At the beginning, I really liked this game.  I really did.  The graphics, for being free, are amazing.  This game is MUCH better than Golf With Friends. It really is like a golf MMO.
However, that loveliness is short lived.  The difficulty ramp is just obsurd.  Plain and simple.  You're given Missions (quests if that term is more your flavor) and completing those helps ramp your skills up.  Which is great! And then you "level up" to being a Junior Pro.  And this is where the game just takes a nose dive to awful.
The amount of courses you can play where you feel viable are sorely limited.  If you're sub level 20, then you're pretty much in 2 courses.  So if you're good with playing those 2 repeatedly, then you may enjoy the game.  I don't and I do not.  The words "Very Easy" are sort of a slap in the face because ALL courses can be labeled as "Very Easy" but their not.  You'd be lucky to escape each hole with a Bogey.  So you try again and again.  But the courses get harder and harder, the greens get steeper and tougher, WAY too quickly.  There is no easing into the higher end portions of this game.  Just a pure hard slap in the face and get ready to eat more bogeys than an Air Force Veteran...because that is all your diet will consist of.
The bonus of having power up items ("potions") and enchanting, yes you heard me right, enchanting your clubs to get bonuses are great...until you realize how utterly useless each of them are.
I wanted to like this game, but when I'm consistently getting bogey and double bogey unless I play 2 certain courses, then I'm out.  I'd ask for a refund if I paid anything towards this...which I haven't.

Sledgehammer (aka Gear Grinder) is one of those weird games that can only come out of Russia...  in a parallel future, where trucks can transform from jet-engined superracer into an armored and heavily armed beast, and police are packed with gatling guns and more and enforce laws with lethal force, you have been executed for slaughtering innocents with your truck, but you woke up mysteriously next to a shiny new transforming truck... and was told to get through some training so you can undergo some missions for this mysterious benefactor...
Basically you drive around like some weird vigilante who needs to cause maximum destruction. You have front bumper spikes, side spinning saws (later), front firing weapons (primary and secondary), and rear mine dispensers. Your truck can also be upgraded with better armor, transmission, engine, and so on.
The fighting is about what you'd expect in such a game... You are in 3rd person but very low, so your truck will obstruct your view ahead. Fortunately you can pretty much run through almost anything in your way, or your shoot your way through. There are missions that are pure racing (where you use racing mode, complete with afterburning engines) pure combat (survive arena for X seconds), or run-n-gun (fight enemies as you try to make it through checkpoints). The more you kill the more time on the clock you get, but the the more damage you suffer. There are a few oddball missions such as "pilot a RC bomb drone" or "max speed into a cafe".
The problem is the first level's "end mission". Instead of a boss fight, you're basically put into a gauntlet that's basically 3 missions together. First is a checkpoint race where you need to pass through little tokens to get extra time. When you reach a mall you crash through to land and found the way's blocked, and you need to kill X police cars to get out. Then it's a long run-n-gun to the final endpoint... where I've tried about 10 times, with max upgrades, and I keep running out of time (the only way to gain time is kill the cops, and they sometimes aren't fast enough so you can't kill them (or I'm taking too many go-fast upgrades?!)  So I can't even get onto "level 2" (i.e. next city).
Voiceover is atrocious, storyline is outrageous, sound is... mediocre. Graphics are tolerable. This is a weird game. If you like your idea of wanton destruction, give it a try. But not quite my cup of tea.

Hard but addictive and inspiring. A classic turn-based-tactics mix of keyboard chewing rage and fist-pumping exhilaration. More on that later.
This game is unforgiving, RNG-driven, and distinctly un-casual. You gotta focus and get as much right as you can and grit your teeth when it goes wrong. Here's a few tips to start:
Gang up on enemies all the time --- Avoid the more scattered deployments --- Always Launch AND DEPLOY to keep your warband close together --- Only collect Warpstone / Loot if it's en route to joining up to gang up on enemies --- Ditto with secondary objectives --- Loot all enemies if you have inventory space, once you've learnt what loot is valuable --- Don't buy skills until later in the game --- Don't forget to switch your weapons around if you're having to put reserves in --- Don't worry if you have a small warband due to injury, it will be more manageable small vs. small --- Take heed of the initiative order and consider using delay or disengage to maximise your combat situations (but beware of missing dodge / parry stances) --- Be wary of ambush stances pulling your units out of group position --- Enemy impressives get stuck a lot, cheese them --- NEVER Abandon Mission --- Scout carefully to avoid ambushes. Etc.
So yeah it's tough. But THERE are tactics to use to deal with it, and take into account the RNG, mostly stacking the odds in your favour with what you can control. And then it works and it's got the classic XCom EU thing of shouting at the screen "YES F**KING COME ON DUDE YOU NAILED HIM"....not many games have that much engagement and satisfaction when your little dudes get it right.
(I'm playing Skaven, which might make me more emotionally attached).
Seriously. It really is worth the effort. I left it alone for months after I royally screwed my warband by Abandoning a main mission (do not do this). Came back and got hooked again. I have to really focus each mission but it's rewarding.
What else? The movement system is really novel amongst turn-based strat and can be used pretty well, as well as adding immersion. The warbands have plenty of character (my Skaven certainly do, I wish they had Orcs and Gobbos tho). The graphics are distinctly previous-gen BUT are well themed and stylish. The city is proper warped even if it is quite repetitive revisiting the same areas. In short it's presented well for turn-based tactics.
Give it a go :)

This is a game for a narrow pool of gamers.
Mordheim is a brutal tactical game. You will lose more than once due to sheer luck.
The game does give you opportunities to counter or play around the percentage chances to hit. That however require some research into the depths of the games' mechanics.
Some players will like this, others won't. I do enjoy the fights and the campaign mission. SO a recommendation from me.
However I have recently seen why some new players rate this game so low.
Anecdote time.
I recently started a new warband with fresh warriors and 31 hours of casuel offline playtime.
First mission went without a hitch. Good start.
Second mission vs a evenly matched AI and I got shafted by the luck machine. Setup to match:
Five vs five fresh warriors. No special endgame/midgame skills. No super soldiers to rely on this early in the game. Almost random gear for everyone. Just strategy and raw power/luck. All soldiers (including AI) scattered randomly around the map. Four out of my five soldiers spawn close to eachother. One does not. When the match start my opponent goes first with most warriors. My loner gets pummeled in the first round. No counterplay possible. No amount of skill or setup could have prevented it. He did not even get to move before he was defeated. The match proceeded with me on the defence with one man down. I lost.
If I had been a new player I would have quit the game right then and there. It would simply seem unfair to lose such a match. As it stands, I still enjoy the game and will continue to fight in the city of the damned. But if such a loss would deter you from playing this kind of game, don't buy it.

Many people complain about the UI and extreme RNG. I can get over that. What killed the game for me was the lack of challenge. Not that the game was easy, mind you, but that the difficulty level of the game was still as the Pacific Ocean.
In similar games like XCOM and Valkyria Chronicles, the fun part is the asymmetry between your dudes and the aliens/imperials. Sometimes your dudes are miles ahead of the enemy and you enjoy how powerful your dudes are. Sometimes the enemies way better than your dudes and you have a challenging, fun time figuring out how to overcome or salvage the mission.
Mordheim has none of that. Every little aspect of your dudes, from their level to their traits to their injuries, are given points. Whenever you go into a mission, those points and your team composition is mirrored by the AI. So, when you bring a high level hero and three high level troops, AI will bring a high level hero and three high level troops. When you bring your awesome rat-ogre, AI will also bring a rat-ogre (or equivalent). The AI will mirror your composition.
This means that the challenge level of this game (at least in Singleplayer) is really static. Which gets boring, fast.

It's a complete mystery to my why my highly-trained, elite warband is unable to open a door . . . this is already ajar with nothing blocking it. The map is completely uninteractable - there is nothing to break, move, or shift and determining line-of-sight from a window is a coin-flip.
This coupled with the numerous bugs I encountered (I had a warrior on ambush, basically a melee overwatch stance run PAST the target he was ambushing and into a wall, my soldier was then stuck in his run animation cycle. The game could not resolve the turn  and simply hung there with my guy eternally smashing his face into a wall - a fitting comparison to this game, really) means I cannot recommend this game. It's a shame, there IS potential here, but it needs polish and expansion.

Three words:
Best Civ ever.

One of the best strategy games of all time, Civ4 has aged well is still a worthy competitor to the more recent Civ games. While those games add another tactical layer on combat (that unfortunately the AI can't handle), Civ4 has a lot more depth in some of its economic aspects. The graphics still look good, the gameplay is solid and the interface is quite usable. It is also very different from Civ5/6, so it isn't redundant with those games: fans of strategy games should play both.
One of the greatest things about Civ4 are its mods: the game had insane modabbility, leading to the creation of many awesome mods like Fall From Heaven 2 (fantasy total conversion), Rhye's and Fall of Civilization (more historical simulation), Caveman2Cosmos (more of everything), BUG (better unaltered gameplay) and its successors BAT and BULL, star trek mods and many others. Those add a lot of replayability and improve on many aspects of the game (including graphics and quality of life). Definitely look into mods rather than keeping limited to the (still awesome) vanilla game.

This is almost good, but I feel the rebirth / new life mechanic is missing.  Your character really can die at any time, and if you've invested any amount of time into him, it really is a letdown to have to start over again with nothing gained.  A lot of roguelikes have new skills learned or powers unlocked after a nice playthrough so that you can feel some kind of reward for your wonderful effort on your now dead character.  This game needs something like that to enhance replay value.  I know you can unlock one new class for each playthrough if you had gotten far enough in the game, but it doesn't make death very satisfying.

1. It is difficult, and only has checkpoints after a while, meaning that you will constantly have to restart long levels.
2. In order to switch dimensions, you must hit the shift key. You will also be holding the shift key a lot, meaning that your computer may often exit the game, asking if you want to activate sticky keys.
Also, the beginning has you walk to the right for a long period of time before starting the real challenge. However, this is part of the level, so when you die, you have to repeat the walk over and over. Not a major issue, but very annoying.
All in all, I would not recommend buying it for $2, however if you receive it for free or on a good discount then it is worth playing.

I have pretty conflicting feelings about this game. When I played it originally on the PS2 around 2005, I loved this as much as RE1-3 because I felt it brought a lot of new gameplay and game design elements to the series without straying from its roots. Since I haven't played it in about a decade at this point, this was almost a new experience for me to replay it and I have to say: it hasn't aged well. Resident Evil 4 is hard to recommend in the current year; if you can tolerate some older game mechanics and unintentional cheesiness, you will enjoy the experience but it definitely isn't for everyone.
The biggest game design issue I have with the game are surprisingly the controls. While I loved the tank controls in RE1-3, they feel out of place in a third person shooter. Leon always feels stiff and slow, as if you're steering a bowling ball instead of the Hollywood action hero the game thinks he is. Two control methods are available but neither really fixes this problem. "Classic" controls are the way the game controlled back in 2005: tank movement with mouse aiming and your POV locked to your aiming or movement direction. "Modern" controls acts like a twin stick system, with freedom of movement with WASD and camera/aiming independently being done with the mouse. I would normally prefer the Modern system but there is no camera snap/reset option available. This makes movement very frustrating because you have to constantly aim the camera manually while walking around. Coming from games heavily inspired by RE4, Dead Space 1 & 2, the default controls feel really archaic and the modern controls feel unnecessarily clunky and cumbersome. I don't expect the original game released before DS1 & 2 to have better controls than its "predecessor" but I would expect a "Modern" control scheme to function with better nuance.
Apart from the molasses controls, you still have the original RE4 experience here along with your post-game padding. Replaying RE4's Leon story in 2017 feels like two separate games; Up until the Salazar fight, the game's atmosphere is much more survival horror-esque but feels aimless and meandering. Salazar's fight feels like something out of Code Veronica, after which the game completely jumps the shark and is practically a different game. If I could just replay the B-movie absurdity of the post-Salazar campaign I would replay it almost annually like RE2 & 3. Unfortunately (possibly because I beat it 3 times previously) half of this game is a cheeseable snoozefest thanks to the RPG-7 and the ever-present Merchant & overly frequent saves.
RE4 is still a good game worth playing in 2017, but in hindsight I now prefer RE2 & RE3 for annual replays. Much of this game feels like padding and without better controls it is frustrating to play. I would still recommend it to fans of the series but only once you're tired of replaying RE1-3. The HD upgrades have improved it visually but there aren't enough new enhancements to make this worth purchasing again if you already own it on another platform.

Pretty good game.
You run around from room to room killing enemies and solving puzzles.  Occasional empty rooms provide areas to expand the story or allow dialouge.  Run around manipulating gravity and use a physics based gun to manipulate objects/enemies.  You also get a rock blaster which acts as an overheatable machine gun/ grenade launcher.
Puzzles and enemies are easy for the most part.  You'll still die every once and a while as your character can't take many rounds before going down.  There's a checkpoint just outside of pretty much every area where it's possible to die, so it only takes a few seconds to get right back to where you were.  What makes the game enjoyable is that it has a very nice flow to it.  Usually you'll run through 3-5 rooms of enemies/puzzles, go to one empty area with some dialogue or something, then run through another 3-5 rooms of enemies/puzzles.  There're very few instances where you're spending several minutes running through empty meaningless rooms.  This means there's very little downtime where you're being bored because nothing is happening.  It also helps that the game is fairly lighthearted and your main character is an entertaining protagonist, occasionally spouting off some enjoyable lines.  Controls are solid with a controller.  The music is also enjoyable throughout.
Only real complaints are the lack of enemy variety and their simplicity.  The final boss is also very easy.  Puzzles could've also been a little more difficult to solve, though there is an occasional one here and there that'll make you think for a minute.  Story could've been better as it's predicatable.  Characters other than John are one dimensional but that's not necessarily a bad thing in a game like this.

Now let's go over the cons and cons.
-Gameplay is boring and repetitive
-flashlight mechanic is broken (when my flashlight was off the battery still was being used)
-Sound design is terrible; Your footstep loop is real short and repetitive and it really got on my nerves since that is basically the only thing you hear for the majority of the game

I could probably list a few more cons but I don't want to think about this game ever again. Don't buy this game, DON'T.

Simply put, the game doesn't work for me.
I got a key for the game on a bundle of mystery games, then decided to give it a try despite all the negative reviews, since I'm a fan of horror games.
I start up the game and after the two logos that come up, the entire game is black. I can't see anything. Meanwhile the character is talking and explaining the story. If I walk, I can hear the footsteps, so the black screen isn't normal. I try restarting the game, doesn't work. Reinstalling the game, doesn't work. I look around for solutions, nothing. I run the game again and start trying using TAB and the console key to see if I can do anything and, somehow, using the console actually temporarily solves the problem, so I can actually see stuff.
When the character is done talking, the game's logo comes up, then the controls and it gives me a "press space to start" message. I press space - nothing, controls are still on screen. Once more, I can hear footsteps if I walk, but the screen is stuck. Meanwhile the flashlight is draining away. Fiddling with TAB and the console doesn't work this time. Eventually the character dies because the flashlight ran out of battery. I press R to restart and it's right back to being stuck on the screen showing the controls.
I restart the game and try everything again. Exactly the same: had to fiddle with TAB and the console to get the screen to work during the intro, then I get stuck on the screen with the controls.
And from what I've read around, I'm not an exception - this seems to happen to quite a number of people. Also, reading other reviews reveals it's an incredibly short game with little to no challenge and that's barely scary at all.
So, in short, this is a game that shouldn't be sold. If people can play a good horror game like Black Rose for free, why would anyone pay for a game that might not work and, when it does, it's not actually good?

A Games Workshop fan of the 1980's will probably remember this. I however was neither of these. In fact it wasn't until the Exploration Sale (2014), that I found this game whilst browsing the usual Warhammer 40k games and came across this little gem. Since I'm neither a child of the 80's, nor was I a Games Workshop fan, I believe I can provide a fresh, unbiased review of this game. So please bear with me.
First off, this game is completely about the luck of the roll. You roll for everything in this game, and I love it! You begin the game with a comic strip intro, and then you begin the game. You have to roll d6's to get your stats. There are no RPG "select this stat?" After you have rolled for your stats, you get some basic points that you can use to aquire weapons, HTH (Hand To Hand) weapons, and or clothing. But you must keep in mind you have a very, and I do mean very, limited amount of points, which usually for me, winds up being one gun, one HTH weapon, and that is all.
After all this prep you begin the game full. You are thrust into New York with a background picture, on your left are cards, to your right, your actions. You turn a card face up, and then you proceed from there. Once you turn it face up, if it is an enemy, you must roll the d6, depending on what you chose. As a short example. Say you turn over a card and it is a zombie, you select say HTH, once done, a combat roll will happen and based on your starting stats, you must equal or beat a certain roll. Or conversely, you can use your weapon, say a rifle. If you roll badly though, you can and will miss and as a last resort, you will be forced into HTH or even made to try and escape the threat.
You go through the apartment blocks, and roll your way to victory! But not all the cards are of course enemies, you have some empty room cards, to which you must roll your d6's to see if anything lurks around the corner. You can get item cards, medical pack cards etc. But the majority of what you will be doing is rolling against the cards that are enemies. Once you have a chance to escape a building, you must roll through some more cards to make it out alive. Which if like me, you have been left with nothing but your HTH weapon, can be very tense.
To make it to the end you need good rolls, and you need to watch your bottom bar which includes a venom and radiation meter. If either fill up, it doesn't look hopeful for you. Amongst the threats lurking behind each card backing, is the ever present timer. Everything you do takes time. Be it reloading a weapon. Using an item. And such. Once it becomes night, your stats may go down and it may just get that bit extra harder. As if it wasn't hard enough!
I'd recommend this game based on it's original HARD difficulty alone as it is brutal and who knows if you will get the rolls you need. If you're a die fan, then sadly this game only uses d6 dices. The game has the mentallity for just "one more roll, I just need one more good roll!"
You will be pulling your hair out with bad rolls.

A very enjoyable card game that keeps me at the edge of my seat from start to finish. You can make your roll checks easier by choosing the easier difficulty setting, though Darkness (the final boss) will still have his way with you unless you're very lucky. A card-based game, developed by Auroch Digital, it brings this Games Workshop title to life on PC. The concept and story are relatively simple: You are a super-soldier, and New York is about to be swallowed up by a black hole caused by ‘the Darkness’, a mysterious unknown entity of evilness and evil. It’s up to you to chainsaw the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the Darkness and its forces, and to not let New York be sucked into an abyss in the process – you have an hour. Good luck!
As simple as the premise is, so too is the gameplay - you do anything, you roll dice. Essentially, the gameplay consists of location cards, each of which holds a certain event, and you need to deal with that event using your weapons, items, or just by moving on when there’s a clear room. Of course, chainsaw-ing a zombie in the face is still satisfying.
The sound is simple, but you’re basically just looking at the same screen with a different card all the time, so there’s not much complexity to be had, and whilst the art for the cards looks nice, don’t expect too much. Again, cards, not a 3D FPS or the like.
This particular title will probably be of great interest to Games Workshop fans, but new adopters may want to at least check the title out through reviews (see our video above) and the like before buying, as the replay value of it might be rather low to many.

I may not have played the original card game, but this digital adaptation is simple yet marvelous. The game itself plays out like a randomized card-game version of a rogue-like. I've seen many complaints about the unfairness of this game, due to its randomized nature and all, but I can't help but feel it's an unfair assumption to assume that just because it's a card game that this game is inherently intended to be a purely strategic experience. What it is at its core, is a quick-playing ride into hell.
Winning is a rarity - I haven't even won one game myself, but I still like to come back to it for a quick playthrough now and then, because it's easy to learn and fun to experiment with. It's nothing more than quick romps through bloodshed and randomized weaponry, but it doesn't pretend to be more than that either. That, and although its randomized nature - including randomizing the player's selection of weapons and items - may make it seem as though there isn't any room for strategy at all, the game does indeed have strategy in the same way most gambling games do. You're hedging your bets. Betting that larger firepower won't be necessary, betting that the monster around the bend WON'T be a radioactive sludge beast, betting you can open that door without wasting bullets and thus saving precious extra in-game time to complete your mission.
You'll come close, it might be painful. But this is the kind of pain I like from a game.

##EDIT: This game unfortunately due to being released in 2001 has horrible optimalization for modern hardware. The worst part is that you find out about it in the middle of the main campaign, since the area of gameplay gets bigger and more armor is getting involved in the conflict. Either use an older PC for this or use VirtualBox (though I haven't tested it). I finished the last mission of the main campaign below 20fps, and couldn't even finish Resistance due to the amount of lag. Unless you never get irritiated by stuttering and you're that willing to finish OFP fully, be warned.
I firstly bought the game under the name Operation Flashpoint but the new title doesn't decrease the amount of punishment you will get by playing it.
After the first missions it creates a fake illusion that the only challenge you will have is who will spot who first - the enemy you or you the enemy. It's this moment where the strategic element comes into play. You WILL repeat levels tens of times and change your manouvers while being filled with rage just to try to finally surprise the enemy. You WILL treat your fellow squad members as cannon fodder in order to ensure that you will survive to the end to the mission, not caring about your score. This game will make an animal out of you, which knows how to use a map.
Theorically, the game (not Steam) says I have 10h of game time, but that's just finished levels. I'm sure the rest of my game time on Steam are replays.
A huge positive about this game is the availability of choice. You may even travel across the whole map before you finally decide to engage the objective, and what's important, you will meet enemies on the other parts of the map even though that if you played normally, you would never meet them!
The downside of that availability is your results do not usually matter in the aftermath. For example, there's a mission where you need to only find the location of three Shilkas on an island, and you may as well destroy them after locating. In a later mission, you have to destroy them, and if you did that before, you... have to destroy them again anyway. So yeah, I soon gave up on wiping the whole map out of enemies.
Time modifiers are the most useful thing you will ever use in this game (default: - and =), as sometimes you will have to wait tons of time before anything happens. You need to be careful with them though, as overusage of them can skip scripts and dialogue.

This game had potentional and is a Warhammer game with reasonable production values. Not as high as THQ's, but higher than other games outside of THQ's and Creative Assembly's. However, whatever promise it has is bogged down by questionable design choices.
For starters,  rather than an isometric view like most games of its type, the game uses more of a 3rd person view like you'd find in a RPG. Whilst unique, its also really hard to navigate and tell where everything is. You can undo movement, at least, but its still awkward to play through.
Deployment is especially a pain, as you have to cycle through each deployment point with the keyboard. Why can't I use the map to deploy my warband?
There is no grid system either, so there is no frame of reference for have far everything can move. The game tells you that a unit can move a certain number of meters per strategy point, but it doesn't tell you how far that actually translates to in game. If they had a grid system, where each square would be 1 meter, then the player could effectively plan out his strategy as he would then know exactly where everything can go (you know, like every other tactical wargame ever). But as it stands the player is effectively blind when it comes to judging distances in game, and that's a bad thing. There isn't even a grid system on the map, where you'd think there'd be one.
You don't actually have that many options for customization, and your warriors will tend to have the same face. You do get a large suite of skills, at least, so you can customize your warriors in that sense.
The stances aren't quite that well thought out.
Parry and Dodge do functionally the same thing. Parry allows you to attack if procced, but only if you have enough Offense points, which you probably won't have enough from as you'll want to spend all of it attacking, and as such its no different from dodging, which like parry avoids damage. Wouldn't it be better to allow a free attack? Its not as if such a concept in the game doesn't exist; if you flee from combat every unit on the opposing side gets a free attack. Why are there free attacks in that case, but not with parrying?
Overwatch and Ambush are flawed in so many ways. For starters, there's hardly any counterplay; it has a 360 degree field of vision, so you can't flank it, and ambush doesn't tell you where the enemy's ambush zone is, so you have to inch forward and pray the charge prompt shows up. Which it won't, because the AI always seems to have longer ambush range than you, and knows where your ambush zones are, so it can always somehow find a way to circumvent it.
Charging, btw, does ignore Overwatch and Ambush, but it has short range and its still counterintuitive; in most games abilities like that are supposed to stop charges.
In a system where the ambush ranges are variable, you have to show its range. Otherwise the player wouldn't know what to do, and stumble into a situation that could have been avoided if it had been designed properly.
The singleplayer compaign is fine at first, but it becomes repetive once you realize that the AI will always copy your composition; if you have 2 heroes, an impressive and 5 henchmen, the AI will use 2 heroes, an impressive and 5 henchmen.
Not to mention that the optional missions are nearly impossible to do, as each mission ends before you can gather the wyrdstone in time, or still their banner and take it to your cart.
The loot system is similarly flawed; as the mission abrubtly ends once a warband breaks, you can lose loot that's right at your feet, as the game won't let you manually loot it. Would it have been really that difficult to automatically add loot postgame that's in your warriors' control zones? This makes the marked for death optional mission harder and more tedious than it needs to.
Likewise, the morale system is a little clunky in that instead of testing to see if the warband breaks at the end of the round, where you'd think it would come in, its tested when a warrior's turn comes up in the initiative order. Why? Shouldn't it be at the end? I could have 5 guys to use afterwards to do stuff and grab loot, but the game won't let me due to how the morale system works.
The story quests are terrible. All they are are fetch quests where you have to make sure a special unit doesn't die as well, all while having to fight constantly respawning enemies. In a game where healing is hard to come across, this quickly becomes an exercise in frustration.
Furthermore, whilst the DLC units and factions are locked behind a paywall for the player, the AI will use them against you. Its obvious that the files are in the game on the player's computer, but the player still has to pay for them. This is no different from on disk DLC.
I can't say much about multiplayer, as there appears to be hardly any activity on skirmish mode.
There's a bunch of bugs as well concerning line of sight. You could clearly draw a line of sight from a warrior to a target, but the game won't let you attack for some reason.
Now don't get me wrong, I like this game. I will keep playing it. However, its also really flawed, and as such I can't recommend it, especially with a 30 euro price tag + about 28 euros of DLC.
Apparently the Devs are making necromunda, and I am looking forward to it. I just hope they don't make the same mistakes they made with mordheim, and avoid that DLC nonsense. The devs do communicate with their playerbase, and I appreciate that, which is why it bothers me to see such irritating design flaws in a game that could have been much more.

The short and sweet.

Could be fun but too frustrating This game has a lot of potential but it is faaar to slow and frustrating to play.
Each turn takes a long time as you have to wait for each enemy piece to make its move, which is all the more aggravating when you realise you don't know any of the maps so you end up entering buildings that are dead ends and then having to spend turns doubling back on yourself. Then when you finally reach the enemy you often only get one attack per team member with which there seems to always be some 50% chance to miss. So most turns you get your troops into battle only to see "dodge" appear above the enemy when you swing, yet of course when the enemy strikes you your dodge chance seems to be non existant.
Then you have the juggling of micromanagement. You need to simultaneously defeat the enemy in hard battles while constantly looting wyrdstones accross the map (harder than it sounds as the moment you split your warband you are at a serious disadvantage) then on top of all that you need to pay the salaries and medical costs of your warband which you can barely do since the wyrdstones you need to send off to your faction who don't even pay you for them.
Then to top all that off you also have to handle party members being injured for several days (missions) which means you have to pay even more gold recruiting new members and pay their salaries and medical costs too!
So you are fighting this uphill battle to win the mission, loot every stone you can see, pay your warband, deliver the wyrdstones to your faction, cover the healing costs and then do it all again the next day.
Now that's without even mentioning the annoying little parts of the game which just seem unnecessary.
For example the goal of the game is to collect wyrdstones on the map to send to your faction. The problem is when you send your wyrdstones it takes three days for the shipment to deliver, but bear in mind you only have 10 days to collect the wyrdstone to start with so that only gives you 7 missions to do it. Why not just make delivery 1 day, why the need for such an arbitrary delay?
Then you have the gold looting. All items sell for like 1gp and most loot on the map is 2-3gp. But you need to pay about 40-50gp in salaries and medical costs per day. Not to mention that you need hundreds of gold pieces to train skills. Now you are meant to be getting gold mostly by collecting and selling surplus wyrdstones, but since those wyrdstones are needed for your faction, plus you can't easily collect the stones since you need to focus on killing the enemy, it all just seems so difficult.
Then you have the days of delay for everything. Want to train a new skill? Well thats that character out of action for 3 days. Someone hurt their leg in the last battle? Well that's five days of that character being out of action. Need to send a delivery to a faction? Well enjoy the 1-3 day delay again. Need to buy another bog standard metal helmet? you have to wait 7 days for the shop to restock.
Last of all you have the UI. Everything in the game is done with the right and left mouse button. It's so pointless, we have an entire keyboard here so why are they using two mouse buttons to do everything?! Then you have the option to deploy your warband on the map, this is essential but good luck doing it as instead of picking a spot to deploy you have to press Q and E to cycle through each possible deploy location (where there can be upto 30). So that takes forever too.
It all adds together to make a thoroughly frustrating game. Now don't get me wrong I am still going to play it as it's sort of a unique little game and does have its fun moments. But I just feel like I need to warn people about the fustration this game gives. Basically it's like a fantasy version of Xcom but a lot less fluid. I would recommend it if you are really into some mix of Xcom, Dark Souls and roguelikes.

A breath of turn based fresh air in a modern twitch happy world.  You review a game like this on it's own terms, not in comparison to Grand Theft Auto 29 or NBA 2k.  And on it's own terms Mordheim was a grand success that I hope inspires the developers to not only angle for sequels, but to potentially put their engine and craft to work for other franchises.  It's been a long time since I logged so much time with a good ole turn based squad game, in fact you might have to go all the way back to Jagged Alliance 2, perhaps the best of the whole breed (and hmm...this is exactly the sort of revival treatment poor old JA needs itself).  What Mordheim gets very right is it's fighting and progression system, which is addicting and never ceases to be challenging.  Where it falls short and could have used more devlopment is really in the window dressing -- in the storyline and between battles structure. The fighting system is a remarkable pen and paper port, looks great, and offers endless tactical options.  But somehow the developers did all the hard work, and then seemed to skimp on the fun fluff that would have taken the whole thing to the next level.  The types of missions are limited, the settings a bit repetitive (the same maps are cleverly altered from battle to battle by the addition and removal of rubble, doors, ladders etc.), the economic system very basic, and the storyline just kind of tacked on to give you a reason to go out and fight the next day.  In fact the half hearted attempt to add story missions in with the daily tactical battles actually turns out to be the lest interesting, and indeed at times aggravating, part of the game.  But that fighting system and character development...if you are, or ever have been, a fan of turn based squad level tactical fighting, then this game will legitimately be hard to log off from.  I leveled up 6 different squads (well 7, as it took me 2 tries to get Chaos right), one for each of the races/combatants.  Fought hundreds of battles, killed over 1000 opponents, and if the developers released a 7th species tommorow, I'd be right back at it.  Major kudos.

Important: This review is mostly based on my experience playing the Skaven single player campaign for long, long hours.
I wish I could recommend this game, but I instead urge you not to buy it. This game has been abandoned by their developers so they focus on another game (Necromunda).
The main issue is that I don't feel this is a completed the game, all the core features are there, but it has some major flaws that I thought would be fixed over time and that won't be the case.
The AI is mostly challenging because of the brutal RNG (I’m fine with the RNG). It gets stuck trying to reach one of your units, and instead of turning around and going the other way it just stays there. You know it’s stuck because it does a weird dance in front of you. The AI also tries to hit all the units basing them instead of focusing on one (let alone focusing on the one they are more likely to harm). The AI ranged units would watch as you murder their friends in front of them if they are not close enough to shoot and not even try to get closer if they are perched on top of a building.
The side objective types are underdeveloped. The AI won’t bother stealing anything from your cart, let alone your idol for the “Crush their will” side mission. There are only 3 side objective types, and of those only the “Wyrdstone rush” is the only one worth choosing because A: you always need Wyrdstone and B: you’ll also get bonus XP for completing it, just like any other side objective, but the others won’t give you any extra benefits so why bother if the AI doesn’t bother as well? (the only smart thing the AI does….). They should remove the Wyrdstone rush optional objective, add a few more side objectives, and add different type of rewards for completing them (an additional day to fulfil requests, items, money, henchman….).
The crypt horror also needs some balance too. Visually it looks like a big impressive unit and your natural instinct is to hide inside a building… until the crypt horror goes inside and murder all your units. Model-wise, the crypt horror looks even bigger than rat ogres because the former have bones sticking out of their back or something, but they can get inside narrow places…..
The worst, worst part for me are the scenarios, which I only completed because the voice dialog and acting of the Skaven camping was funny (unlike the Chaos faction which is ultra bland). But the scenario maps are really bad designed. It's difficult to find anything, they are needlessly long, and you could die out of nowhere trying to fulfill something that doesn't even feel that important. For some scenarios grabbing an item is fine, but imagine your furstration when they tell you "ok, after doing all this BS go and store that special item in your cart" and by some random event an enemy comes out of nowhere and kills your dramatis persona. After spending almost 2 hours on a scenario where most of your team died, having also this happen is like rubbing a big chunk of salt on a wound. The worst is the library map… whoever thought about that scenario probably sold their soul to the devil and needs to torture people in order to make up for it.
As other reviewers has suggested the interface is bad. It’s neither good for controllers nor for mouse and keyboard. The combat seems more controller focused, but as soon as you are done with that good luck using it and trying to upgrade your warriors or buy new equipment without using a mouse.
Something else I find annoying is that if you choose the Marked for Death objective, it’s difficult to tell which units you have to kill. You need to keep opening the map display and remember their names. They should have put a marker on top of them even on the 3rd person view and only have trinkets and personal items for units marked for death.
Picking up items is too annoying too. Even if your character model is stepping right on top of several wyrdstones you can only pick some of them. Then you need to proceed to do the Wyrdstone Jiggle Dance and move your character bit by bit to avoid spending movement points to pickup something that is just underneath you…. Please, if the unit model touches it, let it pick it up :\
If you have junk items and then you find the mother of wyrdstones and you want to throw away the junk or swap it, good luck with that. Why can’t characters dump the items they are carrying? (shrugs)
So, all in all, no, I can't recommend this game. Don't buy it. I wish I could recommend it, but only if the developers were to fix the issues with it, but they won’t. Never buy a game that won’t be supported.

Note I have played this game for years off Steam.
A fantastic game for the series, Civilization 4 Beyond the Sword improves the base game in so many ways it will forever be a must have expansion for this classic. The game run's smooth and with little to no bugs, and there is never a dull game if you love the Sid Meir series. The base game improved with a variety of new units, buildings, and civilizations that are all a blast to play and add a new flare to the game which makes it feel fresh. Classic Civ at it's finest.
The game also has some of the most diverse and incredible scenario's to ever grace a civ game. Not only have they pulled scenarios from some of the best old mod of their time, such as Ryse and Fall and Fall from Heaven, but also a host of unique scenarios that almost feel like DLC within a DLC. Next War adds an entire new era and story allowing archology cities and clone armies to devastate the world while Road to War throws you into the war torn WWII era Europe and Pacific. They even added 2 scifi mods, one a traditional 4X space empire game and a Turn Based game controlling a team of cyborgs. Heroes of Might and Magic: Clash of Heroes, Tales of Vesperia
You are some hero dude. The spell of destruction is being cast and the world will end in 30 seconds. Chosen by the time goddess you become the warrior of the goddess. Though the goddess loves money above all else so every time you want to turn back the clock you'll have to pay up. Various weapon, and armor upgrades are spread out throughout the levels. Sometime the level will give multiple ways of finishing it and sometimes doing so will lead to separate paths. The run at each other combat is automatic unless you have a special item. You must find who is spreading the spell of destruction and stop him.
The game levels play out a lot like different puzzles which is great. It makes fun of itself and the JRPG genre in delightful ways. The soundtrack is nice and retro. It offers two different graphic modes. Once you beat the main story other gameplay modes gradually unlock. It is important to note that Princess 30, Knight 30, and Evil Lord 30 are different in retro mode then in cartoon graphic mode which means even more variety. Finding all the secrets in the levels is actually pretty fun.
The gameplay does repeat itself and it very fast paced so it can wear on you. This is a port of a port and the menu setup is not the greatest if your hoping to customize controls or options. I used a 360 controller and it worked great by default, but the button prompts always show keyboard keys. They don't explain hardly anything so you'll have to look at guides to even know what stats do for example. The human characters in cartoon mode are very bad compared to enemy design.
If you love combat  mixed with puzzles in combination that are fast paced this is your kind of game, but if not I suggest staying away. Though to be honest it's hard to imagine somebody totally hating this game. It's just a silly fun game.
I'd suggest buying the 2nd game and getting this one free. So if you do that at the $10 mark you'll get a great value here.

We're talking about easy QTEs that no previous version ever had me struggle on, but stragnely, they're passable by temporarily locking the FPS at 30.
Resident Evil 4 is one of those games that I got swept up in. Back in 2005, it was hard to pull me away from my many playthroughs, and it's a good thing that this game is long and packed full of content. I loathe the game many times when I reflect upon it for ditching the survival horror and going full-on action, but when I pop it back on, it's too fun to deny. I understand why Capcom made the design choice, and I certainly enjoy the newer camera and perspective, but everytime I play I can't help but wonder at how much more intense the game would be if the ammo was scarce and you weren't getting rifle rounds off of pitchfork weilding peasants, or even grenades from a crow.  The common enemies would provide more scares in my mind if it were more like the first few entries in the series where you had to pick your battles. Imagine blocking yourself in a shack with 50% health, enemies trying to get in from every window and only a scarce supply of ammunition. Retweaking the whole game to make this a reality I'm sure would be too big of a task.
And so, it's indeed Resident Evil 4. It's one of those games like Super Mario Brothers or DOOM. You already know it, you know if you'll like it or not. The best in the series to some, the one that turned it into something it's not to others, but this game to me is a milestone and a classic either way you look at it. If you want this game on Steam, aside from the QTE issue I noted for myself before, they didn't do it wrong here. When I first played this on the Gamecube, it truly felt next-gen compared to most other games we were seeing at the time, not just in its visuals, but in the tight gameplay.  Over 10 years have passed and the game still feels fresh and exciting.

Tl;dr - Controller options need to be improved, gameplay causes much unneeded frustration, visuals are gorgeous, soundtrack is great, just a few tweaks would make it so much better.
I wish controller support for this was improved.  My main issue is that for a controller to work on this, it requires at least 3 axies, meaning that if your controller ONLY has a d-pad and no analog triggers, sorry, but you're screwed.  You can't switch between realms without another axis, which then presents another problem: convenience of control.  If you have to use another axis on a controller that only has buttons on the shoulders instead of triggers, that means that you have to use the other analog stick, which takes your hands off of the jump button.  It's one big mess that would have been simplified if the developers had given an option between analog and digital controls.  I'm lucky enough to have a Logitech f310 Gamepad, but anybody else who doesn't have one of that series, an Xbox controller, or a PS4 controller is screwed and forced to play with the keyboard.  This just bothers me so much because I had at least 3 other controllers I wanted to try out on this game.
As for the rest of the game, the gameplay is very stiff.  Your character can move forward and backward and can look up or down to slightly pan the camera. Platforming consists of jumping and switching dimensions at the right times do you don't fall to your doom.  When you jump, you are committed to holding that direction until the bitter end.  If you let go of the direction at any point, your character stops dead in its tracks.  There's very little control once you leave the ground unless you're in a wind gust, which does allow for free movement, albeit very sensitive movement.  This makes many portions of the game much harder than they look.  It makes you think more and react faster.  If you fall from too great a height, you will die.  Same goes for falling in a pit.  However, something the game makes you figure out is that you have to destroy these huge floating spheres around the levels to progress.  That's an issue that this game has: Not explaining anything past the controls.  You have to shift dimensions as you come towards a sphere and release only when you are touching the red circle in the center.  The main issue with this is that the hitbox for it is very small, so many times you'll miss it when going through our will be falling too fast to hit it.  This aspect of the game is very confusing to first time players as they are not told that these even exist.  This happens with several things throughout the game and is very frustrating.
Moving on, the visuals and music are what everybody says they are: amazing.  The game has a polished pixel art style that works well for setting whatever tone it wants to.  The music is invigorating, even the slower tracks.  It never really gets old... Except for when you've died almost 100 times on the same level.  The music restarts every time the level does, so that can get slightly annoying at times.  Otherwise, the music is very well made and is one of the best parts of this game.
In short, this game is a very good time waster if you can look past the difficult controls and gameplay.  I'll give an update on replay value once I finish the game.  I do recommend it, but be prepared to get frustrated when you die for the 86th time because you just barely missed the center of the sphere.

So I am over 780 hours in this game. I like the game. It's fun, and I do recommend it. But. To address some of the things other reviewers have pointed out? It's arcade golf. Seeing Chainsaw Warrior on sale for $2, and knowing that it was a digital version of an old Games Workshop game I figured I would give it a chance. In the worst case I would get a few steam trading cards and kill some time.
In this game you take the role of a soldier whose job is to save the city. You have a limited amount of gear and a mere 60 minutes to fight your way through two decks worth of monsters and traps before using your Laser Lance (or implosion vest) to destroy “The Darkness”.
The game is very unforgiving and you should expect to lose. It is strongly recommended that you start with easy mode, the game is brutal enough that you will still need to fight tooth and nail for victory. Though the mechanics are mind-numbingly simple, the pressure of saving the world in “60 minutes” was surprisingly intense. Perhaps I just had the right mindset, but I thoroughly enjoyed it.
If you haven’t already, watch the official trailer on the store page. It shows you exactly what to expect. The rules and interface of the game are most at home on a tablet, it makes no use of desktop capabilities. In fact, unless you want the steam cards, you should buy the tablet version instead. To those who haven’t watched the trailer, you click to turn over cards, you click to choose an action, you click next and then repeat the process.
Though the game is largely mindless clicking with everything determined by dice rolls there is an element of strategy. You have a limited amount of time and resources to defeat The Darkness. Do you shoot now knowing you won’t have enough ammo to shoot through the next door you encounter? Do you run or hide? Do you charge head on with a chainsaw? Do you take the secret passage to travel faster but possibly miss out on finding supplies? There are lots of little choices which influence the game.
To enjoy the game you need to overlook some glaring flaws. As previously mentioned everything is random, even the equipment you start with. You may need to restart several times just to have a character with a fighting chance. There are also encounters which destroy equipment making the game even more unwinnable. To top it off there are the slimes which can kill you with one lucky roll.
Despite these flaws I am thoroughly enjoying the game and intend to play until I complete all the achievements. Its an excellent time killer and you can save and quit whenever you want. I don’t really think its worth $5, but its certainly worth getting on sale.

So, it's hard to judge this game for two reasons. First of all, it's a digital remake of old board game. Second of all, it's a 2014 now.
Game developers had not so many options to make it nice to old fans and new-coming players (Should I mention fresh digitalizers like Space Hulk and Talisman or should I search for something older?). At least they can make user interface perfect, while you are not able to change or improve game mechanics. Why I can not turn "intro" comics OFF by default? Why the hell all three active areas (Cards deck, HTH-Shoot-da-Whoop and Roll buttons, Continue button) are in three different corners of the screen? Why asking always for something, that's present in single (weapon for Hth, for example). Why always Rolling character in beggining with SO many dumb button press? There is a rule of thumb: program should wait for user interaction IF and ONLY IF user can change the state of program. Here you have to press 7 times some "skip"-like button, just to see numbers appear on the screen. Hell, thanks, but no.
On the one hand, game mechanics are pure random in nature: "adventure map" - shuffled card deck, combat - dice based. You'll be shouting on your PC :D for sure.
On the other hand, game is hard to play and has a "moment of choice", moreover game will always punish you for mistake. You are not only skipping turns, waiting for some "random" output and lucky end. You have enough possibilities to change outcome, though they are limited.
The original game lacks of "horizontal balance": most of ingame items (cloth, weapon, device) can be separed on usefull in 100%  cases and useless in 100% cases. That's bad. Another problem is small amount of such items at all.
With all that said: it was fun to play. Please read AGAIN the total score I put in header for this game. It makes more sense than it seems to be:

This game has some good points, but also a few bad ones, which are MAJOR bad ones.
The dice-roll-combat system is okay, but frustrating when your chap misses 4 80% shots in a row and the enemy lands all of his, killing your skirmisher without being able to hit back. The slow pace of the combat means that you have to hope every roll works for you otherwise you're set back a huge amount. And your team breaks after only 3/5 members down, which happens very quickly after the enemy is first sighted. The AI will gang up on you super easily. Setting your own warband members to move in to do the same is super awkward due to the stupid 'no overlapping zone of control of your own players'. Meaning you have to faff about with the mouse and camera and movement keys to get to the right angle for a charge/attack/shot.
The camera is overall terrible, with locked-to-your-own-characters camera and no opportunity for an overview of the 3d battlefield, something the game sorely needs as the minimap is about as decipherable as wet mud; not differentiating between levels and generally making it very hard to find the navigation to objectives between using the camera and minimap. In addition, when the enemy is making their turns, if you can't see any of their players, you have to stare at your dumb warband members in super-closeup and the scope for planning a larger strategy is so limited by the dumb camera and controls. Given that a game lasts 40 minutes I've found for all of mine I have to keep my members together and can move forwards no more than 1/3 of the map before the enemy rushes me. It's frustrating.
The game has excellent character customisation and the weapon choices seem quite varied and the development of your members good, but is it worth playing 7 hours to win 2 games struggling with the camera and controls all the while? Frankly, no. Go play Fire Emblem or XCOM. At least you can decipher the map in those.

This is a tough one to recommend but I'm going to do it all the same. I got this game in early access because I loved the tabletop game growing up and jumped at the chance to support a video game of it. I absolutely do not recommend it at the current price. Wait for a sale. That said I do not regret paying full price for it.
This game is slow. Ploddingly so. Every thing about this game requires patience and investment. Per warrior, there are 9 upgradable stats, 11 resistance types, 10 active skill types, 10 passive skill types, head equipment, chest equipment, 2 weapon loadouts, et cetera...
It is a deep game that has a really old school PC vibe. It reminds me of the level of detail of something like Baldur's Gate. Be prepared to spend a LOT of time in your warband management screen considering every minute detail of each of your squad members.
The graphics are phenomenal, and it's most of the reason I recommend this game. If you have any familiarity with the table top game, this game has lovingly adapted it to be gritty and personal as you get down to your soldiers' level.
The actual levels will take you about 30 minutes to an hour to complete, so you really have to carve out a chunk of time to play this properly. There's a lot of "stance posturing" animations, and the inventory management is very annoying. I think they made a lot of concessions to try and make this controller-friendly, and missed out on a chance to really utilize a mouse and keyboard properly. A lot hinges on RNG, but that's true to the tabletop as well.
It's hard to recommend at full price and to newcomers to the setting, but for that niche audience out there, who want a hard boiled, mature, "not going to hold your hand" Turn based strategy/RPG experience,  I give it the thumbs up.

Perhaps you're like me, a longtime fan of Games Worshop "Speciality Games" - all the way back from Chaos Warbands, through the original Necromunda and Man o'War and, eventually, Mordheim itself - and are enticed by the idea of playing a game that recreates that experience in digital form.
This is not the game you're looking for.
I'm not going to evaluate the mechanics, balance and campaign elements of the game as not only have others done that better than me - it's also besides the point.
The game suffers from two major, and immediately obvious, flaws that, for me, are each enough to make it completely unplayable on its own.
First, the UI is a complete pain to use with mouse and keyboard. Even something as simple as deploying your fighters at the beginning of a mission tests your patience to its limits as you're forced to pick spots, among a dozen or so different ones, for each fighter not by simply clicking on the map but by cycling through, using inconvenient keyboard shortcuts, for each one. Forcing you to also toggle back and forth to the overhead map for each position to confirm that, yes, this is the actual spot you want to be in.
This experience repeats for every single action you make that isn't running into an opponent and beating them up.
In addition each action, including deployment, have to be confirmed or cancelled by the left/right mouse button. To say that this will lead to frustration and misclicks is an understatement.
The second cardinal sin is the camera, which is locked in 3rd person view for each model and blocked by... everything really. You can zoom out a minimal amount, unless you're in a building, behind a pillar, under a bridge, standing next to some crates or whatever, but even if you're lucky enough to not have the camera blocked the 3rd person lock means you can't really see anything of the battlefield anyway.
This game desperatly needs a free-form, unlocked camera that allows for a top-down view of the battlefield and much greater zoom distance. And one which isn't blocked by in-game objects.
I'm all for action cams, to a point at least, but if I wanted to be locked into 3rd person I'd be playing Diablo instead.
Finally, if a lesser complaint than the ones above, is the fact that you can't really move around on the battlefield in any meaningful way. You can't open doors, squeeze past heaps of trash or crates or jump through an open window-frame or anything like that. You can't even climb a wall or jump down a canal unless there's a specific waypoint placed at the spot in question.
All in all the game is, unfortunately, an exercise in frustration long before the mechanics or gameplay itself becomes worthy of evaluation.
Avoid.

Dracula Origin is a classic point-and-click game from 2008 with many of the good and bad things that come along with it.  It doesn't belong alongside the beloved classics, but I think it's a good game that's worth playing.  Unfortunately it hasn't been in a bundle for almost 3 years.  So on to the pros and cons:
(+)  Pretty nice graphics for 2008, and it holds up pretty well, IMO.  Animations are a bit stiff, but the still shots are very nice.
(+)  Very good Dracula atmosphere.  I don't consider myself a huge Dracula person (although it was my go-to trick-or-treat costume all though my childhood) but I thought it was well-done.
(+)  Polished, and completely bug-free in my experience.
(+)  Standard Dracula story, but executed well-- and with good length.
(+/-)  All dialog is voiced, but the voice acting is spotty, IMO.  Some of it's really overacted.
(+/-)  Some reading is required; there are letters and documents and whatnot to sort through, most of which contain some kind of clue you'll need.  This approach isn't for everybody.
(+/-)  Puzzles range from very easy to quite difficult.  I think this is a good thing, but some will be annoyed at the too-easy and too-hard puzzles.  But IMO they are all logical, even if part of the puzzle at times was to determine what the logic was.  In some cases, I gave up and looked for a solution online.  In other cases, I persevered and got that fantastic feeling of solving a difficult puzzle.
(+/-)  A fair amount of pixel-hunting.  So much to mouse over, and while most are obvious, some are very well hidden.  This doesn't bother me personally, especially because you can click spacebar to reveal hotspots.
(+/-)  Extremely linear, as was often the case in 2008 point-and-clicks.  You literally can't leave a room sometimes until you've done everything you need.  This wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for...
(-)  Several moments where you know what to do, basically how to do it, but you haven't looked at some hotspot and gotten a dialog confirmation, or you haven't fully combined some item, and you are completely blocked in your progress.
(-)  There's some real "game logic" moments...you know, where you have to make completely bizarre item combinations, or the next step the protagonist takes seems completely out of the blue.
(-)  Locked into 4:3 aspect ratio...hard to get used to these days.
(-)  Sudden and confusing ending.
TL/DR:
I think if you like classic point-and-click games from this era, can put up with some of the drawbacks of such games, and aren't put off by some disturbing or gruesome visuals, then this will be a game you'll like.  If Dracula is your thing, then you should pick it up even though it hasn't been in a bundle for years.

The game itself is visually very pleasing and seemed to hold my daughter’s attention very well. The art style is great, game scales up nicely to 3440x1440 monitors (not even most recent games do that) and the sounds are spot on. One big plus here is that there's no violence in game, no pushing, poking, banging or hitting.
All in all, game is simple and easy enough for children to understand, though some of the puzzles might require adults help. The puzzles/minigames can be played again in the main menu after you have completed the story once. Some of them were really fun in my daughter’s opinion and we played most of the puzzles through at least 1-2 times.
Steam says I've played this almost 6 hours but the actual play time (not card idling) is only 1.5 hours, which we played in 3 shorter sessions.

Before I begin let me tell you how much of an AVID gamer I am. I wake in the morning with my mouse and keyboard in hand. I dream about games and buy all the latest titles on the release day.
I remember waiting outside my local poundstretcher for the midnight release of Nintendogs:Chihuahua Edition and let me tell you, the excitement I felt on that cold November night doesn't even come close to the euphoria I experienced playing this masterpiece. I honestly think God is a better title than developer when it comes to Teddy Floppy Ear - Kayaking. 3 years ago when this piece of history was first announced, the TFE:K club was set up by myself and several members of the gaming elite from around the world. It's been hundreds, if not thousands of days since TFE:K's inception and we've still not ran out of great new things this game has going for it.
STORY: I'd almost jump at the chance to give this a perfect 10/10, but there was a distinct lack of romance scenes and QTEs, so it's gotta be just a 9/10. This issue has thankfully been fixed in later titles in the TFE series.
CHARACTERS: Another 9/10. What would have been a flawless cast and voice actor lineup is let down by the lack of Latvian voice actors for diversity. Once again this is fixed in later titles.
GRAPHICS: 2 words- PER FECT! The masterful art stylings from in house animation teams have led to a game that is discernable from reality. It's only fair to give this section a 10/10.
As a side note, the Teddy Dakimakura that comes bundled in a printable pdf is a wonderful addition. Just make sure your printer can handle the 4K, no, 8K Teddy textures this game puts out for maximum immersion.
In short, GET THIS GAME. It has changed my life for the better, and made me an enlightened individual.

First released 12 years ago, RE4 has aged better than any game of that era. The gameplay is still perfectly paced and exciting the whole way through, the story is still surprisingly engaging given its simplicity, and the set pieces feel distinct and stick with you well after the end credits roll. Only the graphics have suffered over the years, not so much in the character models as the scenery. In particular the backgrounds in the distance of several sections, which looked okay a decade ago, are now shown to just be some fairly low quality flat images with trees or whatever on them. If this game were given a full visual update with modern graphics but identical everything else, there would be no hint that it was three presidential terms old.

There's too many issues with this game.
It looks and sounds great for the price it is and whilst I am a huge fan of the lack of hand-holding it really does not work when certain mechanics are not at all obvious:
Phasing into the orb? Why would we think that. The only time in a video game I would really try to phase into an object is if I was breaking it or making a map on halo 3 forge.
Jumping into an exploding orb to boost higher? Why would we think that, it uses the same sprite as the kill ball.
Then there are just some other issues:
Jumping into the exploding orb for a boost seems to decide when it wants to work.

The game punishes people for not being insanely accurate and that's a problem because it doesn't reward you in the slightest when you do get to the end or get something done right; there's no 'level complete' where it could tell you 'new time record' or 'lives used' or any other form of information, something that would make me want to go back and try and do better.

Lastly the fact you ask the player to drop from island to the one below and yet they cannot skip one in the drop is just insulting; you have no health so how do you magically die from a little higher a jump?
These things fixed this really could have potential but even at 70 pence it was not worth the money.

Eron is a game that looks phenomenal at a glance. Great art, beautiful music, a fun sort of flow to the running/jumping/dimension shifting gameplay.
But I didn't play more than ten minutes before I saw where we were going. Let's get something straight here: Unclear design work isn't the same as "lack of hand-holding." Things like standing on a platform out in open air with no visual cue of where to go and having to plunge randomly to your death in order to find the next platform isn't the same as "challenge." Bare bones lack of interface is artsy and immersive when it is done well. When it isn't, you wind up landing on a platform and instantly teleporting back to the previous one, unsure of why because there's no death animation or screen fade or anything. Three or four falls later, you might realize that the game has fall damage - or rather, fall deaths at a very specific height.
Eron feels like someone with a lot of artistic ability had a vision, and their talent shines through. But in terms of actual nuts-and-bolts game design, it feels like a student project that forgets things like perceptible mapping, important bits of animation/mechanical cues, and, most importantly, fun.

Rochard (that's pronounced ro-shard, mind you) seems to be a 2D metroidvania with gravity puzzles. The first 15 minutes were great and I hated to put it down. It not only introduced you to the controls, but it also introduced you to the world, the characters, and the humor. This has probably been the best First 15 yet.
You're a space trucker/miner on a broken down oil rig held together with chewing gum. I only got as far as the boss threatening to shut you down if you don't find something, and then you find a mysterious alien structure. Things aren't looking good for your team, though. Your health insurance is suspended whenever you do something remotely dangerous. The boss gives you the day off, then sends missles your way for your time off.
The puzzles are all gravity based. You have a gravity gun that can grab and launch objects. You also early on get the ability to turn the gravity of the station on and off at will.
Well worth the money, if you like the Portal game you'll love this one.

Chainsaws are exciting. Warriors are thrilling. And yet, somehow, Chainsaw Warrior is not quite the be-all-end-all of gaming experiences I hoped it would be. Even so, it's still more enjoyable than any other sci-fi horror Solitaire game on the market. In this PC port of a one-player card game from Games Workshops, you play as the eponymous CHAINSAW WARRIOR, a cybernetically-enhanced combat veteran called back in for one more job - to save New York from a teeming horde of extra-dimensional monstroids led by the entity known only as DARKNESS. After a bit of preliminary character creation (which you have almost no say in), you are sent out into the urban disaster zone to murder your way to the top, hopefully with enough equipment remaining that you can take down the big galoot at the end and save New York from devastation.
The game plays out simply, and although it's highly dependent on luck, there's enough strategy and decision making involved to keep it interesting. After character creation, you head out into the city and are given one hour (120 turns) to plow through the two decks of encounter cards. Although there are some helpful encounters out there (empty rooms, ammo dumps, or short cuts if you're really lucky), most encounters are monsters or traps. Each encounter is likely to injure, poison, irradiate, or simply delay you, any of which will eventually kill you, so it's in your best interests to rush through encounters as quickly as you can. Actually clearing out both decks is next to impossible, but fortunately you (probably) won't have to. The final boss, DARKNESS, is shuffled randomly into the second deck, so you might only need to draw a single card from it to face him... or you might plow through all but one card and die, having performed a Herculean feat but still losing anyway.
Which brings me to the fact that this game is just absurdly unfair. No matter how skilled you are, six-sided dice are fickle things. One bad roll against a monster capable of killing you in a single hit will just end your game. The last boss can only be killed with two particular items, and they can be destroyed or run out of ammo along the way. An early encounter with a monster that reduces your stats permanently can hamstring an otherwise promising hero. Heck, just rolling awful stats in the very beginning, or getting lousy randomly selected equipment, can ruin your chances of victory before you even set foot into the battlefield. It's all aggravating, and the character generation process is drawn out more than it needs to be, and there's no quick reset option, and aaaaugh i hate you i hate you i hate chainsaw warrior diiiiiiie.
...But honestly, winning isn't everything. There's something satisfying about the unpredictable generosity of dice rolls, very much along the lines of rolling a nat 20 and wresting victory from the jaws of defeat. As you play, you learn what threats you'll encounter, how the various items can compensate for your lousy stat rolls, and when it's justifiable to pull out your big guns and waste your precious, precious ammo. And on top of all that, the art style and general aesthetics are just the right kind of schlock 80's cyberpunk crap I adore, mixing Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoonery with the occasional spot of authentically disturbing monster design... Just try to ignore the painfully bad voice-acting in the opening cut scene. I'm not about to call this a good game exactly, but it's certainly fun for a while, and the price tag is very easy on the wallet.

Let me start by saying the ideas at play here are fantastic. Probably my dream game if it could follow through on execution and had a few more classes and passive skills; I love every part about the game except for the combat but considering the combat is basically the game, that's an issue. The factions are nice and unique, though again a few more passives would be nice to give them a little more depth. I love the design of the units. The campaign setting is great, and the basic design of battles is really unique and effective.
If you are planning on buying this game, do not ignore the other steam reviews when they say that the RNG in this game is nuts. You will not just miss 30% of your 70%+ chance to hit, you will miss around 60% of the time. Whatever it says your chance to hit is, half it at the least because if you pay attention to the way that the game displays your hit % you will become filled with rage very quickly. Wyrdstone is a huge mechanic in the game but you will routinely need to take more than half of your available inventory to pass the quotas for optional quests and every time you pick it up you roll for a debuff that can be something fairly negligable like -10% melee defense or something that destroys you like -2 AP (in the beginning you have very few units with more than 3).
It's not that the AI is too smart, it's that literally everything is stacked against you. Sometimes you go on a good run of RNG and win a few missions but then as soon as you choose a tougher mission you will be destroyed by RNG when you least expect it, your units will get injuries which buries your game economy (which I could write an entire separate post about but suffice it to say, Gold is a resource in constant, critical demand and universally short supply). If you are comfortable with your success being entirely dependent on RNG, this game might not bother you, but realize that no matter what your gear or levels or tactics are like, a bad run on RNG will wipe you out fairly quickly on even normal difficulty fights.
