There's probably something of substance here, but it's all so dependant on so very many dice rolls that much of your enjoyment from this game comes down to chance. That's not in itself a bad thing (such is part and parcel of the genre, after all.
The trouble that I had with the game was the feeling of a constant uphill battle; whether against the AI or other players, I always found myself outmatched, outgunned, outsmarted, or just plain at a sizable disadvantage. The feeling of struggling against long odds is something I look for and enjoy; this game simply has too much of it. One shouldn't be dreading the each new battle. Fights just seemed to boil down to letting the RNG decide how bad your losses were, and the frustrating mechanics (a diameter-based movement system akin to Phantom Brave, but with occasional traps or ambuhes that keep you from correcting your missteps, for example, or a gold-earning system that does almost as good a job as American capitalism at keeping the have-nots as have-nots) exacerbate your suffering almost as much as the unconvincing, Oblivion-esque graphics and animations.
I want to like the game, since a lot of its aspects seem right up my alley -- but despite repeated, patient, and openminded attempts, I just can't. I admit that I don't really know (or care) about the Warhammer franchise, so maybe if you're a fan of the IP, you'll find something in for you that makes it worth all the teeth-gritting you'll have to do.

To preface, I also own the other adaptions (manga, and the source Light Novels), I have to say this is a really faithful adaption of the light novels, though they do skip out on a lot of detail and shift some things around, for a 25 episode series it does fantastic with what they were given, and the time restraints (heck, they even doubled the size of the first ep to get all the important introductory details and often times skip the OP/ED, or mesh the ed in with what's going on at the time, and one episode not only did all of that but was also extended by a couple minutes) so all that said, they tried their damndest to fit in all the important details to the first 3 arcs of plot.
This series has the best characterization I've seen in any medium thus far, it's incredibly easy to connect and relate to the characters and the actions they take, the story is incredible and heartbreaking, as the main character struggles with losing everything, over and over again... As you probably know from the summary of the anime, when MC dies he returns to a checkpoint, where he's the only one who remembers what happened before, as described by him a "Time Leap" reminiscent of Muv-Luv & Steins;Gate(ironically enough, the art of this anime is by the same company who does Steins;Gate as well).
As far as the story goes, this is probably the best way I've seen this genre done... You don't feel like it's the same story every single time it repeats, the smallest effects change the entire coming events (the butterfly effect) so no two loops feel similar at all, and the story stays fresh and compelling, and there's so much detail packed in that you can rewatch a ton. The story itself is fairly dark and gory, not quite what you'd expect from the genre but it does it so magnificently.
The adaptation itself is on point, there are some important details removed (but to be fair, the super important ones that were removed only pertain to the future arcs, and I mean, about 3 arcs past where the story ended here, where this season covered arcs 1-3) some things are moved to a different point in the story, covered by a different person but it could've probably still canonically been done that way in the novel as well. Overall I'm very impressed with how they adapted the story, you can see the love and care in the episodes and how packed with details they are, yet the flow of the episodes are still like you'd expect.
Art and sound in my opinion are fantastic, the artwork for everything from the characters, to the magic, the fighting and the gore are all wonderfully done, along with the sounds, from character voices to sound effects are all fantastic... And then you have the amazing soundtrack/music score, from the op, ed, to the music that plays during the scenes, it's on par with Steins;Gate, in my opinion, with those two having the best music score of any anime.
My overall impression of this anime is quite easily one of the best, if not the best I've seen, it compelled me into buying all of the light novels and manga (including future pre-orders) soon after buying and completing this series... and the source novels are even better than the anime(which isn't too surprising, given they usually are, and explain things in more detail, tying up loose ends of things that didn't make sense in the anime and so forth), this is the one anime I have to say is an absolute must see (unless you can't handle gore/dark settings,) further more it also has my favorite episode of any anime whatsoever in it, but I won't be spoiling that at all since the build up to it is in my opinion absolutely flawless.

Dracula Origin is an interesting take on the Dracula myth, brought to you by Frogwares, who are responsible for the relatively recent slew of (pretty good) Sherlock Holmes games (and for creepy Watson). This isn't quite on par with their detective-centric offerings, but it's okay, and unintentionally hilarious at several points.
As the the title of the game would indicate, Dracula Origin explains how everyone's favorite vampire got into the blood-sucking immortality business, and why. A lot of globetrotting, in part to try and save one of Drac's victims, uncovers a trail of mystical entanglements and less-than-ideal choices made by several parties that unleashed the vampiric curse upon the world.
There's not that much to say for the game, in fairness. It's a fun if not particularly memorable romp, with decent puzzles and nothing too frustrating. The frequent changes of scenery are a nice touch, and the story reads well enough, despite being a bit cliche. In some ways, I feel the game's core revelation kind of takes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Dracula, and one wonders if he'd be wearing a fedora and making whiny YouTube videos had either been invented in his time. But yeah, it's okay. You could play worse.

Eron is a rather short one-gimmick platformer, similar to many modern indie puzzle platformers. Unfortunately, the hour and a quarter I spent with it was mostly spent cursing at the frustratingly-designed controls, and I left having given up on the final level and with nothing in the way of good feelings for the game.
The control issue is somewhat strange, since it's not that the controls are unresponsive, but that... well, for instance, midair control is very strange - if you don't keep pushing in a direction during your jump, you stop and fall straight down. However, midair control when being propelled by air currents requires you to constantly push in each direction in order to stay "straight" in the air current... and since leaving it causes you to fall straight down, this means riding air currents can frequently kill you. It's IMO bad design, rather than bad coding.
Anyway, beyond that, the artstyle didn't click with me and the actual gameplay was rather simplistic as to what I was supposed to do. Once I realized I could rocket-jump off the big black sphere things, it was just executing it that was hard and frequently took a ton of tries.
Yeah, not recommended. I'd say something about how it doesn't even have cards, but since Steam made it so you need to play for two hours before you get any card drops, that's fine for a game of this length. :P
(To make it clear: I didn't beat Eron, but I got to the very final map before I gave up. I feel this counts as having experienced the entire game, but also I may as well note it.)

Since the blowup of the "Indie Dev" scene there have been many successes, many mediocres, and plenty of flops. In this "BTN Gaming Review" we are going focus on "Eron" by Red Splat Games which, unfortunately, falls into the category of mediocre at best.
This game called "Eron" really strives to add a new perspective on Platform games. It does a pretty good job for the most part. It uses a feature that makes the player have to shift between realms in order to complete the levels. The controls are rather simple as it uses the keyboard arrows, space bar to jump and Shift to well... shift. Now upon first glance, it's easy to see that it is inspired by the olden times of Atari and that is a wonderful starting point. It makes the player almost feel like they are holding that oblong, awkward controller as they make their way through the levels. The "shifting" aspect of Eron is unique and it really makes the player think on how to approach each obstacle. Each movement needing to be calculated and precise, otherwise the poor tribesman of the planet is sent right back to the beginning to try it once more. Although this can be frustrating, it pays a certain homage to the games of old, which is also a nice touch.
The overall challenge of Eron can be described as both irritating and satisfying. Games today seem to be drifting to the edge of boringly tired in order to reach out to a broader crowd. Eron, although simple, is in fact a challenge to work through and though it may get more than frustrating at times, it's exceedingly rectifying when a level is finally conquered. Combine the simple controls with this fact and there is so much potential for Eron to become a truly great game.
Now, on to the reasons why this little game can't quite make the cut. For starters, there is very little story. The only story that the player gets is in the Steam store page and even then, it's just a little snippet. There is no true development. This is sorely detrimental because although the environment tells a little bit of that story, there's no real element of purpose as to why the protagonist needs to carry on. It slowly becomes a mundane challenge of overthinking levels and dealing with the frustrations of failing more than succeeding. By no means should the game be easier, but there should be some sort of motivation put in place for the player to feel like there is progress being made.
While story would add some motivation to the overall gameplay, the idea of adding some sort of "enemy" or even active ability to compliment the "realm shifting" would add so much more depth to the interaction between player and environment. This in turn would help the levels fortify a story as well. From the Steam store page, the story snippet explains that Eron is being destroyed, but destroyed by what? Is it self-imploding? Is it an invasion? Is it an infestation of a nuisance gone out of control? There is nothing in the levels that clarifies this. That is why a hostile element would a welcome addition.
The final reason as to why Eron falls short of a stellar review is the simple fact that there are numerous glitches or bad environment interactions. The idea of causing the black spheres to rocket jump the player is great, but sometimes, even though hit perfectly, there is a disconnect between the jumping player and the sphere. Add to this the fact that there are places in the game where the player can be stuck in  "permajump," unable to move whatsoever makes it difficult to play without the need to add that frustration.
Given all of the information above, Eron has so much room to grow, and Red Splat Games has a great idea. All they need to do is expound on it and show Eron a little more love. Work out the kinks, the glitches and bugs. Try adding some sort of story-driven concept and/or possible a "hostile" environment aspect. Once those are in place and perfected, there is no doubt that Eron could be all that it was intended to be: a modern day homage to Atari Platform games.

Resident Evil 4 is a fantastic game that's stood the test of time. While it does feel aged in some regards now, its core gameplay is so well designed, polished, and varied that it remains far more enjoyable than most games that have come since. Simply put, it's one of those games that just feels right. In particular, I always liked how differently the enemies react to various weapons and even to exactly where you shoot them. Head shots, arm shots, leg shots, all have different results and may or may not be the best choice based on the current situation. Factor in deciding which gun is best for which time, and whether it's worth using the bigger guns and their rarer ammo at this moment, and it's a game that rewards good choices as well as good aim. And on top of all that, every new area of the game provides an interesting layout and set of enemy placements to deal with, often with no single safe spot to stand. Don't focus too much on holding one path because odds are, there are more enemies coming up from behind you. The end result is an action-packed game that stays interesting from beginning to end. Though with that said, newcomers to the game may need to give it a little patience at first, because as noted, it is a product of its time.
Most notably, that means you have to choose between moving and shooting, which will probably feel pretty awkward to those used to modern third person shooters. Resident Evil 4 was designed around this limitation however, so its not nearly as much of a problem as you might inititally think. Simply put, the game never throws anything at you that requires you to move and shoot at the same time, enemies move and react in a way that gives you time to move in and set up a shot between attacks, or pull of a shot then run out of the way of their retaliation. Ultimately, I'm not saying the game is better for nailing you in place while attacking, but it's not worse for it either.
However, more annoying to me is another issue that also used to be common for its time - the narrow field of view. While it was perfectly normal for back in 2005 and never bothered me back then, it does drag the experience down now. The games's till tons of fun, but I really do think that for an "Ultimate" HD version, the option of a wider field of view should have been there. Not being able to properly deal with enemies simply because you can see so little of what's immediately around Leon did get in the way of my fun at times, and unlike the other mobility issues, I don't think the game design really neutralizes poor visibility as a problem.
And of course, the are the visuals. Despite running at a higher resolution now and having been brushed up a little here and there, It's still a 2005 game at heart, and it's still pretty much using those 2005 art assets. The characters themselves actually look pretty presentable still, but the environments do look fairly bad now. Mostly due to the muddy, low contrast lighting in my opinion. And then followed by the low-res, weirdly grainy textures. Nonetheless, the game itself is so fun that ugly brown environments and poor lighting can only really drag down the experience a little. And occasionally, the game still looks legitimately good even by modern standards. Just not so much in those dim, generic ambient lighting caves.
And as long as I'm complaining, the game could really use some audio options. Like, literally ANY audio options, because there are none. Personally, I think the default volume is too high, mostly in terms of the music. I would have very much liked to turn it down a little while leaving the sound effects as-is, but nope. Closest I could get was just turning my PC's master volume down so that RE4 wouldn't be slightly too loud, at the cost of making its sound effects a little quieter than I'd prefer. It may not be a huge problem, but at the same time, there's no excuse for Capcom not including the most standard of audio options that practically every game has.
Other than the audio though, I'd say it's a good port, everything worked fine from the start and the game never once crashed or locked up on me, which is all too rare for any PC game I've put this much time into. It may not be exciting, but until the time that PC gaming finally gets overall stable, I say any game that runs reliably deserves having that noted in its review. I didn't even have any weird minor problems that required a trip to Google to answer.
Ultimately, Resident Evil 4 isn't perfect, and I think it could benefit from a few minor updates and tweaks, (and totally redone lighting, maybe just a full HD facelift for the environment visuals overall,) but it's still an extremely good game I'd recommend to anyone and solidly in my list of favorite games ever, even twelve years after its release.

Great fun.  Decent game engine and a few nice course designs (and some strange courses).
If you can enjoy playing against yourself or against friends who don't spend loads of money on this then it is 100% possible to have a wonderful time without it costing you a penny.
Randomisation as to whether it's a push or a pull when you don't hit the sweet spot (rather than predictable behaviour depending on which side you're on) brings an element of randomness into it that isn't there in, say, Tiger Woods - where you can shape your shots as you like.  With luck this will get changed in the future, but even if it doesn't this still has a decent feel to it.  Shots are taken with the tried and trusted three-click method (or two-click if you're putting) and it all works pretty well.
Playing "special" shots uses up your stamina/mentality points which are regained between holes (but it's OK, you can buy them back with real money by getting energy drinks and giving them to your caddy to carry around - if you're not prepared to be careful planning when you use non-standard shots so as not to exhaust yourself) which is a limitation.  In the special shots category are things such as power shot to hit ten yards further, straight shot to narrow the error window, draw shot, fade shot, punch shot, backspin shot, and a few similar items.  You're limited in what you can use by a) which shots you've actually unlocked by improving your stats, and b) which shots you choose to equip before you start the round.  You only have a limited number of slots (more if you spend real money) much as you have a limited number of slots to carry extra equipment like stamina-replenishment items or longer range golfballs.
Whether you feel the need to spend money to get fancy clothes and clubs, or to kit yourself out with snacks and energy drinks, will be a personal choice dependent upon what you're hoping to get out of the game and whether you want to be competitive in the global tour rankings.  The game is free to try though, and you'll be able to get many hours out of it without investing anything other than your time - which should leave you in a good position to decide whether this game is for you.  It's worth remember that you can turn the ridiculous "commentator" (and I use that label very loosely) off.  If you don't then you might end up starting to like it, which would be bad.
If you enjoy golf then this is certainly worth a trial run.

Chainsaw Warrior is a game that is very challenging, and is not for everyone. For those that can get into Card and Dice based game play, then you will find this a fun and challenging treat. Based/Remade to resemble the 1987 board game, this game pits one cyber commando on a near impossible mission to wade through tons of traps, mutants, abominations and zombies until he meets and defeats his hardest foe yet, Darkness!
The game uses a simple D6 based rule system. One of the really neat features of the game is you start off by rolling your character stats and equipment options. The built in tutorial does an ok job of explaining everything, there where a few occasions where i was left wondering how the game decided on a certain number i had to meet or beat.
This game is no pushover, and sometimes a bad roll of the dice will just ruin you. For me, that's the fun in it, trying to bounce back from an already bad situation. Even though the odds are stacked against you, there are plenty of goodies and items to help you along your way. All items offer different perks and stat boosts, allowing you to approach the game in a few different ways. Sporting three difficulty modes, it helps oneself get used to how the game works and allows for you to experiment with weapon and item combinations.
Its a simple game at its core, but it has excellent replayability due to its hard difficulty curve and random encounters/events. Pick it up if you are into boardgames or looking for a challenge. The Doctor Approves.

For $5.00, is this game worth it? My answer would be yes, as despite the random, luck based nature of the game, and its brutal difficulty, there is some enjoyment to be had here. It's based on a single-player card and dice game from the 1980s. I hadn't heard of it until the release of this version. I find it odd that it is single player as I can see the premise working well with multiple people, but I digress.
In this game, you choose a difficulty, and roll dice for your stats. Depending on your difficulty, you'll roll 1-3 dice and take various values, explained in game for your stats. Then you roll for so many equipment points, and you decide what type of equipment to take with you on your journey. From there, it comes down to what cards you draw and what equipment you have.
Your goal is to get through one deck of 54 cards, and then through a second deck until you find "Darkness", the ultimate evil looking to destroy the city. Oh, and you only have one hour to do this. Every time you draw a card or engage in combat you lose 30 seconds, and you can lose time for other reasons as well. If you run out of time, well, that's it, you lose.
This game takes pleasure in screwing you, in various ways. For instance, it's entirely possible that the only weapon that can defeat the final boss, The Laser Lance, can be destroyed during the course of your game, or you can run out of ammo for it, and have to start a deck all over to get a new one. You can be forced to start over due to running into a giant chasm, running into a locked door without a way to open/break it, etcetera.
Despite this frustration, there is enjoyment to be had here, and for $5.00, you can't really go wrong.
Don't. Just don't. Unless you're actually old enough to have nostalgia for this game, it's not worth it.
You like card games? You like strategy games? Then, go play Pokemon or Magic because this game is crap.

Short version:
If you like Tactical games and dont mind the heavy use of RNG then this game will grab you and never let you go.
Long Version:
As far as gameplay goes this plays kind of like a Valkyria Chronicles game set in the Warhammer universe, but without the nice story and the carefully designed and balanced missions (advantages of being a linear story driven game, wich this game isnt), on its place you have a fully customizable warband of any of the available factions and a lot of randomly generated missions and enemies

Let me first say that I am one of those players that falls under the category of not liking actual golf but loving golf video games. You could march 20 professional golfers in front of me and short of one being Tiger Woods I wouldn't be able to recognize any of them. But anyway, ever since the NES version of golf I have been in love with golf games and curiously enough 20 years later the swing meter follows the exact same concept.
Now that we got that out of the way let me start off by saying that the basics that make for a fun golf game and game play are present in this game. Whether or not you have some necessities to actually make your experience enjoyable is another question. You start off EXTREMELY hobbled. I was struggling to not get triple bogeys on every hole. The swing meter is VERY unforgiving and can get you very frustrated. As you go around and start playing rounds with random players you start to notice that other players do not seem to have as much trouble as you do. Then you notice they have certain clubs, buffs, accessories, enchantments. You start shopping around for these things and notice in order to get anything worthwhile you have to purchase them. Hey, no problem. I can do that. Then you notice there are two types of currency. Gold, which is in game currency you earn through matches and missions and the precious platinum which they give out to you in drips and drabs every once in a blue moon.
The platinum is what you purchase with actual real money. the going price is $10 for 5000 platinum. I know what you are thinking. You are thinking, "Wow, I bet you can buy a lot of sh!t with that." WRONG! For example, there is a buff used when you putt that gives you a projected path of the ball. Trust me, this is almost mandatory when you get on some of these greens that are crooked as fk. They sell them by the 100 for guess what? 5000 platinum! The prices on this game are out of control. But nevertheless there is still alot of crap you can buy with the inhouse gold. One way to make a lot of in house gold is by using the challenge option. This is where they match you up against certain PVE computer players of different ranks. Depending on the rank of the player you can get a certain amount of gold for defeating that player. The only problem is you are only only allowed play three challenges a day and if you lose all three of them then you are sh!t out of luck. Not only do you not make any gold but it cost you money to enter these contests. So guess what happens when you go and try to play after you have expended your three limit challenge? Yep, you guessed it. You can circumvent the three limit by paying platinum currency. This game just oozes greed.  In my guesstimation you are probably looking at spending about $60 to really enjoy this game. Perhaps more down the line.
You may say well $60 is not bad. Most triple AAA games cost that much. This ain't no Triple AAA game bruh. The graphics  are OK, I would say 7 outta 10. The optimization is absolutely TERRIBLE! It is common to drop to 14 FPS in town's square which ain't no big deal since that is not where the actual game play is. Its not acceptable but not a huge deal. But occaisonally you will get a drop like this in game play and that is fkn unacceptable. You are giving me 14 FPS with mediocre graphics set on medium and there ain't even 50 guys running around on screen like most MMOs? GTFO here! And you have the nerve to charge an arm and a leg for petty buffs and clubs? I cannot recommend this game even though I really wanna love it since I love golf games and as I mentioned the game play could be fun with the right equipment AND no frame rate drop. The frame rate drop is what caused me to down vote it. You cannot have a jumpy screen when trying to peg that swing meter. Impossible. As previously mentioned, without buffs just pegging the meter slightly to the left or right means means rough, bunker or even worse hazard or OB.
I think if in a few months, they realize no one is playing any more and they decide to work on the graphics and for fks sake get that FPS to a minimum of 30 with a full server, then maybe it might be worth giving it a shot. I personally think they should A) fix the graphics, B) charge 15$ to actually buy the game and C) drop the P2W model entirely and go with p2p with charging for REALLY special packages but make most of the good clubs and buff accessible for reasonable in game currency. The game has potential to be really popular but as of now I cannot recommend.
EDIT: As of today (11/16/2016) the putt guide buff is selling for 2500 platinum. Maybe they are starting to realize they are asking too much for stuff.
EDIT2.0: As of today (11/26/2016) the game is STILL struggling with FPS drops to the point of making the game practically unplayable.
EDIT3.0: After playing the game for a solid month and a half and no longer experiencing FPS drops or swing bar skipping I have changed my vote from No to Yes. The rest of my comments about the outrageous prices still stands though. Game is fun and with the main technical issues resolved it is now worth giving it a shot.

Single player card game where you dig through two 54 card decks on a time limit to defeat the very uniquely named big bad, "Darkness". Most card games have enough randomization because of the shuffling of cards, luck of the draw, and so forth, but for some reason Chainsaw Warrior feels the need to add die rolls to almost every action, including stats during character creation. On Hard difficulty the game can be over before its even begun because of bad die rolls for stats or bad card draws for equipment (because you're only allowed to chose catagory, not specific items). [Quick anecdote: Mark Rosewater at WotC noted that the main reason the Star Wars CCG failed was because fans hated having to roll dice for everything in a card game.]
Even if you perfectly pick your loadout and get decent stats, many cards in the play decks have incredibly gamebreaking abilities. For example, one card makes you reshuffle all the cards in the deck and start over, another will break your sole win condition weapon, and another will make you lose several turns (randomly decided how many, of course). The most frustrating part is these cards might as well say "You Lose!"... but they just tease you into playing an unwinnable game. Many cards also have stat debuffs (zombie venom or radiation) that stack over time and are difficult to remove, providing yet another way for you to lose the game.
Of course, being a cheap, direct iOS port also brings a slew of other issues. A touch screen interface with gigantic oversized buttons, "click-click-click to play" gameplay, and worst of all, savescumming. The decks are shuffled at the start of the game and are never reshuffled unless you trigger a certain trap. While this is realistic, it makes for bad video game gameplay. To put it simply, you can save the game every card and reload if you make a huge mistake or if you want to redo a fight (even the end boss!). This removed all of the challenge and distilled the game down into simple die rolls and restarts. While it is ignorable, you will still probably restart the game when you pull one of the previously mentioned "almost game-ending" cards.
Chainsaw Warrior was probably a lot more fun to play sitting on the couch on a weekend afternoon but is a huge headache in its poorly ported video game form. Only recommended for nostalgic value or for owners of the original game.

One of the first Games Workshop board games of the same name, this single player card and dice based game faithully recreates the experience in the digital world.
Drenched in 80s sci-fi design pathos, Chainsaw Warrior drips in macho macheesmo and over the top mutated baddies.
Gameplay is based off rolls of the dice, and drawing of cards consisting of "Traps", "Enemy" and "Empty". Each drawing of a card will subtract 30 seconds from the timer. It's a simple mechanic that's easy to grasp and makes for some truly random game sessions. Controls are simple, sounds and graphics are passable, and the UI presents everything on screen that is needed in a clear and easy to read format.
Staying true to the original , it can be quite challenging and depending on the luck of the draw, you could be restarting within the first few minutes. Not for those who will be frustrated easily with "unfair" losses and bad luck. Those looking for something unique, and a decent time waster that you can hop in and play for a few quick sessions should consider this a go.

I'm a big fan of TD games and I found even the tutorial for this game extremely aggravating.
- The tutorial doesn't pause between waves. The next wave starts while you're still trying to understand your options, before you've placed your towers.
- The tutorial forces you to let some creeps through on the very first wave. Yes, it's just a tutorial, but this is very annoying.
- The controls are very clunky and require far too much clicking on locations spread out all over the screen. Let's say you want to upgrade a tower.
(1) Move your cursor to your tower.
(2) Click on the tower.
(3) Move your cursor right to the build icon for your tower.
(4) Click on the build icon.
(5) Move your cursor up to the upgrade tree that pops up.
(6) Click on the upgrade that you want.
(7) Move your cursor down to the upgrade button.
(8) Click on the upgrade button.
Most TD games just require you to click on the tower and then choose an upgrade from an array that appears just above that tower. That's (1) Move (2) Click (3) Click. Contrast that to the 8-step process we have here. Indefensibly annoying.
- The towers don't always upgrade in a regular manner (e.g., mortar tower upgrades to freeze tower). I'd imagine it wouldn't be a problem after a player gets very used to the tower trees, but for a new player, this coupled with the lack of time to think is quite the problem.

One of the best games I've ever played, but not the best platform to play it on (that goes to the 360 version). There are still some bugs in the PC version, the controls are kind of a mess in some of the PSP modes (ie. the "Princess 30" PSP mode has the key bound on the right to shoot left, key bound on the bottom to shoot up, so it's advised to rebind these keys before starting, but the keybind menu doesn't make it very clear what button does what so it does induce a bit of frustration to get working), and cheaters on the PC version ruin the point of attempting of competing on leaderboards, but otherwise this is a solid game. It's a mashup of what makes all golden-age RPGs great, without some of the things we conveniently forget makes those games a bit of a chore to play these days.
If you don't have a PSP or 360, then it's still worth checking out the PC version. However, I think the 360 version is the best, as I have yet to see any evidence of cheaters on the leaderboard (booting up my copy of the 360 version shows I still have top 10 scores from when I first played it at launch, and the people beating me are only doing it by slight margins, signalling that people aren't cheating and just getting *marginally* better times on the best possible solutions for each map), and they did away with the PSP modes that didn't feel all that great.
Unfortunately, they couldn't emulate the success of this game in its sequel, but this is one of those games that I think will get more appreciated for what it was as time goes on. It's in the same tier of SNES greats like Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy, and Dragon Quest as far as I'm concerned.
8/10 on PC due to bugs, control issues and cheaters ruining the leaderboards, 9/10 if you play it on 360 (no bugs, no cheaters, guts the boring PSP modes in place of more story-centric adrenaline-fueled puzzle mayhem), PSP is somewhere between those two.

Eron is a 2d-sidecrolling pixel art masocore platformer in which you play as a tribesman who wishes to achieve his quest of destroying the aliens that have invaded his world and destroyed his villiage.
Eron has a pretty interesting concept in which you "shift" through 2 parallel worlds in order to land on platforms which are scattered along these 2 worlds. Landing on these platforms might sound easy, but you need to be precise, co-ordinated and quick with your shifting.
You are thrown into the game without any instructions, which I found to be a plus point. Considering that this game was meant to be a difficult platformer, being thrown into, blank, adds to the difficulty. No idea how to do what, take time figuring out and getting used to the controls, I found that to be a plus point in terms of difficulty.
The level design is quite good. The puzzles were pretty challenging but not as much as I thought them to be. After you've caught on to what's going on and actually focus, they turn out to be quite simple. Of course, you learn through trial and error.
As you progress through the levels, you encounter spheres that you need to destroy and explosive ones that you have to evade. Shifiting worlds saves you from the explosions caused by the explosive ones. You have to be really quick in shifting in and out as majority of the time, platforms underneath you shift as well. Won't be saying more, "puzzle" eh?
The story has really no effect. It's just basically another level that drags on until you finish it. That's kind of the main problem, there's no "motivation" to play further on other than just finishing the game. The art style was cool and all, but not as much that would push me further to see what the game brings on in the next level other than a different puzzle.
The jump mechanic is kind of weird, once you stop in mid air, you're just going to fall down no matter what. You can't do anything to change that outcome. In a way, it's a good addition to the difficulty but also quite an annoyance.
The shifting mechanic sometimes just breaks, randomly, there's no going back. You have to die to start back at the beginning of the level to get it working again. It's quite irksome to have to do the entire thing again and it not being your fault. Pretty cool if it gets fixed.
The soundtrack is pretty retro and quite catchy. Does suit the atmosphere of the game, but after a while, it gets really, really repetitive. Not the type of repetitive that would be fun to hear to, though.
Overall, considering the up and downs of this game and its price, I'd recommend it.

Black Shadows sounded like a good idea at the time.
=======
CONS:
- MONOTONOUS: Find the key, open the door. Pickup batteries to keep the flashlight lit.
- LACK OF STORY: No real story here, but it's telling a narrative about a lady and her recurring nightmares. It's interesting, but... lacking. It gives enough monologue to let you know that something is happening (no spoilers for ideas and interpretations), but not enough to make it feel fleshed out enough. It's just.. lacking.
- LACK OF SCARES: It's not scary :( The only slightly creepy thing was seeing Silver Surfer appear in front of me, slightly perturbed by his own lack of clothing. No offense meant, devs~!
- ENVIRONMENT/TEXTURES: Somebody really likes empty wire-spools, metal shelving, and fire extinguishers. The only interesting thing in the game was the teddy bear, and I couldn't even pick it up! It disappeared :(
- NO REPLAYABILITY: Play it once, beat it, you're done.
- TOO SHORT: It's exceedingly short. I finished it in less than 20 minutes :l
-/+ Voice Acting: It's not bad, but, it's not great. I can tell that it was done by someone who was invested in what they were doing, but, it's a little, well... lacking. I can't think of better words here, but, overall this game just fell short of what I believe they were aiming for. It could have been well refined, tweaked, and expanded to create a more interesting environment and playthrough, but... as with that, the voice acting could have been more intense to suit the mood. I'm including this one under both PROS and CONS, because she didn't do a bad job, but rather, it was just lacking. That's up to the dev to get right (assuming they're not the same person...? I didn't pay attention to the credits... Sorry~!)
PROS:
+/- Voice acting: She did a fairly decent job, but... it's just not intense enough, yadda yadda yadda. You've read this already under the CONS section. I've placed it in both, so it neither weighs for nor against it.
+ BUILD-UP: When I say "Build-up", I mean this one point where "you've been seen", and "he's coming for you". It really threw me into a slightly cautious mindset, because I didn't know what the game was going to throw at me. Sadly, it didn't really deliver... but, it did have a surprising "alert" reaction from me, and that is always welcome in games like this. Well done, but, overall, again, it was lacking. The only time you really need to feel uncomfortable is if the flashlight runs out of batteries. Then you start again. ...With all the previous doors you opened up until then still open. And no extra batteries. Oh yeah... Just. Keep. Moving. You'll find more around the corner, as long as you didn't already pick them up.
+ VERY FLUID GAMEPLAY: The smoothness of the gameplay for me was great. I know there wasn't much too it, but it was a plus seeing that it wasn't choppy, bloated, or overly grainy on textures. It looked pretty okay, and ran like butter. Very nice~
=======
Do I recommend?
No, I can't.
Overall "BlackShadows" was just... well, there's that word again: "lacking".
It had an interesting direction, though was very short, and did not deliver on the scares.
When I beat the game, I was a bit confused, hoping that it wasn't the end, so it would have at least one more shot at scaring me, but... it was over.

tl;dr: If you're new to the Civ series, get Civ5 instead. If you started with Civ5 or Civ6, try this-- you may or may not enjoy it, it's a totally different experience than those games.
For exposition, I started the series with Civ5, and have played Civ6 and CivBE and love them all. But this is a totally different experience than all of those.
I can't really decide whether or not I like this game. There are so many aspects that I adore that they didn't return in Civ5, but there are so many things Civ5 improved on that I feel this game is missing.
First I'll start with things I love:
+ The culture system. I think Civ5 did culture a lot better, but it's very different. The culture system is the one biggest thing that makes me keep wanting to try this game out-- I love the idea of being able to peacefully flip tiles and cities. I wish Civ5 had this; I think it would be great especially with the tourism addition.
+ I love being able to zoom out the whole map and see a globe.
+ A very great selection of leaders; multiple leaders per one civ.
+ The victory conditions for domination and space race are honestly much, much better than in Civ5. They're more dynamic; in Civ5 you just gotta own all the capitals to win, which is kinda lame.
+ You can (and actually are encouraged to) play wide.
And the bad:
- Everything is connected to your gold treasury. Your science, culture, etc. outputs are all determined by how much money you put into them. It's weird though because I don't understand if there are really any penalties for having 0 gold...? You can't go negative and your output per turn won't go lower if you have no gold left.
- Square tiles, I know everyone complains about this but, for real. They're really unbearable coming back from Civ5.
- There's not as much of a sense of scale in this game compared to Civ5. Games feel a lot quicker, more like you're just rushing through eras.
- And of course, the tiles of death. What can I say that hasnt been said?
Conclusion: It's cheap, so try it if you're used to Civ5. Honestly, everyone gets something different out of these games so it can't hurt to try. You may love it, you may never pick it up again.
I'm honestly going to need to keep trying it. There's so much I love, so I'm gonna give it some more chances.

The overall presentation or interface of the game hasn't been improved by the expansion either. Additionally, there are undoubtedly small balances and tweaks that are sure to be coming down the pipe over the next few weeks. As for the scenarios and mods, some are definitely more interesting and polished than others but your mileage here will vary according to your interest.

The cute exterior of Button Tales hides a devilishly difficult match-3 game with a strange mechanic: you can not only swap but also flip the tiles, which creates complex, although sometimes chaotic scenarios.
Some match-3 games rely on luck, some rely on speed, but I cannot recall any other match-3 game like Button Tales, which relies on the player’s memory. Its main feature that sets it apart from its uncountable siblings is that you cannot just swap neighbouring tiles to create matches, but you can also flip them between two pre-determined states.
This feature is an essential part of gameplay, because all 100+ levels limit the amount of swaps the player can make, meaning we simply must rely on tile flipping to progress.
Combine this restriction with the usual match-3 obstacles and some extremely tricky level layouts, and we suddenly find an almost frustratingly challenging game. The child-friendly graphics and design may suggest otherwise, but finishing Button Tales is a long, difficult journey, something that should occupy match-3 enthusiast for quite a while.

Button Tales is a nicely done Match-3 game, with bright coloful graphics and a unique twist  - or should IU say flip?  Howeve, even with this unique feature, the game play is too slow and too limiting (in "timed" mode).  I kept wanting to like the game so I played until nearly half-way down the trail, restoring building, and unlocking all the power-ups.  The flipping is just too tedious and I ended up switching to the "relaxed" mode, which I normally never do.  Even that though did not change the gameplay into the more traditional Match-3.
I am going to recommend the game simply becasue the author made a great effort to add a new element of gameplay, but if you enjoy the "faster paced" Match-3 swapping, this game will quickly become boring.

This is a basic match-3 puzzle game, with all of the basic features you would come to expect.  Various power-ups to use in levels, different level layouts and objectives to meet, and a loose, not very interesting story holding it all together.  The cutscene art is very lackluster but it does the job and can be skipped.  One part of the game that's a bit different then normal is how the pieces you play with occasionally change design throughout different intervals of the game.  I rather enjoyed the last set of pieces near the ending of the game, but some were outright ugly.  It made me wish that I could set my preferred style in the options instead of getting stuck with an ugly choice for several levels.
Regarding the only main difference this game has to others of this style, the mechanic that lets you flip any piece, was a pretty good idea and it was decently executed.  You may or may not have noticed this from the trailer, but there isn't any correlation between what the piece looks like and what will be on the opposite side.  Say, for instance, a piece has the yellow design on front.  Instead of correlating it to always have the purple piece when you flip it, it could be any of the other pieces.  This mechanic allows for more variety as the board can hold more pieces then normal since you can flip them over without needing to use any moves, as opposed to other games like this where you would be much more limited on what you can do.  A yellow piece in other match-3 games would always be yellow and couldn't do anything else, without the use of some power-up, but here every piece has another color to it and can be freely flipped.
The way they designed the game makes it so that using this mechanic heavily is downright necessary to make progress, and it is rather time consuming since it is random.  The only way to find out what's on the other side is to check and you will flip pieces multiple times each level, especially with the way some stages' objectives work.  So in one sense this game gets more longevity through this game mechanic, but it does get grating after a while.  After playing through the whole thing I would rather have seen the pieces pair up to a specific color so I'd know what to expect and could more strategically play.  Plus it would have saved a considerable amount of time.
There was nothing inherently wrong with the game though and it has 100 levels to play through, so you get a pretty good amount of content.  I recommend it as a casual time killer, though I do imagine the target demographic for the game was the revealed character in the final cutscene, the one who caused all the destruction at the beginning.  *Spoiler Warning* It's about as stereotypical as you'd guess, but I found the ending message cute if nothing else.

Don't be fooled by it's look. It's not a easy match-3. The possibility of flipping buttons could have been a good idea, but the problem is it's impossible to guess which color is behind. Competitive tower defense is one of those holy grail genre crosses.  Fire With Fire makes you wonder why it every seemed like a difficult design problem.  Players simultaneously build their defenses, and can launch attacks on a cooldown.
ATTACKING:
Attacking is very simple: you choose which enemies attack in what order, for example two groups of armored units then a group of fast ones.  Ranking up one type of enemy to level 3 unlocks another, and flying units have to be unlocked so players can tell if you're working towards them and prepare.
The attacking units gain levels each time they're sent to attack, so players are encouraged to attack as often as possible.  There is a clear timer until you can be attacked again, so there are short windows when it's safe to sell and reconfigure your maze.  This all combines to just work on the attacking end, without taking too much of your attention off of your defenses.
DEFENDING:
On the defense side, players get to decide how to arrange their maze.  Enemies spawn from two points, so usually you'll want to merge the incoming streams.  Clear dotted lines show the paths of enemies from spawns to your tree, and as you are placing towers you can see how each one will change the paths before you build.  You are not allowed to place towers that would completely block a path.
When you start a game, you can choose three schools of towers.  Each tower has a base tower and a tech tree with two paths of two more unlockable towers (5 towers per school total).  Building the base towers give you tech points in that school which can be used to unlock more advanced towers or to level up individual towers, so one way you gather resources is to build low-level towers.
A major choice in each game ends up being whether to build a quick, mediocre defense which might get out classed if the game lasts to long, or to architect a complex combo of towers (like stun and splash) that can handle anything but might get you killed before it is completed.
OVERALL:
Fire with Fire is a great structure for a style of game I have been looking for for a long time.  It already blows away most of the similar Starcraft mods I have tried.
There are some interface issues - things like upgrading a tower or building two different types of towers often just take more clicks then feels neccesary, which can be irritating.  Sometimes it takes too long to find an opponent.
The game still needs more content.  (duh, it's early access.)  There are only a few different options for which towers and enemies to take into each game, but it does still feel like there are a wide variety of options and tactical choices during each game.  There are still towers I haven't seen.
All and all this is a great game, and I'm excited to see how it develops!

I got this game while I was looking for Warhammer franchise and I thought I might give it a try, because I used to like the skirmish games in the tabletop original. Now it's one of the greatest games I have played so far and I feel it's much more than just Warhammer franchise: It has tactical depth, a difficult campaign and a role play-like level up system for the characters of your warband. It's pretty addictive to see each member getting stronger. What I especially like (and sort of hate at the same time), is that each member of the warband can also be impaired permanently. When they are eliminated during battle, they need a bit of luck to survive or to not loose a limb or their minds.
Also, since each race is so different and a complete campaign takes quite long to be finished, the game grants countless hours of joy (and frustration). Absolutely worth the money.

Is this game for everyone? No.
Does this game do what it set out to do well? Yes, for sure.
If you've read and understood the description for the game and watched some gameplay and are interested, then know this: The game does deliver on what it advertises; If you are interested in what you read/saw, get it (maybe wait for a sale, $40 does seem a bit much for the base).
Do note though what a lot of other people have noted. There is no manual save/reload feature. Every move once submitted is final (alt f4 does not get around this). If this is a deal breaker for you, then don't get this game. (While I understand why this feature wasn't included, I feel it was a mistake from a marketing perspective as it certainly limits potential buyers). If you can get past this, or normally play on ironman mode anyway, then this may be for you.
Don't believe what people say about this game being unfair. It's entirely fair. You can see the dice rolls. Sometime they're for you, sometimes against. I've won when I absolutely shouldn't have at least as many times as I've lost in situations I seemingly had the upper hand (both of which are fairly rare to be honest, usually if you play reasonably smart, what 'should' happen, will).
The game is an interesting combination of forgiving and unforgiving. On one hand, there's the previously mentioned inability to reload. There's also the fact that when a soldier gets taken out of action, they can die or receive permenant injuries that leave them in a state where they may as well be dead anyway, and there's precious little you can do to prevent these once it's gotten to that point. On the other hand, there's plenty you can control before straits get that dire. There are basically no one-hit KO's (looking at you XCOM) .It's almost unheard of for a unit to be taken out of action by a single enemy or even an entire enemy round, which provides you a round or two to either send back up or retreat even if one of your units is ambushed. And unless a unit loses all of their health in a single mission, they will make it out without a scratch (crits may take them out of action for a couple days but no permenant injuries), even if they were on the brink of death beforehand, with no downtime for healing.
In conclusion, it's a hardcore yet fair turn based strategy that will appeal to some and not others.
Fantastic turn based strategy, reminiscent of the original board game in a highly enjoyable way.

Rochard is a really nice 2.5d sideways scrolling platform action puzzler.
It doesn't really add any innovation to the genres, but there is enough diversity in the gameplay mechanics to keep it interesting for the 6 hours the main campaign took me.
It's a game that lets you start off with just a fraction of the tools you'll have towards the end, so don't let the shallow gameplay at first put you off.
The star of the show is your gravity gun, which after enough upgrades end up being as overpowered as it's supercharged sibling in the end of Half Life 2 which probably inspired it.
Toying with gravity is a key component to the gameplay, and you'll be able to turn on low gravity at will. Other sections of the game will have you reverse gravity at certain terminals in order to solve some puzzles etc.
I just wish the devs had put more time into coming up with some interesting foes, because all you get to fight is bland braindead humanoids.
I played the game with a Xbone controller and the default configuration was nice.
The presentation in this 2011 game is where things fall a bit short - the visuals are OK by 2016 standards, but the realtime rendered cutscenes are just soo poorly animated plus the voice acting sounds really forced. (Rochard is played by the dude who does Duke Nukem). Sound effects are mediocre.
The story was flat, and the attempts at humor were duds.
But who cares when you can have this much solid gamplay for a bargain price. And if you like it, but felt it was a little on the easy side, I can also recommend the "Hard Times" DLC which I bought for less than a buck. It's very short, but it's worth the few pennies regardless.

Its sensationally colorful retro-futuristic and cartoonish art style looks fantastic. The soundtrack in particular is outstanding with its 80's vibe, professional voice acting and good humour. Overall everything is highly pleasant about the game.
It also plays very smoothly. New mechanics and variations are steadily introduced up to the end, keeping the gameplay and level design fresh throughout the entire game, with a perfectly balanced and completely accessible difficulty curve.
Especially interesting low-gravity mechanics and energy fields that only let certain materials through give way to intelligent puzzles. Minimal combat spices things up a bit without compromising the leisurely pace. The challenges remain fairly effortless with lenient enemies, rapid health regen and regular checkpoints.
I only found the aiming controls to be a bit too sensitive with the right stick (playing on an Xbox 360 controller) and the button configuration was a bit unusual at first, but none of this is disconcerting.
While the story is rather conventional it provides purpose to each level, and it's good enough except for a disappointing ending that unfortunately sets the game up for a sequel that will likely never happen. It would have been great to play more in the same style, but Rochard nonetheless stands proud on its own.

Here's my initial impression of Eron:
Pros:
-It looks pretty cool, and starting off getting straight into the game is pretty nice. This is nice pixel art.
-It saves on the stage you last left off. That's always nice for a platformer.
-The game is cheap. I got it on sale for 30 cents. Would I pay for the full non-sale price of $2? I'm not so sure.
Cons:
-No tutorial. I mean, the first couple levels are meant to ease you in, which is fine, but I seriously spent a good deal of time thinking that I was missing some extra controls.
-The soundtrack is okay once it starts going, but the at the speed of the game you're only likely to hear the first bar or so. That's a problem because the first bar is really annoying.
-Fall damage. I'm fine with a game allowing me to fall to my death, especially since this "split between worlds" dynamic is in place. What I'm not okay with is dropping onto a platform only for the game to decide that I have to go all the way back to the beginning. I can understand that if I've somehow missed an objective, but when I've made progress and would be otherwise able to proceed I'd rather not get sabotaged because of fall damage.
I do intend to continue playing Eron, as I like pixel-graphic designs like this and I like the idea of the transfer mechanic, but I think it is notably flawed. However, I feel that the cons of the game very much need addressing in order for me to recommend this game. At the very least, I'd recommend waiting until Eron is on sale until you try it out.

attack chopper hiding in the back. The gunner of the M113 takes out the two in quick bursts and I tell my men to board the Hind. "Out of fuel" 3 in my squad tells me. I find a fuel truck hiding behind a wall and refuel the Hind. As we start the chopper me and my men get ready for what comes next...
As we fly our way to Guba's base, we evade enemy anti aircraft vehicles, namely the  ZSU-23-4
. A little while later, we spot a friendly assault on the frontlines. An M113 supported by a group of infantry heads for Guba's base. A few yards beyond them, we see the diabolical ruskie tank, the
. I tell my gunner to engage the T-80 before our friendlies get slaughtered. I hover the chopper for my gunner to lock on and we destroy the T-80 just in time before it fires a shot at the M113. As we see the friendly assault push forward, we return to our main objective.
We hover over Guba's base and spot him in a UAZ, getting ready to leave for good. Luckily we catch him before even sets a good distance into the Shilka infested lands. My gunner guns down any infantry and spetsnaz units guarding Guba and we land to apprehend him. As we finally apprehend the mastermind, he speaks in Russian of how the island will be nuked with his SCUD launchers that is set up somewhere on the opposite side of the island. Lucky for me, I can translate what he was saying and report it to command. Command replies that our new objective is to take out the SCUD launchers ASAP. As we board into the Hind once again along with our whimpering captive, we search for the SCUD launchers...
I hover around the coast and spot a group of Shilka AA vehicles firing at me. A little beyond, I spot the SCUD launchers... Ready to launch. I tell my gunner to fire at will at the Shilkas but we take too many hits. My gunner and a few others in my squad are dead... I tell my remaining men to ditch as our helicopter moves closer to the ground... crash landing...
Me and a few others, including the captive ditch the chopper just before we hit the ground. I find my legs bleeding and look at the crash site. I call all my units to report their positions to me. Only three of my men were left, along with our captive. I tell them to stay put and look after the captive. As I look infront of me, I see the SCUD launcher's nuclear warhead. I'm lucky to be so close to the nuke... but not so lucky to have my legs broken. As I crawl my way to the SCUD launcher, I spot the same ruskie Shilkas that shot down our chopper. Pros:
Extremely large believable world to relive your military fantasies of World War III. ArmA: CWA delivers in breadth and really astounds. There is quite a lot to see and experience in the game that you'd probably be wanting to replay the campaigns long after you've completed them.

You essentially get Cold War Crisis and the Resistance expansion updated to run on modern systems.
The mission editor continues the life of the game indefinitely.
Cons:
You character will die very often, so make sure you save. This brings me to the next point...
Unfortunately you can only save once for every mission in the campaign.
Missions usually take more than 15 minutes to complete. Make sure you have catered time to play them.
The missions are scripted to the point that if you deviate from your objectives too much, you may find yourself not able to complete the mission.
Vehicle physics is very simplified... don't come away from reading this review expecting realistic vehicular simulations.
The base 3D models for humans is unimpressive.
There is that irritating shouting of instructions by your squad leader where nothing can be done about it.
The game still has the rare crash to desktop problem; make sure you save your missions.

As I launch the game my greatest fears were confirmed : BlackShadows doesn't have any menu. Instead of opening on the title screen the game throws you directly into gameplay, where the scary part actually ends...
Basically, the game consist of making your way through a dark maze-like environment with your flashlight. Since batteries in indie horror games can't last longer than any generic brand batteries sold at Walmart, you'll have no choice but to pickup new ones every two minutes.
In addition, the game features only one level and it lasts no longer than 20 minutes. Once you get at the end of the game you will feel no sense of accomplishment since nothing explains what you have actually done to solve the mystery behind the paranormal phenomenon that afflicts the whole humanity.
To conclude, BlackShadows aka Black Shadows is nothing else but another indie game that tries to cow milk on the success of great horror games such as Amnesia and Outlast (let's not talk about Slender, please). To do the best shot you need to hit the sweet spot on the swing bar, which after level 20, and with a pretty good gaming computer, I can hit about once in 20.  This is really frustrating..  There are specialist skills which make very small changes to you swings/hits so you feel like there is nothing worth aiming for in terms of skill development.  If anyone played Pangya, I just want to compare its swing bar mechanic - in pangya if you clicked the swing bar at the power you want, and then realized you were long or short, you just let the swing bar go back to the start and you can try again.  Not so with winning putt, once you select power you are stuck with it.  This is really frustrating.  What makes it worse is that you can experience an accidentally 'double click' on the swing bar, which is a reported glitch and basically your click registers at the incorrect spot and so, since you can't just let it reset, you tank the shot and ruin the hole.  Some of the courses are nicely designed as you'd expect and then others are so monumentally stupid in design, that again, causes nothing but frustrating to a point where I got today and thought ' why am I putting myself through this. Note: By "click" I mean either pressing the left mouse button or the space bar, depending if you use mouse or keyboard.
Pros:
- Graphic is pretty good
- "Free" to play
- Big variety of courses
Cons short version:
The swing meter is broken, clicking anywhere below 100% power will result in way less power then the displayed one (50% power translates in reality to 15%-30%, which forces you to pick a weaker power club and hit that on 100% to hit that distance) and missing the sweet spot for accuracy results in really strange and seemingly random flying curves, the hit bar also accelaretes toward the ends of the swing bar, which I think is unnecessary and makes clicks more unpredictable.
Cons long version:
I don't really know if the p2w is true or not, but I am giving a bad review because of the (seemingly) random mechanic of the game.
If you've played any other golf game, you'd be familiar with the 3-click-system, as in click to start the bar moving, 2nd click to determinate power and 3rd to set accuracy.
Now I have this huge problem with the 3rd hit, you can literally use the same club, 100% power and even though if you hit the same accuracy, the ball will always fly in a different pattern if you don't hit the sweet spot (dead center).
Here's what I mean, lets say you start, hit 100% and click the 3rd time 1millimeter (0.0394in) to the right of the sweet spot (noted as slight push in the game), once the ball will fly almost straight with a really small curve (what I expect), but another time with the exact same click the ball will go nuts and fly left/right in a 45 degree angle (and I mean hitting from the fairway, 100%, no rough or bunkers, no OverSwing, and I am still talking about a slight push), as if there is a build in RNG (random number generator) to randomly add or substract from the hitting formula to frustrate you, it seems there is absolutely no learning curve as I tried clicking some "hooks" (inaccurate shots) in the driving range, on purposly hitting about 1cm (0.394in) to the right of the sweetspot (clicking too early) and I was amazed, that sometimes the ball curves to the left and sometimes to the rigth, as if there wasn't a fixed mechanic. Or sometimes no matter on what side I click (still same distance from sweet spot) my ball always curves to the right. In other games I played, hitting too early (on the right) sends the ball flying to the left and hitting too late (on the left) sends the ball to the right. I wouldn't care if this game does the opposite, as long as it would be constant.
To test something with the power, I used my I8 which had 90y with a new accuracy character (to have a round number devidible through 10). My 2nd click was on 50.1% the game even stated so, (lets calculate as if was 50%), and my 3rd click was exactly on the sweet spot, noted as nice by the game, I expected my ball to travel 45y (which is 50% of 90y), of course, the ball flew 14.35y and rolled 7.73y (tested on the practice short game) which gives in total 22.08y. Since hitting from the fairway gives only 95%-99% power, i'll reduce the expected 45y to between 42.75y and 44.55y. So WHY is there such a huge difference between the mathematically calculated and stated 42.75y to 44.55y and the result of 22.08y? I also did a test with my DR which has 162y on the driving range, again I hit on 50.4% and on sweet spot, ball flies 26.06y and rolls 3.97y (since it didn't even fly past the rough) so again, instead of the expected 83.16y I got 30.03y, why?!?
I also couldn't find how to finetune where to hit your ball, like hitting the ball left or right, at the bottom if you have nice wind with you or hitting on the top if you have wind against you; oh, and the wind, I had strong wind 11mph (thats 17.7km/h) against me and my ball flew normal, as if the wind icon is just there for nothing, not affecting my ball flying trajectory at all.
Also, keyboard-players are in a disadvantage compared to mouse-players, because mouse players can just click and hold the right mouse key to see the orange trajectory bar WITHOUT MOVING (no sliding the mouse left or right), whereas keyboard-players need to press A or D to see it (which effectively moves your shot angle), holding Shift just softens the problem, not removing it. Maybe have it so when someone presses and holds Shift, the orange trajectory bar appears without the need to also press A or D to move.
Final verdict:
I really can't recommend the game.
The power calculation on the swing meter being wrong just breaks the whole purpose of calculating where to press. You need to hit less than 100%? Just pick a club which has that distance as 100% and use it instead. Already using the weakest club? Well, tough luck... It seems other users have commented on that issue as well.
The accuracy calculation is frustrating. You do same hit from same position with same accuracy but get a way different result.

There is a number of problems with this game.
First off, a thing many adventures used to pull in earlier times, the "click every single corner of the map to find a miniscule object". The moody pallete of the game, although good for the feeling of the source material, makes this even worse. A black veil on top of a tomb that could have been an aristic depiction of shadow? A metallic grey pulley in the ceiling with grey cinder blocks in the background. Yeah, not a lot of fun having to resort to a walkthrough to find those.
The puzzles overall are good and the game's strongest point, although be warned it is old-school. You will find no instructions, hints or a skip button. It is up to you to decide if this is your thing or not. Personally I feel like that some puzzles would need at least some form of hint from the protagonist (e.g. the pentagram puzzle).
The atmosphere is hit and miss, with the Cairo music being probably the worst. Even worse and probably the worse part of the game excluding "hidden objects" is some of the interactions. Need water that hasn't touched the ground? Just take some from a trough and boil it. Throw a jar of bugs at a bug-eating minion that ignores you completely might sound weird but can be explained to morality, if only you didn't set another minion ablaze later. Make a key out of a strange goo (don't ask) and pretzels in front of the innkeeper you want to trick and he is none the wiser or use a dead beaver as part of a funnel system. And the list of absurd interactions goes on.
Unless it comes heavily discounted or part of a bundle, avoid. If you find it discounted, have patience, a walkthrough for the "hidden items" and want to have a few laughts, buy it, Frogwares has moved on to better games since, so at least you are helping them.

Whilse I like this game let me place the biggest cavet emptor I possibly can in the largest font size, bolded of course, that steam will allow.
With that out of the way, who is this game for then? I mean every game in existance is possibly not for everyone afterall. Well, this game scratches an itch no other tower defense game has ever managed to scratch. PVP. Infact PVP is all this game has to offer! If you were hoping for some VS AI or team play or anything else then this game doesn't have it, sorry.
The way the game works is as follows. You have 45 seconds to build up your base defenses AND select a creep wave to send at your opponent. You both get money for attacking and defending successfully.
If, however you think you can just sit back and let your opponent do all the work while you gain massive money then you are in for a shock my friend. Everytime you send your creep wave, they level up. You don't
to send your creep wave every 45 seconds if you don't want too, but it behooves you to do so otherwise your enemy will level up faster than you can keep up and leveling creeps up is free, they just need to be sent on a death march to gain a level.
After 3 level ups they can evolve into even more annoying fodder, usually ending the match outright.
You can however let the opponent level up while you farm their fodder and build the ultimate defensive wall. Its an interesting conundrum and shows surprisingly good design because their is no 'wrong' way to play the game, except by not placing any towers whatsoever but at that point why even play.
You seemingly gain nothing for losing and if your foe quits, you automatically win, likewise if they disconnect. ♥♥♥♥ing hell, just take that in for a moment and then realize that Capcom couldn't even add that for Street Fighter 5.
The game isn't without its downsides however, first of all, their is only the tutorial whereby you can learn the ropes of the game. This is annoying but not game breaking. The tutorial will serve as a testing ground for your various build ideas over time so it is good that it at least exists.
The game also features a shop and some of the items in the shop, well, yeah. Its a free to play game so its what you'd expect, units that seemingly have an advantage over people who don't pay.
Also clicking feels off, can't put my finger on it but if i had to guess, I imagine this game is also on mobile.
Finally their is no single player campaign at all and wait times for matches are pretty long due to a low player count.
I can think of some quality of life fixes for example allow us to save a specific creep loadout rather than picking every wave, with the option to change it if we want, mid match. I often go with the same early creeps, just to level them up and picking them game after game is just repetitive.
With all that said, I had some fun with the game. It isn't deep like a CCG nor is it as good as multiplayer co-op tower defense games like Bloons TD5 but despite all the reviews saying this game is bad, I honestly enjoyed it, even if I won't be clocking in a lot of hours into it.

Rochard is a charmingly styled and thoroughly enjoyable to play, even if the storyline can seem a little obvious at first. The run and jump gameplay is bolstered by a low-gravity function that can be easily toggled at almost any time, and a steady, slow flow of weapon upgrades or modifications keep things relatively interesting. Don't expect too many options though, health stations increase maximum health but there are no shields or recharge changes. Weapon modifications can be found but only installed or not, and with no maximum to the collection you'll find the changes very linear.
The game offers a little replayability with golden icons to collect, upgrades to find all of, and a speed run achievement to hit. Ultimately, however, not something that will be replayed often, with most users clocking in around 10 hours of gameplay.
A reasonable enough deal, with some super-cheap DLC for 4 "Challenge Mode" levels if you found the main game a little easy.

Did you like Chainsaw Warrior as a card game or do you enjoy simple randomly generated games with little influence from yourselves in a neat setting? If yes then you will enjoy Chainsaw Warrior for what it is. If you were expecting anything more then you won't find it here.
The game involves creating a character via the use of dice and a selection of equipment cards. After that you'll go into the main game which has you clicking through a deck of cards to see what random events you come across, which can be traps, monsters, secret passages etc. At each event you can select between a couple of choices like using a item or attacking. Everything you do is delivered through the dice.
The presentation is okay. The art is mostly from the card game I guess, animations are basic and sound assets aren't anything special, the intro comic is quite neat though. But to me it feels so much more could've been done with this setting, like having the Warrior and Mutants visually on the screen and having them fight it out etc.
I bought the game during a sale for a couple of dollars which to me feels like the right price for this game. The game is ok but I wouldn't really recommend it to anyone except to people who want a digital version of the card game. The game length is also very short, but due to the random nature it can take you between 30 minutes - 3 hours depending on difficulty.

Similar Game(s):
Chainsaw Warrior The Board Game
The Good:
A quick pick-up & play game that can be played and beaten in 15 – 40 minute bursts (depending on how well you roll your starting stats)
Due to the board game it is replicating, all the mechanics are in the open and based off six-sided dice rolls
Opening comic is very slick and sets the scene for the upcoming game-play
Artwork is well drawn and retains the original board game’s motif
A high difficulty level that rewards diligence
Card descriptions are straight-forward and easy to understand
Very rewarding to finally beat the game, on any of the three difficulty settings
The Bad:
Tutorial is lacking for those not familiar with the original board game from 1987
Unexplained abbreviations are common and some important game-play mechanics aren’t fully explained (I’m looking at you, guns)
Moderate level of chance present with every play-through, which can cause frustration when having a lengthy play session
Admittedly this is less of a problem for the Easy mode, which allows you to pick your equipment before heading forth to save the world
The difficult-to-beat ending was anti-climactic and gone after a mouse click.  It would have been nice to have been treated with another interesting comic
Voice acting during the comic is a little monotonous, which doesn’t fit with the well produced comic animations
This is very minor, but I must have sat through 20 “how to play the game” tutorial iterations before I noticed the “Replay Tutorial?” button in the options screen
The tutorial was quite helpful the first time around, but maybe after that it should automatically switch the option to “NO” in the options screen
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
I felt like the artwork was a little too gory for them to be taking in.
Though the gameplay is pretty tame (virtual dice roll across the screen in place of “actions”), I feel the zombie pics on the cards would be a little too much for younger ones.
Did I make time to complete it?:
I felt compelled to beat the game on Easy mode.  The learning curve was steep in the beginning (not having played the original), but I persevered and became victorious!  A little achievement pop-up hasn’t felt so rewarding since beating Super Meat Boy.
