Ah Mordheim. The city of riches and fame, but also danger and death.
Theres hundreds of reviews that explain the finer elements of the game so I wont flog a dead horse, although its interesting to note that you can in fact find dead horses in the game. But I digress...
Those that played the tabletop will know the RNG element that comes with this, but this game is even more unpredictable to say the least. To put it bluntly, dont assume that because you have a 95% chance to hit, that you will be hitting 95% of the time. Oh no, that would be too easy, and Mordheim is a city that does not forgive nor offer mercy.
Alot of people find the brutal RNG can be too much to deal with, and while its tempting to make a comment along the lines of separating the boys from the men, it really can be frustrating to have your carefully thought out plans utterly destroyed and find yourself on the receiving end of a multiple crit/stun barrage out of nowhere effectively leaving your warriors cannon fodder for the AI scrubs to beat down on. But then again, from the midst of this certain defeat, that one archer who isnt pinned down will fire off the gamechangers and crit/stun 2 of their strongest warriors and letting you pull that victory out of the bag. The god of change Tzeentch is fickle.
All in all, if you are the sort that likes a game that lines up all neat, that takes pleasure in reading all the guides and setting things up to perfection, or if you have OCD...this isnt the game for you. Your carefully laid plans will crumble at the drop of an unexpected hat, and those warband members you have spend countless missions and gold training to assassins of legendary proportions with the very best weapons and armour can and will die a paupers death to that zombie you didnt see lurking round the corner with the rusty sword and 1 leg missing.
If on the other hand you like a bit of...Chaos in your life, then enroll in your nearest mercenary warband and come join us in the City. Of Mordheim. Where every day is a roll of the dice, and the game might or might not be rigged. Fancy your chances?

I don't spend too much on this game, as i found it's not that fun. I already asked for a refund here. There's some pro's and cons about this game after playing it for an hour and 6 stages of sprint rally. Please note that i'm an average gamer who likes some racing game and already spent about 130 hours on dirt rally. And to give perspective, I'm giving the comparison by (sometimes) comparing this game to Dirt Rally, the game that i played long enough til i knew i can drive in it (not being the best driver out there, but at least i can handle their cars till finish lol). So here they are :
PROS
- Fully Licensed WRC Tracks
In terms of choosing between Dirt and WRC always like choosing between PES and FIFA, FIFA is fully licensed, PES isn't but fully moddable. For Rally, The Tracks and stages on WRC is very variative, while there's only a few places to choose in Dirt. It sucks as a Dirt player knowing you can't simply just add tracks there. Another plus point is, if you start the career mode in WRC, you'll play those tracks according to a real WRC Calendar.
- Fully updated WRC Cars for 2017 season (including some bonus cars too :) )
Damn i really gonna miss driving those Skodas, i just love that Fabia. It really brings me back to the era when i still play WRC PSP. This game includes WRC Cars from all teams and manufacturers participating in the season, and WRC2 Cars (R5 class they call? CMIIW), WRC Junior (is it only ford fiestas there?), and Bonus Cars like the retired VW Polo 2016 WRC, and DLC including a Porsche. Not to mention real teams and real liverys, all with their respective driver. Now what Dirt has? they do have some cars included here in WRC 7, but not with all those teams and liverys, so you gonna need to mod that up.
- Great career mode
The career mode is just like FIFA one in their the journey mode. You're the driver, they give you contracts. Win more you get better relationship with your team and maybe bigger lucrative offer will also come later. Contracts last 1 or 2 seasons.  And Each team has their own perks, use it accordingly to your driving style. Simple as that. You can still configure your cars and tell them what parts should they repair. And it's more forgiving in WRC where you got 45 minutes out of 60 minutes for repairs, where in Dirt Rally all you got is 30 (if it's a rally). As of this writing my playtime is under 2 hours, but I finished it on the 360 a few years back.
The premise is pretty unique: each level has a 30 second timer and has a boss that must be defeated. In those 30 seconds you must grind, buy equipment, and solve issues NPC's might be having that are preventing you from reaching the Dark Lord (like a broken bridge). You also have optional bosses in some levels and allies that can be recruited.
Luckily you have the Time Goddess on your side, and going to her statues allows you to get the timer back up to 30 seconds (for a fee). Each time you use this service the price goes up, so it becomes prohibitively expensive if you rely on it too much (you shouldn't be taking that long with levels anyway).
Battles in this game are really simplistic: random encounters consist of your character running to the right with the enemy coming at you from the left on a 2D plane, and each time they bump into each other you each take damage. If you're stronger, they die and you continue onto the right, going back to the overworld screen. Grinding is insanely easy in this game, and the challenege lies in speed-running the level. There are also alternate paths in some levels that can be unlocked, so you'll be replaying a few. Each level also has 2 'achievements' of sorts in the results screen. It's a simple title, like 'Kelp Lover' or 'Stranded' that gives a hint as to what you should do to unlock it. If you're a completionist, there's a lot to do.
Probably one of the best parts of the whole game is the characters and writing. It has a fantastic sense of humor that I can totally dig. Since each level is meant to be passed in under a minute or so, the scenarios don't take themselves seriously and wind up being silly, like a boss casting the spell of destruction because he has massive ears and overheard it. There are a ton more, but its been years since I played this. All I remember is that several of the scenarios are pretty funny, as is the Time Goddess. After completing the main 'game' there's also, like, 5 unlockable extra 'quests', with some having you play different people. All I remember is that the last one is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to pass, so I never did.

So, RECOMMENDED. Let's just get that strait right away.
TL/DR at the bottom for those who find reading painful.
Do you like golf? Well, that's what this is.
Do you like boobs? Well, there's more bouncing boobs than golf in this game.
Do you like games you can just download and play for free? Well, game's f2p.
Do you like p2w games? Well, this game's got you covered.
Do you like MMOs? Well, I never thought I'd see such a thing but this is a golf game that feels just like an MMO.
The graphics are good enough. They look nice, but it's not brilliant. I like them but I don't love them. I have no complaints though.
The performance is okay, but not great. It has some jitters and stutters, and fps is sorta mediocre. Nothing game breaking though. It runs decent on my Alienware i-7 GeForce GTX  650 ti 6G RAM, but could run a bit better.
About p2w, it's not bad, but it's kinda there. You can beef up quite a bit with real money, but it doesn't mean you can't win without spending $. The game really is more about skill than buying the Winning Putt (see what I did there?).
About the Store, you can buy a lot of things with in-game gold, and other things with cash-money. Most decent clothes are buy-only.
About the community, um...well, naked. The community tends to be naked...so be ready for that. :p
Overall the people are nice, and we always laugh about how naked everyone is. Just a bunch of hot chicks jumping around in their bra n' panties. Sometimes you'll see guys jumping around in their whitey-tighties (yep, the game gave them whitey-tighties)...(priceless).
The golf itself is about what you'd expect from a good golf game. A classic 3-click system for swining, 2-click for putting, and general aiming with the mouse to decide the ball's destination. You have weather, which adds wind or rain.
You can play at night. There are days and nights, so you don't have to wait until morning to go golfing, you just golf in the  lights.
Friendly matches, Ranked matches, 4-way tourneys, challenges from NPCs like simply playing a quick 3-hole on a new course or getting a good score on a 9-hole, and other ways to play and quotas to meet.
You get something of a Q-school challenge, and take a test to graduate to higher levels so you can go pro.
You can play on Steam or not. You don't need Steam (game has its own site), but it's an option.
About bugs, currenly you'll occasionally get a frozen screen and need to restart. Not too bad, but still a thing you might deal with at some point.
Customization is actually better than I expected. No boob slider though! <--
There's a Chest slider that sort kinda adjusts boob size...a bit. No worries though, females get an automatic D-cup. Guys will be ripped with like 5% body fat, but you should fully expect only boy-band options. That's what your guy will look like, either a boy-band or Abercrombie type. You can't really be old n' wrinkly, so you won't be seeing anyone like that. You'll basically be in a fashion show with 1 too many people wearing the same thing. For example, you'll see a ton of girls in a pink mini-skirt with long strait hair, and all ladies get the same standard black bra n' panties.
The NPCs are annoying. You need to repair your clubs a lot, and you normally do so by walking over to Evan, the repair guy who will fix your clubs, but not before flirting with your girl hard and basically suggesting...stuff. Every time. He is a♥♥♥♥♥♥
And the girl at the Academy talks to you like she is a 2nd-grade English teacher (assuming you play in English). I don't have a problem with proper grammer, but jeez...you don't need to try so hard. When you first turn the game on and choose your girl, she sounds even worse. Cracks some cheesy pun and laughs like an idiot. It's like how they talk in a kid's show.
Example: Remeber the hot blonde teacher from Billy Madison? Remember her pattern of speech when talking to her students? Like that, only more playful. You'll notice this the most at the beginning when going through the tutorial at the Academy.
The way people talk sounds like a kid's show or 2nd-grade English class, yet everywhere you look you see girls in their undies bouncing around for no reason other than to bounce around in undies. These 2 things make for an odd combination.
Winning Putt is generally a really fun golf game with tons of challenges. The mechanics and physics are pretty good. The ball basically does what you'd expect it to. The courses are nice, and the game is not too easy/not too hard, though you will have a hell of a hard time trying to get a birdie on any hole of certain courses until you level way up and get much better clubs. The way courses get harder in this game is they simply get longer and longer, making you raise your swing power up exponentially, or you simply won't get the distance to get to the green before the stroke quota has been reached for par (let alone birdie). Like an early course may have par 4's that span about 300 yards, and the next course you unlock will have par 4's at around 350 yards, and so on until low-level characters have no chance.
I have plenty of fun playing, and it's a relaxing game. The AI is pretty good too. They don't really make a lot of super-stupid mistakes, nor are they totally perfect at everything. Don't underestimate a human opponent though. This game has power-up potions of sorts. Like if you got Halloween candy, eating a piece will give you +30 swing accuracy. That is quite an advantage. some things wil give you a major advantage like +80 accuracy or +40 power. The AI doesn't seem to use items like these, but human opponents will. Some of these cost Platinum, the game's equivalent of real money.

Eron is a challenging, but rewarding game that has you switching between two parallel realms in a speedrunner type scenario. When I first bought the game, I hated it. The lack of interchangeable controls angered me because I'm left handed, and not once did I ever let go of the sprint key, making the walk option useless. Ironically enough, after I returned the game, all of these problems were removed. I decided to give Eron another shot, and I bought it again using the money I got from returning the game. The beautiful scenery and the upbeat, nicely done music make Eron an immersive experience. The only complaints I have are the fact that there's a very cheap feeling fall damage mechanic, the lack of checkpoints, the inability to change direction in midair, and that the music repeats everytime you die. Don't let those discourage you from buying this game, however. It's a must-have in your Steam library and at a price as low as that, who could disagree?

It's a game with a great potential but it is flawed on so many levels. Firstly pros:

-RNG
-overall lack of polish for a £30 game
I would love to see more customisation options for your warband (akin to army painter in DoW). Faster animations and more life in the characters and more variety of missions. Decent story line with different story missions for each warband would be a bonus as well.
I would like to see a sequel I think game has a great potential of being fantasy type response to xcom. The world is rich and  well established. Plenty to build upon.

This is a game which must sell entirely on nostalgia value.
I've never played the original - I bought it because I'm a fan of Games Workshop's non-core lines (Blood Bowl and Necromunda in particular are favorites), but I'd never even heard of this.
The game is a series of dice rolls with no real strategic decisions to be made. The largest amount of influence you have is to decide what gear you buy at the start of the game, after that a Choose Your Own Adventure novel allows more player agency. You get to decide whether to try to shoot before engaging in melee with enemies. That's the full sum of your available decisions in at least 90% of the average game.
I suppose if you are really bored it might be worth it at 50% off. Do not buy this expecting the Games Workshop magic, though. This is one of their earliest offerings and it shows.

So Chainsaw Warrior is definitely fantastic... if you played the board game. It is pretty much a perfect recreation of the game with some added value like no shuffling or card management and easy/medium modes. Even on easy where you get a thumb on the scales for your stat rolls and you get to choose your equipment, it's not guaranteed that you'll make it through to kill The Darkness.
You might hit the chasm, not have a rope launcher or the climbing skill and have to backtrack out of the building and lose time. The wretched lunatic might steal your IR goggles or, god forbid, your chainsaw. You might fail a reflex roll and break equipment in a fall. There are a lot (!) of ways to fail.
And hard mode, which is the pure board game form, is brutal. Satisfyingly brutal. Killing The Darkness on hard is a nice mix of good choices and good luck.
Having played and loved the game once upon a time, it's hard for me to peek out from behind my nostalgia colored glasses (for us children of the 80's, it's probably a Miami Vice pastel...) to know whether to recommend the game to folks without that tie to the past. The game is certainly fun, but there is a certain amount of clicking through mob zombies en route to more interesting cards that's not especially exciting after the first 50+. And a lot of the game is watching what unfolds. There are actual player decisions to be made, but not every turn. A lot of times you are sort of reacting to what the cards have in store for you. It's almost a randomized adventure game in that sense. And the mechanics are a bit unbalanced. Shooting requires a reflex check to even be able to fie and has limited ammo whereas hand to hand is one roll. If you play on Easy, take the Chainsaw. :)
It's a great version of a great old board game. Hard as nails, patently unfair, good for a quickie 20-30 minute gaming session and deeply satisfying when on hard with randomized equipment you make your reflex check and shoot that smug prick The Darkness in the face.

Very fun game. I love the fast-paced, yet not too difficult action. Essentually you have 30 seconds to beat a Zelda 2-style level, and you cannot finish it unless you grind enough EXP. You gain gold and EXP for battling enemies found randomly on the map, much like in Final Fantasy. This gold can be used to buy equipment such as armour, weapons and potions. But most of the gold you earn will be going towards praying at the Time Goddess' shrine to restart the timer so you can continue the mission. There's always a hurdle to get over,  like a broken bridge or a a locked gate that you need to go elsewhere first to pass through. This can be something as simple as getting an axe from town to cut down a tree, and later on can be as engaging as clearing a cave of baddies to get a gem, put the gem on the mountain, have the sun's rays intensify through it, creating a beam of light strong enough to burn down the blockade in your path.
At the end of every level is a villian who was taught a spell of destruction that will destroy the world in 30 seconds (hence why you only have a half minute to complete the stage). He is much stronger than you when you start each level, but given 1-1.5 minutes of battling fuzzy forest imps and giant wasps and 400 gold worth of praying at the shrines and you can literally just walk right through him.
The dialogue is witty, the game is addictive, and it has enough content to last you 8-12 hours, depending on if you want to get all the unlockable armours and weapons.
I strongly recommend listening to the theme song on youtube. Amazing track. A game like this is definitely worth a try, especially if you are a fan of retro-rpg's, and would like a new take on the format.
There's one thing I would not recommend doing: passing up a 50% off sale for this game. Final verdict is a solid 8/10. Well worth it's asking price.

Half Minute Hero: Super Mega Neo Climax Ultimate Boy is a set of different campaigns each with their own playstyle. The first playstyle resembles a RPG, the second is a top down action game where you play as an evil summoner, the third is a top down shooter for lack of a better term. Each campaign has at least 30 lands (levels) that have a 30 second countdown with the potential to get more time. This is a dialog heavy game with a comedy slant if you couldn't tell from the Super Mega Neo Climax Ultimate Boy in the title. I'm happy there's a one button skip everything. I didn't need to read anything, because its all so simple.
The first campaign is the main appeal. In 'Hero 30' you have 30 seconds in each land to save the world. In the first land, you'll meet the Time Goddess. For a price she'll reset the timer back to 30 seconds. Each time you need her, she charges more and more. The only time the clock isn't counting down is in the towns. If you don't have enough money to reset the clock, the goddess will still grant you a reset, but she'll repossess your weapons and the timer will forever count down to 0 even in towns. There is a world map consisting of lines and dots where the lands are.
The little lands each have a few towns, caves, a castle and a boss. The only place to explore is the overworld. Towns, bosses and caves are all single screens. Combat is automatic, your character will bump into the enemies and do damage. When time is of the essence, you can run, but that costs health. When you die, you respawn with minimal health. Sometimes its quicker to die, respawn and use the Time Goddess statues in town than risk a game over from running out of time. You can also run from combat.  When each land begins you start at level 1, but you can quickly grind your way back up with most battles giving you a level or two.
Before going into each land you can equip weapons and armor, but you won't be able to change them while in the land.  You can only buy new things to equip them in a land. Each piece of gear has its own weight, making you slower, but preventing knock back from enemies. If you get knocked back off screen from an enemy, you don't die, but the battle has ended. So it becomes a push-of-war. If you buy equipment in further lands, the game will not let you use the gear in previous lands. Other equipment has special uses like the swimmers ring which does uh.... I forget. Some weapons are insta-kills against certain types of foes, the bug swatter, the demon slaying silver sword. It makes for nice choice when replaying a lands for the 30th time trying to kill a giant sub boss far tougher than the main boss.
Towns consist of single screens with many NPCs. Each land has at least two side quests. The world map highlights the name of each quest to give you a vague hint. Some of which unlock other lands. Its not that difficult. Most if not all lands can be finished in under 2 minutes. The tricky part is the two extra quests and fitting them in while beating the boss before you run out of time or money. Hero 30 makes use of time, because the 30 seconds are an entire day, so different events happen at different times. You may see the tide come in and block a path or a destructive fire destroy a town. Its a nice touch. After each land, the credits scroll by. Every time! Like you've just watched a 30 minute episode in under a minute! Then you are taken to a hint screen where four people don't ever have much to say unless you missed an extra path to a hidden land.  Some of the lands are setup in such a way that even if you beat a level your path doesn't continue without completing certain quests.
There is a multiplayer where you can compete with people online on different lands to see who is the fastest. In a fast paced game, it makes it even faster. Plus there are leader boards for each land of the Hero 30 campaign. The game will also notify you of where your Steam friend was where you are in each land. To keep pushing the pace, your friend will beat the land in 3 2 1. It will even show you their recorded ghost in the land or your own depending who was faster.

The second campaign, 'Evil Lord 30' is a top down action game that feels more enjoyable and deeper than the Hero 30. You have three spells that summon different types of creatures. Ranged creatures, brutes that bluntly melee and nimble which dodge attacks from enemy supporters. You also have the ability to push them into battle, but I never used it. Around you is a magical set of circles. The larger your outer circle, the more powerful the creatures are. The inner circle is your current magical power to make those creatures. If you get hit, the outer maximum circle shrinks. The time goddess can restore the size though. This time the goddess hides in golden barrels and takes all the money you have each time you use her. Luckily each enemy drops coins. The goal of each land is to kill, destroy or touch something.
The third campaign 'Princess 30' is the top down shooter. You are a princess surounded by your soldiers and can shoot north, south, east and west. The longer you shoot in a direction the more focused your arrows become. When you take a hit, you lose some of your soldiers, which is your firepower. When you leave the castle you dash one direction, then collect an item at the end or defeat a boss. Then you dash back. All with the 30 second timer ticking down. If you run over a red carpet, you gain time. There are even fairies to pick up for additional firepower. It felt like a fun minigame, but it was the same every time, just with different enemies. In fact all of these feel like minigames turned into a campaign. Its perfect for on the go like a PSP or DS.
'Knight 30' is a top down action strategy game where you are a knight defending a sage against monsters. This fourth campaign needs to be unlocked. It can be more difficult than the others. When the mage is standing still on her own, the 30 second clock will count down to 0. Once it reaches zero you complete the area. Control wise you can grab and use the sage or other objects. You can dash, call the sage over to you and set traps such as fences, spikes, bombs and scarecrows to bait birds. When you dash it will drain your stamina. Without any stamina you put down what you're carrying. If you die, your spirit rises and will need to touch the sage before you can do anything else. If the sage dies, its game over. It is more difficult than the other modes since there is a lot to keep track of. Its interesting and employs strategy.
Overall, everything feels very easy even with a 30 second timer. I never ran out of time in all 30 lands of Evil Lord and Princess. They were a breeze. For the hardcore out there, you can unlock Hero 300 and Hero 3. The 'Hero' campaigns all have a good dynamic of gold vs time, forcing you to complete each land before you can't earn enough gold to reset the clock. The non Hero campaigns feel more fun than the Hero campaigns even if they end quickly. I also have to question why the game says the 360 controller is the Ultimate way to play and then has keys for everything on screen instead of buttons.

Everything that's initially great about Rochard wears thin surprisingly fast. The mechanics are good, but the puzzles never get terribly complicated - you'll solve them faster than it takes to execute them and the subpar shooting sequences are over-stressed.
Rochard's best facet is its humor and ability to lampoon the sci-fi genre. That's why it's so unfortunate when it trades its more heartfelt humor in halfway through. What does it trade it for? A series of racist tropes denigrating Native Americans. The shift makes no sense and it becomes severely uncomfortable very quickly.

This is a great little platform game. You are a space miner, John Rochard, and have stumbled onto something more. Your mining tool can grab items and hurl them at other objects. It gets upgraded to shoot bullets and explosives and finally lets you grab people and swing through crates.

Skyrim won't be that cheap any time in the next decade, so by all means, if you're as big a nerd as me, and want a taste of what we old ♥♥♥♥ers used to play BEFORE the Playstation 1 even existed, then it's surely worthwhile as a curiosity piece if nothing else. By the time I conquer all three difficulties I probably will have wasted five hours of my precious life, so that's about a buck an hour. Chainsaw Warrior was an old board game by Games Workshop, created in 1987. This version is a direct adaptation of that game. For this reason, it may appear overly simplistic for many computer gamers.
Beings from another dimension threaten to destroy New York and you, a cybernetically enhanced elite warrior (think 6 Million Dollar man meets Snake Plissken) have 60 minutes to get in the quarantine zone, fight your way through zombies and mutants and reach the big bad "Darkness" and hope you'll be able to kill it.
You roll 6-sided dice to create your chainsaw warrior and pick your starting equipment.
How many dice you roll depends on which one of the three difficulty levels you choose. While all have the potential for the same stats, on higher difficulties these are more random.
Equipment is either chosen freely on Easy or blindly on higher difficulties.
The game comprises of you turning over cards from a deck, each card being one room you search. Once the first 54 card deck is done, you proceed to the second one which includes Darkness. But the clock is ticking: each turn of a card, each round of combat, each other action are 30 seconds and there are 108 cards to turn. So you have to move through the building as fast as possible, conserving ammo and trying not to die of radiation or poison or zombie bites. In the end, when you finally get to Darkness, it may all come down to one stupidly lucky roll of double sixes. But that is what suicide missions with only a remote chance of success are all about.

A brilliant adaptation of the original Games Workshop boardgame for the PC. Incredibly difficulty at its best, no two playthroughs will be the same because of the variety of weapons and the high chance of failure. I highly recommend this game for its fast paced action, simple mechanics, and sadistic sense of diffficulty.

I recently started playing this masterpiece again and it has quickly become my favourite game of all time.
The main storyline takes place across 3 different islands which are very expansive. Without spoiling too much of the story, a renegade Russian general takes control of a small portion of the red army and plans to seize the 2 nearby islands, one of which is under NATO control. Naturally NATO doesn't like this and a small war begins. There are 4 protagonists: an Infantryman who later becomes a leader of his own squad, a Tank Commander, a Pilot and a Spec Op. The pilot really doesn't get many missions and he isn't too great of a character but the other three are good.
It normally comes with 2 campaigns(the main one and Resistance) but there is another one called Red Hammer which is a campaign from the Russian perspective and it has to be downloaded from the internet
The main campaign has 41 missions and all of them are very unique. In one mission you are inserted behind enemy lines and have to locate enemy AA guns but not actually destroy them as they could be quickly and easily replaced. In another level your squad gets wiped out and you have to escape from the island as it's crawling with Russians. The Red Hammer campaign is also great and has diverse missions, of which there are 20. The most unique missions in my opinion are the last one or the mission where you can order your soldiers to build fences to defend from an armored offensive. Resistance is in my opinion the best one even though it has the least amount of missions(18). It is the only one where the weapons you collect in previous levels carry on to the next. So for example if you find a sniper rifle and put it in a one of your trucks or you finish the level with it you can use it in the missions to come. If you drop it somewhere, however, you will lose it. The same applies for soldiers. You only get 2 medics throughout the storyline and if they die you'll have to play through the missions with the injuries you sustained in the previous ones. This however only applies to missions that are set to happen on the same day. If a mission is set like a couple of days after the one in which you were injured then you will start off healed.
There are also 'single missions' and these can be played whenever you wish. Among them is possibly one of the best missions in this game and it's just called Battlefield. You basically start with a force that's half as strong as the enemy and you have to occupy a territory and then fight off a
counter-attack.
All of the Arma games(this one was originally called Operation Flashpoint, though) are hard and this one is not an exception. 3 shots at most is what takes to kill anyone and if the bullets don't kill them they'll injure them heavily. Serious leg wounds will render your legs unusable and you'll be forced to crawl around unless a medic patches you up. Arm wounds make your aim twitchy. There is also a funny bug where a character may sometimes survive an explosion or bullet near their head and their face will be covered in blood as if they face-planted into a bowl of ketchup.
The AI is intelligent and you can actually trust them to do some work on their own. This makes some levels very interesting as you can split your squad into 2 groups and order one to complete one objective while you complete the other objective with rest of the men. As a squad leader you have a large selection of orders for your squad. Things such as making them scan the horizon, look in a certain direction, be stealthy, make them heal or rearm.
This game comes with a mission editor. The same editor was used by the developers to create all of the levels. Whatever you see in the campaign you can build using the editor. You can place down soldiers, tanks, helicopters, boats, sandbag fortresses, trucks, cars.
Also, certain programs allow you to extract the mission files from the campaigns and check how they were made in the mission editor. This can help you learn how the developers created the amazing campaigns.
Each level can be tackled in infinite ways and that's why I always come back to this game. For example, if you feel evil, in one of the missions you are tasked with destroying a scud missile and the easiest way to complete that mission is to tell one of your squadmates with a rocket launcher to follow you to a spot from which he can shoot the missile. Tell him to stay there and run back to where you started. From there order him(via radio) to destroy the missile and after doing so he will be quickly hunted down and killed by the guards. Mission complete and you not only made someone else do your job but you also got them killed.

Soundtrack is amazing.
Multiplayer is dead as Gamespy was shut down but you can still play using Hamachi or Evolve and other similar programs.
A lot of the levels have interesting easter eggs, secret objectives or alternate endings. In one mission you can go to a nearby forest and find 2 people standing next to corpse, and it looks like they want to bury it. In another mission where you are tasked to meet up with the other 3 protagonists to have a drink you can find the resistance commander in his castle and invite him to join you. In another mission you are tasked with clearing out the enemy infantry in a town and you get the job done but your squad gets wiped out then your character will be informed that they can't risk a helicopter to pick just him up so he is left there, forced to find his own way home..
Until Hard Mode... then it's the devil.

You can make millions and millions of different scenarios, whether it be a massive combined forces assault on some  village, a fighter jet dogfight or simply a tractor race you can make all those missions by yourself in not much longer than an hour. The game also has a massive and I mean massive modding community. I'm pretty sure there are still mods being created on it today, not many games have such dedicated communities. The campaigns are really nice as well, maybe even better than those of newer ARMA games. You feel very vulnerable and unprepared all the time, you never know when a single stray bullet might hit and kill you and you really feel great when you survive against all odds, it's a truly great feeling. Sure there are some serious problems that this game struggles with, like bad voice acting, stiff animations and obviously outdated graphics but you have to remember that this game was one of the first games to have a massive and a truly open world. You will probably have such a great time playing that you won't even notice these problems much. So, grab a buddy and go play it, I promise you, you will probably have such an amazing experience that you will remember it for years to come, I know I still do.

This is a strange game. Eron is a rage-inducing platformer that will probably catch your attention with its very nice visual style. I was curious when I saw it, and I certainly didn't expect a hard platformer from its presentation.
Still, I gave it a go. It infuriated me time and time again. Honestly, I thought I'd just do a negative review many times because of how frustrating it was. It's the kind of difficulty that will feel unfair and will make any flaw stick out like a sore thumb.
But I stuck with it 'till the end. And honestly, that was the worst part. But I've managed to finish it. And surprisingly, I did another run after finishing the game. I'm pretty sure that beating the game took me 3.5 hours. 1.5 of which were spent just on the
!
Still, I was curious to see how much I had improved. And I beat the game in 20 minutes...
What?
It's strange. And yet, that last level required you to perfect every single skill that you had been exposed to in the previous levels.
Despite how infuriating it is, there's something quite masterful about that last level.
It's a really long level, requiring you to lose lots of time repeating the same sections over and over and over... but in the end, it pays out!
The game has some bugs that will make you die unfairly. The game has hidden obstacles that you won't see until it's too late. The freakin' music doesn't have continuity, meaning that you'll be listening to the same intro to every single song until you're bleeding from your ears. There's a Running button that you
have to unpress. Why is it even a button, then?!
Some of the mechanics don't work quite as you would expect...
So yeah... it's flawed. And its flaws make the game very unfair, at times, and incredibly frustrating.
But it's 2$, and it has a beautiful artstyle. AND, for all its flaws, it still managed to show signs of brilliance at the end.
Personally, I think it's too frustrating to recommend to 99% of people. Despite of that, though, there's talent here, and I'll be looking forward to what else comes from these developers!

Half-minute hero is what you'd call a parody on RPGs - you've got the leveling system, enemies, and bosses all scrunched up in a tight little package that encourages playing as fast as possible. In truth, it plays more like a multi-level time attack game: can you save the world in 30 seconds, or do you need to extend it to make the deadline?
That being said, the entire feel of the game is a bit... "whatever." Combat is automatic, NPCs do nothing when not helping you forward the quest, and the humor is perhaps a bit simple. Most of the game is bashing sticks together until you get a positive result, and optionally fine-tuning the mechanics so you can make it within 30 seconds (which can take a few tries).
It's hard to find a game to compare it to, but if you've played flash games, it's in a similar vein; simple premise, simple execution. Perhaps a bit too simple, as the game randomly throws rewards at you while not making failure threatening. There are hints that the game may have some secrets, but with the meat of the game feeling like a mess of random junk incoherently thrown together, the details don't compensate.
I don't like writing negative reviews, especially not when I've only had an hour's playtime, but there's just nothing to captivate the imagination here.

WRC7 is a solid entry into the world of Rally racing titles.
I have not played WRC6 or any previous, so my opinions are based solely on my experience with WRC7, in comparison to other racers like Dirt Rally (of course) and the other standards like iRacing, etc.
The greatest thing about this game is the stages.  They are excellently created, look gorgeous, and are fairly true-to-life from the real WRC stages that are run during the season.  I can't say if they are "exactly" the same in the way iRacing copies tracks, but they are close enough that I believe they match the real-life stages.
I've read some complaints about the co-driver, namely that it sounds "robotic," but I have to say that I've been very happy with him.  The calls are very timely and very accurate.  I've also read complaints about the "Brake!" calls, but again, these have been super helpful when roaring up to a blind hairpin.  Overall, I am quite happy with the co-driver calls and quality.
In terms of physics, this game is not a pure simulation.  The developers have even stated as much - the aim of the title was not a full simulation.  That being said, with the in-game settings on the most realistic setting, it feels good.  Having never driven a 2017-spec WRC car, I can't say for certain, but it certainly matches my expectations and doesn't feel "arcadey."  This isn't the strongest point of WRC7, but it doesn't detract either.
The wheel and FFB settings are my first serious problem with the game.  The key bindings are clearly not made to favor a PC gamer, especially not one with a wheel.  I am using a Fanatec CSW 2.5 with Universal Hub and v3i pedals.  I struggled to get the game to recognize the appropriate axes for pedals, and had to futz with the setup for around 30 minutes to get it right.  Furthermore, the FFB settings have some weird items in there, including engine idle (?) which is clearly a carry-over from the console/controller settings.  The same, unfortunately, goes for the sensitivity settings.  I have looked long and hard for a clear way to set my steering, acceleration, and braking to a simple 1:1 ratio.  I have yet to find it, and I don't believe it's possible.  I tried 100% but I'm not convinced it's accurate.  Again, I believe this is due to the wheel settings being a carry-over from the controller settings, where sensitivity in a non-1:1 ratio might be more useful.
Despite my frustrations with the wheel and FFB settings, I have thoroughly enjoyed the game thus far.  It's campaign/solo mode is rewarding and seeks to emulate the WRC season.  It does so admirably, and keeps me coming back for "just one more stage" over and over again.  This is a huge improvement from Dirt Rally, where I ultimately didn't care too much about the seasons because they were supported so little in game.
My final bit of feedback is the lack of view support.  The FOV is only adjustable from a "near to far" perspective, and means you must adjust it to certain settings for certain cars in order to see the gauges/revs/gear.  The FOV is also not adjustable in terms of degrees, meaning it cannot support multiple monitors or proper FOV setting based on monitor setup.  Finally, no VR, or even TrackIR support, means you are stuck to a single monitor with a single point of view for the entire game.  I can (unhappily) live with this, but going forward, this MUST be remedied for future titles to be relevant.  (A patch certainly wouldn't go amiss in this department either...)
Overall, this is an enjoyable racing title that fills my need for a satisfying WRC/rally experience.  It doesn't offer the most hardcore simulation available, but it offers a great deal in how it emulates the WRC season both in the "campaign" and the excellent stages.
Recommended for those who enjoy rally, with an enthusiastic recommendation being reserved for problems with proper wheel and FOV support.

It looks good, sounds good, and has some really nice ideas. In fact, it just feels like they almost certainly had an incomplete/cancelled fantasy MMO and decided to turn it into a golf game instead. Everything you'd expect from a generic fantasy mmo is here. Experience, leveling, skill trees, upgrades, gear, etc. Just, in this case, instead of whiffing on fireballs while you level up, you're slicing balls into deep rough when you're almost positive that the shot should've been safe. It's unique- usually with golf games, if you have the player skill you can just dominate immediately. But this game forces you (even a bit artificially) into doing poorly when you're a noob- creating an actual sense of progression. Prepare to struggle for bogeys and pars for a bit.
The real downside here is, that instead of going with (what would seem to be a slam-dunk) real money only for cosmetics, the cash shop items are DEFINITELY in what would be called the "pay to win" category. Money makes you better in every single way, by leaps and bounds. Gear, skills, stats, better caddies- you're flat-out at a disadvantage versus other players if you don't pay.
That being said, I'm having quite a lot of fun playing a round or two a day by myself as a Tiger Woods subsitute. Your call.

A free game always gets a thumbs up from me so... But to the golf.
The good:
1. Nice leveling system.
2. Gives you leveling up clubs as apposed to having to buy them (at least till lvl 12)
3. You can 'win' stuff you can only buy with real money by playing - but it's random.
4. Graphics are kinda nice... but options are really limited. This looks like a conversion so graphic tearing occurs, no anti aliasing or vsync and the power bar flickers when a shot begins - mine's stable after that but...
5. Nice atmosphere to the game.
6. The options to play others or by yourself are varied and so good.
7. As a free golf game you can't really go wrong if you want to play it casual.
8. Loads of quests to keep you busy - you can finish several in one round.
The bad:
1. P2W. Two ideas, either you get x amount of shots or the effect is timed. Things which will help you play better basically work this way and are really expensive considering what you get.
2. Arcade golf. The ball's run never ceases to amaze me - a driver can stop in 2 meters when hitting the green while a sand wedge can get a good twenty meter roll... go figure.
3. Wind seems to affect randomly.
4. Height of landing area effect (if your shooting up hill, your ball won't go as far) is random.
5. If it's raining your ball acts as if it's hitting mud.
6. You must stay online or the game closes - like your internet drops for a second? Bye, bye... if you log back in the round you were playing is lost, even if you were playing it alone.
7. Think the recognition of you hitting your space bar/mouse for your aim (when the bar's coming down and you have to hit the sweet spot to hit it straight) is linked to your internet... so feels a little random to me.
8. If there's something to your right and you slice your ball? Your going to hit the object in question - even if it means your ball has to shoot wildly to the right, it will.
9. The lay of the ball, expecially on slants, doesn't really seem to work properly.
10. Slightly slicing or hooking the ball, if your playing close to the rough, in the direction of rough will put you in the rough - meaning your ball will slice or hook alot more than it should to hit the rough.
11. The putting is waaaaay more affected by slope than other golf games. Against tiger woods (which is what I'm used too) I have to change direction to what I feel is right then add half that again to putt in this game.
So arcadie golf rather than realistic (played a 4 player match - one guy was in full scuba gear, the other looked like a power ranger) but if you can get your head around that it's not bad - I played 'Everybody's golf' on the ps vita and plays alot like that... as if the AI is actively trying to make the game more dramatic - be it putting you in the rough, bunker or hitting something.
I can see the arguments for and against. It is what it is. If your ok with this you'll enjoy it. If not, you'll want to throw your pc outta the window in fustration.

New rule: never ever do a point and click game in a kayak or canoe or any other paddeling operated boat again unless it controlls with WASD/arrow keys. While mountain adventure controlled fine enough even if somewhat glitchy and slow, the controls in this one feels very sluggish, unresponsive and at times downright doing the opposite of what you tell them to.
On top of the abysmal controls we have the issue of the story and missions also being much worse than in mountain adventure. EVERYTHING in the game is a sidequest, even the main story, and it has an unreasonable ammount of backtracking, presumably so they wouldn't have to produce more background art for new locations.
Instead of having a somewhat decently sized area to explore, we now have tons of very very bad mini games that control worse than free Flash games, and will probably have kids with less patience than adults ragequit eventually too.
There is also much less "so bad it's good" enjoyment in here in the dialouge itself. Outside of an amusing scene involving random off screen kids berating a cat fish for being poor at math (it makes sense in context... sort of) the dialouge is very plain and the over the top overacting isn't as present or cheesy as in mountain adventure.
Basically, I can't recommend this one to adults looking for some cheesy camp value nor kids looking for a fun adventure. Grab the other two Teddy Floppy Ear games instead.

Ah yes, DDO ... a game that gave me thousands upon thousands upon thousands of hours of pleasure.  I've seen it all: the starter's island, the low levels, the mid areas (which are the best i.m.o.), the festivals, the high levels, the raids, the good loot, the outdated loot, the absurd build options that are a powergamer's dream, ... For a game that I spent so much time on, I really MUST write a review ...
Ignore my Steam time, I only used Steam to download the game but never ever even started it through the Steam link. No reason. I played this for years, almost every day. I don't even dare to think about how much time I wast... I mean spent on this title.
Oh yeah ... quickly, before I lose the TLDR crowd:
The good:
- The best character building out of any MMO out on the market, period.
- Seriously, even better build options that most single-player RPGs!
- Quests that are actually quests, not "go and kill 10 yellowtail rabbits".
- Seriously the quests are damn good.
- The "handcrafted quest" is not a marketing blip, most quest locations are pretty sweet.
- The progression through monster types as your increase in level is excellent.
- Heavily instanced, no need to wait for your turn in a dungeon shared with others.
- The only MMO I know that feels like a single-player game yet with other people.
- Active combat. You are moving around during combat, DURING attacks. Rolling, evading, sidestepping, haha your fireball missed.
- Atmosphere! Everything feels connected, part of one living world.
- Tons of lore if you care about it.
- This is basically B2P: buy-to-play, not free-to-play, not pay-to-win, not relying on microtransactions.
The meh:
- The current player base is quite impatient and does not welcome new players at all.
- If you care about your looks, you have little options and likely will have to buy cosmetics in the store. But who cares?
- The "end game" of DDO is actually centered around reincarantion: replacing your high level guy/gal with a more powerful level 1 toon and restarting the game.
- No real PVP.
The bad:
- Graphics are outdated.
- Raids are very boring "beat on the meatsack while doing other stuff" endeavours.
- Player base is active during peak hours but at other times some servers are empty.
- Game developers have been catering exclusively to veteran gamers from 2016 onwards.
- Also more focus on pay-to-win aspects since 2016, in the form of loot that is getting ridiculously more powerful with each upgrade, requiring everyone to buy the latest quest pack to remain competitive.
- This is buy-to-play, the free-to-play label is a trick! THE FREE TO PLAY PART IS BASICALLY ONLY A LARGE DEMO!
- Game forums are the most toxic, vile places of filth known to man. Even the Blizzard crowd is civilised in comparison.

I recommend this expansion for one of the best mods I have tried. - Fall from Heaven 2. A mod that adds so much to the game that the vanilla game is like a mud hut next to Taj Mahal.
The mod is set in a dark fantasy world, recently waken up from a long period of winter due to the god of winter reigned unopposed until a hero emerged and slew him. An armageddon count which turns the world into fiery hell terrain as it climbs closer to doom. Lairs and dungeons to explore. Occasionally, along comes a game more demanding than the most lusty of succubi; a game that will truly suck the essence out of you, and you love every minute of it. Civilization 4 was such a game; from the moment you played your first turn, you knew it would claim far more of your time and energy than you were sure you had to give. Just one more turn? No, just one hundred more. And now that the latest expansion has dropped, it's time to re-evaluate your schedule once again.
Before we launch straight into all the new stuff, let's get the game's most noticeable flaw out of the way: Leonard Nimoy is no longer the voice for the game's pithy quotations. And since the tech tree has been considerably changed up, you'll be hearing Sid Meier's voice, and not Nimoy's very early in the game. Sid's a nice guy and all, but he's no Mr. Spock.
The expansion brings with it a host of changes, additions, and re-balances of Civilization 4's old formula. The benefits of the previous expansion, Civilization 4: Warlords, are rolled right in as well. Among the new systems are the espionage system, the corporation system, an advanced start system, and an army of new combat options. This is before we even look at all the new scenarios and mods that come packed on the disc.
Espionage makes for an interesting addition to the game. Unlike the somewhat awkward spy unit of pre-expansion Civ 4, the re-worked espionage system provides for a variety of different options. By spending espionage points, which are generated much as research points are, you can work on counter-espionage, foment rebellions, gather information, attempt to steal technologies, sabotage buildings in opponents' cities, influence local civics and religion, or even poison the local watering hole. Most of these require you to send a spy along to a target city, but there are still some passive benefits to building up espionage points, most of which are just gaining inside information on your foes' activities. The espionage system doesn't really require you micromanage carefully, so it's a pretty rewarding system all around. While you shouldn't be expecting to watch James Bond murder his way through the Soviet Union to make certain your civilization comes out ahead, it's nice to know he's on your side.
Excuse me a moment, I have to conquer Mongolia.
[3 hours later] Crap, it's that late already? Alright, well, let's talk about one of the other new systems quick – the random world events. The addition makes a lot of difference to the game, and they're worked in amazingly well, frequently playing off of the events that are already ongoing in the game. Random events pop up due to wars between civilizations of different religions, over-farming, failed royal marriages, or just plain chaotic weather patterns. In a lot of respects, the random events are reminiscent of Galactic Civilizations 2, though they generally feel more balanced and less arbitrary.
Some of the new systems don't go over as well, though. The corporate system in Civilization 4: Beyond the Sword presents an almost nightmarish window into our own corporate structures. Founding a corporation is an interesting proposition, as it may very well harm you more than it benefits you. Corporations can potentially generate massive profits, but they take a great person, access to specific resources, and a fair amount of startup capital to get off the ground. Even after that, they can end up costing a lot to maintain, and getting rid of them is hard.
Spread a branch office to your foe, however, and suddenly the maintenance burden is lessened, because your neighbor is now shouldering some of it. It's a weird, and eerily accurate, process, where frequently no one but the corporation really profits much. When you feng shui your trade routes, resources, expenditures, and diplomatic relations just right, however, corporations can generate an impressive amount of income – finding and maintaining those balances is the trick, and it's not a simple one. Overall, corporations can be far more trouble than they're really worth, so players that aren't trying to eke every last benefit out of the game should really just stay away from 'em.
The combat refinements - including some considerable changes to artillery units - change up warfare in some interesting ways. The new specialized units bring some flair, and can help define some civilizations' preferred ages. Likewise, the new rulers (and in the case of Rome, a change in the ruler) also help spice things up in some interesting ways, and help to provide an even more varied experience. The new changes and additions help the game's replay value immensely – though it's not as though it was needed in the first place.
Hang on, Egypt's getting uppity again...
[Another 3 hours later] Well, I'm happy to report that the pharaohs have made friends with my cannon balls. A few rounds through their fancy stone walls, and suddenly we're the best of buds again! Hatshetsup was positively grinning when she heard I wasn't going to put holes in the roof of her palace – but it's not cause she asked me real pretty, it's because she always serves the best beer at her diplomatic functions.
The A.I. in Civilization 4 has been revamped immensely with the new expansion – for once, you can't win the game just by keeping up with the science and agreeing to the occasional demand. When I first took up Civilization 4, I got into the habit of playing on "Emperor" difficulty level and doing alright for myself, but Beyond the Sword has forced me to scale back to "Noble" to break even, and "Warlord" to do well for myself. Between the new complications and the much cleverer A.I. opponents, I've found the game to be a renewed challenge, and a heck of a lot more fun. Given that the game was already siphoning off shreds of my very soul to power its dark simulations, I fear I might need the services of a preacher before I'll rid myself of this game. What's worse is that I'm not even clear I'll want to get that exorcism.
Getting away from all that's new to the gameplay, the expansion also comes packed with a variety of mods and new scenarios. Some are great. Some are really quite bad. There's a total conversion packaged with the game that's frankly terrible; it attempts to be some kind of tactical RPG, but ultimately comes off as a clunky turn-based strategy game with ugly units. Though it's interesting to see what can be done with the platform that Civilization 4 was built upon, it's a poor addition to the expansion. There's also a fantasy total conversion packed in, which fares reasonably, though will likely not distract you much from the main game. The varying new scenarios and little mods add some extra amusement to the game, especially the Next War mod, which expands into futuristic, sci-fi technologies.
Overall, Civilization 4: Beyond the Sword presents a lot of additions to what was already a great game. It's a good expansion, and capitalizes a great deal on fixing some of the weaknesses of the original. That said, the expansion doesn't do anything that will make someone who did not already enjoy Civilization games dance for joy. The expansion is absolutely great.

Eron is a difficult 2D platformer that requires precision and coordination. Its pretty untraditional, because instead of just run and jump buttons, you also have a plane shift button. Shifting planes will make things transparent or bring them back to solid. You can travel through anything transparent including enemies and spheres. Most of the game focuses on your coordination to leap through transparent spheres and pull the left rigger to destroy them. You're never told this, you just need to figure it out on your own. You need to have precision timing or else the sphere won't get destroyed and you might fall to your doom. Each of the large spheres needs to get destroyed in order to disable a red electrical field at the end of most levels.
As the levels progress, it introduces small spheres that look like the large spheres, but these are explosive. Lucky for you, shifting planes will keep you safe, but chances are it will make the ground transparent as well. So you'll need to jump, shift and unshift before you land again. Eron uses this tactic over and over again, but it'll try to trip you up like having the ground turn translucent when the spheres are not.
Later in the game, there's an air gust mechanic that will push you up in the air the longer you stay in it. The only problem is that if you fall from too great a height, you'll die. Its like that in the earlier levels, you'll need to drop through a platform to land on a sphere, then turn it translucent to destroy it from within again and again.
It all just takes coordination on a 360 controller (or keyboard) having to hold the right trigger to run, left trigger to shift (letting go shifts back) and the A as a jump button. You'll get a workout. When you start the game, the only thing that you're told is left to shift, right to run. You'll always be using the run trigger, because the game has a lot of far jumps. Some jumps are so far that you'll need to use a sphere jump technique where when you jump through a sphere and destroy it, keep holding the jump button to hurtle yourself even further! I sincerely wish the game told me any of this, but thankfully the developer himself told me or else I wouldn't have gotten past the third or fourth level.
One of the real missteps to Eron is lack of jump control. If you pull back in mid jump, you'll fall straight down. Its just odd to see something like that. If you're caught in one of the wind gusts, you can move left and right freely, until you leave the gust. Then you're stuck going one direction.
The game looks amazing and we wouldn't be here if it didn't. Every few levels the theme changes to offer something new and beautiful to see all while maintaining the same great atmosphere. In terms of music, you'll hear some fantastic chip tunes reminiscent of something from the late 80s. It sounds fantastic, but hearing these tunes restart over and over with any death makes them get annoying. That's what Eron boils down to, death after death. You have unlimited lives, which is always great, because you'll need them. Each death restarts the level and the music.
While the game boasts a story of finding your village burning to the ground, its really just another level. There really is no story, maybe it wasn't even your village. Its never referenced that its your when you play only outside the game is it ever mentioned. That's fine I don't need to have a story in my platformer, but its hilarious when other reviews are covering the story with fifteen minutes of gameplay. You play as a silent protagonist that carries a staff, but never uses it. I'll assume its for shifting or hiking and not for combat.
In fact the smoke on the village level is a detriment to gameplay. It causes input lag that could easily get remedied if there were graphical or resolution settings, but you won't find any of that in Eron. There's not even a menu. You're just dropped in the game. There's not even a way to restart the game from the beginning. You'll just have to keep going with more difficult levels rather than replaying the game. Even getting out of Eron is cryptic. You'll need to pause the game and hit the back button. You can't move any sort of cursor to the exit.
One of the strangest glitches I've ever found in any video game is an alt + tab glitch where I can leave the game to get into a different program, but when I return the game sends me back a previous level. Its just so strange and something that only I would notice. You can still exit the game and restart it to get back to the level you were at. I also encountered a consistent error that prevented me from shifting. I could still jump and move, but I just couldn't shift. Death fixed the problem. Neither issue ruined the experience.
With everything said, I did make it far, but without a story (outside of what it says in the storefront) or fun gameplay, I'm just not invested enough to overcome the challenge and finish the game. Eron is such a challenging game that its certainly a feather in the cap for anyone that can beat it. The big problem is not having achievements to acknowledge your hard work and perseverance.
While the game is an uphill challenge so difficult that I can't consider it fun, as I continued to play, I got more focus and it became easier to play. Perhaps that meant I had gotten used to the controls, but I still failed a lot before I was able to get through each level.  The $2 price tag is worth the risk to anyone willing to face Eron's learning curve and master its controls to see beautiful retro vistas and hear some fantastic music. I'd also like to thank RedSplatGames for giving me a copy of the game.

Eron is instantly appealing with it's gorgeous art style and chiptune music. The gameplay, while fairly simple, is still potentially fun. Unfortunately it sabotages itself with sloppy programming.
As a twitch-style platformer, Eron demands fast reaction times from you. It's fundamental flaw is that the control system completely fails to give you the necessary tools. Both keyboard and joypad controls are hard-coded. The keyboard controls in particular are terrible and require ungodly finger gymnastics. This wouldn't be so bad except said controls fail to respond half the time, regularly leading to unfair deaths.
As a programmer I think the problem stems from the game using an even-based control system rather than polling the controls in the main game loop. The game stutters regularly on my system (4 cores @ 3.2GHz, 16GB DDR3 RAM) and so performance problems are going to lead to events firing late or not at all.

I have mixed feelings for this title, as I really do enjoy a challenge every now and again when I play a game, but some of the game mechanics are a bit buggy. Take the fourth level, for example. You're able to boost off of the floaty sphere thingies when you phase into one dimension and back into the other while you jump to gain just enough boost to make it over to the other side. Sounds easy, right? Well the only prolem with that, however, is it is nearly impossible to do. You absolutely have to hit the "eye" of the sphere at just the right moment in just the right spot in order to become the chicken who crossed the road, and make it to the other side. Now you could always just jump on top of the sphere to jump over to the other side, but you need to destroy all of the spheres in order to move on to the next level, making that solution no longer an actual solution. What the game lacks in controlability (trust me the controls are pretty awful, forcing you to turn your left hand into a jumbled mess of knots in order to play the game even somewhat correctly) it makes up for in artwork and music. This title has an excellent, calming soundtrack, which very much helps you not throw your monitor out the window at the wonky mechanics of the fourth level (still can't beat it, by the way) and has smooth, bright graphics that make you fall in love with the game.
This game definitely has its pros and cons, but with a reasonable price tag on the title, I recommend picking it up, inviting a few friends over, and kicking back and relaxing as they tear their hair out trying to beat the fourth level.
Overall, I'd give this game a 6.5/10. Artwork and soundtrack are solid, but the mechanics definitely need some fixing.

Not to much of a let down at 2 bucks but it's sad to see such nice art go to waste.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is a harsh mistress, seductive but malign. She is pretty, with her sceneries leaving enough to the imagination to come back for more. Her treatment of your warband is harsh and cruel, and makes you want to come back and prove her wrong.
One of the problems with the game though is that at some point it is starting to feel unfair.  The percentage system is seems to be faulty. "90%" chance to hit often results in a  6 out of 10 hit or worse. Which gets extremely frustrating when you fight increasingly difficult fights and your troops always seem to fail at the most crucial moments. Some might say it is similar to Dark souls in ways that it is hard and punishes you fast if you make a mistake. But Dark Souls has an element of skill in there as well. Where as with Mordheim you are completely dependent on the program to confirm whether you hit or were hit by anything. So it gets really painfull when with a 90% hit ratio you can still manage to miss 3 times in a row. It lets the investments you make in the individual soldiers feel futile.
All in all a fun game, but because of the somewhat sadistic nature of the game it gets really hard to play it for a longer time.

I really want to like this game. Mordheim is probably my favourite tabletop game, but this game just feels like a straight up slugfest where who wins depends purely on the random number generator.
It always feels like the computer is cheating, and the whole thing seems to dissolve into finger-crossing, then feeling like you were robbed due to % chances.
There are so many stupid design decisions it boggles the mind, -have an item stolen, kill the thief and then win before you can loot their corpse? You don't get the item back! Win before you can loot some stones? You don't get them. It gives you incentives to delay winning the fight. When you fail 5 95% chances in a row you want to just quit. The enemy tends to have fully upgraded warriors, something you can't afford, and always has as many as you, so the incentive is to use as few of your warriors as possible. The AI is non-existant (just attacks with no thought for numbers or strategy) so the game compensates by giving flat % increases to AI warriors. You might have fun for a while, but it's frustrating, and not the sort of game you can play to relax, whenever I want to play this game, I have second thoughts due to remembering the feelings of rage at the random number generator in the past, and often quit from the title screen without loading anything. It would be easy to fix as well (just make a generator that rolls twice and takes the average).

Let me begin this by saying I started playing NosTale on the UK server back in 2007, transfered to Global on release, then went back to UK after the death of Global. From 2007 till around late 2014 (with a few breaks) NosTale was one of my main games to play. It was by far my favorite MMO, and even became a social outlet for me. Most of the time, I could just log in and be happy to socialize with fellow Family members, or just passing time sitting in town, surrounded by the pixel faces I had grown to love. Two of my most important friends in the entire world I met in Nos. Just passing the time together, questing, and eventually leading to a leap of faith that many other players would never do. These are the reasons I loved this game, but unfortunately the game was a horrible excuse for an MMO, and eventually became an Unbalanced Cash grab. Towards the end of my time playing It became less and less fun, and slowly but surely a lot of the community died out. Unfortunately the common ground we shared, in raids, pvp, and TimeStones, was all lost, and most of those people are gone, lost across the world.
Although, a great man once told me "A true Nos addict never quits, you will be back, and you will grind for your 95 bow mats" - Ky
Which is true. I've "Quit" and came back multiple times, thinking I would be finished, and gave all my EQ and gold away, only to come back and grind it all back and re gear my main. I had multiple Charachters in the top level bracket, and can comfortably controll all 3 in raid. I've grinded for 95 eq, and smashed Pea Pods for days to get every 80% fairy maxed. I can say that I've experienced Everything this game had to offer me, and most of it was not worth it. This game is trash, and the novelty from the OG players will die out quickly. The only ones that will stay are the ones that have been there the whole time. The botters, the hackers, the sandbox players with every buff on standby in their mini land, but most importantly, The addicts. The ones that never grew up from NosTale, and only stuck around because they felt like they were on top in something. I loved my time spent in Nos, I would never trade that for anything, but the actual game, and gameplay it self is just awful. NosMallers run the Economy, and if you aren't willing to drop money for some NosCash, you better be ready to gamble your way to R7 and pray you can get a +13 SP. To say it's impossible to do this completely F2P, is crazy, but if you do it you probably are. I've never given a dime to NosTale, and to the game I loved so much, I don't Think they deserve it.

Greed comes to tower defence in a pretty bad implementation.
Ignoring the technical issues that come with early access (like inability to login, progress being wiped, tutorial failing to load, etc) there are several fundamental problems:
1) Inconsistent graphics, some are top down, some are 45 degree angle, and generally do not feel cohesive, more like random clip art placed on a random background.
2) Pathing operates on a 1x1 box where towers operate on a 2x2 box which limits possibilities & strategies
3) The interface is clunky, especially only being able to quickly access 3 towers at a time
4) There's no conversion path for towers already built so once placed it's either sell & replace with a newer version to convert or try to make due which is a cumbersome playstyle
5) It appears to be setup to be a F2P model of game without the quality of other F2P TD games... or just incredibly grindy which isn't good when you can't find people to play against
6) You have account creation etc with no privacy policy prior to being setup
7) My account was setup upon loading the game with my Steam credentials but still made it seem like I had to provide my details again.  I was sent confirmation emails which I did not confirm but was still able to connect & play which is concerning
8) Reliance on MP - the playerbase for this is not going to be huge so there needs to be more than the tutorial level and MP available. (currently blocked from MP because progress was reset and the tutorial won't load, can't just jump in and play MP without first doing the tutorial)
Generally speaking this seems like a copy of one of the first TD games I played with slightly better graphics.  I've played a LOT of TD games and this needs a lot of work to become anything worth checking out.

This game is a wonderful intermediary between the "arcade sim" nature of Dirt 4 and the balls-to-the-wall difficulty of Dirt Rally. If the steep learning curve of Dirt Rally puts you off but you aren't interested in an all-inclusive simcade like Dirt 4, this game is your golden goose. It provides a professional, realistic, accurate, and most importantly fun rally racing experiece that pays a very keen eye to detail as far as the source material (this past years WRC season) and the painstakinly recreated tracks (of which there are many) from real-world locations down to every detail (even -haybales- can be found in game where they were near the courses during the actual races)
Though I personally found the physics a bit sluggish and hard to get used to (I'm typically careening ahead with audacity in Dirt games), I cant argue against the realism thats represented on the tracks/roads. Like any racing simulation (especially rally), it simply takes some getting used to and you'll be feeling it once you get your bearing and find yourself climbing up the time rankings. Just make sure you pay attention to your cars intricate hardware. I personally was ready to shelve this until I saw I could use hard tires as opposed to soft, which made driving the cars much more enjoyable on certain tracks.
Also, much to my enjoyment, this is one of the few present day rally games where I'm able to just pick a track, car, team and be racing in only a moment. Theres options for custom events and the like, but this is a very welcome thing for me as I usually find practice/pleasure in driving on random tracks to perfect time trials and obstacle avoidance.
My only gripes are things that were not touched up or flat out missed. The co-drivers sound like robots and lack the fluent, more human tone of Dirt Rally's much-venerated (and apparently standard setting) co-driver. For me, listening to a co-driver is one of my favorite things about rally racing/sims, so having one that has no feeling or soul is a bit of a killer. Given that I only understand English fluently, it's kind of a bummer to be stuck with a British co-driver who sounds like the love child of Max Headroom and a Game Boy speaker.
Secondly, I personally do not like how there is -zero- means of using a H pattern gearshift. Seriously, you just cannot do it. I fully understand this was not included given how all present day rally cars use sequential shifters and realism was a key objective, but it is still a real bummer that I cant use my Thrustmaster TH8A the ideal way when playing this game. Sequential shifting is easier, but kind of boring and lacking in the thrill of jamming on a H-pattern gate during an intense set of turns.
All in all, this is well worth your time and purchase, especially since this is easily the best entry in the series after a string of mediocre entries in the series. Buy with confidence and enjoy.

PROs.

-As you level, quests and campaigns become increasingly complex and introduce new challenges that force you to adapt.
-Multiple viable builds that all have their own unique play style vs other MMOs that force you to build only one/few ways.

-The Mail System
-Many upgrades and amenities can be accessed by playing for free.
-Subscription gives you in-store points to use to permanently unlock content.
-Multiple story lines, including heroic/iconic series
CONs
-High base monthly subscription costs (decreases to 10/month if you buy 3 months, but that's still an amount)
-Even with subscription, certain content will still be restricted until you buy it with in-store points and/or unlock it via gameplay (not really a hard con, I guess, but it irks some people)
-Lots of grinding/restricted content while free to play (as to be expected. They can't give you the whole game free)
-Buying all expansions/amenities is VERY expensive. (Over 100 dollars bare minimum)
-Small community currently. Need new folks.
Overall, I give the game an 8/10. The subscription model could be adjusted and it needs more people (that is the 2/10 missing) but otherwise, I highly cosign it. And best of all, unlike PUBG, you don't need a $10,000 dollar supercomputer from NASA to run it on the best graphics. :)
