I have been playing this game for years and only recently started playing it through steam. I would say my actual hours are probably closer to 2000. this is a huge, well established MMO with tons of content. if you like customized builds, look no further. you have the ability to create your character from the ground up. you choose where every ability, skill, feat and enhancement point goes, and you can even multiclass. ever wondered how an Archer Monk Wizard would fare in combat? Now you can find out.
Quests are anything but the repetitive "find 12 of this". most quests have you go through intricate dungeons that have puzzle solving and traps and interesting story lines. while the game is less biased to balanced parties than it used to be, you will certainly reap rewards by teaming up with friends or other players although solo play is quite viable.
The game is nearly infinite in how playable it is. once you reach max level you have a variety of options that allow you to continue improving your character by "reincarnating" back to a lower level, different class, etc in exchange for more feats, enhancements and ability points. as I mentioned earlier there is also a massive amount of quests and content to go through, and the devs regularly come out with more.
The game is free to play and I would say it is fairly free to play. expansion packs are the only things you have to purchase with real money (if you want them) other than that all the quest packs and quality of life items can be purchased through in game points that you gain from completing quests. I am very much against the pay to win trend you see in alot of f2p games and even paid games these days however this game is not one of those. if you get serious about the game you probably will put real money into it in order to buy the expansions or pick up some of the adventure packs you don't want to grind for but there are no lootboxes or gambling and everything is reasonably priced. Getting to max level as well as getting good gear is very achievable without paying anything. out of all the games I have spent time on, I would say this has actually been one of the least expensive when I compare how much enjoyment I have gotten out of it over time. If you are into MMOs and like excellent fantasy lore, challenging dungeons, highly customized characters and don't want to spend alot of $$$ for a full gaming experience, I would highly reccomend dungeons and dragons online.

I recommend this game with a caveat: don't go into it expecting it to build a character for you. That's what most fantasy mmo's do. You wind up with some superficial choices that May help differentiate you from other people playing the same class. DDO was built off of DND 3.5 though, so you've got a lot more complexity in your available choices, not the least of which is multi-classing. This means that it can be very easy for you to make an abysmal character build that can barely fight it's way out of a wet paper bag.
This also means that you can make a character whose abilities represent what you want out of the character you want to play. The addition of character building elements like the Enhancements system provides further depth to your character build, giving you options that, in 3.5, might have otherwise not existed or been a part of prestige classes.
While I haven't played it long enough to see all the content, or even push into the mid level stuff, with 98 hours under my belt, it's already provided me with more hours of fun than many recent AAA game titles do with their anemic storylines. And while a lot of the quests are one time per account pay gated, DDO has plenty of well built quests around for you to play through.
Unlike other MMO's, DDO works best with at least one other person in your party. Having someone who can deal with traps is important, having someone to provide healing is necessary, and being able to deal damage is not the end all be all of the combat in the game.
It's not a perfect game. It's over 10 years old (which is A decade, not decadeS), so it can have issues running on modern systems. It started as a pay by the month game and went free to play years ago, so it's business model may feel out of date. And I did have an issue getting one of my steam purchased packs to apply to my DDO account. Oh, and character visual character customization is rather limited.
But, if you don't mind the graphics, the age isn't that big an issue. The options for putting money into the game boil down to: pay by the month and access 99% of everything for 15 bucks, or make a long term investment and buy stuff permanently open on your account (there are worse business models out there). And while I did have an issue, tech support resolved it within a few days with absolutely no muss, no fuss, no problem. Yeah, not much I can say in defense of the character customization being as limited as it is. It's an old game.

Unnecessary lack of checkpoints. I'm not asking the game to hold my hand, but after the 5 minutes it took me to actually be able to "run" due to a lack of direction I expect to be at least compensated for wasting my time so early in the game. Areas are short, but the controls mean constant restarts - the controls mess with your head, holding run, holding jump to jump longer and holding the phase shift button means your mind's going to be confused on which button to release at the right time. The difficulty is due to the lack of an intuitive control scheme and lack of tutorial. It's not what the game gets you to do that's difficult, its your mind that is focusing on too much at once... It's like you're playing Rock Band Drums for the first time with no prior experience, you'll forget the bass pedal - and when you do remember it, you're going to miss some of the drum/cymbal notes. Imagine every time you missed the bass pedal you had to start the whole song again. It's just too much going on with your motor skills at one time. No tutorial and lack of a reasonable checkpoint system earlier on in the game makes for 10 minutes with this game more than enough time to know I'll just end up being frustrated if I keep playing. Don't letthe game's visuals fool you - it looks great, it doesn't play great and that's really down to whether you're ambidextrous and have great hand-eye coordination, not due to the game being designed with its difficulty as a selling point, like Super Meat Boy or something.

Eron is a 2D side-scrolling platform game, published by Red Splat Games, in which you play as a local tribesman on a quest to stop an invading race of aliens who have destroyed your home village. It relies heavily on reflexes to navigate in between two separate layers of the game world. Fair warning, be prepared to die. A lot.
Don’t let that dissuade you from playing this game though, as it is immensely satisfying when you do finally get the hang of the controls and are able to progress past whatever particular obstacle is hindering your progress. Although I would also recommend playing on a controller, if you have access to one, as it was clearly designed to be played this way and requires quick reflexes to switch back and forth in-between layers. That’s not to say that it is impossible to play on a keyboard, but due to a lack of button mapping options, you will be stuck with the default keyboard layout which is probably not the most efficient setup.
The level design is incredibly well balanced, with each level being just long enough that it can be completed in around a minute, which is rather handy, considering how often you are likely to die before you manage to master the techniques required to pass each challenge. This in turn means that you can be back to where you were in anywhere between a matter of seconds to just a minute or two.
The difficulty increases fairly across each level, adding a new element of danger to the ones found in preceding levels. The only real issue I have with level design is the large, red and black balls that you have to destroy in order to progress through the level. It’s not eliminating them that is the issue, but the sensitivity of them; you must be almost directly in the middle to destroy them, so phasing into them at the edges will cause you to just pass through them without destroying them. There is also a point where you must clear a rather large chasm by jumping into one and using it as a booster for your jump. However this technique is not explained at all in-game, and so can be a little confusing to pass until you figure it out for yourself.
The graphics are simple and effective, although I personally believe a little more work could be done to the main character, as well as differentiating between the large black and red balls that you need to destroy in order to progress through most levels, and the smaller, but identical balls that will kill you on contact. However it is the nostalgia inducing 16-bit music that really sells this game for me, with each level having its own distinctive style that fits beautifully within the game.
For only $1.49, this game is worth every cent, and provides a solid and challenging platforming experience.

A rough gem. I wont lie, like the paradox games, it needs time to grow on you. But.. If you stick with it, you will be rewarded with an immersive engrossing tactical warband sim.
The game is basically you managing a warband by recruiting members, equipping them, choosing their skills on levelup, sacking ones you no longer like or need and then controlling them in tactical turn based combat in instanced maps of the ruined city of mordheim with the goal of acquiring warpstone and defeating the opposing warband.
A few things to bear in mind:
There is no quicksave, no save scumming and no reloading before it went wrong. Not a lot of visual customisation, the camera view can be annoying at times and it can feel a bit rough around the edges but read on.
Now what you have to realise is that this game is designed around the ups and downs of failure and success. Missions you choose to take are done to find warpstone in various quantities which you can sell for money to help improve your warband/increase faction reps or save to fill your quota to your overlord. You have a period of time to do this. you could fail 3 missions in a row and get no warpstone but get a lot in the next to make up. The failure of the mission is not nearly as bad as the potential injuries to your members.  Success or failure is just part of the journey.
If one of your characters is killed/ko During the battle, there is the possibility they will be injured/recover with no problem/take on permanent effects for example: one of my skaven was put down in his first fight, after the battle he had to have his arm removed. Time for a reload you would think... Well, it was a good and bad thing it enabled him to become more adept at dodging but he could no longer wield two handed weapons so it was not necessarily the end of his career in my warband. At worst he could gather warpstone for the group until he was replaced, and so it goes.
Now when you initially start this you really could do with taking the time to browse the ingame tutorials or some online guides before diving right in and hitting a wall of frustration. Think paradox games, you know a gem is waiting once you spend some time digging it out of the dirt.
If you are prepared to take your time with it you will be rewarded. There are a handful of different factions and campaigns to play thro. A couple available by dlc. It seems to be designed around the idea of playing your warband until they eventually fail so that you can restart with another. This is made easier by the veteran system which is an ongoing group of benefits/buffs that carry over each time you start a new warband. So dont fret if you have to restart, your experience will make it a bit easier and your veteran status earned will make it a bit more interesting.
Good luck. You will need it.

Mordheim is an unforgiving turn based strategy game with RPG elements set in the fantasy Warhammer universe. You build a motley crew from one of 4 factions; mercenaries, bible bashers, methheads or rats, and fight rival gangs over territory and money.
Your gang members gain experience, level up and can be customised with equipment and skills, however they can also be injured permanentley, or die even, if they fall in battle. As your gang earns victories, you are able to recruit more warriors, and even field an "impressive" warrior, which are your ugliest and strongest units.
The game is RNG based, so everything is determined by a dice roll, with chances of success dependant on each warrior's stats. As such luck swings it's erection around both ways, resulting in either earthly pleasure or a throbbing♥♥♥♥♥♥ That being said, good strategy and planning will win out regardless of dodgy dice rolls.
There are a few flaws to the game however; the UI is an eye sore until you learn how to hide it, there is a bit of a learning curve as you learn to play and learn to equip/utilise your warriors correctly, and RNG can screw you over so badly you want to cry/punch your monitor in frustration.
If you want a pleasant, easy going game, give this a miss. If you like a challenge, strategy games and the satisfaction gained from crushing your opponents, pick Mordheim up.
Edit: play with a controller if you have one!

Back in the days before DIablo and The Elder Scrolls ruled the land, Japanese RPGs  were king. Run throughout the land, gaining levels and equipment until you meet the biggest, baddest, eviliest cliche' in the game and kill him. No stat and skill trees to master, no pointless customization, just you on a quest to vanqish an evil that's almost always different than the one you originally set out to defeat. Just you and your countless hours spent grinding away.
This game is all that, except each nefarious fiend must be killed in less than 30 seconds. While this sounds impossible and at least somewhat silly, the way the game presents itself makes it one of the best JRPGs I've ever played.
The game is basically seperated into over 100 mini RPGS with a small overworld in each where you run around and defeat monsters to gain enough power to defeat the resident Evil Lord before it casts its world destroying super evil spell of evil, in 30 seconds.
Since it is basically impossible to even get to the baddie in half a minute, the benevolent Time Goddess will reset time for you at any point, for a fee of course, giving you another 30 seconds to level up, make it to the boss, and kill him. Along the way you gather new equipment that you can keep across stages, although your level resets after every boss,
This all may sound overly simplistic, but there is a lot more under the hood than it seems at first glance. Beat the game and you unlock new modes to play. Complete challenges and sidequests in each stage. Multiplayer, anyone? There is a lot of content for a game that expects you to save the world in 30 seconds!
If you liked the old-school JRPGs like Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior, this game will make you smile so wide it will connect in the back and your head will fall off. If you just need a quick game to play on break or whenever you have a few minutes to kill, this is better than most.

I'll admit I don't consider myself to be much of a competitive person, but there's just something about this game that grabs hold and refuses to let go after an adrenaline filled run. Push harder, get faster, rank higher.

Crates. Since the dawn of the digital age, man has struggled with crates. Inexplicably, video games contain about a hundred times more crates than exist in the known universe, some to be pushed, some to be broken, and some to arbitrarily block your progress. Rochard is, first and foremost, a game of crates. There's shooting, there's some cute writing, but there's mainly a lot of crates.
If you're like me and have been wondering what the hell kind of name "Rochard" is, it's the name of the pot-bellied protagonist, John Rochard. A blue-collar asteroid miner down on his luck, you control the surprisingly spry fellow on a day when everything goes to hell. Your main tool in this adventure is the G-Lifter, a gravity gun knockoff that can lift crates, drop crates, launch crates, and do some other stuff like double as an assault rifle and grenade launcher. You'll also get control over gravity for much of the game, and the interplay between your crate gun and gravity manipulation is the basis of most of the puzzles.
Generally your challenge is getting from point A to point B by stacking crates, swapping fuses, and finding ways around force fields and chasms. The force fields are actually a nice touch, with some blocking organic matter, some inorganic, and some energy like weapon fire. They're color-coded to function, and my favorite puzzles are figuring out how to get yourself and the items you need through networks of force fields. Still, I have to stress that a lot of your puzzling will depend on crates, so if the stacks and see-saws in Half-Life 2 burned you out, you might not last long with Rochard.
The other major part of the game is combat. Rochard is way more combat-heavy than I expected, with most puzzles needing to be cleared of enemies and turrets before working out the solution. Your G-Lifter can switch to pew pew mode with the touch of a button, and crates make very deadly weapons here, so combat is at least integrated pretty seamlessly and offers plenty of entertaining options. You'll get weapon and life upgrades as you progress, and there are collectibles to find if you need a little extra puzzling, but most of the game is very linear and offers the same challenges in mounting degrees.
Look, do you like crates? That's really all this boils down to. Rochard looks, sounds, and plays really well for a platformer, but everything revolves around crates and what you can accomplish with them, and at this point in our lives I'm not entirely convinced we really need much more of that. It's a solid game that'll last you 3-4 hours (plus some additional challenges) so as long as you know what you're in for, it'll fill your crate quota.

The year is 2017 and a lot of games came out that have improved on the formula set by Resident Evil 4. But does the King hold up today? It's safe to say it does; it holds up extremely well. Granted, its successors improved on the speed, controls, and horror but in terms of a perfect balance of horror and action, Resident Evil 4 still holds the crown.
The protagonist, Leon Scott Kennedy, is a US government special agent sent by the POTUS to find his kidnapped daughter, Ashley, from the clutches of a cult called the Los Illuminados who are situated in a remote area of Spain. He is escorted by two local officers but is soon separated and forced to conduct his investigation alone when the villagers attack. Later, he finds out that the villagers are infected with a parasite called the Las Plagas which grants them speed and power and frightening mutations. Leon's goal is secure the President's daughter and successfully exfiltrate, but he is met with overwhelming odds stacked against him.
The story of Resident Evil 4 is serviceable and does its job. After your initial playthrough of the game, you unlock Separate Ways, another campaign featuring a different character, which has its own story that fills in the gaps of the main campaign. The personalities of the characters come through the well directed and well voiced cutscenes.
Resident Evil 4 is a third person action adventure game that moves into an over-the-shoulder perspective when aiming. You will shoot, knife, grenade and even perform context specific actions like kicking and suplexing through mobs of enemies. The infected villagers (aka, the Ganados) put up quite a fight and they'll come at you with everything from simple tools like pickaxes and knives to instant killing chainsaws. They'll flank you when they can, weave in and out of your targeting reticule. Leon can literally break heads with a well placed shot or suplex but that may not always result in a death for your foe as they can have their Plaga come out of their head. Factor in 3 different types of Plaga, and you can see Leon definitely has a lot on his plate to deal with.
You'll also face monstrous foes like the acid spewing, bug-like Novistadors or the horrifying creature called the Regenerator who, as its name implies, regenerates the damage you deal to it. You'll find Ashley early in the game and you have to protect her while she is with you. Enemies will either bee-line straight to her or carry her away (both leading to a Game Over screen if they manage to do so). You can give her rudimentary commands like Wait and Follow, and even have her hide. She even has her own playable section later on in the game.
Where Resident Evil 4 truly shines is through its brilliant boss battles. These encounters will test your mettle to the fullest. While challenging, the game is fair and perhaps, most importantly, fun. Leon is only able to take a few hits before he keels over so the game has to be fun for the player to keep returning to it.
Through the help of a Merchant, you get to buy weapons, items and even upgrade your arsenal through through the money and treasures you find in the game. You start off with a handgun, but as you progress, you'll be able to buy shotguns, magnums, sniper rifles and so on. You are, however, unable to buy ammo (which is kinda funny because you can see the Merchant with ammunition all around, but I suppose this is deliberately done so that the game doesn't become cakewalk because players happened to buy a crap ton of magnum ammunition). You'll also have access to a fun diversion in the form of a shooting gallery where you can unlock collectable Bottle Caps of characters in the game. The game has QTEs, both in-game and in cutscenes, so you have to pay attention.
The game has numerous set piece moments like riding a boat to harpoon a monstrous lake beast, and a mine cart sequence where enemies drop in from above, so the game does a lot to keep your surging on adrenaline. After you are done with the main campaign, you'll unlock Professional Mode (aka Hard Mode), and a bunch of extras - Assignment Ada (a short campaign where you have to find 5 Plaga samples), Separate Ways (a full fledged campaign that fills in a certain character's role in the main campaign), a movie browser, new costumes for the main campaign, and the excellent Mercenaries (a very fun time attack mode where you play across different maps using different characters and score points by killing enemies).
Resident Evil 4 is purely a single player game. There is no multiplayer or co-op of any kind in the game.
The game sounds great and the soundtrack is well done with some memorable tracks like the 'Save Theme' and 'Serenity' (the song you hear when you are with the Merchant). The enemies sound terrific and send a chill down your spine (the labored breathing of the Regenerators come to mind). Sound effects are excellent and everything sounds very convincing. Do yourself a favour and play this game with the headphones on.
Resident Evil 4 boasted some of the best visuals back in 2005 on the Gamecube and the PlayStation 2. The PC port supports higher resoultions, 60 FPS, extra filters, and HD textures. If you want the game to look even better the vanilla release, download the RE4HD mod; it is still a WIP (work in progress) but makes the game look insanely good (google RE4HD and see the results for yourself). If you have the rig to handle it, you should download the mod.
The artstyle of the game does a great job and the game still looks decent to this day. The game does have film grain but it's not overblown like in Resident Evil 5.
The PC version of RE 4 is not perfect - I encountered crashes in the Garden Maze section in Leon's campaign which I managed to overcome by quickly making it through the maze, but the crashes for the same area in Separate Ways required me to stop the TabletInputService in the Services tab of the Task Manager and modifiying the game's config.ini to have the game run at 15 FPS. This is the only way I got the game to stop crashing in the Garden Maze section in Chapter 3 of Separate Ways. If you encounter crashes in any other areas, try following the above steps and see if it helps you.
The game also doesn't run well on low end rigs. My potato of a laptop had no problems playing Resident Evil 5 at 720p and 30 FPS with a mixture of medium and high settings but this game runs worse than a game that came out in 2009. I was forced to lower the resolution to 800x600, turn off AA and motion blur, have shadows on Low, and play using the default textures to get the game running well at 30 FPS.
Resident Evil 4 is more than the sum of its parts. The game stands the test of time despite it being  12 years since release. It's evident that the game was a labour of love back in the days when Capcom was great and not Crap-com. RE 4 is easily one of the best games of all time.

I think Mordheim is an overall good game but it suffers from a plethora of issues. Here is my small list:
1. The AI cheats in more ways than one. This is probably to make up for poorly programmed AI.
*  If any enemy warriors spot even ONE of yours, they all know exactly where ALL your warriors are for the rest of the mission.
*  They always receive a wounds (essentially HP) and damage bonus, even at normal difficulty.
*  They can bypass your ambush stances by charging even when movement range is equal. Not humanly possible.
*  They LOVE to target your lower rank guys first, so good luck keeping them out of harm's way.
2. Progression is mirrored with enemy warbands. This is both good and bad because it makes every fight more of a challenge but at the same time
. To clarify, if you equip one of your guys with a nice weapon, the enemy warband also gets one. Same with training skills for your guys, the enemy will also get skills.
3. The graphics are pretty bad. More specifically, textures are really low resolution. There is very little facial animation, save for mouths opening now and then. This is not very important for me but they overall look pretty dated. Screenshots are misleading.
4. Aside from just going into missions, there isn't much else. You have your generic missions and then there's story missions. That's the entire game. The multiplayer scene is largely dead.
5. No mods. No Steam workshop. Sayonara, longevity!
6. The balance kinda sucks. Obviously subjective but Skaven for example have a massive advantage because of their increased movement and thus can perform important optional objectives much easier and rally to engaged allies. The Undead are also kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with their terror-toting vampires (extremely powerful early on) and inconsequential (but undoubtedly durable) zombies. The rest I think are fair.
7. The units feel "dead". With this I mean that they never talk, ever. They only do grunts when attacking, taking damage then there's a war cry upon victory and a death cry when dying. I really wish they'd say something. In other words, there is absolutely minimal voice acting.
That's all the bad things I can think of. I still come back to it, despite being shafted by real ♥♥♥♥head mechanics and cheating AI. In the end, I think it's worth a buy on sale. Keep in mind that it's abandoned for the moment, no more updates. No more DLC. The devs are working on a game called Necromunda.
If you want to read about the positive things about this game, look elsewhere. There's plenty of chumps that've that front covered.

You fight enemies for gold and xp/levels, buy stuff in towns, talk to people and do sidequests all in this short time limit, but you can turn back the clock by paying the time goddess increasingly large sums of gold. I don't typically hold free otome games in high regard because my experiences with the mobile app versions tend to be piddling amounts of story followed by relentless microtransactions, or a hurried first offering for a new developer focused more on presence than quality or even quantity of content. Cinderella Phenomenon is a game that I gladly would have paid for, and gladly would have supported on KS if I'd known it was running at the time. Almost every aspect of the game is so carefully crafted, and with the length and variety of content for all ten routes, plus the teaser/epilogue, it can easily hold its own in the myriad of VNs presently on the market. The characters are well fleshed out, the background music delightful, the background art a painterly treat, and the attention to lore just the plum in the pudding. I blazed through five routes a session until I'd gotten every CG and enjoyed every word on screen, and I only wish there was more, potentially some twisted romances with Varg or the elder Mythros, or attention from a lady or two, simply so I could spend more time getting to know more characters and watch the icy princess defrost at the hands of another's guidance still. Good show for a first game, and I can't wait to throw money at them for their future endeavors!

Nobody expected a free indie game made by three girls from London to be that good! It truly exceeds expectations. I'd like to give my two cents to support CP so I repost my tumblr review here.
PROs:
- The game is plot-driven (oh god, finally!). Developers have emphasized the fact that they boosted a lot of energy and resources into the plot. It’s captivating and action-packed.
- MC. One of the best (if not the best) otome heroines I’ve seen. She enthralled me from the first lines (I’m not exaggerating here). At the beginning of the game we see Lucette as a selfish, cold and arrogant person. She's alone and unhappy. Then she gradually experiences a great character growth. Truly refreshing for an otome game. I also like the balance of Lucette’s character. She's independent, but she doesn’t become an overly badass fighter. She's strong, but she stays feminine (unlike some western otome heroines whose gender becomes blurry).
- Various characters. Creators clearly took a step aside from usual otome cliches. Significant part of the story is based on the idea about fairy tale curses. Every main character has his own curse loosely based on a famous fairy tale. The curses are not revealed at the beginning and they are not plainly obvious since original fairy tales have been reworked. In some cases, these curses becomes a real engine of character’s growth.
-Side characters are very detailed, every one has a backstory.
-Beautiful sprites (I liked CGs less), great facial expressions. Beautiful backgrounds and interface.
-The story itself is well-written. I’ve mentioned the plot already, but the game is also packed with touching and even thought-provoking moments. A really 3-dimensional family conflict included.
- Music is remarkable. Truly, the soundtrack is rarely notable in otome games.
- Every route has two endings. It’s pretty easy to make the preferable choice due to the “right choice indicator” that appears shortly after the choice is made. You won’t need any walkthrough.
CONs:
- I can find faults of anatomical sort in the CGs, but overall the game is so great that it’s easy to ignore. I believe that the team who has already achieved this amazing result will progress further, including the quality of drawing.
- Some reviewers note that the game doesn’t provide enough interaction and you just follow the plot, for example, you can’t make Lucette completely evil, like in some RPG. I disagree with this point. There are many games now that provide a semblance of choice (not only VNs). And every time you end up following the plot. The best ones (like Telltale games) provide you with different ways to reach the final point, the very best games (like Witcher 3) create several endings, but it’s not about the freedom of choice at all. When I start to play a VN I expect an interesting story so I don’t mind that I won’t be able to make Lucette an evil queen.

I was looking for a free online multiplayer game back in May 2010 when I found DDO.  I found out that it coincidentally had just gone free-to-play three months prior.  I quickly met some cool people to play with who were patient enough with me to let me learn how to play.  (I started out with a pre-planned Cleric of the Healing Font, and I actually let the game choose my level awards for me all the way up to Level 20.)  I already knew what I wanted to do in the game, but I needed help learning how to do it.  7.5 years later, I'm still going strong with it (at least 10 hours each week, mostly on the weekends) and playing with people I met back in 2010.  (I didn't start playing DDO on Steam until about two years ago, which is why it says I only have 1,000+ hours on here.)  So I definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes developing their own character and playing with online friends, even if you have no experience with Dungeons & Dragons, like me.
Some recommendations for new players who are willing to give DDO a try:
1)  Don't spend any money for a while.  Once you've played two characters each all the way up to L20, you can then start imaging what is worth your hard-earned coin.
2)  Standing Stone Games (the game's developer) runs sales every week.  When you are ready to start spending money, try and coincide that with the sales.  It's better that way in the long-run.  Try to moderate your impulses.
3)  Join a guild, whether it is to build-up a low-level one or benefit from a high-level one.  This is a multiplayer game, so make it about socializing and coordinating with other people.  Solo-players in multiplayer games are lame.
4)  Multi-classing in DDO is basically only going to help you build a melee character, with very few exceptions.  If you want to build something other than a front-line character, then avoid multi-classing.  The rewards for taking a single class to the top are much better than simply exploiting a few melee stats.
5)  Always quest and guild with like-minded people.  You will find them.  Stay away from the Community Forums, as they offer very little relevant or helpful information, as most of the posters there do no represent the DDO community at-large.  The forums are basically there for a few dweebs to tout themselves; but you wouldn't want to play with those people in the game.
6)  The expansion packs should only be bought when they are on sale.  You can actually get most of their content by using the in-game currency rather than real money, though usually it is much faster to spend real money to get in-game currency.  Again, wait for 'Double Bonus Point' sales and such.

Imagine all the annoyance and absurdity of XCOM's RNG combat and crank that up to 200...that is Mordheim. You will NOT make it far on your 1st playthrough nor your 50th because no matter how well you plan every mission, how carefully you position your troops, or how much money you throw at your warband, this game only wants 1 thing: To see you suffer. You can build up a unit and throw hundreds of coins at training their skills as well as equipping them with the best purple-quality enchanted gear but in the end they will just fumble all their 90% to-hit rolls and 50% to-dodge rolls and die to some poorly-equipped zombie who will then steal their stuff from their corpse and run away and THEN even if you win that mission by rout the zombie STILL HAS YOUR STUFF BECAUSE SCREW YOU!
You will find yourself deleting your warband constantly because it is impossible to recover from even minor defeats when your ranged unit lose an eye, your fast units lose a leg, and your heavy units lose an arm because once again SCREW YOU! You do not recieve enough crowns (the currency) from any 1 mission to consistently hire new replacement soldiers as well as buying new gear for them. Not even to mention that gathering Wyrdstone (aka Warpstone, aka the other currency, aka the whole point of the game) during missions is horribly detrimental and will weaken you so the A.I. has an easier time stomping you, while you also cant keep gathering after you win so even if you are lucky enough to survive the fight and beat the enemy you will get less reward meaning you cant afford to pay your troops meaning they wont fight for you because once again SCREW YOU!
Presentation-wise it is actually rather cool, perfectly befitting of the source material in every way from the gloomy atmosphere to the brutality of the combat. Even more-so a shame that the 2 most powerful factions are locked behind DLC (Witch Hunters which are better versions of Sisters and Mercs, and Undead which dont care about petty things like "morale" or "poison" or "putting a staff on a necromancer instead of bow because LOGIC!").
I cannot try hard enough to tell you to walk away now before you get sucked into agony because unlike other RNG-based games such as XCOM this game NEVER GETS EASIER! The stronger you get the more stacked against you the odds become. There are no difficulty options, A.I. intelligence modifiers, or shortcuts you can take. The closest is the Veteran system which carries over points every playthrough but be warned: If you use that system to start a new warband at level 5 you get level 1 troops in a level 5 warband...which means you get to fight against level 5 troops in level 5 warbands with all blue gear and tons of trained skills...because once again...SCREW YOU!

is a turn-based roleplaying/strategy game based on the skirmish-sized supplement to the tabletop wargame
. It is set in the ruined city of Mordheim, which was devastated by a comet impact and has now become the battleground for four (later five and then six) factions all seeking to collect wyrdstone, highly valuable shards of the shattered comet.
There have been plenty of games based on the Warhammer IP, but Mordheim stands out because it brings the tabletop experience onto PC and console. Players take control of warbands, completely customiseable teams from each faction, and lead them on wyrdstone gathering missions with the aim of accruing enough to meet regular shipment requests from the faction's leader. Of course, on every mission you are opposed by an enemy warband, and any of your warriors who are put Out of Action run the risk of receiving an injury or even dying in the post-match rundown. Those who survive receive experience points which can be spent improving their stats, and levelling up grants points that can be spent training special abilities. This makes for a very narrative experience, where your favourite hero could lose an arm in any battle and weak henchmen can rise to become powerful warriors.
Where the tabletop experience comes in most strongly is in Mordheim's combat mechanic, which calculates damage and chance to hit for every attack as well as warriors' chances of Parrying or Dodging. Plenty of people hate on RNG but in this case it is just like rolling the dice on the tabletop: sometimes you'll roll 6s, sometimes 1s. The mechanic does not leave everything up to fate either; the better your warriors' Agility, Weapon Skill and Ballistic Skill, the higher chance they have of Dodging, Parrying or hitting with a ranged weapon. However, what is often more important is their Initiative value, for this decides the order in which you and your opponent get to use your warriors within a turn. During missions the Initiative wheel scrolls along the top of the screen, showing the order in which warriors will get to move and attack. Getting your guys in first can be the tipping point between victory and defeat, as on their turn outnumbered warriors most perform an All Alone check which decides whether they will stand their ground and fight back, stay put but be too demoralised to fight or flee in terror after each of their assailants gets a free swing. Once enough of a warband's warriors are put Out of Action, their Morale will drop below a predetermined point and they will be forced to take a Rout check, which if failed means defeat. Passing a Rout check can keep a warband in the game long enough to force the enemy to Rout, but Rout checks are retaken each time Morale drops again, until the warband does Rout or no longer has enough units in action to win.
For the most part Mordheim's mechanics are solid, but for those without human friends willing to play against them versing the AI can be a frustrating experience. AI warbands are not sophisticated enough to pursue the secondary objectives which can turn a narrow win into a crushing victory, nor are they particularly concerned with gathering wyrdstone. For the human player, this means you must fend of the mindless full-frontal assaults which are the only kind of attack AI warbands can stage, while also trying to gather wyrdstone, take out specific enemies or, hardest of all, steal the Idol from the enemy cart and carry it back to your own. Worse, there are a few issues with the AI pathing, and in almost every game on of them will get stuck on a wall or at a Jump Down point, or they will path into another unit and trigger a 'bounce-back' that ends their turn. This can be great if you're happy to exploit it, but detracts from the smoothness of an already somewhat clunky game. Things get somewhat better on the higher difficulties, where the AI will begin to ignore obvious targets in favour of ganging up on your weaker warriors and set up more effective ambushes, but the problem never goes away completely.
One of the most satisfying elements of Mordheim is warband progression, where levelling up your warband as a whole (as opposed to individual units within it) unlocks access to new hero types and allows you to field larger forces. A beginner warband consists of 1 Leader, 1 Hero and 3 Henchmen, but by level five you will be able to field 1 Leader, 4 Heroes and 5 Henchmen, or swap out two of your Heroes for a single Impressive, the most powerful units in any faction. The main flaw with this system is that it peaks too early; going up through the first five levels is exciting as you unlock new units and increase your warband size quite quickly, but after that level ups becoming progressively harder for paltry rewards. Thankfully individual unit leveling does not have this problem, and reaching Level 10 with a particular warrior is always worth it.
To its credit, Mordheim is a fairly well-balanced game. None of the factions feel overly tough, and each has their strengths and weaknesses. Human Mercenaries are excellent for beginngers as they have a flexible play-style with the most units able to wield melee or ranged weapons of any faction. Sisters of Sigmar have almost zero ranged capacity, but are the toughest melee fighters off the bat and have the best access to magic. Cult of the Possessed are well-balanced between ranged and melee units and become devastatingly good at melee on high levels, but all of their Heroes and their Impressive are subject to a random mutation system which gifts them with mutations at Levels 1, 4 and 7. This can be excellent if your Possessed ends up with an array of eviscerating bone-blades instead of arms, but can really suck if your best ranged hero suddenly develops a mace instead of a hand and can no longer shoot. The blessings of Chaos are fickle indeed.
Skaven are my faction of choice, though they are not the easiest to play as you mast take careful advantage of their high Initiative and speed to compensate for their low Strength and Leadership. Witch Hunters were the first DLC faction added, and are basically just a remix of Human Mercenaries with a heavy metal aesthetic and less ranged options. Undead, the second DLC faction, have a significant psychological edge as most of their units are immune to All Alone, Fear and Terror while a higher percentage of them
it than in any other faction. Vampires are particularly fun to play as, but zombies absolutely suck.
The cruel and unyielding laws of probability that govern Mordheim reward those who survive to veterancy by making them statistically more likely to survive than newer warriors with inferior stats and abilities, and if you play a particular warband long enough you will most likely develop a core of elite veterans who keep pulling through while the new guys you hire to make up the numbers bite the dust. This can be a big problem if one of your powerful veterans does die, as it is very difficult to train replacements up quickly. On the whole Mordheim rewards conservative play, though the fact that you have to pay each of your warriors after every mission means that it is sometimes not enough to just win, you must win
. Gold can be found in Loot Points around each map, but a better way to make money is by looting your fallen enemies and selling any weapons they were carrying that you don't want for yourself. Calculated risks are the name of the game in Mordheim, and if you miss four wyrdtsone shipments in a row, your warband is done.
Overall, Mordheim is an excellent game that I have thoroughly enjoyed playing. I don't have room here to go over the single-player campaign aspect, so keep an eye out for some walkthroughs coming up in the next few months. Enjoy!

The game still looks good inspite of it's age, something that really helps it in this regard is how in the eraly game units will look different depending on what part of the world they come from, the faces of the various world leaders are expressive and really nice to look at.
The combat in the game starts off pretty simple as mostly just rock paper scissors until the ages move on and new tech is made on these fronts, becoming more complicated with artillery and aircraft being thrown in to the mix.
Building an empire is fun, as populations rise and cities and buildings are constructed the appearance of said cites change  in size with the various buildings being visable inside them.
Researching technology is a neat experiance; every time you have completed on you will be given a lovingly narrated qoute and a short description of what you accomplished, and after certain techs are resaerched you will enter a new era that will be accompanied by a change in the ambience music will change along with the asthetics of your cites to signify the age your people live in.
Espionoge mixes things up quite a bit, it gives you opportunites to see what your friends and rivals are resaerching and with enough intelligence you can do everything from poisoning the water hole to learning every single last move the target of your spies is making.
Wonders are great buildings and monuments that offer special bonuses such as The Great Wall, which will prevent barbarians from entering certain parts of your borders, The Oracle, wich will give you a free tch of your choosing, and The Taj Mahal, which gives you a golden age- a event that lasts a number of turns which will give boosts to virtually everything.
Another thing that can occur is the creation of Great People: Great Builders, Great Prophets, Great Merhcants, Great Generals, Great Artists, Great Scientists, and Great Spies. These guys can give you a variety of different boons from starting a corperation, expanding your borders, giving more experience to some of your units, and giving you a free tech.
You can manage you system og government from it's humble beginnings of tribal barbarism to slavery, police states, free speech, state property, theocracy, etc. These can vary in terms of expense but can also effect what kind of special events that can occur along with how other nations view your country.
Diplomacy is another thing that is simple at first but becomes far more complicated over time, between wars, religion, charity, various events, actions made by your friends, and many, many, other factors can change how the leaders of the world view you- or even how your own people see you.
I think above all others however in importance is the world maps, randomly generated that still manage to retain a sense of organization and beauty that are never the same, your experience will be different every time you play.
There are many other details that I think should be learned from playing or have been described by others, but it is mostly for the reasons I have described above that I have nominated this game for the Test of Time Award.

Well I decided to take my time and write a review as there are no english reviews at the time I'm writing this.I have played the game for a fair bit and I kind of can tell how good the game is,what it does wrong and how the overall experience would be for new players.I have also restarted playing about 2 weeks prior to the steam release announcement so I can tell you how it feels like to start from 0(Most people give a lot of good stuff from their mains to their new characters,but I didn't do that so I can objectively say how it's like to play without anything to help you out)
First of all I'd like to say how the game is not pay to win,despite the fact that a lot of people have that ingrained in their minds.For instance when I poured most of my hours in was when I was a child who didn't know how to make money in the game,so in turn I had really bad equipment but I still could do everything by myself(besides raids obviously).That character is lvl 74,so if the game would actually be pay to win It would have been hell for me to do anything by that time.Honestly money in this game is not hard to make at all.There are 3-4 main ways of making money but I won't go in depth now as this is a review not a guide.Besides these 4 ways,you can make a ton of money by spamming event raids which mainly are easy to play and people let anyone in.The one exception to this is the easter raid.People there only want you to play with certain specialists and are really a bunch of ♥♥♥♥tards towards newer players.Aside from that the community is really nice.When I asked for help with something people always helped me.
Now that I mentioned it,you are probably wondering what a specialist is right?Well they act like some sort of subclasses that you can always change.You get a quest at certain levels(you get the first 4 out of the 8 specialist cards by doing missions given to you from a stone.The other 4 are received from certain raid boxes).That stone is a dark purple rhomb on the map.My advice would be to do them as soon as possible.You can get 5 specialist cards from these stones.In the order you find them do the first one at lvl 27,the next at lvl36,after that at lvl 46,followed by the lvl 55 stone and last but not least the lvl 65 one.The only reason to play this game is for the specialists in my honest opinion.Being able to play in so many ways on just 1 character is really great,and it really feels rewarding once you get the quest done and have a strong new class at your disposal at any given time.My advice would be to get special point chargers from the bazaar.You normally only have 10k points for using specialists daily,but for about 6000 gold you can add 10k more on top of that in a bar that starts draining as soon as the free 10k points are donzo.Buy 10 for 60k total and you will have enough for at least 2 weeks if you play 24/7.
As much as I really love the game,I have to say that until you start getting specialist cards the game feels really generic,and the monster designs are not all that interesting until later on.
The first time you make a character,you start as an adventurer.He pretty much is a character who is weak,feels boring to play and is just not fun in any way.You have 2 exp bars.One for your normal level,and one for job level.Job level is used to change from an adventurer to a swordsman,archer or mage once you have 20 job levels on the adventurer.By playing normally you'll get that done at around lvl 18-20.Job level is also a requirement for using specialist cards.You need X job levels to equip Y card.
Honestly,the first 20 or so levels are hell,but please try to play it for longer.You can get to level 25 in like 1 day.Quests award a ton of exp up until like lvl 55 so you level up fairly quickly compared to other MMO's.Once you start getting into the meat of the game it will be one hell of a trip.The story is not all that intriguing either.It's divided in 6 acts and the only act I actually feel is interesting is the third.
This game also has a huge amount of pets/partners.You can capture most monsters you fight,and you can also buy/unbox better pets so to speak.There are some pets which kind of give you useful bonuses but even though they are really good,they don't impact the gameplay up to the point is hard to do well without it.Partners are kind of sucky to be fair with you.People kind of only keep them around for the looks.Oh partners have specialist cards too,but sadly most of them are only obtained from the item shop or by buying them from someone.There are 6 in total you can get from raids.2 for each partner type.The mage,the equivalent of a swordsman and the ranged ones.
Specialist cards are kind of in a position where it's hard to buy them though,same about pets which have been taken out of their original bead.In order to trade these and big fairies you have to put them in a bead and a card carrier respectively.They can only be bought from the item shop and go for 5mil+ depending on the bead/carrier.I understand having a bead for pets/partners as they actually level up and stuff,but why do I have to put big fairies/specialist cards in a card carrier?That's just stupid and greedy if you ask me,so keep that in mind.
The playerbase,even though it dropped quite a bit is still pretty big.You won't find many people to play with at the lower levels as most people just made new characters so keep that in mind.It's going to be hard to play with someone if you don't have friends.
Well this is all I can come up with now.I might edit it if any new things come on top of my head so keep in mind that this is a WIP.If you have any questions/would like to know more then please leave a comment here or add me as a friend.I might also write a guide regarding what items not to sell and what to sell.You can make easy money by only selling certain things on the bazaar which is to Mimi's right(She is one of the more important npc's so there's no need for me to tell you where you can find her).Anyways best of luck and I hope to see you around!

I have played it on and off with my friends for years, while the biggest problem I have with NosTale is the power creep. All the major updates are fixed an focused on making the strongest and richest players even stronger and richer (since they are the only players who can complete in the new content for the first few months). The only way you can properly catch up in this lifetime is by spending a small fortune.
Introducing the game to steam might save the game, for sure there is an awesome community but it's been around since 2006 for the Korean audience it's also kinda dead as only high-level players roam the game. There are new servers to play on with the launch of steam, so everyone will get a new fresh start.
If you like playing by yourself  most of the time or are a casual gamer then it's absolutely an awesome mmo. While there are missions that open to groups as small as 4 players with as many as 15 being able to tackle some missions.
NosTale also offers pets which you can catch in the game world and use in battle (you can only have a single active pet at any time). By training these pets they will gain new skills and can prove to be a powerful ally in battle if used properly.
NosTale has good class diversity although it only offers 3 base classes which players must select upon reaching level 15. These base classes are the Swordsman, the Archer and the Sorcerer but upon obtaining further levels players can choose from a further 4 options per class for a total of 22 second tier class options.
Don't expect making a lot of gold or progressing as easily it's a time and money sink if you want to compete with high level players. As an old player of the game unfortunatly I can't recommned this game to new players.

Call of Duty is a 2003 first-person shooter video game developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision. It is the first of many installments in the Call of Duty franchise. The game simulates infantry and combined arms warfare of World War II using a modified version of the id Tech 3 engine built for Quake III: Team Arena. Much of its theme and gameplay is similar to the Medal of Honor series; however, Call of Duty showcases multiple viewpoints staged in the British, American, and Soviet theaters of World War II.
The game introduced a new take on AI-controlled allies who support the player during missions and react to situational changes during gameplay. This led to a greater emphasis on squad-based play as opposed to the "lone wolf" approach often portrayed in earlier first-person shooter games. Much of Infinity Ward's development team consisted of members who helped develop Medal of Honor: Allied Assault.
In September 2004, an expansion pack called Call of Duty: United Offensive, which was produced by Activision and developed by Gray Matter Interactive and Pi Studios, was released. On November 10, 2009, the "Hardened" and "Prestige" editions of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 debuted, including redemption codes for the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 versions under the title, Call of Duty Classic.

This is an absolutely incredible visual novel that I would gladly have paid money for.
The characters are so complex and they are all very likeable, making it impossible for me to pick a favourite or say which of the 5 boys' routes was the best! Each is afflicted by a different curse based on a classic fairytale, and you try to break their curse as they help you try to break your own curse, the Cinderella curse. You have gone from riches to rags in order to learn an important lesson, and the game doesn't just focus on your bachelor once you choose him - it has an amazing supporting cast as well who will make you feel every emotion, from anger to sorrow and everything in between.
While the story is the most important thing in visual novels, the graphics here are also of high standard, which really helps to immerse you in the story. The music isn't repetitive or distracting, and it changes throughout the story to suit the scenarios you are in, which just adds to the experience. Once you have seen a particular dialgoue, you can then fast forward through it, and even skip to the next unseen dialogue or choice, which is very useful for the replays as there are 10 chapters to each story and they are very long.
The replayability is fantastic - there are 5 pursuable male characters, each with a good and a bad ending. It took me 14 hours to read through everyone's story, but skipping the dialogue I had already seen during my second playthrough of that character. Everyone's story gives you more information about the world, and every bachelor has his own unique path due to them having different curses. Two of the characters' routes are locked to begin with, and I liked that because their routes wouldn't have made sense had I played them first, and it gives you something to aim for aside from the achievements.
This is an amazing game and I highly recommend it to any visual novel fan, but especially those who like a bit of fantasy and magic.

A lot of people divide games by pros/cons but that sometimes feels like looking for things to point out that are bad about a game. No game is perfect and I always feel that the number one thing a game should always be is fun, which this one is. However, since this is a review, I'll break it down by different components.
Gameplay: 2D puzzle-platformer that does not treat the gamer like an idiot. You need to actually think on how to solve a puzzle and there are a few different ways to solve each which can be combined with the combat in the game. The puzzle solving and combat can at times go hand and hand which adds a level of difficulty to the game which is all the more satisfying for completing it. The combat itself can be straight forward but that mostly depends on you as a gamer which makes the game feel all the more freeing because you can choose to simply shoot the enemy or figure out a complex way to kill them.
Voice Acting: The cast is small but that is not a terrible thing, Lani Minella who has voiced over 500 animated/video game characters plays Skyler while the main character John is voiced by Jon st. John who is famous for being the voice of Duke Nukem.
Design: The game design can feel almost reminiscent of classic platforming games from the earlier days of video games and that is not a bad thing, the character and level designs are bright and eye catching. John, the main character, isn't your average muscle bound hero, he's an over weight miner just trying to make a living so it's easier to put yourself in his shoes and sympathize with him.
Music: The music is great, though I have a bias since it was composed by Markus “Captain” Kaarlonen from one of my favorite bands, Poets of the Fall, who also composed/wrote music for the game Alan Wake. and had work featured in Max Payne 2.
I would recommend this game and the price isn't that high, considering there are far worse games on Steam asking far higher prices.

I don't really know how to make a case for this game, but I don't think it's bad.  You play a redneck asteroid miner with a physgun and solve puzzles in order to save your friends and uncover a native-american-alien-conspiracy whatever along the way.  The plot doesn't really go anywhere and the ending might as well have just said "Congratulations, you did the thing, the end."
However, the production values are extremely nice for an indie game.  The voice acting is great, the game opens with an awesome song by Poets of the Fall, and the graphics and art are visually pleasing.  However, I get the feeling that this is probably the reason why the developers have been MIA for about two years (as of late 2015).  The link to the game's official website is dead, as are the social media accounts associated with Recoil Games, and although they talked on Facebook about their desire for a sequel, they said that they didn't have the money to make one.  So you should probably not expect any sort of closure unless they suddenly make a kickstarter.
The game itself is an indie puzzle platformer (if those three words in sequence turned you off, this is easily the least pretentious indie game I've ever played) with a focus on gravity, so imagine a 2D version of Half-Life 2's physics puzzles with a button that lowers gravity.  It's pretty fun for what it is and it nicely kept my attention for five hours, so I'd say it's worth saving for a rainy day if you got it in a bundle like I did.

My first statement was "after only 4 hours I can already say that this game is better than the rally part in Dirt 4.", but now, after 18 hours, I have to update this. I am actually starting to think that it's even better than Dirt Rally! Quality of stages in WRC7 is pretty much on par with stages in Dirt Rally, except here you have much more locations to drive on, with an ability to play each location in "epic stage" (one very long stage, instead of more shorter stages).
Handling of the cars is very good. I don't think it's as good sim as Dirt Rally (while connected with the road), but that it's somewhere in between D:R and Dirt 2/3 handling models, where handling is more accessible, while still being very rewarding. The biggest drawaback is the weird FFB, so I switched to gamepad, where it plays a lot better.
Visuals are...mixed. During sunny days, dawns and sunsets, it looks VERY good. But when it comes to rainy, foggy, or night conditions, it looks very bland. Optimisation is great. I am running it with mostly stable 60 FPS, all settings maxed out on my GTX970. I only experience some framedrops to 40's during foggy conditions, but it happens very rarely, so it's not that big issue.
Sound... well, car sounds are OK. Engine sounds in particular are great, but after playing Dirt Rally/4, you will quickly notice that a lot of sounds are missing, or sounding kinda meh. Co-driver on other hand is just terrible. Listening to his robotic voice was giving me a headache for the first hour, but eventually I got used to him.
All things considered, it is a really good rally game with a few minor flaws. If you were disappointed with Dirt 4 and it's deja-vu track generator, you should give WRC7 a chance.

This game requires a good deal of dedication, yet it's very much worth it!
Now for the long rant if you want it
Regardless of what my playtime might seem to indicate... I've been playing DDO for years (shortly after they bumped up the max level to 20 ... somewhere over 7 years ago but not sure exactly, it gets fuzzy after a while).
I have been playing games since the Commodore, and to this day I find this to be my favorite game!
However it's not for everybody, some of the negatives worth mentioning:
* It's a very complex, detailed game and it takes a long time to get the hang of it; so if you're not familiar with Dungeons and Dragons you have a lot of reading ahead of you (which you can do on a need to know basis)
* This game is a cooperative game, and although it is possible to fight other players this is not really fully developed and there is very little demand for it. Simply put classes are not necessarily balanced for this, but all of them can be useful in a dungeon.
* The game is old and some people have a new graphics fetish ... The game looks good, but there is surely something out there that looks better
* Configuring your inputs is a chore... my settigs file is sacred :P
* It updates often and slowly ... so you gotta have it update while not playing
* Some quests take a long time, so this is not a 5 minutes in and out kinda thing but rather an evening long kinda thing
Now for some of the positives:
*  First off, if you ever wanted the creators of Dungeons and Dragons to narrate your adventures, there are two adventures packs where you get to listen to them - Honestly this game is historic
* Character development is extremely in dept, and it couldn't be anymore flexible. By that I mean, there are a tons of classes, with differents customization options, races, customizable and craftable gear, etc. And, if that's not enough developers are constantly monitoring the forums and although changes come slowly they take a lot of input from the users
* It accomodates a lot of different playstyles, a barbarian works similarly to link (legend of zelda), while a Artificer is more of a shotemup kinda thing (doom)
* Dungeons only have actual human players in your team that you know (save for hirelings), you don't get a public area with other people competing for rewards (unless you chose a bad party, but it's not public all inside a dungeon are a team and must to best of their abilities work like one)
* No click and forget... I like Diablo, but I need a lot more interaction. Here you control your player fully as in arrows in your keyboard or a joystick rather than click and forget about em; to me the playstyle straddles the line between a FPS and Platformer gameplay (not as fast and not twichy like a FPS and not as platform oriented, but you are always in control of your character)
* Quests are super varied, from puzzles to exploration, to hardcore gauntlets - oh and then there's traps ... loooots of em
* Dungeon master narration makes the quests very inmmersive without having to stop the action.
This game has a Dungeons and Dragons experience that has action at the forefront and actual dice rolling calculations hidden away (d20 in its core, some very intersting numerical analysis pops up in the forums every now and then, with plots and all that good stuff; if you want to look into it, it's all there; however if that makes your head spin you can never look into it and and still be a top performer)
There is a lot to explore, and a lot to do but you have to put a lot into it. Quests are long, and you don't have access to everything right of the bat (unless you have a heck of a wallet, but if you want that don't complain about spending money). Some people complain because the expansions are not free... Well they didn't exist years ago and the game was already huge, and its only gotten larger since.
So if you can relax and let it slowly charm you, show what it has to offer, and develop your character while you get immersed in its fantasy you should have a great time. See you at Eberron (or forgotten Realms, or ... anyway see you there)

Although the graphics aren't much to look at, this game shouldn't be passed up. It isn't "pay-to-win" because the only micro-transactions in the game are for either cosmetics, or to purchase access to certain special dungeons/instances/quest lines. You can technically level-cap without purchasing these, and if you feel that you want to purchase them, you can earn in-game currency to do so instead of spending real money. The game has incredible diversity, and has a role that caters to every possible player. The story-telling is wonderful, and just about every quest/dungeon is narrated to provide that classic table-top DND feel. If you're a fan of DND, or if you just like a good RPG, I urge you to try this game. The ONLY downside is that it can be incredibly difficult to complete some necessary dungeons/quests without a party (though, that's the point to DND) and the game can become boring without friends to liven it up. But it's still a great game!

Fire with Fire is a clever twist on a classic premise; You alternate between playing the attacking and defending forces in a tower defense game. The rules are simple and mechanics are easy to grasp. I'm almost worried they are too simple, because the game might be too easy to master. In order for the game to be competative, it needs to consistently provide challenges at every skill level. There's a good amount of interaction with the game, and it's fun to fine tune both your offense and defense depending on the enemies strategies. The game could use some more inirtia. As it stands, while using bad strategies, the game could go on forever. This could be fixed by slowly making the mobs stronger over time. As it stands, the games go on for too long. Additionally, if you're behind in the game, it is pretty difficult to catch up. If, while making the mobs stronger, the mobs also did more damage to the tree, then it would be easier for someone who is losing to make a come back.
All in all, really cool game and I'm excited to see how it evolves over time.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: The easiest way to imagine Half Minute Hero is that it is the Super Meat Boy of the RPG world. By that I mean that there are many small scenarios that you have to complete (the exact number is 30) within each mode. I'll be reviewing this game on a mode-by-mode basis, as there are four major modes: Hero 30, Evil 30, Princess 30, and Knight 30; each with their own variations, at least on classic mode. In fact, if you don't know to switch to Classic mode after you've beaten the game, you'll end up missing out on quite a bit of the game. This wasn't really mentioned anywhere - or at least that I remember - so do keep that in mind when you play through the game.
To start, we'll talk about the "vanilla mode," Hero 30. This mode consists of you traversing a given map and leveling up to the point where you can easily defeat the boss of the area. Of course, beating every single area in under 30 seconds would get tiresome after a while, so there is usually some new design concept per level. To compensate for longer levels, the game allows you to turn back time to the 30 second mark with a Goddess statue located at most villages. The fee for turning back time increases by 100 gold each iteration, and if you end up getting careless you could end up trapping yourself in a then-unwinnable situation. You kinda have to be trying to do that, though, so don't worry too much about that. Apart from that, it's pretty standard RPG fare: you can usually upgrade at least one of your equipment per map, you can carry one healing herb with you to heal should the need present itself, and battles are handled automatically with the main influence you have on the fight being that you can run in (running consumes HP, by the way) or turn back and run. Pretty straightforward stuff, but then again; depth isn't exactly necessary when your mission can be beaten in under a minute. It's also worth noting that unless you switch to Classic mode, the following three modes will be one mission long and play out roughly the same way as Hero 30.
Evil 30 is, as mentioned above, pretty boring on non-Classic mode, but on Classic mode it becomes a lot more interesting. This plays a little more like an RTS than an RPG with you being able to summon three classes of allies to fight three classes of enemies (as the Evil Lord himself put it, a game of Rochambeau). Your summons become stronger the more filled up your summon ring gets, so that prevents against spamming, and this ring decreases when you get hit. This ring can be easily filled back up by going to the Goddess barrel (it makes sense kinda), but unlike Hero 30, turning back time takes all your gold, so there is an extra element of strategy to it. This one's my second favorite mode of the bunch.
Princess 30 is my favorite of the bunch, as it plays like a SHMUP. The way that time is factored into this mode is that different terrain can slow down your squad, and the more you get hit, the slower you go. Turning back time is done by "flying" over red carpets, which take a certain amount of gold per tick to turn back time that amount (I don't know the rate, but I'd guess 10 Gold/0.4 seconds in four ticks per second). It is kinda easy to get ganked by some of the bigger enemies, but that never really caused me to outright lose the match, as I had plenty of gold to get time back. Definitely the best mode of the bunch.
Knight 30, however, is the worst mode of the bunch by quite a large margin. The whole mode is essentially an escort mission with the most erratic difficulty curve I've ever seen. It tries so much to be a sort-of tower defense thing, but either the strategies you can make with the items are useless or impractical, save for the Fence which is the only thing you should make ever. There's just a lot of stuff here that is either unnecessary to the game or outright frustrating to play. Unless you're a completionist, give this mode a pass.
All in all, though, I still had a lot of fun with the game. Sure, Knight 30 was awful, but at least it was only an hour or so of the total gameplay. I don't know how the hell Howlongtobeat has an average for this game of 18 hours, since I pretty much completed all the single-player stuff in a third of that time, but I still had a good time nonetheless. 8/10.
Story: There actually is an over-arching storyline between the modes, so that's good. It's pretty standard RPG fare, although I think that was mainly for more of a parody angle than a lack of creativity. Also, this game is great if you've got even a slight bit of a Japanese sense of humor. Plenty of laughs to be had in here, even if some of the gags were predictable. There isn't really much else to talk about here, other than the Evil Lord being the strongest pervert. 8/10.
Graphics: There's two graphical styles to this game: the "modern" tile sets and the classic tile sets. The modern looks (presumably) intentionally uninspired and kinda lazy, but that's to the game's benefit. Classic mode of course has pixel art, and the pixel art ain't bad, honestly. In fact, it's quite alright. Both are definitely good in their own ways. As for the technical side of things, of course anyone who can run at least Windows Vista shouldn't have any problem playing this game, since this is more or less a port of a PSP game, but the game handles fullscreen in a weird way. It does fullscreen to your native resolution, but it also upscales from 720p, meaning that you don't have true 1080p graphics or whatever your native resoluton happens to be. Because of this, I ended up playing windowed which worked fine, but I still would've liked proper 1080p. Also weirdly enough, the game prompts you to use a 360 controller at the start of the game, but all the commands on screen are listed as keyboard prompts. I'm sure DirectInput had a function to detect whether input was from a 360 controller or a keyboard back then, so excluding that seems really weird. Nevertheless, the two art styles this game presents are pretty good, but it is unfortunate some of the more quirky technical issues. 4/5.
Sound: Only music to talk about here, and man does this game have a good soundtrack. It covers quite a few genres as well, from orchestral to rock to industrial... yeah, and it's all quite good. Definitely a game worth grabbing the OST for. Apart from that, there really isn't much else to talk about other than Evil 30 classic had the best songs of the game. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 8/8/4/5; cumulative score of 8.3/10. Worth your time and definitely worth more than 30 seconds.

Are you a rat? Cause I am. Do you enjoy being a rat? Cause I do. Would you like to help guide your brethren through the hellhole that is escaping pest control? How about annoy the heckle out of those pesky humans and steal their stinky cheese? Cause I would.
Rat Simulator is a work of art. It takes such a simple concept of living your daily life as an ordinary house rat and expands your rat-world into a twisted reality based in dominating humans by infecting their houses and taking their food. It takes rat-kind back to the golden years- back when The Black Plague™ was a thing and we were feared! No! Not because we're rodents- but because we had power! And now we have that power again! We can infect their homes and spit our infectious saliva at the humans! Rat Simulator takes this idea and runs with it in the modern age in a way I wasn't expecting.
I thoroughly enjoy this game and would say it's worth the pickup if you are even a slight fan of simulators. Or rats.. However if you are a fan of rats Rat Simulator is a must have.
----------------------
The only gripes I have with the game are...
Pest control is very inconsistent when spotting/eliminating rat-kind and I feel it happens a little too fast, not enough time to hide after getting spotted by a worker unless you're near some where they can't reach
Turning is a little wonky in my ratpinion.
Tutorial not having a save when you get outside/to the dumpster the first time.
(I spent a good hour getting reset and trying to not get ratted by pest control)
----------------------
All in all those are just some small gripes and I have a feeling most of the complaints anyone has will get fixed or be looked at. But at the very least it is worth what you pay for it and I recommend 9.4/10.
