WRC 7 is a fantastic rally game!  This is easily the best rally game to come to us since Dirt Rally.  While not without flaws, WRC 7 is a most worthy rally title and definitely the best of the series by a long margin.
Pros:
+Physics and handling:  WRC 7's handling model is shockingly authentic and realistic, the performance of the cars reflects the WRC 2017 cars more faithfully than any title.  Side-by-side comparisons of gameplay with on-board footage makes for a hilariously similar show.
Force Feedback was not so great on release, but update 1.2 has improved this hugely.
+Stages:  The stages of WRC 7 are some of the best in the genre.  They're beautifully crafted, full of variety, challenge, and rhythm.  I have nothing to complain about here.  The Epic (Endurance) Stages bring us some of the longest rally stages ever seen in a rally game, and it is gold.  Every locale of the 2017 WRC is represented here!
+Career mode:  The style of career mode aims to reproduce the 2017 world rally championship season, and it does this well.  Complimented by a full set of stages for every location, it's a ton of fun to fulfil the fantasy of being a privateer climbing up to the top of the World Rally Championship all the way from a junior driver to hopping into one of the blisteringly fast 2017 WRC cars.
Neutral points:
*Graphics:  WRC 7's graphics are very adequate but nothing particularly groundbreaking.  I have experienced some struggle to maintain a full 60fps as well.   Again, not alot to complain about here, but nothing to get excited about either.
*Sound:  Similar to the graphics, the sound is adequate and nothing more.  It's a huge improvement over WRC 6, but it still can't compete with Dirt Rally.
Cons:
-Camera customization:  There really aren't many choices to adjust the camera to your liking.  There's no FOV control, and you can't adjust your sitting position in cockpit views.  As a result I just drive with the bonnet cam, which is fine, but It'd be nice to feel like I can drive in cockpit view and still be able to see the stage well.
-Lack of setup saves:  You can't save custom setups in WRC 7 so if you have a custom setup for certain stages or conditions, you'll have to write them down elsewhere and re-customize to implement them.  The setups you can save are limited to gravel, tarmac, and ice/snow, so if you edit the gravel setup, that setup is used in all gravel rallies. It would have been great to be able to save and share setups.
Conclusion:  WRC 7 is absolutely worth a buy if you're a fan of Rallying.  The excitement this game provides can only be rivaled by Dirt Rally or Richard Burns Rally, and in some ways I think it can be even more exciting and authentic.  There are minor flaws, but I have a hunch that the developer will patch this soon as some of the problems have already been patched within a month of release.

This game is really improved above WRC 6 especially the graphics ... the initial settings found in the options are set to maximum however with tweeking the game is fantastic so do not get discouraged ... frame lag is due to maximum resolution in the graphics settings in the game ... around mid range resolution probably fixes frame lag on most computers with some relatively new video card ... for those who prefer the hood and bumper cameras not unlike myself the suspension & spring settings should be around zero to stabilize the bouncing of the cameras ... the brakes should be 100% ... with these settings the game plays really very good ... on easy i was able to place third on my first try ... there are 52 routes at this time ... the physics & handling are excellent with further options to tweek the car without it being some complicated car mechanic sim ... there are options for different time & weather conditions including night driving which is difficult ... all routes are available to drive in solo mode ... big major improvements without the eyestrain from grainy graphics in WRC 6 ... the roads appear quite clear with excellent effects such as wet roads & sunshine ... x box one controller plays great ... great game.

I'm amending this to be a postive review. The game has now been patched (2nd patch) and now runs correctly. I should have mentioned previously the issue was not so much the framerate as frametimes which caused skipping and stuttering.  Happily issue is now resolved and frametimes are consistantly 16-17ms.  I'm running the game in 4K@60hz vsync with SLI enabled and it's working perfectly.
I don't find WRC7 to be a huge leap over WRC6 but has certainly improved. It is markedly different to Dirt 4. Handling is looser and vehicle settings more limited but feels closer to expectations of what a rally car should feel like. I was a bit disappointed by Dirt 4's generated stages as they tended to be very generic and devoid of any signficant scenery. The designed stages in WRC7 imho are far better. Vistas, drops, hamlets and unique road features make driving the courses more visually interesting.
One significant problem for me is the in-car view on some stages. I think there is a problem with how the game handles HDR. On some tracks the in-car view is very dark, to the point you have difficulty seeing the road and affecting times. Go to the bonnet view and things are much brighter. For example on the Bakers Creek stage, at midday in clear conditions the view is very dark however, oddly, in what should be dimmer rainy conditions the view is much much brighter.

This game holds the dubious honour of being the first I've ever requested a steam refund for. Almost two hours of tutorials followed by a main campaign that reveals you've got to work to unlock the fun or even vaguely effective stuff.
Forget about customisation too. That's possibly the saddest part because you can see the plans for customisation that never really got carried through. Most of the warriors I checked had half their 'sliders' greyed out because only one option exists and even those you can adjust the appearance of look near-identical in the end. Forget about skins too because while every warrior has the button to open the list, only a couple in the game actually have them.
I got through two campaign missions after the lengthy tutorial. For the first I spent the first 5 rounds with half my 5-man warband running around picking up warpstone while the other half searched for the enemy. I then spent the next few rounds running my warpstone gatherers half way across the map to back up the two unlucky fellows who found the entire enemy warband. The mission ended after I killed two and the rest of the enemy fled, leaving me with a single casualty of my own.
The second mission was almost entirely the opposite. I kept my warband in a loose group and advanced toward the enemy cart, letting them gather the warpstone with the intent of looting it from them. Two turns in I got attacked by the skaven warband which cut down my two best warriors and engaged two others while my fifth man turned out incapable of shooting through a window at them and instead had to spend two turns climbing down, out and around the building (that he apparently couldn't open the door of and save himself a turn of movement) just in time for my warband to be routed.
Maybe I'm just awful at the game but I really don't see a way to play this game that's both effective and fun.
All in all it feels like a half-finished game that I've regretted buying even at a 75% discount.

The game itself is pretty good--unique playstyle compared to most MMOs, action based but you have limited mana/resources to manage between resting points inside dungeons, so you have to manage mana more carefully than in most games.  Most exp is awarded on completion of specific quest steps and at the end of the dungeon, rather than per kill, so there is almost no standing in one place grinding.
Dungeons have an enormous amount of lethal traps and puzzle mechanics.  Most content (at least up to level 20, haven't done much 21+) is soloable/duoable with an NPC hireling, except a couple dungeons that have puzzles that specifically require more, and even they can often be completed with smart use of the hireling and summoned creatures.
A lot of the subscription only/cash shop content can be unlocked ingame, though expansions still need to be purchased separately, and having a subscription in the first place will make getting those unlocks a lot easier.
Unfortunately, the company that owns it has a nasty habit of charging people for subscriptions long after they are cancelled, combined with the fact that they don't have a functional customer support phone number and may take a long time to respond to customer service tickets.
Edit - changed my review as they did eventually reply to my ticket and refund me (and I do like the game itself).  This still happens, but at least they're addressing it.

I definitely would recommend this game if you are into RPGs, retro style games, or speed runs. There's ton of playablity in this game and some replay value as some stages have two different ways to complete it or have missable objectives that you can find in a new replay of the stage. Speed and time management are key in this game. Level grinding takes a few seconds to a few minutes so you aren't going to be playing for hours to reach level 100.
After you beat the game there are tons of game modes that make the game different by giving you new challenges and gameplay styles different from the main hero. If you are an achievement hunter my advice to you would be to switch the game to classic graphics so you can unlock some of the achievements from the other game modes. When you change the graphics to classic to neo or vice versa the game style changes too. For example the Princess mode in neo graphic mode you rush enemies and try find certain items to save the King while in classic mode it's more of a shooter instead of rushing into foes and you have a time limit for reaching the objective to help villagers and saving the King. Either game mode you are bound to have fun and if you are fast enough you might make your way on the leaderboard. Good luck and save the future.

First off, this isn't a game that everyone is gonna enjoy, if you don't like gitting gud, or would just rather play a more casual game then "Absolver" Isn't the right option for you. There is also a chance that you will just not enjoy the game for any specific reason, and that's okay. I won't judge you for your opinion
However, if you do enjoy getting your butt kicked, learning new moves and the feeling of grinding your skill rather than just stats then you might like Absolver. A lot of the game is based around "decks", basically it's your moveset. Those decks can barely ever actually be countered (if said deck is good) since it's more about your abillity to outplay your opponents moveset, rather than just simply having a better one yourself.
The game does have low amounts of players, but it's never unplayable. In fact throughout my time with Absolver I never actually felt lonely, there is always someone to spend your time with. So, Absolver is not dead, but is it going to die soon? Well unless the devs will give up on it, I doubt it will die anytime soon.
What about balance, you might ask. In that case I can't say anything more that the game is very balanced, I rarely feel cheaped out from a win, every loss is my fault and my inabillity to counter my opponent. I didn't metion that the game has 4 styles (with more to come!), their skill ceiling is almost limitless. Those short dodges feel so satysfying, pretending to be drunk before kicking your opponent into a different dimension never felt better. Im confident that whatever it is you want to do in Absolver can be done.
Soundtrack is a little bit dissapointing, espacially the boss themes. Except the last one there was not a single track that got stuck in my head.
The fighting system altough rather easy to understand takes a lot of time to get good at. Fainting, moves with special abillities, mindgames, dodges, blocking, parries, it's all here for you to enjoy.
So what are you waiting for?
Make your move.
Good luck, Prospect.

Art- 8/10
Story- 5/10
Combat- 8.7/10
Soundtrack- 6.8/10
So, this was honestly a hard decision to make. While I haven't quite "grinded" absolver like other games, I finished the story in a solid 4 hours, because I had some rough encounters. However, I'll get to that.
So, PROS:
- Absolver has beautiful landscapes in particular, and doesn't overdose on things such as particles, sunray effects, or foliage to create senseless lag.
- There IS replayability in Absolver. After defeating the few bosses in the game, you can return to them at a later time to challenge them at a higher bar of difficulty.
-Absolver is by NO MEANS an easy walk in the park. If you're looking for a easy cake-walk game, Absolver is not for you. You can't pull a protagonist in Absolver and waltz into a crowd of three enemies and expect to beat them with a couple of hits. The combat is the most important part of the game, with skill taking priority over levels or gear.
- Absolver has variety in a multitude of playstyles. Not only are there 3 set styles to choose from at the start of the game varying from a "parry" ability, "dodge," or "attack absorption" abilities, but also movesets and stats. The game features more than one type of "attack" stat, meant for dedicating yourself to a playstyle, or you will hit a roadblock when you met someone who did. There is also a "mobility stat" meaning that your walk pace is increased, helping to close the gap between you and your opponent in a fight, or get away from them in a fight, to kite, or simply keep an unrelenting assault on them.
- Character customization is indeed a part of Absolver. However, there is little importance to it. The initial character creation allows you to choose your character's visuals. The equipment and attacks you unlock later in the game are far more important by leaps and bounds. The only important part of the initial character customization is the aforementioned ability class.
- PvE can be completed with random people you stumble upon, or friends who may have the game as well.
- The story rewards you appropriately- defeating bosses have the chance to drop equipment the possess.
Now... the long-awaited CONS of the game:
- First, the servers can sometimes lag. They sometimes drag you across a server mid-fight, which may end up with you taking unneeded damage. However, this never occurs during a special boss instance, as it is a one-on-one experience.
- The game is not intended for a PvE experience, personally. The story lasts a short time if you stay committed for a couple of hours, and is not entirely fulfilling.
- The community, at times, can be extremely toxic. People may randomly attack you for the sake of having fun, using utterly unbearably annoying spam moves that have little cooldown, extremely high speed, and low stamina cost to spam you until you die. When you try to block, they instead use moves that wear out stamina immensely to block. The only resolution to this is to either kill them, or when you die, the off-chance that the game moves you to a different server when you respawn.
- The moves learned from fighting enemies, at times, can be frustrating. Not all enemies know all the moves, so you may have to search for enemies who know the moves. This can be particularly hard to get sword moves, as few enemies have them. You may have to resort to feeding enemies swords for this.
- Aforementioned skill-lacking spam moves can ruin the whole "combination of moves" theme from the game, and makes the PvP seem more like a "how should I spam to win" feel instead of a "how should I organize my combo chain to win."
- The soundtrack is limited to fighting moments. There are no other moments that the soundtrack plays besides when you fight. I have no direct opinion on the fighting soundtrack, as it is limited to that, while most fights seem to absorb me more than the soundtrack does.
- There lacks weapon variety. Greatly. I understand that the game is generally new to the market, however it lacks variety. There are only two sets of separate movesets; normal fighting, and swords. Your bare-hands and war glove movesets use the exact same moves, so there are no differences there. In terms of sword techniques, there most definitely lacks variety in these. Adding things such as daggers, rapiers, cutlasses, greatswords, spears or other polearms would vastly increase weapon variety in the game, allowing a more customizable playstyle.
- To access the replayability section of bosses, you must first become somewhat adept in PvP.
To explain my initial scores:
Art- 8/10
-The art is a bit rough, but it fits the atmosphere amazingly, so it deserves a high score for blending well.
Story- 5/10
-The story is incredibly short, and has little to no backstory to who we are, our past, race, language, or why we fight.
Combat- 8.7/10
-The combat is the best part of this game, as you can never be too good at it. You can keep improving and improving, mastering both retreating and rushing.
Soundtrack- 6.8/10
- Aforementioned soundtracks are all fighting soundtracks. If there was music for walking through the woods or Colosseum or such, it would bring out a higher score by leaps. However, the fighting soundtrack does not distract oneself, and may motivate some.
Tl;dr, the game is an experience for players who enjoy short PvE experiences, and highly value competitive PvP. As of right now, there is maybe 4 hours of story, with many more hours of PvP.
"Is Absolver worth $29.99?"
Personally, I do not believe the full 30$ is worth this game. 20$, yes. 24$, sure, why not. $28, hey, you're pushing it. As I personally came here for the PvE experience, it was a bit of a letdown. However, as it has replayability, I do recommend it.

Overview: I love this game. It's so much fun. But I can tell you the pros and cons.
Pros:
-Gorgeous art. Cannot stress this enough.
-Customizable. Both your character and their combat styles/moves are completely customizable. Moves are not limited to fighting styles, and each move flows to a different stance.
-Very fun combat
-The seamless multiplayer is fun. You meet people even doing just the single player stuff. They can help you too.
Cons:
-No real multiplayer ranking system. The combat levels for multiplayer only ever go up, so there's no real way to have even matchmaking. This means your first match in 1v1 may be very jarring. and it's likely you'll be unevenly matched
-Some single player stuff is locked behind levels only gained though 1v1 and 3v3. If you wanna fully beat each boss all 3 times, you have to 1v1 or 3v3.
-When NPCs gang up on you, it becomes a little ridiculous how easy it is to die. But maybe I'm just bad at the game.
-No real map/minimap, so easy to get lost. Not that big of a world though, so it's fine.
Conclusion:
One of my favourite games despite the flaws. Crafting my own moveset is immensely satisfying, especially when it successfully KOs another player. The game is lovely to look at with its breathtaking art. Combat is addicting and fun. Love this game.

My mother was the one that introduced me to video games. I can remember playing games for as long as I can remember being alive. It started with the Atari and moved onto the Commodore 64, the Apple IIe and other computing dinosaurs of the early to mid 1980’s. I was addicted to playing games before I was old enough to really know what I was doing in them. It’s stayed with me throughout my entire life. I remember games such as Jumpman, Toy Bizarre, the original release of Tetris and pretty much the entire list of games that  RETREAM list in their Steam description. And to think that I have my mother to thank for this addiction that has stayed with me throughout my entire life. Thus, you’ll understand when I say this that RETREAM have given me yet another reason to wish that she was still alive. I wish that she had have seen and played Huenison. It’s the exact type of game that I can see her getting her inner geek on and playing until all hours of the morning. We would have shared an enormous appreciation for this game.
Before I was granted an opportunity to review this game my contact at RETREAM, the lead and perhaps only developer, a lovely person by the name of Simone Bevilacqua, made just one request. He asked that I take a deep look at his game rather than just a short shallow look at their game.  He claimed that although it appears to be just a simple arcade game that there are a lot of interconnected facets that produce a complex product and that this is simply unable to be seen on a ‘shallow play’. Personally, I think that Simone was selling his game short to me. Certainly the game starts easily enough and one may first think that it’s just another Tetris clone with a couple of simple mechanical changes – and perhaps this is what he were implying – but one needn’t be a brain surgeon to gain an almost immediate understanding that the game is so very much more than that. In that fact I believe that the game does possess the type of beauty and soul that is lacking in many of today’s pick up and throw away games.
Thankfully the Steam Description, below, does a very good job of explaining the soul and concept of the game. You do shoot at falling bricks with a cannon that is capable of shooting multiple different colors. You must hit each brick with the right colored cannon fire. If you do not then the brick will not clear. But the game is deeper than that. Some of the falling bricks have different powers. For example, some you must hit multiple times, some change color each time you hit them until you’ve cycled through the entire color range, others you have to hit four or five times before it’s power has weakened to disappear and of course there are power ups when you kill the brick they will turn white and magic happens when you destroy your next block. If you don’t get to the blocks in time they will add a line at the bottom of the screen while if you miss a shot the dreaded zapper line at the top lowers a row. In the latter’s respect it feels like Tetris on steroids.
You need to consider the total sum of every component of the game to truly appreciate Huenison. Thankfully there is a very thorough demo of the game available on the Steam store page. I definitely would recommend playing the demo if you’re on the fence with this game. I can only describe it and praise the game so much but actually playing the game will have you forking out the fiver needed to purchase the game at full price. And at that five dollar mark I would tell you that it is an absolute bargain. It’s one of those games that possesses the quality of addiction that you literally could spend countless hours playing this game.
The graphics and the chiptune music capture the very essence of what video games were like thirty years ago. However, they also help transform what could be deemed to be a very niche product – a game that only appeals to those of us who were alive to enjoy 1980’s gaming – to a presentable status to a modern audience who should be able to appreciate the vast quality that the classic style gameplay contains. You’re not going to find anything that looks, feels and sounds as genuinely classic as what Huenison does without it actually being a true classic. In that regard it is perfect.
Mum, I wish you were alive. You would have loved Huenison and I hope that Steamified’s readers will too. It’s one of the most outstanding indie games that I have had the privilege of not only playing but featuring on Steamified this year.
Steamified Score: 8.5/10 – Powerfully addictive. A greatly appreciated reminder of the types of games that defined my childhood. A game with a beautiful soul.
For more details on how to be successful within the game I invite you to take a moment to read the developer’s fantastic Tips ‘n’ Tricks post that he contributed to the game’s discussion boards. You can find the thread here. In all honesty as much as I can write about the game within the time that I have played it – I’m presently at over three hours and would love to spend significantly more with it but that will not be possible in the time that I have before posting this feature – there are just far too many nuances in the nine game modes for me to write much more effectively about the game.

I can't say I've played many games based entirely on their theme song, but Rochard is one of them. Thankfully I ended up satisfied with my time with the game.
Rochard is a sidescrolling platform, action, and puzzle game. You take control of a miner on a distant asteroid that has had little luck finding resources. Your team stumbles upon an important artifact that your boss hurries to investigate when pirates attack and things go awry.
The story is pretty thin, and while they seemed to get the space redneck Rochard just right, some later Native American themes felt pretty out of place. I emphasize the story, setting, and characters so much because that damn theme song sold me so hard. I'm a sucker for space cowboy antics.
Rochard, the protagonist and player-controlled character, uses a mining gun to pull objects close to him, shoot them away, and eventually shoot lasers and bombs. Throughout most of the game, Rochard is able to alter the gravity of the level, which becomes second-nature and part of the player's elegant jumps, swings, and attacks. It's fun to take on enemies by dropping boxes on their heads while leaping gracefully over a platform. There are collectibles for people who want to test the limits of their abilities, too. I didn't bother with every one, but I liked the additional challenges.
If you're like me, you got this game from a Humble Bundle a while back and never gave it a try. If anything I shared here interests you, load it up! I enjoyed my several hours with the game.

First thing first: I'm a huge Warhammer and Warhammer 40K fan (and lets not mention anything Age of &*@#). Not a fanboy, mind you, and not even a proper gamer. I spend more time painting my models and reading fascinating fluff than actually playing.
There is now a family of tabletop games consisting of Necromunda (1995), Mordheim (1999), Shadow War: Armageddon (2017), and an upcoming remake - Necromunda: Underhive (November this year). As I was late for the first games, I only recently got myself acquainted with Shadow War, so I can say I am familiar with the basic mechanics. I'm also a huge fan of turn based, skirmish level games, from first Fallouts, Incubation and Jagged Alliances to brilliant XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, Darkest Dungeon and Battle Brothers.
I'm revealing my background to show you that I was a perfect candidate to be biased and to fall in love with Mordheim: City of the Damned from the get-go. And yet it took me awhile. Three times precisely. The whole game looked so convoluted and unnecessary awkward that I couldn't force myself to carry on. And I lost at least a year of great fun. Actually, I was that close of losing opportunity to play the perfect turn-based skirmish game. And a Warhammer game. A game of my dreams to be honest. Yes, I said that, and now you can call me a biased fanboy, but I really don't care, as I can't really hear you, wandering off towards the treacherous alleys of the wretched Mordheim.
But if you care to accompany me on the way I can explain myself. Rogue Factor's Mordheim catches the atmosphere of Warhammer Old World perfectly. For me, Warhammer was always a satire and to some degree a parody of an epic high fantasy tolkienesque worlds full of brave and mighty heroes and deus ex machina wizards. Here you have a grim, down to earth reality, and a brutal, unforgiving world. F.e.the fact that there is magic in this world does not make it more colourful and, well... more magical. It only makes things worse, bringing ruinous chaos powers to your neighbourhood. So far, no other game could show this world better than the story of a bunch of miserable, desperate and greedy mercenaries, trying their luck in the ruins of Mordheim. I was nowhere near that attached to my XCOM squad, as I am to my Reikland henchmen. Even though one of them has only one arm now, and the other received such a strong hit to the head, that he is practically imbecile, loitering on the battlefield completely useless. But they are MY boys. We fought together side by side, and we almost stole that cursed idol from the Warrior Nuns. If only Mother Superior had left her mace at the dormitory...
Does this game have issues? Of course it does. Is the UI still convoluted? At the begining yes. But it all makes so much sense eventually. Could it be better? I hope we'll see that in the upcoming Rouge Factor Necromunda and I keep my fingers crossed for the guys, wishing them well. Is Mordheim a hard game? It's as hard as an Ogre punch in the stomach. It's brutal. But it's not unfair. Usually you are punished for you mistakes or for that another Wyrdstone, which was just round the corner, and I could almost reach... Bang!
If it's so hard, how can it be satisfying and fun you might ask. Well, you have no idea, unless you've completed the mission with side objectives, brought that wonky wagon full of strange unearthly gems to your camp and celebrated with your merry band of misfits. Shame, that Otto didn't make it though. But If he was with us now, I'm sure he would like us to laugh and drink while we can, pray to RNGesus, as there is no other god in Mordheim, and carry on my friends. And if you are undecided whether to give it a try on the streets of Mordheim, I will not  try to convince you. It's not for everybody. But the rewards are magnificent, believe me.

Resident Evil 4 is best described as the turning point in the series where it left the old style of first 3 entries and started going in a more third person shooter style of direction. While not as action focused as RE5 and RE6 are it stikes a balance between horror aspects and your traditional third person shooter with action elements mixed in. This of game is of course a remaster of the original Resident Evil 4 with all the extras for it and you can toggle between the original SD and HD textures in the options menu. Unforuntatly you have to do it before you actually start playing it which means no mid game toggling between the two. On the upside though because it includes all the extras from the orignal gamecube and PS2 versions you are getting a solid value for your money. Unfortunatly not all of the game was remastered and some cut scenes namely the ones for the Seperate ways missions are still in their original SD format though the core gameplay does remain with the HD uptick. The only other real downside to this remaster is the lack of achievements you can earn as they're pretty much regulated to the main game with none for the Seperate Ways camapagin or some of the other extras. While not a big deal it would have been nice to see some achievements set aside for the extra content included.

Truthfully, going into this game, I didn't know what to expect. With the name telling me I have 30 seconds to complete a mission, I thought it was going to be very easy. This is far from the case. As others have mentioned, this game makes you think strategically about when to grind, when to spend your money, how to spend said money, when the best time to fight the boss would be, etc. It's this balance while forcing you to think on your feet that makes it so interesting. Some missions you may beat the first time, others, especially the bonus missions, may take you two, or three, or even more attempts at them, but you will most likely end up loving it every time and, at least in my experience, rarely, if ever, ever give up in anger because it's that fun and addicting.
Would I say it's one of the best games I've ever played? eh, not really, but it's definitely up there high on the list. Reason for this is while yes, the game is fantastic and addicting, it's also really repetitive. This is probably it's biggest, and only flaw in my eyes of the game. Now don't get me wrong, each stage is set up to give you a new challenge to get to the boss, such as monsters are absent from the map so you can't level up, an avalanche can hit you causing you to lose all your armor and weapons, etc. but at it's core, it's the same thing each level. Grind early, reset time, buy items, grind a bit more, reset time, proceed to go through the stage, reset time, fight boss, go to next stage, repeat.
If the thought of repeating the same core gameplay every stage doesn't appeal to you then I'd recommend watching a few videos on youtube or watching other people play it on twitch or something first to see if it really isn't your thing. If you can look past this flaw then you will most likely enjoy this game and for ten dollars, it's not too bad of a price if you can afford it.

I bought this game within days of its release several years ago.  At the time, I was a call center worker, and wanted to support a fellow grunt.  I was moved by the story of a developer who had made a game based on his experiences and was terminated as a result.  I wanted to support the creator in his quest to become a developer.
In itself, this game is a short 5-10 minute window into what red tape feels like.  It illustrates the difficulty of something as simple as an address change, gives you a brief but accurate perspective into a few moments of the life of a call center worker, and may teach people how to not be a difficult caller.
You play the role of a call center rep who receives a call from someone claiming to be a Mr. Swarth.  The caller is somewhat disagreeable, unprepared for the call, and mostly clueless.  Caller requests an address change.

.
The reason I do not reccomend this game is not because it is short, or the art style is less than optimal.  That's all fine.  I do, however, fundamentally disagree with the message of the game.
The game's message appears to be: call center jobs are soul-sucking, and it is your job to not help people.  To this effect, the achievement for actually completing the call with the desired outcome is designed as literally impossible to get.  100%ers beware.
However, the game's message should be: following the law is a beautiful thing.  While we were unable to help the caller, we actually did a real service to the actual Mr. Swarth; As it is impossible to verify the caller's identitly, Mr. Swarth's information has been protected from potential unwarrented disclosure or tampering.  Also, in real life, I was and am very good at my job, and I believe there is no claimant, customer, or beneficiary who cannot be helped.  As I write this review, I work for Uncle Sam; I do my job with a rigid iron rod lodged firmly up my backside, and I am an extremely effective public servant regardless.
I will not reccomend this game unless and until the developer makes the requisite amendments to the game per the unfulfilled goals stated for the game's future prior to the steam port.

Empire TW is an upgrade on the management side in some ways but a downgrade for the rest, let me elaborate on that.
Pros
- The campaign map is huge, you can conquer America, Europe and India and they are inhabited with their appropriate factions
- Development, you will get towns the more population you get within a region which let you customize things a bit more
- Research system is fun but quite slow
- Diplomacy is much better compared to M2TW, I was able to maintain 2 alliances in my first long campaign quite easily and you get long-term benefits for keeping trade rights which is really nice and you won't get backstabbed every 5 turns now.
- Sound design is well done, it's nice to hear the gunshots and cannons annihilate enemy troops while listening to battle music
- Graphics are good, a bit chunky for my taste sometimes but overall great
- Lot of history stuff that you can learn while having fun
- Events that are linked to real history happen adding up to the immersion
cons
- The AI is really bad, It's almost always complete confusion in the enemy ranks that it drives me crazy at times
- The pathfinding in battles is horrible, especially visible in siege battles which makes you want to slam your desk for just placing something on the walls. Also ordering multiple troops to attack 1 unit is really unorganized to the point that your troop could stand in front of another one and still shoot, you need to place them 1 by 1 because they don't give a crap how terrible their placement is.
- Agents, the fact that you cannot recruit agents and they will recruit themselves whenever they want is really stupid and pointless, I had so many useless agents by the end of a campaign it was ridiculous.
- Regions are tedious to manage and poorly divided. They do have a building browser that is a bit bad to use, it would've been nice if you could actually manage your buildings from this window and not having to go so every single buildings and do your action from there. Also regions are sometimes cut way too big, like France for example, it's one region, like the present day France that is a country and if you loose the central city you loose the entire region.
- Naval battles, they are long and almost every time a snore fest, it's not pirate of the caribbean and you will be tempted to auto-resolve everytime you get to fight one.
- Speaking of auto-resolve, I don't know what they did in this one but I saw some pretty ridiculous auto-resolve situations that made zero sense to me
Overall, the game was somewhat fun, it was a good bit of changes from it's previous title but I just couldn't overlook many problems I had with it. So if you're a fan of the era and really want to play something like that, go on it's probably just my picky nature acting up. If you're here for the gameplay however you might want to go for the next one instead or get it on sale.

I've played this for years and still have a lot of fun. New expansions and content constantly increase the play and variety. While a lot of content requires purchase or subscription, you can also earn points from playing that will allow you to purchase that same content. Admitedly the totally free route is much more of a grind, so you may find you want to purchase or subscribe for convenience. Overall a beautiful full 3D game, with movement in all directions including high altitudes and deep pits and water you have to swim through. There is day, night, rain, sunshine, multiple moons moving across the sky and beautiful sunsets. And yes, there be dragons too! There are a lot of areas, but you seldom have to run too far as there are telporters and guild ship docks all around to move you quickly to the various regions. Choose the difficulty that makes your play the most fun while still challenging - casual, normal, hard, elite and the new "reaper" mode. Many in-game Guilds welcome players - players' "renown" build up the guild and your character receives numerous buffs as the guild level increases. A rather unique feature in DDO is the ability to reincarnate. Tired of your current capped build? Have it start again from level 1, but stronger and better each time you reincarnate. While DDO characters only have 30 levels there are 5 sub-levels within each level. Each of these sub-levels or Action Points are roughly equivalent to a level in other MMOs, so it's comparable to 150 levels in other games. There are hundreds of quests to play either on your own, with your friends, with potential new friends, or even purchase an AI hirling to help out. The game starts in the D&D Eberron world, but has expansions to Forgotten Realms and soon Ravenloft. There are also questpacks for D&D modules Against the Slave Lords, Temple of Elemental Evil and Haunted Halls of Eveningstar. Normal quests have up to 6 players and raids have up to 12 players. There are so many ways to customize your character, You can even take multiple classes and try to combine benefits from both. But it's also fairly forgiving and if you make mistakes you can adjust the difficulty, rebuild your character or just wait and reincarnate into a better version. While the game has a lot of features, is very "learn as you go" and you don't have to do everything. E.g. Craft it you want or skip it altogether. Most of all I simply enjoy playing and experiencing the various worlds within the game.

I got this game because of the number of reviews that claim: "This is a balanced fighting game!" What they all really mean is: "Since this is a customizable fighting game, so long as you go a high Dexterity, high Mobility build, then you are balanced and the same as everyone else."
In the end, the entire metagame is the Kahlt Method (chosen at character creation) plus high speed attacks; the only non-directional counter move plus quick damage return to "combo" with its "drawback" . . .
While I initially liked the way moves are learned, it requires hours of gameplay to obtain them. Those that have the quick, dodge high/low double-tapping moves dominate PvP, and you can't learn them because you almost never take them down due to the high health regain they recieve when your character is taken down. Learing moves PvE would take somewhere around 100 hours, and only if you can find NPCs in the world who use them, then grind them over and over again until completed. This also makes unpopular builds nearly impossible, because no one in PvP is using those moves for you to learn them from . . . This quickly results in your character having learned the bad moves (because you beat those opponents) and becoming fodder for those with strong ones, as you are unable to take them down, and therefore unable to learn them.
This game holds a lot of promise. It is unique and beautiful, and really doesn't neet to have more content. But before I could ever give this game a "thumbs up", it needs extreme PvP balance fixes.
In truth, I would have returned the game, but the developers did a great job requiring you to put far too many hours into the game before you realize its extreme pitfalls. This makes it ineligible for return, based on Steam's return policy.

This game is unfinished. Unapologetically so. The one thing they did finish is the combat.
Simply put, it is the most enjoyable, intense and fluid combat of any game I have ever played, period. Everything from the animation, sound, responsiveness and clarity is polished to near perfection. The only part that needs work is the balance, but that's going to always be a work in progress no matter which MP game you play.
It is an absolute joy to learn and master building a combat deck and then try it out against other people. Combat is strategic and skillful. Reading your opponent and learning their moveset is paramount to success. Baiting, countering and dodging all important factors. And it's all FUN. Outplaying your opponent then landing a 360 spinning kink to their head is sex levels of satisfying.
However, as I alluded to earlier, the rest of the game is just not there. This game should have remained in development for at least another 6-12 months. The world, while beautiful, is empty and mostly a chore to move around through. (No fast travel). The PVE content is okay for learning how to play, but past that it offers no challenge outside of outnumbering you. The bosses (all 3 of them) are boring and far to simple. None of them forced me to change my playstyle.
Once you have finished what little PVE content there is, (took me about 6 hours to grind through) all there is to do really is play PVP and experiment with new moves that you'll be unlocking. And like I said, this is still fun, but if you prefer PVE games there really isn't a lot here for you. There are few NPCs scattered around the place, but all they do is give you a few unvoice acted lines in a dialogue box with a bit of lore or a few tips. There are also items to find around the place to find, but they aren't really hidden, they're kinda just there to encourage exploration of the pretty enviorments.
I'm still going to recommend this game. The combat is worth it by itself. And the developers have stated they have more content coming, both for PVP and PVE. Like I said, this game isn't finished, but at least the developers are still working on it. Don't get it if you are looking for an interesting world to explore, or a cool story, get it for the combat and the fabulous cloths to find.

Cinderella Phenomenon is an Otome game that centers around an 'Icy' princess that has been cursed and demoted (from riches to rags) in order for her to thaw her heart and learn kindness. At the start of the game, the princess can choose between five other cursed individuals in order for them to help each other lift their curse. The story in itself may seem simple enough, but as long as the routes are played IN ORDER, the plot of the story will get progressively thicker and at some points darker.
The character routes that will need to be played in order will come as follows (based on the how plot driven the routes are) from least to most:
-Rod
-Karma
-Rumpel
-Fritz
-Waltz
While personal character favorites from best to least come as follows (this is my opinion):
-Waltz
-Karma
-Fritz
-Rod
-Rumple
In all honesty, the game is so good that it is kind of shocking to see that it is a free game. The story is well written (favorite being Waltz), artwork is really beautiful with no visible flaws, and the music is nice and beautiful. A definite recommendation.

Did you like X-COM? If you didn't, you probably won't like this.
Mordheim is a game about playing the odds and testing your ability to recover. Yes, it's heavily RNG. So is any tabletop game that uses dice. Much like with D&D however, it's possible to maximize your odds of success through smart positioning and, as the game progresses and you can afford more skills and spells, tactical choices.
This is not a fast paced game. That is important to note. There are often waits while the other team is going, and that can get boring if you don't have a show in the background or something else to do for brief spans. However, having to wait for the AI to move isn't exactly a new thing with turn based strategy games, I remember having some pretty lengthy waits in Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.
A lot of people have some pretty strong opinions about how saving works here. I was pretty annoyed at it myself while I was still learning my way around the game, but now that I have I kinda understand the difference in playstyle it leads to and while it may not be for everyone it IS rather engaging. Unlike most other games, your every decision matters. You can take nothing back. If you want to test your ability to respond to unfavorable situations, this game will give you plenty of chances to do so, and it makes victory all the sweeter when you manage to outplay a stronger enemy.
If you are going to pick up this game, you should probably accept that, in all likelyness, you are going to be pretty bad at it at first. That's normal, it's got a bit of a learning curve, and anyone I know who's good at the game has had their share of bad defeats and abandoned warbands. On the bright side, part of the progression is independant of your specific warband, meaning that if you play a lot and start a new game, your new warband will start off with more resources and a higher level than they would otherwise.
Personally I haven't suffered from any of the bugs that I'm seeing people talk about. I'm not doubting that they've run into them, but I've never had my characters get stuck in terrain, I've never dealt with it crashing, and at least on my machine it's been quite reliable in its performance.
If you have patience and a tactical mind, this game is great fun.

TL;DR - A "should probably buy" for DiRT Rally fans disappointed by DiRT 4.
The question "Is WRC 7 more realistic than DiRT Rally?" does not have a simple yes-or-no answer.
The question "Is WRC 7 a better game than DiRT 4?" does. The answer is yes.
It's brilliant. It is not, however, Richard Burns Rally 2, nor is it DiRT Rally 2. If you're looking for a "more realistic" experience after putting 1,000 or so hours into DiRT Rally, this might not be the solution. The realism or believability of the handling varies from surface to surface.
In Rally d'Italia Sardegna, it feels almost like you're playing RBR. The car is ludicrously skatey and floaty, but in a fun, satisfying way that is easily controlled using your throttle and brake. Moments like this are where the game really shines, handling-wise. It's responsive and lively like DiRT Rally, but slippy and elegant like RBR.
In Rally Finland, the car feels like the tires were manufactured by Gorilla Glue. I don't just mean that you have a lot of grip (you do). I mean the cars tires, through my G27, literally felt sticky. It's a strange and not-so-true-to-life experience. Sometimes you'll find yourself going flat-out around bends that would have killed you in DiRT Rally or RBR (or real life), planted firmly to the ground without a bit of lateral motion. Other times, you'll suddenly frisbee off the side of the stage and cut down more trees than the Finnish Forestry Commission. It can be inconsistent.
Besides the variable handling in terms of expected grip, as a player, the handling was almost immediately intuitive and comfortable after bingeing on DiRT Rally while the game downloaded. DiRT 4 felt confusing and alien - it took me several hours to even gain the ability to hold a line or a drift angle, and even then never for long, or to my satisfaction. The cars in D4 practically begged to understeer into an outside spin at some times, and refused to move the rear out a single degree at others. In WRC 7, the cars love kicking their tails out. All it takes is a solid flick (or tap of the handbrake) and a feathering of the throttle, and the cars take an angle and - more importantly - HOLD that angle so long as you keep it steady. They'll turn in or out at your behest, or hold fast and drift like crazy if you tell them to.
That's the main thing for me. Even if the game is - on average - less realistic than DR, which was never an incredibly realistic game to begin with, the cars are intuitive and they behave. The rear does what you want, and you rarely feel confused or frustrated by the car making its own decisions in terms of angle or balance.
PROS:
+Stage design/stages from actual WRC events
+Career mode
+Sometimes handling
+Multi-surface stages
+Fun and intuitive, to contrast with D4's incomprehensible feel
MEHS:
~Performance
~Lack of FOV options
~Wheel compatibility issues (my G27 worked fine but there are tons of reports of issues here)
~Sometimes handling
~Graphics (vary from solid to ridiculously dated on a moment-to-moment basis)
CONS:
-Overall, less "realistic" than RBR or DiRT Rally in most handling cases
-Co-driver is robotic and kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I didn't mind so much in terms of playability
-Sometimes handling
-Lack of car variety
-Controls are wonky without tweaking, no clutch(?) and handbrake does unexpected things to the car

Space Leprechaun (or Space Lepricon as the game says a lot of the time) is a horizontal space shooter, without much going for it. The game is just long, dull, devoid of enemies or challenge. Each level lasts 15+ agonizing minutes of emptiness.
There are primarily two types of enemies, rocks and orbs. Shoot a red orb to replenish your red weapon, shoot a yellow orb to replenish your yellow weapon. The colors don't matter, its all about whatever gun you need ammunition for as there's a maximum. For other enemies, there are bosses and every so often a flying saucer appears.
Because the  enemies are sparse and easy to avoid, you fire one projectile at a time, although the trailer would lead me to believe that you can get better weapons.  Changing between your seven weapons is a bit cumbersome as you need to press a the number to the weapon. In a way its okay because the weapons have the same effectiveness. Any color of your weapon can kill any orb. When you run out of ammo you have to change your weapon, but if all weapons are dry, that's it, you have no other opportunity to regain ammunition at least in the early portion of the game. I should point out that while the weapons are all color coated, the projectiles are all the same rainbow laser.
The scoring is simple, destroy something and get a point. Even matching orange weapon to orange orb fails to net you any additional points.
Full disclosure, I never made it far in the game. Its just far too dull. I keep watching the timer tick by and watch the meter indicating how far you are in the level. Its just disheartening. I never played far enough to get upgrades or better weapons.
You start with three lives if you need them, but since everything is so easy to dodge in the early stages of the game, the only way you can die is via suicide.
I would appreciate shorter levels with more action and a greater variety of enemies. Leaderboards would also enhance how replayable the game is.

There are definitely pros and cons to this one; personally I can't help but recommend it for its quality and message, but I was disappointed at how short of an experience it is, and how simple it is to work through.  Getting all of the achievements will be a bit of a slog, maybe impossible, but it is entertaining enough to come back to after a break.
Essentially, you are a customer service representative dealing with a difficult customer on the telephone.  Unfortunately the title of this game is literal; there is only one customer and the call never changes.  It's possible to interpret this as part of the game's message, but for a piece of software that costs money, there really should be more content.  Be prepared to 'finish' in less than ten minutes, and whilst it is perfectly understandable if that represents bad value to you, I'm personally glad I played it.  I'm sure there will be sale prices that are more justifiable, so maybe wait for that or get it in a bundle.
The voice acting is great, as it really should be in a piece which is primarily audio based.  The developer has opted for an (I think intentionally) janky MS-paint visual style, which is humorous and adequate since there is really nothing to look at in a desk job like this anyway.  And that is the point; to convey the horrible banality of such work, being treated badly by customers as a matter of course as if the guidelines you follow are your fault when you've come to despise them as much as they do; anyone who has worked in customer services, tech support or telesales will find this resonates uncomfortably with their everyday experience.  Perhaps the work presented to us if we want to get those achievements is a reflection of that.
(Also, it is nice to see a game start with an anti-GamerGate message.  It's old news by now, sure, but people are still sore from that experience and it is nice to see devs acknowledging that within their games.  Obviously this can't be a factor in a review of the game itself, but kudos for the bravery).

When my birthday rolled around, a friend of mine gifted me this. I had heard about the Resident Evil series for a long time, how good some of them were, how the movies were terrible (which isn't very surprising considering most game-based movies suck), among other things. So I was excited to play this, considering it was, apparently, one of the best games in the franchise, and was hailed by many as one of the best games ever made.
So I played it, and, to my surprise, I had a blast playing it.
So, first off, is it one of the best games ever made? Well, it's honestly one of the best horror games I've ever played. It has some flaws, some more noticeable than others, but they don't ruin your experience. They didn't for me, at least.
Second, is it one of the best games in the franchise? Well, considering this was my first game in the series, and that I haven't played any of the others yet, I can't make a complete opinion at the time of me writing this. However, after seeing gameplay of most of them after playing this, and also before playing this, I can conclude that the original Resident Evil, as well as this one, the 2nd one, and the 7th one, are my favourites. 3 is good, 5 and 6 are eh. There are other ones, but I haven't cared to look at them.
Third, what did I think about it overall? Well, I did mention I had a blast with it. First off, Leon Kennedy is, in my opinion, a great character to play as. He is developed quite nicely in the opening cutscenes, with him remembering the events of Raccoon City in the 2nd game, as well as some other parts. Ashley Graham, however, is one of the most annoying sidekicks I've ever had to deal with before. Her voice is so high-pitched, it felt like I was listening to someone scrape something on an old chalkboard everytime she spoke. She's also the President's daughter, so yeah.
The weapons you get in the game are basic, but are very important to your survival. Resource managing and the ammount of ammo you have for your weapons are two key elements you will have to keep in mind while playing this game. I've read the 5th and 6th games focus more on action than horror, which can be good in some ways, but not necessarily if the series was built around horror. That's what I think, at least. Throughout the game, you will be running around lots, either running away from the Ganados, running & gunning, escorting Ashley, etc. Also fighting some bosses along the way. Some parts are very fun, and they give you a sense of tension, while others build up dread and uncertainty.
The setting is quite unique : rural Spain. The atmosphere is very cloudy, dark, and unsettling at some parts. You have to have a sense of dread and uncertainty in some parts to make you feel on edge, and this game excels at that when it needs to. For one of the first times in my life, I was genuinely terrified at some parts, mainly at the halfway point of the game and after that. Mainly because enemies came out of nowhere at times where I thought I was in the clear. Also, the Regenerators. If you don't know what I mean, either play the game, specifically at night with most of the lights turned off and the sound up high, or just look them up. Not kidding when I say this, those things scared me good at one part.
Last thing I will talk about here is more of a flaw. The controls. At first, the controls are really awkward and hard to understand. Especially when you have to use a keyboard. However, after a while, I got used to them, and I can now play the game pretty well with no issues involving the controls.
Overall, I had a really fun time with this game. The story was interesting, even though it was flawed in some parts, there was a sense of dread that really worked in a lot of parts, it had some memorable moments for me, as well as some pretty decent characters. I recommend this to anyone who likes survival horror, because you'll probably enjoy this quite a lot.
Final score : 9/10.

Just went through with my bi-annual Autumn tradition of replaying this game. I've lost track of how many times I've finished this game over the years and on all different versions. Comments about the port can be found later down in the review.
It's hard to write an unbiased review for this game - simply put, this is my favorite game of all time. It's got a great mix of a spooky atmosphere, deep combat system, campy storylline with hilarious catchphrases, great artistic direction and a very nice sense of pacing - the game knows when to dial up the action and knows just when to dial it down for you to take a breather with a bit of puzzle solving/exploration. The weapons are immensly satisfying to use - the shotguns feel like a force of nature, the magnums are the definition of a "handcannon"; even the pistols feel like they pack a punch and each time you land a headshot and see the enemy's head blown clean off it just makes me happy in ways that I cannot describe.
In terms of structure the game is linear but there's just enough hidden pathways and hidden treasures to be found that it doesn't make the game feel like a straight corridor to the finish line. What I probably love most about the game is how varied it is - it always manages to throw in a wrench in the works so you are fighting enemies in interesting ways; be it on diffrent points of elevation, on a minecart or in a labyrinth so you're always watching your back. The game even does escort missions right - the girl you're escorting always stays glued to your back (unless you tell her to wait somewhere) and never gets in the way while adding tension to the encounters yet also giving you a break from your escorting duties at certain points in the story so that you're not always doing the same thing.  I should mention that I don't find the game very scary - it is infamous for breaking away from the previous games in the series' horror roots but taken as an action game on it's own terms this game shines based purely on it's refined gameplay.
The game is also full of content when you finish the game: you unlock a New Game+ mode where you have access to new weapons/costumes, you get two (one very small and one 3+ hours) campaigns featuring a side character and the addicting Mercenaries mode which can be described as a "horde" mode of sorts where you're killing enemies to add to your timer and chase highscores; Mercenaries is so fun and has enough playable characters and stages that you could easily waste 20+ hours on it alone. You also unlock the Proffesional difficulty mode which I wish was unlocked from the start for returning players.
Now in regards to the port I feel that this is a good version of the game but I had some annoying hick ups in the game. I played through the game using a controller - the M+K controls for this game is nothing to write home about but since the game was originally designed for controllers I can forgive it for that. The button layouts for controllers are not customizable - you have three different layouts but none of them were exactly how I wanted them - not a dealbreaker as I managed to adapt but still very odd that such a simple feature wasn't included. In regards to the controls I had a very annoying bug happen during a boss fight - a quick time event popped up and the button prompt was for a keyboard button even though I was using a controller so I had a few unnecessary deaths. I had to put the keyboard in my lap and take my hand of the controller when the QTE popped up - not the end of the world but it felt sloppy of the developers. I also had the game crash on me when entering a door forcing me to replay a lengthy section of the game.
The positives of this version does outweigh the bad though in my opinion even though it isn't perfect - this was my first time playing through the game in 60 FPS and simply put I'm never going back to an older version of the game; it really felt like I saw a game I knew like the back of my hand through new eyes. In terms of visuals the bump in resolution is appreciated but certain assets end up looking pixelated - these assets looked like this in the original release so I'm personally used to it but it bears mention. You do have the option of switching to newer textures - these look all right but many elements of the game world lack the gritty worn down feeling that the originals had. For example, the original plank wall textures really look nasty and worn down - the newer textures look like they were cleaned last week. I could take it or leave it honestly as I prefer to play with the original textures. Also some animations are locked to 30 FPS - the reloading animation of the sniper rifles being a notable example but these are far and few between. I should also mention that load times were close to non-existant on my Nvidia 960GTX/Intel i5-6600K/16GB RAM rig with no slowdown whatsoever.
All in all I recommend this version of the game. Some newer players might find certain design descisions a bit strange - infamously you can't walk and shoot at the same time, but the game is designed around it - but this game was very influential on gaming as a whole when it first came out and I believe there's still a lot for new players to love in this game; it really feels like a unique beast being released at the end of the PS2-era while at the same time introducing features that still can be found in games released today.
I'm already looking forward to Autumn 2019 when it's time to give this game a playthrough again.

The first impressions from looking at the store page is already a negative one. The "About This Game" section is poorly written and attempts to be comical. The horrendous video and screenshots aren't lying. Defenders of Time really does look bad, play badly, and even performs badly. It's out of date, it doesn't innovate and it most certainly is one of the worst tower defense games I've ever played.
Aesthetically, Defenders of Time looks like the results of a project from an early graphic design college class even at maximum settings. The game completely lacks polish and presentation. There is no story, no lore and no interesting factions or units. There is nothing that grabs a hold of your attention in any way. There is nothing to play for or to experience. From when you boot the game to the glorious moment when you click the "exit game" button, you will feel as though you could've spent your time doing something else. Anything else. This game adds nothing new to the tower defense genre. There is nothing to enjoy.
In addition to it being uneventful, uninspired, dull, boring and mind numbing, there is no single player campaign to speak of. This game was designed for multi-player alone and no one plays this game. What we have here is a game that was made in hopes to have a massive online multi-player community, and it doesn't. It never will. Even if it became free to play, there is nothing attractive about this game to bring in players. The single player portion of the game is just picking a map from a total of six and waiting for the mindless enemy units to make their rounds. There is nothing else. Also, even though the game runs smoothly at 60 frames per second, it will constantly take up between 20% and 30% of CPU power at all times. If all of this isn't bad enough, you are also required to create a separate account in order to play the game. Having a price tag of $20 is ridiculous. The developers couldn't have expected this to be a success, could they?

I've been playing DDO since its release, and I'm still learning new things about the game on a regular basis. If you're looking for in-depth multiclassing, this is the game for you. See below for pros and cons.
Pros
------------
- D&D 3.5 rule set (loosely followed)
- Dungeon master voices things (with new DMs for many dungeons)
- Everything (in theory) is acquirable through play.
- Updates bring new content somewhat regularly.
- Don't like your build? Reincarnate, and try again!
- This game has alot for players to learn
- Lots of statistics manipulation and class customization (if that's your thing)
- Multiclassing
- Lots of replay value
- Lag monster is becoming less frequent
- Scalable challenges for veteran players (reaper mode - The DM wants you dead!)
- Ravenloft and Intelligent items coming soonish (new xpac soonish)
- PVP is not really a huge thing.
Cons
-------
- Lag Monster can/will wipe parties
- Graphics and engine is out of date (the game is old, this will eventually happen to EVERY game)
- Content is locked behind a grind/pay wall (grinding is doable, but VERY tedious.)
- 60% of the time hirelings are garbage EVERY time (I've never seen hireling AI this bad. Its shameful.)
- PVP is not really a thing.
Give the game a shot. I enjoy it quite a bit and you might too.

"This game reminds me of Limbo. It looks like Limbo. It's like a shorter Limbo." You'll hear phrases like that a lot in regards to this game (and pretty much any platformer with puzzles whose graphics are mostly gray-scale). While there are similarities in those regards, I wouldn't
say it's a straight up clone or anything. The atmosphere feels somewhat different from Limbo for instance, as pretty much every creature you meet is actually quite friendly
and will help you on your spontanious quest-as long as you're willing to help them in return.
+ A decent atmosphere and setting with some interesting looking characters.
+ The music is alright.
+- The graphics are fine if you like this style. If you don't or are sick of seeing it, then this game probably won't change your mind. A few character's sprites look kind of weird to me though.
+- It's a very short game, lasting an hour at most if you're really bad at puzzles and/or platforming, although you'll likely finish it in under an hour otherwise. If you like longer games, this could be a problem, but the issues with the game may make its short length a positive.
- The controls are one of the biggest issues of this game. The game is surprisingly awkward to play, with inputs either not registering or having a large delay. I'm fairly certain this is an engine limitation though, as the game was made in RPG Maker 2003 and, to put it bluntly, RPG Maker isn't a very good engine for platformers. If the dev wants to make more platformers, my advice would be to not use RPG Maker, or at least not that version.
- There honestly aren't many puzzles in the traditional sense in this game, and a couple of the puzzles that are there either feel gratuitous or are held back by the poor controls. The rest of the puzzles are pretty much either "avoid the hazards" or "just guess for this bit".
-+ It didn't really feel like there was much of a point for your character suddenly going for a dangerous stroll
. The ending was also kind of confusing. Those are just small personal gripes for me though. And who knows, maybe you'll get it more than me.
The game has several problems, but at the end of the day, it was a quick free romp in a world filled with animal fellows and a cute wrap-up ending cutscene
, so if you just want to play a cute, short puzzle game and can look past some bad controls and non-puzzles, give it a try and play it on a  rainy day.
All of that said though, I hope the dev takes the criticism and uses it in any future games, cause while I can look past those problems in something like this, a longer game with the same problems would likely be an infuriating experience.

Rochard is a sci-fi platform game which was initially released on the PlayStation 3 network in 2011, but was eventually ported to he PC later in that year.  The game  revolves around taking control of gravity, and using the gravity gun called the G-Lifter. This is used to manipulate objects around the levels.  This game has it all, increasingly challenging environmental puzzles, action, a rich story line and plenty of humor.
The game play is a two dimensional side scrolling platformer that takes place in three dimensional scenes. You work your way through the environments completing a series of puzzles and combat encounters.  You are able to change the gravity in the room very easily at just the press of a button. All of the puzzles are easy enough for you to not get stuck on them for ages, but hard enough so that you can't just stroll into a room and instantly be able to figure it out. It hits the sweet spot just right.
The graphical fidelity is very pleasing, it has a nice art style which works well with this type of game. All of the character models look well polished and has brilliant animation. The voice acting is also top notch here too, something a fair few games manage to fall down on.
While the single player story mode took me about five hours to complete; I felt as if it managed to fulfill its potential in that time. There is also some DLC available for a very cheap price which includes four new challenging puzzle levels. Granted there is more of an emphasis on the puzzle solving as apposed to the combat, but even for the most experienced puzzle platforming players you'll find them difficult. I did have to check out the walkthrough because I was stumped at times.
This is a really well ported game, I didn't have any technical problems, you are able to play in higher resolutions and the game does work with the keyboard and mouse, however it is highly recommended you use a controller with these types of games.
I would recommend Rochard to people who really enjoy the puzzle platforming genre, people expecting an action packed side scrolling shooter will probably not find the thrill they are looking for. But if you want a couple hours of figuring out puzzles in a sci-fi environment, you may as well try Rochard

Sorry for huge review if you don't want to read. Tl;dr is the game can be fun but has stupid design decisions that limit your choices and impact on the game, wierd power spikes and a lot of useless skills/spells that take time to learn about, causes you to fail even if you didn't do anything wrong, often punishes you for no real reason, and fanboys of the game will defend these things as all being more "challenging."
Oh boy, where to start with this game? A complicated bundle of enjoyment, acute disappointment, and annoyance.
It's not a bad game, but it's also not a good game. My biggest complain is that you have relatively less control over the outcome of the game than in comparable titles. Oh sure, there's rng that determines results in a ton of games, especially squad based tactics games like this, the Xcoms, and Wasteland 2. Mordheim has them too, but its nothing really worse than those two games.
The difference I noticed in Mordheim is that you can't affect the rng directly. In Xcom you could hide behind cover to protect yourself or flank enemies/blow up thier cover to increase your chances of hitting them. Anything like that in Mordheim? Can you flank or surround enemies to decrease their dodge/parry rate? Nope. How about attacking them from behind (the direction the character model isn't facing)? No. Attacking them while they are in a corner? Nope. Automatically that limits the things you can do for a tactical advantage by a huge amount compared to other tactics games.
Sure, you still can make intelligent decisions and they still do have an effect on the game... it's just less than it could have been if the developers included some of these things. A lot less. So the smartest tactic in this game for the majority of situations would be to consolidate your units in one group as soon as you can (not a hard thing usually, given movement speeds compared to map size in thsi game) and mobbing the first enemy unit you see. This is exacerbated by the fact that the AI seems to recognize this as well, and tends to immediately move all or at least a large majority of thier units towards the first of your units they see. This strangles my ability to affect the outcome of the game, and puts most of it into the hands of rng and my units' stats instead of choices I make during the fight, even in pvp.
It's true that the optional objectives for the mission will occasionally encourage you to split up, or at least do something slightly more complicated than mobbing the enemy, but they are usually more trouble than they're worth. I understand the fact that optional objectives ought to be difficult and not always possible, but what happens in Mordheim is that the act of pursuing the optional objectives will sometimes cause you to Fail the optional objectives. I know. Mindboggling.
The first optional is to steal the enemies' idol and take it to your cart, but merely taking the idol off its pedestal heavily penalizes the enemies' morale, often causing them to route and forfeit the match to you, giving you the victory before you can take the idol back to your cart and get the extra objective done. This happens often early and midgame even if you've only killed a minimal number of thier units. It become slightly less of a problem late game, but can still be an issue.
The second optional objective with this problem is the Marked for Death, which has you target one or more enemy units and steal a bounty token they are holding. The units chosen are usually the leader and hero. Guess what happens if an enemy leader or hero is killed? Yep, you guessed it, a hefty reduction to morale. About half the time you can loot the enemy in the same turn you kill them, but the half the time you can't do so (due to being engaged with another enemy or just running out of action points) you automatically forfeit that.
The third optional objective is item collection, its only problem is that it's boring.
What else? Right, the enemy has an unlimited inventory, whereas you will probably only have space for 3 items early campaign and maybe 5-7 late. The gist of this is that if the enemy kills one of your units and isn't immediately engaged with another of your units, they will loot your guy for all of thier weaponry and items, and if you kill them, you might not be able to pick it back up because of limited inventory space. So if you win and kill the enemy that looted your stuff, some of the time you lose most or all of that stuff anyway because they route before you can grab it or the unit you have over it already has other stuff in thier inventory.
The game has scaling Offense points with level and whether or not the unit is a henchman or hero. It also has different Offense Points costs for different weaponry types like ranged, dual-wielding, single-handed or two-handed. This leads to strange power spikes and valleys, most notable the fact that ranged henchman are pretty useless until level 3 when they suddenly go from being able to attack once per turn to twice per turn, effectively doubling thier damage. Also, before level 3 dual-wielding and two-handed melee henchmen can attack once, and at 3 they still can only attack once per turn. But after level 3 a single-handed henchman can attack twice, thus doing comparable damage while having more defense. Why? Just why? It's so gamey to have to suddenly switch up weapon load outs because your character leveled up.
Approximately a third of the skills in the game are wastes of space (read: every active endurance skill except for insanity, skills that increase your chance to climb, fall, and expecially leap. leaping is useless). Most of the other skills and spells are kind of boring, even if they're decently good.
Yes, I understand there are ways to get around some of these issues. I've used these methods. But those ways are stupid as hell. These issues just shouldn't exist in the first place. Yes, they make the game harder, and I like a challenge. However, not everything that's hard is a challenge, sometimes it's just a ♥♥♥♥ing chore.
