The game is fun but it's
! I never thought I'd say that about a game, but it takes probably 200+ hours to unlock everything with a single warband, and after about 60 hours with a single warband it starts to feel very grindy. I have almost everyone in my warband up to the maximum level, but it'll still probably take another 100+ hours to reach top rank with the various guilds. I wish I could win a playthrough with a single warband in maybe 30 hours so I could move on to another type of warband, but as it is I feel like I'll have to just give up on my current warband without finishing and I really wish I didn't have to do that. Most people probably don't have enough free time and motivation to finish the game. It'd be nice if the game had an option to change the overall length.
That said, the combat and mechanics are very solid. Each warband type plays differently and there are a lot of skills and weapons to choose from to customize your group. Some skills are clearly more effective than others, but within each type of warband there are many ways of playing. The risk versus reward is well-balanced, and the game has a good feeling of progression as you become stronger and able to take on harder missions and take bigger risks within those missions. You won't be able to win by getting stronger than the AI because the AI scales with you and is almost always stronger than you are. (They have the same number of points you do plus a hefty damage bonus.) Your wins will be based on having better tactics and synergy between your skills and characters. Luck is a big factor too, but player skill can overcome bad luck in almost all cases, at least once your warband is developed. (Early on, expect to lose a lot of characters.)
The graphics and sound are good - not amazing but definitely good enough for me. The level design does a good job of depicting a city corrupted by evil forces. One downside is the map, which doesn't always clearly show which ways you can go, especially if you're playing a warband that depends on vertical movement.
Some people complained about the game's controls. There are quirks and it's possible to get stuck on terrain for a turn if you're exploring inside a building, but once you learn how it works it's rarely a problem. I thought the controls were pretty good, overall, but I do wish it did a better job of choosing default actions so I could avoid a bunch of unnecessary button presses each turn.
The DLC at $10 per warband type is fairly expensive. I suppose one could argue that each new warband type adds another 200 hours to the game, but most of that time is just grind. I think they'd be worth getting on sale if you really like the base game.
Unfortunately, the game gets so grindy in the end that I almost can't recommend it, but if you like turn-based tactics games and you're okay with giving up before the end or if you have a huge amount of time to waste, then it's definitely worth trying.

This game has scratched an itch that I didn't even know that I had...
I bought this on sale on a whim (i.e. had enough Steam credit that it didn't hurt to buy) despite actually having marked it as "Not Interested" in one of my discovery queues. But as I have been waiting for X-COM 2: War of the Chosen to come out, this one popped up as a recommendation. I decided to give it a chance and I have been blown away!
It's not overly polished, and frankly it's very repetitive in gameplay (deploy your warriors and scoop up as much loot as possible before the inevitable battle begins and hope to God that the RNG is favorable, praying that no one in your team gets permanently injured or at worse dead). However, I am finding myself nearing 70 hours of gameplay and I still don't feel I have scratched the surface of all the game seems to offer. I am currently on my fourth warband, haven't even tried any of the "campaign" missions, haven't even touched any of the other warband types other than the mercenaries, and I still can't wait to get back to it for just one more journey into the City of the Damned to try my luck and skill just one more time hoping to get to the next warband level, getting more experience for that lower level grunt, and hoping to find that one superior looted item that will make you a little more stronger the next time you go in for more of the same.
It's a numbers game as much as a skill game and I am loving it! My first two warbands went horribly wrong and my third one actually started to get reasonably strong before I decided it was time to scrap it too after all of the lessons I had learned on what not to do in my first failed attempts. And that's when the game really starts to come into its own. Unfortunately the game can be very, very unforgiving to a newbie such as myself and that's what keeps a lot from going on further with it. I can understand why so many are turned off by it but also see why there are those dedicated players who have also literally put a thousand hours and more into this one. The ecstasy of a well fought victory as well as the utter dismay at a battle gone wrong are an addicting contrast, though I have finally really been learning to have more victories than defeats (around 90% won with my current warband) with the occasional disappointing fallout for an injured warrior even under victory conditions.
This game is definitely not for everyone. I can understand that. But if you are looking for a game that really makes you think out strategy as you position your warrior pieces and the tacticts to get them there, this is a game for you. Even a small skirmish can take extra time now that I have learned more about the game mechanics and the opponent AI. If you know where to look and are patient, you can make good judgments about where the enemy will be. You can know pretty much what you are up against and position your warriors accordingly. Also, learning tips such as stay together, don't always ambush, and don't be afraid to disengage or even flee from battle at times, can make a big difference after failing to do some of these things the first time(s) through.
Also, mitigating damage, is something you need to be prepared to do. There are some great skills and some awesome buffs, but be aware that almost everything has its negative effects as well. Do you take the potion or leave it at camp? Do you apply this enhancement or save it for later knowing that weapon or armor might be the next to be lost? Do you spend the gold for that skill that could be lost forever when you get unlucky with that warrior the next time you send them out. It's loss manager's dream! The first time you cast a spell and have your warrior permanently knocked out for the rest of the battle is one of the worst feelings you can have. However, when you see the enemy attempt to do the same thing but not only stuns himself, but also your three warriors that are currently pummeling on him, you just have to smile (the enemy still ended up being toast that very same round). It really is a masochist's dream, but I am now convinced you can get better at this game despite the random nature of so many of its events. I haven't even come close to experiencing all I can with this warband, and I am already envisioning which one I want to start with for the next playthrough AFTER I finish at least the first and maybe second campaign mission with this one.
To be honest, recommending a game like this which has almost absolutely no story and absolutely no purpose other than building up the most versatile and ferocious warband you can actually seems ludicrous to me, but I still can't recommend it enough. If you don't want to pay full price to try it, I understand, but you might actually like it. I liked it so much that despite buying the base game on sale, I missed the sale for the DLC, but bought it at full price anyway (a reason for many of the negative reviews you might be reading) because I have truly enjoyed it that much and didn't want to have to wait for the DLC to come back down in price again before trying it.
You have been warned. This game is definitely not for everyone. Some will wish it had never been programmed. But some of you on the edge just need to give it a try and you might very well find yourself as sucked into it as I have been. Just one more mission into the City of the Damned!!

I've found myself warming to this since I wrote the last 'review'.
While I still won't recomend it (Mostly because of AoS2 being localized) I can say that the soundtrack isn't as bad as I first pointed out, now that I listen to it outside of the game I find myself liking it but seriously, that VIsitors mix (Used for the title screen) is awful.
AI isn't great, most characters can be beaten by sitting on top of the screen as Saki and carpet bombing them with her maracas, looking into the situation of this translation/Steam release (I.E. looking at a translated page on Orange_Juice's website) reviels that a character was added for the Steam release, this character happens to be Sora, who has the most broken AI in the game and from what I can remember was very difficult to play as, which makes me wonder why the AI was so difficult to vurse. Then again, it may be because I was still very bad at Suguri at the time. "Why?" Before anyone asks 'How do you know Sora was added?' I will say this, she has no dialouge, never apears in either of the stories and is only found after clearing one (Or both, I did them one after another and thus wouldn't properly know) of the stories, even QP gets some dialouge in the second story.
Art! In the story dialogue the artstyle changes completely, to something more reminiscent of 200% Mixed Juice with the pixels toned down by quite a lot, I even think they recycled a couple of images for 200% from this, this different artstyle works for me... somehow, again I can't say why I liked it, maybe because it was different from the other art and came as a bit of a shock to me.
The main Story is much more laid back then in Suguri, it does have it's funny moments, where as Suguri tried to be very serious at all points, but flopped when a midget calls another midget 'short'.
The second story...
No I should stop and complain again, why not stay on topic with the stories?
There are two of them, both with 6-7 fights in them, and with each fight on a 90 second timer along with the game being generally easy even a bad Suguri player can get through them on easy very quickly... While this review has gone on for way too long than it needed too I feel I should write a conclusion. So, here it goes.
Since writing my first (Very poor) review I've warmed to the game, and mostly it's soundtrack, it's AI ranges from pitifully easy to very difficult but there is no middle ground. There is a slightly confusing story as to why Sora is a playable character which revolves around the fact that the game was six years old when it was first localized and eight years old when put on to Steam, the actual story has some comedic vibes to it and ends rather abrubtly, the story modes end very quickly and are very short, a joypad or controler is recomendable for a few aspects of the gameplay, the multiplayer that the game is sold on was poorly done, may have LAN support and dosen't have any lobby system, requring you to directly connect to an IP and a port.
I just remembered, there is another aspect of the game that I havent touched on. Besides from the story modes there is a larger story telling aspect with this game, a series of unlockable cutscenes featuring a character talking in the first person, telling their story, answering some questions about the lore of the entire series, the first one you unlock is Suguri telling her story, there will be spoilers here, for the entire series.
Some time after the end of Sora's seventh stage (Max six years) Suguri wakes up for the first time in six years, she has been given her powers and is ready to fix, single handidly, the destruction caused by the war Sora fought so hard to stop. She gets given a mirror and remarks about how her eyes have turned red at some point between before being operated on and that moment in time. Suguri's dad, of whom she talks so highly of during the events of the first game, explains that she has been 'asleep' (I.E. In a coma) for six years, Suguri remarks that she is now "old enough to drink" (Seeing as the drinking age in Japan is 21 we can estimate that she was placed into a coma at least by the age of 15) From this comment Suguri's dad decides to throw a party, to celebrate his daughter waking up, the repair of the earth, and the six birthdays Suguri missed out on. So the first thing Suguri would do after waking up from a six year coma is help her dad cook. Suguri then remarks that she acknowledges that if she takes care of herself she could live for "hundreds of even thousands of years". Jump forward many years, right to the end of the first game, just before fighting Hime, she mentions that she is "over ten thousand years old", Suguri simply replies "Same." Giving a big thumbs up on this one. Only in my WRC2 career so far but what an improvement over the previous two releases by this developer. Their first attempt WRC 5 was truly godawful, the second WRC 6 was a dramatic improvement but still lots of gamebreaking moments like driving at night and in bad weather the graphics didn't stand up. I am delighted to say that third time is the charm. There are still minor flaws but this is a GREAT game at a GREAT price. Having said that is it Dirt Rally no, and it doesn't try to be. It even plays smooth as butter on my laptop with a GTX 960m, even though I know some higher end rigs had stuttering issues, but I had none and it does seem the developers are working hard to iron out the very few bugs that are there. First of all, I'm not a Sim-gamer. I'm playing with keyboard. Therefore I can't and don't want to rate the wheel-driving physics of this game. But I can tell that this game has absolutely fulfilled nearly all of my expectations. I have played all WRC games before. None of them have been left more than 30 minutes on my PC. Somehow, WRC 7 for the first time hit the goal and found the way to my heart. The graphics are astonishing, sometimes I've just searched my chins under the table. The lights, the particle effects and the great track design together creates an atmosphere which I have never seen before in any rally game.
(Dirt 4 graphics are nothing to this, maybe the rain effects could have been polished a bit in WRC 7.)
I also fully satisfied with the content regarding the countries and tracks, however, we could use some more cars, because the list is pretty weak (I know, that official ars are included, but still, couldn't they be just added from previous years as well?). I also satisfied with the voices, engine and background sounds, here I can only complain for the co-pilot voice, which is a bit frustrating. With keyboard I did not have any issues to drive the cars through the tracks, I got used to the handling within 10-15 minutes.
Finally after 17 hours of gaming, I'm not disturben by the flag rules, however a bit more agressive damage modell could be added to the game.
But most importantly, I can't explain the feeling when I started my first round in WRC 7. I've felt nostalgy for some early Colin Mcrae rally games, I've felt rejoice about the graphics and car handling, I've felt...This is It!
Overall I think that with the 7th game in the series, WRC games are at the finish line to finally beat the DiRT series and be one of the best rally games. Of course there were some minor technical issues in the background, and the game could use some more optimization to eleiminate strange stuttering effect at some points, but the developers are already released their third update and the game is getting better and better. Hopefully they will not stop here and add more patches to the game. Nowadays when no game is released without issues, I think this can be forgiven :) Codemasters should really do their best if they want to stay on the throne.
My best regards to the developers! Keep-up the excellent job!

WRC 7 makes good on the promises of WRC 6. I bought WRC 6 thinking it might be a nice game to play around with when not playing Dirt Rally. But the handling was too erratic (albeit with promise), the stages were wide and too arcadey, and the FFB was really bad.
Happy to say that WRC 7 improves on WRC 6 in every regard.
Car handling is up there on par with Dirt Rally. The feeling of the tyres digging into the gravel is not quite up to DRs levels, but the distinct grip level changes between different gravel types is real nice. Tarmac handling feels quite nice and believable. The cars feel like they have mass, and weight transfer is modeled nicely. Overall the handling has been a big surprise, and overall I find it more believable than DRs.
The stages are quite nice overall, much tighter and more technical than WRC 6. There aren't a lot of stages for each location, so I suspect they'll be feeling stale after a while (like in DR), but they're varied and distinct and many of them are absolutely fantastic. While I personally give DR a slight edge with their real to life stages, there are some stages in WRC 7 that I feel are better than DRs. And the epic stages are awesome, so much fun to finally drive long stages.
FFB is much better than WRC 6, but still nothing to write home about. I'd call it adequate on my T300RS. Not much to adjust, and it feels a bit like canned effects. Still, when you get the levels right (I found about 50% strength felt right) it works quite OK and communicates what the car does in a decent way. So fully functional, but can get better.
Codriver calls are overall OK. I find that I can trust them overall, and I seldom get caught out on bad notes. There are times when the note pace gets a bit off, but generally OK. Codriver voice is a bit sterile and machine-like, hopefully something they can improve for the next game.
Graphics are OK, neither good nor bad. Car models and stages look OK in general but "wow" moments are rare (there are some, like Mexico).
Sounds are OK. Gravel kickup and tyre squeals are good, as are brake sounds. Engine sounds range from slightly bad too OK. Some sounds feel quite off, like the loud bang when the suspension punches through that just sounds completely wrong. Crash sounds are also very muted and undramatic.
Stability wise I had some troubles for the first week, where I was one of many that got the heavy stutters even though I have real good hardware. Big Ben handled the problem well though, got a thread up about the problem and got some testers fast. New patch came out which fixed the problems for the vast majority and it seems to be trouble free now.
Overall I'd highly recommend this title for any rally fan. Surprise hit game of the year so far for me.

Absolver has wonderfull combat mechanics, and if your a dark souls player this game will come naturally to you. Of course sometimes the combat animations dont seem to work quite right, but its a minor concern and often the animations work quite well. 1v1 combat is fun and where this game truly shines, though combat with groups can also be fun if you approach it from the right angle or if you have friends.
The graphics are decent though if you dont have a great GPU (like me) you'll find that youll have to lower the settings, though on the lower settings the game sometimes has graphical errors (Small sprite issues and light flickering mainly.) That being said the game is perfectly playable on the lowest settings if you dont mind the lighting changing in a few buggy corners of the map.
The audio is great, both the music and the sound effects are well done and fit the mood of the game. Unfortuantely sometimes it seems as if the music is a little lacking in between fights.
Customization in this game is good, most clothing sets look good, and you can mix and match items fairly well. The armour isnt necissarily great from a realism perspective, but few items in this game are flat out ugly.
The bosses can be a bit of a letdown (I beat all of them first try) but the fights will grab your attention at the very least.
In the end Absolver is a fun game, that could use a few more patches here or there, but is pretty solid as it is. It's a bit short so you shoudl proboboly wait till a sale, but the main life of the game is supposed to be the PVP matches. In Dark souls terms it captures a similar feel of the combat and the co-op really feels like dark souls in some instances. It's worth a play if you like souls like games, though it'll lack the same oppressive difficulty if thats what your seeking.

Rochard is just about my favorite puzzle-platformer of all time (though now it has to share that honor with The Swapper).  This game pretty much fell through the cracks when it was released, and it's a shame, because it's a delightful pleasure almost all the way through.  The main mechanic is a special gun which gives the hero (John Rochard, a working-class stiff beautifully voice-acted by Jon St. John) the power to grab things at a distance (like the gravity gun from Half Life 2), control gravity, swing himself into the air, toss people around (eventually) and so on.  The gun also can be used as a gun, and the main weakness of the game is an occasional overreliance on straight combat instead of puzzle-solving.  However, eventually you learn to combine both fighting and environment manipulation while playing, and then the game is serious fun.  It's also light enough and short enough for casual gamers (like me). I wish enough people would play this so we could get a sequel.

Although the game overstays its welcome imo, it was a highly enjoyable experience from start to finish. What I mean is that when you start to get to the later levels it seems like it's never going to end. It seems like it lasted much longer than the 6 hours it took me to beat it. However I suppose that isn't entirely a bad thing because most games it seems are too short nowadays.
Rochard takes a great idea and turns it into a great game. Your beam gun and eventually laser attack gun are a lot of fun to use to figure out puzzles. I never really found the game challenging. Pretty easy actually, but still fun. Most indie game purposely try to be hard it seems nowadays so having a fun casual experience was a welcome change. It isn't too super easy though. Some parts are a little challenging. The music is pretty good and the sound effects are good, and the voice acting is great. The effects are done well and the game looks really nice too. Overall it looks more like a AAA game than a indie game. If you want a real challenge get the hard times dlc. I tried it for a little bit and it has some challenging puzzles and stuff, but I got my fill with the main game and am moving on since I have a ton of other games to play through.

To all intents and purposes, this is Darkest Dungeon in 3D, with all that entails. It looks good, the environments are interesting and detailed, and the atmosphere is delightfully dark, with some wicked humour lurking beneath the surface. Warband building and customisation is extensive, with new options and toys being drip-fed to you at precisely the right rate - you are rarely overwhelmed with options, and there are always new toys you can get after 'just one more game'.
On the negative side, the UI and controls can be fiddly, the AI can occasionally be a bit daft (although hardly a game-breaker), and like DD, you have to watch out for RNGesus - If he is against you, you'll suffer. That said, even these defeats add character to the game - My Vampire lord lost an arm on his third outing and I couldn't afford to replace him at that point. So I rebuilt him as a dodge-tank instead, and now Wilhelm the One-Armed Vampire is the terror of the Merchant Quarter!
If I had one major complaint, it would be the warband story missions - some are very good, but others are a brutal, unforgiving slog. (Looking at you, library missions).
At heart, this is an interactive board-game. Bear that in mind, and it's easy to overlook it's faults and have a blast leading your merry band of murderous miscreants through the City of the Damned.
(Although I do have to make a complaint about false advertising - to the uninitiated, the screenshots might suggest there are Skaven in this game. Everyone knows that there is no such thing of course, and anyone who says otherwise is a vile heretic!) See you on the streets!

Hmm. This is a bit of a complicated one. It’s not a complication that stems from trying to explain what Resident Evil 4 is, because that’s fairly easy to do – it's a survival horror and action hybrid, seeing you taking on hordes of violent villagers and sinister cultists in a mission to rescue the president’s daughter from a dark and terrible plot. Nor does the problem come from gauging the general public opinion surrounding it, which essentially sees it lauded as being absolutely brilliant and arguably one of the best games ever made. The fact of the matter is that the complication lies in the simple fact that despite this nigh-on critical acclaim, and against my best efforts, I... Uh... Don’t really like it very much.
It took me a little while to work out why. At first I thought it was the story; after all, the voice acting is laughably awful, and there are not so much plot holes here as much as there are plot ravines. Yet after the initial wave of cheesy lines were spoken in a manner that made me facepalm so hard my hand nearly came bursting out the back of my head, the sheer audaciousness of how bad the plot is becomes somewhat charming. This is a schlocky, over the top B-movie experience and the game knows it, with so many quotable lines being flung your way that any initial scepticism soon fades away into unbridled joy for the whole camp spectacle.  Nor was my problem the sound design, which is non-ironically excellent - with chanting, foreboding music and much more working together to create quite a menacing atmosphere throughout the whole journey.
My problem, it turns out to be, purely stems from the gameplay and level design choices that are on display here. There are just so many little issues and bugbears consistently appearing throughout, that they mar the core enjoyment that comes from merely shooting the bad guys in the face. To provide examples; some areas require you to stand and fight while others require you to flee, and often it takes far too long to differentiate between the two. In cases of fleeing, there’s no point even trying to put up any sort of combat effort, because enemies will just continue to infinitely spawn without warning. And, despite the escort sections being reasonably thought out, there were still too many moments which felt like I failed purely due to the AI behaviour being a little too unpredictable.
On the issue list grows, with even core concepts of the game floundering - I don't mind the idea of not being able to move when firing, but the reality is it doesn't actually translate into gameplay that’s particularly riveting. It's more of a case of fire at the enemies, run away a bit when they get close, then repeat the cycle. This comes to a head with the boss fights, whereupon in most situations you can dodge these eldritch abominations and their devastating attacks by simply slowly jogging past them.
There's also so many rooms and areas that feel as if they only exist to burn away your time in some fashion – most of the roadblocks to your journey simply require you to get the funny shaped key for the funny shaped door, and that never proves to be a simple point A to point B endeavour. At one point I even came across a hedge maze and was struck with an overwhelming desire to simply turn the game off, such was my certainty in knowing I’d have to wander around for far too long shooting enemies that were practically destined to appear.  Anyone familiar with this game should also know exactly what I mean when I say "water room”, and I'm not having you argue that as the pinnacle of excellent level design.
I’ll concur none of gameplay faults listed above are truly horrific, and perhaps some of you out there would even find them endearing – defining traits of the series as a whole. Yet to me they just lower Resident Evil 4 down to a level that for the most part I would describe as “distinctly average” – a far cry from the flawless masterpiece that I was perhaps expecting to encounter.
There's a reason why I think this doesn't feel like a stellar experience nowadays, however. Oddly enough, I think it stems from the fact that back at the time of its initial release, it was the
stellar experience.
was the game that invented the idea of the over-the-shoulder perspective in third person games.
was the game that also created the precision aiming system that went hand-in-hand with such a perspective. Heck, it could even be argued that it was this game which made quick time events into something that you can’t escape from in most action titles even to this day. If Resident Evil 4 didn’t exist, you most likely wouldn't have titles such as Gears of War. Or Uncharted. You certainly wouldn't have had a series such as Dead Space, and I could keep going with this list if you had several hours to spare.
Put simply, it was the title that set the benchmarks. Yet by doing so, it also devised the means by which it inadvertently shot itself in the foot. You see, so many games have since taken those benchmarks, and refined and honed them via a great deal of time and effort into something that approaches perfection. To therefore go from playing the polished titles of today to the system that's in place here... Well, it can't help but feel like a step backwards, a regression into something that can no longer hope to provide the same sense of satisfaction. In many ways, I feel like Resident Evil 4 should be considered a museum piece; something that should be respected, remembered, and admired. It's just perhaps not something that should be taken out of its case all that often.
In summary, if you were to turn to me and ask me to recommend a good action title or survival horror, I'm not going to turn back round to you and say that you should be giving Resident Evil 4 a whirl. I simply ended up confused and frustrated too often for me to say I had fun with it, despite what it manages to do right. That, however, doesn't mean I don't respect the game for what it is and what it managed to do to the industry. If you're looking for a piece of history or a trip down memory lane, you've come to the right place. Otherwise, I'd think twice before taking the plunge.

Resident Evil 4 is a game that I have played for years back when it first came out on Gamecube and to this day, I still find it a game that I have highly enjoyed after over a decade. This particular PC port of the game is great, but it does have its fair share of problems that do hold it back from being perfect.
For just the game itself, Resident Evil 4 is definitely a game that is easy to get into plot wise if you did not play the previous Resident Evil games. There are references and a few things that only the older games can explain, but if you are new to the series, you can easily grasp what is going on in the main plot at least. Really all you need to know is the basic premise, you play as Leon Kennedy, you are sent to retrieve the U.S. President's daughter who has been kidnapped and is in Spain being held by a cult of parasitically infected people. That's all you need to know and it is a good plot with some admittedly enjoyable conversations between characters here and there. The gameplay is what really kept me playing the game for over the years of playing it since it first came out. It played like every other Resident Evil game with pressing one button to aim and the other to shoot, but this was the first game in the series to have the over-the-shoulder camera that allowed you to aim for body parts of enemies which they reacted to accordingly depending on where you shot them and you could kick them or even suplex them. You could carry much more, the merchant to purchase weapons and a few select items and also upgrading those weapons. It was still challenging and it was a mix of horror and action. Even with how action packed it was, there were times that I did feel some fear or uneasyness. Each of the 3 main locations of the game, the Village, Castle, and Island, have a good amount of length to them and I never did find myself bored with any of them. The main game itself will last anywhere from 7-10, depending on difficulty, rather you want to go for side treasures, and how thorough you're going through each area of the 3 locations.
On this port of the game, the controls, in my personal opinion are good for the most part. Using the mouse to aim and shoot, shift to run, W and S to move forward and back, A and D to move, and Space bar to use the knife. What was weird though was the inventory controls. WASD moves you in the inventory and enter to pick up and move an object, but to turn an object in a direction to have it more easily fit is mapped to the Pgdn/Page Downbutton. I will not understand why of all buttons it is Page Down is the button to do this. What could've been better was Q and E and I have to wonder why Capcom didn't make it them. Aiming did feel a bit weird as in it kinda felt sluggish sometimes, but it's something that I can easily get used to. As far as I also remember, there were no ways to rebind keys in the options and I can assume you can through the .ini files, but it's not exaclty practical. QTEs are controlled with X, C, and the mouse, and again, these work fine for the most part. There was one instance that I can remember where something really was off about it, and that was near the end of the Castle during the Salazar Statue Chase sequence on the bridge that leads to the final area of the Castle. You have to rapidly press X to keep yourself from falling, and I do not know what is up with this part because I pressed X as fast as I did in other sections that require you to rapidly press it, and failed just this section multiple times. In my experience, I would say that using a controller is better for this game as it makes QTEs better, it's not as weird to move stuff around in the inventory, and it feels better with the aiming.
Returning mini-games from past versions of the game are Assignment Ada, The Mercenaries, and Separate Ways/The Another Order.  For those who do not know, Assignment Ada is where you play as, of course, Ada and you have to collect 5 samples from a certain sections on the Island and you can not upgrade or purchase new weapons. The Mercenaries is where you pick a character and stage and you have to get as many points before time expires and if you get a certain rank at the end then you'll unlock a new character. Separate Ways is basically an unlockable side story, it plays out like the main game, except it's shorter, you can buy and sell, but can't upgrade weapons, you play as Ada, and it shows what she did behind the scenes in the story in the span of 5 small chapters. Now I do have one big annoyance between this side stuff, and it is just with Separate Ways and it's something that also happens in the game, albeit not nearly as much. Every single cutscene, every single last one of them, is pre-rendered and not rendered in-game and the quality of the cutscenes are not really good. I would actually say that its bad, and the jump in quality from in-game and to pre-rendered is very noticable. They looked fine back then, but the jump to HD did not take well to the pre-rendered cutscenes.
There's also another weird thing that happens with the game and it's with the sniper rifles, and quite possibly with Minethrower, but I have no idea since I haven't used it. For whatever reason, both of the sniper rifles in the game have some weird FPS issues. Both of them have lag when reloading, and also after every single shot with the bolt-action. With the semi-auto, it only affects the gun as everything else will move at normal speed while the semi-auto reload just looks like it is lagging, and I think it's even worse with the bolt-action and I think, although I can't quite remember, actually lags the entire game.
As for Ashley's AI since she's one of the main parts of the game as you escort around the entire game, in my personal opinion her AI is not bad. She always tries to stay right behind you and follows right behind you, and she crouches down if you ever aim in her direction. She'll hide, stay in one place, or follow you when told. However there were times where she stayed crouched for a while even though I wasn't aiming and she could easily run away from enemies, but those barely ever happened.
Weapons that you will be using in the game range from different types. You have 4 different types of handguns, 3 shotguns, 2 sniper rifles, 1 SMG, and 2 magnums, and this is not counting the unlockable weapons. Each of the weapons feel unique in their own way, so much that even the weakest of guns have their own strengths that does give some sort of incentive to try out each one. For example, the standard pistol you get in the game is weak, but it has a change of popping heads easy when fully upgraded, while the Punisher pistol is weaker, but it can shoot through multiple enemies, or the Riot Shotgun has a tighter spread and has better range than the other 2 shotguns, but the Striker Shotgun has largest magazine capacity. It's not hard to tell that some guns are better than others, but each gun acts a bit differently and each one can be useful in someway or another.
There's not much that I can say about this game really. It's a solid fun game with a good story with some enjoyable moments, has a nice blend of horror and action, various enemy types and bosses, 3 locations that are expansive and you'll feel in a way that you are going on some sort of adventure, various types of guns that act differently, different enemy varieties, and the game has plenty of content to play.
In short, I do recommend this game to the highest for both fans of the Resident Evil games or people who are new to the series.

A very nice surprise this year. I had abandoned the WRC series after 4, but now that rally games have been having something of a renaissance since Dirt Rally, it's good to see that the WRC series has upped their game.
The game was marred by a terrible stuttering issue upon release, but a recent patch (September 26th) fixed it in my system. With a 6-year old i5-2500k and a Geforce 970, I can play the game at very high settings and 60FPS without any issues.
The content is what one would expect - stages (including SSS) from all the locations of the WRC, and cars from the Junior WRC, WRC2 and WRC itself. There is a serviceable career mode, and daily stages. I haven't touched the multiplayer part of the game yet.
Graphics and sound are good, if not spectacular. It is unfortunate that apparently motion blur can't be disabled on replays, and FOV can't be adjusted comprehensively, which is a big sin.
But! It drives excellently (I am using an X360 controller - haven't tried it with a wheel yet), the stages are varied and mostly very interesting, so the rallying itself is great, and that's what counts. This is really what makes WRC a very good game.
One should note that there's nothing in the way of a tutorial or rally school, only a (somewhat flawed) test to determine your "skill level", so if you're absolutely new to rally games, you're in for a bit of a learning curve.
I would like some sort of DLC pack with extra stages. (but then again, everyone would always like more stages for rally games!)
If you don't own Dirt Rally yet, I'd still recommend getting it first instead of this game because of the much more varied car selection.
However, if you already have Dirt Rally, or if you're only interested in the actual WRC cars, it's almost surprising to say that this game is a no-brainer. Get it, you'll have fun. (I don't own Dirt 4 so I can't include it in the comparison).

Dirt Rally fanboys need not bother, you are never going to like or play another rally game.
For those who actually enjoy rally games, not just 'a' rally game, WRC 7 is the best game in the series so far. It's worth playing if you know what you are getting.
Disclosure: I play the game with a gamepad, in cockpit view, and with an Nvidia GTX 960 card.
I'm also playing this in single-player only, since I don't care about multiplayer gaming.
So what's new and improved?
The first two things I noticed was that the roads are narrower and bumpier. I also feel that there is a stronger sense of momentum behind the car, for example when you go downhill you have to brake earlier than you would in WRC 6. There's a stronger sense of weight behind it.
These combine to make the stages even more challenging than they were in WRC 6, and in my opinion much tougher than the stages in both Dirt Rally and Loeb Rally.
The third thing I noticed was that the AI seems more balanced. In WRC 6 things were either too easy or too hard. WRC 7 feels more balanced, where 'medium' actually feels like medium.
Lastly, the road surfaces have a stronger difference to them than in WRC 6. For example, driving on certain gravel stages feels quite slippery, which is how it is in reality.
So what's bad?
I tried the bumper camera view and had noticeable framerate drops. Not serious enough to hurt my driving performance, but enough to be noticeable. I did not have this issue in cockpit view.
The game defaults to a steering aid on some difficulty settings. These kind of aids have never worked well in *any* racing game in my opinion, whether it's Dirt Rally, Loeb Rally, F1 or MotoGP. It makes the steering feel very odd. You can disable it by picking a higher difficulty.
So what's more or less the same?
The graphics are only marginally better than in WRC 6, which already looked great to me.
There are more details in the environment though, for example driving in one of the Polish stages you'll see a swarm of flies or mosquitoes as you enter and exit a corner. Smaller details like that.
The content is quite similar to WRC 6, some stages feel familiar, most do not. Similar teams, game modes, and country locations. WRC is a real-life event, so naturally the game is limited in terms of content compared to the Dirt and Loeb games. I would draw parallels to the F1 and MotoGP games here.
All the weather and daytime effects are the same as before: fog, dust, rain, snow, night racing, etc. I also don't notice much difference in the damage model, except that repairing things take longer than in WRC 6, and is thus more punishing than before (since you have a time-limit for repairs).
On the whole the driving physics model is not astonishingly different from WRC 6, it's not like going from Dirt 3 to Dirt Rally for example. To most people it's probably 'more of the same' really. The main change is the above-mentioned momentum effect. Again, I would draw parallels to the F1 and MotoGP games; a few tweaks here and there.
If you haven't played a WRC game before I would compare the driving physics to the Dirt 1-4 games. Dirt 1 and 4 being the closest matches. It is not as difficult to handle as Dirt Rally and Loeb Rally.
I feel the main challenge in WRC 7 comes from the stage designs, not the actual driving physics. This is complete opposite of Dirt Rally and Loeb Rally, where the physics *is* the challenge.
So there's a different philosphy behind the game's development. They made the game highly intuitive to play, where you don't have to think that much about the car behaving badly, and can focus more freely on the road. The big challenge comes from the narrow and bumpy roads, the hazards that are close to the road, and stages that are very difficult to master at speed.
The philosophy behind Dirt Rally and Loeb Rally is the completely opposite; you have to learn to become good, and pay full attention to every movement the car makes. The stage designs are not as freaky and wild as in WRC 7.
So why play WRC 7 if you have never played a WRC game before?
* The content is different, with different stage designs and countries to drive around in.
* The physics is different, 'yes' this is a positive thing. Why on Earth would you want every racing game to have the same or similar physics? that would be extremely boring.
* It simulates a real-life racing event, with all the roleplaying it brings, as with the F1 and MotoGP games. You get the real teams, drivers, and cars to immerse yourself with.
* It's fast-paced rally fun, where unlike Dirt Rally and Loeb Rally, you can really go for it. You don't really have to master a car, instead it's about mastering the road.

, but I honestly don’t see many other people enjoying it. I might be wrong, tho. But well, let me talk about my experience with this visual novel.
It’s a kinetic novel, you don’t make any choices and you only read about the MCs fate, Will. He goes to Japan to work as a researcher at a Japanese university, and there he meets his three coworkers: Yuri, a girl that loves water bears with a burning passion and talks about herself in third person; Suzukake, the main researcher and which also is very connected to Yuri; And there’s Yae.
The art style is gorgeous, I really have no complains. BGM was okay too, and the VA was awesome. The story starts very light and suddenly things change faster than you can say f*ck. The thing is,
makes no sense. Its contents are divided between three episodes (which covers Will’s coworkers routes), and none of them are connected. So it’s basically three different stories
. By the end of episode three, it gave me a feeling that all of the episodes were clues for the player to try to solve the big mystery of this VN. But I don’t know, it lacked something. Not that everything needs a clear answer (at least to me, a lot of readers like to have answers and that’s totally fine), but this title made me feel like I was reading a cheap rip off of Higurashi. The concept of Malus Code was somewhat intriguing to be honest, but in my opinion the writing was the biggest problem here. Things are so mysterious that it just ends up being like a total f*cking secret and you barely have hints of what’s happening. At some point it made me not care anymore about the mystery.
4/10. I only recommend this game when it’s on a big sale, if you like random creepy stories,
if you don’t mind unanswered questions. Also, I only gave a thumbs up because of Yuri’s story (the first episode).

Okay. I finished it. I think, anyways.  This damn thing was confusing as all Hell.
Overall, I'm on the fence about this little VN.  Unfortunately, I feel that the negatives outweigh the positives, so I'm saying "steer clear"; unless you get it in some form of a bundle or *HEAVY* discount.
First, on the plus side, the graphics are top notch. Yuri is cute, Suzukake is naughty-librarian hot, and Yae makes me feel funny and then I feel funny for feeling funny.
.  The VN utilizes the Emote system - which I'm definitely a fan of.  It helps bring the characters to life.  Going hand-in-hand is the fact that the 3 main characters (besides you) are also voice acted (in Japanese, as per usual).  Production-wise, Malus Code is great.  But that's about where the positives end.
The VN is kinetic, but also has 3 routes.  Yeah, I know it doesn't make sense.  Trust me, nothing in this makes any sense at all.  In order to access the 2nd and 3rd routes, you play through the first story (Yuri's).  It ends . . . abruptly/poorly/badly/stupidly/WTF-ly.  Then you get a new title image and start route 2.  I still don't get how these routes fit chronoligically. I'm going to assume they're more "alternate" endings and plots than anything else.  The problem is the game attempts to be very X-Files with it's "more-questions-than-answers" formula, but falls flat by basically just giving questions.  Mostly, the question is simply "huh?" and then it ends. I imagine it's intended to be creepy and mysterious, but it's really not.  It's bland and befuddling and nothing seems to have anything to do with anything else.
The characters themselves are odd at best.  There's not really much depth or even consistency to their personalities.  Well, that's not true.  Yuri always seems like a mental child, Suzukake is always kind of the hot-but-smart ♥♥♥♥♥, and Yae is . . . whatever the Hell Yae is. The mian problem seems to be with your character, Will. He's a student, or a researcher, or an agent of something or another.  I'm not sure really.  Truthfully, I just didn't care.  The "romance" is horribly forced and makes little sense.  One minute, Suzukake is scolding you and the next she's dressed as a succubus at a theme park on a date with you.  The Hell? And that's saying something because this game is chock full of "What the♥♥♥♥♥♥did I just read and why?" moments.
There are other issues as well (like the total lack of a coherent plot to individual routes, let alone a larger story arc), but I'll leave this there.  At this point, I think you get the picture that while pretty to look at, the game is a mess of randomness that is just plain bewildering.
TL;DR - Huh? What? No. Just . . .  what? No.

Where to begin, where to begin...
I was really ready to give this game a "mixed" score after I completed the second route, but after completing the whole story I seriously cannot recommend this game whatsoever. The story is split into 3 routes which each focus on a single character, there are no choices in this game (which I am fine with) but there is also a disproportionate amount of filler / story in each route (which I am not that ok with). The relationships that the game builds are vapid and just really uninteresting in general, there are obvious arcs to these relationships but they’re all really predictable with little to no conclusion. I am fine with a story being told in little chunks to make it more impactful, but the story segments that actually matter in this game (not the random chatter between our characters that does nothing but waste time) are seriously lacking in content. The game builds up this idea that there is something bigger going on beneath the surface of this supposedly cutesy charage game but it really just stops before anything that you may be questioning is explained. If you are confused and you expect something to be explained later you are going to be seriously disappointed because you will get no context or reasoning behind scenes that you see in the early game. Even the point where the genre shifts into horror it really didn’t feel that impactful and it just left me feeling confused, which is a feeling that persisted all throughout this game.

Acceleration of Suguri is the sequel to Japanese indie developer Orange_Juice's hit bullet hell game "Suguri". However, rather than make the game another bullet hell, Orange_Juice took an... odd path in making the sequel game a bullet hell and fighter hybrid. However, it worked out surprisingly well!
AoS is a bullet hell and fighter hybrid, however, it leans more to fighter than bullet hell. You choose your character before fighting, each with her own different playstyle, giving a nice variety to play around with. Each fight takes place in a circular arena, in which you are allowed to move in freely. There are various different attacks, each executeable by either pressing or holding the button or by dashing and then pressing the button. Most attacks are projectiles, but there are a few melee attacks. You can dash to get around the stage faster or to dodge energy-based projectiles (so don't try to rush through a missle). By doing damage, you can unlesh various different special attacks.
- Great music, all of which are remixes of songs from Suguri
- Nice artwork
- Responsive controls
- 7 playable characters at the start, and 5 more unlockable characters, for a total of 12, each with a vastly different playstyle

I am a Technical Support Specialist.  I usually do my work onsite, but I still feel some kinship to the fellow in this game.  I come face to face with people every day who have insurmountable problems that have severely impacted their ability to run their business.  I can usually resolve these issues with a simple Google search.  Sure, sometimes I run into real problems where I have to call on some dedicated hardware support, or developers whose software has so many dependencies it could be considered a welfare state, but what I specialize in, and the calls I am given most often, are “user error” issues.

Rochard never gained enough traction because of its small marketing efforts and smaller demographic, which is a shame because it's the quintessential small, charming indie puzzle platformer game with personality and care. This was one of the earliest games to utilize the Unity Engine. It benefits from it, and will feel current for many years.
Without its charming indie feel and homely 80s personality Rochard would've been just another, slightly above average, platformer. But some really symbiotic design and gameplay elements elevate this to something a little better than the rest.
* Great characters that didn't even need to have personality but were given tons
* Incredible voice acting for a game of this budget
* Above average lighting and background design
* Fairly challenging at times, brain required
* A good, 80s-feel soundtrack
Platformers are relatively simple in their design and tend to need combinations of good mechanics, unique or useful collectibles or alternative ways of solving things. Rochard suffers from a lack of these and often feels bland and samey.
* Very annoying AI and level manipulation at time, repeating the same mistake a few times is jarring when it's the game engines' fault
* Mechanics, despite working well, feel repetitive after so long
* Bland and slow paced at times
Rochard clocks in at 6 hours play time and doesn't have much re-playability, but it's relatively cheap; £7.99/8.99€/$9.99 at the time of review and it goes on sale for up to -90% regularly on Steam, so is definitely a buy at less than 1 Buck, Quid or Euro. It's available on mobile and a ton of other platforms and comes up in bundles, so look out for it being cheaper somewhere else if you care about a few cents.
* The
is pretty difficult and challenging, and only adds challenge maps. It's probably only worth considering buying after completing the full game.
* The voice of John Rochard is played by Jon St. John (
), who also helped voice elements of Duke Nukem, Dota 2, Sonic Adventures, Guild Wars 2 and Amnesia.

I love this game.
If it is your kind of game, you will understand me.
You level up your heroes until they are super tanky, or can hit hard or just stand on a rooftop and play sniper - but with one bad roll of the dice it's all gone. In my opinion, anyone who complains about the game's randomness being "unfair" has never played a similar boardgame based on dice. They ARE unfair! You always have a chance to fail miserably and make your charakter loose an arm.
It is a hard game. No question. The tutorials offer you an insight on the game mechanics, but there's still a lot to learn. You may fail with your first hero, but you'll know what to do with the next one. And honestly - I have a smuggler with only one leg and she's still running around and killing stuff. So don't worry too much about that.
Just give it time. Don't give up if it doesn't work for you when you play your first game!
Many reviews complain about the long loading times and the AI's turns being to long. Just think of the boardgame and its setup. It takes much much longer, and your opponent might take a lot of time thinking as well. The same happens to you here.
I'd love to play this game online against human opponents, but I already like it against the AI. I played it over 100 hours and there's still stuff for me to find out, so I'm excited to play a lot more!
Long story short: If you like strategy games that don't give you anything for granted but only if you work hard for it - pick this game up! If you don't, then don't.

I can say that Mordheim is one of top 5 most favourite games of mine and definiately the best game based on Games Workshop license.
The game will kick your balls, punch you in the face and spit on you, you thought that Dark Souls were hard? Nope, in DS you can master all of the skills to play it but in Mordheim there's this cold, unforgivable calculation in the gameplay. Oh, your hero have 95% chances of dodging the attacks? It would be shame if he wouldn't do that and die afterwards. Your sorcerer was casting a spell and you rolled really bad on the curse table? Puff, your character exploded just like that, -9999dmg.
But I highly recommend not giving up and keep trying because this game is one of the most satysfying things I've ever played. I could lose half of my highly skilled warriors to skaven zerg rush only to meet them once more later and obliterate them.
Last but not least - be warned, it's highly addictive.

Overall this game falls into the catagory of highly difficult but highly rewarding. You need to think really tactically, using buildings and choke points to your advantage, if you can lure a foe to hit you and get them stuck in a door, but keep enough room avalibe for your hidden unit behind the wall to join in the fight, you will have an extreme advantage.
The game has a high difficulty curve, but unlike games like Dark souls it is less on pressing buttons at the right time and skill, and more on tactics. RNG will not be your friend, but in turn will not be the friend of the enemy at times as well.
I would like to see some more warbands, although we would be treading into the unofficial warbands most likely from here on out. special hero units should be a lot cheaper as well, but this is just going to fall under the dlc craze most games have now adays.
Overall I reccomend the game, if on the condition that it is a hard game to play and you will lose. But it is one of those games that I will keep coming back to after being frustrated with it for awhile.

So lemme just start by saying if you're looking for a super complex fighter with a bunch of systems. This isn't that.
I enjoyed playing through this game. It's fun, the art style is fairly unique and the few characters you meet are somewhat interesting.
However... the combat system is really not that complicated. There's a stamina meter you have and essentially just 4 combos, you cycle through these combos with alternative moves which can be used to interrupt the combos. You can also cycle through them with the right analogue stick whenever but whatever. You can of course change every move your character does to be whatever after you unlock said move.
I think the system for unlocking moves is neat(you block or take another defensive action against the move as it is used on you and you gain experience towards learning that move) I think the experience bar fills kinda slow though, and there should be ways to just buy moves with the sort of ingame currency you earn from scrapping gear, but there isn't.
My main problems with the combat system is the Kahlt are crap. Their ability Absorb is essentially just a crappy less rewarding version of the Forsaken's ability Parry.  HOWEVER more importantly, there's not really much you can hope to do against an opponent who knows how to block properly. Most fighting games have a grab or guard break but there is no such thing in this. There's a stamina bar which if you drain someone by hitting their block enough you get a couple free hits on them if your moves are fast enough maybe even 3 free hits but whatever. There's also weapons in the game, and when I say weapons I mean a sword. Doesn't really matter what sword you choose since the only notable difference is aesthetic.  All styles use the sword the same reverse grip way, The only other weapon type is gloves which doesnt change your animations at all just lets you have a different deck of combos.
SO I gave this game a YES, because I think it CAN become a good game. At the moment it's a dumb enjoyable one, but not a very deep one. Given some time and love it could be great. It's not now though and if multiple updates haven't happened between you reading this and my posting of it on 12/31/2017 I don't recommend buying it for full price. (I bought this when it was on sale)

Oh where do I begin?
If you are familiar with the anime/manga "Higurashi no Naku Koro ni", you have seen where various scenarios play out with the characters, usually resulting in a different ending, usually bad. Underneath it all is a overriding story that explains a little better what is happening and then it all makes sense.
After playing this game, I got the scenarios, but with nothing of substance to tie it all together. That was a little disappointing.
The story premise was pretty cool and would have made for a really interesting VN, but the idea was scaled back and turned into this. While this might have been the developers original intent to make something different, I felt like I was dragged along for the ride of a lifetime, then kicked out of the car while it was turning a corner and left to walk back home myself.
Oh well, time to move onto the next game and hope it is better.
I do have to give thumbs up to the Emote engine. I really like the motion of the characters, hair movement, mouth and eye movement, everything! I hope other VNs will license this technology going forward because it does make the game more enjoyable than a typical static display.
----
TL;DR - at full price, move on, if in the bundle with TSL and two other games, a much better deal, but you might wish to get your 5-6 hours back once you are done.

One of the best third person shooters ever made.
Rather than churn out some generic & serious conspiracy story with a cringeworthy story RE4 delivers a completely bizzare and off the wall cospiracy story that plays up the camp factor for intentional and self aware laughs.
Resident Evil 4 even still today remains the best 3rd peron survival horror shooter ever made.  The campaign is an absolute blast from start to finish; the story feels like it was made by Japanese people who grew up watching bootleg copies of Rambo, Die Hard, and other classic American action movies and then they mixed that level of action and ridiculousness with elements from classic horror movies; movies like Evil Dead and campy slasher movies.
Chances are you already know Resident Evil 4 is amazing and you're just watning to know how this port is.  On the bright side, it looks amazing.  No doubt; visually this is the best way to experience this game.
Unfortunately, this game has some pretty bad technical bugs at times.  The worst of which is that it'll slow your game down to feel as though you're playing in slow motion.  It's like getting 5-10 FPS but instead of being choppy it's like someone but you in a bulletime sequence from Max Payne or the Matrix and you got stuck there.  There's multiple times throughout the campaign that I encountered this bug and each time it's about 5+ minutes of basically truding through the much that is the cancerous FPS bug.
Even though this bug is certainly a hassle, it's a minor marring on an otherwise amazing product.  This HD remastering and improved FPS (except for the aforementioned bug) are no doubt the most visually impressive way to experience the masterpiece that is Resident Evil 4.

Worse than that, though, is the pacing. Most of the game seems to be spent staring at a featureless screen waiting for opponents' characters who you can't even see to do whatever it is that they're doing. When there is a fight, your characters spend a good few seconds staring at each other between actually doing anything. Even during game changing battles between powerful characters, there's no drama.
It's just a basic stab animation. A loooong pause. A basic slash animation. Long pause, while deciding what ability to use next. Stuff happens offscreen to opponent's characters. Slash. Pause. Stab. Pause. Etc.....
I want to like this game, and I do like many aspects of it. Character progression, the mixture of PVP and PVE for the same warbands.

In my opinion Mordheim: City of the Damned is a fantastic game. It delivers on all of it's promises. If you enjoy turn based, tactical, skirmish combat games and enjoy having lots of ways to customize your team you'll greatly enjoy it.
This does come with a word of warning however, Mordheim is secretly a harcore rogue-like.  (TL;DR warning)
We usually reserve the term for games that instantly take advantage of any weakness you show and punish you harshly for it. Normally you see this manifesting in games as instant, or near instant death. You make a mistake, all progress is lost, restart at the latest checkpoint.
Mordheim however, punishes you differently.
Characters in Mordheim follow the standard RPG system. Every character has a list of stats that determine how well they do things. As a character progresses those stats increase, they gain skill points, and in combination with equipment you can specialize and customize the character. To fully level up and customize a character takes a lot of time and energy, and it shows in the mechanics of the game. Characters in Mordheim as a whole are worth more than the sum of their stats, skills, and equipment.
Mordheim features an injury system, every time a character runs out of HP they have a chance of facing something worse than a nasty bruise. Generally this is something that fully heals within 2 days, in bad cases sometimes 5 days. Sometimes however, the injuries are worse.  Every time a character is knocked out there’s a chance they could permanently lose some HP or become worse at aiming due to a maimed hand. For the full list look here,
, and it gets even better!
Combat is unforgiving. Positioning is essential and the game does an amazing job making that difficult. The maps and objectives will make you want to weaken your positioning constantly. Assuming you position yourself perfectly, there is still RNG, and thus still a chance for everything to go horribly wrong. This combined with a warband's story being a marathon means things will go wrong eventually.
All of this together means that sooner or later, your characters are going to face permanent injuries that are often career ending. All of your time and effort will be swept away by picking up 1 more wyrdstone than you could have.
There are no save points, there is no easy mode, and there are no guarantees. This is a hardcore rogue-like.
Mordheim: City of the Damned is a marathon obstacle course that will kill you by a thousand cuts and the occasional bonk on the head. That's what makes it satisfying.
TL;DR, Think fantasy XCOM permanently on hardmode, then add more RPG, make it 5 times as long, and there’s 4-6 unique factions.
P.S.
Start out with the Sister's of Sigmar. All of their units excel at being super tanks, and their casters can AOE heal.

If you've been interested in bullet hells or shmups, but never found a good game to cut your teeth on, Jamestown is a must buy.
It has foregone the portrait-screened arcade style, cute'em'up aesthetics, and oppressive difficulty that makes every serious entry in the genre feel niche and inaccessible. The full-screen game feels much more natural on PC, and it's clear that gamepads and keyboards were the intended input devices. A very distinct and fun visual style, and tongue-in-cheek story told through cutscenes, give the game a style all it's own that feels much more open and fun than the anime girls and arcane plots often found in bullet hell games.
The difficulty of the game starts much lower than arcade shmups like DoDonPachi, Danmaku Unlimited, or Ikaruga - only the Divine and Judgement difficulties provide the wall of bullets genre veterans will be expecting. This is excellent for new players, as it lets you practice your skills in a less frustrating environment before the game forces you to take the next steps by locking the last few stages behind completion of higher difficulty levels. Though this content gating is initially offputting, you'll quickly discover the game won't put you in over your head unless you ask it to, and you should be capable of completing the whole campaign, even as a beginner.
A final blessing for new players is the story and mission structure - this eccentric tale is broken down into six levels, and the level select screen is front and center in the main menu. This saves new players from the frustration of slamming their heads against a brutal, arcade-style, six-stage grind as the only way of playing the game. You can go back and practice levels at will, or even just replay the missions you like most without having to slog through a typical arcade experience. However, The Gauntlet offers the traditional unbroken string of missions for veterans or those who want to test their skills.
In conclusion, Jamestown is the perfect entry point for the world of bullet hells. It drops more off-putting genre trends in order to fully embrace new players.

This is more an update review than a fresh one.
Let me first state that the wheel I used to play this game was a Logitech G29.
When I first played this game when it came out, it didn't impress me enough to keep it. While there were certainly a lot of pros, there were some serious cons for me that I simply could not overlook.
I've now picked the game back up again after the recent patch (I hoped) might have fixed some of the issues I had.
The only small issue I had was with the co-driver calls being a bit rubbish, but I didn't expect that to be fixed. It's only a small preferencial problem and nothing worth slating the game over.
The two main issues I had were with the way the game handled my steering wheel and the flickering bug.
I can happily report the flickering bug is gone.
However, I still have a major issue with my wheel. While the addition of several extra settings for steering wheel FFB controls have been added and are very much appreciated, I still cannot alleviate the terrible chattering my wheel makes with this game. After talking with a few people, I think I can say it comes down to my wheel itself. The G29 uses gears to control the wheel instead of a rubber belt. This unfortunately will lead to chattering noises when the wheel receives multiple tiny FFB signals. With a belt driven wheel, you would simply feel the tiny tugs and pulls at the wheel. So does the fault actually lie with my wheel? Well.....no. See, I can play games like Dirt 4, Dirt Rally, and to a lesser extent Assetto Corsa. Granted AC isn't an offroad game, but I can still feel when the very edge of my wheel is on the apex. None of those three games make my wheel chatter one tiny bit, yet the feel of the FFB in those games far surpasses what I can get from WRC 7.
The other problem I have noticed now after reading a post on the forums is the fact I seem to be suffering from some incredible input lag. As one person wrote, "It feels like your steering column is made of rubber". I couldn't put it better myself.
So those are the only REAL problems I have with this game.
As for the pros, I can only echo what everyone else says. The tracks. Amazing. I love them. Varying from teeth grinding technical stages with narrow roads, to wide sweeping stages and insane speeds. The tracks are the best I've played. Yes, even better than Dirt 4 can manage. On par with Dirt Rally, as every single stage in that game is real. Even the surroundings on the stages are varied and changing all the time. It keeps the stages looking and feeling fresh rather than seeing the same bland environment over and over.
Graphically the game isn't amazing, but it's certainly good enough. Lets face it, in a game where you get tunnel vision using extreme focus to keep your car on the road, next gen graphics aren't your top priority.
Sound quality is....on par I guess, borderline sub-par. It's the least impressive aspect of the game. Engine sounds seem fine, but the collision noises and the sound of your car bottoming out remind me of some old arcade boxing game from the early 90s. In a word, lacklustre.
Menus all seem pretty clean and good looking, no complaints there.
Overall I would probably rate this game a 7/10. If the sound quality was better, the co-driver wasn't awful, and I had no issues with my wheel, it would be a very solid 9/10.
If you can overlook the sound, co-driver, and you don't have a Logitech wheel, then by all means buy this game. You won't be disappointed. If you do have a Logitech wheel, be prepared.

This review was negative before due to stuttering issue and it is why developer answered below. I have upgraded my graphic card from old HD 5770 1GB to GFX 750Ti 2GB and the game started to work as it should. Do not believe minimum system requirements on Steam store. They are false, they differ from what is written on box version. You definitely need a 2GB VRAM card to run it without stuttering.
To start with, WRC 7 is a improvement over WRC 6 in terms of stage design. This is the biggest change and it is a big step forward, due to the fact stage design next to handling model dictates how good a rally game is. Stages are bumpier, much more narrow, with less undestructable objects (like in WRC 6) and longer (epic stages).
On the other hand, most of the stages are not new, they are the same as in WRC 5 and WRC 6 but a bit redone, and many of them are just reversed. This is poor approach to the game, critical argument to stop yearly realeasing rushed game and make updates to one product instead (examples: Assetto Corsa, RaceRoom, Automobilista).
Handling changed too. It is a positive change however I did not find good wheel setup yet. Maybe it is because I use Logitech Driving Force Pro which is not officially supported (btw why? Force GT is and this is almost the same wheel - developers laziness?).
But I must say there is a learning curve, so newcomers can be put on a tree. And it just does not feel precise like for example in DiRT Rally, it is just a bit different. The car is unpredictable, feel like floating in some way. Bad thing: you can't set camera steering buttons on a wheel (look back, look left etc.). They are fixed to keyboard numpad or pad's right analog, and there is no such setting in control button menu). Inside the car - the inputs seems to be not fully analog but the wheel jumps when it reaches certain amount of turn degree, according to steering wheel animation.
Force feedback is bit werid. We were given further settings (after a patch) in options menu but they do not work properly. For example when I hit some soft fences (this cloth on sticks I mean) my wheel vibrates/jumps like mad, even if I have any vibration/colision vibration off to 0%. This is very distracting when attacking a stage cut a tiny bit and may lead to losing control over the car... Those options under wheel settings are fake, other settings than overall strength/vibration are simply doing nothing.
Graphics improved a lot, but still it is missing something. On smaler resolution (mine 1366x768) it looks pixelated due to no real AntiAliasing implemented (MSAA forexample). There is only FXAA which makes it all blurry and is useless in my opinion.
Online gameplay has not changed too, so there are still no players to race with apart from friends you invite.
In conclusion - I am pleased to play official WRC 2017 content so I leave a positive review and must say this game can be very enjoyable if you will give it a chance. However I would suggest to buy it on sale.
