Like many other simracing fans I'm surprised at the mixed reviews.  This game is a huge step ahead of its predecessors.  Physics are intuitive, stages are absolutely amazing, and after some tweaking of the wheel I found it more immersive than any other rally game out there.  This truly wonderful game deserves VR and an analog hand break.  If we got these two things I wouldn't be able to stop playing.
In terms of specific car physics, I can only compare it to the real life.  If you have only driven the Fiesta in this game as the Junior WRC entry, then you might be sceptical as to how you can trash it around so hard while the car maintains so much grip and feels sort of like a rear wheel drive car.  I own the same gen Fiesta, and with summer tires, rear sway bar, and front and rear strut bars, my car feels exactly like that.  And I can't imagine the upgrades the rally car goes through to make it what it is.  I also own a heavily modded WRX track car, and I have to say that the nimbleness and accuracy of my Fiesta with limited mods over my WRX with fully upgraded suspension and far better and wider tires still boggles my mind.
I own a fanatac v2 wheel and my graphics card is a 1080, and with everything maxed out I had no issues that people are speaking of.  The stages truly are a work of art! Not only how they look, but even how many surfaces change over a stage, and for example, how a patch of ice can feel different from one area to the next.  I also love the attention to small details like tracking of each tire on the gravel and snow surfaces, how twigs break and shatter after you have hit them, the sparks from hitting a guardrail, and how the interaction with each of these objects effects the car in a way that I would expect it to in real life.  It's too bad the replays right now can't show off these amazing stages in the right way.

Even still, I believe this is the best rally game out there today.  I say game, because it's not quite a simulation, but pretty darn close to it.  It crushes Dirt 4 in every aspect except graphics clarity, which can be a bit of a turnoff, I have to admit.  That motion blur really has to go you guys!  I can't stress enough how important it is for the graphics to be crystal clear in a driving game.  The game has plenty of sense of speed, and does not need anything to enhance it.  It's better than Dirt Rally for sure, unless you play with the RFPE mod.  RBR is only better in terms of the damage and setup.  The physics in RBR are really not relevant anymore, no matter what people say, and I do still love the game.  Assetto is still king in terms of physics for tarmac rallies (especially if you have a motion rig), and stage mods by Simtraxx and others are amazing!  This reminds me, Sim Commander software absolutely needs to support this latest WRC title now.
WRC 7 really captures the essence of current rallying, which the developer did a masterful job of.  The speed of the cars also feels right.  The time and control it takes to execute a hairpin feel perfect to me, but you have to really get the game and wheel settings right.  With that in mind, it's not about how fast you are going through a stage, but just the enjoyment of driving and getting the technique right, which naturally results in fast stage times anyways.
Keep in mind, my review is solely based on playing the game in simulation mode.  So, for those casual arcade racers, sorry you had to waste 30 seconds of your life readying above writing.  I have no idea if you would like this game.
And lastly, although I fully understand the financial reasons of creating the game that reaches a broad audience, it's too bad this can't be an out and out simulation game, because it's clear that the team really has the talent and the ability to make that happen. I was really disappointed in the last WRC title, but now I'm back being a fan again in a big way.  Keep up the good work, and please don't forget about us drivers out there ;)

---First impressions---
I had no expectations firing up this game and I must admit I was very skeptical first and not sure buying it after reading all the mixed reviews but what a ride! Seriously, I'm happy I did these devs a chance! This game came out of nowhere and it look amazing and plays very well.
The reason why I thought it would be a nice idea to put this review together is to try to describe how exactly the handling feels as I've scrolled the whole steam page reviews without knowing exactly what I was buying and wanted to help others like me. Also, if it can be of any help, I really hated WRC 5 and 6 handling and I'm more a fan of sims like Richard Burns and DiRT Rally.
---Handling model---
The physics of this game to me feels close to Sebastian Loeb Rally Evo. The best I could describe it is a kind of blend between WRC 3 and SLRE physic-wise, but with better axle pivots and a more dynamic suspension geometry modelling. Don't get me wrong, WRC 7 is still a simcade game.
It's very fun to drift around corners (much better than DiRT4) and seeing your suspension working over bumps is a real joy to experience. Inside the cockpit, models are a bit rough around the edges... you see just a bit of the steering wheel, you can't adjust seat and FOV and I must say with a pad, the handling doesn't feel as dynamic as the exterior view or bumper cam. But with a wheel, it feels much better, I would not say as great as DiRT Rally, but it's actually surprising.
I plugged my T300RS + T3PA Pro pedal set and the game instantly recognized them with the buttons mapped accordingly. The FFB effect is not very good and the slider in option menu is odd as it doesn't let you select each angle... I wanted to put it to 540 degree but it just let me choose between 508 and 560 although you can go straight up to 1080 degrees?!? Also, the virtual steering wheel look out of sync and I do get some minor input lag.
The handbrake could make you slide more as right now it make you stop to a dead end. The cars behavior doesn't feel as predictable  as DiRT Rally, the cars feels more floaty and less responsive making them harder to drive than DR but they're intuitive and you will experience countersteer, oversteer and lost of control without ABS. The only negatives worth mentioning here I think is the landings after a jump and interaction of your car with the roadsides... it feels a bit clunky at times and you have that weird looking cloud of particles effect going in the air.
--- Graphics and stages ---
About the graphics and stages, the shaders to me looks better than DiRT4 (specially lens flare and reflections), the vegetation is luxurian and very dense but above all, the road are a real blast to drive... they're narrow, bumpy, packed with elevation and camber changes. I'm happy to finally be able to drive between vineyards on these narrow Germany roads, something DiRT Rally is lacking. You can feel the immersion as you're going deeper in these wonderful forests. The stages have been crafted to perfection and are amongst the best I've seen, if not the best ever in any rally games. You can go from a mountain top to a valley and back into forest, etc. the landscapes are so much different, we can easily see these guys were very inspired when they've designed them. The landscapes are never the same and the saturation of colors in Australia and Wales are top notch. The textures looks very natural and realistics, and each country look different and are packed with lot of trackside objects. So far, having always been impressed by the DiRT serie stages, I think these guys could show some tricks to help Codemasters refine the variety of their environments but one point goes to DiRT Rally for having more detailed road surfaces. Speaking about the graphics,I think the car models could benefit from more polish (especially rims) and the watersplashes effect could be reworked. This game is one of the few featuring the great Kopecky's Skoda Fabia R5.
---Performance---
Lot of reviewers complain they have microstutters, and some of them have killer rigs. It's not the case for me. For reference, I have a first generation i7 920 with a GTX 1060 6GB and 12 GB DDR3 and the game run perfectly fine at a constant 60 fps locked, even using local splitscreen which is a nice addition btw. Hopefully a patch will come soon to fix these microstutters but on my setup, game runs like a charm.
---Conclusion---
As it is currently, it's still too early to talk about the career mode as I just finished the first country, but so far, I've been very impressed. I recommend this game to any rally enthusiast out there looking for a different racing experience.

It was the Space Debris music in the trailer that sold this game to me. So having just bought the Soundtrack Edition of the game, I listened through the soundtrack first before playing the game. Yes, Space Debris is such a great track, but the rest of the soundtrack certainly didn't disappoint either; from the '90's 'Independence Day' feel of John's Theme, to the excellent Tangerine Dream techno-ambience of The Fight, the Rochard OST is so enjoyable from start to finish..........so what about the game itself?
Rochard is a light-hearted physics-based side scroller set in a future-grunge world of space mining. Playing as John Rochard, you use your grapple gun and anti-grav physics to overcome environmental obstacles and enemies.
The production of Rochard is top-notch and the physics superbly done. The game starts off easy enough and the first couple of levels act as tutorials easing the player into the physic-based system of the game. It's too early for me to say how the game pans out, but I think it's hardly going to disappoint from what I've experienced so far. Great characters and enjoyable cut-scenes, I'm genuinely looking forward to spending more time with John Rochard & friends.
Edit:
As it turned out, Rochard was an immensely enjoyable game from start to finish. The game was lean with no padding. Checkpoints were frequent and positioned so there was rarely any grind to get a previous position after dying. The length of the game was also satisfying, never threatening to outstay its welcome.
Playing with a PS3 controller (360 mapped), the controls were very responsive and satisfying. There was also a good balance between combat and physics-based puzzles.
There are Gold badges to collect throughout the game. They don't contribute to any weapon upgrades, etc, but are positioned in the levels to add extra challenge for the obsessive collector. After beating the game, I find I can select individual levels to find badges I've missed which adds to the replay value. I'll probably enjoy playing through Rochard a couple of more times whilst patiently waiting for Episode II.

A genuinely fun game for about 20 hours. Then you realize that most of the PvP skill comes from grinding endgame moves. The game is praised for its combat system, and it really is great. But your average move sets are simple attacks, while hard to get endgame moves evade, provide invulnerability and stagger sometimes all at the same time. So most of the moves are just fluff and filler, where only a few dozen proper ones actually count.
People defend the system claiming once you know the pattern you can defend against it. But it doesn't take a genius to understand that mathematically if your opponent's moveset leaves 50%+ less openings for attack than yours does, and you have 50% less evade options than they do, then it's about much more than just pure skill.
Other than that, the game runs smoothly, and looks gorgeous. The gameplay is good, although the controls on both keyboard & mouse as well as gamepad suffer from some illogical planning when it comes to your ability bindings: With a pad, you basically need superhuman thumb speed to switch between right analog and buttons as you need them virtually at the same time, and with a keyboard the action is hard-coded to jerkin your mouse around. You can switch the sensitivity for it, but it switches the overall mouse look sensitivity too.
I do recommend the game however. For its price, especially on sale, it was real solid fun for 20 hours or so. Really something quite different from the usual game.

One of the most consistently fun games I've played. It also has the most badass thing I've seen in a video game: suplexing a cultist so hard his head explodes.
At its core, Resident Evil 4 is a game about action and resource management. Your ammo matters, how and when you engage enemies matters, and what you decide to keep in your inventory matters. You will have access to powerful weapons, but with limited ammo you have to decide when the best time is to use them. The over-the-shoulder tank controls will feel awkward at first, but the inability to run-and-gun like an action hero adds to the survival horror setting in my opinion, as it forces you to pick a spot and stand your ground.
One thing that RE4 nails is its difficulty. The game always has me in a constant tug-of-war, dreading the next scenario it will throw at me. Each section of the game is unique and memorable, with different kinds of challenges to keep things fresh. It also ramps up in difficulty quite early on, letting you know that this game isn't a walk in the park. However, while it is challenging, RE4 is not cruel or sadistic; if you die, you are sent back to the beginning of the area (or sometimes a checkpoint in the middle of an area), so you never lose that much progress.
With that said, there is one issue this port has. The game logic is tied to the framerate, and since this game originally ran on 30 FPS, setting it to 60 causes unusual things to happen, as well as more aggressive enemy AI. I would recommend leaving it at 30 to avoid having to deal with any bugs. I also recommend playing the game as it was originally designed, on a controller. Mouse and keys make the game a little too easy.
In my opinion RE4 is a must play, even if you've never played a Resident Evil game. It's incredibly fun, dynamic, replayable, and a testament to excellent game design.

I bought this game with the day-one DLC and from the get-go it was an absolute nightmare.  My specs for my computer are:
Intel Core i7-7700HQ/ 32GB DDR4-2667 RAM / GTX 1060 / OLED Screen (Yes, it's an Alienware)
That should be plenty to drive this game considering that its "recommended" setup is only a GTX 780 with a skylake CPU.  BOY was I wrong.  First, the game was slow.  This was attributed to the fact that the nVidia drivers did not recognize that WRC 7 is in fact, a GAME, and not something like an office document or YouTube video that can work with integrated graphics.  Second, it started up every time in non-fullscreen AND windowed modes.  I had to go into settings multiple times to change this before the settings finally stuck.  Lastly, the input lag was monumental.  I get that there will always be some lag because of latency from input controller to machine, but when some inputs lag upwards of half a second before the input is seen by the user, it's not a "game ready for release"; it's a game that was released because WRC's design studio realized that Dirt 4 came out.  Put simply, this game was caught sleeping.
Moreover, stuttering was terrible.  Not "this is too slow to run this game" stuttering (which I would accept if I had an ultrabook with only Intel UHD or HD graphics), but rather "this game's programming code was not tested thoroughly.  What the game has in difficulty, it lacks in fps consistency and it lacks in smoothness.  Cockpits look generic, with no real attention paid to things such as how the speedo / tach / other dials look, and while I like the copilot's dry readout of directions (adds to accuracy), I do wish that there was sarcasm when the player messes up (ie: I never knew a right 6 was a right 9... you sure you finished grammar school?).
The idea is there, but sadly much like WRC 6, DiRT is far superior, even though DiRT gives up realism and actual tracks in favor of a far more polished experience.  Wound up getting a refund.

One of the best Otome games I've ever played. The story had excellent set of characters, scripts, and the characters were completely fleshed out which made the story feel that much better.
You could really see and feel each characters perspective which made the game feel so unique not like other games that I have played that feel liek they have the same characters replayed.
This game will also bring you to tears. This story will likely have you emotionally attached to the characters so be well prepared if you choose to play this game.
The art and music add to the fable-like story and characters really well.  I was really surprised that the choices in the game such as the choices you need for the good endings weren't always the virtuous type of decisions and that the story wants you to know each characters way of thinking before you can get that good ending, but being the good ending seeking type of person I always saved before the big choices so I could always get the good ending, but when I finished and started doing the bad endings I found out that wasn't always the good way to go.
The bad endings left me feeling really emotional because the good endings really made me feel attached to the characters personalities, but I won’t spoil any of the endings for you.
I have to admit that Delora and Parfait played two great roles in this game helping move the story forward.  (For those who don’t know those are two of the characters that you see in the game.)
I honestly can't wait to see more games from the Dicesuki and I really hope the sequel will be somewhat similar to this storyline because I would love to see how my past character choices affect the future of the game.
Pros.
•	Music placement, it felt in place during each scene, chapter, or act in the story.
•	Unique music, I loved the intro to the game and the songs throughout the game they made me happy, frightened, and sad.
•	Great script, I didn’t notice any errors during my play through and it had me laughing, teary, and unhappy during my play through the game.
•	Memorable characters, I can’t forget any of the characters I met during the story they were indeed very memorable.
•	Memorable endings, both the good endings and the bad endings were so very memorable, but the bad endings that I have done actually had me tearing up.
Cons.
•	Repetitive music.
(Although it wasn’t an issue to me, I know there is definitely someone out there who thinks the same music is too receptive and how they would much rather have a different song playing, but it I don’t think it will affect the story or game for you.)
•	Choice bug where if you clicked anywhere it would pick the top choice.
(It stopped after I loaded my save thankfully, I just wanted to bring it up and also it only happened once for me so it shouldn’t be that big of a problem as long as you save.)
•	Made me have sad feels.
(Warning if you are emotional you will get sad during the bad endings and in some parts in the story.)

A very short review after just over an hour of play. More to follow, but I want players to know about this game while it's still SO cheap.
Amazing graphics, pretty good story, great voice acting, stellar music. This is a thinking player's game, heavily involving physics. Gravity, and gravity control is a big part of this game, and so far using gravity to place and throw objects is used instead of traditional weapons. I must say, squashing bad guys with huge, heavy boxes, or grav-throwing explosives at them is FAR more satisfying than just....."bang". (Nothing wrong with "bang". I LIKE "bang".) And to grab an errant robot with a gravity beam, then smash it rapidly against opposing walls is oddly....calming.
If you typically avoid platformers, or like me, buy them expecting to fail, "rochard" may be your solution. Many, if not most, of the multitudinous puzzles seem to have more than one solution. One, the typical "brute force" sort, but also a much easier, more "scientific" one.
Very good learning curve. Short, reasonable checkpoint intervals. AND a hero who looks and sounds much like so many of us! MOST importantly, this game is really a LOT of fuN!
If PORTAL was a platformer, it just might be "rochard".
At this price, WHILE it's this price, you owe it to yourself to at least take a look at the Store Page. What's to lose? $1.49 is all! ($2.09 with soundtrack & artbook.) At this price I have to give the HIGHEST possible recommendation.

I bought this game on sale to play with some friends. Honestly I read the reviews before and didnt think much of it until I actually played it. Ive refunded it after 2 hours and heres what I can tell you:
Pros:
- Clean fighting mechanics if youre fighting someone your level
- Complex and combo based fighting system
- Online 1v1 games are balanced (skill based, your items and upgrades are negated - same applies to 3v3)
- AI isnt stupid and can effectively 1v1 you like a real player
Cons:
- Small player base
- Lack of Singleplayer content (if you dont play online 1v1 or 3v3 gamemodes)
- Can get really repetitive and boring in an hour (personal opinion)
- Loot and items always seem to decrease the stats that your fighting style requires
- No AoE moves, so if youre stuck in a 1v3+, youre screwed
- Multiplayer theres a lot of spammers and "no-skill" fighting styles that people choose instead of the (more fun in my opinion) combo based and dodge based styles. I chose the Windfall fighting style which requires more skill and dodged based timing. Then there are to other people who chose the *forgot the name* style which requires the player the spam left and right click to do charge attacks. As my class you should be able to dodge it easily, which is wrong. I am able to dodge 50% of the time where either I successfully dodge or it curves and "autolocks" and hits me anyway. In the case of a successful dodge, they go right back to spamming and I cant fight them at all. To prevent that, the game has a stamina bar that drains to prevent spamming, but apparently for them it takes virtually no stamina cost to spam on me.
TLDR: Theres a spammy and broken no skill class that ruins fighting 90% of the time
Grey Space:
- Multiplayer 3v3 never goes as the trailer shows: people dont choose one opponent from the other team and they all fight each other like separate 1v1s. While one idiot goes and takes the objectives, the other 3 people gang up on the other person and violate him alone. Now this is either a good strategy or a bad strategy and its your opinion.
- You can just chose the broken class and player like a Smash Bros spammer online or play the base game content and actually enjoy using the class you built and the move combos you set up
Most of this is from personal experience. People have told me to counter the spammers, just dodge. However as Ive stated before that never works no matter how hard I try. Usually I dodge then punch them (as the counter is supposed to work) but then as I pound them down they just block and go back to spamming me when I run out of stamina.

I wish I could recommend this game, but I really can't due to the said state of affairs with regards to mission balance and risk vs reward. Rng is absolutely devasting in this game, and can ruin the most careful planning. You can lose a normal mission, which is 1 of the lowest ratings you'll find, in part due to bad rng. You can surround an enemy hero 3 to 1 and still waste a huge amount of time trying to take him down, while your own heroes will lose 1v1. 1 Mission ruined a promising Sisters of Sigmar run because I was stunned 3 times in a row, and enemies were landing every blow, while I missed 3 times in a row. Each loss reprsents a huge lose of vital men and material that is very difficult to replace and there seems to be a high probability of receiving debilitating injuries each time a hero gets knocked out of the fight. This game treats a rout as if your character was knocked out during a fight, meaning you have a high chance of losing an entire squad. My last mission cost me 6 Sisters, 1 died, and 5 received wounds that put them out of action for 2 or 3 days. If you want a game that arbitrarily punishes you, then this is the game for you.

Jamestown: Legend of the Lost Colony is caught between new and old ways of thinking about shmups. The game is obviously heavily influenced by arcade shmups dating back to the turn of the millennium. Cave’s Progear has been cited by the dev team as a particularly strong influence, but larger elements of Cave and Treasure’s house styles have also been found. But Jamestown tries to go in creative directions most arcade shmups don’t, with mixed results.
The shooting in Jamestown works, although it’s more mechanically simple than a lot of shmups. The player can choose a ship before starting a level from four different options, this choice is then locked for the duration of a level. This means a commitment is made by the player to execute an entire level in one particular style for its duration. This makes Jamestown a less dynamic shmup than other franchises like Raiden with its scaling/switching weapons or an Ikargua with its phase switching. In its place Jamestown has a bullet absorption mechanic in Vault that rewards players with points. It’s less exciting to play, but timing of Vault brings a tactical level of score building to Jamestown that other shmups lack. Jamestown’s mechanical design encourages the player to replay levels in order to determine when/where is best to use Vault. Success on the leaderboard isn’t tied to level clearing so much as clearing levels efficiently. Jamestown’s mechanical simplicity encourages the player to master level planning, not reflexive skill to get good. Ikaruga has some of this with its combo mechanic, but that game’s difficulty keeps the player more focused on the actual “playing” than Jamestown’s memorization focus.
Jamestown gets away with a tactical approach because it’s positioned differently from the classic arcade games that inspired it. Unlike most shmups, Jamestown was designed from the ground up as a home release. As you can replay levels instantly without paying new quarters each time the player can change, and improve their strategy gradually with practice. In an arcade game this would feel like a cheap grab for more coins.
Jamestown doesn’t go far enough though in benefiting from its home platform. If you play the story on either the “normal” or “difficult” difficulty setting you’ll learn the end of the game is only present on the higher difficulty settings, without any warning before hand. And this isn’t just a secret ending, start on “normal” and you’ll find 60% through the game that you have to start all over at the beginning on “difficult” is you want to continue. Same with that difficulty level 80% through the game. Having started on the first difficulty level, I was force to play through the front half three entire times to get to the final level, it’s a cheap way to artificially pad out a shorter game. This means the player will spend more time re-playing the easy, less interesting levels over and over. The game is structured to show the player its duller side more often than its more exciting content, a baffling decision that can make this game awful dull to slog through.
This also totally breaks the difficulty curve. Playing through the game the third time on “legendary” is still quite easy as so much of the difficulty in Jamestown is based on memorizing enemy placement and attack patterns. The player learns these things the first two times through the game, making the third pass very easy until they arrive at the final level. Playing an unseen level on “legendary” is much harder than doing it with practice, creating a massive difficulty spike right at the end of the game that ruins the established flow. The problem isn’t that the game gets hard, it’s that the game’s structure masks the difficulty before turning it on all at once.
As is Jamestown’s multiple modes don’t contribute to each other at all. It feels as if the game’s tried to include all the variations you would find in home releases of arcade games. While I always appreciate more modes, the game refuses to let them interact in any way. This makes sense for a home port, where they are fluffing up a short experience. But Jamestown is a home release and these modes could very easily be integrated into a more cohesive whole. The challenge mode or gauntlet mode should be incorporated right into the campaign as a means to unlock the later levels. Replaying so much of this game over and over is a weird decision. Jamestown ends up feeling like less of a love letter to classic shmups, but more of a tribute to their awkward home ports. Ports that much like Jamestown, show off the worst parts of the games proudly.

First let me say that this is a very enjoyable set of stories.
Now that that is out of the way, what you should expect. This is not a choose your own adventure novel or one of those games with a large, dizzying array of choices. This is a visual novel with clearly defined paths that walk you down a story. The choices, while deciding the ending, don't really alter much. This is one of those Visual Novels that are more novel than game. That is not bad, in fact I quite enjoy such things, however, it is not for everyone.
Criticism wise my biggest issue is the bad ends. They feel kinda tacked on. As stated above this could be more looked at as a series of short stories about the same characters where events play out differently. It feels to me as if the choices and the dual endings for each route were forced in to make it more game like. This is mostly because the bad ends could have been much more. I dearly wish they had done an epilogue for the bad ends. Even if Rod's curse failed to be broken in time, in his route Em and Lucette got closer so there could have been an epilogue about them seeking comfort from one another and becoming true sisters. Etc. Long story short, don't expect much from the bad ends. They could have been so much more, but instead they just end and leave you wondering about what would happen next.
The second criticism has been brought up in other reviews, but it can be a trick at times to tell when Lucette is thinking to herself or speaking aloud. Not a big deal since it can be easily figured out from the scene as a whole, but a bit annoying nevertheless.
What it does well is making Lucette a complex character. Boy, did I hate her during the prologue. If this were a longer game they likely could have made the prologue start earlier, during her childhood, to give you a better feel for her instead of doling out the relative bits as dream sequences through out. That said how they did it does work very well form a literary point of view, it is just that the first bit can be really offputting for some folks who don't want to read about someone like what Lucette was at the start.
Music is great. It is too bad the digital art book doesn't come with a nicely formatted OST for us.
Artwork is. . . Ok. There are times when the art is just a bit wonky. For example during Rumpel's kiss scene his arm is going through Lucette's shoulder. However, the art does what it needs to do, even if the style may not be for everyone or if there are odd bits here and there. Plus, free game. The art is really good for that production value.
In the end I highly recommend this game. There are things I wish were done differently, but nothing is perfect or so they say. Still, I can't help but wonder what the result would have been if this were a true kinetic novel, a visual novel where you have no choices. Instead of choosing a partner we could follow Lucette as she sought help from all the members. It just always felt to me like each route here was missing something since it was so short. We skip so much time, time that could have displayed other interactions she had. Of course pure kinetic novels tend to get a poor rap at times, but they can be so beautiful and I think this had the potential to pull that off.

Rochard is a fun little physics/puzzle based platformer with a decent enough (although rather cliched) storyline to go along with it.
- Combat can get a bit boring as you basically have the option of shooting or throwing stuff at the enemies but it's not a major part of the game anyway.
- The mechanics of the "G-Lifter" and the fact you can manipulate gravity at will (remotely by manipulating "gravity generator" on each level) makes each level somewhat challenging to begin with, but once you see the solution you'll kick yourself for not seeing it sooner.
- The graphics aren't going to blow anyone away, it is built on a fairly old version of the Unity engine but they're perfectly acceptable and go well with the game.
- It has collectibles hidden around each level. Although they all look the same, it adds a degree of replayability to the game for those who like to get every achievement in games.
- The soundtrack is very enjoyable and always fits the situation perfectly.
- The voice acting is decent, especially that of the main character, John Rochard, voiced by Jon St. John, the voice of Duke Nukem himself.
Overall, it's worth buying, although wait for a sale. There isn't enough content for £8 but there's certainly plenty for £2.

Carrying some of the principles and mechanics of the game Suguri (i.e dashing priniciples and heat gauge), Acceleration of Suguri X-Edition HD takes into to a world of arcade fighting style where you can not only just play your favorite silver head female Suguri but you can now play an extra cast of eleven more characters each with their own attacks, method of attacks, hypers, and devastating combos. Not only are you are presented with new characters, you are presented with now reworked background stages, outstanding bgm, and vigorous fighting styles which now you can take to friends since you can versus each other online.
Alright, so more on to the aspects of the game itself: The game, unlike Suguri, doesn't have that vast arsenal of weapons. Those weapons are now replaced by combos and abilities so don't expect to be unlocking weapons.... Not gonna happen. Another thing to mention is that the game only presents you with two storylines of which you have to play a certain character and battle you way to the end. In addition, this game may get repetitive since it only offers you only arcade style of playing these storylines against the same characters.
What are the in-game differences?
-There is actually only character that can actually recieve the title as a boss.
-Sicne there are no bosses, the difficulty settings are now reduced to just easy, normal, and hard. There is no special. T^T
-You actually have this option of where you can activate a shield when not using a hyper. This shield requires to 1 hyper gauge. (Pretty nice when it comes to outrageous situations)
-Each character has more than 1 hyper that can be accomplished by combos associated with the hyper button. You can even execute the character's ultimate hyper by having 3 hyper guages and slamming the hyper button+dash button+attack button.
-Like I mentioned before, it can get repetitive, howeverm if you like arcade style gaming and like the amazing combos you can do with these characters then it probably won't get that repetitive.
-Some of these characters contain abilites of which you can spam.
Do I recommend this game? Of course, I do. Now this is just coming from a huge Suguri fan. :v I recommend playing it to see if you like it, or just watch gameplays of it to see if meets your standards.

I've been playing DDO on and off for 8 years and it is still one of the best MMO's out there. FIrst impressions for new players can be bad, dated graphics and no help from other players on the starter island can scare off the kiddies but give it a chance and it can give you one of the best game experiences in an MMO.
It is not and never will be perfect, I've quit countless times but it will draw you back. It offers rareties that you seldom see in games.
You earn in game store points just by playing, if you want to try f2p it can be done (just takes a long time to buy everything). The ressurection system means you will never have a capped useless toon, you can go back to level 1 from levels 20 up and everytime you do you add a little bonus to your toon, not a lot but they add up. Don't want to go back to 1 then fine, there's a level 15 res option as well.
The game is really PVE only, the PVP option is never used, the difference in classes and gear mean it would be pointless. The PVE combat is brilliant, as good as any in MMO's. The class/race options mean you really can be/do anything with your toon, want a halfling zombie mage with a two handed sword that can still hold its own in epic content? easy.
Although experienced players go back to level 1 a lot they tend to solo the starter island meaning there is no support for new players but don't let that put you off, there are lots of guides out there and
has a full write up on every quest in the game.
Quests are handled a bit differently to other MMO's, most quests are given by npc's in neutral areas, you just go to the entrance, pick your difficulty level and off you go. Wilderness areas are more like other games but each party has its own instance, there is no fighting over resources or loot, every toon gets thier own. Like crafting? good there are 15 types.
In short it is an old MMO,  the looks have gone, forums are rubbish, a lot of content needs to be bought (you can grind/earn it) its laggy at inapropriate times and the population isn't what it was but it has staying power, its past 10 and pretty much evreything you'd want in an MMO is there. You can play f2p but buy thier cheapest package (used to be £2.99) and your account goes to premium, its worth it. Personally I'd say buy a month's sub (you go vip then after the month your account goes to premium) and blast the hell out of it.
A tip from me, press O and choose grouping, no group for what you want? make one, this game has the best pug grouping system of any MMO I've ever played.

I've been following the development of this delightful game since its first Android version: this new "Meowgically Enhanced" edition is great, full of funny references to cartoons and popular games. My little daughter is enjoying it a lot but don't be fooled: the game gets harder and harder, some puzzles will really test your patience! Very recommended! <3

.Story.
You’re a cat who wants nothing more than to be a wizard. Unfortunately, the wizard academy is much too far away for you to attend.
You’re in luck, little kitty, for you receive a package in the mail for distanced learning of the magical arts. Your training begins with spell books.
.Gameplay.
Your mouse is the only thing you need to play Spell Casting as you’ll be using it to draw various shapes. If you have a drawing tablet, this makes that task much more doable.
The game is divided into spell books, each of which allows you to practice a number of spells until you’re satisfied that you can remember how to draw them. Each practice will show you where to begin (open circle) and end (closed circle) the spell as well as give you a written cue that will hopefully spark your memory later.
And you’d better be confident because once you start the exam, which is unlocked once you’ve completed each practice with any score, you’ll be expected to recall and accurately draw each shape in a random order.
This can get quite challenging as you have to draw the shape from the same starting point that you learned earlier, lest your wizard cat chastise you with an “ah-ah!” and screen shake that can be made more or less intense in the options menu.
After you’ve passed the exam without too many errors (you only need a three star rating in order to pass each shape), you unlock the next book and move on to the next set of spells.

.Atmosphere.
The music is the same track set on a loop, so it’s not all that impressive. The majority of the game’s charm comes from the cutesy doodles that look strangely familiar and the accompanying text.
.Longevity.
The game will take you a couple of hours to beat at max.
There’s no real reason to replay anything except to get a perfect score, though you will get achievements for your efforts.
.Pros and Cons.
.Bottom Line.
Spell Casting: Meowgically Enhanced Edition is a casual and charming experience and worth a buy for the nerd-dom references alone. If you’re the artsy type and you’re looking for a way to kill some time, this title is worth a look.
If you’re not the coordinated or patient type, however, I’d advise you to steer clear.

What a game! I played this over 10 years ago and the gameplay is just as good today. Back then it was called Operation Flashpoint - Cold War Crisis, from 2001 but due to copyright issues it has been renamed under the ARMA brand in 2011. This game is a war/army simulator and as such it is bound under certain simulation rules. For example everything is hard as balls to operate. Tanks, helicopters, boats ... and planes, holy hell is it difficult to fly planes! But once you learn it, it is fantastic! Flying around in an Apache helicopter and raining hell down on all those shiny tanks is AWESOME! All this is present in the single missions but mainly the campaign. The campaign does give you missions and an outline on how to do them. But you can just ignore all that and do a lot of the stuff your own way! Place C4 to destroy 4 tanks? Nah, get in one of the tanks and wreck everything (including low flying choppers). Carefully use stealth to get to the extraction point while avoiding BMPs and patroling soldiers? Nope, just steal a Skoda 120 car and zig zag between the tank and soldier fire.  Examples like these is what made the game great for me. What extends the experience even more is the missions you do yourself in the editor. However there are downsides too - graphical glitches, stupid AI sometimes and carboard graphics. Multiplayer is pretty much dead except for LAN. But if you manage to hook up a MP game with some friend(s) you will not regret it. Yes, it is a bit laggy because the network code is rubbish, but it still is loads of fun. I recommend this retro game that despite the flaws is just so much fun!
The game does contain the expansion Operation Flashpoint: Resistance. However, it sadly does NOT contain Operation Flashpoint: Red Hammer due to copyright issues. See more

Took me about 80 hours to beat the Witch-Hunters campaign, no idea if that's average, but I do like to rampage.
The game is hard but mostly forgiving, in my playtime I think I've only had 5 or 6 warriors die, though one was my highest ranked leader when I had to abort a campaign mission due to being trapped by a bug.
I've fired a couple of cripples who had head injuries too, had 2 priests get insta-smited by the 9999dmg backfire (both survived with no injuries) and seen it happen to the AI once.
It's a tough game but if you stick with it, it does get better. The campaign missions can be a lot of back and forth to complete objectives, enemy impressives seem to have pathing issues (rat ogre and the chaos thing are too large to move easily), and I've seen a fair few enemies stay up on a ledge going into ambush stance every turn instead of trying to walk a short distance to join the fight. AI also won't sacrifice a unit to block a path or tie enemies up, so I'd say you always have the advantage (as long as you keep line of sight for your ranged units)
I have a Templar with I think around 106% parry chance, so he was total cheese when he's fighting 3 or 4 enemies at once, evading or parrying everything, immune to fear/terror/all alone tests and slowly grinding them down while the rest of my team swarms the enemy. Except Chaos mutants, who wear bracers that prevent parrying, but there's a lot of little things you learn as you play that make it easier (like spells or ranged attacks that cause a bleed type effect).
Optional objectives can be a chore, but then they're optional, and for the reward (3xp and 3 random loot items) usually not worth the risk.
Definitely a game that rewards planning over aggression, it's pretty slow but at least you can "speed up AI turn" in the options. I played about 7 hours originally and then didn't touch it for a year, so I guess they patched that in.

Pros:
Turn based version of the Witcher if your into that sort of thing.
The huge degree of specialization enables you to build teams to fit your style
Watching your characters modify over time via injuries (usually a really bad thing) forces you to adapt and adjust your style, making matchups a bit more interesting.
Cons:
The terrain in this game is laughably poorly constructed, making it nearly impossible to use the terrain advantage. I lost one match because the two leaders were fighting, and the angle prevented my hero from joining in combat against their leader, enabling him to kill my leader, and wipe me out.
The triggers for ambushes are very poorly designed, but computers can "Trap" you into an ambush. I placed my character in an ambush outside a doorway, and the AI walked right past it, and set up an "ambush" right next to my character, ensuring i would be attacked next turn.
The movement mechanism in this game tethers your units to multiple nodes in your walking trail, rather than checking the radius from your origin point. This makes it literally impossible to maximize your units mobility, while the AI is free to run the full gamut, and ensure maximal position advantage.
AI take forever to make their moves. This make each game take forever to progress through, and there's no payoff for waiting through it when you lose.
Ultimately, these issues make the game unwieldy, random, and slow. For hardcore fans of these chess-like xcom games, it might be worth the 10 bucks, but they lost my vote.

There are vast improvements over the previous installments but that is not to discount the glaring issues currently experienced by this game, namely in graphics and controls.
From a pure physics standpoint, this lands solidily competeing with the likes of RBR and Dirt Rally, but with the FFB issues and inability of the game to recognize some controllers, its hard to enjoy those physics, much less get a bead on them and improve times. If the game had propper FFB settings, I'm imagining it would feel like magic.
Content wise...its the FIA World Rally Championship. Locations, cars, drivers, everything is here. Nothing special, but nothing negative about it either.
Graphics are last gen, and that can't be argued. So what makes this a negative even more is that there are glaring performance issues from dropped framerates, stuttering, and INSANE amounts of screen tear (My rig sports a 7700k and a GTX 1070, so having said issues on this hardware is a HUGE problem). If these issues didn't exist, then one could look past the lack luster graphics, but this is more of an issue because of the performance.
Audio? Meh. The co-driver seems to be asleep at times (even when setting him to call corners and hazards to the "far ahead" option). Cars somewhat sound muted, but the outer environment sounds nice.
At best, this game is meh to boarderline unplayable. If performance and control issues are resolved in future patches, then this game should definetly be in any sim racer's library. Beyond that? Skip it until then.

Massive step forward from WRC 6 in the physics department. Still not a full sim, but it never will be because of brand restrictions. Considering the low ceiling hanging over the dev's heads, they've done a great job with the game.
Visually it's fantastic, and the stage design is certainly a benchmark for other game studios to hit, with incredible attention to detail and landscapes. And yes, narrow roads!
Sounds have slightly improved, but only sound relatively good when using chase cam, which by the way, is a great camera angle now because it behaves like GTA V, or the old WRC games by Evo Studio. But yeah, sounds still need improving, especially the co-driver; still a pretty robotic and lifeless delivery of notes.
I suppose another negative is still not having the ability to set a proper FOV for the helmet cam, but it's doesn't really hinder my enjoyment of the game.
Overall, it's good stuff.

WRC 7 has surprised me as an overall package. The epic stages are in some cases very long and a real challenge. The cars behave differently as you transition between road surfaces and the physics model is improved and credible. Not an out and out sim but edging in that direction. Graphics are very good and each country has a different atmosphere to it. The potential is all here for a great game.
There are a few aspects in which the game lets itself down however. I experienced very bad stuttering depsite having good FPS. This seems to have mostly sorted itself out somehow with all manner of tweaking and experimentation. My Thrustmaster T500 wheel is detected and works but my other USB devices do not, so my Clubsport V3 pedals needed a work around to make them even semi functional. Hoping for a patch to sort this issue! Force feedback took a lot of tweaking until it felt natural but is not bad once you have got your settings right. The game uses both spring and damper effects so be sure to turn them on to some degree in your wheel settings.
I would cautiously recommend this game, the good points out weigh the bad. The epic stages are a real draw and should satisfy even die hard rally fans. But be aware that if you are used to jumping straight in and having everything work it may not be the case with WRC 7.

Seeing as Steam thought my review was too long to post in its entirety, feel free to check out over here:
A snippet:
Disclaimer
Before I get started, I want to say that I acknowledge there are a lot of people having issues with stuttering, getting supported wheels to work and the ol’ multiple USB issues from previous titles. To clarify, I have been using my trusty XBOX 360 controller during all of my gameplay and not felt the need to mess with any controller settings. I personally have had no controller or performance issues with the game so I simply can’t comment on those aspects during this piece. I am playing the game on the maximum possible details at 1920 x 1080.
Basic PC Specs
Intel i5-4690K @ 3.90GHz/Nvidia GTX 1070/16GB RAM
My Background
I want to mention this, because I think it’s actually pretty important. I’m both a gamer and sim racer. I differentiate between the two because I approach both differently. I take sim racing very seriously, with hours and hours of practice put into events. With games outside of that, I want to feel immersed in the world I’m playing in, with it also being accessible. I want to feel like I’m part of something expansive. I very much play based on how the game makes me feel rather than outright “needing to do well”. That is the angle I approached WRC 7 from, not the sim racing angle.
The Great and the Good
I’ll be honest, I’ve been having a blast with WRC 7. “Why is that?” I hear you say. There is one very big thing that this game gets right that other rally games simply haven’t in recent years – the stages and the environments. I have played the original Colin McRae Rally (and subsequent PS1 and PS2 games), the PS2 WRC series, V-Rally 3, Richard Burns Rally, DiRT Rally and DiRT 4. Very few of those games have ever quite nailed the individuality of location feel that WRC 7 has managed. Not since the PS2 WRC series has a rally game really captured my imagination in the way WRC 7 has. It really has stirred the ol’ memory banks from my youth. Lets be honest, nothing can really beat a bit of nostalgia. Of course, the stages aren’t the only reason the only reason I’ve poured hours into this game since it launched last Friday, but the challenge they offer and the immersion they bring certainly gets me playing again and again. There are stages on offer in this game that are narrower and more dangerous than some of those in Richard Burns Rally. That should tell you something.

First of all, this is a very good game and should be considered for trying by every rally fan, especially those who like Dirt Rally and RBR.
- Stages. As for 2017 these are easily the best rally stages compared to any rally game of any time. They're both beautiful and challenging, short and long (including so called epic stages that are 15-23 km long), what else could you dream about?
- Physics. Driving cars in this game is pure fun. If I'm to compare WRC 7 to Dirt Rally and RBR, I'd say that handling in WRC 7 is closer to RBR's which is personally to me is a good thing.
- Graphics. Not the most beautiful racing game out there, but it gets the job done.
- Modern WRC cars (obviously).
- Co-driver sounds unnatural, robotic and annoying. Many improvements can be done in this department.
- UI in this game looks like something from games of early 2000's.
- Lack of overall polishing and lack of minor quality of life features like UDP output, saving/loading tuning presets and adjusting FOV.

I can confidently say that this is the second best rally game in my steam library behind DiRT Rally. I'm having a great time with this game. That being said, I do have some criticisms:
1: Performance is really inconsistent. the game looks amazing but certain stages in Germany, Spain and Italy (I think) really hit the framerate on anything above medium settings, while other areas such as Poland are completely fine with everything maxed out.
2: There are enough stages overall, but the individual rallies feel a bit short. An option to run every stage reversed or even mirrored would greatly enhance the feeling of doing a full rally, rather than simply a few events. These are some of the best stages ever in a rally game and I would love to enjoy them as much as possible.
3: Replays are a huge issue. Firstly, the quality of the replays is poor, with bad camera angles except for the helicopter one and not enough roadside pans. Also, it resets your in game viewpoint for the next stage if you watch a replay which is really annoying.
4: GIVE US AN OPTION TO REMOVE/REDUCE HEAD/COCKPIT SHAKE! It is really annoying and kinda makes me feel sick.
In all however, Kylotonn has done an amazing job of WRC 7 and this has turned out to be the most surprising gamen of the year for me. The old days of having New Zealand stages in a WRC game are long gone, but now I can race Hayden Paddon's Hyundai through amazing stages in a licenced rally game that is actually good!

With over 700 hrs played I can not give this a bad review. This was the very first Total War game I ever played and the one that got me hooked on the series.
Pros
-stunning graphics (even if they are a little dated)
-helpful tutorials which I strongly recommend you play if your new to the series
-the music on the campaign map gets a little repetitive, but the music for both the land and naval battles get me pumped for an epic battle. (My girlfriend always says it sounds like star wars)
-lots of "x factors" effecting unit moral including exhaustion and losses, like wise dicisively winnning against the enemy can make your soldiers fight better. Ships can be effected with loss of masts, men and hull damage. Also accidents like misfires from both cannons and muskets killing your own men , with the addition of friendly fire add to the realism of war. Later steamships can be researched, they have superior sailing capibilities but have a higher chance of blowing up realisticly showing how primitive they where for the time.
-great beginner title to enter the series.
-naval battles (from what I understand a first to the series with this game)
cons
-calvery units are really only good for skirmishing and running your enemy down, most linemen can ward them off
-espioniage is a little limited in this game, something the really expanded in Shogun
-building damage in land battles is kind of "meh" compared to the epic ship damage in naval battles
-city fortresses, of all cons this was my biggest complaint, you can't repair city fortresses and any damage done reamains. If you want to "fix" this you have to destroy and rebuild it to square fort and then upgrade it if you want a star fort This just wasted so many turns.
Other Thoughts
The naval battles are the hardest to get used to, and I noticed alot of my friends who play this game hate them. Unlike land battles naval battles are easier to manage when you group your fleets, I find line formation works the best hence why the called these ships"ships of line", you get full use of your broadsides this way. I only command individual ships in smaller fleets. Once you figure out the tactics you'll have one of the most awsome 18th cenury naval battles ever, I'll never forget the first time i saw my opponate's 1st rate explode rate down the middle!
All and all I give it a 9/10

This game is hard.
And not just in the Dark Souls sense of the word, with trial and error being a core component of the game. (It still is.)
The game is hard to get into, and hard to master. It starts with learning how to make a deck, which can be incredibly frustrating if you don't understand how the deck building system works. Once you've got that down, it can be hard to learn new moves, as you defend and counterattack as your movelist slowly builds. Back to deckbuilding. Still hard, and even more complex with new options.
And then there's PvP.
Absolver is a game about getting knocked down and, hopefully, getting back up. A lot of people in the reviews complain about the level difference in PvP. However, after every match you have the option of messaging the player you just fought and asking what happened and why you lost, and the community is built in such a way that you'll often get a helping hand. You can join one of the discords, talk about decks and abilities, the subtleties of feinting, and just how tight your outfit is.
This game isn't based around being a coolguy out of the gate. This is a game based around learning. And, after 300 hours of learning, it's one of the most satisfying experiences out there. Players you went up against and would demolish you? You know all of their tricks now. The previous struggle of building a good deck? You can fit the pieces together in newer and flashier ways. The game is martial arts all the way through, especially in its philosophy. Comparing this to Dark Souls doesn't do the game justice. The game is like competitive Dwarf Fortress, where you've got so many options and a learning curve so steep that pushing through feels like you've climbed Mount Everest.
Things to keep in mind: I'm not talking about PvE. The PvE in this game is fun, but relatively short. It's like a very long tutorial to prepare you for PvP, which is where the game absolutely shines. It has its bugs, but when the game behaves as it should (which is only getting more consistent) It feels fantastic.

Jamestown is a game developed and published by Fianl Form Games
Jamestown is an extremely solid shoot-em-up, with one really fantastic advantage over other games of the sort
As a single player game, the bullet patterns and level designs are solid but also a bit bland and lacking in strategic variety.

It's probably the best co-op shoot-em-up ever made!
It also has one of the best and most creative settings and aesthetics for a game. The theme, music, pixel art, and setting are excellent
If you don't have anyone to play with (local multiplayer only), then Jamestown is a decent shoot-em-up that should probably be somewhere in your wishlist
However, if you have some friends to play with, it's an absolute must buy!

So, I've basically been playing this game since it first came out, and recently transfered it to steam.
I generally give this game a 8 out of 10.
There are some issues which need to be resolved, I'll list them though I doubt turbine or whom ever is running ddo now days will actually fix them.
The graphics for this game are in my opinion excellent. Character control is on spot and easy. Play through and challenges are variable and allow the player to set the difficulty.  The story lines and quest lines in this game are absolutely amazing and well thought out for 90% of them. Some are just cheesy, but that happens in every game.
Constant updates and additions to this game make it one to stick with.
Seasonal events make the holidays more fun.
90% of the game will be inaccessable unless you go vip and/or buy the expansions/adventure packs.
Mneumonic potions, store bought item only. These replace lost mana which is used up via spells. Needing these is pretty much key for playing a blaster caster, or glass cannon. Saddly they don't seem to drop anymore in chests or quests. They seem to be a store bought item only, thus you will have to pay to win to play a wiz/sorc.
Wizards/ Sorcs- Best dps, glass cannons. Highly reliant on some form of wall and mana potions which are ddo store bought only. Familiars still haven't come into existance dispite numerous requests and complaints. The one exception to this is going pale master on wizard and being able to summon a skeleton companion (which isn't overly powerful, or useful.)
Fighters, this class is so woefully under powered that it's more of a joke rather than something actually playable. You will be vulnerable to everything, you wont be able to deal out adequate damage, you can't heal yourself, no magic, and lets forget about locks and traps. There is one word for this class, screwed.  (This is not how it was in the past, a good up front sword and board use to be a very valuable thing in parties, saddly no longer.)
Barbarians, slightly better than fighters, more hp, but still 95% useless.
Warlocks, a favorite class lately it seems, though their blast and aura damage output sinks them behind sorcs and wizards, and even clerics and paladins, and even a well made rogue. Still, when mixed correctly with other classes they can add many benefits.
Artificer, this is probably the best soloing class. High dps, magic, buffs, can deal with locks and traps. Robot dog companion which can actually heal you faster than any regen int he game.
Rogues - decent solo character if built correctly with high hide, ms, search, spot, open lock, disable trap, high hp, and dual wielding with the correct feats. Fort will be your down fall, but rogues or trappers are absolutely required for this game. With out one you will miss out on loot, extra xp, secret doors, etc.
Druids - They come with an animal companion and magic, haven't played one yet but I imagine they are some where between clerics and wizards as far as casting power goes.
Clerics - amazing class to play when going through the multiple undead quests, otherwise you might just get tacked onto a group to play doctor while doing very little for the rest of the dungeon. High solo ability, or dual party with a rogue for multiple dungeons and quests.
Rangers, other than the artificer the ranger is an amazing ranged dps you can go with. Some magic, no animal companion as of yet dispite requests and complaints. Some healing, no traps or locks.
Paladins - the word tank seems to fit these pretty well. Paladins have taken the place of the old fighter it seems for sword and board, having magic, resistances, auras, etc. No mount as of yet dispite requests and complaints.
There are several premium class/race options available if you want to pay for them.
There are multiple dungeon areas if you want to pay for them.
There are multiple expansions/dlcs if you want to pay for them.
If you go entierly free account then go on each server and get your favor up to 125 with your first character there, this will give you enough money in the ddo store to buy some adventure packs at the very least with out dropping a dime.
Invest in the monster manuals if you want extra xp, astral shards, ddo coins.
Pets/companions/and hirelings - These are great resources when they work, though usually after about half an hour of playing (and some dungeon chains can run you 3+ hours) they tend to stop working. They stop fighting, healing, protecting you, etc.  So, if you dump money into hiring the gold seal ones from the store be prepared for soem faulty ai junk after the first half an hour.
Some things don't actually calculate as their descriptions say, which might leave you wondering what's going on.
Cr rating/level rating - these ratings are to inform you of what level you and your party should be when doing a dungeon. These ratings are accurate for casual and normal dungeons, if you go to hard or elite difficulties expect the level/challenge rating to be at least two to five levels off. Ie, an elite lvl 12 will actuall have cr 15-20 creatures in it making it actually impossible for a level 12 to do it alone unless you spend butt loads of money on rez cakes in the ddo store, or hirelings, etc.
Xp is calculated incorrectly since the challenge/level ratings for the dungeons are calculated incorrectly. Expect xp to be on the low side unless you invest in xp tomes and potions.
Stat tomes are a must if you want to increase your survivability from 25% to 60%, maybe that's a little ascewed on the lower side.  These can be earned after many, many hours of game play, or you get lucky with a drop, or you just buy them from the ddo store for an absurd amount of money. Once more, pay to win.
Guilds - there are lots of guilds out there. . .you can get buffs and extra xp and such from being in a high level guild.
Loot - half of what you find will be bound to your character or account, so don't think you'll make a bunch of money on the auction house trying to sell rare things.
The auction house - the majority of servers sell things at about 200 -500% mark up. Yes, these are common every day drops. Nearly every servers auction house is so woefully over priced that you're better off just trying to find the stuff your self by farming dungeons. This however is a player based issue, not a game issue.
There are multiple advancement trees and many, many options on how to form and build your character. You can make them weak or strong in multiple areas.
Boss fights- Don't expect over 50% of your spells to work on bosses, stick with melee, ranged, or damaging spells. You have to litterally nickle and dime some bosses to death.
Raids- There are multiple raids and events, but you will need at least a group of four to twelve to do any of them. Only a few are actually soloable. This is due to levers, pressure plates, and all sorts of other annoying bs which has to all be done at the same time in order to open doors, etc.

InFlux. Another unknown game of mine that i'd had in my library for a while, never looked at it, heard about it, or played it. Happy to say i enjoyed this game very much! Its, a ball rolling, puzzle solving adventure game, where you gather little orbs to unlock puzzles to progress around the map, which doesn't sound appealing, but it really grips you from the start due to it being so easy to play and get to grips with. Graphics are nice, It's not too long, puzzles make you think, not too much, but enough to make it moderatly challenging. I played through it in a night, 5 levels, around 12 puzzles, not too many bad things in this little gem. Loading areas can hit your FPS quite harshly, making the game stutter a bit, and the ball controls aren't always the easiest to control, mainly when you're mid air!
Simple. Effective. 8/10

A short length and oddly implemented mechanics keep the proverbial ball from getting rolling.
InFlux manages to create a rather unique and interesting world for a ball rolling game. You traverse more traditional terrains on a semi-tropical island collecting orbs to unlock puzzles that progress you to the next part of the island. The terrain just doesn't work with a ball though. Its too natural and rocky and bumpy for a ball. Its rarely fun exploring these sections and they're an easy chore more than anything. As for the puzzles, they are more umm "futuristic" and clean. Much more on par as to what you'd expect in the genre though again, unique. The puzzles are quite inventive sure, but are all unfortunately very straight forward. With little room to make errors you simply don't. Which ultimately makes them unsatisfying despite how cool they are. A huge sour point in the game both in and out of puzzles is a lifting fan mechanic (fan on the ground, blows your ball upwards). They rarely lift you to the height required without some finagling and are all around poorly implemented. Toss some loading hiccups and hangs (especially early) on top of it all and its mostly a frustrating game. In a bad way, not a good challenging game way.
I clocked it at under 3 hours from start to finish. So on the shorter side. Its no reason to avoid a bundle by any means. But I'd have a hard time recommending it outside of one. I will say it was interesting to see a metal glowing ball, in a canoe, on a whale. So there's that at least. Plenty of other better single session time killer games out there than this though.
Not bad until you get to a point where you need precise control of the ball for platforming in puzzles but the controls are anything but.

Mordheim is not for everyone. Its unforgiving, slow-paced, and grindy. There is no save-scumming, permanent death/injuries, RNG, and the chance to lose a great deal of progress with a single error. After you figure out the mechanics and rhythm of the game those things are more limitations on your progress, instead of significant impediments.
Its main drawback is a result of the nature of the single save and the punishment for failure. These are good mechanics and needed for the dark setting of Mordheim, but ultimately forces you to rely on a single strategy for all standards missions. Essentially, there is no good reason to ever take risks or seek out you enemy--it ALWAYS makes more sense to pick a good defensive spot near spawn (making sure to always pick missions with a tight deployment) and wait for the AI to trickle its fighters into your ambush. While the potential for RNG can still get your warriors killed if you are careless, this strategy essentially decides all your standard missions. Thus instead of a highly strategic game, it often feels like a tedious game of waiting for the AI to rush to its death. The story missions are different, and show a glimmer of how difficult this game could be if you were forced to fight the AI in a more aggressive fashion.
All that said, this game is weirdly fun to play. All the factions share similar mechanics but play significantly different. The customization isn't great or expansive, but enough to feel attached to your warriors who have the potential to acquire grizzly injuries. Progressing your warband is an achievement mostly of the player's patience, but rewarding all the same.
Overall I think its a great game to pick up when it goes on sale (which it does with regularity).

A puzzle-platformer based around gravity and throwing boxes around.  It's a perfectly functional game, everything works well and I don't recall any glitches.  Unfortunately, that's as far as I can praise it.
The puzzles start out very easy, and for the most part stay there.  There are some interesting mechanics, but they're never taken far enough to actually be interesting.  From beginning to end, you'll pretty much be solving the same few basic puzzles over and over again.  The gravity swinging is the best part of the game, but again it never goes beyond very basic use.
Combat is a chore.  Point at the enemies, hold the attack button.  If you're feeling daring, throw a crate.  It's very easy and serves no purpose other than to pad out the game.
Rochard, the titular character, is a space redneck working for a mining company.  The game tries to present him as some heroic badass, but he's mostly just annoying.  It doesn't help that he has a groupie/love interest following after him, singing his praises.  The villain is a short German guy, and the vast majority of the enemies you'll be slaughtering throughout the game are flamboyant homosexual stereotypes.
I don't consider any of this a spoiler, since from his very first appearance it is blatantly obvious that the German guy will turn out to be evil.
The game is functional.  A completely standard puzzle platformer that does nothing to stand out.  Puzzle-platformers are hardly in short supply these days; in a genre with so many excellent examples I really see no reason to ever play Rochard.
The DLC is the best part of the game by far.  The puzzles are actually somewhat tricky.  But again, they never go beyond fairly basic and the whole thing is quite short.  Not worth buying or playing the game for.

Mordheim is how tactics games should be.
Let's be honest and up front here: this game has a few issues. The load times tend to be long, and the RNG and AI combo can be punishing for your characters and your sanity. However, I don't think these problems eclipse the fact that Mordheim is FUN. The different warbands are cool and diverse in playstyle, and loyal to the originial Warhammer universe. The balancing act of in-mission decisions and of managing your warband between missions provides a nice tactical counterpoint - cost/benefit analysis is important at all stages. The pacing of missions allows you to make the measured decisions and careful considerations that a tactics game should require, and the different objectives and conditions throw curveballs left and right; that's how it should be, in my view. If you like a game to challenge you, you got it.
Mordheim is HARD, very hard, and combining high difficulty with a single autosave file means decisions (and mistakes) have permanent consequences. It can be discouraging - but if you like games that make you work for it, this is a winner. The payoff for time invested is a very real sense of accomplishment.

I'll start by saying that this is not a game for casuals, if you want to have a game that is incredibly compelling and complex and rewarding to learn, this is your game.  While Civ 3 remains a complete mystery to me, I can say I have played all the others, and this one is by far the best I've played.  You might say "what about Civ 5?", but I highly prefer it to Civ 5 for several reasons (unit stacking ***Figure out how to use collateral damage people***, tech/espionage/culture slider, much more micromanagable empire, better system for unit and city maintenance, far superior espionage system, more interesting promotion dynamics with military units, unrestricted leaders, non gimmicky leader traits, non gimmicky religions, far superior map option, way less annoying barbarians, way less buggy multiplayer, etc etc etc...)
I have dumped hundreds of hours into this game on steam (untold hundreds more on my non steam copy) multiplayer on the steam servers just last year and still have no fatigue of this game.  The replay value is incredible and you can even find interesting strategies with unrestricted leaders.  If you like Civ 5, and have never played Civ 4 BtS, and want to take your Civ experience to the next level, I highly recommend you this game for you.  It can be overwhelming at first, I know, but give it time, it's a seriously good game.
Don't let my seemingly low play time fool you, after 10 years and several thousand hours this game hasn't even gotten close to getting old.

Now, where do I even start. Think of this as a fighting game, except bullet hell. My one complaint would be the fact that it pretty much assumes direct control of your desktop. You can't alt+tab unless you press esc first, and the steam overlay doesn't work. Now, I do want to point out his review is based on my experience. Apparently some people are having problems running the game, it's unresponsive to their controls, or they can't get achievements. Bravo Developers!.... Now for starters it does seem to have some issues with Nvidia Graphics cards which hopefully the developers patch. The game stutters. I have personally found a fix for my gpu the 1080ti. In the Nvidia control panel goto manage 3d settings and the click program settings tab. Add the game. On power management ive set it prefer Maximum Performance, Triple Buffering is on, Vertical Sync is on and then Virtual reality pre- rendered frames set to 4. In the game Graphics settings i have shadow quality set to medium, Texture quality High, particles on low ( this seems to be a big cause of frame drops) Visability Distance  High, Vegitation density medium and the last two set to high. Game is running in 4k at 60fps for me and looks fantastic. Still get the odd stutter but its much improved with those settings.
As for the game itself its a huge improvement from last year. The graphics are a hugh improvement and so are the tracks. If your a rally fan you will love this game. I think it sits between Sim and Arcade. Which i prefer personally. Overall its a fantastic rally game and the developers deserve a clap for the improvements to last years poor effort.
Hopefully the settings i put above help people out.  Enjoy!

DDO is different from most MMO's I've played in that instead of hundreds of players all trying to kill the same monsters you have public non-combat areas to do your shopping, etc... and private instances for your party to adventure in.  Some adventures are F2P, all others are accessible by monthly subcription or can be purchased individually and thereafter available to all your characters.  If you're familiar with DnD 3.5 then you know 90% of the game mechanics but you also receive points to spend on "Enhancements".  What enhancements you have access to depends on your class, and multi-classing is possible so if you want a  fighter with a couple levels of bard you can have it.  Some purchaseable features such as the Drow playable race can also be gained for free after completing a certain number of quests.  Also, the dungeons are beautifully crafted with a dungeonmaster occassionally giving you descriptions for atmosphere.  The Temple of Elemental Evil adventure has discoverable playback snippets of Wil Wheaton describing his own early experiences playing the pen and paper game.

Jamestown is a pretty incredible game. It is definitely one of the best local co-op games I know of, and is still fun to play solo. It has very nice-looking graphics, an amazing soundtrack, and a story that is compelling, but stays out of the way of the gameplay. The difficulty ranges from "unchallenging, but still fun" to "mercilessly difficult, but still fun" with the bullet-hell gameplay always maintaining an intense, hectic feel. It rewards success, but doesn't overly punish failure, making it so very easy to just play one more game.
Jamestown consistently impresses my friends when I show it to them, and the only real criticism I can give is that I find some of the characters difficult to use effectively. About half of the characters are fun though, and I only really play one of them anyway. If you have similar gripes about the characters, the DLC is worth considering, as it adds four new characters which are all pretty nice.
Overall, definitely worth the price, on sale or otherwise, and an absolute 10/10 in my book.
