Ok, this one is tricky.
First things first: the music and sound environment are gorgeous. They convey perfectly the extreme emotional intensity of the game.
My personal opinion: it is not suitable for the very young. Don't be fooled by the great art, in the end the game is all about sad, dark and morbid events. The orchestration of the story and the way the characters are fleshed out are so much well done it amplifies significantly the emotional impact of the events.
Now, the ♥♥♥♥♥ing: a bit too much reading, but I guess it contributed a lot to the growth of the emotional bubbles. Technically, this game did deserve better, animation wise and for its narative expression power. I kind of felt the constraints of the engine to build the puzzles and story unfolding, even though I know what to blame: resource limitations (not all projects can have tens of devs, artists, etc).
On the overall, it's obviously a great journey.

I cannot possibly recommend this game more. The art is lovely, the music is absolutely breathtaking, the story is so delicately well crafted, and the down-to-earth writing of the script is second to none.
Laura Shigihara and co. have created a love letter to 16-bit RPGs. Despite there being no random battles or any of the gameplay staples of that era, the bright and colorful world and zany characters, as well as a couple more literal nods to influential games, really do that era of gaming a justice that I have not seen in years. The world feels like Earthbound meets Secret of Mana meets Chrono Trigger. As a SNES kid, this resonated with me deeply.
Emotionally, I feel like it's easily in my personal top five most emotionally touching games.
If you're on the fence about this game and happen upon this review, please do yourself a favour and support this wonderful piece of art. You will not be disappointed.
NOTE: Due to weird Internet instability, the "Hours on Record" displayed are incorrect. I believe this game took me in the neighbourhood of 10 to 12 hours to complete.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is a tactical, turn-based, party game based in the Warhammer universe. The core game is based around sending out your warband to explore the ruins of Mordheim to gather the lucrative resource, wyrdstone. Each warband is made up of the different factions (Skaven, Empire Mercenaries, Sisters of Sigmar, and the Cult of the Possessed; Witch Hunters and Undead are paid DLC) and have an array of different units to use. The units have their own set of perks, weapons and armor they can use, and skills. Building a solid team to succeed is paramount to your warband’s survival. Failure can lead to temporary and permanent injuries that are costly to fix and can have lasting negative effects for the injured unit. The game allows a good deal of customization in the makeup of your warband so you can easily design a team to fit your playstyle.
Combat and actions are all based on your typical dice rolling chance system to determine success or failure. Each unit has so many actions it can do each turn from strategy or offense points. What actions each unit can do is of course based on things like what weapons and abilities they have. When two units start fighting they are locked into combat and can’t move unless they sacrifice strategy and offense points to flee or disengage. This allows you or your enemy to easily move in more units to quickly overcome the other. Complicating the situation though is that each unit has a circle of engagement that stops movement through the area, so one enemy can block a doorway or an alley. This flows into allowing players to set up kill zones where for example one melee unit is holding down an alley while his archer buddies are above raining down death.
There are secondary objectives to each mission but the overall goal is rout the enemy team either by killing them all or enough of them that they fail a morale check. While trying to overcome your enemies though, there’s wyrdstone to be gathered around the map. Wyrdstone is the lifeblood of your warband and you have to walk a fine line between gathering it and keeping your units alive in combat. The wyrdstone itself is volatile though and every time a unit picks some up there is a chance they can receive a buff or debuff. The end result is a hectic battleground filled with hard choices. Many times I’ve had an unfortunate unit get caught out in the open and have to decide whether they are worth saving or not. Overall it can make things stressful but its extremely rewarding gameplay when a well thought out plan works or you overcome a difficult situation. Outside of missions there are wyrdstone shipments that your faction will demand from you to deliver within a set amount of time. The rewards for fulfilling them are gold and reputation that eventually will unlock perks. There are other factions that have shipment requests, but they are just requests and not required. They also have their own reputation and perks though so you have to decide who to supply wisely. If you fail the required shipment, their next demand will be bigger and you’ll have less time to fulfill it. After four failures its game over. At the same time, you have to pay your soldiers and pay for their injuries. Injured soldiers can eventually succumb to their wounds and unpaid soldiers will leave resulting in your warband being disbanded, or in other words, game over.
Each faction has story missions to complete on the campaign map that’s unique to them. There’s also randomly generated secondary missions you can do to your heart’s content. Story missions can get really frustrating with vague mission details and worst of all, infinite enemy reinforcements. When the whole game is based around your decisions having lasting impacts and possibly end the game for that warband, poor design on story missions can quickly kill the fun. In the end, I had a lot more fun with side missions and started to avoid story missions.
There’s also 1v1 multiplayer matches called Skirmishes. Skirmishes come in two types, exhibition and contest. Exhibition is a purely for fun match using one of your single player warbands. There’s no rewards or punishments for the outcome of the match. Contest skirmishes act just like a single player mission in that you have to not only pay the upkeep of your units but they can become injured. You keep the fruits of your labor too though making it a highly competitive match. Only problem is that there is never anyone with a match setup and good luck getting someone to join yours. The matches are only 1v1 too so unless you and a friend enjoy killing each other’s warbands, multiplayer is nonexistent.
My Two Cents
After weighing everything else in, there’s an immense amount of replay value in the game, but sadly only in single player. With each warband having different units and you being able to craft each unit to how you want, it keeps each playthrough varied and fun. There’s also a veteran system that you earn points for the more you play the game. This allows you to have an easier time right off the bat when starting a new warband and gives you something to look forward to. The game gave me exactly what I expected from it, but it doesn’t strike me as a game most people would sit and relax with. It’s a hectic fight for your warband’s life and some of these fights can take quite a while to complete. If you have the time to sit down and think things through, Mordheim fits the bill nicely. For a game that started in early access and delivered on its promises with a plethora of gameplay features, I think Mordheim is worth its $39.99 price tag and your playtime (once again, not a sit-down and play a few minutes kind of game).

Civ IV is my most played game ever, and a pinnacle of the strategy genre. I have installed it on every computer I have owned since it came out. The Steam play time reflects that I played from my CD-ROM copy of CIV 4 complete until recently when my install discs became incompatible with Windows 10. I feel that the Civ 4 gameplay is the most balanced and addictive of Civ 4 series games, with strong ai, diplomacy, building, expansion, religion, commerce, and war all providing great depth that makes playing just one more turn addictive. In my opnion, only the great Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri has comparable all around strengths and innovations for its time, Moreover, Civ 4 has given me unparalleled replay value because it is the most modable Civ game.  Besides the usual tweaks of the vanilla game on can find in Civ 5, Civ 4's structure enabled the creation of many complete overhaul mods that transformed CIv 4 with new gameplay and graphics, including historical, fantasy, and sci-fi mods. For example, in my opinion, the Civ 4 fantasy mod, Fall From Heaven 2, remains of one of the best 4x strategy fantasy pc games ever made.
Civ IV, however, does show its age when compared to more refined interface of Civ V. Civ 4's maps of square titles and battles with stacks of units on the same tile, also give a less sophisticated first impression. However, when I compare the gameplay between Civ 4 and Civ 5, I find Civ 4 AI is usually more challenging, sophisticated, and strategically effective than in Civ 5, with regard to both combat and non-combat activities alike.
Install Civ 4 complete (Civ IV, Civ IV Warlords, and Civ IV Beyond the Sword) and join the addiction!
Note: I have reviewed Civ 4 and its expansions as a single game.

TLDR - Fun little platformer with an interesting game mechanic.  Definitely worth it when on sale, maybe not quite at regular price.
It's not very long, and it generally is pretty easy, but it's well-made, has interesting mechanics, and is overall quite fun.  I found the "ancient Native American legend" bit of the storyline a little goofy, but that doesn't detract too much from the enjoyment of the game as a whole.  The look and feel of the design is great, the voice acting is quite good, and the music is enjoyable.
Some might find the game too easy, but I like the feeling that I am making progress, so it didn't bother me that much.  It is a little short, but that just means that I enjoyed it enough to want more.  It's short enough that I'm not sure I would have paid full price for it, but on sale it was absolutely worth the money.
My biggest complaint actually has to do with the ending - if you die, the game has you restart from the last checkpoint, which works well throughout most of the game.  In the final battle, however, the last checkpoint comes before the fight starts, before the villain does his stereotypical villain monologue in a cut scene.  And there is no way to skip that cut scene.  I died several times before beating the final boss, which means that I had to sit and listen to that monologue over and over, punching buttons and hitting keys in hopes of skipping the damn thing.  Oddly, the same thing happens when the final credits begin to roll.  You had better enjoy that theme song, because you are going to have to listen to the whole thing - I could find no way of skipping the credit sequence.
Overall, however, I quite enjoyed Rochard.  If you enjoy a good indie platformer with a heavy dose of puzzle solving, I recommend it, especially on sale.

I really dislike this game and I will try to elaborate as much as I can. I hope that my arguments against this game will be justified and fair.
This game is a puzzle-platformer most of the time and this is one of the better elements done in Rochard. Puzzles and mechanics aren't clever or original (main gimmick is a gravity gun and lowering/increasing gravity force), but most of the time they are nonintrusive. I also liked some sections where you are performing Tarzan using mentioned gun. This was pretty fun.
Unfortunately, all other important aspects fall flat for me. ESPECIALLY combat. Sometimes you are forced to shoot some dudes. I can understand that it was added to vary the pacing, but at the end it was implemented very badly on many levels. One, ludonarrative dissonance. Your protagonist is presumably a nice and caring guy, yet you gunning down mercenaries like heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Two, gunplay is pretty boring and unsatisfying. You basic gun makes only minor "pew pew pew" and most of the time shooting you feel empty. Three, enemies are morons. They literally get crushed by the slow moving elevator without any reaction. "Moving away from the lowering platform? Nah, I will stay here! Nothing important to consi..." <Dead>. This is a overall how they function. Expect idiots everywhere.
Story is extremely problematic. You can see first plot twist from mile away and game expects you to be shocked. Dramatic scenes are made laughable thanks to poor and repetitive 3D animations. Characters are really bland and except for the main protagonist, they have no personality whatsoever. I'm a person that can ignore story problems if characters are likeable, but this is not the case. Mid-game they are trying to set up the "big reveal" at the end. Of course there are no actual hints or information what's going on, game only insist that there is a MASSIVE revelation down the line. After pretty weak bossfight at the end of the game you will learn the truth! SPOILER ALERT You get nothing. To sum up: uninteresting characters, no actual story development, weak villain, no pay-off. Nothing.
Graphics look kind of nice, but level design is uninspired (many annoying forcefields of different kinds that block you, block things you carry or block your shots) and art assets are reused very often. best looking locations are to ones that are more unique - Third level for example.  Game has also a VERY bad habit of not telling you important things. Example: "Great! You found an upgrade station!", "What does it do?", "I don't know!". Other example: You are expected to lower gravity in one room to reach higher ledge in one of the early levels. I was stuck there for few minutes, I didn't know that I can do that. No button prompt, no voice information. This could be understandable in more basic game, but in that moment I was thinking that I'm getting a puzzle wrong. Until I checked the control scheme and discovered the button for gravity change (note that effect of button press is not instant), I was painfully stuck
Overall, I would call Rochard an unpleasant experience. Puzzles are okayish, but combat, story and questionable omissions in basic game design make this one part boring, second part infuriating and third part plain mediocre. I simply cannot recommend it. People may like this game, I don't know how, but that's good for you.

For someone who has never played Resident Evil before, I wasn't 100% sure what to expect. Now that I'm partway through the third chapter, I can confidently say that I love this game.
Being dropped in the middle of what I presume to be Spain... At night... When it's "zombie weather" outside... With nothing more than a picture and a purpose. You soon learn there's a lot more to the village than meets the eye...
The first levels are a tad bit linear, but the storyline and mix between survival, exploration and action more than makeup for it. More than once have I been caught by a villager from behind when I never knew there was a path there in the first place. Definitely adds to the horror aspect.
The boss fights are unique and quite challenging at times (especially when you're boxed in the barn with Mendez). If you misclick, you suffer, and hard. Some bosses can kill you in one attack set, in fact.
The weapon management system is really nice when you have lots of items that you need to pack in before the next upgrade. Rotating your guns also saves a ton of space, and you'll need it.
You also don't get a lot of ammo. Ammo during the first castle fight gave me a tough time; took almost everything I had just to get downstairs and flip the switch, let alone get to the water challenge with Ashley.
Overall I'd say it's definitely worth the buy. Runs great on lower end systems, and it's an enjoyable tactical survival experience. Be sure you have FAST fingers.
Cons:
-Quicktime prompts appear for a fraction of a second, making them impossible to react to on the first go. It also CHANGES from M1 and M2 to X and C, so I just mash both of them at the same time.
-The tap X quicktime events are bugged; you have to smash the X key so fast or else you fail instantly and have to redo the ENTIRE (starting with) minecart segment. I have to somehow press it at LEAST 7 times per SECOND. Not even talking about the Salazar statue run...

Pentium G4600
8GB DDR4

It's clear that there's probably dozens of pages just about all this background information about the world.
All five of the routes made me feel, with deep characters who learn and grow for the most part, and the music is absolutely gorgeous. There are things I felt needed a bit more work, but I understand that a. this game is free and b. by a small indie company, so not all my wishes could be met. The only one I would like for an expansion of the story is maybe an LGBT route or two. I also have friends who would prefer proper evil routes, which this lacks.
I would recommend this game to pretty much anyone, whether or not they are into Otome Games, since the world and characters are amazingly crafted. If you just like Fantasy stuff, this is your game as much as if you're into the genre.

Puzzle platformer where you're a ball. You can roll and boost to move and you can attract and repel certain objects to accomplish goals.
As a puzzle game it's pretty decent. The art and settings are nice, gamplay is fairly smooth, and the music fits the mood into a nicely relaxed atmosphere. The main menu is a bit obtuse. Some clipping and invisible walls (i've gotten stuck inside a boulder and shot myself into tree branches, though the latter I could escape from), plus your ball isn't big enough to get over some terrain types, so that can halt your momentum in some areas as you find ways around and sometimes in the later areas you can find yourself on small ledges that weren't meant to have paths to progress so you have to kill yourself.
You get generous checkpoints and don't have to reload if you fall somewhere and "die", but you can't save progress in the middle of an area and leave the game. If you come back you can go to the area you were in. but it will be as if you just got there for the first time and all puzzles need completing, so make sure you have time for 3-4 puzzles, at least.
If you want story about why you're a ball, what your goal is, why these puzzle places are around, I'm afraid the game gives nothing on that front, which is too bad. There's enough unique things about the setting and gameplay to interest you about the reason for it all.
Overall an enjoyable experience, though.

Heartomics 2 is a grinding game to boost your stats to fight monsters. You can do three different things each day and that's it. Although it's Heartomics 2, i believe that there is no relation between the first and the second serie at all.
There are two musics in this game and it's very nice and relaxing.
This game uses anime style characters and they looks nice. The backgrounds are also good looking. However, the main menu and the UI is horrible. The main menu only shows a low resolution Heartomics logo and a "New Game" button. The buttons are also designed horribly with no effort.
The game doesn't give much story to begin with although i believe that there is a story branching in this game since i play this and got a game over without doing anything significant.
You'll be shown a screen of a girl with bunch of icons after pressing a New Game. With no way of knowing what icon does what, i decided to tinker around until i found out that most of the icons are used to raise your stats. There are tons of stats such as HP, strength, defense, magic attack, and magic defense for battle. There are also other stats which i don't even understand what is it used for such as art skill, endurance, confidence, and a lot more.
You can do three actions in the game by pressing the icons. You can train, work, or even going somewhere. However, you can only do each of these actions once per day although after playing it for a few days, i feel that i need to go to other places more than once because you can buy a status boost potions and trigger event which i believe is used to progress to the story. Sadly, you can only do it once per day.
There is also an option to kill enemies although the combat system is horrible. There is an attack, magic attack, and counter command. Both attack and magic attack will do attack to the enemy (no, you don't get to choose which "spell" that you have to cast in magic attack command) while the counter will... counter the attack that the enemy do (if it's attacking, that is). Your attack can also get countered by the enemy which makes it to be a guessing game. The enemy is also way too strong to beat if you didn't grind for stats beforehand.
You can also see your status although it's divided into three sections and all status (such as HP, strength, and defense) informations are displayed in separate dialogues. This is also happening when you're training and working. You'll get a "Your strength increased by 10!" kinda message three times in one action.
There is a closet option where you can buy clothes to change your character outfit in the screen. I don't think that there is a stat boost by using different clothes but there is a weapon shop in the town where you can buy a weapon to boost your stat in a small amount.
Honestly, i still don't know what's the point of this game. I just clicked through the options several times and waiting for the dialogue to roll out. The game also has auto save (no manual save) which make me have to reset the game completely if i screwed up. In the end, i got a "game over" (although it doesn't say so) after i advance a day without knowing what happened.
Actually i want to stop playing this game just after a few seconds, but i hold out until i got this "game over" screen.
Pros:
- Changeable clothes.
Cons:
- No tutorial.
- Unclear goal.
- Terrible battle system.
- Too much useless dialogue.
This is a stat grinding game with no clear point on what to do.

Before:
An extremely skill demanding turn-based tactical-strategy chess-like card game, the main focus of the game is on each player's ability to make the right tactical and strategic decisions rather than luck.
Each card is balanced, every single mechanic has a counter and all the non-free cards get countered by free cards. A free deck can beat a non-free deck. There are no better cards, they all serve a purpose and are situational to a wide variety of different strategies, non-free cards offer different strategies.
You can get every single card on the game by purchasing them with gold or diamonds. Gold is a currency you get every time you win a quick match game, by winning a bet on a quick match game, or by purchasing gold using real money. Diamond is a currency you get by purchasing it with real money.
Being that you can only get gold by winning a quick match game or a bet, the game is very punishing on players who lack tactical and strategic abilities, or are new to the game. But if you learn the game and have the skills needed, you'll see yourself getting a lot of gold.
You have 3 decks instead of 1 main deck. You can grab a card from any of those decks at any time you can draw a new card. This makes this game more skill based than your normal 1 main deck game. You can divide those 3 decks in early -
mid - late game, or units - damage spells - control spells, or whatever you like, the choice is yours.

Not the most new player friendly game out there but if you can get into it you will find quality fun not found in most other MMOs. I've played for over 6k hours as of writing this and I'm still having fun with friends.
The graphics are dated but still do the job well. The gameplay is meaty with a lot of gameplay systems to learn. Not the most friendly MMO for new players (complex gameplay, very difficult to solo at first so you want friends) but if you can get into it there's nothing else like it out there right now.
Pros:
Very deep character customization. Want to be a melee Halfling Wizard wielding Greatswords? Well you can do that.
Action Combat. You can actively move out of the way of incoming arrows and avoid traps with careful timing.
Almost no fetch quests. Each quest has it's own story (over 400 quests so far) with many of them feeling like a true adventure.
Cons:
It costs money to truely enjoy past level 10. The game is basically free to try until about level 10 when you will start running out of free quests. I bought Rakuen in hopes that it will deliver the same emotional impact that To the Moon did - what I ended up getting is a beautiful and captivating story which for me makes up for a slightly less impactful yet still emotional ending.
The utilization of RPG Maker is really the only setback I could think of with this game since actual gameplay is limited to "fetch quests" and movement of your character is very rigid. That is to say however that this game's ~7-hour story and world-building is something that is definitely worth experiencing. The characters are likeable in their own right, and many of them have their own stories attached to them that portrays a related, valuable message.
Some of the gameplay elements are inconsistent in some ways. For example, in getting tasked to obtain two quest items, one of them took 20 minutes to get while the other just required less than 5 minutes. Although this is just something minor, I feel like this could be improved upon given the significance the items have to the drive of the story.
The world-building, to expound, is really nice with colorful and creative design. The music was great as well, especially given the fact that this is produced by RPG Maker. Some areas in the game act as a sort of obstacle in a sense that it requires a couple of seconds to uselessly circumvent passages that could be better of not being their in the first place. I guess it's part of making the world feel big and less forgettable - but I find it more of a hindrance honestly.
Overall, the story and the characters really are the driving force of this RPG, and does have the potential to make you shed some tears. I'd recommend it to fans of story rich games since it's somewhat inexpensive and can use up a good number of hours. 6/10

I've put a little bit of time into this game and I'll do my best to describe my experience with it.
If you are a fan of the Warhammer universe and tactical games similar to X-Com than this will be your cup of tea. There are plenty of options and ways to play and I'll expand on this further. The warbands you have to select from (this does not include DLC) are....
The Sisters of Sigmar - Unfortunately have not gotten around to using them yet, but their heroes are serious trouble makers for anything, even impressive tier units.
Skaven - The tactics for these guys are pretty simple, you are playing ratmen so you must do ratmen tactics. Swarm them and give them no chance to group up and counter you and you'll decimate the opposition. Has a few fun ranged units to play with as well.
Chaos - My first warband, in my opinion the most fun/difficult. They are difficult in the early game, especially due to the henchmen units not being able to retreat and disengage so take fights only if you know you can outnumber and chop them down quickly. If you can get past the early game and level up your men accordingly, you're gonna have some SERIOUS heavy hitters. I made my best henchman a dodging, twohanded weapon user and could cut down impressives with no issue. A good tactic for getting past the hellish early game is the use of choke points. Your hero units are bound to be mutated once you hit specific levels which can be a bit of mixed bag. Lets say your mutant has focued on archery but receives a sword hand mutation, you're sorta screwed so level them to be heavy hitters. The impressive for these guys is interesting in that, if it is downed in combat, it will not get injuries but can be sent back to the warp with a 10% chance.
Empire Mercs - These guys are extremely fun. Easily the best warband for noobs, they have great ranged weapons as well. I would rock two hunting rifles on my archers, and a youngblood with pistols. If done correctly you can make a good area of security and shoot down any stragglers that push on you. Hero units are fun and pretty straightforward. Use a shield for your important guys. The ogre unit for these guys is really slow, so if you decide to have one just keep your men around him while you set up on a good spot and wait for the enemy. The ogre might be the best impressive IMO.
My review is trying to explain this game isn't as hard as people claim, just EXTREMELY unforgiving. You must play like your best units could be lost at any time because they CAN be. Don't get overly confident. The story missions can be the worst parts of the game sometimes. Expect to lose those often when you are learning them and have patience. Game has immense replay value as you learn and try new loadouts and tactics. Hope I didn't ramble too much on this review.
Also; there are some customization options but dont expect anything too in depth. It's mostly used for color coating your men (or sisters) to look spiffy.
I loved it, it has a really good plot. There's many plot twists I just couldn't stop playing.

Rakuen is primarily story-based, but it also lends itself to a fair bit of adventure in terms of gameplay. The world is imaginative, and characters are disarmingly unique in both art and personality. I especially love the graphics, which are so engaging it made me atttempt to interact with everything lying in my path (and I'm still irked that you can't move the wooden basins, they just look so interactable). The soundtrack is simplistic and incredibly atmospheric - and even if you don't play the game I'd say that the music by itself is totally worth the buy. That said, Rakuen isn't completely well-rounded. There's a fair bit of running around, and the puzzles are noticeably imbalanced in quantity as you progress, which made the gameplay feel rushed or dragged out in some places.
Still, in terms of story, Rakuen is a beautiful tale of acceptance. It's loaded with recurring themes and concepts that, from start to finish, subtly conveys the story to the player without explicitly revealing facts. For me, those moments of dawning realization (and tears) were the best parts of the game. If you're looking for a short but heartfelt experience, I'd say play Rakuen. There's nothing to lose (except your tears), and much to learn (or at least ponder) if you do.

There's a bit of a learning curve at first, but once you get the hang of the game mechanics and controls, you start to get used to the extremely punishing world of Mordheim.
The aim of each outing is not to complete the objectives or collect wyrdstone or defeat the enemy warband. The aim is just to survive. If you prioritize surviving, you will go far. Get distracted or greedy, go for the glory and you may well lose everything. There are no saves, no safety nets, no concessions.
There are definitely arguments for adapting the mechanics of the tabletop game more to the computer experience, but really once you get used to game and how it works, it really does make sense. Also, I really wanted Mordheim (the tabletop game) growing up, and this is really the next best thing.

Jamestown honestly might be one of my favourite bullet hell games of all time. Great soundtrack (scratch that, *amazing* soundtrack), nice graphics, not the hugest amount of content, but all of it is well balanced, fun, and even after playing through the game some 50-60 times it still feels interesting. 10 different ships, most of which are fairly good (only real outlier is bomber, which is absolute♥♥♥♥♥ not a fan of gunpowder either, but it's atleast decent), all with their own feel and mechanics. There's also two ships with which you randomly get one of the other ones every time you spawn, pretty fun.
Even with the fairly small amount of content (only seven levels in total with the DLC, five in the main game), there's also a bunch of challenge levels (which are all pretty great), and gauntlet modes. The levels have some really neat attention to detail, such as a land war going on beneath you with your allies shooting enemies in the first level, and stationary cannons actually being fired by enemies (meaning that, if you kill the guys before they get there to fire it up, they won't fire at all).
Only played it solo and in two-player, so can't speak much for the 3 and 4 player modes, but co-op is fun, especially on the challenge levels, trying to synchronise stuff. Playing with the random ships in co-op is also pretty fun, especially the sighs whenever someone spawns with bomber, heh.
For 13€ or whatever it is with the DLC, it's absolutely worth the money if you're a fan of the genre.

Sim racer here.. love sims like AC, rF2, RaceRoom, Richard Burns Rally, Automobilista. Went into this game VERY skeptical, but end up positively surprised.
WRC 7 is surprisingly sim-like, WAY more a simulation than any past WRC titles. Actually I rate this game higher as a SIMULATION than the disappointing Dirt 4. (Well, Dirt 4 Rallycross was okay, but their "physics upgrades" effectively sucked the fun out of rallying)
This is close to Dirt Rally good.
Best stages in any Rally game, period. Detailed, narrow, full of danger and surprises. Puts Dirt 4 to shame. Think these actually surpass even Dirt Rally.
Actually, they are quite realistic. More convincing than Dirt 4, who would have thought. Not far off from Dirt Rally either (while these are modern WRC cars, so can't be directly compared to Dirt Rally), tarmac feel is actually better than Dirt Rally.
Definitely way more sim, than past WRC games. Only thing bothering me is the braking, the cars just stop a bit too easily. If you lock up, in real car you would get into more trouble than here I feel (while I haven't driven a real WRC car obviously). However, tyre wear is simulated and if you abuse the tyres (two compounds selectable, Soft and Hard) early on, you'll regret later.
People saying there isn't weight transfer are clueless.. There definitely is weight transfer, and you can use brakes to load the front and rotate car around corners. Sliding feels very natural, controlling drifts feels spot on. Steering with throttle is very much possible, unlike the terrible understeery mechanics of Dirt 4. Different surfaces truly affect the car, even overheating tyres will work like you'd assume. Tarmac, snow, wet, gravel, all feel different
Check also this video (not mine), closely matches not only WRC 2017 car pace, but the movement over bumps and in corners:
Game has also the 2016 cars. 2017 WRC season brought aero upgrades, which makes cars more planted at higher speed. You can really notice the difference in the game too.
52 stages in 13 countries that all really look and feel different. Longest one is 23 km.
Cars are the 2016 and 2017 WRC, WRC2 and WRC Junior cars. So no historic stuff, but to be expected. Career, Custom Championships and Online challenges should offer plenty to do.

Note that Physics and FFB are a separate thing. Physics in this game are good, car moves and behaves very much like real cars. You can see that from the visual feedback. Game can have great physics, and poor FFB. While they are connected they aren't the same thing. Good FFB doesn't exist without good physics, while good physics can very much exist without good FFB.
FFB in WRC 7 is serviceable, while not mind blowing. Make sure you have Spring effects in your profiler at 100%, otherwise FFB will be dead. Damper I prefer at 0%.
I'm assuming many people complaining about the FFB had their driver settings wrong, this game ABSOLUTELY needs Spring to feel right. Many sim racers have disabled or lowered it from their driver, which will feel horrible in WRC 7. It's programmed effect here (not constant Spring), and forms the core of the FFB.
Don't expect Assetto Corsa or rFactor 2 here. FFB communicates what the car is doing, but it's not the most detailed. Feels very similar to Dirt 4. But the better physics make it feel actually better than Dirt 4.
No music to speak of. Cars sound okay, while not as good and detailed as Dirt Rally. Basic engine noises and backfires are fine, transmission whine, chassis flex and such things aren't there though. Sound is okay.
Actually, it's pretty detailed. However, same as Dirt Rally, the cars are a bit too tough. You can keep going, when IRL you would be on a tow. Wish in "Simulation" difficulty, the cars would get totaled easier. You can do it, just takes a bit too much effort.
A bit wooden, but gives 99% right calls. Also supports multiple languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Chinese and Japanese).
I didn't have a problem about it, while it's not great. Does it's job. You can set the calls later/earlier and adjust the detail level of them. I wish it didn't tell me to "BRAKE!" though because it tells me that, even if I've just messed up and barely moving.
Edit: Actually you can delete the braking callouts, game works and they won't be played:
C:/Program Files(x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/WRC7/WIN32/Sounds/Voice/EN/PACENOTES
The game seems to have native D-Box support. There is D-Box .exe in the install folder, which has loads of settings. So it clearly outputs required telemetry.
But at the moment SimVibe is not supported, if it ever will be is a mystery. For me SimVibe is pretty important for immersion. Hopefully they can add support, but past WRC games don't have it.
Triples image is stretched, while otherwise works fine. So, just like in Dirt games.
WRC 6 had experimental VR support they showed in conventions and such. Didn't make it to full release. And this one still doesn't have VR, sadly. A developer said on Steam forums, they don't have plans for adding it.
You can't adjust the seat height. Which is too high for Triple Screen users. Also getting the camera close enough isn't possible either, even with "Very close" dashcam setting. I ended up using the bonnet cam. Which I wouldn't normally do, just works better here. Hope they could patch this issue.
Game's understanding of multiple input devices is bit of a mess.
There is a function called "Axis detection" which is supposed to recognize unsupported & multiple peripherals. But currently it's not working very well. However, you can get separate pedals working by assigning them as buttons. For some weird reason, they will still work as Axis in the game. This is very confusing, and needs patching ASAP.
Was able to get TH8A working as a handbrake by this method. Seen also footage of people driving with high end pedals and wheels, with separate USB connectors. However, I've heard some having trouble getting a G29 to work in the game. T500RS worked out of the box.
Suggest testing with your peripherals. Steam refund works flawlessly, used it many times.
So, there's that.
The performance is fairly okay though. Able to run triple screens 60 fps with 980ti, by dropping from Very High to High and dropping Post Processing SSAO to medium.
Run the game in borderless window. For some people it works flawlessly even in full screen, for me only in borderless, or using Alt + Enter twice (into desktop, and back to full screen)
I'm using also V-Sync (A mode) to get smooth experience, which I wouldn't do normally due to the input lag it creates.

An big step forward from WRC 6.
Cars less easy to control, slide around more - generally feels more realistic, harder to learn and 'pick up' straight away, but is very rewarding & fun when you get it right and eventually learn how to drive the different cars. Things like windscreen wiper control, with the windscreen gradually getting dirtier on gravel stages, increase the challenge in an authentic way. Stages are narrower, bumpy and challenging at times: some are very long ('epic stages') and with no flashbacks these require concentration. The rest of the stages are by no means short as well, roughly 5 minutes on average from my experience so far.
Some things could still be improved, like the co-driver (which is the same since WRC 5 I believe) who has a tendency to shout BRAKE! and panic me into braking too early (come on, just say 'Caution'!), and the tutorial deciding that in fact we're not capable of reading and we also need to have the text read to us at a very slow, patronising pace.
The career mode has largely untouched been since WRC 5. I'd love to see TV interviews after the stages which affect morale of the team and social media reactions from fans. I'd love to see the co-driver as a fleshed out character and other team members (think Jeff in F1 2015+ or Emma/Chris in 2016+), little things to help bring you into the world. It's amazing what the little cutscenes and just sitting in the motorhome does to bring you into the world of F1 in that series, I feel that could do a whole load of good for the WRC games - don't how how easy it would be for Kylotonn to do that though; Codemasters and Kylotonn are probably not quite comparable on budgets.
To sum up - WRC 7 is a challenging, yet rewarding rally game - straddling the line between hardcore sim and arcade racer. It's not so easy that it's not hard, but yet it's not so hard that it's not easy. It does a great job of capturing the 'on the edge' feel that is evident when watching real life rallying, you feel like you're on the edge of control. In that sense, it captures rallying perfectly. Overall, I'm enjoying what I've played so far - much more than WRC 6.

Pink Heaven is the sequel to Pink Hour, which was the prequel/side-story to Kero Blaster. Pink Hour was made as a demo, of sorts, for the experience in Kero Blaster. Pink Heaven was made in response to the reception of the original demo. With that little bit of explanation out of the way, let's delve into the good points.
Well, for starters, it's free. That is always a nice plus. Even if it weren't, I'd feel fine in saying that the game is worth your time. It's short (clocking in around 10 minutes), but there are two endings and an unlockable Hard Mode.
Hard Mode is much more distinct than it was in Pink Hour. It's level design is remixed to a degree that it almost feels like a bonus game. It's also quite difficult, relying on mastery of the controls and speed of your character. It makes for a nice little challenge, even if it's only double the length of the regular mode.
My only complaint is that Hard Mode is a lot easier to unlock than in Pink Hour. It's funny, since Hard Mode in that game wasn't much different and felt a bit needless, but I can't really complain. Having two radically different versions of the same level is awesome (especially in a freeware game).
Seeing as how both this and Pink Hour are incredibly short, there isn't much reason to write an in-depth review. The game doesn't have layers of nuance or introspective story. It's just a cute little 2D shooter that is a throwback to a bygone age.
It also works to give you an idea of what Kero Blaster will feel like. Since that game has been well received (and out for some time on Playism), you should know how well this will be. If you are undecided, then just give it a shot. The worst thing that can happen is you waste 10 minutes of your day.

With the release of the Half-Minute Hero: The Second Coming I think its appropriate to take a long look back at the first game. Half-Minute Hero is a silly and experimental RPG developed by Opus releasing in Japan and the US in 2009 on the PSP. After weak sales on the PSP the developers gave the game a second chance on the Xbox 360 and PC platforms. The game is split between 4 diverse game modes "Hero 30", "Evil Lord 30", "Princess 30" and "Knight 30" all centered around the half a minute theme.
"Hero 30" is the star of the game as it distills everything RPG down to their most basic elements. Each level is essentially a full RPG campaign where you'll start off at level one, talk to NPCs, gather info, take on quests, buy equipment, and grind your way up to the world destroying Evil Lord all in 30 seconds. Fortunately your allowed to turn back the clock for an incrementing fee of gold. This cost will eventually force you to find a quick way to complete the stage, so you'll need to move smart as the game values tactics over reflexes.
Battles are automatic affairs where you and the enemy will ram each until one of you dies. Fortunately you have input through dashing which drains life so you can move faster (useable out of battle), use an item like a healing herb, and running away. Combat goes by in a flash but can be surprisingly tense as you'll have to worry whether you made the right preparations for a fight.
As you can imagine such a simplified set of mechanics requires creative level design to make the most  out of it and you'd be right. Levels are packed with content and often provide a lot of freedom in completing an objective which will likely lead to repeated playthroughs to find secrets, collect gear, and find the quickest way to complete a level.
Next up is "Evil Lord 30". This mode is a real-time strategy game where you play as a Evil Lord, where you play Rock, Paper, Scissors with creatures you summon against various enemies you'll face.  There are 3 types to account for and you can summon: high damage dealing Brutes; fast Nimbles; and long ranged Shooters. You're limited in how quickly you can summon creatures by the magic circle around the Evil Lord the smaller it is the weaker the creature you summon, so keep an eye on the size of your magic circle. Its quite satisfying to watch your army of massive minions trample over an enemy force when you've gotten a hang of exploiting enemy weakness. Unfortunately the simplified control scheme tends to work against this mode as you lack any precision when commanding your minions, since all you can do is tell all minions in your magic circle to charge in a specific direction.
"Princess 30", a scrolling shoot-em-up where you control a princess and her soldiers as she blasts her way through enemies with her crossbow to find a cure for her fathers sickness. The objective usually involves traveling across the stage by shooting enemies and avoiding hazards to defeat a boss or pick up an item, and make it back to the castle before time runs out. The stages will have you frantically avoiding obstacles and keeping you on your toes with some pretty interesting variety of enemies. But it can get repetitive due to having less variety in its objectives than the other modes so it's best played inter-spaced between play sessions of other modes.
Lastly there's “Knight 30” where you control a perpetually optimistic knight who must guard the sage who brought him back to life. There's a surprisingly strong somber atmosphere here as you desperately search for a hero who will purge the evil that infests the world, through desolate settlements and castles you've been to before. The trademark humor is still present so it never gets particularly bleak.
This isn't exactly just a set of escort mission either as the knight is too weak to actually kill any monsters, so he must depend on the sage's magic which takes 30 seconds to charge. The knight's job is to stall the creatures with anything he can his hands on such as rocks, sticks, and even his own body. He can also move the sage by either lifting him or calling him over, which will not only be necessary in finding a more defensible position. But also to get to areas that will speed up the sage's magic. This all plays on the strong level design of these stages as you need battle against new environments to keep the sage safe.
There's also a multiplayer mode in the PC / 360 releases and it plays like "Hero 30" only multiple players will compete over who defeats the Evil Lord first on multiplayer unique maps. Its also very difficult to find people playing multiplayer, so I have little experience here.
There is actually a over-arching story tying these campaigns together which come together in fairly satisfying manner despite their simplicity. But its really the dialogue and self-aware humor that stand out as it has a lot fun with various RPG conventions/tropes. While still providing plethora of humor for those less experienced in the genre. Your constant companion the greedy Time Goddess is always good for a laugh as well.
Something to note is the surprising moments of sincerity that almost seem to come out of left field. These rare moments juxtapose with the general satirical atmosphere while using the episodic nature of stages so well, that I found them completely unforgettable.
All the story sequences are also skippable which makes replaying stages a lot more convenient.
The game has great presentation sporting a 8-bit art-style harkening back to the early Dragon Quest games. Alternatively there's the default paper-craft graphics of the PC release which you can switch between. While its not quite as fitting it will scale better on larger monitors. Half Minute Hero is an awesome game and you should buy it. At the very least, you should watch some video gameplay. This game is an innovative mashup of different genres (primarily JRPG and Puzzle). If you enjoyed the PSP original, ever enjoyed JRPGs in your life, like to play puzzle games, or like quirky/innovative games... you should just stop reading and buy the game. If you're on the fence, I'll do my best to describe to you what this game is and what this game is not. I'm going to write a lot, but it's necessary to give a good picture of this game.
(If you've played the PSP version before, skip to the end of the review for a list of changes made.)
As you can tell, I'm a huge fan of this game. I enjoyed it a lot on the PSP and I enjoy it even more on the xbox. I'm going to be very enthusiastic in this review since I don't think many people even know the game exists and it can use all the hype it can get. But I seriously encourage you to at least try the demo, it's such a interesting concept that I think most gamers should at least experience it.
I can't guarantee you'll like it. But who definitely won't like Half Minute Hero? People who loathe solving puzzles, the JRPG concept, japanese-quirky games, or non turnbased games. People who like the genres they're already playing and don't want to try something new. People who buy it expecting it to be a traditional JRPG. People who need top of the line graphics and voice acting to enjoy a game. People who need to spend more than 60 hours on a 10 dollar game.
Needless to say, this game does not take 30 seconds to beat. It's not a 60 hour game either, but there isn't any fat... no grinding hours for items or toiling on mindless tasks.
- Gameplay -
The gameplay is a JRPG stripped down to its barest elements. It is not a traditional JRPG, although it uses the JRPG elements. The game is composed of several stages that could be mini-JRPGs in their own right (complete with title screen and credits.) You start off each stage at Level 1, although you can use any of the equipment you've found in previous stages. You get into random battles to kill monsters to get money and level up, buy equipment at villages, read through walls of dialogue, complete quests to progress the story, complete optional side quests to gain allies or special items, then ultimately defeat the Evil Lord threatening to destroy the world. The twist is that you have a 30 second timer to do all this and once that timer hits 0, it's game over. But you can pay an ever increasing sum to reset the timer to 30 seconds at any village. You can also dash around to move faster and avoid random battles, but while dashing, your HP is consumed.
Battles are also stripped down to their barest elements and made to go as fast as possible. Battles are viewed from the side where you and your opponents simply run at each other. You clash, damage is dealt based on your respective stats, and you repeat until one of you is dead. You can choose to dash, which eats more of your life but makes the battle go faster, or use a healing item, which can be expensive and you need money to reset the timer, or run away if you don't think you'll win. Battles are still strategic... you have to decide when you can take an enemy and you can equip items that can cause the battle to be a lot easier (such as equipping a Silver weapon that can One Hit Kill demon enemies.) They're still exciting, especially late in the game when you might finish battles with milliseconds to spare, then need to rush to the nearest village to reset your time.
The game parodies the JRPG genre and the different stages address the many tropes of JRPGs. Some stages focus around you needing to collect special equipment to defeat the big baddie, others have you do fetch quests, another has you chase your rival around, while others send you hunting for special monsters. There are 72 different stages and they're all really creative. As the game goes on, some new gimmicks are introduced. Most of the stages have different paths you can take to complete them. Sometimes you'll unlock hidden stages by finishing levels in unconventional ways. Some of the secret stages are really challenging.
In my opinion, the best part of this game is the level design... there is so much packed into each level. In order to beat the stage at all, you'll probably play the stage one to three times. To unlock the titles (you gain titles by performing certain tasks in levels), collect all the equipment, or get the top times you'll need to play the stages a lot. It's a joy to go through them. Playing through a stage is like solving a small puzzle. And you can get that satisfied feeling of leveling up in a game and overpowering your enemies.
Let me explain how a stage might work. I don't want to spoil anything, so I'm just making up an example, but the stages play out a lot like this. Here's what you can expect:
In your first run through a stage, you might grind for a few minutes, pay 300G to recruit a mercenary ally from a bar, complete a sidequest for him by finding a memento left for him by his deceased wife in a cave that boosts his power, grind some more, reach level 60, then finally be strong enough to take out the mini-boss and the boss. You unlock a title and completed the stage in maybe five minutes (throughout the stage you'll be stopping at villages to chat, learn some backstory, heal, and reset the timer.)
But then you play again. You grind for a bit and recruit the mercenary, but don't do his quest. You remember a townsperson in the first village mentioned something about a hidden village you ignored the first time, so you go searching for it this time. You go through a cave of monsters and find the village on a peninsula in a hidden patch of a forest. The shop there sells a demon slaying sword for 200G. You may need to grind for a minute to afford the sword, but now you can rush through the rest stage and One Hit KO the miniboss and boss. This will get you a new sword to use in future stages, unlock a title, and it took you only three minutes instead of five.
Maybe you're satisfied with what you've done so far. Or maybe you want to get a lower score. Speedrunning may not be your thing, but it doesn't mean you won't enjoy the game. Even without the speed running, the stages are still really fun to go through and you can beat them no matter how good or bad you are at games. But if you want more of a challenge and want more gameplay, it's definitely an option.
Let's say you looked at the leaderboard and saw people were beating the stage within 30 seconds and you want to figure out how. So you play the stage a ton of times, finding several new paths through the stage and some time shaving shortcuts. You finally get the 'Aha!' moment. You equip some armor that lets you swim, shoes that make you dash faster, and a sword that increases your base HP by 30. You don't equip a shield so you can move faster. You start the stage and dash off to a forest in the east, where there's a really weak monster that drops 230G, but no experience. Once you got the gold, you dash off to the village on the peninsula, taking a shortcut through the water this time. Because you're using the sword that boosts your base HP, you don't need to stop by any towns on the way to refill your HP. You use up all your money to buy the demon slaying sword and heal, but it doesn't matter because you're aiming to beat the stage within 30 seconds, so you don't need money to reset the timer. Now you rush through the rest of the stage, again through the water, and beat the mini-boss and the boss with a second to spare. You get nothing new, this playthrough was entirely optional, but you have the satisfaction of beating the stage in 29 seconds rather than three or five minutes. I'd like to start out by stating what may not be obvious at first, Half Minute Hero: Super Mega Neo Climax Ultimate Boy is a combination of the PSP and XBox versions of the game.  If you've played either version, or both then you aren't missing much here.  With that said I this review (like most I suppose) are based entirely on what you believe to be important in a game.
The premise of half minute hero is that an evil lord is working a spell to destroy the world, and you have 30 seconds to grind, upgrade your equipment, complete quests and defeat the 'Evil Lord'.  As frantic as it sounds (and can be) you have the Goddess of Time on your side, but as we all know Time is Money, and she will charge you for resetting the clock - while this isn't entirely burdensome it does become expensive quickly which encourages you to move quickly through each quest.
The battle system is pretty straight forward requiring very little outside of keeping an eye on your health and using an herb if needed.
The PC version has three modes: Hero 30 (which is RPG based), Evil Lord 30 (revolves around summoning minions) and Princess 30 (shooting), plus three unlockable modes (which I honestly haven't unlocked yet).
The PC version also includes two graphics modes, retro and 8-bit which was released with the XBox version.  Personally I enjoy the retro look, but that's simply a matter of opinion.
The charm and replayability of Half Minute hero is in the humor, multiple branching stories, collectible titles, and equipment.  Although the humor didn't always hit the mark with me, it was still charming in it's own right and although I haven't played through the entire Hero 30 (which is the core game-mode) I did find that collecting titles and unlocking branches could become a little onerous since some of the tasks and hints can be oblique, even with assistance from your caravan.
I was initially hesitant to make this purchase because many of the reviews I had read weren't descriptive enough for me (which I hope this fixes for others), but overall I would give this game an 7/10, and dispite it's shortcomings there is more than enough content to justify $9.99, especially if you haven't played the PSP or XBox versions, if you have and you're still interested I would wait until this goes on sale.

Jamestown is a work of art. The superb way every attack forces you to calculate Vaunt perfectly, the many varied ships with hunderds of unique designs, everything comes together to make what is certainly the greatest indie game, bullet hell game, and roguelike of 2016.

Jamestown is a top-down shoot 'em up with a strong retro vibe and local multiplayer support. It's clearly inspired by the various Japanese bullet hell games, even if it isn't quite as good as the best of them.
As a single-player game Jamestown is passable but not particularly great. There's nothing truly innovative here with either the gameplay or enemy designs. The soundtrack is great but the art design is somewhat uneven. I quite liked the level art itself but wasn't a massive fan of the ship designs.
The campaign has only five short levels, which shouldn't take too long to finish. Be warned though, that the developer did make the highly dubious decision to force you to play on higher difficulties to unlock the last two levels. Personally I didn't have too many issues playing Jamestown through on legendary, but if you are not very good with these type of games you are basically stuck playing only the first three or four levels.
Not really recommended for the single player experience unless you are a big fan of bullet hell games. It's probably much more fun in local co-op, however.
The good:
- Great soundtrack
- Beautiful retro-style backgrounds
The bad:
- Quite short
- Rather ugly ship designs
- Aggressive ingame marketing of the DLC pack
- Later levels can only be unlocked on legendary or above
Kind of short ultimately, but tons of options on how to play.  Get together with some friends and you have a fantastic indie co op here.

Disclosure: I marked “received this product for free” because I received it as a gift.
Jamestown: Legend Of The Lost Colony is a game that I wanted to play at one time.  Before I make a purchase I typically check out reviews (both good and bad) and the Steam Discussions to see if there is anything that might make me think twice about buying.  If the game crashes on start or has some sort of other technical issue there is a good chance someone will be posting about it.  In the case of Jamestown, one doesn't have to look far to find some dirt.
When I looked through the discussions I learned that Final Form Games appear to have completely abandoned the PC version of the game (it looks like they stopped support to focus on PlayStation 4's Jamestown+). The developers haven't posted since June 24, 2015.  There is at least one somewhat major bug that they're aware of and haven't fixed as of today August 28, 2016.  For many users, every enemy projectile in the game is currently a dull grey color.  The color of bullets in shooting games is kind of a big deal and there is a good reason why they often are colored brightly.  How are you supposed to dodge them if you can't see them clearly?  I've played quite a few shoot 'em ups and this was enough to convince me not to buy the game.
A fix exists, but it doesn't work for all users.  It involves reverting to a previous version through the properties menu of the game in Steam.  It ended up partially working for me.  It fixed the colors but the game became unplayable unless played windowed.  I strongly prefer fullscreen so decided to keep the grey bullets.  Aside from not being aesthetically pleasing, there were only a few parts where I found them to be particularly detrimental.  I also experienced odd controller bugs if I was holding a direction immediately while spawning. I'm not sure if it was my gamepad or not, but it wasn't difficult to avoid once I realized what was causing it.
Jamestown isn't really a standard arcade style shooting game.  Rather than being one continuous run, the game is split up into five stages.  In order to unlock all five stages the player is required to beat the earlier stages on progressively higher difficulty levels.  The later stages do not feature lower difficulty options at all.  This serves as a nice and slow introduction for individuals inexperienced with the genre.  In addition to the regular stages there are challenge levels that feature special objectives such as flying through rings, getting a certain score within a time limit, or surviving a brief onslaught.  The regular stages are enjoyable but I had even more fun with the challenges.  The only campaign stage I didn't like was the final one which unexpectedly introduces environmental hazards which aren't in the earlier levels and felt out of place.
After completing a stage you are rewarded with ducats that can be used in the store.  Among other things the store sells alternate ships, additional challenges, and the gauntlet mode.  Each ship has a primary attack, a special secondary attack, and the ability to vaunt.  Activating vaunt mode provides temporary invincibility, a damage bonus, and a score multiplier.  Picking up coins prolongs the amount of time your retain the bonuses.  The Gauntlet serves as the game's version of an arcade mode where you play through all the stages consecutively with limited continues.  It is also worth mentioning that the game allows up to four players. I never tested multiplayer out myself so I can't say how well it works.
Although it's a little unorthodox when compared to classic Japanese arcade shooters, Jamestown is one of the strongest entries into the shoot 'em up genre from a western developer that I've ever played.  It's truly sad that Final Form Games has let it fall into its current state.  The game is gorgeous, the soundtrack is great, and the overall presentation is outstanding.  Due to the solid package and enjoyable gameplay I'd recommend this game, but with a warning about the likelihood of encountering bugs. There is a lot of fun to be had here and it's playable even with the grey bullets, but I think it's important that potential buyers know that there are bugs that may never be fixed.
Just buy this already.

This game is good, like really really good! Everything from its crushing difficulty, to the lack of any type of story! Its amazing how such a small team could make such a great game! SO let me quick list pros and cons for people who are reading this review.

-MOST spells are very fun to use (summon monster)
::CONS::
-The only reward **really** after dying is the increase in your skill

-No type of ingame guide to monsters(You can't see monsters' stats for example)
-Small development team means updates are few and far between, meaning that the game(after it's been beaten) fails to hold my attention, (Though as of the new year 2018, They have kicked it into high gear in polishing the game! meaning frequent updates!)
-Cooking is underutilized
-Act 3 is a difficulty spike, and Act 4, though freakin awesome, is a cakewalk afterwards..sometimes
-Unspoken prerequisites, what I mean is that you "need" certain abilities for certain Acts(a gear check if you will) or else its extremely difficult lemme quick list (im not covering the secret acts, although they are the worst offenders. ::NITPICKS::

-Shops are useless in the endgame, and shop keeps are freakin robust in multiplayer.
-Mentioned this already, but Swing weapons don't have place with any character's abilities

This game might be great for the casual gamer, as it looks fantastic and have
great stages. However, I want a game with great handling where the car reacts
to my input, similar to real life.
SIMULATION MODE:
Started the game and liked the way I was taken straight to what mode I wanted.
Simulation and hardcore. But from there it went downhill.
Suddenly I was thrown in the car with the view from the camera behind the car.
Since I had not set up my buttons yet, I had to hit ESC to get this sorted out.
While I was in the menu, I turned down a lot in the graphics settings, as the FPS
was very low, down in the 20s.  I noticed some flickering, and then the game
crashed, and took Steam along with it.
After getting the game up and running again, I ended up setting every graphics
setting to low, which still looked surprisingly good. I did not need to turn everything
to low, but I did not want to waste my 2 hours by optimizing graphics.
After getting all settings sorted out, it was time to drive with hood cam. OMG...
The lag! I changed view to headcam, and there it became obvious:
How can they release a game with horrible lag like this? And just to be clear,
I do not have any other controller connected.
I already had all the graphics settings on low, so it can not be that that causes
it, and I tried with VSync on and off, but the lag was still there. This made the
handling feel terrible. I played around with the wheel settings, but the car was
no joy to drive.
Wheel rotation cannot be set as you like. It was something like 256, 298, 346
and so on with strange values. I usually drive with 270, so this was a
disappointment too.
Then there was the problem with the FOV. There is not wide enough FOV for
3 screens. On top of that, the FOV is changing as you brake or accelerate.
WHY?? If you are going to simulate that your body is moving because of
acceleration and braking, you need to move the point of view, not the FOV!
Seriously?
I wanted to check what FPS I had, so I went to window mode and enabled
on-screen display in RivaTuner. Game crashed again.
At this point I had already decided that this game is not for me, so I uninstalled
it and got my refund.
THOUGHTS:
I kind of expected this game to fail, based on my experience with earlier WRC
titles, but really hoped to be proven wrong, as we need a new rally game to
replace DiRT Rally.  This could be a fantastic game, but seems to be made by
people who just don`t understand what it takes to make a great sim. Handling
first, then everything else...
I don`t know if there might be some workaround to get rid of the lag, but since
there are no DEMO, I`m not wasting my refund trying to find out if some setting
might fix it.

Rochard is a very nice platformer game in which you play as John Rochard, a miner. He has a gravity gun that can move objects, and he is also able to manipulate gravity. Through the levels you have to kill some bad guys and use your skill and gun wisely (especially in the Hard Times DLC).
For me, Rochard is an interesting and awesome mix of Half Life 2 (because of the gravity gun), Portal and Constant C, all of which I really enjoyed playing.
So yeah, I would recommend it to everyone, who loves this genre or the games mentioned above.

7.75/10.0
+ Very fun and fast paced, intuitive controls, enjoyable abilities, great soundtrack
- Difficulty curve lowered towards end, predictable plot
Not much more can be said about this well-convcieved title. Rochard isn't your everyday side-scrolling platformer as it creates its own identity in the mask of its weapon. As the main character you're capable of shooting bullets and grabbing objects by holding down on the mouse. Release will throw objects away or use momentum to swing yourself around like spider-man.  You're also given a few unique grenade throwing options that aid your progress.
The main downfall is how upside-down the structure of the level designs are. Flipping the game around, it would make more sense because the starting levels are more difficult than the end ones. Levels get shorter and puzzles aren't as crafty or unique. My biggest gripe was honestly the shining moment of the game: the final boss fight. It was incredibly fun and after it was over, it left me wondering why the game lacked these kind of fights throughout the game. Don't get me wrong, blasting one guy into another, or throwing a mechnized shooting turret into a group of enemies has its positives. Yet I would have loved to see some unique fights take place at the end of each world.
Buy: For the gameplay
Don't Buy: For the plot, difficulty

As some one who's put a ton of hours into this game, I can say it is a very tactical game that can be unforgiving for your mistakes.  This game is rather fun and rewarding knowing that when you succeed, you did so in the face of risking catastrophe.  I've had many a round where I can almost flawlessly win a battle and then when I get overconfident or careless and spread out or try to reach wyrdstone with quick and agile characters, I get picked off and unable to help my units.

Disclaimers: First off, my gametime is misleading, since Steam only clocks hours while connected to the internet. I lost the internet for several months awhile back, so my actual playtime is probably closer to 150-200 hours than my listed 70. As well, my computer is not particularly powerful, and as such, I need to play on ultra-low settings. If you care about graphics, I advise you find another review to satisfy your curiosity.
Mordheim isn't for everyone. Not everyone wants to calculate risk management versus potential reward. Not everyone wants a game they can't just breeze through. And that's fine. However, Mordheim is about that risk management, and people who don't want that can save their money by looking elsewhere.
In Mordheim, like most difficult games, knowledge is power. You may lose repeatedly early on as you ease into things, but once you understand the game, it is highly addicting. While I disagree with the notion of "git gud" (as I personally find it highly elitist and dismissive, a slap in the face to people who could otherwise become valued members of the community if people offered actual advice instead of acting like they have a superiority complex) I highly recommend you disregard any reviews with only 3-10 hours that whine about the difficulty, and instead consider the following:
Most of the time, if something bad happens in Mordheim, it is your fault. If your warband started scattered and your lone unit got ganked before you could get help over there, ask yourself "Why did I select the mission where it said warbands would start scattered? Why did I not pick the one where units deploy near the wagons?" If one of your mages takes 9999 damage from a spell gone wrong, ask yourself "Did I mitigate the risk by using a staff or equivalent weapon? Did I cast repeatedly, thus increasing the odds of each subsequent cast being disastrous for me by a further 15%, and the game literally shows you the number increasing each time so there's no excuse for not noticing?"
Pros:
- Great SRPG combat, complete with stances and utility actions like climbing, and a 3rd person perspective similar to games like Valkyria Chronicles, Lost Dimension, Natural Doctrine, and the like. Terrain makes a critical impact in battle, and not just in positioning, but it affects the game right down to the combat rolls, with ranged attacks being affected by cover (how much terrain obstructs the shot; there's no mechanic to actually take cover) and height difference. There's also seperate point pools for tactical actions (Movement, reloading, dodge stance, etc) and attack actions (Charge, Overwatch Stance, Ambush Stance, spells, and so on) with some actions, such as switching weapons or carefully aiming shots, using points from both pools.
- Four vanilla warbands (+2 DLC warbands) bring numerous playstyles to the table. The Sisters of Sigmar, for example, are basically an army of Paladins and Rogues if you break them down into RPG archetypes, without access to archers until they gain enough reputation to hire mercenary marksmen. The Skaven, on the other hand, are poison and ambush specialists: Frail, but sneaky and hard to pin down in the hands of a good player.
- Character Customization: You can change the name and appearance of every last unit you hire. Some units can't be customized very much, but being able to select a unified color scheme for the warband, at least, is a nice touch.
- The permanent injury system is more merciful than a lot of games with immediate permadeath if someone is defeated. This gives individual members character, and makes you think back to the time they sacrificed themselves to hold a daemon off while the others completed their mission. It may make amazing characters useless if they get a crippling injury, such as if an archer loses an arm, but it adds so much character to your roster, I can't even express how neat it is.
- Multiple Multiplayer modes, including friendly spars and fights with full consequences as if it was a campaign mode battle. Having an option for the casual battles and the hardcore scraps for keeps is very welcome.
- Enemy AI warbands are scaled to you: If you only bring 2 henchmen instead of a full 5, so will they. If you don't field an Impressive, neither will they. It prevents you from being completely SOL if you find yourself in a tight spot, like if you have an impending shipment request deadline and can't take time for everyone to recover from injuries.
- The music is atmospheric and really captures the mood: Not knowing what's around the corner, but knowing that you could be fighting for your life at any moment. The music remains unchanging even when your units are engaged in battle, because not being in battle isn't even really any safer.
Cons:
- It's pretty resource intensive, so it won't run on lower end machines very well. This isn't an issue if you have an amazing rig, but is worth noting for people on machines that are a few years old and were only okay at the time.
- The permanent injuries can be stressful. It's not for everyone. I, myself, have had absolutely key members of my warbands completely ruined by one bad mission, like a mage becoming megalomanic (Can't use ranged weapons/ spells become more expensive to cast) or an MVP gunslinger losing an arm. The feeling of losing a ton of souls in Dark Souls just can't compare to the despair of a fight going south and dreading what awaits at the end.
- The tutorials, while good, are tucked away in the main menu and only teach you on a turn by turn basis, jumping from one thing to the next. Having a tutorial-assisted first few campaign missions for first timers may have helped people remember these lessons. From what I understand, most people jump right in without even looking at them.
- The maps themselves are largely kind of samey. While there's variety in story missions, the bulk of campaign battles take place in maps like Merchant Quarter 2 Noble Quarter 3 which are all so similar. Yes, the layouts are different, but variery in the overall aesthetic might have been nice.
- I wish there were more customization options. For example, I'm not a fan of the hoods worn by the cultists, but I'm stuck with them on the Magistrate and Brethren. I'm also not a fan of the Witch Hunter hats. Or the head thing worn by the Matriarch when equipped with a helmet. You get the idea. More variety would be nice.
- I swear the AI knows your objectives and trolls you. Oh, you need to claim this character's trinket as proof of defeating them? Expect the AI to hold them back so you can't get them before they rout, the battle ending with your objective left incomplete. While there's no penalty for failing these, the rewards for completing them are very nice, and being able to complete them more reliably might be nice.
Overall? Mordheim is a great experience, albeit one that can only be truly enjoyed by apecific subsets of gamers. I wouldn't expect it to ever garner mass market appeal and become mainstream, nor would I want it to.
