I must say this is the first time I've played an Otome game that immersed me into its world so deeply that I feel the need to leave a review.
The creators did a marvelous job in weaving an interesting story influenced by well-known fairytales and adding their own twist to them. The story itself drew me in, but what kept me glued to the screen, re-reading bits and pieces here and there, was the excellent writing that (in my opinion) is on par with some commercial games that huge development companies release. Each character - even the antagonists and the supporting cast - has something special to offer, which makes the journey all the more pleasant.
The main character is complex and as she likes to emphasize every so often, she's no damsel in distress. Her development is well-paced and reasonable and I couldn't help admiring her confidence and elegance with which she held herself. She made even questionable morals and choices sound justified with her wit. She is flawed but that only makes her even more likeable and real as she learns from her own mistakes.
The gentlemen that our Lucette can romance are not ideal nor are they brooding over their "Difficult Past". Each one of them has a story to tell from which a player can learn a thing or two (I definitely did). What makes the playthrough even more enjoyable and different is the fact that depending on which route you're currently on, the general ending plot varies slightly and at the same time finishes the story. Every route uncovers different facts that others may lack and I personally think it is important to play through all of them to have the best experience (and love all of them, cause they definitely deserve it), leaving the most rewarding and satisfying one for last (Waltz's). The supporting characters were also very charming and made me want them to have seperate routes just to befriend or get to know them and their stories better, which only shows that they had depth and were very well-written.
The BGM was beautiful, well-suited to the current situation or mood and not disturbing at all, smoothly easing emotions from the pit of my hollow being. Personally I would've prefered the Opening song to be in piano version, but it was still really pretty and well-done. The Ending one stole my heart, not even once did I skip it after finishing a route with a good ending and I found myself searching for it in the music section of the gallery.
As for the art, it was breathtaking in all cases, be it the background, the CG's or the sprites. They were all very detailed, sometimes hilarious when it was needed, sometimes heartbreaking or full of happiness. Overall, my hungry eyes were satisfied, although sometimes the proportions or sharpness of certain features looked odd. However, the colours and designs made it all seem insignificant (I'm just picky about graphics, don't mind me).
Overall, I fell in love with this story, its various characters, from villains to brooms, and wise and beautiful morals that stuck with me until now.
I applaud the team at Dicesuki, for they made a masterpiece. Some of the developers could learn a thing or two from you ;)
I look forward to the Fandisk and your future games. If I could, I would shower you with my nonexistent money.
Thank you for making it available to everyone <3

Amazing environment and love the interactions with objects.  If you are a bang bang shooter up type you won't like it.  If you are of the MYST genre and like atmospheric environments, you will love it.
That being said, there is a lot of inconsistency in the game saves and it's down right frustrating.  I don't understand why the developers made this feature so user unfriendly since the ability to save your progress is probably the most important feature of any game.
Be warned that unless you just leave the game running on your computer, you won't be able to save any progress that you have made on your own.  Rather, it seems mostly random.  For a while it seemed like it was saving at each glass building once you entered.  But I found that NOT to always be true.  Occasionally after you have finished in the glass building and are dumped into the next environment, thinking that your progress has been saved, you exit, you find upon reentering you are back at the beginning of a glass house puzzle, and not necessarily the one you were last in.
Also, if  when bouncing around and playing in an environment, you land "inside" a rock or piece of graphic, you often can't get out, even with the power surge.  And if you bounce into a section of the game you've already completed (because they sometime run side by side) you more than likely can't get out.  Murphy's law dictates that these are the times when the game chooses to save for you.
So I would rate the in game exerience an A+ but the whole saving thing a big fat "F".
Oh, there is a feature called go to last checkpoint.  But that again is up to the game to choose and not you.

This is a beautiful little game. It's deceptively simple but almost impossible to master, and with enough complexity that it has extraordinary replayability. The different character classes are all unique with their own starting equipment, stats, and abilities, which allows for a wide variety of play styles. Want to run around all the enemies and attack from a distance? Be an acrobatic rogue and roll, jump, and climb around to your hearts content. Want to just brute force melee everything? Be a berserker wildling and solve all of your problems with fists. Finding a method that works for you is important because the game can be mind numbingly difficult.
The games mechanics are very classic rpg and rogue-like: simple melee, ranged, and magic attacks with stats that control each; a variety of potions, scrolls, and magic spells; and a plethora of different weapons, armor, and gear, most of which has some sort of magic property. However, the most notable feature that makes it a classic rogue-like is that preserving health is critical. If you're not careful you can lose a lot of health fast, and healing is infrequent. In addition, the enemies get much harder with each subsequent stage, even relative to any stat boosts from leveling up and better gear. This is why after over 500 hours of play time logged and a death count in the thousands, I've beaten the game exactly three times.
However, skill is only about three quarters of having a successful run, and the rest is luck. The randomness of the loot can be one of the most challenging aspects of the game. Skill is critically important: just through muscle memory, good reflexes, and learning the attack patterns of the enemies, it should theoretically be possibly to beat the game with no gear and unarmed. That being said, better gear make the game infinitely easier. Besides boosting your stats, one of the most interesting aspects of the gear system are the magic properties of the items. Most weapons and armor have some sort of magic property, the effects of which range from detrimental (such as cursed items, although the curse can be lifted, or super speed boots, which make it nearly impossible to have any sort of precision to your movement), to useless or niche (such as underwater breathing, or heavy boots), to helpful (such as double or triple jump, dealing additional poison or fire damage, or having a familiar that fights with you). There are also some that are ridiculously over powered or way more useful. Things like life steal and homing arrows make the game a breeze, but are proportionally rarer.
Co-op is fantastic with this game, and while I haven't played much online, my roommate and I play couch co-op all the time. It is a little easier with more people, although starting stats and health are slightly nerfed when playing with more than one person to make it more balanced, and the quantity of loot stays the same and must be split amongst the party.
It's hard not to keep raving about this game. It's strange to me to think that I've put so much time into such a simple game, but the simplicity is part of the appeal. Everything about it is so minimal and uncluttered, while retaining and refining to a point the things that make a great rogue-like. The developers have done an amazing job with this game and keeping it updated. The next update should be the end game content and the game will move out of early access. I can't wait to see what they do, and hopefully the official release will expose more people to this game.

In a somewhat odd move, developer Orange Juice's sequel to its bullet hell shooter Suguri all but ignores standard sequel protocol in Acceleration of Suguri, a bullet hell shooter/fighter hybrid. Adapting the end level boss mechanic from Suguri, wherein the player faces off against one of a number of flying, hyper-weapon toting anime girls, AoS offers a ridiculously fast paced aerial combat title for two players filled with more multi-color pellets, techno music and short skirts than an otaku convention!
Each fighter comes equipped with two unique weapons, each usually containing two abilities of their own, along with a super attack, shield and the ability to dash around the sky-high arena at a breakneck pace whilst dodging all manner of weaponry. Weaponry is very distinguishable, there are majorly no similarities between loadouts and abilities, and successful play styles vary between each character. Stow any fears that lack of buttons and combos make for a dull combative affair, AoS requires just as much forethought and cunning as it does quick reflexes if you want to best your opponents. That said, it’s entirely possible to get by on reflexes and button mashing alone, but better players will have no problem putting you in your place.
The arenas themselves, aside from differentiating backgrounds, are indistinguishable from one another. Their only purpose is to provide a backdrop to the girl-on-girl action. A similar lack of variety comes in the single player experience. Aside from a standard arcade mode and two separate side stories, each with their own individual tourney, the experience is limited by your want to better your scores and skills by taking on higher difficulties in arcade. Luckily, AoS features local and online multiplayer, from what I’ve sampled, the online works surprisingly well, aside from the occasional disconnect. It’s even easier to battle friends with an option to only search for friends’ lobbies. Since there’s no group tourney mode, nor any lobby option larger than two, it’s a much appreciated feature.
The HD artwork is crisp and colorful, and the accompanying techno soundtrack is supremely catchy and fits well with the hectic nature of the gunplay. Really, I can’t stress how fantastic the menu theme is, I’ve found myself leaving the game on the menu screen and enjoying the looping beat while I take care of other business. It’s very catchy. It’s a shame that there isn’t more music to the title. I’m not sure I’ve heard even a full handful of unique tunes in my several hours play time.
Aside from a lack of solid single player options and only slightly fewer fighters than I’d have liked, AoS offers a unique experience that a very niche audience is going to adore. The sheer pace of it all will undoubtedly alienate some, but for any shmup buffs
, fighting fans
, or anyone just looking for something new to smack their friend around in to a techno beat
, then look no further. It may be limited in its single player offering, but as long as you have a willing bud to play with, you’ll be hard pressed to find a similarly unique and hectic experience to waste away an afternoon in.

I think a lot of people can easily hate on this game when they are used to being successful with minimal effort in other games. The RNG can be frustrating, but that is life, and most importantly, it is Warhammer. A 78% chance to hit is not 100%, so if you miss those from time to time you just have to roll with the punches.
As someone mentioned earlier positioning is important. Having cover from one or two sides will protect you from getting flanked, and if you can get the enemy single file or otherwise block them from maneuvering around you, it offers a great advantage in combat. That being said, there is a lot more to it than this. Early in the game you can win fights by just having a better position, but if you dont have the right skills or equipment, the enemy will whittle down your fighter and eventually defeat him. Even more so if the enemy team has a magic user, a few Sigmar's comets is enough to bring any fighter down, regardless of position.
Leveling up is pretty basic, if you perform well in combat everyone gets some XP and maybe a skill point or two to spend on advancement. Getting better equipment comes pretty quickly after winning a few fights, but getting magic and enchanted equipment can take a long time which I feel is a good balance.
Early on you will be hurting for gold, and taking a lot of risks to get wyrdstone to complete your shipments, which I feel is a good comparison to the actual Warhammer Mordheim minitaures skirmism game. I played a lot of that back in the day and the whole thing was a scramble for resources and I feel this video game kept true to that feeling.
The story missions are fun, but a lot more challenging that norming campaign missions. I appreciate that they take place in unique locations, especially the burning library with a huge demon inside of it.
Overall a good game and a faithful representation of the original Warhammer tabletop skirmish game it is based on. If your only exposure to the grim and perilous world of Warhammer is video games, you may want to temper your expectations of the level of success you might obtain compared to the level of tactical effort you must put forth. In short, if you try hard you might win. If you dont try hard, you wont win.

Despite what you may read in most reviews of this game, it is not actually that difficult of a game. Complicated? yes. Difficult? no. You develop your dudes outside of battle, always seeming to have to work with far less money than you think you should have. The battles themselves are basically all about moving into just the right spots to exploit the tact-less AI. The game rewards positioning above all else, and it is not hard to learn where to place your dudes to avoid walking home missing a few arms and legs.
I think that the "difficulty" of the game comes from the sudden and severe way in which you can be punished for abandoning safe positioning. You know that guy you've been training and building up since day 1? Well you moved him just a little too far out to pick up some wyrdstone and he got surrounded for an AI beating that ended up killing him permanently. Also, you should always elect to choose your own positioning before battles, or just avoid choosing the battles where you are forced to split your group up into 3+ groups. You will never be rewarded for splitting up your party during combat. Once you get combat (read: positioning) down, you will get pretty bored pretty quickly realizing how stale the action is, how cardboard the environments really are, and how totally annoying it is that your agile jumping/climbing guy just lost his leg.

If you're the sort of person who plays XCOM games on the highest difficulty then you should definitely check this game out.
If you're unwilling to accept losses -- i.e. the RNG goes against you and your favorite characters gets debilitating injuries or is outright toasted -- then you'd best stay away from this one.

This is Resident Evil 4. It's the same terrific game it always was, and isn't overhyped imo, although I do think the number of ports for the game are excessive.

The game pioneered a camera and control scheme that was only seen again in God Hand, a combination of tank controls and an 'over-the-shoulder' perspective. You'll always be able to see what you're doing. This is a scheme that I wish was still relevant as I hate adjusting the camera in the middle of games.
I think some of the puzzles are throwaway since the game switched from its Metroid-y adventure roots to a linear game. I also don't really care for babysitting Ashley. You can put her in a dumpster in some rooms, but I'd still prefer her to not be there.

GAME PLAY
You search for items, solve puzzles, and unlock (mostly) linear paths. You can sell items, buy new ones, or upgrade what you have. To win, you must complete the story. You´re also required to protect someone, at some point.
A controller is recommended. Movement is digital, aiming is analogue, and enemies react in response to shooting at their different hit-zones.
LORE
It's a fictional story, that takes place in imaginary Europe. Although the fourth in the series, most characters are properly introduced. The story is told as you move forward. It's main protagonist, Leon S. Kennedy, is part of an anti bio-terrorism organization. When he arrives at a Spanish village, a horror unfolds.
SKILL
Item management is important. There are different combinations of gear you can possess. Gear is interchangeable because of it's trade system. Knowing what gear when to pack or upgrade, is beneficial.
Multiple difficulty levels, random item placement and enemy behavior; all add replay value.

The main problem with InFlux is that it doesn't matter that you're a ball.  Rolling physics games, like Marble Madness, rely heavily on conservation of momentum as a game mechanic.  InFlux does not.  You have very good control over your movements and can arrest your forward momentum at any time.
Moving slowly often makes the uneven ground difficult to traverse, but that's more an annoyance than a gameplay mechanic.  There's no incentive to dash madly through levels, not in the least because you spend the navigation levels searching for hard to spot motes of light that you need to unlock the next puzzle.
The game has some ramps, but you don't so much roll up them as you hit them at speed and bounce into the air.  Once the game introduces the boost mechanic all semblance of ball relevance goes right out the window, as you can use it to easily turn on a dime at tight angles and even essentially freeze time in mid air to target perfect landings.  Overshot your mark?  No problem, just boost again and turn yourself around.
There are some puzzles that involve rolling a ball into a receptacle but that ball is not you.  It's a different ball.  And you don't manipulate it by hitting it like a cue ball or a bowling ball -- you have telekinetic powers.  These puzzles would have been much better if you were the "scoring" ball and the game actually forced you to behave like a ball.
But instead, InFlux is just a mediocre first-person puzzle game with some reasonably pretty landscaping that is in no way relevant to navigation by a ball.  You might as well be a tiny person with a gun that fires attracting and repulsing waves -- in fact, I have definitely played games where I was a person and my momentum was more difficult to control than it is in InFlux.  At the end of the day you are a character with a motor skills deficiency trying to solve spatial puzzles.  The net result comes across as unfortunately frustrating.
It's obvious that the developers put a lot of work and care into this, but it suffers badly from some poor design choices.  I can't in good conscience recommend it to anyone but the most diehard of spatial puzzle fanatics.  I definitely don't recommend it to anyone looking for a ball physics game.

The entire time I spent playing InFlux, I kept wondering to myself and trying to discern just
about it was causing me to dislike it so much. But ultimately it became clear that there was no one thing that was so abhorrent as to destroy the game, but a long list of mediocre mechanics, frustrating moments, and missed potential stacked upon each other to create a game that is not fun to play.
And you really wouldn't notice this from the outside, so much is the subtlety of InFlux's deeply permeated problems. What appears to be an average, but solid physics based ball puzzle game is instead a amalgamation of poor design decisions and tedious level designs.
The most easily called out of these issues is the sluggish and clunky controls of your ball. There is such an absurd amount of momentum attached to movement that it's nearly impossible to retain any control even when moving slowly. It's as if there's a second invisible player playing beside you which constantly wants to go in the opposite direction, and you are left to try and wrestle control back away from them as you try to move forward with anything resembling precision.
This of course bleeds into the actual puzzle designs, which naturally require excessive amounts of control and constrained movements in order to complete, something which is nigh impossible given the previous paragraph. Compounded upon this is the astounding amount of tedium built into each and every puzzle, often placing you back at the beginning of long sequences for the slightest mistake, and making completion feel like a brief relief before you're put right back into an even more aggravating level. There's nothing clever or satisfying to find here, just an abundance of cheap failures and unrefined design.
This finally ties all the way back around to the clash of styles presented with the presentation. The game is split into two parts: that of navigating a realistic, occasionally rather pretty world ripe with nature, and that or completing the actual puzzles in a sterile white box floating somewhere in the cosmos. The transitions are glaring and abrupt, and turn the parts of the environment that are actually interesting to look at into little more than glorified conduits to carry you from one stale puzzle to the next. This isn't to say the overworld (for lack of a better term) is actually a compelling place to explore, as it feels as barren and underdeveloped as anything in the game, but in comparison to the drab color pallet of the puzzles at least presents an occasional bit of eye candy to counteract the monotony of constantly being in the same room.
There might have been some point where InFlux was coming along into something decent (I'd like to think so at least), but if so something went terribly wrong at some point and sent the entire game careening down the crapper. No matter how hard I tried to enjoy it, every single moment I spent with it was nothing but dull and frustrating, leaving me feeling like the game was just waiting for me to give up on it so it could roll over and die like the lifeless creation it is.

I've played this game for 4 hours, and I still don't have a clue what it's about, or if I'm anywhere near an end, or even a middle... I love it!
InFlux is a neat, relaxing game where you take control of a small metal ball and do pretty much two things: 1. roll around looking at the pretty environment devoid of any other presence despite obvious signs of previous haitation and even civilization, and 2. roll around in giant glass houses where you push buttons and guide other objects to goals to move on to the next area.
While exploring this strange place, you'll find small lights that you can attract to follow you, and you need to gather at least 3 in each area to unlock the glass house for that region; I think this is brilliant, since it gives an excuse to explore the gorgeous landscape while breaking up the pace of the puzzling glass houses and still giving an excuse to go slowly through the game.
You'll also get access to abilities as you progress, like being able to push or pull some objects, charge up a speed boost, and slow down time for more precise manuvering; these add a freshness to the play, and the speed boost specifically can be used to pull of some really amusing tricks, including jumping over/on top of mountains or clipping through walls. in the short time I've played, I even managed to find a relatively large skip in the game using a clip in one of the early glass houses, which really appeals to the speedrunner in me.
For some negatives, if you're playing on a laptop more than maybe a year old, you'll probably experience some slowdown or lag, which for me is a pretty important issue. Additionally, as far as I can tell, there isn't really a point or story in the game; that might not be a bad thing, and maybe later in the game I'll learn something about why I'm alone in this big world and the complete absence will make sense, but for now, it's just a bit of a bother to me. finally, while the controls are fairly easy to use,  it does take a bit of getting used to, and momentum plays a major role, meaning hairpin turns aren't feasible, and you'll have to constantly modify your speed and direction to keep going even in a straight line, a problem that's just compounded when you factor the environment filled with slopes, bumps, rocks, logs, and even just uneven ground.
Now the positives, first and foremost, the beautiful atmosphere! Your journey takes you through fields and mountain passes, caves, small villages, mountains, beaches, and A FREAKING VOLCANO! Combined with the very mild and unobtrusive audio, the experience is one that I'll probably remember for quite some time. Speaking of the audio, the backround music is faint and plesant, even in the glasshouses where it changes, it only serves to set a mood, and it does very well. Even the sound effects are simple and quiet, which is a major plus for me. The puzzles in the glass houses are also very well done; you are introduced to new mechanics slowly to give you time to understand each new concept and play with it for a while. You can press a switch to turn the entire room on its side, get blown up by a giant fan to a higher platform, be launched by a catapult, and tons of other things that will take up too much space in this already lengthy review to go into detail about. And having mentioned the controls in the negative section, I feel like it's only fair to mention that they are always fair. You'll never feel like the ball was just ignoring your input, and you always have plenty of room to move around so the tiniest mistake won't ruin your progress.
So tl;dr - I would definitely recommend this game. $10 isn't asking too much, and I think it's well worth it for the experience you get. If you're okay not having a ton of direction, you want something relaxing and calm, you don't mind thinking a little, and you apreciate beautiful things, you can't go wrong checking this out.

Acceleration of SUGURI is a fun and surprisingly competitive bullet hell/fighting game hybrid. Battles are extremely fast, with both players throwing multiple projectiles and bullets while weaving through them in attempt to catch them off-guard. Not just that though, you have to manage your HEAT bar which dicates your ability to dodge/dash and your hyper meter stock, which is used to perform hyper moves and furthers the fighting game similarities.
There's a good amount of variety in playstyle between the cast members, where you have your more zoning-oriented types like Kyoko or rushdown types like Kae each with a large amount of moves which can vary based on proximity or charge time.
The only problem with the game is that there isn't that much singleplayer content. There are a few arcade-esque story modes with entertaining characters if you've played Orange Juice's other games, but this game is purely versus-oriented and it excels at that. So if you're looking for something that's unique and are a fan of fighting games, SHMUPs or both then I definitely recommend this title.

Serious review:
I've been playing this game on both PC and Ps3 since 2011. Game is amazing. Fast, Frantic, Hectic.  I describe it to friends as a "High-Movement, Versus Shoot 'Em Up". and it's pretty accurate.  You control a character and fire weapons and laser swords and giant fists at your opponent to reduce their hp to zero at an alarming rate. The game is simple on the surface and allows very deep and quick-reaction strategy. When you become more skilled you both see and feel its rewards.
There are tiers of "this character is definitely better than this character", but there are no flowcharts. It's a matchup-intensive game but it is driven by KNOWLEDGE, and by ADAPTATION. Any character can win. You have be very cognizant of situations and understand when to push, when to back off, when to set up. There's a lot that goes on constantly. You have to watch the camera, you have to watch what's /not/ on the camera, everything is nuts because it all happens so fast.
The first fifty or so rounds that you seriously play in this game will be a blur of "I have no idea what's going on and I have no idea what i'm doing." This is -normal- and you'll acclimate quickly from there. It's just like watching or playing anything for the first time.
There are cons, but to me they don't mean anything compared to the pros.
- Some people don't like the camera functionality. (I think it adds a layer of strategy and meta
- Despite what I said above, some characters really do struggle in every match.
- Please never pick QP unless you're being a nutbar. She's too good and is banned in competitive circles.

The RNG in this game is utterly broken. I've run a handful missions, all complete disasters. My team almost never hit on 70%-80% chances, and the enemy almost never missed. This happened again and again, the random function doesn't work right, it's either broken or outright cheating to create the illusion of difficulty. Fight after fight I miss and wiff and the enemy takes me apart; twice the enemy warband had identical composition to mine, same faction, same units, almost identical equipment, and they crushed me taking almost no casualties. I've had enough and I would recommend that if you're interested in a game with honest difficulty rather than the psuedo-difficulty of a busted RNG then go look elsewhere.
Edit: I've read some other reviews and discussions and I'll admit, the RNG might not be broken. It's the balance; in order to compensate for the idiot AI the enemy team is given an advantage, a way too big advantage. I've just given the game one last chance, and I got team wiped on my first mission. I missed literally every attack and I got critted several times at least. The game balance is terrible, the AI is way too overpowered, especially for early game. I hadn't seen the enemy for the first couple of turns, set my units to ambush, but didn't take. The enemy came round a corner, charged and I lost two people without being allowed to react.
I wouldn't be so upset at this if I felt the game offered options, if I felt like this was my fault, but it's like this on the first mission, where you're equipment and unit options are very limited. There's no tactical options outside of outnumber them in melee and MAYBE they'll run away (more common they stick around and kill all the people surrounding them, who constantly fail to hit them). This isn't fun xcom or fire emblem tactical challenge, there's no interesting strategic or tactical thinking or options, no way to swing the balance in you're favour with clever tactics, you're just stuck facing an opponent with a huge statistical edge and the only option is to either exploit AI bugs (the not fun kind of tactical thinking, akin to exploiting pathing bugs in dark souls) or just hope the RNG swings your way for once.

The RNG gods were cruel when they saw fit to test my warband. They waited till I was reckless. What could I do when the post battle summary brought news from the Merchant District? This game is absolutely well done, since as it warns you from the start you have to make the best out of the worst situation and as soon as you master the way you ought to play in tough fights or when gathering wyrdstones, it becomes an awesome experience. The campaign arcs for each faction are well done (especially the maps, I remember getting stuck in a cursed library with the witchhunter team) and the story keeps you interested.

The multiplayer isn't anything special, but it gives you and a friend a chance to either kill eachother brutally or have a fun match with no repercussions.
Overall this game is a fine addition to the whole turn based universe of Warhammer and along with its great atmosphere it delivers a very challenging playthrough for each and every faction you choose.
8/10!

I have played "Civilization III", "IV", "II", "V"  and "VI" (in that particular order). "Civilization V" is my favourite, but "Civ IV" has also a lot to offer and it's worth playing not only for nostalgic value. Everything what I'm saying relates to "Beyond the Sword" expansion and I highly recommend to purchase all the expansions, because, without them, the game is incomplete and you have limited mod and civilization options. (Actually, I don't understand, why people play vanilla versions. For "Civilization" games, it's usually like this: they release an incomplete game with some gameplay faults, which is substantially improved with following expansions – not only in terms of content, but also in terms of mechanics. I believe this will be the case with Beyond Earth, as well.)
Here are some things that "Civ4" does have that "Civ5" doesn't, and things that "Civ4" is better at (well, imo, at least):
+ More customisation options (e.g., no limitations regarding how many civilizations could there be per map size; an option to assign leaders to different civilization, for example, Ghandi as a leader of Russia).
+ By far better interface (except, for one thing - when you are offered research/tech choice, you need to make decision right away - you can't examine your empire first. You can change it afterwards in the same turn, but, anyway, it's not very convenient). Apart from that, it's more easy to review the overall state of your progress. For example, howering over a tech gives you a detailed explanation of what you can achieve with a tech (units, wonders, bonuses for discovering first, etc.), why it's important and where it leads. Also, in "Civ4", there is the option to see the network of global politics or what a particular leader thinks of other leaders or what he wants or is willing to trade. I also prefer "Civ4" icons over "Civ5" icons.
+ Unit appearance is different for each civilization and religion (and not just in terms of colour). For example, Korean swordmen will have different swords than European swordmen, a Buddhist missionary will have a different outfit from that of a Christian missionary.
+ Cool wonder animations.
+ Civics (ideologies) are available much earlier in the game, you can change them more easily and they are not linked to culture points. In "Civ5", many of the civic system functions are transfered to the relligion system.
+ Map trading
+ Cultural victory is actually a feasible option contrary to "Civ5", where it is possible only in rare occasions.
+ Inbuilt World Builder (In "Civ5" it's available only from the "Workshop")
+ Workers can build forest preserves (that add happiness)
+ The rather unique "Afterworld" scenario and "Final Frontier" mod (which both feel like and actually are completely different games – full-conversion mods, if you like).
+ Vassal states (you can push other leaders to become your vassals).
+ No lag on large maps, since it is a much older game and requires less system resources.
+/- Random events instead of city state quests
+/- Workshops and windmills are tile improvements instead of buildings.
+/- Religion doesn't have that much impact as in "Civ5". But it does have a considerable impact on diplomacy.
+/- Culture bombs work in the same way as great general citadels.
+/- Different great persons may discover different technologies.
+/- Corporations - spread them like relligion and each corporation will have different effects. "They are mechanisms that can add substantial production to a city, at the cost of higher maintenance costs. Thus, in essence they convert gold into other basic goods (food, hammers, science, and culture)." [From Wikia]
However, there are some aspects in which "Civ4" falls behind "Civ5":
- Square tiles. Hexagon tiles are far better for strategical gameplay and layout.
- Unit stacks. I know that I will be condemned for this and for a while I missed the stacking option in "Civ 5", but, when I got used to it, I must admit that one unit-per-tile limitation actually improves the gameplay a lot. With this limitation it matters much more where you put your units. You can manage your army more easily. The city placement has a bigger impact on your attack/defence strategy. And, finally, if you play smart, you can save more of your units (sometimes even win the game without loosing any unit), whereas in "Civ4" you are bound to throw your units into the battle as cannon fodder. "Civilization 5" feels like chess in that matter. And I prefer it that way.
- Ranged units (Archers, Crossbowmen, etc.) don't have a "ranged attack" option. It is available only for siege weapons ("bombard").
- No city states. I actually like how city states provide bonuses, quests and influence the diplomacy. I think it's a better mechanic than influence points. Although, on the other hands, AI leaders in "Civ5" are completely irrational, their attitude sometimes doesn't make any sense and there is little you can do about it, whereas in "Civ4", you can at least change your civic/relligion or influence those of the AI leader.
- "Civilization 4" is harder than "Civilization 5" (although it might be a good thing for some players). In "Civilization 5", I feel comfortable on "Emperor" and with a bit of luck I can manage "Immortal" on smaller maps, whereas I struggle on "Noble" in "Civilization 4". Perhaps, it's because I haven't played "Civilization 4" in years and hadn't developed any strategy when I did.
- Technology trading. This actually makes the game rushed, unbalanced and it's much harder to make that technological gap between you and AI players. Although, there were moments, in "Civ5" multiplayer, when I wished there was this option. But, now, I see that research agreements are actually a much more balanced mechanic. Luckily, you can turn "technology trading" off in "Civ4".
- "Civilization 4" pushes you to expand early (as mush as possible). "Civilization 5" pushes you to build army early (expansion is less crucial than in "Civ4)". I don't like any of the two, but, I think, that the fact, that AI civilizations are expanding so rapidly and that you need to keep up, makes "Civilization 4" unbalanced - it's hard to maintain positive stats and to manage the cities and units. In "Civ5", you can win with less units, less initial cities and the overall pace is slower, which allows you to build your empire in a more balanced way. "Civilization III" had the same problem btw.
- No "Steam Workshop" support. But you can still use 3rd party mods.
There are probably some more differences that I've forgotten, but, in the end, I would like to say that "Civilization 4" is a great game and offers many things its successor lacks. For that reason it's worth purchasing even today – not only for a nostalgic value, but also for the different and fun experience it offers.
My overall rating: 9/10

I recently got into this game because my wife and her brother used to play the crap out of it when it first released. Now we have a full party of family members all playing together. If you enjoy D&D 3.5, you'll be glad to know that every rule in the game came straight from the tabletop books, to including multi-classing. It sticks true to its roots of the original format, but also makes a pretty good MMO. The community is also very friendly from what I've seen (Khyber server) which I assume is because it's age (and possibly it's limitations on free players, more on that later) has driven off the bulk of players, leaving only the ones who really enjoy it.
As a note, this game released 11 years ago, and while I personally appreciate that it doesn't need a dream machine to run smoothly, people who are accustomed to 4k HD might find it off-putting. Also, if you have a friend (or a few) who you're going to play with, I highly recommend using a third-party chat system such as Discord, as I don't think that the in-game mic chat has been updated since 2006.
The only fundamental problem with the game is that as a free-to-play, free players have a bit more limitation than what I've seen in other games. This could actually be the reason why the community is so nice, but I digress. There are a few races and a few classes and even several missions that are only available to those who purchase VIP, but if you don't mind spending a little money I highly recommend giving it a whirl.

I would say it's worth it after about 2 hours of play.
The physics and graphics have improved vastly compared to last year. The stages are also so much better and a lot harder. I would go as far to say that WRC 7 has the best rally track design i have seen so far. The terrain is filled with bumps, tight corners and moments for high speed. Going off track is not as forgiving as it used to be.
It also features random car crashes which is a feature i love! I just saw a Yaris hanging on for dear life over a cliff in a aussie stage.
What i don't like though is the force feedback. It's not very informational, and it's put to max at default which is just incredibly stupid. I turned it down to 15% in G27 now it's okay but far from perfect. Still though WRC7 is a must buy for rally fans imo.

First few stages suggest this is a huge improvement over 6. I can't wait to get back in there! It's hardcore, you know the score.
More info, now I've played some more: Stuttering. Yes, I've seen it. I saw some stuttering at the start of some stages, but it went away pretty quickly. I definitely think there's something going on (didn't we have the same issue when WRC 5 and WRC6 launched?) but thankfully it wasn't a game breaker for me.
The audio is MUCH improved. Love the sounds of the cars now. They sound meaty and proper.
My Logitech G27 steering wheel worked perfectly, although the button remapping screen is suffering from a serious recurring bug from the first release build of WRC6, where the 'remap' button ends up getting captured as the button you want to remap rather than letting you press a new one. This problem calls for some extreme messing around trying to remap anything (I like my handbrake on the top right button of my wheel) and should have been caught by some proper QA.
The stages are amazing. The bumps and dips and little details on the roads makes it special. Really nice sense of speed, too. Like others have said, FFB could really use some work. It doesn't communicate the weight distribution enough and it's hard to get a feel for where the weight actually is. I hope that they can work on the FFB and fix this up in a future patch because it's a shame to see this awesome game being let down by this.
The only other thing I don't like about this game are the replays. I've seen reviews where they said the replays were bad and I completely agree. They need to be more cinematic - they need to try and recreate something closer to the official WRC event coverage footage instead of some outdated old videogame. The replays are buggy (clipping issues with the co-pilots head, as well as culling problems) and they're flat. Not at all fun to watch. I really hope K will go back and put some more effort into the replays. We want to see a cinematic WRC event coverage style replay, not .. well, whatever this is. It's not good enough!
Above all else, though, I am having an absolute blast. I think it's well worth the money and I know I'm going to be playing this game a lot. Rally-heads will probably get a real kick out of it.

The tracks are fantasic. They're narrow - They're unpredicable. Exactly what rally games need.

The suspensions feel welded solid. Jumps feel like something beyond gravity is artificially yanking you back to the ground as soon as possible.
I went into this really excited and wanting to like it - I can put the poor sound and graphics aside for a good game but this really disappointed.

Good enough to make the game easy to pick up and play with no fuss which is a positive in an era of endless options.  I went straight to simulation and manual geabox settings and the cars handle well without being overly difficult.
The trial stage to get the settings and difficulty level right seems to work well too.  That big jump on the Portugal stage is fun.  Needing to turn on your own lights and wipers is also a good touch.
The WRC cars feel like real beasts and starting out in the WRC Junior cars is a bit of a shock after trying the WRC cars first.
At this stage, after my initial impressions I'm content to recommend this game.  Similar in driving feel to DiRT 4 but the graphics and locations look far more detailed and real.  At the price it seems good enough to me.

Rochard is a fun, leisure time puzzle game. It boasts barely 4 hours of gameplay and it won't be one of those games sitting in your log waiting to be finished.
For it's short playtime however, it boasts a good amount of content; you're just speeding through it because it's easy to get a good pace - once you understand the basics, you can maneuver through the part-platform-shooter puzzles with narry a pause.
However, for more experienced puzzle and/or platform players you might feel the gameplay falls short; only the DLC brings any real challenge to the puzzles, and there's not a lot of variation outside of the DLC itself.
And sadly, for people who like to delve into a story of a game, it's nothing to write home about either. It has very predictable plot twists if you've ever seen a movie in the last 20 years, and you're gaurenteed to watch the ending of the game with a bad flavour in your mouth.
However, it's a perfect pick-up for people who don't have a lot of time to play games or just want to fill a weekend with a new game - it's also a good gift for inexperienced puzzlers/platform gamers who might feel it to be more of a challenge. A veteran might be too critical to the flaws, and might forget the game has good, smooth graphics, very easy-to-use controls and some familiar voice acting of quality!
All-in-all, I wouldn't recommend it if you're looking for the hardest puzzle game of the year, but if you're up for a small brain teaser to occupy your weekend afternoon, it's a good purchase.

This game gets a bad rap, but it really is something special. Fighting games have always been niche, so low player numbers should never have been a surprise outside of the fighting game titans like Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat and Marvel VS Capcom.
It's a game with a story that cuts itself short when it feels like the adventure's just begun.
It's an experience like no other in the combat, but the game does lack in a couple crucial places that would have really given it a huge chance at shining. The combat is needless to say, just incredible in a lot of aspects. It takes traditional fighting game combat and adds a touch of realism, combining it with aspects of a deck building game. With up to 2 different fully customizeable movesets in the secondary weapon, things can get really deep before even landing a punch. On top of that, aside from just a few moves that see less use than others, every attack available for use in your combat deck is surprisingly balanced across the board.
There isn't any other game in the market at the moment of this review that has the same gameplay experience that Absolver offers, that's for sure. It's up to you to decide whether the game is for you though, because its divergence from the fully traditional fighting game will turn away many people.
The problem of the game lies in its poor initial reputation (partially due to having similarities to For Honor which also had a bad reputation and kind of still does), and lack of overall diverse content. There's the very short story, unlocking new moves by blocking attacks you haven't learned before, the semi-open-world PVP, and the instanced formal 1-on-1/3-on-3 PVP (with more modes to come, I believe). Besides that, there's some gear to collect if you didn't do that as you played the story. There's nothing in the way of meaningful PVE, nor a major goal to work toward.
The content is there and it's satisfactory enough, but it really feels like something more could have been done.
It's one of those games that end too early, leaving you hoping for more of the story behind it all, thrusting you into the vortex of multiplayer that many games do these days.
The developers DID assure us that the story wouldn't be very long and to not expect much in that department, so there is so lenience I can give there, but it's almost too short even with the preemptive notice. It leaves me more sadly disappointed than anything else, since the world of Absolver itself does seem genuinely interesting.
It's really something, but as it stands, I think it's best bought on sale. That said, the developers do seem to be diligently chipping away at refining the game and adding more content.
It's a real shame, though, because I believe that with a few more months of polishing before release to change the fact that it garnered a poor first impression from many after launch- Absolver could've been a lot more than it is.

An excellent game for arcade, puzzle, or RPG enthusiasts. It's a good thing I don't have a hard 30 second time limit to write this review otherwise I'd be broke with no equipment since I'd have to pay the Time Goddess so much.
Enjoy the world of Half Minute Hero, where you play as one of several characters who are associated with a stingy Time Goddess who enjoys every bit of gold in her pockets.
This takes every single trope that RPGs implement and runs with them. All in less than 30 seconds (per stage). While it is an RPG, the RPG aspect is replaced more by a puzzle aspect and requires you to balance your gold and time to defeat those pesky Evil Lords trying to cast a spell of destruction on the world. There's a good amount of humor, and I found myself laughing almost everytime I turn on this game. There's also several game modes, including Hero 30, Princess 30, and Evil Lord 30. The game puzzles can get rather hard with all the frantic action that happens (considering you have a 30 second time limit, it's not surprising). Just make sure you can think on your feet otherwise you may be on the receiving end of the Spell of Destruction by the Evil Lord across the street!
But underneath the absurdity and the humor of the game also lies a well done story, not often seen in games. Don't think that this is a comedy through and through!
Now if you'll excuse me, I need to pay the Time Goddess (again).

There's not a ton to say about InFlux other than it is clear that the college that the developers attented, RMIT University, is clearly a million times better than the scamtastic joke that is ITT Tech that I went to for game design. InFlux is a simple and fairly relaxing ball puzzle game that is best described as Marble Blast meets Q.U.B.E. . If you played any 3D ball puzzle game like those or Super Monkey Ball, then you have a rough idea. The game world is continuous in InFlux, as you gather orbs of light with your attact ability spread across an island paradise and drop them off into to totems/torches that activate puzzle segments. You then can enter these segments which are relatively easy puzzles involving trying to get an orange orb into an orange box (in one case, there was a second, green orb and box). Solving the puzzle activates a pillar of light and when all the puzzles in an area are finished, some sort of sequence will activate, allowing you to the next area. Puzzles generally involve rotating the room or parts of the room with blue switches and moving yourself and the ball around with the help of platforms, air vents, and bouncing mechanisms. The hardest part of the game and puzzles is probably the platforming, and I belive most gamers, even those not good a puzzlers should be able to solve most of these relatively easy puzzles.
I really like the art style, specifically of the ball, it's lighting effects and look and sound of it's abilities. The island has a nice asthetic, though graphical quality is comparable to a mid-era PS3/360 game - textures up close can be pretty muddy. It's unclear as to what or why anything in the game world is happening. You're a high tech looking ball with an internal light source and "magical magnetic" ability rolling around what looks like a real world, primitive tribal island where human-like life exists or used to exist. There are tree stumps and man-made structures all over the island, but no signs of life beyond flora and a single whale-like mammal you encounter a few times in the game. *Mild Spoiler* It is implied that you are from another world OR that you are trying to escape this world. *END SPOILER*. Regardless, it is never made clear exactly what the story or plot really is; you roll around the level, entering puzzles that seem to take you to another dimension, finish them and eventually leave the entire location. That said, exploring the world is mostly calming, especially thanks to the very nice Chillwave/downtempo soundtrack from Johnathan Yandel - I have added it to my Bandcamp wishlist.
My few complaints are minor. Due to the level design and physics engine, your ball will easily hop around on some ground surfaces on the island, even if it is an apparently flattened trail, but this isn't a problem in puzzles and most of the game. I had a couple bugs where I got stuck behind geometry and once even went straight through a wall on a puzzle room - in that instance, I didn't see how I could complete the room without that exploit. Platforming is annoying as the ball doesn't jump and instead propels, bouncing off anything it hits, which sometimes means you will miss jumps or worse, bounce off a wall into oblivion. Thankfully, lives are "infinite" and you are generously returned to a checkpoint. I also had a bug where I lost some of my sound for the attract ability. Lastly, I'm confused into why I'm even playing this or what I'm doing exactly. InFlux ALMOST has the mark of something pretentious, but never clarify or signal much of anything.
Still, it's a nice puzzler that likely won't strain your brain, time, or wallet as it can be completed in under 4 hours and costs only $5. I enjoyed my experience, and I recommend it to fans of the genre and casual/semi-casual gamers. I even recommend it to gamers that don't like puzzle games - since the puzzles are generally easy. However, all that is the biggest drawback to some of the biggest fans of the arcade/puzzler genre: there little content or challenge, and next to no reward.

Rakuen is a game I truly want to like, but a few aggravating flaws resulted me unable to keep playing.
Its first sin is the engine of the game can only render a very small window of the game, or run in full screen with incorrect aspect ratio that causes everything to be stretched.  I am not sure how the creators of this game overlooked this glaring UX issue, but I guess I’m not actually looking for an excuse; it is not excusable.
Let’s talk about the plot next.  I liked the first chapter where an interesting cast of characters reside in a hospital, facing an unknown thief who has been stealing stuff.  But it took a down turn when the mother of the boy protagonist encouraged the boy (and also accompanying him) to the fantasy world in a story book.
Maybe the story would later explain why the boy, who appears to have some serious cancer that must be hospitalized, can make a trip to the book’s world and start doing cliched RPG-ish quests for fluffy cute NPC.  Even worse, the mother of the boy approved all these with seemingly blatant disregard of the boy’s health (and the consequences of their disappearing from the hospital).
In the end, I think the only thing the game does very well is the sound.  The bgm tracks are gorgeous, and little details like the footstep sound from across the wall, to progressive louder ticks when you move towards a clock, is quite impressive.
It’s unfortunate that to protect my own eyesight and sanity that I have to quit playing this game.  Hopefully the developers will learn a lesson here and make their next game a better one.

Rakuen may have some blind spots in writing, some not so great gameplay ideas and slower-paced story moments, but at the end of the day, it delivers the goods. You know exactly what I mean by that, when you consider this a heavily story focused game in the style of To the Moon.
This title shares a lot of common ground with the one of the biggest indie tear-jerkers. It uses the same engine, controls, it lacks any combat and it also focuses mostly on telling the heart-touching story. There are several major differences though. Rakuen, in opposition to To the Moon, offers noticeable more gameplay mechanics, more open-ended world to discover and far longer run time. I believe that those changes both damaged and helped the game in several different aspects.
Story takes place in the hospital where a small boy with his loving mother discover portals to the alternative universe via family-inherited story book. In this colorful, fantasy world, interconnected with the real one, everybody has its own counterpart that faces similar joys, problems and fears. To awaken the legendary forest god and get granted a wish, boy and his mother need to help other patients in the hospital. This involves delving into their past experiences, learning their tragic stories that shaped them into who they are. Games jumps from helping one person to the next, dividing itself into seamless chapters, ending up with the climactic finale where developers bring up the biggest "guns" to this feels-train.
Game has a lot of plot ground to cover and added gameplay mechanics in form of fetch questing, exploration and some very weird puzzle solving also extend the playtime. The world and challenges are mostly alright, but I think that thanks to atrocious RPG-Maker style controls and feedback, game seems to drag a little in many places, especially when the story doesn't run on all cylinders. You can start to feel somewhat little disappointed, especially when some earlier characters' stories and general plot movements aren't remarkably memorable or engaging (ex. I think that Mom character was very underutilized in the beginning).
That being said, you should not worry about the earlier parts of the game, since title really picks up the pace later on: putting some more interesting characters into motion, pulling some unexpected revelations and very pretty powerful moments. Some of those scenes, on top of being quite emotional, are also extremely clever with hints of foreshadowing hidden in the plain sight. I was very close to performing a standing ovation on the few last scenes.
- it's the sentence I would like to share with the developers in those exceptional parts.
Despite my initial doubts about Rakuen having a fair chance against other titles in the genre, I would say that the ending and the game overall, brought a very satisfying experience worth recommending to anybody interested in story based games. If you liked To the Moon, you will definitely like this one too!
Rakuen may lack focus, presentation and polish sometimes, but I believe that it will be a pleasure for you to help this boy get his wish.

Jamestown is one of the strongest 'against-the-flow' feelings i've had against a game; here is this clearly beautifully crafted thing that for some reason i can't enjoy or appreciate. Everyone says it's great, the reviews do too--so why don't i like it?
Jamestown is, in my mind, not a schmup designed to be a schmup. The rudimentary gameplay is not interesting or challenging enough to sustain prolonged interest, the enemy types are forgettable, the stages are bland and mono-paced, and the same song plays for every level, minus the last--an unforgiveable sin, to my mind, in this genre where ZUN and so many others have set such a precedent and high standard of quality for soundtrack composition. Everyone says this soundtrack is great, and i disagree--it is orchestral, emotionaless, unintuitive, and not at all designed around the experience of FLYING A SHIP SHOOTING STUFF. At the end of the day, Jamestown feels like an experience not designed around itself--the fluff is what makes the gameplay, but the fluff is stupid (no, it's /really/ stupid), and i don't like it and you can't make me like it, and therefore the game doesn't hold much weight by itself. The 'Vaunt' system is kind of cool, but ZUN's done better in every Touhou from 8 onward, so that's not much to brag about.
Anyway. If you think there's a chance you'd enjoy a mediocre shooting experience with an impersonal movie soundtrack and terrible writing, buy Jamestown. i feel i was tricked. this review is brutally honest. i apologize for anyone's feelings that it hurts.

I must admit that when I had the opportunity to review Jamestown, a title developed & published by Final Form Games, I immediately jumped at the chance - being the avid shmup fanatic that I am. And let's face it, within the Steam universe there certainly exists no shortage of mediocre ones to play...those that tried to emulate the heart & soul of arcade shooters but which ultimately lacked that certain magic and polish to them. However I always heard very glowing accolades about this particular title, but are they warranted? Let's find out below.
The game touts itself as having "lovingly handcrafted pixels", and it is my pleasure to report that these retro-styled 2D graphics are absolutely superb, easily evoking the look & feel of its 1990's era arcade brethren with its charming yet familiar style...making me quickly feel right at home. And I must also say that it's a very colorful game as well, sporting vibrantly rich hues and pretty bullet patterns which instantly dazzle the senses.
The artwork itself is themed from a "17th-century British Colonial Mars" motif, and it seems to work quite well, especially since it also includes a matching storyline to add a bit more distinction to this title. The story itself is wholly superfluous to be sure, because with a shmup we all know gameplay is truly the cornerstone of the experience, but I found it to be a nice touch nonetheless and there is a decent amount of skippable text which can be read by those seeking to capture the full essence of Jamestown.
As far as its music & audio go, it was superb all around...with punchy bullet & explosion sounds overlayed atop beautiful orchestral arrangments which seemed to perfectly fit in with the theme of this memorable game.
Now getting back to its gameplay here, this is a dreamy kind of bullet hell indeed in that it's very challenging yet always fair. And the wonderful part about it is that you have both primary and secondary weapons which can be alternated seamlessly throughout each level, as well as a tertiary "Vaunt Meter" which is a time-limited power-up/shield combo whereby you first have to collect gold from destroyed enemies to recharge before using again (you simply move toward the falling gold and it scoops up automatically within your proximity).
And if that wasn't enough, what truly impressed me most about it by far, is the ability to play both online and local co-op with up to four players. This adds a very interesting dynamic to the game since the way it is uniquely implemented consists of only one player needing to survive the level in order for the entire team to succeed, whereby everyone respawns once more to continue off playing the next successive one. And I must confess that with so many bullets flying in Jamestown, having the ability to lean on your team-mates in this way is a definite plus. Because death can come surprisingly fast and unexpectedly when playing on any of the several difficulties higher than normal - just massage one single bullet the wrong way and you're a goner to be sure! Which in the end makes it all the more addictive and challenging, undoubtedly infusing a lot more replay value into it.
But nonetheless I do have to admit that I was somewhat disappointed by how few levels there were to enjoy (only 5). It's just so much exhilarating fun to experience, that I very soon wanted more Jamestown to play...perhaps twice as much. In fact easily twice as much. And while there is a DLC available which adds in more ships, I somehow felt that the base game just wasn't quite meaty enough for my taste...but then again at its price-point I suppose this can be somewhat understandable...but still...I did decidedly expect a decent amount more content in this regard.
Having said that, you will be absolutely spoiled in no time after playing this gem...make no mistake about it. It hits all the high notes with ease as far as its frenetically fun gameplay & presentation goes. And it certainly plays very well with no discernable issues noticed. I suppose I will have no choice now but to pick up the DLC for it, because while immersing myself within this one, it felt just like I was being transported back inside the 1990's arcades...with those unforgettable chains of explosive delight ricocheting between my ears...and eventually soon finding their way to a soft spot inside my heart.

This may be the first time I've ever felt the need to write a Steam review for anything but this otome/visual novel struck a chord with me. An overwhelmingly good one - enough so that I'm staying awake to write this when I really should be sleeping. I have done my best to keep spoilers out of this review.
Positives:
A whirlwind of emotions and compelling storytelling, this visual novel may very well rip your heart out in all the possible ways. I laughed, I cried (both in sadness and in joy), and I grinned ear to ear whenever something happened not just to the main character, but the characters around her. You see, with Cincerella Phenomenon, you don't realize you've fallen, not just for the main and her romantic interests, but also every single side character until you're cheering them on whenever they come on screen. I absolutely loved the characters - even the unpleasant ones - and that is a testiment to fantastic writing.
The writing itself, characters aside, was glorious. About halfway through the game (3/5 good endings unlocked) I spent an hour telling a friend about the lore of the story. Had I not spoiled it for them, they said they would have played simply for the story - and they do not play visual novels, much less otome games. Anyway, the story is so rich with bits of lore scattered throughout. You simply cannot only play one route - you have to do them all in order to understand everything. Typically when I play otome games I pick the guy I like best and only do one playthrough with him before tossing the game aside.
Not this game. I binge-played it in 20 hours, unlocked all of the good endings (and one bad - the others I'm still working on), and am even planning to buy the digital artbook just to support the creators because this- was- fantastic. I literally could not stop playing this game because the story is so rich that I felt like I was reading a book.
Negatives:
My negatives will likely not be too similar to those of the comments here that I have read. Cinderella Phenomenon touches on close to taboo topic(s) in certain areas (you will understand if you play it) but that wasn't what bothered me - if anything, I found the topic(s) interesting and would likely shove that up there in my positives section. No, what bothered me about Cinderella Phenomenon was a particular route that I will not go into too much detail with. I am trying to keep this spoiler-free, after all.
Anyway... I enjoyed all of the routes, do not get me wrong, but there was one in particular that felt a little... "mish-mashed." It is simultaneously my least favorite and favorite route. This route is not like the others and is messy, complicated, and feels ridiculously long in comparison to the other ones but it is the one that has the most feels (good or bad, I will leave that a mystery). As such I'm not sure if I can actually make this a true negative of the game, but it's the best I have got.
Cinderella Phenomenon was phenomenal and I eagerly look forward to more by this company.

What secrets is everyone hiding? Can someone who has closed off her heart be able to do good deeds? Can we trust others? Lucette or our protagonist faces these questions and more.
It's a masterpiece of storytelling. The five story routes tie in together. Even the side characters are well fleshed out - most of them are dynamic and round characters. There are lots of surprises in store.
Unlike other Otomes games, Lucette or our protagonist (you can change her first name), has a personality. Instead of wish fulfillment, the game tells a story as we join Lucette on her and her friends' journey.
Play this for the story. The game play is the usual for a Ren'Py visual novel. There's even a right choice indicator to show you which choice scores a point with the character. Outside of getting the Guided by Intuition achievement once, with the right choice indicator, this is a pretty easy game if you invest time in it.
The programming and execution is top-notch. There are barely any bugs and the game is gorgeous.
Rather than a translation of Japanese, this is a full blown English language and culture story. It's so satisfying to see them do curtsies and English mannerisms and values. (I've read too many Chinese Imperial Court stories and Japanese stories by then). Finally, a good Otome game in English based on English culture.
This is THE English language Otome/Visual Novel I never realized I was waiting for. How is this free?! I'm surprised this is only Dicesuki's 2nd published game. Thank you too to the Kickstarter backers that made the game even more gorgeous! I can't wait for Dicesuki's next game.

For the order of routes, here are my recommendations:
> Whichever excites you most between Karma, Rumpel, and Rod. I really enjoyed Karma's route. I would have quit the story if I played Rod's route first. I suggest getting the guided by intuition achievement in Rod's route.
> Play Fritz's route fourth. It's got a lot of drama/revelations that may make the other three routes pale. But it can get depressing. You do NOT want to play this route last.

I've put up my own series of guides and a play through on  youtube for the Skaven faction and I had invested a lot of hours in this game and I kept thinking maybe this game can be great, I mean otherwise why would I put so much effort into making an entire youtube channel for this game?
The thing is, this game is very unique in that it is basically a tabletop strategy game that was turned into a computer game making it more accessible to the more "casual" players. It has the potential of being almost as popular as chess. BUT the devs didn't understand this potential and didn't understand how to unlock it.
The Good:
-This is a very challenging strategy game that involves  a solid understanding of Strategy concepts and players who crave a deeper experience or who have read and know how to apply The Art of War and/or have military background would enjoy this game.
-This game is exciting and draws inspiration from a fun franchise.
The Bad:
-This game does not have a lot of players who play and due to the decisions made by the developers this game is likely going to only be played by the most die hard fans.
-The developers only focus on graphics and it took several months after release for them to fix the random teleport/rubberbanding issues which would cause your units to teleport randomly around the map which will likely get them killed via being put too close to the enemy by being too separated from friendly units.
-This game does not really have a smart AI and therefore once you do have a good solid grasp of how to be strategic or use positioning to cheese the AI you will be able to pull off victories without any loss of units every single game and this makes the single player very dry and boring since once you've reached that level of understanding (by following simple rules like 1. Damage comes from surrounding enemy units with multiple units of your own, not giving each individual warrior high damage... 2. Reduce the enemy's damage by taking them out at chokepoints if facing superior numbers so that doorways become key real estate to control. 3. Pulling your low health units back and switching to ranged weapons if any makes your units be able to carry on fighting even if they are low on health and in this way reduce their risk of dying while still getting usefulness out of them.)
The Ugly:
- The way the Devs made this game, the game is extremely punishing in that if you lose a unit in combat they might die or get a permanent injury that will make them useless and all those hours of upgrading them is wasted. Then there's the fact that if you lose a match your entire team will take damage and possibly die. There is no way to prevent this.
- The game's brutality is further compounded by the fact that multiplayer is the same exact thing where if you play multiplayer your team will also DIE if you lose and even if you win any unit that was knocked out will likely die or take permanent damage. There is a "no deaths/penalties" mode in multiplayer but because of the overall brutality of this game where you can't save so you can't reload, nobody plays multiplayer anymore.
- The no saving, every decision is final, permadeath, devs only care about releasing DLC's and upgrading graphics part of this game makes this game prohibitive for new players who want to play and also makes this game exceptionally hard to get into because unless you are a seasoned pro at strategy games (like myself), you WILL struggle and cry bloody tears when your favorite units die in horrible ways because of a simple misclick that you made and there's no way you can take it back.

Pink Heaven is the second demo/preview/ad for Studio Pixel's new game, "Kero Blaster." It continues the story of a little pink secretary, which started in the first game, "Pink Hour."
Pink Heaven expands on the originals simple premise. Instead of one weapon, there are two weapons. Instead of one stage, there are two stages. And instead of one boss fight, there are two. (if you want to tackle Hard Mode). It is very short, and relatively easy. There are multiple endings, just like Pink Hour, which is an incentive to replay the game. The story is very simple, but it's cute. I especially like how it utilizes characters who are NPCs in the main game, Kero Blaster.
Where Pink Heaven really shines is in its Hard Mode, which unlocks after getting one of the multiple endings. Hard Mode doesn't give you less health and enemies more damage like most other games with varying difficulties. It completely revamps the familiar two levels from the main game, and even has an extra boss fight. Hard Mode requires extremely precise platforming, and a cool head during the final boss. Beating it took me multiple, multiple attempts, but the feeling of overcoming Hard Mode was immensely satisfying, and I'd recommend at least trying it out.
Pink Heaven (along with Pink Hour) is the perfect way to advertise a game. It has me invested, even if it's just a little, in these characters, and it showcases the gameplay style and overall feeling of Kero Blaster while remaining its own little side-game. With the price of 100% nothing, both games are worth playing through at least once. They definitely have me excited for Kero Blaster's Steam release.

This is pretty much going to be the same as my review for Pink Hour, as it's a sequel in the same engine, so here goes:
Pink Heaven is the second free platformer released as a "demo" of sorts for an upcoming game by the same developer, Kero Blaster. It provides around an hour of fun, or twenty minutes of fun followed by an hour of ragequitting, depending on how good you are at platformers.
Honestly, it's a pretty well put together platform/shooting game, with the biggest "drawback" being that it's fairly short - something that would be resolved by buying the game it's promoting, obviously. Though, well, even less so as compared to Pink Hour, being as Pink Heaven is about twice as long! The only real issue I had was still that Hard showed that it might have some issues with precision jumping, as I found myself falling short or overshooting on those segments reliably, especially the ones with the moving elevators, which was more annoying in this than Pink Hour since that segment was near the end of the game, and thus failing there required going through everything until that point again.
That said, though, it was a good hour and a quarter of fun for me, and free, so I can't really help but give this a thumbs-up.

The main question everyone will be asking is: Is the game good? Yes. Is it worth £25? People that love brawlers 100% Yes.
If you don't, I suggest at least trying out the game at first. The game is extreamly fun with a very good combat system and a very interesting deck system which allows a lot of variations between fights during Combat Trails(PvP). However, I picked up this game at a reduced price on sale and honestly at the point Absolver is right now I don't think its worth buying at full price, however if you love brawling games like For Honor, or Tekken this game is probably worth the full price. The game looks beautiful and has a massive amount of potential. The game also has a very nice customization system and you are able to dye gear which I love. Personally, the best part about the game is that the community is extreamly nice and are really helpful to make the game's high skill cap much easier to reach as Absolver is an easy to pick up, but a very hard game to master.
On the other hand, sometimes camera angles are absolutely horrible due to the third person view you have and the somewhat small arenas(depending on the area/arena). At low levels Combat Trails, its almost impossible to win (in my expericence, it could just be that i was just unlucky, or just that i flat out suck at the game) as you will most likely be matched up with someone who is a much higher level than you, this might be due to the small community so there may be much more higher level people than low levels, but this is just me being salty about Combat Trails tbh. Finally, my biggest complaint is that the story seemed very very short, as just in a few hours(approximately 5/6 hours if you dont skip all the npcs like I did, but i dont reccomend this as you dont learn any moves and I was with a friend so I only had to worry about solo bosses), and the ending wasn't exactly what you call, "satisfying". But overall, Absolver is still in early stages and can be developed much more over time and has loads of potenial, and I hope to see the game evolve and the community increase in size.
