Absolver offers a fresh new take on the melee genre.  Instead of confining you to a rigid combat system that feels highly limited and nonfluid, Absolver's combat feels very natural.  The story and exploration themselves are well put together and very immersive, and the music and minimalistic art style ties it all together.  There is character customization - yet, your character's face remains hidden the entire time.  I really think this makes it quite easy to get into the roleplaying aspect of the game.  In addition, although there are other players present pretty much at all times, there's no sort of communication beyond emotes.  I'm a pretty big fan of this, as  it adds to the minimalistic feel that the devs seemed to be aiming for while still stimulating player interractions.  It certantly makes the open world PvP part of the game a little spicy at times!

I most definitely suggest using a controller. I'm not even a controller person (in fact, I generally avoid the use of controllers altogether) and I have been absolutely loving the controller scheme of this game.  Whoever set up the default controls really did a fantastic job.

My only complaint is that the co-op grouping is a little odd.  You kinda have to jump through some hoops to join games, and respawning kicks you out of the group (but not out of the scenario, thankfully!).  I personally do not find this to be something that makes me not want to play the game, but I'd definitely keep it in mind when making your purchase.  You can totally work around it, but it's just not as easy as other games make it.

Absolver is a very thoughtful and artistically done melee combat game that is totally worth every cent, whether on sale or full price. If you're a fan of melee combat, this is definitely a game that you don't want to miss.

I absolutely love this game, and this might be my favorite English Visual Novel/Otome game yet. Each route is very well-written, and it's fun to see how Lucette gets along with her chosen partner. The central theme of the game is also very original, seeing curses that are based off of Fairytales.
I also love the fact that Lucette is not your typical Otome protagonist. Instead of being a blank slate, Lucette has personality and starts out with a frigid heart. As you progress through each route, you get to see her character develop to a warmer personality. The reactions of all the guys when they see her smile for the first time is always fun to see, and you'd likely have a similar reaction when you see it; it's a very nice smile.
Every guy has a unique personality, from your tsundere stepbrother, to a crossdressing and secretive man, to a nearly shameless flirt, to your personal knight, to the mysterious child street magician. I must say that I really like Waltz' route in particular for several reasons. He's enjoys giving puppet shows to children, is very protective of Lucette, knows how to do magic
Let's not forget how adorable he is while he's cursed, as well as when he blushes.
I've already finished all the routes, and I just can't stop replaying each one. Although I've already seen all the good endings, I'm reluctant to get the bad ones. I purchased the digital artbook recently, and the bad end CGs are rather heart-wrenching. I will warn anyone who plays this game to watch out for such moments, because when you reach them, you'll likely have to reach for a box of tissues.
Overall, Cinderella Phenomenon is a very nice Visual Novel/Otome game to pick up if you have never done so before. It's completely free, so there's no harm is trying it out. Also, I heard a fandisk will be released sometime soon, either by the end of the year or early next year, so keep a lookout for that. I'm extremely excited to get it, and hope to get closure for the routes then. I recommend that you head to Dicesuki's official tumblr account after playing, since they sometimes give answers to little bits of trivia and some further insight into the personalites of the main cast. I don't usually get this excited for these kind of games, but I'm glad to say that this one has rekindled my interest. I hope that when you play this, you'll feel the same way. Happy playing!

I used to play a lot of visual novels, and I'd often lose interest about halfway through and not bother trying to get all the routes completed. I'd just play my favorite character and be done with it. In Cinderella Phenomenon, I have a legitimate drive to want to complete each route for all the available bachelors, not only because all of the stories are very well connected and intertwined, but because each one of them has something unique to offer. The fairy tale theme lends itself extremely well to this. All of the characters, main characters and side characters, were likeable, well rounded, and interesting. The game gives you the opportunity to get to know several who otherwise might have simply blended into the background.
What I really appreciated about this game was also the writing of the main character/heroine, who is extremely effective in the story the game is trying to tell. There's nothing shallow or empty about her, you honestly feel connected to the character while playing her. She manages to be a strong female lead who doesn't have to compromise her feelings or personality for the sake of pleasing any of the bachelors. That was incredibly refreshing to see.
Overall, I definitely would recommend this game to anyone looking for a sweet, interesting little story (with a price that's unbelievable-- you can't really beat it, haha). It has nice artwork, a lovely soundtrack, and very good writing. 100% recommended.

Get some quarters, grab your giant headphones and get down to the mall arcade.  It’s time to play a game full of bullets and explosions, where only your reflexes will decide if you win or lose in Jamestown.
The year is 1619.  England and Spain are at war, and the conflict has spilled over into the New World.  Only we’re not in America.  We’re on Mars!  Join the colonists of Jamestown as they fight back against the Spanish Conquistadors, search for the lost colony of Roanoke, and more.  This top-down bullet hell arcade shooter is everything awesome about video games.
Play through the storyline with four different ships, each with their own playstyle.  There is four player splitscreen co-op.  The action is tight, fast-paced, frantic, but fair.  At times the screen will be positively filled with bullets, and your only hope will be to deploy the Vaunt, a temporary shield that makes you invulnerable and gives you a damage and points boost.  Knowing when to deploy it, and when to gamble if you can make it through an attack is a huge factor in your success.  Because you only get 2 credits before the level is over.  Then its back to square one.
The graphics are charming, full of beautiful depth and vibrant color.  Enemies are unique and interesting, backgrounds are lovingly detailed.  The art in Jamestown is among the best I’ve seen in an arcade style video game.
The music and sound effects are equally top notch.  Especially the final level and boss fight, which get my blood pumping and adrenaline racing.
Final Form Games really set the bar high with this game.  There’s very little I could nitpick that is wrong with it.  I would love to see this in a real arcade machine, with an actual joystick and buttons.  This game is screaming to eat people’s quarters.  It excels at letting you think you’re just one run away from beating the level, every time you fail.  Just one more try…
The story of the early American English colonies is a fascinating tale of survival and hardiness.  Throw in Martians, steampunk flying machines and beautiful pixel graphics, and you have a winner of a shooting game.  If you call yourself a gamer, get this and play it.  It is excellent.

A very playable old-school top-down shooter with well-drawn graphics. Controls are fairly simple, and both keyboard and gamepads are supported.
Difficulty is adjustable; normal is nice for getting started and casual play, but later levels are locked until you complete earlier levels at higher difficulty levels. Enemies fire many more bullets in higher difficulties; it only takes a single bullet to lose a life so a key skill to learn is slipping between gaps in the hail of bullets.
Jamestown seems oriented to co-op play, however I have yet to try a co-op game. Players can select ships with different abilities and some ships are more effective for certain enemies than others, so mixing up ship types in a co-op game is likely to be a good strategy.
I recommend Jamestown for casual arcade gaming and casual co-op gaming with friends. With variable difficulty levels it is quite playable even for those who consider themselves non-gamers.

Game sucks on so many levels. It's a mystery why anyone likes it.
First off, the camera. That type of camera was done in many games, and never has it been that  bad. Leon covers roughly 30% of the middle of the screen and the camera is apparently attached to his feet because you get his entire body in the frame, the camera is locked directly in front of him, rather than recentering after a while like pretty much all good third person games do. The aiming controls exactly like Deadrising, except you got the shakes on top of the stiff unusable aim. Also there's film grain you have to mod out because the game gives you a headache otherwise
The enemies are all boring. The ganado just exist for you to use all your ammo on, which you never run out of, so they exist to be a waste of time. The chainsaw men just get pinned to the floor by the shotgun, but you have to sink like 6 shots into them because a weaved bag over your head is apparently better armor than the actual suits of armor.  The crossbowman just serve to make you take damage if you don't abuse line-of-sight mechanics. Honestly the only challenge you'll encounter is the House of the Dead♥♥♥♥♥♥throwers that just throw their weapons at you and you can shoot them out of mid air like you were playing House of the Dead. Early on in the game the enemies just get a random chance to sprout a second head if you kill them. It doesn't make them harder, it just serves to make you use more ammo. The blind knife men are alright. They hear you if you run and they hear you if you shoot. However you have the magnum by that point so just being behind them means an instakill. The shield guys also would work great if you couldn't just kill all of them with one sniper shot. And I do mean all of them, they always line up and their shields don't block sniper shots so you can ge triple kills often. I haven't had a chance to see the regeneradors yet, but from what I understand they're just chainsaw guys that you need a rifle to kill instead of a shotgun.
The bosses also suck. The Big Boss Bass never even attacks you, you just take potshots at it with a harpoon until it dies. The Troll in the Dungeon bosses pretty much just require you to have ammo because you beat them by walking between their legs, shooting them, repeating until they fall over, QTE their spaghetti then repeat it 2 to 4 times depending. You fight them alot too, I think I fought 4 so far. The fake eye guy does nothing too. He walks at you like a common enemy until you shoot him in half, at which point he's still just a common enemy but now he's attached to one of the 6 beams on the ceiling. The Right Hand is pretty much just a question of "Have you looked at the cans before the fight?". You freeze him, you shoot him, you repeat it for 2 canisters, you win, there's no challenge because all his attacks are dodged with QTE. Even if you didn't know that, the guy is going all Adam Wesker on the screen so you know you can shoot him.
The scenery is boring. Have you played Return to Castle Wolfenstein? Then you've seen all this game has to offer.
The gameplay isn't great either. You could either run past all of the enemies because they're all designed so they can only hit you as long as you're trying to shoot at them, or you could use your shotgun, round them up in a nice pile, and fire one shot to kill all of them at once. Every other gun serves only as a replacement when the shotgun runs out of juice, except for the magnum, which is for killing bosses. Then once you did that, you have to just run around hitting the improperly colored decor items, because they're breakable if they're not the right color. Then you sell it all to the merchant. There's barely any real puzzles, although there are puzzles. There's a matching puzzle, where you have to match the shadows to the drawing, there's a sliding puzzle, where you have to slide a picture into the right position with 1 square missing, there's a weighting puzzle, where you have to remember you can tell Ashley to wait on the platform to open the door, there's a ton of shooting puzzles, where you have to figure out what to shoot in the environment to proceed. Basically, puzzles for 12 years olds or Legend of Zelda players. Sometimes they don't even bother with a puzzle, you just have a riddle and then you press 2 switches or you put 2 objects on a pedestal and that was the puzzle.
The characters suck. You have Leon, which looks like that kid you had in high school, that was bullied by absolutely everyone on account of the fact that he looks like Leon, you have Ashley, which you just spend the entire time you have her hoping she dies. She doesn't, as far as I can tell, she just gets captured over and over. But it's almost like she died when you're finally rid of her. You have Carlito. He's just Carlito from Dead Rising except he's not a terrorist, so he's way less cool. You have Ada. Not really though, she appears like 3 times to tease the fact that she's in the game. Saddler is boring. I mean really boring. Salazar is a weird midget. Except it doesn't really matter, he acts identically to a person that's tall, so there's no point to him being a midget. Actually he reminds me alot of Frieza. At the point I'm at they teased some Wesker looking dude with a beret. I'm gonna assume it's Wesker.
If I'm being honest, the game would have been better as a House of the Dead title. It works so much like a rail shooter. The enemies take a ton of shots to die, you can shoot projectiles out of the air, the bosses don't do much and you have to stand still to shoot.

I hav played D&D alot and it carries over so much that it feels almost nostalgic to play along with being a pretty good MMORPG experience. My only problem with the game is that it becomes very quickly impossible to play alone. I don't mean "I can't play it alone so its bad", I would be completely fine with playing with other players, the problem is that the player base is so small that if you are tying to even get 1 other person for a quest it takes over 10 minutes (this would be fine i guess if it was end game stuff, but I am only level 3 and can't find ayone). So you must have friends to play with you just so you can do the basic quests. Other tuff that does not translate well from the board D&D to the MMO D&D is stealth mechanics. If you do not start as a rogue (althouh i believe bards and rangers also get stealth stuff) then sneaking is almost impossible until the upper levels of the game. You obviously have the "Hide" and "Move Silently" skills from normal D&D and the game gives you a toggle ability called "Sneak" on every character, but it accomplishes nothing. There are missions you get alot early on that require you too sneak through a dungeon without killing more then 5 or 6 enemies (which is very little considering after you get out of th tutorial there are more then 5 or 6 enemie per room even in solo dungeons, although that isn't too bad), but the problem is that your are detected instantly upon entering a room while using "Sneak" if you only hae average "Hide" and "Move Silently", even by sleeping enemies. You can;t run past them and ignore them because all enemies are faster then the player, even with no armor on, so they will eventually surround you and you will be unable to move or jump over them and they will interrupt you when you try to use levers or open doors.
On top of all that, the game is very unforgiving of Free2Play players. Many events, stories, quests, items, skill trees, classes and races are all locked if you do not buy the VIP subscription membership or outright buy them individually, which locks you out of leveling easier or getting many better items. Even the forums run by the developr do not even allow you post a reply, let alone post a question on their forum unless you are atleast a VIP member, so if you have a problem, but aren;t subscribed then your problem doesn't exist.

I won't sugar-coat this.
This game is dated as all hell, and it shows mostly in the graphics department. Beyond this little bit, the game is VERY fun, can be incredibly challenging (scaling difficulty), and is in my top 5 favorite games of all time.
It's based around 3.5 rules in terms of character creation, but apart from only being able to multiclass into 3 total classes, the character levelling process is staggeringly varied, and the best part is that most builds will work to some degree, whether it be a niche setup, a full out min-maxed badass, or some fun little generalist you enjoy tinkering around with. You might not be clearing Epic Elite Reaper 5 difficulty quests on everything, but there's many settigns you can try, as well as solo/group support on every quest and dungeon.
If you've got some spare time and are looking for something MMO-based, but still want the ability to explore on your own, give this game a shot. I bought this game when it came out and level cap was about 5 or something. I have gone back to it several times over the years, as apart from DM'd NWN stuff it is for me one of the best dungeoneering adventure game experiences on a computer.
Caters to people who want to min max or casually enjoy some fun adventures without the need to devote hours to each session unless you want to. From the first little adventures to the epic stuff it is a class act with friends or solo. There have been many changes and power levels are pretty extreme as you'd expect in a game of this age, there are a lot of systems, craftings, grindy bits etc which can be intimidating but to be honest they aren't required unless after joining in on the ultimate challenge levels (I haven't), and you can find challenge in many other ways in the game - but more importantly you can find a boatload of fun adventures.
It is worth your time and your money - the adventure system used with its narration was a genius touch at the time and is more satisfying than the story modes a lot of later MMOs used - adventures are group instances so may not be your thing, but if you like small co-operative adventuring it was made at a time people were mad for MMOs and it shows, and it has developed a huge amount of content of differing types. The combat and adventure skills are great too. Not flashy, but just right and allowing for a huge diversity of character builds - both effective and erm, flavour. It doesn't handhold but there are websites which can answer just about any question you could ask so not an issue and people are helpful.

InFlux is a rather unique (from my experience) ambient exploration/puzzle game.  You play as a ball exploring an island and completing puzzles to unlock new paths to continue on your journey.  It seemed like a perfect fit for me and it is somewhat, but I can't help but feel like the game is a bit of a missed opportunity.
The island is a visually great place.  While the game doesn't have cutting edge AAA graphics, and it shows, the visual design is very pleasing.  The ball itself looks surprisingly good and the light generated from within adds a nice effect while you roll around.  The puzzles themselves take place in a sort of virtual world which have a nice clean design that is unfortunately marred by some of the most poorly done motion blur I have ever seen with no way that I have found to turn it off.
Past the visuals, the rest of the game really isn't up to par.  Rolling around the island can be a chore at times with lots of sudden changes in the ground surface that will stop you or send you awkwardly up into the air.  The puzzles are for the most part quite simple and can be completed with ease, but the levitation fans and vents you come across often don't bring you as high as they're supposed to, and the game's own hint of aiming up in order to go higher when boosting simply doesn't work.
The other main issue is performance.  While the game ran plenty fast for me, my framerate was amazingly low for the graphical quality and it makes me concerned about running this game on lower end hardware, even video cards that could manage newer AAA games just fine.  Coupled with this, the game doesn't seem to take advantage of the Unreal engine's dynamic data loading so the game stutters badly whenever it needs to load new data, often at strange places while you move around.  At one point the entire game froze for 2 seconds due to this.
So while I'd like to recommend this game, I really can't.  With additional and more complex puzzles, a better controlling ball, and some work in the engine department it could be a really great game.  Where it is now, I'm just disappointed that it isn't more.

Impromptu Games creates a fantastic puzzle mystery which keeps the gears in your brain continually grinding. InFlux offers a serene ambience with melodic music that produces a peaceful environment that is calming.
Influx is the story of a small ball and its adventure to complete mazes, explore an island, and collect orbs. You must collect orbs in each area in order to unlock the maze that allows you to progress to the next section. The island continually grows as you progress through this amazing campaign and the emptiness keeps you wondering at every turn. I completed the game in about 3-hours, which means it’s not a very long game. You could spend more time exploring the landscape although because of the poor mechanics of the protagonist exploration can seem rather annoying at times.
The rhythmic music and simplicity of Influx creates at times a very peaceful experience. The game offers a very vivid environment without any traces of even the simplest story. Without a story to follow Influx produces something most games lack, answers. I found myself continually wondering why there were empty houses on the Island, how the modern maze structures formed, why I was even solving the puzzles, and the list goes on and on.
The protagonist, a small ball, is able to roll and boost in order to accomplish tasks. There is no point where this character can jump, but by using boosts correctly you can launch yourself into various places. An interesting feature behind controlling the character is that you can boost while in mid air allowing you to change direction. Boosting also slows down time which allows you to gain a view of your environment while deciding how to act in a fast paced situation. Although there are time where controlling the character can be tricky the overall experience is relatively easy.
If you like puzzles, modern graphics, beautiful scenery, and melodious music then this would be the game for you. Despite there being more cons than pros I would recommend this game, but only if you can find it on sale for at least 75% off. InFlux is a short, but very riveting puzzle game. If you are a fan of puzzle games then this is the game for you.

Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This has to be one of my favourite visual novels. The storyline is well written and gets you gripped so quickly, the characters and their development throughout the story makes you love them all so quickly (even one of the antagonists, if you can call him that in the end).
Here's my pros and cons of the game and my overall thoughts and feelings:
- Storyline is well written, it's an intriguing story which develops well and clears everything up at the end of Waltz' route so there's no confusion. The recommended route order is on their store page (Rod, Karma, Rumpel, Fritz then Waltz). This order is best as you learn the entire story with no gaps by the end. Plus you can't do Fritz or Waltz' routes without doing 2 endings first.
- Character development was on point in my opinion. I loved Waltz the moment I first spotted him reading this story, I knew his route would be my favourite and it was, closely followed by Rod! You learn everything about the characters and even a considerate amount of their backstory to understand them better as a person, it makes you feel like you're part of the story developing with them.
- Art design, I personally think the design is beautiful although there are minimual background changes and they're repetitive but that didn't matter much to me as the story had me gripped more than the backgrounds. Each character is unique with their own style, they're beautifully drawn.
- Music. The music used in the visual novel really set the mood for what was happening or what was about to happen or simply for how your character is feeling. They set the moods perfectly for me.
- Routes, however only having 2 endings, good and bad. They don't fail on the emotional side of them, Rod's and Karma's bad endings had me crying like a baby but I enjoyed them nonetheless
- Lack of choices. There is only 3 choices per chapter (chapters 1-9) there is a chapter 10 however that's just the finale so it's pure reading until the credits.
- Routes, as it is a pro it is also a con in my opinion. Simply because the bad endings aren't very long, they're short and simple which kinda sucks. The longest bad ending is Waltz' but it's still very short in comparison to the good ending.
I loved the reading, it was fun and enjoyable. I honestly couldn't put it down, I was stuck at my laptop reading it non-stop until I'd finished everybody's endings. It was happy and sad, gets the waterworks going when the worst happens but it's still so amazing. It's free so why not give it a go? For a free read it sure will leave you pleased and if you're not, well you didn't waste cash, just your time so don't complain too much (it could be a lot worse).
If you do decide to give this a go then I do recommend following the route recommendation on the store page:
because it will fill in ALL the blanks by the end of Waltz' route.
Enjoy and happy reading!

I must admit, this is a tough one. The things I liked, I really liked. The things I didn't like, I really didn't. Would I recommend this VN? Absolutely. At its current price (free), you really couldn't ask for a better VN. Its sheer length alone, minimum twelve hours gameplay, is admirable for a free VN - and it isn't long, nor wordy, for the sake of extending the experience.
What did I like?
The protagonist is really likeable and relatable. Her situation is very much exaggerated, but I think there exists a little bit of Lucette in everyone. Even in the beginning, when her character is very one-dimensional, you instinctively know that there's more to her than meets the eye and you want to learn more. I think one of the things the writers did best with this our Cinderella is how she matures DIFFERENTLY on each route, based on the things she's experienced.
The love interests are varied and there's something for everyone here. Can't go into too much details without spoilers, but every route is unique.
The choices aren't obvious; it isn't painfully obvious what is the "right" choice. This VN actually offers a right choice indicator, which I did not use for my first playthrough, as I play a lot of VNs and figured I could easily trigger the good ending. I failed three consecutive times before turning it on. Telling your love interest what you think they want to hear isn't always the best choice; sounds like real life, doesn't it?
The amount of work put into the aesthetics of this game is praiseworthy. The game has a full soundtrack, which I believe was composed for the game, and at no point during the story does the music not step up to match it. Most of the songs are short instrumental clips, but they do the job properly. The art is plentiful: each character route has 10+ CGs, and there are 20+ common CGs. And, more importantly, the art is gorgeous--this goes for characters as well as backgrounds, which to me is often overlooked in VNs.
The different routes tie into one another very well. Just because you picked romantic interest A does not mean that B, C, D, and E disappear. They're all interwoven into one another's fairytale journeys. This is also very important to me, as I believe it makes the game much more believable and submersive.
What didn't I like?
This is the only free VN I know of to include a theme song and theme song animation. The animation is nothing to write home about (features very little original art not already seen in the VN), which is fine; but the song is HORRIBLE. The singer sounds like he was recovering from a loss of voice when he recorded it. It's scratchy, off-key, flat (in the musical sense). It would have been much better to omit it completely than to include it in the game.
The writing isn't very balanced. I feel like some routes got way more attention than others. There's one route in particular where the romantic interest is literally absent for half of the entire route. In certain routes, I could feel our Cinderella falling in love and I was falling in love too. In others, I had to go "What?" as dramatic changes just kind of occurred without rhyme or reason.
The writing is a bit too formulaic. Every route has a set number of chapters, with a set number of choices in each chapter. It was also a little bothersome that you needed to make no more than two wrong choices, out of 27-30 total, to trigger the good ending for each character. And even this seems to be somewhat random: I tested it with three different romantic interests, and made exactly three wrong choices in each of their routes. I triggered the bad ending in only two out of the three. So not too balanced.
Certain characters are far too cliche. I understand that fairytales are a fundamental theme to this VN, and thus it makes sense for a love interest's route to align with their particular fairytale. However, just because a person is put under a curse that relates to a fairytale does not mean that person automatically transforms into the one-dimensional character from said fairtyale. Also, I found that only certain curses required the one cursed to reflect and grow as a person (for example, there's one curse that's broken by finding an object). It's impossible to discuss this in detail without irreparably spoiling the story, and probably some people will disagree with me on this point. That's fine. Play for yourself, and see.
Asymmetrical character development - relates to my last point as well. Certain characters have their past shown in great detail whereas others barely get a one sentence mention. Certain characters are flawed, but are redeemed or at least are given an explanation, and are given a chance at sympathy. But other characters (the most important being the primary antagonist) stay the same the entire time, and it really destroyed the story for me as I completed more routes and got a better understanding of the overall world and situation. It's not up to the writers how their audience feels about the characters, but every character should at least have a chance at making the audience feel something. And especially when someone as important as the primary antagonist is sidelined, it sucks. In fact, most of the antagonists suffer from this. In a game that is literally about fairytales misleading and corrupting people into thinking good is only good and bad is only bad, it's horrible to not give the antagonists a fair representation. It undermines the whole story.
Conclusion:
I did thoroughly enjoy Cinderella Phenomenon, and I will be remembering it for a long time to come. It's definitely one of the best VNs I've ever experienced - in certain areas. However, I do feel that this game has certain flaws that cannot be ignored, and that keep it from being as good as it could be. I would love to see more from the developers, and I hope their next project is more well rounded.

I enjoy Mordheim a lot, and heartily recommend it, but ...
it is not a game that everyone will have fun playing.
In Mordheim,
You can plan and prepare, carefully choose skills and equipment, even pick and choose which battles you fight ... but you *will* at some point suffer a crushing defeat despite everything.
Just as you will at some point, in an inspired moment of tactical brilliance, shatter a vastly superior warband and win plunder and victory that is all the sweeter for how difficult it was to achieve.
Sometimes, you'll collect a huge haul of loot, and crush the enemy warband with barely a scratch on your own soldiers.
And sometimes, the enemy will do that to you.
Mordeheim is unforgiving of mistakes, and requires careful consideration of risks.
The game doesn't fudge anything to help you win.
Difficulty indicators start at "Normal", and swiftly escalate through "Hard" to "Brutal".
There are no do-overs.
Nothing is guaranteed.
The cruel vagaries of statistics reign unimpeded, and favour neither you nor your enemies.
Losses of men and materiel are inevitable.
Soldiers that fall in battle are "out of action", and with treatment can often recover to near peak condition. Permanent injuries can and do occur, but sometimes your soldiers can draw lessons from their defeat, emerging stronger from their brush with death.
And there's always the need to salvage more wyrdstone, to satisfy your sponsor and keep your warband supplied.
Get too greedy, and your warband might get caught out of position, unable to support each other.
Get too cautious, and you might struggle to keep your soldiers paid and equipped.
Gauge the risks well, combining preparedness with planning and a few smart gambles ... well, you might just have a fighting chance.
Welcome to Mordheim.

I've played allot of MMOs, and this is my favorite by far [I even like it more than my first MMO, which I played for 4+ years and still love]. Not because it's D&D; I don't care about that. DDO has the most complex, demanding, and rewarding game mechanics I've seen - by far. The dungeons are carefully crafted to [on the hardest settings, which you can control completely when subscribed] require intense strategizing: if you screw around for a second, if you don't think your way through every moment, you will fail. But, when you learn the system, and set the difficulty correctly, it's also completely fair.
The dungeons provide an extremely wide variety of carefully crafted strategic situations, and regularly surprises you as everything suddenly spirals out of control due to intentionally placed surprises - this, however, becomes a nonexistent factor once you've played through them once [changing trap locations aside]. The intitial dungeons [levels 1-3] aren't a great example of my claims, especially on F2P, since you won't be able to increase the difficulty to the hardest settings without first playing through the easier [normal, hard, elite] settings. But, give it time. The game is also stellar for team-play: every class has dramatic strengths over other classes, which when combined, make your team that much more powerful.
Though I personally consider this game to be, mechanically, decades ahead of all other titles, it has many flaws.
Though the mechanics are extremely complex and fair [both the character building system, and combat], the game nevertheless has a wide variety of minor yet annoying bugs. Game-breaking? No; if we exclude the atrocious hireling AI. I don't recall ever being deep in a brutal dungeon and losing because of a bug. Nevertheless, you'll just have to get used to issues which have always existed on this old engine. Nothing to be done about it.
And while the mechanics function correctly, and are precisely fair, there are a wide variety of issues when it comes to understanding them: there is very little explanation of how many of the mechanics work [even ddowiki, which is your best source of information, has blindspots], so you'll be spending allot of time researching from multiple sources. For example: If you want to multiclass, which opens an extremely wide variety of game-play styles, there's very little information ingame about it - even simply sticking to one class can be a very complicated process. And, ontop of all that, many tooltips for spells and skills are incomplete or blatantly inaccurate.
Another issue to keep in mind is that the game can be a serious money-pit, even when carrying a subscription: there are numerous convenience upgrades which can only be bought with real money. Though many of those upgrades can be earned ingame through simply playing, are available as long as subscribed, and a subscription includes currency which can be spent toward those upgrades.
All that aside, when deciding whether or not to commit, keep in mind that I have understated the complexity of the system, and that you will have to learn a great deal if you want to play on the level of difficulty which I love. Also that, to be completely blunt, you will need to play with at least 2 total people - ideally 3 or more, if you want to get the most out of the game. Though you can simply turn down the dungeon difficulty, and use "hirelings" for most situations while soloing, there are nevertheless many which demand specific classes and multiple people. There are plenty of player groups [guilds] to join.
In total: If you're the hardest-core strategist, if you love extremely tight team-play, this is the absolute best option for you - though remember that you need to carefully calibrate the difficulty settings, and your second playthrough of a dungeon will remove the surprises. Still, it's a flawed masterpeice; you will have to take the bad with the good.
To whomever was in charge of building this game's mechanics: I consider myself in your debt, for the joys you've granted me. I appreciate and understand the intense mastery you possess and hope you are given your due.

Background: D&D 3.5 DM and player of Pathfinder & 5E
Combat Mechanics: Outdated, but True to Form for Dungeons and Dragons. Throw Dice at it...more dice and eventually you may find a different result.   This game like the Tabletop version is very Team oriented and much like the Tabletop experience. At Low Levels Non-Casters thrive, but at High Levels It is those with a Casting Ability that really start to take the Lead.  Some will find this system of standing in a room and holding down Left Mouse Click to kill something...Tedious...Boring...Overdramatized when it should be contact with enemy produces some kind of visible reaction from the enemy whether I miss or not...I have friends who have told me the exact thing. This Game and its mechanics are not for everyone.
The Pay to Play Thing: Yes some classes are Paywalled but everything can be obtained through lots of hard work. Turbine points are given for in game progress but can also be purchased. Quest Packs are purchased and unlocked in the same way. So is the Druid Class. If you have a subscription you get all the Quest Packs and 500 Turbine Points a Month.
The Pay to Win Thing: Now there is an opposite side to these Turbine Points. Not only do they unlock classes and quest packs, but they also allow you to buy ingame Convenience Items that make most of the game; Stupid Easy. Like Resurrection Cakes that let you Free Rez inside of a Module, or Items to allow you to Craft Epic Pieces, Unlimited Lockpicks, you name it.  While This is not cheating it does fulfill a model to create revenue because at the heart of any MMO is a Business and Businesses need money. I do not fault their decision to offer items like this, but it irks me sometimes at their offerings.
Social Mechanics: Given the age of the game and that fact the Devs are still pushing out content (Turbine and WB are somehow still producing stuff) and the mostly active community. The Social side of DDO still has enough active guilds and Power Runners who've literally memorized the maps and quest sequences that you are bound to find a group if you look hard enough.
Final Thoughts: So this game was made a while ago. By today's standards it is like World of Warcraft in that it should be scrapped and a completely new, graphically intense game of the same name needs to replace it, like yesterday.
That being said I am a diehard D&D player and DM so part of me knows the frustration of trying to Disable a Trap and then roll a 1 and get completely obliterated. The other part of me knows...this type of gameplay is not a positive example for a RealTime Game like DDO.
100% Watch Low and High Level Gameplay before you Get a Membership. Remember this game can be 100% Free 2 Play and you will evenentually have everything a VIP has Except for a few character Slots.

I just started this game, and I already know I am going to enjoy it. The "outside world" is relaxing, with very serene scenery and ambient music. The "cube world" has a puzzle game feeling. Together, they create a fantastic blend.

Overall, this game is a very atmospheric experience. Between the hybrid of natural and abstract environments, you will find an immersive world full of puzzles waiting to be solved.
Controls for the most part were very responsive. (I used an Xbox360 controller which the game immediately recognizes and alters the menu screen accordingly.) Controlling this sphere reminded me of the Morph Ball from the Metroid series assuming Samus was stripped down to just pulsing magnetic fields and using speed boosts to get around.
The game's puzzles offer a decent challenge on what you are supposed to do. I think only two puzzles glitched on me, but in both cases, the puzzles did eventually work leaving me wondering what I did differently.
In terms of game time, this game is on the short side. I spent about 3 hours give or take on my blind run of the game. To be fair, I can think of one other abstract game that's probably even shorter and still gets lots of praise anyway: Portal.
My one real complaint is the apparent compatiblity issue with Windows 7 32-bit OS in which the game apparently runs out of memory and crashes. Thankfully, the forums offer a workaround which certainly made the game palyable for me.

Got this on the week long deal, and for what I paid, I'm pretty impressed.  Makes good use of the Unreal engine, the environments are well built and with the settings turned up it's a good looking game. The natural hub environments contrast nicely with the more artifical puzzle aspects.  Gameplay wise, this doesn't provide any real additions or major change-ups to the puzzle-platformer genre, but executes it nicely in a comfortable and relaxing style.  Usually the goal is to move color-coded spheres into the matching recepticles using a fairly diverse set of standard puzzling mechanics, including push/pull, lifts, buttons, and level rotators. Gamepad support worked flawlessly for all aspects (I used an Xbox controller, you'll want something with two joysticks), and I didn't encounter any bugs.  It was a bit annoying that sections of the hub environments would load during roaming, and this did create some lag, but the load times were fast so they didn't last long, and didn't occur too often.  Overall a good game for the price.

This is a very mellow game, great chill soundtrack, and puzzles which can be at once simple and frustrating.  The environment is lush and welcoming, and control of the sphere feels natural.  However, I felt that the game seemed short.  There is a fine line between having too few puzzles and too many, and the size of each of the levels could have crossed that line with another set of 3-5 cubes, so I understand why the developers made this decision.  As with numerous other exploration/puzzlers, plot can be a secondary concern, but the motivations and background of the events in this game were murky at best.  A sphere falls from the sky and powers up the machines for the next part of its journey.  Why were the machines here?  Who built them?  Sadly, one is left with more questions than answers, but it may be left to the player to ponder and draw one's own conclusions.
I will say too that I initially had some issues with it stuttering fairly heavily when loading new areas of larger maps, even after turning my settings all the way down.  I was ulitmately able to solve that by counterintuitively turning the settings up or on, but is more likely an issue with the Unreal Engine.
All in all, though, this game is definitely worth a few hours of your time if you enjoy puzzle-type games.

I could not get over how annoying, spoiled, and mean Lucettex is. It was cool to see her grow, but I feel like there was so much time in the beginning showing how cruel of a person she is that made me NOT want to help break her curse. That in itself didn't really encourage me to continue playing the game, but I did because a friend recommended the game to me.
I played through Rod's route, because Rumpel is an annoying womanizer, and Karma ... I wanted to play through Karma's route, but I disliked their art. We're introduced to Karma as a Beautiful Woman, but I thought Karma was easily the least attractive character. So I played Rod's route, because honestly he was cute. I couldn't really believe that I could win Rod over, and I sort of didn't even want to. Rod comes in saying that life is better without Lucettex. Of course it is! She's a binch! Rod's family deserves to be happy without her. I didn't want to disrupt that, but I wanted to get to Waltz' route, so I went ahead with Rod's story.
Rod's route didn't make sense to me. There were some choices that seemed pretty similar, but you only got points if you chose one of them. Sometimes the choices were inconsistent: Sometimes you don't get points if you choose the option that's more confrontational; sometimes you DO get points if you choose the option that's more confrontational. I found myself saying, "What!" when I chose the nicer option and didn't get a diamond; then loaded a save and chose the more confrontational option and then Rod would blush and the diamond would appear. You started off not liking when I was more brash; and now you like it? What do you want from me!
[SPOILERS] I was very dissatisfied with Rod's ending. I thought it was going to end with Delora giving Lucettex an option to be a princess again but she wouldn't be able to be with Rod; or stay as a maid and be with Rod. And the best ending is to choose to stay a maid because you realize that Rod's family is happier without you, and now you get to be with Rod. But?? Instead you become a princess and sneak out with Rod every once in a while to be with him? And Rod's sister and mom are OK with that? That doesn't make sense. Also that's not an ending to a story; that's a beginning of another one. They can't possibly be satisfied with living a life in secret... again! Also there was no resolution to Lucettex's relationship with her father or the commonfolk. And what happened to Fritz? He turns into Varg, doesn't he? But what happens to Varg? The last we saw of Mythros was that he's stuck in an ice sculpture, but ... what happens after that?? Did I miss some text somewhere? If so, then that's totally my bad. But if those loose ends were never tied up, then... [END SPOILERS]
After I was done with Rod's route, I said OK, now I can finally do Waltz' route. He's cute. And nice. So I started going through it again. The new Fast Forward feature I unlocked brought me into a debug mode of the game or something? A weird screen where I had the option to ignore the problem and continue forward... so I did? And instead of hitting Fast Forward this time, I just sped up the text. And that's when I realized just how much text there was just setting up the story and grounding me into hating Lucettex. I don't think there should be
exposition. I also realized that Lucettex is a janitor for such a short period of time if you chose Rod's route? So short a time that it really didn't even need to be included in Rod's route.
Then I realized that I needed to complete SOMEONE ELSE'S ROUTE BEFORE UNLOCKING WALTZ' ROUTE! At this point, I gave up. I don't really want to look at Karma, and I think I'd be too annoyed at Rumpel's route. And I'd just be annoyed at Lucettex the entire time. All of this is not worth playing Waltz' route, which might be just as disappointing as Rod's route anyway.
OK. So that's all the narrative stuff.
In terms of art, I like the cutscene art, but the in-game art during dialogue looks flat and is considrerably not as pretty as the cutscene art.
The music is good! I found it stuck in my head after hours of playing the game. I did catch it stop its loop once, though, if you let the game sit there for a bit, so I know it's not an
loop. I'm not a programmer so I don't know how hard it is to loop audio, but the programmer might want to change that.
I do want to end this with saying that it is cool that pretty much one person made the whole game, the art, music, story, etc. That's very respectable!

Rochard is a physics puzzle platformer, which came out a few years ago, long before the current glut of physics puzzle platformers. In retrospect, Rochard is obviously an older game with many design flaws that were the result of not being able to learn the mistakes of other titles in the genre.
First of all, the game's positives: Rochard has fairly good graphics and 90s cartoon art style. The protagonist is not a faceless muscular commando, but a working stiff with a potbelly and some personality. The supporting characters are similarly varied, and the entire cast has decent voice acting. The writing is nothing special, but the style of story does fit well with the cartoony art aesthetic, though any plot twists are obvious from a mile away.
The problems with the game are that it focuses on both combat and puzzle solving, but does neither very well. Combat is done using a combination Gravity Gun/Laser Blaster against mercernaries or bots. Enemy AI is simplistic, reminiscent of very early console platformers. There's very little challenge in that area, so you would expect something more from the puzzle department. Unfortunately, that is not the case, as puzzles are equally simplistic, never reaching the level of mind-bending challenge that a dedicated puzzle game like Portal or The Swapper provides. So what's left? Nothing. No high score mechanic, and no exploration. There's a barebones badly executed attempt at Metroidvania elements for collectables which forces some backtracking, but that's not at all enjoyable due to lack of fast movement abilities, and lack of enjoyable combat.
All in all, Rochard is simply less than the sum of its parts.

Take this yes with a _massive_ grain of salt. I can't simply bring myself to say "No, do not buy this game", because to be honest I enjoyed it. However, there are a lot of things holding the game back.
First off, let's talk about what I enjoyed about the game. The premise of the game is to complete a bunch of puzzles by activating a certain box, which is by far and away the most inadequate explanation for a game, but it's the most I can say without spoiling the game. This is a very interesting concept, and I did have fun solving the puzzles. It's very important for a puzzle game to leave you thinking "Boy, I solved that puzzle! I'm pretty smart!" On another topic, this is a very "artsy" game, and the atmosphere has to be (and is definitely) executed beautifully. The "story" had me wondering what on Earth, or where on Earth, I was. The minimalism put me in the position of having to wonder exactly what I was doing, and it definitely had me guessing, in a sort of existentialist way. This all comes together to make a nice game, and I believe that lots can be done with this premise!
Now let's talk about all the glaring downsides of the game. This game is absolutely gorgeous. I think. I wouldn't know, I played on low graphics settings and at times I found myself rolling up a hill whose texture looked like I was rolling up / through a set of stairs. Then again, I'm playing on a Dell i5 laptop, so I wasn't expecting much from the graphics department. The low settings may also explain why whenever I plunged into water that kills me, I see myself falling below the game world for half a second. Or is that the physics engine? One of those two departments has to fix that.
Speaking of game physics, this is to me personally the most infuriating flaw of the game. More than once I have found myself stuck _inside_ the ground. Other times, when I break the sound barrier, I fly _into_ rock formations. No, they don't shatter, I just seem to become one with the rock. That's easily escapable though since rocks are actually made of air in the middle. There's also this one part where there is a current that drags your ball to the edge... of a pool... for some reason... and if you don't act quickly you're going to be stuck there for the next few minutes trying to boost your way out. Finally, there are parts where you will encounter the infamous Invisible Wall. Even though the game is trying to take you in one particular direction, it does it in such a way that, if you didn't have the Invisible Wall blocking your way, you can hop onto the top of the edge of the area that you're currently in. I was incredibly let down when I saw this. If I was able to roll on the edge of the arena, that would have given me the feeling that I'm "beating the system", and mastering how to control the game.
On a personal note, I was disappointed with the lack of difficulty of the game outside of the puzzles. To access each puzzle, you had to wander around a world collecting X-thingies to activate Y-thingies, and open the puzzle. It turns out that you only need to collect three X's to unlock each Y. This killed my ambition to go hunting for X's, or spending effort to catch the X's that are hard to reach, essentially eliminating a possibly very interesting game mechanic.
This last oversight is so big to me that I have to count it as a flaw. No level editor? Really??? The level designs were really impressive in the game, and here they are not taking advantage of the potential creativity of their audience. A level editor would practically have the players make the game themselves, minus the artsy portions.
So why do I say "yes" when the list of downsides is more than thrice as long as the list of upsides? I feel that there is so much potential with this game, and I am willing to bet that Impromptu Games is not done with it yet. It may not be the longest game (though I feel that for the given premise the story length is perfect), and it may look incomplete, but I firmly believe that the Devs have more planned for InFlux. Perhaps a game patch, a level editor, or multiple story arcs with each journey eliciting different emotions. Whatever it is, I'm excited for the future of this game.
As for the price, I'm very confident that the Devs can make this game easily worth $10 and then some. But for now... it'd be best to wait for the Steam sale.

As a fan of marble games like Marble Blast Ultra, and Switchball, it's an interesting blend of the two. It's broken apart into six different hub worlds, each containing 3 puzzle areas. These hub worlds are wide open natural vistas, whereas the puzzle rooms look a lot like those Marble Blast Ultra. Most of the puzzles deal with world rotation, and getting other marbles to designated areas.
The movement feels pretty different than Marble Blast Ultra, mostly in that you carry much more momentum, and you don't have a button to jump. They introduce a charge boost though, that accomplishes similar goals. It has a small story being told organically through the world, and it's just a really satisfying time. I'd highly recommend it to dudes that dug Marble Blast Ultra/Switchball/Spectraball.

So, this game really is loads of awesomeness. It has an incredibly calm atmosphere, lush graphics, ridiculously smooth gameplay, and aims to bring a new light to problem-solving and virtual puzzles. Its originality in terms of both puzzles and overall gameplay really gives off a great vibe, and in my opinion, it feels like the developers really knew what they wanted from this game. They executed this indie game extremely well and it really shows.
I have not had the chance to play this game with a controller, but for a mouse and keyboard(which feels more natural to me than a controller), the controls are perfect. The developers really struck a beautiful balance in terms of how you control the gameplay, and subsequently, how the gameplay controls you. They left the complexity and problem-solving to the puzzles of the game and made the controls simplistic. Perfection.
On the topic of the puzzles, they also match this game perfectly. As you can see from the teaser video clips, the puzzles take on this abstract form of obstacles within multi-dimensional cubes of glass and steel. Without spoiling anything(or too much anyways), at first glance you would figure this combination to clash with the original atmosphere of the game, but it's quite the opposite; the transfers are done so seamlessly that the player remains undisturbed, and continues to flow through the calm, dream-like gameplay that is InFlux. Most of the puzzles are simple, a couple of them frustrating, but not so frustrating that you want to turn the game off or bang your head against a wall. They always keep you coming back.
At the end of the day, this is a fantastic game with an amazing atmosphere that keeps you coming back for more; and honestly, that is the kind of result you want from a problem-solving game of this caliber. If you are on the edge about whether to buy this game or not, just go ahead and buy it and thank me later. For its miniscule price, you get an experience easily worth ten times the amount(was on-sale for $2.99 when I wrote this review).

To make matters worse, the layout of the singleplayer content is obtuse at best and the featured map is less than useful.
The focus of the game is undoubtedly multiplayer where it features matched 1v1s and 3v3s. There's not much here though. The multiplayer offering is really inferior to other fighting games or just about any multiplayer game. This is the crucial flaw of Absolver. If you want to play a slick fighting game, there are so many superior offerings. Do yourself a favour and buy one of those instead.

Introduction;
I have spent many hours on this game over the years, and even though it may feel a little antiquated now, it is still one of the best RPG's that I have played in a very long time.
It feels like a true RPG, and a true adaptation of the AD&D Rule Set that true AD&D gamers are familiar with.  There is none of that level scaling crap in this game which has become a trend recently.  It is all leveled content.
This is one of the few games which I install every time I have to do a re-install of Steam for what ever reason.
The Game;
The world is huge, to be frank.  AD&D has access to areas of the Forgotten Realms region that, I assume most of us are familiar with, as well as the main city hub of Stormreach, and several huge explorer regions.  For instance, when you get into the Forgotten Realms Campeign setting, you gain access to Evening Star, and eventually gain the keys to the city. If you don't want to be there, then you can go to Stormreach, the Kings Forest, or even the Underdark.
The game has all of the usual enemies which you would associate with the AD&D world, including Dryads, Dire Bears, Kobolds, Druids, and Drow.  The enemies are plentiful, the loot is plentiful, and the traps which can be powerful enough to kill you in one shot, are also plentiful.
It is a true AD&D game in every way.
The amount of loot that can be acquired from various quests is so expansive that I cannot list them all here, but there is everything from +5 Daggers, to +6 Docents, to +1 Kite Shields, to specific, named loot.  It turly is immense, and the amount of ways to get that loot is even more expansive especially considering the depth of the crafting system, and the wilderness areas which contain specific bosses who can be farmed for fat lewt.  On top of that, farmable item sets of great power can be farmed in Evening Star, simply by farming event tokens in the Kings Forest.  That only takes a few nights to get, and you are essentially fully geared.
The quests are plentiful for both groups, raids and solo players.  The main issue with that however, is that the servers can feel a little empty at the minute, but to help tackle this issue, the game does still receive constant new updates.  Later this year for instance (2017), the development team will be releasing the Ravenloft expansion pack.  Besides which, you can cut the need to do low level content out by purchasing the Shadowfell Conspiracy Expansion Pack and start from level 15 with a heroic class.  Furthermore, a lot of the content does not require a group, so there is nothing stopping you from playing solo, scene as every class has access to certain spell casting and healing items.  With all that said, the game is ageing well, for a 10 year old game.
The highlight of this entire game however, is the level of character customisation.  Every character can be specifically customised in a variety of ways, whether it is through the character generation screen when you first start, or through the epic destiny system, or the tallents trees.
For instance I play a mage, that might sound boring at first, until you realize that I play a 20th level Eldritch Knight / Pale Master with 7 Epic Levels in Draconic Lineage.  That makes him one bad♥♥♥♥♥character in both melee and for spell casting.  The range of spells available are not only equal to anything in the original 2nd edition AD&D rule set, but also exceede it, because of these epic level spells and the abilities granted through the tallent trees.
Updates;
As I mentioned earlier, the game is constantly updated, and always in the right direction.  New raids, new quests, new player races are added, and a whole plethora of other things are usually added.  THERE IS NO NERFING which is important to mention, because the trend these days seems to be that if something is deemed too powerful, nerf it and that is usually your update in other games.  That doesn't happen in AD&D DDO.  Instead, we get new raids, new quests, new loot, new hero classes and races, in otherwords, content that we actually ask for.  It is all done right.
I would highly recommend buying both of the available expansions packs however.  In particular, The Shadowfell Conspiracy DLC is well worth purchasing on F2P accounts.  If you plan to do some F2P gaming on DDO, especially as a solo player, without having to pay a subscription fee, buy that DLC pack before you do anything else.  I will tell you why below.
These are probably my two main gripes against the game.
I don't like the fact that you may feel like you are forced to buy content packs to get the most out of the game if you don't want to subscribe to DDO, or want to treat DDO as entirely F2P, but you can work around this by buying the expansion packs instead.
The only times that locked content may be a pain though, is if you are farming for specific loot, and that loot is only available in a certain part of the game world that you do not have access too, or when you may want to do a quest with your friends, and you don't have access to those quests because you haven't unlocked them.
My other gripe is that I really don't like how Spell Points are regenerated via Rest Shrines.  Rest Shrines can be used every 5 minutes, 15 minutes, or once only, depending on the difficulty setting.  This isn't a problem really for classes who don't use spells, but since many of us do, SP management becomes critical, and that is also the chief reason why I chose to play an Eldritch Knight.  Even when my toon runs out of SP, he can still go melee.  The SP elixers should also drop much, much more frequently in game, and I don't think that they should be listed on the store in all honesty.  Selling Spell Point recovery pots may be seen P2W, and may put potential new players off DDO.
Subbing Vs F2P.
don't bother subbing over a long period of time, it is not worth it.  The only real benefit to subbing is the "free" DDO store points that you get each month.
There is a better, cheaper way to unlock most of the games content on F2P accounts, wihtout ever having to pay a subscription fee;
1:  Buy the Shadowfell Conspiracy Pack.  This will unlock a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of content and allow you to start from level 15, as a heroic class character.  This will also make a lot of the lower level, locked content worthless.
2:  Buy the Menace of the Underdark Pack.  This will unlock the Forgotten Realms setting as well as the Drow Race and Druid Class, and give you a permanent xp boost for your account.
3:  Use any store points given to buy the "Hall of Heroes pass" so that you can transfer between Eberon and Eveningstar without having to fight Lolth on a new toon each time.
Subbing for a year would cost well over $100.  Buying both of the expansion packs and the Hall of Heroes Pass costs around $50 and you will unlock a lot of the base games content.  you then have access to that content forever, without ever having to pay a subscription fee and can start a new toon at level 15, with access to those campeign settings instantly, forever.

If you're completely mad for bullet hell-style games then this game is definitely for you, so stop reading here, but as a big casual myself i really didn't enjoy it. The shooting generally feels really light and unsatisfying with anemic sound effects, and the three extra ships you can buy are less fun to use than the one you start with. Moreover, the game as of Jan. 2016 is bugged, with all enemy projectiles displayed as grey, which makes the game needlessly hard-- you can fix it by opting in to the Beta version, but who knows what you're missing out on there.
The music and the setting are unique and carefully done, but TOO carefully done i think-- i'd rather play a game where the game makers' time was all spent on rock-solid mechanics at the expense of the story than the opposite, and this is the opposite in my own opinion. You really need to have your ducks in a row to spend that much time developing the stylistic elements, but it's not a good enough shooter to get away with it so the whole martian-colonialism thing just ends up being distracting/pointless as you die for the 3000th time to a bullet you couldn't see coming (for a shooter that gets it right see 'Sine Mora', which gets away with its elaborate narrative elements in spades, though admittedly the Arcade mode is pointlessly difficult and rage-inducing).
So yeah, as a non-superfan of the genre, i really didn't enjoy this-- it's too bugged and hard and viscerally lacking. I'd dock it further points for having an Infuriatingly Annoying Indoor Level, but then pretty much every shooter has one of those...

The following review will focus first on Civilization IV as a whole, then on the expansion "Beyond the Sword".
Civilization IV was the first game of the Civ-series to go 3d, for better or for worse. The graphics are in fact atrocious compared to the newer Civ 5, and even Civ 3, with its 2d isometric graphics and heavy reliance on shades of brown. But as any fan of the TBS-genre will tell you; graphics are secondary to everything else.
You may ask yourself "why invest in Civ 4 when Civ 5 and BE is out?". Well, apart from having better graphics and adding
certain features, there aren't many differences between these games. Some of the most important differences (or improvements as some will call them) are the limitation on movement and stacking in Civ 5. One may argue that limitations compared to older versions are negative, but the point would be moot when faced with "the stack of doom". So yes, at first glance, the newer games are better. There are however saving graces for Civ 4: Plenty of advanced and interesting mods, as well as a (more) stable multiplayer, the latter of which is laughable in Civ 5.
BtS is arguably the largest expansion to any of the Civ games, and a must-have if you want to use mods, as most of them now require it to work. It adds quite a few new features, including, but not limited to:
In conclusion: If you like the civilization-games, but don't care about graphics, or don't like the limitations of Civ V, or like Civ but want it to be more advanced with certain mods, or just want to be able to play multiplayer for more than 10 minutes without having problems; i would suggest grabbing Civ IV with BTS as soon as possible.

I got this game very early into development. I've stacked quite a few hours into multiplayer with my brother and friends and have watched it grow. The developer has regularly come out with updates and it has grown quite quickly into a very good game that I have thoroughly enjoyed. This is early access done right. It is now climbing towards 1.0 and I felt the need to give a review.
This game is brutal and unforgiving in single player, while multiplayer allows for the possibility of revival. It is very roguelike at its core. Death is the end, and it comes easy. However, I find the difficulty to not be very frustrating. After I die, which is practically inevitable, I am eager to begin again and see how far I can go.
Bosses are difficult, until you start to figure out their patterns. Some bosses will remain difficult, even if you do know the patterns. Difficulty also very much depends on the luck of the draw when it comes to loot, but that is half the fun! Especially when you are rushing to get it before your friends.
The developer intends on working some balance issues out in the future, which I believe is needed. The wildling is horribly underpowered right now, while the rogue is perhaps the easiest way to progress through the levels.
Overall, this game is wonderful. It has come a long way from when I first bought it. I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a difficult game.

I have just finished the initial single-ish player content of the game and I... I really don't know what to say... I'm not really disappointed but I sure am feeling sorry for this game for what it could have been. I'm gonna start with the
Let's see.
First off you should know that the game carries the overall feel of a regular "souls" game; non talkative npcs, difficult combat, feeling lost, exploring and getting gear to get back to a zone you couldn't clear before etc. etc. What this game falls short in term of this aspect is that it lacks a great deal of athmosphere. There are 4 zones you traverse and you fight same looking bosses with brief and shallow dialogues. You cross paths with other players from time to time, who can help you out or be a jerk.
Oh, and you can use the simple interface to ask for co-op, duel or stop a fight, other than that its just emotes.

This game promises quality melee combat and boy oh boy does it deliver. There are three schools you can pick in the game, each with different special abilities and starting move sets. For example the one I played (forsaken) had this special timing block that nullifies all the damage of an attack and stuns my opponent briefly. There is actually another school -they say that there are other school
but there is only one additional school. Which is -you know it- drunken brawling. Their starting move sets are different as well.
So the interesting part; the way you learn moves in this game is quite interesting. You learn moves by blocking them or using your special ability on them to learn even faster, a well timed dodge works too. You get points as you repeatedly block or dodge incoming attacks and upon defeating that certain enemy you get solid progress on that move, if you run or the enemy defeats you, no points for you.
There are two shard-ability slots in the game which you can fill with special powers you get from defeated boss or mini bosses. Namely, there is healing, raised defence, shockwave, stun-like abilities. They didn't feel all that relevant, except for the healing power. I used that a lot in pve.
The third shard ability is a weapon draw. Weapons have a different set of moves. They can be dropped and used against you or you can sheathe them back, there is a time limit to it. Sometimes there are some weapons on the ground as well but those are not all that important since they are rare and break way too easy.
The basics of combat is crazy good in this game. There are four stances in the game and four different starting moves that chain with each other respectively. The slots increase up to four as you level up. Each attack has a starting stance and an ending stance. There are extra four "alternative" attacks that take up only one slot but they increase your combo potential. Say for instance I create a string of mill punch which starts on e stance and ends in q stance that chains to a reverse elbow which starts in q and ends in e so the third move is another punch that chains with the others, I think you get the idea. You can change your attack stance anytime, other than that the "alternative" attack slot means that you can change a chain you got going into another string vice versa. This I think is the paramount feature of the game. The fluidity and enjoyment of combat is really good.
Although picking fast chains and being crazy aggressive seems to work fine in pvp most of the time.
The moves differ in each other as well, some are fast, slow, some have reach, some have high guard damage. Some attacks are overhead which don't get hit by low attacks if they both are executed at the same time or close enough. A jumping kick beats a sweep. Or there are moves that bypass vertical attacks in the same manner.
Although picking fast chains and being crazy offensive seems to work fine in pvp most of the time.
When you kill the final boss you become an absolver and pushed into the pvp section of the game which is 1v1 duels and 3v3 capture-hold point matches. You get shards, buy gear, profit. And you can try higher rank bosses after you level up your pvp stats.
All in all I have to say this is an idea executed pretty decently but leave you saying if they had more budget and time what it all could've been. I give it a 7/10,

THis was a game unlike any other in my collection, something chill and relaxing that I could just throw on at the end of a long day and kind of fade away into.  The puzzle engages just enough grey matter to be enjoyable, but are spread out enough that just exploring the world and finding neat landscapes in between breaks up the experience into a joyful take-at-your-own-pace eerie wonder.  It's so rare to find a game which favours and rewards self-exploration for those of us who just like to meander through every nook and corner for idle amusement.

What baffles me is how developers who clearly had the time and resources to make such beautiful visuals and ambience managed to screw EVERYTHING ELSE up this horribly.
Multiple times I had to replay portions because the game is, as much as I hate to say it, too open world. It's way too easy to get stuck somewhere you shouldn't be and have to restart. And surprise, the game saves itself very rarely and there's no way to manually save it. It's utterly ridiculous. Several of the settings options also seemed to flat out not work.
The game has a lot of those little flaws where they're not big enough to cite for a review, but they pile up. A few examples: Before each puzzle you need to collect an unknown number of arbitrary glowing blue dots lying around the area.
What's the point of this? It's not like getting them is a challenge or something. They're just lying there. Another example, they give you the ability to gain up speed and "boost" forward, yet the collision is so accurate that the bumps in the ground will usually send you hurtling in some odd direction if you ever dare boost across the ground. Yet another "hyper-specific" example: There's a point in the game where you activate a thermal vent that serves as a natural cannon. It's right next to you, you get in it, go flying, aaaaaaand- slam into a stalactite. Upon further examination, when you activate the first vent it also activates a second vent slightly back from where you activate them. You have to enter that one. What? Why is the giant vent that EXPLODES right next to me not the correct path? Why do I have to go backwards? It's a pointless waste of time. And I could go on and on about little nitpicks like these.
The puzzles themselves aren't awful but they tend to be very straight forward and bland. What's awful with them are the underlying mechanics. Citing Portal as the obvious comparison, in that game you pick up, easily move, and place cubes. Since they're square, they stay where you want them. But that would be too simple for this game. You have to use your magnetism powers to attract or repel spheres that just roll around everywhere. I can't for the life of me conceive a good reason for this awkward and frustrating control scheme.
In the end, Influx is visually and thematically beautiful, but not enough so to excuse the incredibly poor gameplay and massive amount of bugs.
