I have to say this is my favorite MMO of all time. I have played off and on since 2006. The game is just different from other MMOs. The dungeons and combat have a way of making you feel like you are in the world. Trapped down in a dungeon. At times you will find yourself just barely getting through a dungeon. The best way to enjoy this game in my opinion is to get a small group of friends (2-6). Even if it's just two of you. Only play the game together if possible, and only run dungeons on elite. The joy of experiencing a fresh dungeon with a few friends, and not knowing what is around the corner is much of what this game has to offer. That feeling of getting one shot by a trap is beyond anything I have seen in a MMO. The game suffers from a few balance issues, but it's acceptable given the amount of customization it has to offer. The microtransactions are fair. I would say just get a sub and everything else is pretty unnecessary. It’s always fun to come back  to DDO and run some dungeons with friends.

In short:
I strongly recommend this game WITH 2-4 friends in tow. Otherwise, given the current state of the community, I strongly recommend against it!
Note:
Some folks are having problems with becoming a subscriber or purchasing in the market. This is a problem with the Steam launcher. To circumvent, you need to go to your Steam folder ...\steamapps\common\Dungeons and Dragons Online\ and run TurbineLauncher.exe.
The long version:
I had thousands of hours of gameplay prior to acquiring on Steam. I have recently returned to check it out.
DDO, iirc, was the first Western mmo to go f2p-microtransactional. With Daybreak Games acquiring publishing rights recently, it's unclear how bad microtransactions will become. The claim is that DBG won't have undue influence, but this could easily be pushed into the P2W zone.
That said, DDO remains the "unique" mmorpg out there. Nuts-and-bolts it was built with grouping, suspense, problem solving, humor, quirkiness and discovery in mind, rather than grind or plain action. In its prime, it had 4 core group roles, with a nod to a fith: tank, healer, dps, trapper and a lil' bit control. The trapper was essential for finding and disarming invisible traps and unlocking key doors.
For newcomers who find a balanced and patient/dungeon-crawl group, the experience is unparalleled. DM narration, complex dungeon/mission mechanics (vs simple boss scripting), puzzles, and slower pacing really do rival your most acute PNP nostalgia.
Like all mmorpg's, however, the dev team has allowed this to degrade into solo'able content, or dps biased grouping. But unlike other mmo's, the original experience is still viable and worthwhile!
The graphics aren't 'modern,' but they have always had an ineffible charm.
Returning after several years. Though graphics are a bit dated DDO is still the same game I used to love. Just a solid game period.

Play Length: Extensive multiplayer matches.  A little bit of single player.
Positives: The most important thing for a strategy game is of course the strategy.  This game has a very impressive amount of depth.  I like that who you choose as your world leader matters, and that each one tends to feed into a different playstyle.  I like that there are various ways to win, including many non-violent ways.  You can not only win through military force, but also through technology or culture.  This is just a very cool concept for a strategy game.  But it's not just that the concepts are neat; they are also well executed.  It feels like the game is pretty well balanced, and that there are many legitimate ways to play.  Now, I'm not very familiar with the meta game, so for all I know in the competitive scene mulitary may be the way to go.  But for casual playing, it feels like there's a wide variety of ways to play, and that's mainly what interests me.
Also, Leonard Nimoy lends his voice to this game.  That's a huge positive for me!
Negatives: While the graphics are perfectly serviceable, sometimes I feel they come acrossed a bit dopey; especially the cartoonish portraits of the world leaders.  This game is turn based, and while I enjoy that style of slow and methodical gameplay, some people may not appreciate that as much.  This weakness can be magnified if you play with the wrong people... it can be annoying when one person is taking a really long time to act every single time.  The in-game music is very timid and fades into the background, it didn't do much for me.  Sometimes it creates a nice ambience, but a more memorable soundtrack would have increased my enjoyment of the game.
Overall: It's one of the best strategy games around, as far as I'm aware.  Certainly one of the best I've played.  If that's what you're looking for, then you've come to the right place.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  Overall score, and soundtrack.  Personally, I feel like game soundtracks are tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a vital factor in getting me into the game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and equal importance.  The meaning of each number are as follows:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
Civilization IV's score:
Game Rating: 7 (Great)

Jamestown is a fast paced indie shmup that features tons to unlock and some pretty damn nice visuals.
In Jamestown you'll be able to select from a number of different ships to play as, and each one play pretty different from one another. Some will have homing missiles, others will have plasma beams, and all sorts of other special abilities. As far as mechanics is concerned it's pretty simple. You have your regular shoot button, then a special which you can charge for an alternate fire, you also have vault as a defensive skill to negate any immediate dangers and bullets, and that's about it! Shoot stuff, collect the coins, then buy stuff with the coins. It's not a hard game to get into but it is a hard one to master.
The game's pacing is great as well. Each level never over stay it's welcome, while offering varied difficulty challenges as you proceed through them. This is a good thing since you'll be going over the same levels more than once in order to unlock everything in the game. It is arguable that Jamestown recycles a lot of the same content, but the developers have introduced interesting ways to reuse older assets to further the variety the game has to offer. From arcade mode, to challenge modes, and even a gauntlet mode, and more to unlock later on.
The game's graphics and presentation is top-notch. The pixel art featured is of a high caliber, with great details and animation. The game's soundtrack compliments the game's excellent presentation and really hits home the atmosphere the game tries to get across. It's just a gorgeous looking and sounding game.
There's a lot to love about Jamestown, but it's not perfect. The biggest issue I drew from the game is it's white enemy bullets. Of all the colors in the color wheel, why on earth did the developers choose white as the color of what's arguably the most important element in a shmup? White blends into the background, it blends in when there are explosions, it blends in where the screen shake. White is just not the color the eye picks up on first. When you're talking about shmups, visual clarity is of the utmost importance. Shmup players don't watch their spirits or the bullets individually, they "feel" them like a 6th scent. Usually in other shmups enemy bullets are as clear as day, allowing the player to ultaize their peripheral vision to "feel" their way around the battlefield. Because the bullets are white, a dull, uncaptivating color, the player is forced to watch every single bullet while keeping a close eye on the character sprite, forcing the player to play with a focus on parts of the game that shouldn't be focused on. The focus should be on the on coming dangers, not the immediate danger. The white bullets is my only real complaint about Jamestown, but it is a major one considering the genre.
Overall Jamestown is an excellent shmup. It feels great, it has a great degree of variety, and the ships are very interestingly designed. It does suffer from visual clarity problems due to it's white enemy bullets, but if you can adjust, I have no doubt Jamestown will be a memorable experience.
Pros:
- Fantastic pixel art
- Fantastic Soundtrack
- Great diversity in ships
- Lots to unlock
- Many different ways to play
Cons:
- White enemy bullets... for a shmup... seriously what the hell were the devs thinking?
(Only one con, but this one is a biggie)

Mordheim is a brutal and dark TBS game that will often punish those who like to re-load failed actions and take chances.  However, if you appreciate the art of balancing risk with opportunity, then Mordheim may just be the game for you.
Pros:  The game runs smoothly and I've never had a glitch so far.  The character models do justice to the Warhammer theme (fan of WH40k since 1988) and the factions all stand out.  All the attributes and skills may be a bit daunting at first, but the community on the forums is very helpful.  The battles are fun, often nail biting and the after battle loot/experience/purchase sequence is intuitive and enjoyable.  Interesting story missions that don't hold your hand.  Games usually last between 1-3 hours.
Cons:  I love the music, but wish they had more of a variety.  The AI could use a bit of an upgrade, but you'll still get a challenge with brutal/deadly missions with great rewards.  At first the game is very challenging, but as you go on the AI often picks lousy skills/armaments, which will get shredded by your focused ambushes.
I believe the game probably really shines in multiplayer.  Something I haven't tried yet for two reasons.  First, I'm attached to my warbands and want to complete the story missions before getting schooled by a pro with a MP focused warband.  Second, my wife is six months pregnant and having 1-3 hours of uninterrupted game time isn't highly likely.
I Love this game! It's so much more like the table top game then I ever expected a video game could be. I'll be playing this one for years to come.

This has been a review I've been meaning to write for a while, and I might not have as much time into it as others, but I believe I have given this tree a fair shake and have a good insight into the nature you should expect if you purchase Mordheim: City of the Damned and any of it's DLC. PLEASE READ FULLY BEFORE PASSING JUDGEMENT!
First and foremost I will share a snippet from a Warhammer 40K universe book that I find gives wonderful mental preperation for Mordheim, where the things you don't know on the battlefield can still kill you. And believe me they will.
With this in mind lets begin the review.
Mordheim: City of the Damned is about mortal men (monstrosities, not-so-mortal daemon spawn, etc..) throwing the dice by looting treasures and other wealth from the remains of Mordheim after a cataclysmic event befell the city. You in particular are a "Leader" of a mercenary group, warband, etc... struggling against other factions of those with like minds. Be prepared for the horrors that now call the once great city of Mordheim home, for they will be many and have no mercy. Be ready to lose not only gold, but equipment, men, time, reputation and even a limb or two. You will be hardpressed to make meets end that your "sponsors" or "patrons" have set you for they have no patience for those with lack of skill, poor judgement calls or even just bad luck.(mostly its bad luck) As you progress through Mordheim: City of the Damned and the gods are with you, you will collect more powerful wargear, loot, items and the all important Wyrdstones.
This game is heavily similar to it's tabletop companion in where whatever can happen, can indeed happen because events are based on dice rolls. It may take you a few tries and restarts to finally get going in the game, as well as to learn a strategy that you can take advantage of. But once you get going you should find it easier and easier to manage. Does that mean you should take greater risks? Not necssarily. Indeed taking a greater risk can result in greater rewards, but the consequences can be equally severe. You should always have a contingency incase a planed action failed or be prepared to lose what you've commited.  Course the game is not completely one sided, many times after a particularly nasty round or route, a soldier I thought lost managed to, beyond all hope, return to the camp with little injury and ready to seek revenge.
This is a game based in a realm of despair, darkness, and unrelenting war. Although you are far from the conflicts of greater powers, you are still in a struggle just as gruesome, bloody and savage as the wars that rage elsewhere. Be prepared to lose it all or find your fortune in Mordheim: City of the Damned.
Pros:
+ 4 begining factions that roughly span the different types of tactics in war
+ Campaign provides some different objectives
+ General customization for each unit, and rename warband
+ 2 more factions in DLC's
+ Individual units can rise above and beyond like in Warhammer lore and stories (a soldier thought dead making it back)
+ Units can individually level up creating strong individual soldiers
+ You can backtrack your movement (as long as something hasn't happened)
+ A good sense of realism from war (you try coming out a fight after being stabbed in the gut and be fine)
+ Graphics capture the feel of Warhammer
+ Enemy Spellcaster can blow themselves up (9,999 damage)
Cons:
- There are some annoying movement and item glitches
- Cannot respec a unit once skill points are assigned (it does ask you if you're sure before continuing)
- Couple DLC are priced a little high (but no higher than other games similar from what I've found)
- Enviroment can get in the way of your camera
- Can feel you've wasted time when a high level unit dies or is debilitated (training extra units can ease this)
- Can get hung up on pieces of terrain that looks like you shouldn't (movement glitch, good thing you can backtrack)
- It does feel like you have little time to explore before Enemy AI finds/gets to you
- DLC Vampires are a little ridiculous ( OP Fear )
- Your own Spellcaster can blow themselves up (9,999 damage)
Note: I did not critque the dice roll system because this is an imperative part of the game mechanics and dice rolls can and will be a thorn in your side at times.
Personally I suggest Mordheim: City of the Damned and its components as an entertaining Turn Based Strategy Game that fits well with the history and the feel of Warhammer.

Rating: 8/10 ("Very good")
Recommended for: People who enjoy VNs, people who enjoy romance. I would recommend this for a first time VN-reader.
My route order: Rod > Karma > Rumpel > Fritz > Waltz. I can’t choose a favourite!
Cinderella Phenomenon is a 100 percent free visual novel with a female protagonist. It took me approximately 19 hours to complete all the routes, keeping in mind that I skipped content I had already read and didn’t start from the beginning for every route. This leaves approximately 4 hours for each route, which seems accurate.
The novel has a pretty interesting and original take on the concept of fairytales, witches, and fairies. The good endings aren’t truly one hundred percent “good” and not quite a happily ever after – good people unavoidably die, no matter what you do, or perhaps
of what you do. Nonetheless, the VN has a good storyline with an endearing message and competently written characters. The main heroine has a real personality as opposed to simply being a self-insert doormat, and she has her own agency. All the other characters, including the male love interests, have varying amounts of depth to them that make them thoughtfully crafted.
There are 5 love interests and 10 endings: one bad and one good ending for each guy. Every route is told in 10 chapters, wherein only the final chapter actually changes based on whether or not you have a good or a bad ending. Overall, the biggest problem with Cinderella Phenomenon is that in the end, choices don’t feel like they truly matter. The VN would benefit from a couple more bad endings earlier in the storyline. In addition, there are no true branching paths. You will do the same things and achieve the same overall outcome no matter what choice you make, which begs the question of, why are there choices in the first place?
The requirements for achieving a good ending are a little too strict. If you deviate even one answer from the guide, you will obtain a bad ending, no matter what choice it was. Case in point: I played the game blind for Rod’s playthrough, and obtained the bad ending even though, after looking at the guide, I could see only two or three of my choices deviated from the given path. You are shoehorned in a particular role and personality – telling Rod off or being honest with him at certain parts of the story is apparently the bad thing to do and will give you a ticket to the bad ending. That being said, it seems that making the wrong choices in chapter 9 doesn’t matter – you need to go back a couple chapters in the storyline if you want to snag a bad ending without skipping through the entire novel from the very beginning. Starting the novel from the beginning isn’t all that necessary, since, as stated, there are no branching paths and no matter your choice you will ultimately have the same outcome. Only a few lines of dialogue change here and there.
But don’t let this dissuade you whatsoever. For a free product, Cinderella Phenomenon is honestly outstanding. Each route tells an
different story. They were all enjoyable – I really cannot choose which route I liked the most, as they were all interesting and never felt boring or bloated with filler. The writing was competent and hardly ever came across as too amateurish, though there were scenes where I felt more appropriate words could have been selected. Cinderella Phenomenon’s artwork is also rather high quality; despite some CGs being a little awkward looking, it’s quite obvious the artist spent a lot of time and work on the art. The sprites are all fantastic, backgrounds are detailed, and most of the CGs are very pretty. There were a few scenes that I felt could have used a CG to bolster the impact of what was happening, but since this is a free work, I think that can be forgiven. Really, almost 20 hours of reading, depending on your speed, for
…
Overall, Cinderella Phenomenon is definitely worth a look. It’s free and has an interesting storyline…you can't possibly go wrong with picking this VN up. I'll definitely take a look at anything else this developer chooses to create.

*STOP*. Save your money.
Terrible puzzle game, terrible anything.
The game tries to focus itself around visuals and fails. It’s using the Unreal 3 engine so the visual engine power is there but the game does not use it (considering its focus this is rather silly).
Level layouts are ugg, invisible walls, bad layouts (dead ends),  getting stuck in crannies (rocks, between puzzle button ramps and walls). For a game that you'd expect to be movement to be fluid it’s just the opposite, lots of  slow breaking to stop, turning around,  hitting ramps at the wrong angles and thus drop to a complete standstill.... Far, far from fluid...
The game flow, I expect, ’s supposed to be a pattern of explore -> puzzle -> explore -> puzzle-> ... etc. Iit’s just executed so poorly, the explore sections are clearly supposed to be *ooo look at the visuals* but it’s more like *oo look at the visuals that look like they are from a game 4 years ago and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (yes I've gone into the settings and jacked everything up). If you stop to look at anything you immediately see beyond the superficial polish into cheap, lazy visual effects.
Furthermore a lot of the ‘exploring’ (feels more like walking around Disney world without a map, looking for a particular ride) is to dead end map sections (you’re on an island with all the outlying water being cordoned off with rocks or bundled timber? Looks really silly), where your entire purpose for going down was either to discover keys (blue floating balls) or the absence of keys, either way you have to stop and turn around. All the exploring is through like… hiking trails very bumpy and therefore very little room for any fluidity and gets repetitive as well (“oh look another trail with… tiki huts… ooo so different”).
The controls are loopy (e.g. forward+ left should result in the ball rolling left, but instead is like an invisible force is pushing the ball diagonally (like a kid playing with a hot wheels car)), the game is buggy (especially with the boost feature, found myself going THROUGH walls and other solid objects and dropping outside the world or in a place I could not get out of (like inside the model of a tree). Or once I touched some water and then for the next ten minutes I heard the obnoxious water splashing sound looping over and over.
My overall impression is that this was some team’s grad school project and they had a great team of modelers, content artists but the game designer and programmers were not so great...
The skills you learn are extremely repetitive, e.g. use 'mouse buttons to repel and attract rocks, here now have twenty rock walls incase using this skill didn’t sink in the other twenty times!’ Or the flipper things, have to use them thirty times in a row; it’s all highly repetitive…
The puzzles are lack luster, very little thinking, just obnoxious trial and error: “oh you got all the way to the end of the puzzle lugging around 2 heavy balls using the attract? Well oops looks like you stepped on the wrong button which requires you use the balls to activate (no way you could have foreseen this). Now watch the balls fall off the platform and roll back to the beginning of the puzzle, DO IT OVER NOW!” Highly repetitive, very little to no satisfaction for solving puzzles as most are extremely monotonous.
Its crap; all in all the game does nothing new (kind of mandatory for a puzzle game) (ok there is ONE new thing, the puzzle maps do flip but really has little effect on your skill repertoire), nor does anything particularly well and it all feels like some poorly executed grad project with no direction other than five people shouting out ill contrived ideas at a meeting table in a student library. It even sounds lame when you describe the games concept out loud “you are this ball thing rolling around the environment up and down ramps placed on hiking trails and occasionally solve puzzles”.
Overall *HIGHLY* repetitive and very mundane.

My advice: If you're new to puzzle platformers, or you're itching for a puzzle fix, get it for around $5.
Genre:  Puzzle Platformer
As creative as this game seems, I wish it had tried to push harder on a few fronts. The story is interesting enough. You're Rochard, a backwater space miner who's down on his luck trying to bring his mining company to new sources of fuel. When they do finally strike the motherlode, Rochard and the crew discovers their find is far more valuable than they anticipated.
Unfortunately, from that point, the story is pretty flat and predictable. The mechanics behind moving your 'weapon' are neat, and using anti-gravity in combination with moving heavy objects around is pretty seamless and fluid. Unfortunately, the puzzles are quite easy, but they did rectify some of this with the cheap DLC. Voice acting isn't half bad, nor is the music, but it's still not enough to get me to recommend this game to anyone but true puzzle fans.

3/10.
The developers had an interesting idea here, but I'd say they flubbed on its execution. The game tries to be a mix of puzzle game and platformer, but can't end up doing a very good job of either one. The puzzles are too simple and repetitive when they're present, and the platforming is oftentimes thoughtless. It's not necessarily that either element is too easy, but that they used no imagination in their execution, take no imagination to solve, and generally feel the same throughout the entire game.
The game would have received maybe a 5.5/10 if not for the story. Aside from a horrible case of purple prose and poor dialogue, it packs more cliches than I thought possible and plays them all straight, without any indication that the writers had any awareness of its laughability. The voice acting also really grated on my ears, and the only reason I finished the game is because I kept telling myself it had to get better eventually.
It didn't. I applaud the creators for their work because creating a game is no mean feat, and it took dedication to get this far. But if any of them should happen to read this review, I suggest focusing on one genre and doing it well, rather than trying to combine genres or elements of genres before you've learned what makes either of them work.
I will not be recommending this to fans of platformers, puzzle-solvers, or puzzle-solving platformers. If you want a recommendation and don't mind a challenge and antiquated graphics, look up Defy Gravity on Steam instead.
This is fantastic puzzle platformer, highly recommended for fans of the genre.

As someone who's never really understood the charm of fighting games, and even actively disliked some, this is the game that tricked me into liking fighting games. Open-world, loot, leveling, seamless PvP and co-op - it just happens to be a damn good fighting game as well. It's simple if you want it to be, but a deep, deep rabbit hole of complexity if that's what you want.
Don't buy this game for the story or PvE though, as that part of the game is more of a prolonged tutorial - it's definitely not bad, I would even consider it good, but it's short and takes a back seat to the actual gameplay. PvP is the end game.
Speaking of, right now the playerbase is kind of small, and the matchmaking (structured PvP) suffers for it. I've not once had to wait more than a minute to set up a match though - the main problem is getting matched with someone that is roughly the same skill level as you. Maybe 25-50% of the time you end up with someone who's significantly better, or worse, than you. This isn't all bad, as you get the chance to learn from the ones that are better, and practice the things you haven't quite nailed yet against the ones who are worse. It's just plain fun either way.
The developers seem intent on continued support as well, and just recently added further customisation options (the ability to dye your equipment - if that's your jam (FAbsolver)), and a 3v3 mode which is quite fun to dip into every once in a while.
This is probably my game of the year (2017), simply because of the uniqueness of the game, and the absolutely phenomenal gameplay - at the moment of writing I've spent roughly 19 hours playing the game, and boy do I feel like I've gotten my moneys worth.
TL;DR: Buy the game. Gameplay is amazing, even if you don't have any experience with the fighting game genre.

A satisfying, deep, and incredibly well-crafted puching game.
Basically, it's indie Dark Souls with punching instead of giant swords. The levels sprawl and have some verticality, you wander around a ruined world punching people in search of especially strong people to punch. The formula is pretty familiar.
But the new tricks are brilliant. To improve yourself, you need to take hits. You learn new moves by blocking them, then use them to build your own combos. It's easy to get the gist of it, but it'll take hours to get properly good at it all.
I just have two issues. The first is that the mouse & keyboard controls are useless. It's almost insulting. There's a reason that we use the mouse for camera controls, and it's the same reason we use our dominant hand to write an essay: that's what it's good at. AND YET as soon as you get into a fight, you can't control the camera anymore and the slightest twitch of the mouse will activate your special ability with absolutely none of the accuracy and consistency you'd expect. Use a controller or prepare to rage when you lose an easy fight because you had to wrestle with the controls.
My second issue is that it feels like an Early Access. There are 9 (i think) areas, none of which are very big, and only a handful of minibosses and two main bosses. Then you go through a door, go on a bit of a sightseeing tour, fight a superboss, then you've won, congrats, hope you enjoyed those five hours of game.
But I did enjoy it, and I keep going back. There are multiplayer duel systems that unlock better equipment, and grinding out new moves from the minibosses is actually pretty fun. Also, you need to go through the "Combat Trials" multiplayer to unlock next-level versions of the overworld bosses. Even though the game feels small, there's a lot to it. The "beta" tag hovering over the 3v3 mode gives me hope that more content will come. That being said, there's really no reason to play it once you've beaten it other than "for fun."
I know I went off on the negatives, but literally everything else is so good I don't even know where to start. In all, a super fun fighting game with expertly crafted mechanics and sound design but rough in a few spots.

A good looking and tight controlled Rogue-like with decent amounts of environmental randomization, a nice pool of unique items and basic Role-Playing leveling mechanics.
Overpriced considering the low amount of randomization as a whole, the very poor developer support and straight up broken controller support. The game also likes killing players instantly with traps that are barely visible, perhaps the developers are underaged. The only unique strength of the game is it actually has online co-op.
It still suffers from the primary issues of these kinds of low-end Rogue-like games; it does not have enough randomization or polish to compete with the price range it is sold in. There are multiple other Rogue-likes you could buy which are better designed and hold far more replayability then this one while costing exactly the same. It doesn't help how awkward the combat can be as well, while the controls are tight in a very satisfying way; the actual method in which players need to land hits using melee is straight up clumsy and unrefined.
It's also to be noted how blatantly the game rips off the mechanics of Spelunky. If the developers were so desperate to save brain power by just stealing another games system instead of making up their own; where did they put all that saved energy into. Because it certainly didn't get put to use in making anything in this game remotely special or innovative, or polished in any way.

If it wasn't already obvious from the store page, this game is a tower defense / action RPG hybrid.  You have the choice of using 1 of 3 heroes - a warrior (tank), bowman (ranged damage), or a wizard (ranged AoE damage).  You can start with any of the 3 at the beginning of a map, and can swap in another if you happen to die before you finish it.  You're also given stars for completing maps, which can be used unlock and upgrade different types of towers to place.  Clearing maps also gives experience, so you can level up any of your 3 heroes.
I played this game when it very first hit Steam, and it had a few issues.  Controls were wonky, I lost my save data.. I gave it a chance, but it didn't work out.  I lost the willpower.
However, I recently came back to give it another shot, and learned that the developers had improved the control scheme to allow WASD controls.  This dramatically improved the gameplay.  Interestingly, I also found my old save data on my computer; apparently the save folder changed during one of the earlier updates.
As I write this, I've just finished the game on hard mode, and overall the whole experience left me with a positive vibe.  It's not without flaws, though.  Below, I'll share some of what I liked and didn't like.
PROS
------
1) The stat progression feels rewarding.  In this game, as you reach higher levels, you start to gain more stats (attack, defense, and health) per level.  This makes it so each level is exciting to gain - I wish more games recognized this and followed the example.
2) It plays well in general.  Bashing into enemies as the warrior, my favorite class, often feels like a pinball machine of pain (THEIR pain), as I bounce from mob to mob.  You can do this as the other classes as well, but they don't have as much defense and health.
3) The 3 separate difficulty modes are somewhat tiered, such that you're not expected to beat hard mode from the start.  This allows you to go back and replay levels for more experience.  Granted, you don't have to beat level 30 on easy to start level 1 on medium.  Each difficulty setting is a good nudge up in both challenge and reward, though.
4) My kids find the talkative fairy creepy, but I think she adds a nice touch to the game.  She never did tell me something about the last boss, though!
5) If there's a level cap, it's high.  I finished the game at level 40, and still have an experience bar filling up.  I like it when a game allows me to decide when I'll stop leveling up, not the other way around.
6) Stable - zero crashes.
CONS
------
1) The stamina system isn't fun.  This is one of the reasons I picked warrior as my primary.  He just bashes into things, and stamina loss doesn't seem to impact him much.  The bowman and wizard, however, are massively dependent on stamina.  Once you run out, you can no longer perform a ranged attack, and have to either use a heart or go to a healing tent to replenish.  This felt tedious, and I wasn't a fan.  The wizard can only perform 9 casts before having to refill.  Gaining more stamina on each level up would have been an easy fix for this.
2) Items with magical suffixes need tooltips.  I never really know what they do until I play with them.  If one replenishes stamina, that would be a fix for the wizard, but I didn't toy around enough to find out.  "Of the gods" gives health regen though, so that was a sweet deal for the warrior.
3) Class balance doesn't seem right.  The wizard in particular feels very underpowered, mostly due to the stamina system, and not being able to continuously cast.  The overall damage from her spells feels low as well, or maybe it's the fire rate that suffers more?
4) Very limited settings.  It's apparent that this game wasn't originally developed for the PC.
All in all, this game delivers what it promises - it's a satisfying tower defense / action rpg.  There are annoyances, but I don't believe they're numerous enough to warrant not buying the game.  5 bucks is a steal; I paid that much for my coffee this morning.  I would recommend this title to other fans of the genre.
Thanks for fun experience, devs.  I hope to see more of your stuff in the future, or possibly more updates to this game.  Nightmare mode, anyone??

Onion Force combines the elements of tower with some light action features which sets it apart from most other games in the genre. The gameplay is true to most TD games, you can place towers that’ll do different things such as attack and heal but the unique thing about Onion Force is the use of a hero to help repel enemies.
You have three heroes to choose from: Warrior, Bowman and Wizard and each has it’s own abilities and attack style that you can use. Warriors focus on Melee and are very strong whereas the Wizard and Archer are ranged and you’ll find yourself a little more susceptible to damage. Your heroes are fully controlled by you and you must defend your king alongside any towers you build. Though your hero can die in battle if you don’t use the heal tent properly you don’t have to worry as you can select one of the other two heroes to continue on with the level allowing you to have a second chance if you just made a mistake. Your hero has stamina and health, both of which will decrease as you play and can only be refilled at a healing tent so you’ll want to strategically place yours so you can both fight and survive!
The game is done in stages and each stage has a boss and as you’d expect the levels and bosses get harder as you continue through the game. Each stage can also be replayed in harder modes so if you want to complete the earlier levels again with a little more difficulty you’re able too adding a small amount of replayability after you’ve completed the game once.
In between stages you have the ability to level up your towers using the stars you get from completing each level. You can also use the onions that enemies occasionally drop as currency between stages to purchase spells but these only last one stage and since the onions are rare you’ll not want to waste them until you really do need them.
The graphics are fine but they don’t scale well onto a larger screen. Everything looks a little blurry and the only options you can change are the resolutions options which don’t make anything any better. You need to play the game on a small windowed screen for the best graphics, I think this may be because it’s a mobile port? The sound is also nothing too impressive, just your run-of-the-mill soundtrack you’d expect in a tower defence game.
Many people have mentioned the heal tent and i’d have to agree, it’s an annoying feature and should be rethought. It's boring/annoying to constantly have to return to a certain point just to regain stamina to attack. I think it could be much more forgivable if it was just for health but the stamina element makes it impossible to not use. I also feel at times the game really does feel like a mobile port. You see things here and there which seem like they were meant to be paywalls yet they haven’t translated well to PC. Lastly, there are some stages that seem severely unbalanced and require you to have beaten many prior stages on the harder levels to beat which can be a pain in the butt if you like you play through each difficulty individually.
Overall Onion Force is very fun and worth picking up on sale if you’re looking for a tower defense where you feel like you’re doing something more than just building and waiting. Although it does have it’s flaws it’s a great time waster and has sturdy enough gameplay to hold its own.

I personally love Tower Defense games, something about protecting my tower (or king in this game's case) really appeals to me.  It has all your typical Tower defense offerings, towers to help with defense (sniper, tar, cal-traps, soldiers etc,) you can also purchase spells between stages which will give your hero the advantage in the upcoming stage.  I was quite impressed by the game, and found myself drawn to it and it's very simplistic gameplay.  Onion Force makes for a nice casual game play experience, it's a game that can be enjoyed by people of almost any age and gameplaying ability.
The game play is simple, you select a stage,
, then you select which hero you want to use..  The levels i'll call them are broken down into various stages..   Each level has 5 stages, with the fifth one being the most difficult and containing a unique "boss" battle, although most of the bosses aren't too much more difficult than the normal enemies.  The game features three different heroes, the Warrior, archer and mage, each one has a slightly different approach on how to defeat enemies.   The warrior is as you may have suspected, the upfront meat head type, continually smash into enemies until they are dead, rinse and repeat, I personally found myself using the warrior twice as much as the other two heroes.  Personally felt the other two were slightly under-powered in terms of beast slaying, although they are viable choices albeit much more options.  The goal of the game is to protect your king from being overwhelmed and killed by the enemies.
Throughout the game you'll get various drops from the enemies, the first of which are coins, which you can collect and use to build your various towers, the second collectible will be onions, which are used to purchase spell buffs prior to the stage.  The buffs can really give a major advantage to the gamer, but require onions which are semi rare, so be sure to not go too crazy buying buffs or you'll run out of Onions on the stages when you really need them.  The game also has weapons which can drop for the various heroes, you can equip them prior to the stage, the weapons increase attack power and sometimes have a unique bonus added to them.  You also get coins by beating stages, which are used for upgrading your towers.  Although this proves to be a double edged sword as each new upgrade, increases the cost of building that particular tower.  The gameplay is relatively fun although can get repetitive after a while
Each of the three heroes has their own unique brand of attacking.  The Warrior bumps into enemies and takes down the enemies health.  He has the most health and deals the most melee damage.  The archer as you may have guessed is given a bow which shoots at enemies from am distance.  You can also bump into enemies while playing as the Archer but don't expect to last very long, the archer can only take 4 or 5 bumps before he's killed.  The mage attacks with an AOE cone of damage, it damages and pushes back enemies, a great tactic involves standing just near a tower as the wizard and continually pushing enemies back so the tower can hit them.
The two bars on your heroes are health and stamina, the warrior loses health and stamina with each attack, the archer and mage lose stamina with each attack and only lose health if they melee an enemy. If you run out of stamina you'll have to rest in a medical tent to continue fighting.  Upon death you are given the option to select one of the other two heroes to continue the battle.

TL;DR
I just finished playing Rakuen and first off, it was wonderful.
This game has so much heart put in to it and it really shows!
If you have been looking for a retro-styled adventure RPG with
good story and music, this game is for you.
Review:
Plot/Story:
The story in this game is fantastic without question. The characters
all have so much life put in to them and many of them really seem
real. Here is a brief rundown of the plot:
Rakuen is a game about a boy in a hospital. You play as him as
you travel through the fantasy world of Morizora's forest with
your mother. Together you seek to wake up the guardian of the
forest to grant your wish. However, the guardian is asleep with
no sign of waking up. In order to wake up the guardian you must
walk a mile in the shoes of your fellow patients and in doing so,
you come to terms with your own story.
Gameplay:
Simple enough, but that is all it needs to be. It's basically an
interactive story with the occasionaly puzzle or quest to solve.
The real star in these kinds of games is always the story though.
Soundtrack:
From a game by Laura Shigihara, you should come to expect an
amazing sountrack and it does not dissapoint at all. I love all of
her other work, especially her work in Kan Gao's game,
To the Moon (which I also recommend checking out).
So basically, if that sounds your style, pick it up! It will take you
roughly around 7-8 hours to beat and is well worth the $10 price
tag. Be ready for the possibility of crying of course. While the
finale didn't actually hit me that hard, there were some parts in the
middle that really got me reaching for the tissues to dry my eyes
so I could still play the game.

The Good:
+ Beautiful artwork
+Good character design
+Relaxing: the kind of game where you can just have fun exploring in different environments
+Honest, well-done message/theme
+Plots with feels. All the feels.
+The puzzles aren't frustrating. You are given information on what to do and, for the most part, you're allowed to use the tools provided to solve them on your own. I felt a little patronized to now and again, but I think this game was meant for children as well as adults, so I won't hold that against it. Anyway, I'm a veteran of Cyan's games (as well as other, more traditional adventure games), so I like my puzzles on the extreme of the "give the player absolutely no information other than what's naturally provided by the setting" side. That's probably not true for everyone.
The Not-So-Good
+Characters aren't explored enough. The plots of their stories are well-done, but the only character who I felt like I actually got to know was Sue. However, I still cried a lot, so it's not like this flaw made the story horrible. It felt more like there was lost potential than like you were surrounded by two-dimensional people. Like you wanted to get to know everybody but weren't given that chance.
+Consistent mechanics are nonexistent, aside from recycled things like fetch quests. Mechanic design is not this game's strength. I see a lot of these arbitrary mechanics in RPG Maker games, and I think that people get the idea that because Ib and The Witch's House had arbitrary puzzle mechanics, you don't need solid mechanics for a story-driven game. But the reason why those puzzles worked in those two games is because the environment was trying to use arbitrary puzzles to kill you. It wasn't supposed to make sense, and that's what made it work and even enhance the horror/mystery element. However, now that my rant is over, I should add that the overall game design flows pretty smoothly.
+The pacing is unbalanced. It's half-RPG, half-To the Moon type story and those two pieces weren't cut to fit together well. The mechanics feel like they sit on the surface of the story rather than working in a symbiotic relationship with it, and this inevitably leads to wonky pacing. Again, it doesn't make the game bad, but it feels like potential was lost.
Overall, I had a lot of fun playing this game and the message came to me at a time when I needed it. It isn't perfect, but it certainly is lovable.

I played DDO on and off for over 2 years and even had a premium content pack or two, but I just gave up. The initial Character mechanic LOOKS like the DnD 3.X, but the deeper layers of the game are built in a fashion to any other MMO. Just because I know what my character can handle on paper doesn't mean my Online character stands a chance. Looking into the forums and fan pages, I leaned that just like WoW/Everquest/et al, the game was built using an engine that encourages decimal point maxing that's even more Munchkin than pen and paper games. If you want to play solo, don't bother. The "perfect builds" have been long since logged and the macro routines are freely traded, thus turning the game into less of a skill/luck game and into a "press this key to execute this routine".
The player population is slim and too many tropes from other games have crept into DDO over the years like meta currency, Alliance based items and abilities and a subtle but painful need to chain play content packs for gear in order to stand a chance at higher levels (as a soloist, I suck at group play).
It just isn't DnD anymore. It has the window dressing at the front end, but it's just a grinder. I disbanded my Alliance, deleted my toons and gave up.

I like DnD as a whole, but not many MMO's have a Monk Class, and if they do, the game itself isn't very good, and even if the game is good, it normally isn't compatible with low end computers. I LOVE fist fight/martial arts style classes, since they are far and few between in the MMO world. This game does indeed have Monk. It is locked behind micro-transactions. At least this was the case for me since I haven't played a ton of the game yet. This to me is not okay, and is not deserving of a reccommendation to play from me. Majority of the extra races are also locked behind micro transactions. So all in all, if you look into the game, and you are fine with not having the premium races and classes and such, it is well worth trying. I am not one of those people, so I am no longer going to give my time to this game.

Father, forgive me for I have sinned.
I did not play Resident Evil 4 until August 2017. A cardinal sin I know, but before you sharpen your pitchforks and light your torches, it has rocketed into my top 5 games of all time. I was uncertain as to how to approach it, as I didn't want to hype it up too much in my own head. However, I am overjoyed to say that it was the fantastically enjoyable experience that so many others have reported.
It starts off as almost a self-aware B horror movie, a theme which runs for the entire game. It almost feeds from this for plot elements which seem almost familiar, but which are laid out in an entertaining and engaging story. It is well paced, starting slow, and then building quite literally up to an explosive climax.
The level design is superb, with many different environments being explored - the castle level being a particular favourite. At the time the inventory system was innovative and it still shines to this day, from which other games could earn a lot.There is also great replayability, with additional levels and stories to play, an arcade style minigame and many unlockables to enjoy.
Most of the readers will be familiar with the above and if you haven't played the HD edition I would thoroughly reccomend it. For those rarer breeds who are new to the game such as myself, dont hesitate. Play it now!

Ever heard of this game? I hadn't. It was in my Steam list because I apparently got it from Humble Bundle 6. Well it looked like an action-y physics puzzle platformer (think Trine) and I like that kind of thing so I went ahead and launched it.  I'm glad I did!
The game was enjoyable, accessible and pretty unique, mostly because there aren't a lot of entries in this genre. Despite the fact that the game flew under my radar, I found the art, effects and voice acting to be pretty top-notch for a game of this type. It's clear that the team loved about this game. It was short-ish, which is expected. About 6 hours. And the story has a fairly unique premise, but it gets kinda mucked up with some really stupid cliches. Despite that, I found Rochard himself to be the game's most lovable character. A rotund, twangy and kind space-miner.
The game spends most of its time allowing you to use a Half-Life 2 style Gravity Gun in many of the same ways Half-Life 2 does, but with a few twists, such as pairing that concept with low-gravity, and solving larger-scale platforming puzzles. It's shameless, but still different.
There's a lot of things that don't fit together with the game's theme... like how many people you actually end up just gunning down as cartoony cannon fodder... and the stupid native american mysticism subplot. Regardless of my complaints, I have nothing against Rochard and genuinely enjoyed my time with it.

[TL;DR] Superb game. Highly recommend.
The Rogue-Like elements are done well. You will recognise areas after a while, but the structure and placement methods keep the same areas feeling different for each run. Though the levels can feel a bit short at times, they are always interesting to navigate and explore.
Combat is satisfying. Button mashing will get you killed, but properly executed tactics are rewarding. In 78 hours of gameplay (at time of writing) I have rarely felt like a death was cheap. Every hit taken, or missed attack is down to my own error, not glitchy hitboxes/mechanics.
Character diversity doesn't feel limited by the chosen class. The, current four, classes each have their own perks, but there is no pressure to play a specific way or use a certain weapon.
Item diversity. Though the selection of weapons may seem limited, compared to other games, the balance actually works in the game's favour. Going for a handful of architype weapons, with stronger varients, and a veriety of enchants means you are more likely to find the weapon you want but you are not guarenteed the stats you want.
My few complaints with the game are so minor, I am not going to bother highlighting them, as they will likely be resolved before full release.

Onion Force is a Tower defence game, which mixes in RPG abilities and the ability to be able to a character of your choose to roam around and kill enemies. There is a variety of different levels and enemies that you may come across as you play throughout the game.
For me, Onion Force started off to be a really good game for the first half an hour. The gameplay itself was fun to begin with and really got me intrigued to play more of the game, but once I realised what the game actually was I really wasn't very impressed with it. The gameplay is sort of like a tower defence game meets RPG styled game, you are able to 'choose' your character and roam around the battlefield to kill enemies. I use the word choose loosely for a couple of reasons.
So when you first start a level you are given three characters you can pick as. Just normal standard classes nothing fancy or nothing, these classes consist of Warrior, Archer and Wizard. My first thought about this was that I would be able to play as one character throughout the game and then play it with another character to maybe add some replayability. I soon discovered this wasn't how this game was going to work out at all. With the three characters that you choose to be you will probably be all of them. because the way that the game works is that if your character dies you will either have to wait for it to be revived or pick another hero. Obviously you will pick another hero because you don't have time to wait around. So getting them to the same level as one another is a grind for the most part, having to replay levels constantly to try to level up your character.
Something that the game is highly dependant on is this heal tent. This will obviously heal your character to make sure they don't die in battle. This wouldn't be a problem if the game didn't have this one mechanic that forces you to always go back to the tent. This mechanic in the game is a yellow bar above your health bar. This yellow bar indicates how much of the power you have left. Every attack move that you use will cause you to lose some power. For some reason this power bar doesn't stay active for very long if you are trying to kill enemies. You are then either forced to go to a heal tent or use a heart to get it back. Trust me, you will visit the heal tent several times in one game.
Apart from this constant grind for exp the game does do a few things quite well. The first is the enemies that you encounter through the game. As you progress you will find more enemies that will have certain weaknesses from the towers that you can build. This is a nice way of making the game easier for the player, and makes them think about what tower to buy an place down next. Some of the enemies are also themed based, getting through 5 levels you will get to a new area and will find new enemies to encounter.
Something else that is rather unique about Onion Forces is the way that you upgrade your towers. Normally you would upgrade your towers when you place them once you have gained enough of the game's currency. Onion Forces however. puts the stars that you gained into upgrading your towers and making them more powerful. This is really good because in most games the number of stars you collect is just something that you collect, you don't find them precious or helpful it's just nice to have. While this game lets you use your stars to help you out later on in the game.
The next point I am going to make is this boost run that you have. Now I'm not really sure how this was suppose to be implemented, I thought that this boost has a cooldown or something so that you didn't constantly run around, but the game doesn't have that. So you can constantly run spamming right click. I wasn't sure if the game meant for this to happen but it seems a bit stupid to have something like that and not have it to be toggled on or off.
The graphics of this game aren't all that. In the new areas that you will find it will seem like a nice change of scenery until you realise that you will have to put up with it for X amount of hours. For me the first 5 levels took me about a hour to complete, the levels aren't really any different from one another and just look the same. Apart from that the colours of the game are nice, sometimes they are a bit dull here and there but overall they are alright.
Onion Forces has a few soundtracks. Unfortunately, these are limited for each new area that you find as you go through the game. For the first 5 levels you will be listening to the same music as you fight through the enemies. Trust me when I say the music in this game isn't very good. I wouldn't even call it music, it just this same repetitive sound that is slightly mixed in with other sounds to try to make it sound different. Really dislike the music in this game.
+ First half an hour is good
+ Nice variety of enemies
+ Use stars to upgrade your towers
+ Standard graphics
- After half an hour the game got boring
- Game forces you to level up 2 or all 3 characters instead of just sticking to one
- Playing as 2-3 characters makes you have to redo levels to gain exp, constantly grinding
- Power bar makes you constantly have to go to the heal tent to attack with your character
- Can constantly run, but have to spam right click to do so. There is no toggle for it
- Music is bad
For me Onion Forces really isn't worth buying. The replay ability is dragged on from you having to replay levels to level up your other characters that need to be the same level throughout the game. The game has alright graphics, but the music I would advise listening to your own if you're going to buy this game. Overall, I wouldn't recommend buying this game.

Onion Force is a Tower-Defense style game that lets you control your hero to add to the defense with spells, arrows, or plain old bump-a-guy-to-damage melee action.
It's a simple, fun little mobile port of an action-TD hybrid.
It feels
like a simple, fun little mobile port.
Onion Force is... well, incredibly average for this type of tower-defense game, which really isn't such a bad thing.  It offers 30 levels across 6 environments, which is about the standard amount of content for a game of this type to keep you playing without losing interest before you're through. The 8 different tower types in the game follow the usual arrow / cannon / slowgoo chain, but there are also a couple fairly originals ones such as the caltrops & barracks towers.   The heroes you control are likewise incredibly typical - archer shoots single foes quickly, mage shoots slowly with area blasts, warrior hits things up close and can take a lot of punishment.  The story is little more than an excuse to fight through the boss map to reach another change of scenery, but there is always a bit of quirky dialogue about the different enemies you encounter and locations you explore to keep you interested, which is definitely a plus.
Unfortunately, along with the averagely well-done game mechanics, Onion Force also suffers from the most common flaws in a mobile port.  The audio sounds nearly as tinny as it would from a mobile device, and the graphics look about the same.  Additionally some of the controls don't work as well as they should (pressing ESC instantly quits the game instead of bringing up a menu, inventory management is a pain, running through a tower-build spot brings up a huge window covering the screen, gold/onions are hard to collect, etc) - but on the plus side, the devs recently patched 'WASD' keys to work as movement, so improvements are being made.
With all that said, Onion Force does everything well-enough to make it an enjoyable - but not exceptional - experience.  However, I would have to suggest waiting for a sale (or price drop) before purchasing, as $10 seems too high for the content in what is essentially a mobile game... and I probably wouldn't recommend this game to those who don't already enjoy Tower Defense as a genre.  Still, if you're a Tower Defense fan, you might want to give Onion Force a shot!

Hi my name is Jtrev23 and I own my own Indie Game Review site,
and this is a copy of a review of Onion Force that I wrote on my site:
Onion Force is an epic Action/Tower Defense game with RPG aspects that was created Queen Bee Games and is available on Steam for $9.99 at the time of this post. I actually already reviewed this game a month ago but that was based off of the demo version and this review is based off of the full release. For the record, I played this game for around 9+ hours according to Steam before beating all the “easy” levels in the game. Still working on beating the “medium” and “hard” levels.
If you haven't read my first review of the demo version then please go here first before reading:
-INITIAL THOUGHTS-
When I first reviewed this game I really disliked the default moving mechanic in which the player moved continuously in the direction of the mouse. Since then though, the full release has switched to WASD controls as the main movement mechanic with the mouse direction as a secondary moving option. I feel that just this small change alone drastically changed the overall quality of Onion Force for the better. Not only is it easier to control your character now, but it greatly helps the player maneuver out of unfavorable situations.
One more thing I wanted to mention was that although this game is a Tower Defense game, it also has many features of an RPG game and should be played as much. I found that certain levels that are too hard at first become way easier after leveling up your characters a bit and I would recommend treating the game as an RPG in addition to being a Tower Defense game.
-PRESENTATION-
I still highly appreciate the quality of the graphics and the variety of music in Onion Force, but after beating the game I’ve found the story to be rather lacking. Yes, this game does a nice job of telling bits and pieces of the story in between levels and spreading out relevant information throughout the game but in the end I feel that there are still many questions that are left unanswered. Without spoiling much, I found myself wondering: How did your team get chosen to protect the king? Who is Lawst related to, or better yet why did he start killing off kings in the land? These questions and a few more are left without answers by the end of the game and there doesn’t seem to try to answer them anytime in the game. Despite my feelings towards the ending and plot holes, I still found the overall presentation to be wonderful and I still believe Onion Force is a great game that I has a nice universal story with interesting plot twists that keep the player engaged.
The visual representation of the enemies are very well thought out and I felt that there was a nice variety of enemies with many different characteristics. I also liked the varying locations that the player has to traverse through in order to progress through the game. The music also flows really well with the game and helps to amplify the tone of each area in the game. Other than the holes in the story, I really had no other problems with the presentation of Onion Force.
-ENGAGEMENT/GAMEPLAY-
There are many reasons that a player may be engaged in Onion Force. The obvious reason would be to complete all the levels and beat each of them on all levels of difficulty. Easy mode alone can be challenging before leveling up your character and Medium and Hard modes seriously tests the player’s skills. However, I can see players becoming engaged because of a particular challenging level, because the player is trying to beat their high score on a level, or because they are trying to level up their characters to a certain level before moving on. Aspects such as the leveling up and having health and mana is what makes this game somewhat an Action RPG in my mind even though the game mainly functions as a Tower Defense game. As for gameplay, I really especially liked the difficulty of the game and the overall tower mechanics. Much like other Tower Defense games, you have to spend a limited amount of money on towers that help to defeat enemies in some way and you earn more money by defeating enemies. For the most part I liked the variety of towers but I feel that the “chance” tower is a little overpowered in comparison to the rest. Sure you aren’t sure what perk you are going to get but it seems that the only negative result is rolling a 1. Not to mention that by increasing the level of the chance tower, increases the number of die rolled at a time which allows for stacking multiple effects on the enemy. Other than that I would say the game is fairly balanced in difficulty but power-ups, special equipment, or perks are needed in some situations. I really like the random special equipment feature. It helps to keep players from experiencing the exact same style of gameplay. In the demo version I mostly used equipment that sped up my wizard but the one of the first items I got this time around was arrows that poisoned the enemy. Needless to say I played as the bowman more this time around and I feel that having the items be randomized like that helps to keep the game interesting and fun.
-OVERALL-
I actually would be happy after spending money on this game. Not only is it fun and challenging but it also the game is good from both a visual and mechanical point of view. I would highly recommend playing with a separate mouse and keyboard though for anyone who plays game with a mousepad. Though rare, those people do exist and I warn you that the game will become very frustrating if you attempt to play this game without a mouse. I wanna preface this review by sayin' that I
Laura Shigihara and her work. Honestly, over my past few years as a 'gamer' Laura has always provided great songs and contributed many great tracks to multiple games.
With that said, let's begin.
Rakuen, on the surface, seems like your typical 'RPGMaker' Game, the graphics aren't the greatest and the gameplay mechanics are basic and simplistic, like I said, a typical RPG of this nature.
But by no means does this mean
is a bad game, in fact, I dare say, this is one of my most cherished Games of all time hands down. If not, one of my favorite RPG games of all time. Why? because it does things right.
As said before, it's mechanics are your typical pixelated game and the mechanics left much to be wanted.
But they're not what makes this game so good. What makes this game so good is the emotionally-rich story within the game that is masked by the visuals.
Not only that, but the soundtrack, is masterfully crafted, the 'lullaby' style theme prevalent in many of Laura's works carry the emotional setting and tone of the events in the game well.
This is a perfect example of a 'balance' with the two aspects of the game complimenting each other rather than 'competing' one another to provide the player with a fantastic experience.
I often found myself crying every 5 minutes because of the songs playing in the background as I experience this wonderful journey.
But it's not without its flaws. The game often asks of you mundane tasks that are very 'repetitious' and requires constant back-tracking to complete.
But that can be easily over-looked not only because of the variety of them but also because they are short and sweet.
Most people say this is where the game shines the most and I agree to a certain extent, the way Laura used her wit and creativity to overcome the technological limitations is interesting and doesn't cheapen the experience at all.
*Also, I can definitely say without a doubt this game will make you cry. That's no understatement, this game will try it's hardest to play your heart like a fiddle so a tissue box on-hand is recommended.*
I'll end the review here because if I go on I'll end up going to *spoiler* territory, but to leave on a high note,
Especially if you're the type to have loved games like Undertale and To the moon, this game will definitely provide.
A round of applause and praise for Laura Shigihara on her efforts and Passion as a contributor to the gaming world, well-done, and Thank-you!
9.7/10

This is a great game for any Euro Truck Simulator (ETS) fans.  While ETS focuses on endurance driving and the freedom of trucking, Trucks and Trailers (T&T) focuses on the technical side of things.
T&T is basically a collection of complicated trucking scenarios which are organized as mini-games.  It is very similar to Scania Truck Driving Simulator.  Challenges range from parking in small confines, navigating through tight corners, and mastering brake control.  The goal is to complete the task without causing damage to your vehicle.  This can be a lot of fun for truck enthusiasts, and there is little doubt that one’s trucking skills will improve.
SCS decided to award Gold, Silver, and Bronze medals based on completion time.  A good driver should have no problems achieving the Silver medal for most challenges, but the Gold times require slightly rushed maneuvers that should never be attempted in real life.  Achieving Gold often requires many attempts, even for the best drivers.  It adds a nice challenge, but in real life, parking isn’t supposed to be a rushed process.
Don’t expect much replay value on this game - unless you want to repeat the challenges over and over.  Despite this, the challenges will take you a fair amount of time (I am still working through them).  If you can get this on sale for less than 5.00 USD, it’s a fun little game to have.  A steering wheel or controller is recommended, but the default K&M controls are more than sufficient.
Expect this game’s graphics to be somewhere between ETS1 and ETS2.  It looks quite nice, and most low to medium spec PCs should have no problems running this.  You’ll probably get a higher FPS on this game compared to ETS2.
For the features it has, and its price point, this is a great game.

Half-Minute Hero isn't a bad game by any means, and is in fact, quite a novel experience. At least, for the first few hours.
The game has a good amount of content, but every level basically plays like the last, and it doesn't have any other redeeming to qualities to make-up for that fact (such as sharp dialogue, for example). So what you're left with might be a monotonous slog that is helped along by, at best, very average dialogue.
The game seems to go for a pick-up-and-put-down experience, and that's exactly how I tried to play it. But even after putting HMH down for a long time, and picking it up again, I always felt underwhelmed after completing a level, and always just wanted to quit.
The other modes (Princess 30 and Beautiful Evil Villain 30) suffer from the same problem, and were -- arguably -- even worse when it came down to being repetitive, and having boring-to-average dialogue. So there are no saving graces to be found there.
HMH is a game that spread its novelty way too thin (imagine if Portal 1 was a 30-hour game), and as a result, eventually becomes a mind-numbingly repetitive experience. It could have benefited from being a much shorter, and sharply-focused experience.

This is a roguelike with some RPG/character building elements. I would not suggest trying to play it without a controller of some sort. (I use an Xbone controller)
Yes, it has RNG like crazy. Yes, deaths can be very frustrating because of being knocked into traps or from a very far height. Yes, it has been in Early Access for a long time. Yes there are apparently very sparse bugs. The difficulty in the beginning can be difficult.
Not everything about this game is apparent or given in the tutorial. There are some functions (D-Casting for the mage, shrines, effects on armor and weapons) that you have to either wiki, look in discussions, or figure out.
HOWEVER, since I had this game gifted to me by a friend, I have fallen in love with it. I love the art direction. I love the multiplayer. The RNG can be frustrating at times, but it makes those good items extremely satisfying.
There could be some improvement on one or two of the classes skill trees but there are updates and bugfixes (I haven't encountered many bugs myself) fairly regularly from what I've seen.
The platforming is solid in the vein of Spelunky (I actually prefer Vagante to Spelunky for a few reasons). The item generation is in the ballpark of mixed Diablo and (if you played it) the mobile roguelike Pixel Dungeon.
The multiplayer is still populated (not extremely populated, but every time I've gone there is at least one game running. It helps to have friends who play too.)
I find this to be an extremely charming game.

Vagante is my favorite game in the past five years.
On the surface, it's a punishing 2D roguelike platformer with simple and fluid combat mechanics; but at its heart, it's a stat-based, skill-tree-building rpg. The two elements combine to make one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I know of.
A lot of people seem to dislike how punishing the game can be. For instance, you might spend 7 hours on a single run only to stumble into a spike trap and instantly die at full health. With perma-death, this is definitely frustrating. But in the age of the Quick Save, where any mistake in a game can be undone by reloading a save point from two minutes earlier, I think it's pretty exhilerating to play a game where actions have consequences.
Other people complain about the how you can have bad luck on a run and end up with bad items, low stats, and at a severe disadvantage.This is also something that happens, but again, I see this as a strength to the game rather than a shortcoming. If I got the ideal items every time and had the eprfect skill-tree, it wouldn't be much of an rpg... I might as well be playing any other 2D platformer.
Other reviews will discuss the excellent artwork and gameplay, but I just wanted to offer a counter to some of the negative comments. I think this game is worth double the price for people who like rpgs, and at least worth the standardprice for people who like platformers. :)
(Note: I have many more hours than my record shows. I played a lot of local multiplayer on my brother's account)

After nearly 25 hours of playing Vagante, it seems funny that I can't recommend it. There are elements to this game that are unbelievably satisfying: Mastering the controls, building up your character from scratch, defeating the bosses, exploring the levels- this game takes much of what makes the rogue-like genre likable and turns it up. HOWEVER, this game suffers from another aspect of rogue-likes in too much of an extreme- that randomness has the ability to cripple and kill your character at any time with very little foresight or control from the player. Here's a few examples:
Traps
Reading through other reviews, traps get a lot of attention, and for good reason- there is no reason for a small misstep or bad RNG to kill a player immediately. While traps do encourage care from the player, the fact that elements outside of your control (Such as being knocked by enemies, or not being able to see an area below you) can immediately end the game is frustrating in the extreme. Traps can be fun, but not when so much of a player's success is dependent on something that can instantly kill you. If the penalty for traps was less brutal, I'm sure they would be fine, but as it stands, that's not the case.
Potions and Scrolls
Oh man. There's an issue with giving a player a huge toolbox but not letting them know what the tools are. In Vagante you find scrolls and potions, but (with some exception) unless you use them, you don't know what a certain color scroll or potion will do (and they change colors every game). While scrolls are generally positive, and using them can simply mean wasting an effect, potions are a serious gamble: poison potions can slowly kill you, and some potions will permanently reduce your stats. Knowing what your scrolls did in advance (because some scrolls can be used to identify other items and potions) would hugely reduce the random aspect of potions, but, again, that isn't how it stands. In most cases, you are left with a huge arsenal of potions and scrolls with little to do but let them take up your limited inventory space.
Cursed and Negative Items
Similar issue to the potions and scrolls, but a little less extreme. Equipping a cursed item means you can't unequip it. Some items severely ruin your stats, making you extremely weak, or slow, or etc. etc. Why they wouldn't remove cursed items so that players could actively decide what tradeoffs they wanted to make with their items? I'm not sure, but it sucks. Cursed items is a lot less of a concern than other items on this list (being that they don't appear that often), but it's another un-fun element of gambling added to the mix.
Difficulty Curve
In Vagante, you progress through a dungeon, a forest, a catacomb, and some sky islands. I truly believe that the first area of the game is the most fair- the enemies are predictable and simple, and they are never in overwhelming quantities or deal overwhelming amounts of damage. If you get hurt by these guys, you know it's you own fault. That's not at all the case with later enemies, who are in higher concentrations, deal more damage, take more damage, and worst- they can stun you or grab you with little warning. If the designers were looking for fairness, they might consider changing one of those variables at a time, but not all of them. While I imagine a more fair game would have a linear rising slope of challenge, the way it is now looks is like an exponential degree of difficulty.
Leveling Your Character
Vagante tries to make interesting tradeoffs in its designs: Do I pass up this enemy, and not get experience or gold? or do I fight this enemy, and risk taking damage? The thing is, most of the time it doesn't make sense to take on enemies, especially as the game goes on. If the only goal is to reach the end of the level, and the only thing preventing you from doing that is taking damage, why risk the additional dangers? An easy fix for this would be to force players to confront enemies before making it to the end of each level, but the game has no incentive to do so, especially with it's current imbalance in favor towards it's enemies. It's almost always better to just try and make it to the end than fight your way through.
I don't want to seem like I'm nitpicking, but these details are glaring flaws in an otherwise very strong game. I have enjoyed my time with Vagante, but there are too many poor design choices in the game for it to warrant any more of my time. Good games should implement elements of both luck and skill, but Vagante relies to heavily on the former than the latter.
