Sonic 4 has alot of problems. Is the game great? No. Unfortunatly not. It does not live up to its name "Sonic the Hedgehog 4".The Physics especially  are not at all like the old classics, wich made them so fun.
Sonic feels a bit too floaty. The Momentum is also really weird, for example running up Hills seems wrong, he essentially can run up Walls with almost Zero Momentum. On the contrary he also looses a ton of momentum when hes turning into a ball while going down. This especially is not at all like the old Genesis Games, where he would increasingly get more Momentum instead.
A lot of Actions also seem automated and take controle away from the Player. Acts are filled to the top with boosters and springs. Enemys are often just there as sacrifices so you can use the homing attack consecutively to skip a pit, basically acting as a bridge for you to cross.
The Music in this Game is also either Hit or Miss in my books. Some Tunes are really Catchy like Splash Hill Zone, Invincibility, Super Sonic Theme and Mad Gear Zone. But others are kind of bland and forgettable like Casino Street or Lost Labyrinth Zone.
Also the Achievement "Enemy Hunter" is completely broken and requieres a certain method to obtain. This was really painful and annoying since you essentially have to grind one act over and over and over again.
The Game also borrows alot of ideas from the original classics and adds almost nothing new to table. Reused Zone Themes and Boss Battles. Even the Final Boss is nothing completely new. They were obviously exploiting the Nostalgia of people who were growing up with the Classics.
Another thing to note is that this Game is also really short. It only took me 5,5 Hours to 100% this Game with prior Knowledge. 4 Zones and a Final Act (Excluding Special Stages) is just too short.
The Graphics on PC seem weird overall. The 3D Character Models seem pixelated even when running this Game with 2560x1600. Maybe its just me but it seemed as my old PS3 had better Graphics and Character Models.
Even tough there are many bad points here this DOES NOT mean that you wont have any fun from this game.
I used to really like this game when it came out sometime after its initial release and even after all these years rebuying it here on Steam I still had a blast playing it. I see the flaws of the game more clearly now that im older, yet I can still appreciate the game for what it has to offer, tough my Nostalgia might have influenced this.
With all that said i unfortunatly cannot recommend Sonic 4. Excellent, hard, and honest turn-based strategy game in the vein of XCOM, etc. You take a warband of character classes into a spooky city and engage other warbands. The game allows for wonderful customization of your characters' stats and you can design a particular warband member
Then that warband member gets annihilated in combat and needs his leg amputated and you have to rethink your build for him because he can't climb walls anymore.
It's an Ironman-mode only game, so there's no coming back from a maneuver, decision, or result. If you aren't thinking about strategy your warband can get wiped easily by the AI, suffer permanent injuries, and you're back to square one and need to hire a few new characters. Do you risk going for loot or a gem and exposing a character to a potential ambush, or do you hide for one round so a few other characters can catch up and add security against a potential engagement? Decisions like that happen on practically every turn, and they add incredible atmosphere to the combat.
It's procedural, so every non-story mission is unique and the replayability is fantastic.
A hard game at first but you eventually get the hang of things and learn to be patient and think
before you act.
There is a nice selection of guides written by members of the community that I found invaluable. They cover things like warband management, combat tips, levelling, which skills to train for X builds, etc., and make many aspects of the game much more approchable for new players.

Wasn't originally interested in using the Steam Link, as I was satisfied using my computer, upstairs.  But with my wife's health issues, she pretty much lives downstairs. Had no problem with installation or finding  my network and it worked passibly with the Steam Controller, but there was lag.  But not just on the Steam Link, but other devices on our system.  So, I purchased a gigabit router for the house and assigned different channels.  The Steam Link is connected to the cable router and all other devices are through the new router.  Response speed improved that I could effectively play pinball games using the Steam Controller.  Was using a keyboard/mouse combo, with an inexpensive keyboard balanced on a cutting board. A great game with some perplexing design issues. I haven't finished Rakuen yet, but despite some extremely transparent plot devices, it's exceptionally beautiful, funny, and well made. The soundtrack and art are fantastic, and the use of more surreal humour in places gives it a great oddball touch... something it desperately needs given how heavy the plot gets.
The downside is that some aspects of design feel strange. There's no sprint function, which starts to grate early on, and so many of the puzzles not only rely on tedious back-and-forthery, but also seem really disconnected from what's going on in the story. They feel like arbitrary obstacles... unscramble a code, push a block, find a thing to mix stuff in even though there are BUCKETS AND BEAKERS RIGHT THERE OH MY GOD. Given how heavily Rakuen relies on symbolism and the strength of its plot and cast elsewhere, thus far all the puzzles I've come across have kind of felt like busywork, particularly the stuff revolving Gemma's plot.
Still, if you're looking for something heartfelt, lovely, and smart, you can hardly go wrong here. Rakuen is still an instant, effortless recommendation more people should be playing.

Heartwarming and heartwrenching at the same time, Laura Shigihara's Rakuen is a colorful experience of a mother and child's journey to cope with living in a hospital. Laura knows how to present to us a cute slice of life story while organically tackling familial and cultural issues. I highly recommend this game-- the music is very worthwhile.

Dear Laura Shigihara,
please let me express my heartfelt thanks for your mailing-list e-mail dated 26 April - usually I never pay mass e-mails much attention, but something compelled me to read yours anyway. And I kept it in the back of my head.
Finally I bought your game last Friday. I can't say I was hooked from the beginning - to my shame, it felt a little stringy getting used to going around the hospital, feeling estranged from everyone and everything. After some days of reflecting on it I know the reason I felt this way - because of my own social exclusion I am experiencing right now. I feel detached from everyone and find it hard to bond to people - whether it be old friends or potential new ones. And after an hour or so of playing Rakuen, I stopped and returned to League of Legends.
Still, after some rounds of League, something compelled me to advance further in Rakuen. I don't know yet what exactly had driven me, because I wasn't very invested then, as I mentioned above. Maybe it was the prospect of a story - most games I play nowadays are sandbox or otherwise have the potential to spread in any direction for an endless amount of time or replay value. I need some constraint, I feel. If you can call it that. I need some constraint for my own thoughts, otherwise they overwhelm me and flow out of me without any sense, scattering into all the directions of the wind, like spilt milk covering wooden floor planks, seeping into the clefts.
I value a good story above all else. Since I am not able to wring some from my own hands yet. I admire you for doing what I cannot.
And a breathtaking story is exactly what I got.
I remember starting crying around Tony's story arc and I don't think I stopped weeping for long periods afterwards. There were so many incredibly strong and meaningful images, elevated by your astounding music, accompanied by your heart-piercing dialogues... I don't want to spoil the experience for others reading this, so I won't put any details, but there are so many ways the fates are intertwined, a song might fit more than one of the story lines, a person you feel is nothing more than a side character becomes the true main character (to me, at least) and it feels enlightening thinking about it and then letting your whole range of empathic feelings take control for just the slightest amount of time - they get so little exposure to the outside world...
Rakuen is a masterly crafted piece of art, an all-encompassing holistic experience that tugged at my soul and made me cry very painful tears that came flowing directly from my stringy heart. The very same stringy heart that made the first one or so hours of playing Rakuen stringy in my own mind. After I overcame my own struggle, your game became something I needed dreadfully at that stage of my life. And which I will value highly as one of the most beautifully written stories in my whole life.
And thus I want to wholeheartedly say "Thank-you" (including the hyphen) - not only for the e-mail I received, because I got music from your bandcamp like an eternity ago, but also for everything you went through to create this game. All the sad nights and the depressing thoughts, all the stressful moments, all the hard work. You as a person are one of my personal heroines - because you do the things I am not yet ready for and it feels like I'll never really be. Which is "simply" doing it at all, whereas I am not even starting. Which is going through with a project that seems impossible to tackle. Which is completing an idea that once just was a small flickering flame in your mind. Thank-you for starting developing this game, thank-you for going through with it, thank-you for completing it and sharing it with all of us!
Thank-you! <3

NOTE:  I received a key explicitly for reviewing Chasing Dead. How I perceived this game whether it’s positively or negatively is entirely up to me.
Chasing Dead is a Zombie FPS that sets on a duplicated earth that appeared near our planet. The US government sent agents and scientist to investigate the planet, you play as Jake who is a marine to retrieve any data left by the scientist and agents in this monster infested planet
PROS
Graphics – While there are few areas that looks mediocre overall the graphics are pretty good compared to the other games.
Plot – While there are many games that uses zombie as a storyline, Chasing Dead still keeps up with the trend and did it decently.
Weapons – A huge arsenal of weapons are available to kill zombies you can even use your arms to kill zombies.
Cutscene – By far the best thing about the game. Cutscenes are made by real life actors which is unique in this time since most games tend to do the cutscenes by CG and cutscenes are delivered with excellent dialogue and sound effects which makes it great.
CONS
Hand Combat – Although hand combat is present in the game, it really feels clunky and unresponsive at some time during the gameplay
Sounds – Weapon sound effects are kind of similar to each other it needs to be fixed.
Animation – For a FPS a reloading animation is a-must but it looks bad right now and I hoped it would be fix in the later patches.
Overall – For its Price Chasing Dead is a good game despite its bugs and somewhat mediocre animation and sounds but I think there’s still a huge potential on improving this game. I’ll give it 7.5/10

Charming story, tenmon and minori delivering as always. As the end of Chapter 1 (actually the prologue) foreshadows a ton of content, I would love to see the rest of the project funded.
Opening - The introduction movie is just gorgeous. I'll always miss Makoto Shinkai's directing in minori's past OPs but Supipara did an amazing job.
Characters - The characters were pretty likeable after a while - Sakura and started off super clingy at first, but you really grow to love her character as she shows new aspects of her personality without the game forcing it in your face. The only character I never really liked was Amano (aka Ange). She was funny for comical relief but her character didn't really make any sense. Part of this may be foreshadowing for her chapter (which will probably never come out).
Story - The story of the prologue is very feel-good - there's little conflict as the player is introduced to all the characters. I'm quite fond of visual novels that establish various relationships between the characters - it makes for a more lively story and more believable story. Lots of loose ends however, simply because once again - Supipara is meant to be episodic, and the lack of readers (aka money) is preventing additional chapters to be released.
Art - No complaints here, pretty standard Naru Nanao character designs.
I vaguely recall buying the Japanese copy when it came out, I'll probably have to go play through Chapter 2 (chapter 1 in Japan) because I need more! You guys should buy the game to get Chapters 3-5 funded!

This game is not for people that like their wins handed to them or for people who can't handle it when things don't go their way because things won't go your way in this game. It's an odds game and you have to play like the odds are heavily against you, because they usually are.
The AI doesn't play fair so throw any notion of being 'honorable' against it out the window. It knows exactly where your units go once they see them (even if you go out of view) and always has boosted stats over your units and will straight up murder you if you make a mistake, so use every trick you can against them. Be nasty, hide around corners and ambush them with multiple units when it sends some poor sucker for that last wyrdstone you left as bait.
Once they see one of your units, they will usually send everything to that location, except sometimes they won't send units that are on the kill list for the optional quest, so use that to your advantage.  You can set up a bottleneck in pretty much any area and ambush them as they come through so it becomes 1 vs 3 while their other units are locked away behind their one ambushed unit.
Probably the best piece of advice, especially for early game, is choose the right missions. If you pick a mission where the enemy AI has easy access to a solo or small group of your units, they will suffer.  Never ever choose a "both warbands are spread out" and avoid the 3 groups split one (for those you can just bring 4 units and make it a 1 group thing). Early game you never want to go 1 on 1 (or worse) with a unit. Later on you'll have awesome units that can murder henchmen solo in 1 round but that takes time. The mission type defines the difficulty so much more than the actual normal/hard/brutal/deadly thing does. Although with brutal or deadly you can get
In the later game ranged damage is really good at level 10 with good passives, but it's a little difficult to get a ranged unit to level 10 because they pretty much suck until level 8 or so.  You can buy warriors that are already leveled up later in the game, so remember that.
If any of this sounds exciting, then this is your game.  I love this game so much more than many other strategy games because it's very difficult at first, and then you get that victory feeling once you start figuring things out.

One of the most frustrating, yet satisfying games I have ever played. I haven't been so addicted since the original release of "Civ II." I actually wake up at 5am excited to get an extra hour of playtime before the day starts.
There is a lot of randomness, and you will die. It keeps you coming back to prove you can do it better. Sort of like "Darkest Dungeon," that way.
Turn-based combat in most games tends to have top-down views and less impressive graphics, which keep you feeling removed and God-like as you orchestrate the strategy from afar. Mordheim feels like a polished third person adventure...only slower. You only get the point of view of the character whose turn it is, and the enemy is often hidden. It's very real and the art is excellent.
After every battle, you get the option to equip, upgrade, and customize your party; hire or fire new members; and sell your booty. Your skill choices are permanent and will greatly influence how effective your team becomes. The costume and character design is very well done: dark, gritty, practical, and aesthetically pleasing. I want to give a hug to whoever designed the Sisters faction. They look like real women. No ridiculous swaths of skin exposed. No gigantic boobs. The leader has a pudgy, matronly face that I adore.
This game is probably not for everyone. If you don't have patience and a passion for strategical planning, best to steer clear. Personally, this is one of the best things I've ever discovered.

Originally I tried to refund this game but I had already played it for too long for that to be an option (2hrs is the threshold). So I put a lot of time and effort into liking this game. I read guides, warband builds, reddit posts and tried to apply all this information. Ultimately Mordheim: City of the Damned just does not deliver an experience to warrant anymore of my time or in all likelihood yours.  This is a big disapointment, as I love Mordheim the tabletop game and was hoping this adaptation would measure up. While there are definitely some things to enjoy about this game, a plethora of major and minute flaws make it overall unsatisfying.
This game isn't hard on the wallet. I got it on sale for $12. But it's a timesink. I have 44hrs in and I haven't beaten a campaign yet. There are 4 campaigns (6 if you buy the DLC races). The campaign is a sparse peppering of special missions that come up as you level up. You level up by doing the unending supply of regular missions which have you fighting other warbands for loot. These are randomly generated and draw from a pool of maps, mission types and warband types. The enemy warbands scale to your warband or are stronger. There is a significant sense of difficulty, you can't screw around or your warband will get wasted. You also can't reload a save or undo a bad desicion so fights can get tense when you find yourself in a bad spot or one of your favorite warriors gets isolated and surrounded. Likewise the RNG system never really lets you feel comfortable or like you can take a battle for granted. The RNG system is fine, people accuse it of being broken or rigged, but it isn't. What it is, is frustrating. Because the warbands are always so close in relative power a few bad rolls can lose you a fight or leave you scrambling to cheese out a victory. Plans go out the window when your enemy succeeds 3 morale checks in a row and you fail your first attempt, meaning you lose. In many ways this is the game's greatest strength. Every contest is so close that small desicions matter, I've played plenty of games that would be vastly improved by some iteration of this approach. Unfortunately I don't think this was executed well enough to make the game fun.
Let's talk specifics. I read a guide which suggested that you would probably have to start one or two warbands and have them fail or become to injured to make it worth continuing. This seems like it would be kind of cool. The stakes are so high that when you finally do succeed it will be that much sweeter. In practice you'll evenutally figure out that you need to build your warband around ganging up on your enemy .If a unit is left by himself, they must make a leadership check or break and run, giving you an oppurtunity to make a free attack for every person in proximity to the fleeing target. This is the game. Surround them, make them run, kill them with the free attacks, repeat. You will basic melee attack thousands of times. There are ranged weapons and magic but don't worry we'll crush those dreams later. Because of the scaling it will never be a good idea to go one on one. My beefed up Cult of the Possessed leader learned this by charging at a Witch Hunter and rolling 3 misses in a row and then getting killed in one round. This would have been funny, if I hadn't put a ♥♥♥♥load of time and resources into buffing up his defenses so this shouldn't happen. This moves us to the leveling up. It's kind of cool as every fight you'll get a few bonuses to make your warriors stronger. This game is full of little micro advantages and disadvantages. My problem with this is that this when combined with the fact that other warbands always scale to your level or above it, you'll never really feel a sense of significant progress. You can devote intense resources to making a warrior intensely tanky or to do a lot of damage but the changes are so small that they will only be slightly different then the generic dude beside them. Likewise the customization is weak. There are few meaningful options. A slightly different haircut or a off color shade of brown is all the seperates your goons from there's. You'll often fight warbands populated with guys who look just like yours. There's no flavour text or background as to why you are fighting, other then they were there. Also don't bother remembering the specific warbands you fight. If you're looking for revenge or to steal back that ♥♥♥♥ing magic hammer they looted off your corpse then you're out of luck. All the enemy warbands are randomly generated so don't look for continuity there.
My leader was a mage and I wasn't getting a lot of millage out of his spells. Infact all the stuff he could learn seemed like a colossal waste compared to him just running in and doing basic attacks. So I read up on magic to see if this was a universal problem. The answer was yes and no. Helpful members of the community were more than happy to point out that nothing was wrong with the spell system, merely that my question, playstyle and general attitude were the real problem. Apparently magic becomes a viable strategy once you get to level 10 and can afford to spend all your gold on spells and talents. For context, 10 is the highest level you can get to. I think this sort of speaks volumes to the type of person you should be if you think you will thorougly enjoy this game. If you think it's reasonable that an entire aspect of the game is useless until you get to the end of the game then sign right up. Likewise ranged combat isn't recommended until your warband has a posse of level 5 tough guys to bodyguard the delicate flowers who can shoot people. This isn't set in stone or a law you must follow. There's probably some masochist out there or someone with 200+ hrs logged who decided to only use spells and guns or something. But after awhile you will get tired of losing and having your people get injured to the point of uselessness or death. Likewise being broke all the time in this game is about as fun as it is in real life. So you will grind out win after win, by swarming people in 3v1s, using basic melee attacks and trying to get them to break and run.
This is the fundamental flaw in this game. For a game that boasts of an immense learning curve and challenges you to eek out every advantage you can, it does everything it can to punish you for taking risks and limits your viable options. Ranged attacks do less damage then melee, have penalties to firing into combat and require complete specialization to be useful. Your spell caster will take a risk to try a spell only to have it backfire, leaving him stunned on the ground, waiting to be pulped by whoever is passing by. Daring flanking maneuvers will blow up in your face, giving your enemy the chance to 3v1 you. These risk vs reward scenarios will tempt you over and over. But the conclusion is that there is no downside to bunching your whole team together and swarming out of position enemy units, it's all reward no risk. Even the special missions boiled down to this. I rarely lose at this game but two of these came when I became so bored with the long and drawn out special missions that I stopped playing it safe. I was immediately punished and a bloodthrister popped out of a closet I hadn't check yet and layed wasted to my spread out team. For me this came down to the game rewarding me for being boring and punishing me for having fun. I would go back to school if I wanted that.
TL:DR - Play this game if you have a lot of time and patience. Otherwise the repeatative gameplay and lack of progression will break you.

Rochard is a bargain and it offers so much. The combat has a lot of depth to it because there are multiple ways of taking down enemies like reflecting bullets with objects or throwing objects at enemies or you can just use bullets or missiles. No method of combat is overpowered enough to use all the time but I've noticed some methods are better in some situations for example I now know not to use the assualt rifle when surrounded by multiple enemies in multiple spots but to just reflect the bullets with objects until there are a small amount of enemies standing then I can easily kill them by throwing the object at them then throwing a grenade or shooting a missile.
The graphic style consists of a nice colour palet of faint blues and greys and strong yellows and oranges, the chatacter models are slightly over exaggerated but hold lots of detail. Textures are for the most part high quality and there are some brilliant lighting effects throughout the game. Rochard also ran at 60 fps at maximum settings on a 650 so optimisation wise the port over from ps3 is good and you're more than capable to play with mouse and keyboard however I preferred to use a 360 pad because I found that it was easier to multi-task moving, firing and appling zero gravity on the 360 controller.
The only issues I had with the game are that it should of been about two hours shorter because it became a bit of a chore to play at the end. Also in my opinion the plot is a bit lackluster but in Rochard's defence the platform genre isn't known for their gripping complex plots even the greats like Fez and Rayman Origins barely focused on the plot however Rochard does but the plot just isn't very good. Whatever I have to say about the story I still liked the space mining theme because it reminds me of the show "Red Dwarf".
Lastly the game brings in new items and abilities often and if you haven't mastered each mechanic in the short amount of time you might fall behind. Sometimes I found myself being overwhelmed with the options I had in combat situations like whether I should throw a grenade, use zero gravity, fire bullets or missiles or block myself with an object, this can be a sign of two many powers and abilities in a short space of time because the player hasn't gathered enough experience with each weaopn or abilty to know when to use each of them at the right time.
Overall I'm very happy with my purchase of around £3 (I can't really remember the price I paid but it was one sale at the time), anyway I got more enjoyment out of the game than If I had used that money to buy a Mcdonalds burger and coke.

A re-release of one of the best Resident Evil games. This has very varied and exciting level design but is let down by being less than the ‘ultimate HD’ edition advertised. Main story takes around 12 hours to finish.
This was considered a classic when it was released for the Gamecube. Does it live up to that high regard today? For the most part it still does. The level design remains more varied and exciting than other 3rd person action games.
As with previous Resident Evil games it borrows themes from classic horror movies (such as ‘The Thing’) but also becomes more action focused (‘Commando’) in the final third. The style of the game is similar to other Japanese action games such as Devil May Cry. It focuses on gameplay at the expense of story.
The gameplay has changed significantly compared to the older RE games. The levels are more linear and your objective is always marked on the map. Puzzles are easier and are only really used to break up levels. The over the shoulder camera is used to make shooting more dynamic and the main focus of the game. There is a large variety of weapons, enemies, quick time events, melee attacks and environmental hazards to make situations feel different. You cannot move and shoot so the gameplay is slower than other shooters but it still feels satisfying to take out large groups of enemies.
As well as the 10+ hour main game there are 2 extra stories for Ada that adjust and reuse levels from the main game as well as the mercenaries mode. This is an arcade mode with a time limit where you use different characters to play for high scores in arena levels.
The main drawback is the technical side of the game. This is a port of a console game and there is no optimisation for PCs. It runs at higher resolutions but I experienced some slowdown when playing at 60 FPS which was disappointing. There are no advanced graphics or sound settings in the game. You can make some improvements but this is through ini settings and mods.
Overall a decent port of a great game, however, It’s hard to recommend if you’ve played before and are looking for a definitive edition.

A parody of the typically slow, grindy, complicated and expansive plotdriven J-RPG, it condenses the game into much simpler 30 second stages. You will need both the reflexes and the smarts to plan an optimal route to beat the clock!
Speedrunners and RPG fans will get the most kick out of this game. It's also a fantastic, fresh experience for any other players interested and well worth the few bucks it costs when on sale.
I highly reccomend playing to beat the >time<, not the game. Go for the gold, and go beyond!
30 secs to do everything sounds daunting, but you have the option to pray (aka bribe) to the time goddess and reset the clock. Kill some random monsters and you can buy yourself some leeway. This is necessary for the much larger stages and gives even casual players the oppurtunity to get through the game easily.
But you're not a filthy casual, are you? You're a huge nerd with the penchant for speedrunning! Enjoy reverse engineering the game mechanics, planning routes and equipment, executing optimal frame-perfect runs, and feeling great about yourself as you destroy your friends' inferior records. Kill those leaderboards, KILL THEM! Many levels can actually be completed under 30 secs without praying a single time. You'd be surprised how the people on the leaderboards got there. (the legitimate ones, that is)
EXTRA DETAILS
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
= Port Features/Differences =
This Steam version mirrors the xbox version. It is missing 1 level that is exclusive to the PSP, but has a different set of 7 stages and equipment (the time beast route). Some levels, items, and mechanics have changed as well; the wiki is somewhat inaccurate in some areas. You can play in the original 8bit style or the new neocartoon look. I reccomend neocartoon for larger resolutions. Multiplayer mode is expanded from the xbox counterpart, but unfortunately very few people are around to play it.
= "60+ RPG Games and Extra Modes" =
The flavor text at the steam page is somewhat misleading. The game advertises itself as 60+ seperate full RPGs; its more truthful to identify them as seperate levels. The main game consists almost entirely of Hero 30 and Hero 300. Knight 30, Evil Lord 30, Princess 30, and so on are advertised as "extra modes" but are in fact seperate chapters that are still relevant to the plot and serve to bridge Hero 30 to Hero 300.
The important thing to note is that the graphics you chose matter in these modes:
- If you play in neo-cartoon mode, Knight 30, Evil Lord 30 and Princess 30 become very short single-level chapters. You'll play different characters with slightly different mechanics, but it will mostly be identical to hero 30.
- If you play in the original 8bit retro-mode, these same chapters become completely different, fleshed out mini-games each with thier own set of levels.
= Bug =
Sometimes entering holes teleport you out of the map and unable to complete the level. It may also cause the game to crash after a level ends. To fix this, you'll have to verify the cache. This glitch is prevalent in quest #22.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Quest #30 (Cursed Hero) is the best level.

I've followed the creators other works for years, so am probably a little biased, but I really loved Rakuen.
Rakuen is one of the best examples of the way games not only tell stories, but allow you to experience the emotions of others. It tells a charming, beautiful, but sad, story about a boy and his mother as they journey through both a hospital ward and a magical land. The pixel artwork is beautiful and the music is excellent.
The game is a little short, but given the weight of the story, I think that's okay. I think I should also say that the story can hit you quite hard, so go in prepared for to cry a little. If you can stand the strong emotions, then the game also has some good replayability in finding the important items and filling out the achievements.
Overall I think this is both a good game and an important game. I think it's worth your money, time and maybe tears.

Rakuen is a lovely interactive adventure story. Gameplay is very light, very casual. Younger players will have no trouble, and they'll enjoy the themes, while older players will get more out of the story, which is deep, and emotionally engaging.
Wonderful soundtrack, gorgeous 16-bit-ish art styles.
Great for fans of To The Moon, as well as Tell-Tale-style adventures that focus on the story more than the gaming mechanics.

I got this as a gift from a friend after I liked Medieval 2: Total War a lot, and I've been putting more time than I probably should into both. It's probably an unpopular opinion, but I actually like this game a bit more than it. Regions aren't just the one city or castle, so there's a bit more incentive to not just hold and wait for the siege as the enemy goes a burnin' through your lands. Some settlements are simply better than others, so you need to prioritize what you defend and what you take. There's more tactics than "charge, hope you have better numbers/units" or "Heavy cavalry all day all the time" - positioning matters a lot so there's more to do than giving orders and hitting fast forward. The sea combat is a nice addition beyond auto-resolving, although it can feel a bit confusing or random in my experience.
Of course, it's not all good. In terms of actual gameplay, the sieges aren't nearly as cool as Medieval 2's, and they're all basically the same - Howitzer/Mortar the enemy until they die if you go on the offensive, or dig in and wait for them to come to you and then hide behind your cover as they just break themselves on your guns and cannister-shot cannons. The AI isn't that great either, without mods - it seems they have trouble understanding the concept of a naval invasion. It's a bit too easy to snowball - I was having reasonable strategic difficulty in the grand campaign as England until I took a few territories in India, and then my economy began to snowball and now I have 40k per turn. Mind however I've only played on Hard Battles/Normal Campaign difficulty. I've had a few bad glitches, usually fixed by rolling back a turn, nothing deal breaking.
All in all, a fun addition in my mind and an incentive for me to upgrade my computer to play more recent titles once I have some disposable income.

I've never written a review before but I really do have hope for this game. However, I'm not going to mention the various other issues that can be seen in the majority of reviews. (many bugs, lack of content, and an unfinished game altogether)
The main selling point of this game, in my opinion, is the combat deck system, in which you're meant to create a unique deck and pit it against other unique decks. On paper, this sounds fantastic, and indeed it was fantastic during the first month or so, despite that being the time when bugs were the biggest issue. However, in practice, this is not the experience you are going to have if you buy this game. This is, of course, due to the "meta" that emerged rather quickly. The game quickly devolved from fighting people and their unique decks to fighting the meta. Now, more often than not, you'll be matched with people with very similar decks that revolve around the "meta" and what moves and abilities are stronger than others. This, in turn, will ultimately force your own playstyle to change, either adopting the meta yourself or tailoring your deck to counter the meta. In either scenario, you're probably not going to create a unique and interesting deck, and that ruins what gives this game its potential.
With the current climate in gaming, it's all about winning because that defines whether or not some people are having fun and the remaining pc playerbase of absolver is just too small to support that. While I understand the win mindset to a degree, it is exactly that reason why this game will not grow any time soon. This is a very niche fighting game and it can be very fun if you fight someone who is also not interested in the meta. Unfortunately, that is a very small group of people in the already dwindling playerbase.
In its current state, do not buy Absolver. That is, unless you're interested in fights that are, more often than not, decided by who can cheese better than the other person. If you're looking for a fighting game that can really test your skills and deck against other people, this is not that game. That being said, the game does have potential and maybe a year from now it might be worth buying, at least I hope so.

I need to say a few things about this game.
First of all, the first day I had it I played it for 14 hours straight as I couldn't get enough of it! On my first character, I grinded her from level 1 all the way to 37 and there's still a whole lot of stuff I need to do yet. Now on to the short review.
Pros:
This game is powered by Unreal Engine 4 so, visually, this game is pretty darn amazing. It's stylized and semi-low poly in a good way! The lighting, the models, the overall environments all compliment each other very well! I was playing it at a steady 60fps on an AMD Ryzen 5 1500x, 8 gigs of 2666 gaming memory, and an AMD RX470 4gb. The system requirements are quite low too, anyone with a modern to previous generation machine should run it with no problem as long as you have dedicated graphics.
Animations are nice and fluid, they each blend together from one move to next really well! I feel like the developers really took their time perfecting the animations in this game. Take it from someone who has used Unreal Engine 4, animations and their blending are pretty easy to do. Also, I studied martial arts and it feels like these animations were done by martial artists, that's how real they look and feel.
The sounds effects are great! I especially love the power of the impact sounds whenever you make contact with an opponent. Environment sounds are decent as well, from birds, water falls, and wind it's very natural sounding and I love that.
From a gameplay standpoint, using what they call a combat deck, you can modify the way your character fights. Each time you battle an NPC or player even and block their moves, you'll learn different moves at a steady pace. My character only knows a small collection of moves and as I said above, I'm still not done yet. Combat isn't too fast nor is it too slow, it's paced just right so just about anyone can get into it. You'll spend a lot of time dodging, regaining stamina, and trying to stay alive while you fight other NPCs and players. The game features a drop in, drop out multiplayer system, similar to Dark Souls. You're also given an option to switch into offline mode so it's just you and the world, so you don't need to deal with players if you don't want to.
Multiplayer has only two modes and I've only played 1 v 1 where you'r pitted against another player for three fights to the death. Again, the game is open multiplayer unless you choose otherwise, so often times you'll run into other players who want the same thing.
Cons:
There's not too many but here's a small list of what I didn't like.
First off, the story is a bit lackluster. You're thrown into a world where you aren't given much context at all. You start off getting chosen from a group of Prospects and are given a mission to prove yourself to the higher ups, fighting to the top and that's about the extent of it. You don't have a journal or quest log, there's absolutely no hand holding in this game. You're expected to know what to do when you first start. Granted, I don't see this as much of an issue, do some research on traditional martial arts :) and you'll see why it makes sense without context.
Multiplayer aspect is great and all but there will be times where you run into another player who just wants to fight without warning and they'll just start punching you. I found myself getting beat on by three people who were cooperating with each other, I stood no chance. This can get annoying, but it is what it is. I wouldn't recommend playing with Online Mode active unless you want to deal with higher level players. I'd say head on into the options and disable it at least until you got some good moves to build a deck with.
One final thing in the cons, sometimes the voice over for your character will go to the opposite sex, it's like the character went transgender during loading times lol. I did find a few bugs with some doors not allowing you to deactivate gate, that's fixed by quitting out and going back in.
All in all, I find this game to be a great experience! It's still early on in it's life and the developers have said that they will be adding more as time progresses.

minori’s Supipara, a collection of five visual novels, the first of which has been localised by MangaGamer, is in an interesting situation. It’s a series that doesn’t quite exist yet.
As the
notes, Supipara is an ambitious undertaking for both developer minori and localiser MangaGamer; while the first two chapters currently exist in Japan (albeit as a single game), and the first of these has already been localised into English, the future of the series is largely up to visual novel enthusiasts.
Rather than relying on crowdfunding as developers such as Frontwing and localisation outfits such as Sekai Project have done in the past, minori and MangaGamer are instead ploughing the combined profits from Supipara’s first chapter and science fiction love story eden* directly back into the series, with various milestones allowing the companies to continue their collaboration and — hopefully, anyway — see the Supipara project finally brought to complete fruition.
Having finished reading the first chapter of Supipara last night, I would very much like to see the remaining chapters become a reality. And if you’re a fan of visual novels, checking out Supipara’s first chapter is an eminently pleasing way to spend twelve or so hours of your life.

If you want to mentally torture your♥♥♥♥♥♥and balls then this game is for you. In something like XCOM a 75% to hit pretty much meant you would hit whereas in Mordheim you'd be lucky to hit on a 95% chance. In terms of punishment Mordheim is really similar to Darkest Dungeon in the sense that bad things will happen and you just have to roll with it, but you get much more skill customization and loot choices to mitigate your losses. RNG: The game. Simple as that.
Its not really about planning, about strategy or whatever. Its all about dice rolls.
You might plan ahead, trying to setup ambushes but in the end all that matters is if you will get proper rolls. 85% chance to hit or 95% doesnt mean anything, you will miss all attacks because this time RNG decided to have bad day. That enemy you flanked and outnumbered will kill half of your people, because RNG will favors him this time. And said half of people will die for good or get absolutely useless due to permanent injures because of RNG. Half of your troops wont even get a chance to attack against that vampire from DLC warband because they will fail all rolls. All your precious weapons will get stolen because your guys will fail their dodge rolls and die. Your units will lose half their hp from charging enemies, because when both you and AI have same range, AI gets advantage, because. And so on...
Of course, veteran players wont agree with that. They will tell you that game is fair and "high level warband gets advantage over AI". Maybe - chances are that you wont reach that high level at all. They will defend system, where enemy warband have same composition and same levels as your own team - except that they wont be restricted by gold and have all those skills you cant learn because you lack money. They will tell you that AI is actually in worse position for picking skills at random - while your own team wont have ANY. They might even just tell you to "get good".
Some say that all the fun in this game comes from losing. If you like being wiped on the floor, then go ahead - you will probably enjoy this. If you want fair game - go play something else.

A very fun game set within the Warhammer Fantasy universe, plenty of depth and customization and all sorts of fun ways to leave your mark, both on your warband and on the faces of your opponents.
I must say, however, the Random Number Generator for this game is seriously perverse, on the verge of being actually bad. Worse than X-Com by a damn sight, anyways. I've missed far more than one in five +80% attacks, I've been hit repeatedly with well over a 50% chance to dodge or parry, and the number of times my warriors have wiffed a 95%, with so much on the line, it's pretty sickening. Not saying the game is broken, but I'm saying there is a surprising amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, not numbers, being generated. I am writing this review after having gotten my warband creamed due to poor rolling, but my complaint stands on it's own merit.

- before: long loading times (so get a SSD, load lightning fast and ignore that problem!)
- skills and progression become deeply interesting only at 1500+ rating, because you may be very puzzled before (I mean that I was)
- before you understand that, the game looks as if it would just "play on its own" and people may find it either too easy or too difficult in the beginning
- developing your warband needs time
I disagree with the luck problem some people mention but that needs further explanation:
To win you cannot just engage a 70 % chance-to-hit warrior vs a 50 % warrior.
A defeat on such circumstances is quite acceptable.
Sure victory is earned by ambushing, retreating, not using all your Strategic Points at once... something I learnt the hard way after a few mistakes. You need to have warriors you can easily use as buffer and others to support the victory, to compensate for the occasionnal stun, etc. Overall fights then often unfold with some difficult episodes but nice story and tactics.
More review:
You begin by picking a warband, and on that part you have a lot of choices.
Some warband have bow or gun fighters and one (the Sisters of Battle) start as a full melee warband with more and more range options thanks to spells later on.
You have access to plenty of classes but some will be unlocked further down.
Overall your warband begins with 5 warband-specific character classes for your party and can upgrade that to 8 classes and more.
In itself, that unlocks many variations in how you build a warband. These variations are deepened further by injuries and every character progression.
After digging the game more I discovered that even if you pick a single, simple objective for a character progression (ie: le's just make him or her a super dodger) there are no less than 7 skills to pick and upgrade for that objective, meaning you would only learn half of them over time. That's for one objective.. .imagine then if you mix that up ;)
About the classes you have:
Last but certainly not least you occasionnaly can even add other races/faction classes to your warband depending on which faction you favored.
Every day you can commit your warband to a battle making your choice on the map.
You bring 10 warriors to the battlefield with others left at camp.
Objectives are random.
Warriors play turn by turn with the highest initiative (ie best Agility etc) beginning the turn.

Every warrior can move and attack:
they have Offense Points (red) to lead attacks and Strategic Points (blue) to lead other actions.
At the end of your turn you can activate a "Stance" that would affect the enemy during his own turn (needs at least two blue points), and your left-over Offense points can also be used to strike back with "counter attacks" (usually needs at least two red points) or to set up an Ambush action. To ambush the enemy, the best move is not to be in an open area to prevent him from seeing you and charging you, but to use houses and indoor obstacles.
You would not understand how to best use the tools you have during your first battles.
Overall the game can be played as a no-brainer in the beginning, it is just that you'll also commit  a number of mistakes.
Mistakes in the game are OK: you can lose a leg, an eye, a warrior... or even many. It doesn't need much gold to replace them. Also, by playing you also upgrade your "Veteran skills" which are warband achievements that unlock powers you'll carry over with your next warbands/campaigns.

Part of the legendary *Civilization series*, this turn-based strategy (TBS) games reward careful planning. Unlike its newer sibling, Civilizations 5, Civ IV allows you to fine tune every aspect of your civilization. For some, this means tedious micromanagement. But for people who like fine-grained control (a.k.a., 'control freaks', like me), this game is much better than (the much-simplified) Civ 5.
The "Beyond the Sword" (BtS) expansion is not only a bugfix of the previous Civilizations IV releases, but also introduces some 'twist' to the gameplay. In addition to the 'Great Generals' units of Civ IV Warlords, BtS expands on the importance of Espionage, and the introduction of the 'Corporations' allows players a 'second attempt' at 'religion', but with more devastating economic effects.
Simply put: If you're not a twitch gamer, but a strategic gamer who likes deep, encompassing games, then this game is for you.

I really enjoy games like Vagante and I read the reviews and was looking forward to diving into a game with RPG elements that had difficulty and depth in a Rouge-like.
The first time I booted it up I was playing local co-op with my two friends and we played for a while and struggled to really enjoy the game despite really fun mechanics, great art, and fantastic and rewarding boss battles. We kept dying and starting over until after about an hour and a half we quit. I wondered why the game got old so fast so I started running some solo games.
10 deaths later I realized the full extent of the issue. Insta-deaths are difficult to balance properly due to the frustrating nature of them. Add perma-death and it becomes extremely difficult to properly manage, bordering on impossible. The way the Vagante developers have dealt with this is by putting instant death traps all over the place. This increases the difficulty by forcing you to pay constant attention, but also means that with one mistake or one unlucky knockback from an enemy you're dead. This is called artificial difficulty and it's a major flaw in any game, but Vagante suffers heavily from it by slapping you in the face with it over and over.
Often games would start wonderfully and feel great due to the art and beating enemies and bosses, then the game would give you interesting loot and reward you for overcoming challenge after challenge, the you miss one pressure plate while fighting off multiple enemies and you die. There is no challenge failed, there is no rewarding glory of death in battle, there is only frustration that you made one mistake or took one bad risk and you ended your game that you otherwise loved.
Ultimately the mechanic is there to frustrate and increase difficulty and time of play, but it falls completely flat as insta-death mechanics so often do. It's unfortunate because the game is otherwise so interesting and fun to play. Until this changes the game is extremely noob unfriendly and frustrating.
9/10 with a reworked trap system, but as it is now I would suggest to all my friends to stay away until this changes.

Okay, so whew, this is gonna be a long one but I think it needs to be written.
So, I prefer not writing what is essentially a review about a game until I manage to "beat" it. For games with no real end (Minecraft, Project Zomboid, Overwatch) this may be up until the point that I run out of things to do or have experienced everything it has to offer, everything being relative to what the makers put in, not mods. With 28 hours logged into this game from periodic play over roughly three years (I know, a tiny ammount in reality but the game has only just become fairly stable in terms of updates and much of my other time, much to my regret, is with a pirated version from a friend) I have finally "Beaten" Vagante. For those whom would like a short version in order to inform their decision to buy it or are just curious here it is: Don't waste your time on Vagante (at least for now).
Now Before Fan Boys (or Girls) get up my♥♥♥♥♥about how I'm wrong here's a slightly longer version: Vagante is a great game that I love but I could never and would never recommend to anyone to play, not even the coarse, experienced, and highly skilled Rogue-Like player. Here's why I feel that way.
Me and my good friend love, I mean really LOVE Rogue-Likes. So much so that we created a kind of "Expectations" or "Guide" to what makes a game a great Rogue-Like.
Now, while this is only our opinions when it comes to these games we think each of these offer a valid point in mind, and thus have only given one game full checks on this ever: Risk of Rain, a game which we have a combined total from online play to local of over 200 hours, a disgustingly large number compared to every other Rogue-Like we've played. So, why do I bring all of this up? Well, because Vagante easily fails four of these, specifically, the four ladder most checks. To clarify lets start with three. The game
with Pixel Perfect Mind Sets i.e. the jumping puzzle before you ever enter the dungeon which nets you the nimble quirk. It's one of many instaces of honestly ridiculous odds. For four from experience with personal play time and online playing no one ever wants to seek out anything truely dangerous for the sole fact that even a little loss of life can spell doom when going into the next level and those that due are often the bane of the part and the precieved reason for failure i.e. the wildling is reckless and draws too many enemies out, then dies causing us to have to rez them or causing us to die and they being unwilling to rez. Bosses (especially in the later half of the game) are typically too much of a bother and the game shifts from a dungeon crawl to a full on hell sprint where the focus moves from slowely taking ones time to trying to rush through without getting hit or fighting to the exit. For five there have been countless games where the only reason I got as far as I did was because I picked up a really strong item early game. Even for my winning game my party and I only made it through because we were blessed with Vit items early on and traded them back and forth while running through. Sure, it forced us to work together and I enjoyed being the hero of the day dishing out stolen vit item we found but the fact that we would have died without it was generally sucky. And finaly number six, easily the most important rule of thumb and too the biggest failure. While many deaths in Vagante are player driven, an equal amount are total and utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥te. To elaborate there are often many games that have ended not due to a player mistake or recklessness but instead and unfair  gimmick (as I refuse to call such things mechanics). Case and point my winning game. My party and I all sit at the bonfire wary but sure of ourselves. I've been pumping shadow to full, and giving myself one point in daggers and archery for better overall dmg. Since looping I've also pushed my Vit up four times and my elusive play style has rewarded me with 120 health points and a full bar along with snazzy armour and some really good weapons, plus some health items to boot. I feel like the hero of the game, my party only barely surviving our inital run thanks to some unfun but well meaning tactics of "Dont't fight, just run, and if you die twice use your skull to find the exit and then lead everyone there". The enemies are stronger but so are we and our team work is nearly flawless. We make our way into the Spirit Forest once more killing the shopkeeper with ease and exploring while loot gathering. The boss is the Plant Monster, my party dives into the fray, with me bringing up the rear. We avoid the plant head though every now and then we're hit but the damage is low thanks to defense and poison resist. everything is going well until BAM, I'm caught and the plant head dives underground with me in it and I get insta-killed. The same happens to our mage and me again when I reform as a skeleton. 118 health (I took a little dmg) to zero, just like that. How is that fair? Where is the test of skill or trial of battle? There was none. I and my teammate were simply killed to an unfair gimmick. The party survived the encounter but my paitence did not and I gave up all of my items, told my new mates fairwell, and now we're here.
Now, I realize that Vagante is still early acess but as is I just can't recomend this game to anyone. I love the art style of the game, looking like a 2d version of my dream game. The score is beautiful composed really setting the mood for the game. The RPG elements are spot on being easily understandable but still complex enough to show off your custom version of classes. Combat, while simple, is for the most part engaging. Crafting is simple and fun to do as minecraft, even though there is little of it. However, with all that said I just can't forgive these other issues. When an entire group of veteran players tell you to run past hard to reach content instead of enjoy it as you would other areas it's extreamly telling of what kind of problems the game has. Again, as is, I can't say I would recomend Vagante nor would I really even play it anymore if I had more options (You win this time developers. I've had and played this game far too long to refund it.) but alas I'm a poor college kid and don't, yet even still I can't say I'll be playing much for a while. Developers, if your reading this please, don't take any of what I'm saying spietfully. I love this game and would like, no, I need you to take this as constructive feedback. I wan't to explore the catacombs and rift as thoroughly as I do the Dark Caves, not run through them barely able to distguish things as I make a mad dash for the exit. It's not fun.

Laura's talent has truly shone on every project she's taken on in the past. But Rakuen is perhaps the fruition of all that work, a game that touched a very rare spot in the heart of any gamer who has been deeply touched by a video game.
It's pretty clear from the premise that we are in for some unique storytelling, but what the summary will not tell you is how much discovering the world of Rakuen feels like the most beloved games of the SNES era. It's not trying to hail back to that time; it's just the sort of game that's too rare these days. Beautiful, heartfelt dialogue and quirky comedy take turns as we learn about our protagonist and the world he inhabits. In all the games I've played over the last 20 years, I have never once played a terminally ill child. This is a brilliant story option and thrilling to me as it's a brand new experience.
Video games are not often tender, but Rakuen is. It has a sense of wonder. It's fully plugged into the human experience and all its ups and downs. And the fantasy side of it is so enveloping that there's never a moment where you don't believe in it entirely. I don't want to ruin any of its secrets, but I will say that the connection between Rauken and the human world is one that left me thinking even after the game is closed. The story is part fantasy, but there's a lot of reality woven into it. Those two juxtapose so beautifully it's made Rakuen one of the most memorable titles I have played all year.
If you miss the quirkiness of The Secret of Evermore and the fantastic worlds of Chrono Trigger you are going to love Rakuen. Surely it was inspired by them, but I think it could easily have existed right beside them in its own right. That's praise I can rarely give to any game – that it could stand right next to the classics and look right at home.

Okay, I more mean this as a "Not ready yet" kind of Not Recommended. When this game is at its best, it brings with it the same feeling of accomplishment that I find when playing Dark Souls. At its worst, it is a tedious, dull, frustrating and empty experience. Unfortunately, most of the experience consists of the latter.
This combat system was not designed for multiple opponents yet the game insists on making enemies agro in groups, forcing the player to rely on cheese tactics if they want they want to effectively deal damage. This could be mitigated if there was a system in place to specifically deal with the people you are not locked onto like in For Honor, or if it was possible to switch decks mid combat if you made one for 1v1 and one for CC.
The Camera, on the other hand, was not designed to accommodate the vast majority of this game's level design. The tight corridors and awkward angles means most encounters are spent looking at unflattering close ups.
Gaining new moves is cool on paper, unique at first, and monotonous the longer you play. The idea that in order to learn something, you have to show you understand how to work against it sounds interesting until you want to actually start learning new abilities. Grinding abilities usually goes as follows: find an enemy with an ability you want, let them hit your guard till you learn the pattern, use your class specific defense to fill meter faster, beat down enemy. If you die before the enemy does, say goodbye to the progress. If you want to learn weapon abilities, your looking at much more tedious process as some enemies may or may not have or be around weapons that they may or may not even use and if they do, you better learn their patterns fast.
Co-op is... garbage-ish, teaming up is fine but you really do need a way to communicate because this game does everything in its power to disband the group. Countless times had me hostile with a friend and having to end the fight and invite them to group up again.
Content is very much a problem at the moment as there really is about 2 hours of story content(1 if you have a good sense of direction), the level cap, and schools. The focus seems to be in the mulitplayer right now so if you are willing to put up with what I will generously call a subpar matchmaking system then you should be good to go.
Just to reiterate, It's a pretty good game. It's just an unfinished game.

Resident evil 4 is an amazing game which started out different and cheesy but then got way better. It maintains the cheesy and corny aspect throughout the game, but for some reason it works really well. Better than any game I've come cross. The action is pretty great and the controls are also great. They take a bit of getting used to, but once you do they are fine. At first i was getting motion sick because the controls weren't what i was used to, but afterwards i was fine and could play for longer periods of time.
My only problems with this game were really the quick time events. The game would make you rely on mostly shooting and running around getting things, and very rarely did quick time events happen, yet when they did it was always the continuous mashing of buttons, as well as changing the buttons. For example, you're running around shooting all the infected villagers, and you killed them all, so you're collecting ammo and such. As you go down a path the townspeople drop a boulder and have it toll down the hill chasing you. It tells you to mash the buttons Q and E and you mash and mash and mash, and all of a sudden it switches to Press R and then T, but it doesn't give a clear warning, so you die. You try several times more and die each time as well, so you pay closer attention, and tehn see that they hosed you. I know it sounds like I'm complaining a lot about a little thing, but it was my only problem with the game. I wish they gave you a warning or didn't make it utterly stupid when they switched to quick time events.
Anyways, this game was a lot of fun and i enjoyed it immensely. I encourage every resident evil lovers to play this because it's so unique and even if you're not a resident evil lover i encourage you to play this game. I spent about 24 hours in game and i loved every minute of it(except for the quick time events)

- - There is PvP within this game, however it isn't really good. If you are looking for a PvP based game, then I advise you to go to another MMO.
3.
- - This game certainly isn't for everyone, it takes a bit of work to get into, so finding groups to play with can be challenging. You have to put yourself way more out there, in order to find other players to talk to/group with.
4.
- - Now I personally dont mind games with bad graphics, however some players might. This games graphics can be hard on the eyes when players are used to games such as... (Skyrim, Blade & Soul, Black Desert, etc)
5.
- - This game is a major grind, since the entire goal behind this game is to utilize the (True Reincarnation system). If you dont wish to utilize that system, then you are better off playing something else.
Looking at the Pros/Cons you might be wondering, "Why...? Why would this guy recommend this game to me?"
Well I will tell you. This game may be finicky, it might require a bit more time invested into it in order to enjoy it, however this game has 2 essential elements that many other games lack.
1. Character Difference
2. Reason to continue playing that character
A lot of the MMOs out there these days lack in both of those areas... With [DDO], You will be able to differentiate your character by selecting things such as, (Race, Class, Alignment, Feats, Skills, Enhancements, Weapons, Armor, Stats, Selecting up to 3 different classes, etc.)
You will also be able to continue to improve upon that character by following through with the (True Reincarnation system). This will make it so a level capped character can go back to the beginning with benefits acquired from your past life.
These 2 elements is what makes [DDO] superior to games like [World of warcraft] For example.
What is it that players from [World of warcraft] do once they reach the end game area?
They get the best in slot gear, then what do you do? They might do some PvP. Then what do you do? They get gold capped. Then what do you do? The game is pretty much dead for you after that right? At least... unless a new update/expac comes to pass perhaps. Yes, [DDO] does get more updates to the gear, and if you dont like to grind, then this game definitely is NOT for you.
Now, im not the best at writing reviews however, I certainly recommend to anyone that is seeking a new MMO, to try out [DDO]. The game is definitely worth a look, and it wont cost anything to just download it and hop in for a bit guaranteed :).

I find Sonic 4 Episode 1 to be quite underrated. Sure, the physics are nothing like the classic Sonic games, but I actually find that to be for the better. I don't know about you, but the physics of the classic Sonic games have sometimes forced me to run into something I was trying to avoid because they wouldn't let me stop soon enough, even after holding the d-pad in the other direction. But with Sonic 4 Episode 1, I can just let go of the d-pad, and I'm safe. Also, I appreciate the fact that the chaos emeralds are not as much of a pain in the butt to collect in this game. Sure, you have to collect 50 rings and enter the giant one at the end of a level like in Sonic 1, and the special stages are pretty tough, but the game's level select makes it less of a hassle. You see, in the classic games, if you failed to collect a chaos emerald after reaching a checkpoint, hidden giant ring, or the end of a level, you could not try again from that same point. But in Sonic 4 Episode 1, if you fail a special stage, you can just return to the level select, go back into the level you entered the giant ring at the end of, and try again. I believe that the two positives I just mentioned about Sonic 4 Episode 1 make it more accessable to more people! So if you're thinking about getting this game, then by all means, get it!

With a game titled "Sonic 4", inevitably there are going to be very high expectations especially amongst fans of the original classic Sonic games from the early 90s and given how the original series progressed then you'd expect Sonic 4 to have more features and enhancements than Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Overall, I feel this game falls well short of deserving to be a true successor to Sonic 3 & Knuckles, however that doesn't mean that it is a bad game, far from it, but this Sonic 4 series feels more like a soft reboot of the original series with a modern touch that moves away from the 16 bit world.
Gameplay:
The controls and the physics of Sonic's movement are generally fine and the homing attack is quite a nice feature which is quite essential for the gameplay given the layout of some of the levels. However Sonic's movement feels a lot more restricted than compared to Sonic 3, for example when in mid-air, Sonic can no longer curl up into a ball which means he is more exposed to enemies that he might collide with.
Levels:
The most noticable enhancements are of course the graphics which has moved very much past the 16 bit era. Whilst I like thr 16 bit aesthetics of the original games, it's also nice to play a 2d Sonic game with more complex and detailed graphics.
The zones are not particularly original and are pretty much updates of the classic Green Hill, Casino/Carnival Night, Labyrinth (albeit with an Indiana Jones flavour) and Metropolis zones. The bonus stage for collecting Chaos emeralds is pretty much the same as in Sonic 1 but with a couple of new elements added. Each zone is split into 3 acts plus a battle with Robotnik/Eggman and overall the game is quite short although I think the original intention of the creators was to create 3 episodes at a fairly low price.
The levels play pretty much in the same style you'd expect from a 2d Sonic game with obstacles, enemies, rings etc. There are a couple of neat twists or elements that adds atmosphere to the game, as mentioned, the Labyrinth zone has an Indiana Jones in a lost tomb feel as Sonic walks with a lit torch whilst overcoming activated obstacles or suddenly the walls start to move like at the beginning of Hydrocity Act 2 in Sonic 3. But compared to Sonic 3, there is a lack of elemental shields, special stages and Sonic is the only character you can play as in this episode.
Boss Battles:
The developers practically reused old boss battle ideas like the original Green Hill wrecking ball but tried to add a few twists which are either quite lame or very effective. I quite liked the concept of the Labyrinth zone boss which starts with the familiar "keeping up with Robotnik whilst the water level is rising" obstacles but then the actual boss battle is a bit like the Final Zone boss in Sonic 1 with regards to crushing obstacles and platforms but you have to use them to reach Robotnik and time your jumps correctly.
The final boss is pretty much a repeat of Sonic 2's final boss but to be fair it gets progressively more difficult after every few successful hits against the boss but watch out for the final hit, if you don't time it right it is instant death and you have to start all over again.
Music:
The composers went for a Genesis/Megadrive feel but with slight modern elements. The execution is better than in Episode 2 but just like in Episode 2, there are some good melodies but the synthesizers used don't really do the music full justice. I like the title track and the first act is very good, there are some other quite catchy tracks in the Casino zone but the boss battle tracks sound like a Carnival/Circus gone wrong.
Storyline:
Pretty much identical to Sonic 1 - Robotnik/Eggman has an evil scheme and Sonic tries to stop him. It's supposed to take place after Sonic 3 & Knuckles but it doesn't look like Robotnik has upped his game considerably except just revisited some old ideas and tried to make some relative enhancements.
Overall:
I'd give this game 6.5/10. It's a pretty solid Sonic title with all the core features that we idenfity with the series but it lacks the charm of the original games and it doesn't feel as innovative as each progressive 2d Sonic game tried to be. The series has gone backwards in terms of the physics of the gameplay but the level design looks quite pretty. I just feel more effort could have been put in by SEGA to make this a truly great Sonic game and I imagine that the developers regret giving this the title of Sonic 4, nearly 16 years after Sonic 3 came out.

I actually enjoyed this game despite its flaws, and I would recommend it to people who detract it without having played much of it.
First let's get the flaws out of the way, since some are obvious. Sonic 4's graphics look lazily made at times, and it stands out as such from the intro animation. The game "borrows" so heavily from the first game as to almost be a Sonic 1 remake, as opposed to a sequel named "Sonic 4" to the classic trilogy. This is compounded by the fact that there is no tails, knuckles nor emental shield powerups, there are 3 acts per zone (meaning less variety), and the special stage is the trippy kaleidoscope spinny ball thing. To make things worse, Sonic 4 has 4 zones before the final boss, whereas the game it compares to (Sonic 1) has 6 acts per zone - and one of the returning zone inspirations is Labyrinth zone, which isn't exactly a fan favorite.
Also, the leaderboards are buggy and have update-lag scrolling through the menus, and the 1000-enemy achievement is bugged to require 1000 enemy kills in one sitting instead of accounting for the total enemy kill counter across playthroughs. The game just clearly needs polish.
And now for the good: Sonic 4's unique charm comes from the fact that it's designed around the homing mechanic, which doesn't feature in the classic trilogy. This means that sonic can move forward and increase speed mid-air, which leads to some interesting platforming exploits. The patterns of floating enemies are placed in such a way as to take advantage of this and provide shortcuts, and being able to home into springs and pulleys are a fun way to gain speed.
Another thing that deserves credit is that each Act introduces a different new mechanic, so playing 3 acts of a zone doesn't get stale.
And of course, the game's music is composed by Jun Senoue so it still has a classic sonic feel with some catchy tracks.
So all in all sure, it falls short of the classic trilogy, and doesn't catch up to the 2D Classic sonic platforming in Generations or Mania, but I was still able to find the game enjoyable.
