(Review by a reasonably long time fan of visual novels with some understanding of Japanese language)
Let me first start by saying that minori, the developers for this game, have previously created my all-time favourite looking visual novel eden*. I can safely affirm, after the 9-ish hour playtime on a reasonably fast auto-mode setting, that this superceeds that game to become my all time favourite art in a visual novel. I'll save any spoilers for the story section so feel free to ignore that section if you're interested in getting the story first-hand. I have completed this (English Chapter 1) story and can confirm that at a reasonably fast auto-read speed, it takes just over 9 hours, which is well worth it for the (mind you 10% off first week) asking price, as the shorter visual novels are priced at around £1/hour reading. I would have happily paid about £15/$20/2000￥ for this game, just on its quality.
GRAPHICS/ART:
As previously mentioned, this is my all-time (as of writing this) favourite art in a visual novel. The game is presented in widescreen 1280x720 (720p) which is a huge step up from the 800x600 visual novels of yore. There is multi-frame lipsyncing for all voiced lines, which increases immersion, and in some walking scenes there is animation of characters bobbing up and down. However, what really makes this game shine is the fact that it is absolutely packed with CGs. Lovely drawn CGs which blend perfectly with the standard portraits. There is a huge amount of depth to the art, and the real draw is how detailled the lighting is, as is what drew me initially toward eden*; there are multiple sets of portraits depending on which direction and colour the light is coming from in the scene, and this really affects the shading on the characters and objects, and this is consistently shown across the whole image. The attention to detail on the art is impeccable. If nothing else, you should get this visual novel just for how nice it looks. Another point I found is that Amano, one of the heroines, is foreign, and this is represented not just by the colour of her eyes and hair as you would expect in any visual novel, but her entire facial structure is designed to be foreign, lacking the large forehead you see in the other characters, and having a longer face in general, something that is reasonably true to life!
LOCALISATION:
I hate rubbish localisations. I really really do, and I will destroy a review of a visual novel if it's done really badly. I can say that this one is actually ok as they go- there was only one (pretty annoying) problem with this localisation, and one small one. Big problem is that for some reason they've localised the ん (n) in 先輩 (senpai) as an "m", and this annoys me. There is no lone m consonant sound in Japanese, shy of perhaps if you have a っ (glottal stop/repeated consonant) before ま(ma)、み(mi)、め(me)、も(mo)、む(mu); even then it's not really treated as a m consonant as it is being treated here. I could understand it if the voice acting was accented enough for it to actually sound like an m but it wasn't so it was a bit of dissonance hearing n but reading m. Small problem is that they rarely swapped surnames and forenames from the voice acting around when writing names.
VOICE ACTING:
Every character bar the protaganist character is voiced (this is not new to the visual novel scene, but kinda a letdown after the main protaganist in eden* was fully voiced), and the voice acting is filled with a lot of emotion and skill. It definitely is at least medium-tier voice acting staff they've gotten. There aren't many names on the list that you would recognise so I'll spare you the details.
STORY/CHARACTERS:
Ah, ok here kinda the spoilers begin. I have not exactly seen this story done before. It isn't a full nakige as you would expect from minori, but I have a hunch that it is leading to it (more on this later). It is truly a novel story, and the characters are nice and varied, each with their own schticks and nuances. I can feel the potential for the story to go in multiple directions just by how much extra detail is given about the heroines. The story in this "chapter" appears to basically be a slice-of-life story, just to get you in tune with the characters and their circumstances. The game appears to be pointing towards a future nakige type development, but this will probably be in the next "chapter". (can I also say that I drew up a genetic similarity diagram and can confirm that second cousins have a reasonably present 3.125% genetic similarity- take from that what you will.)
I use the word "chapter" because this English Chapter 1 appears to be just about half of the Japanese Chapter 1. Unfortunately in Japan, there is only Chapter 1, as the development of this series was apparently put on hold. MangaGamer is trying to get the second half of Japanese Chapter 1 localised, but as always, this requires money. Purchasing this game will go towards first the English localisation of the rest of Japanese Chapter 1, and then will go towards actually completing this series. minori have not made a Japanese Chapter 2, probably for money reasons, and so your purchase of this game and eden* will go towards funding minori to continue this series!

You are Jake, waking up in a plane that is about to crash. Can't get any worse can it? Except there's zombies on the plane that you have to kill.

: The cutscenes and dialogue in this game really surprised me - along the lines of what I'd expect from an AAA game.
: The storyline is really entertaining and fun as well.
: Lots of variety in enemies (zombie in a bikini anyone?) and boss fights.
: I didn't like that after firing your weapon, the crosshair doesn't reset back at the original position.
: Not able to edit options while in game and not very configurable even when you access it through the main menu.
: Melee attacks just feels a little clunky to me.
Even though I had some trouble at the start (you guys may want to add in pop-up help boxes in the plane to help new players), I really enjoyed playing it. The gameplay is challenging enough to give you a sense of satisfaction and the storyline keeps you playing. Would recommend this game to fans of the genre; it has the potential to be great if the game is further developed.

In Chasing Dead you play a character named Jack who finds himself in an airplane that is infected with zombies. After fighting himself through the airplane, he jumped of just to figure out that there are even more zombies coming for him.
Chasing Dead shines in setting a mood right for a horror game. It has superb background music that really gets your adrenaline pumping and keeps you on your toes. Combined with some nice jump scares it really reminds me at the old days when I was playing Resident Evil 4:) And there are not that much games that manage to do that.
The voice acting, especially the dialog between Jack and his friend, is topnotch and up there with any AAA title.
During the cutscenes that you get after completing mission you see real person talking to you. Usually I wouldn't be a fan of that idea but they managed to surprise me ;P The style of the cutscenes really fit the style of the game and they underline the already great horror setting of the game.
The graphics of the game are decent, nothing special but not bad either. One thing that surprised me tho that the game  supported a nativ 21:9 ratio, something that isn't even supported in all AAA titles ;). It is what you would expect from an indie game. Talking of indie games, it does also have a limited amount of setting that you can play around with. You can rebind your keys which is a good thing and switch between preset graphic settings. The only thing that is missing is a mouse sensitivity slider, the option to turn off mouse acceleration and a fov slider.
But that's nothing that they cant add through a future patch, also if you choose to play with a controller then it's no problem at all.
So bottom line is that if you are looking for a great zombie horror game that manages to actually set up a horrifying mood then definitely buy this game!

If you find enjoyment in B Movies, then you wont have a problem to dive into Chasing Dead. The story is pretty straight forward and features a bunch of really unexpected locations and enemies. At some point in the game I'm pretty sure that I killed an invisible Zombie and then ate his heart to gain more health. Hilarity ensues! Also, each level comes with live-action cutscenes that are super fun to watch. I really enjoyed watching those a lot, they kind of have their own charm.
As you can see on the Store Page, the developers of Chasing Dead are also listening to their players. They rolled out several Bug fixes and adjusted their price to 9,99€ which is totally fine for a game that keeps you entertained for a few hours and lets you burst down hell of a lot of Zombies with many weapons. So far I've found a Nailed Baseball Bat, Rocket Launcher, Flamethrower, Shotguns and of course a few Rifles.
The gore mechanics of Chasing Dead are pleasing, as the models of Zombies missing half a face or half of their body actually look very good. I also liked small details, like Zombie heads that stick to your Knife after you gave them a beating. When you run around, shooting mutants and other enemies they usually go flying and get dismembered which is exactly the thing that I want in a game like this.
The only thing that bugged me a little is the AI which sometimes tends to act a little stupid, but then again it's not too bad to ruin my experience of mowing down hordes of Zombies. There also were some issues with the Hitbox, but as I'm writing this it actually got fixed.
This is a very unique platforming game built upon the Unity engine, but is it me, or is the voice acting in this game somewhat tacky?

Extremely satisfying tactical game saddled with a couple of questionable design decisions and a few lingering UI annoyances. Probably my favorite squad level tactics game released in years.
Fans of tactics games can and should just buy and play it, but people considering buying might want to know what those cons I mentioned are. Above all, Mordheim TT players might be disappointed with some of the changes to the rules; I think they largely made smart changes, but purists should adjust their expectations. As for what I consider drawbacks in brief:
The decision to have the AI build a team that mirrors yours is questionable. Every unit has a point value based on its abilities, skills, and equipment. You can field 4 to 10 units of varying tiers--leader, hero, henchman and impressive (a special unit)--in every battle. Their combined point value is your warband rating for a battle. When you go into battle, you select from a pool of missions with randomly generated difficulties--Normal, Hard, Brutal, or Deadly. The AI then generates an opposing team that exactly mirrors the composition of your team in number and tier with a warband rating equal to or exceeding yours, with % bonuses based on difficulty.
For example, if I select a Brutal battle with five units--a leader, two heroes, and two henchmen, rating 1000--I will face an enemy band of five with a rating a bit higher than mine. They will all have +20% health and +15% damage due to difficulty rating.
There are multiple consequences to this decision. The most notable to first time players is that there are no real "milk run" missions to let you learn the ropes. In the first week of a campaign, a combination of fragile low level units, player inexperience, and lack of resources with which to recover from losses means a huge difficulty hurdle. A full party wipe at this point is likely and a wipe means a game restart, given the game's ironman sensibility. The devs have attempted to remedy this by including several fairly good tutorials, that new players should probably play until they can win them, and with a universal experience system--in short, in game achievements can help you start the game with more advantages when starting new campaigns.
Another is the effect this approach has on the sense of progression. Since ordinary battles scale, levelling your units and getting better equipment can feel a little Sysiphean. You will still always be quite outmatched, mechanically, on Deadly missions, whether you're deploying four rank 0 noobs or ten rank 10 veterans. The only exception are the eight story missions, unique to each faction, which have fixed difficulties. I personally feel the game would have benefited from creating districts containing increasingly difficult missions and better rewards and allowing you to complete missions in different areas. The upside to this, though, is that it keeps the game from feeling grindy. You will have enjoyably challenging battles at any point in the campaign and I never feel like I need to grind levels or drops in order to be able to tackle new challenges.
The last consequence is a lack of variety due to the symmetry. You won't have battles where your leader and three heroes fight off a Skaven zerg rush; fielding a leader and six henchmen is always a fairly safe strategy, because your enemy will never decide to take an impressive against that composition. Even skirmishes (vs. other players) don't allow that flexibility.
Another questionable design decision is the implementation of optional objectives and routs. Optional objectives include gathering a certain number of wyrdstones, the game's primary resource; killing specific enemies and taking trophies from them; or raiding the enemy's cart (their homebase of sorts) and carrying their "flag" back to yours. Routing, shortly, occurs when the morale value (I'll spare you the full explanation) of enemies left in action falls below 40% of its starting value and the highest ranked member of the enemy band left standing fails a leadership ability test. Completing optional objectives ultimately becomes a game of keeping the enemy alive long enough to let you complete the objective, since killing them wantonly may trigger a rout. In a sense, the game can feel like it punishes you for fighting effectively, ultimately generating you less experience and less loot.
Lastly, the UI annoyances have been well documented elsewhere. I'll reiterate a short list: you must sit through enemy turns in real time, even if you can't see them, sometimes resulting in several minutes where you just twiddle your thumbs; LoS rules are not always intuitive; your units' zone of control (through which enemies cannot pass) or their occupied space (through which your own units cannot pass) is not viewable while you're positioning them, meaning you will inadvertently cut off routes for friendlies or leave paths through your line to your mages/ranged units open; pre-battle deployment of your units means cycling through the entire list of possible locations rather than just selecting them directly; where you can climb up and jump down isn't always displayed (inconsistently, it sometimes only displays them if the currently selected unit has enough movement points to jump or climb); the order of the different defensive stances (you'll only be good at one if you're playing correctly) changes randomly at times; warband management has a consolized interface requiring you to go down too many levels in order to change minor things.
So, I've ♥♥♥♥♥ed at length about things in this game yet still recommend it. That's because the core of the game is that ♥♥♥♥ing entertaining. Buy it, git gud, have fun.

It would be all too easy to give Mordheim the finger instead of a thumbs-up.
For one thing, this is an adaptation of a complex dice-heavy Games Workshop game so it's likely to be ignored by most and loathed by some. There will be, of course, those who will absolutely adore it but even by Game Workshop adaptation standards, Mordheim's rough exterior makes it hard to love.
Tabletop or PC, the premise is the same: you command a ragtag warband in missions set in the abandoned titular city. Your aim is to grab the wyrdstone, the valuable remnants of the comet that wrecked Mordheim, but you'll first have to contend with rival warbands intent on the same task. This is gang warfare, Warhammer-style.
This isn't a straightforward adaptation of the tabletop game but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Adaptations ought to take advantage of the medium they're being ported to and as a PC game, this is decent enough. The rules refereeing and the tedious administrative tasks are rightly offloaded to the computer leaving you free to focus on battle tactics and warband development.
On the downside, Mordheim's battle tactics and warband development are relatively dull in the first few hours of play. You have few units to command at the start and they lack interesting skills so combat mainly involves positioning your troop, choosing Attack and watching in exasperation as your inexperienced warband contrive to miss wildly. This game will try your patience.
The difficulty is definitely front-loaded. This is partly due to how fragile your warband is initially but it's mostly due to the game's complex skill system. The skill system offers tremendous build freedom -- so much so that overwhelmed new players could make some laughably bad choices. You could, for instance, have a Purifier train the Armor Proficient skill only to discover the character is incapable of donning heavy armour. There is in-game documentation but it could certainly be improved. Build-planning, for example, would be easier if you knew the total amount of attribute points apportioned for each warrior. The Steam guides and the fan-made Character Planner help a lot but this really should be noted in-game.
As your warband gains experience, the game's strengths start to reveal themselves as your trained veterans help realise your preferred strategy. Just as in Blood Bowl, a level-up ding might result in a lot of contemplation because you're not simply improving a single warrior, you're trying to complement the abilities of your other warriors.
Don't get too attached to your highly trained soldiers, though, because they might suffer debilitating injuries if they're downed during sorties. Your Rank 5 Mercenary might suffer a head injury causing him to gawp in confusion for long periods of time during a critical mission; that archer you were hoping to turn into an eagle-eyed sniper is not going to be wielding a bow after losing an arm. Do you soldier on with them out of loyalty or callously fire them?
While the injury system and the limited model customisation serve to differentiate warriors visually, the game also allows you to rename them and even furnish them with bios that tell their individual stories. When you get down to it, that really is the draw of Mordheim: the story of your warband. I could regale you with tales of my Ogre, an absolute beast who destroys everything in his path. I could tell you how he almost succumbed to a sorceress -- he had so little health left there was no green in his health bar -- before miraculously getting two consecutive critical hits to secure the victory. But you don't want to hear me go on and on. You're champing at the bit to tell me about your warband's exploits. That time your favourite Sister was imperilled and how the rest of the warband rallied to save her. Or that time your hapless archer, the one who never seemed to contribute much during battles, pulled off an impossible shot to nail the enemy leader and cause the enemy to rout. Those are the best gaming stories because they're your stories, ones that emerged from your gameplay.
Those personal stories would be enough reason to heartily recommend the game if it were not plagued by irritations. The interface, for example, seems to have been inexplicably designed with controllers in mind. The only reason this makes sense for a PC strategy game is if it was intended to, say, make manual troop deployment as irksome as possible.
Once battle commences, you might be annoyed at how you just can't seem to position troops to outflank the enemy. Can you plant your soldier on this spot? No? What about this one? No? Even grabbing loot from downed warriors can be a challenging mini-game in itself. Can you rummage through the loot bag from this spot? No? What about over here? No? The game does allow you to undo movement in most cases but again, it's plain irritating.
A more damning issue is the AI is, on the whole, far too generous. The AI prefers to send its troops out in piecemeal fashion and since the game's All Alone mechanic punishes units for being outnumbered, the AI suffers badly. This is compounded by the fact the AI delights in putting its leader in harm's way, making it all too easy to destroy enemy morale and secure victory. AI Impressives, the most powerful unit in any warband, continue to suffer from pathfinding issues so your Impressive will be cheerfully decimating the enemy warband while its AI counterpart jogs in place behind an obstacle.
You might even be exasperated upon successfully completing a mission. The game's random missions always feature optional objectives that reward you with attractive bonus items but the game's morale system might cause opposing warband to rout and thus end the mission before you can complete those optional objectives. Mordheim might be the only game that regularly leaves players sighing heavily because they've won too quickly.
The scripted story campaign missions can be irritating as well due to some obnoxious design decisions. One mission features dangerous opponents with regenerating health that might block you from getting the items you need to stop them healing themselves. And to raise the annoyance level further, enemies constantly get reinforcements in most missions. The scripted story missions should have been carefully crafted highpoints for each lengthy campaign -- something to look forward to rather than something to slog through.
(To be fair, it can be challenging to craft story missions for a game that offers so much freedom in warband composition. The player might have a warband without ranged units, Impressive or reliable healing.)
That aside, the developers deserve plaudits for their interactions with their fanbase. They've listened to suggestions, made post-release improvements wherever possible (e.g. mission loading times have been dramatically reduced) and patiently explained why they turned down other requests. This is not a large developer and they're not backed by a major publisher so they clearly don't have a lot of resources to throw at the game but they do seem to have a clear vision of the kind of game they want to make.
The game they've made is not that far off from being one that's easier to recommend without qualifications. Rogue Factor are onto something with Mordheim so here's hoping their publisher gives them the opportunity to work on a sequel with more polish, better AI, better documentation, greater customisation and a PC-oriented interface.
As for gamers, if they want hardcore niche games like this, they must be patient with game developers just as they must be patient with new warband recruits as they slowly gain experience. You're not going to get a Sid Meier's Civilization without a NATO Commander along the way.
As things stand, this is far from being a perfect adaptation of Mordheim but it will do for now.

This is no doubt one of my favorite games in the library, and I highly, HIGHLY recommend it to anyone who likes Action games or Old School RPG satire. The game is about a boy who sets out to save a kingdom and, through a twist of fate, ends up making a pact with the Time Goddess to save the world...which only has 30 seconds until it explodes!
The game mostly parodies people, gaming, and most of all, the classic RPG, and it does it well. The game as a whole is really a parody, making it a point to "Grind, Grind, Grind!" when really getting to high levels only takes a few minutes. While the player only has thirty seconds to save the world, they can pray to the Time Goddess and, with an added fee, can turn back the clock. The story is expansive, and there are multiple paths and multiple endings, as well as multiple ways to go about each level (some story arcs even being surprisingly serious and tense).
And that's just the first mode. There are several modes, some of which tie into each other. This game will last you many, many, many hours, but the best part about it is that it doesn't matter whether you want a game that's easy to pick-up and stop at any point or one that keeps you in for the long haul, because this game occupies both of those roles. Really, I feel that this game should be in anyone's library regardless of whether they like RPGs or not. It's a great game, and for $9.99 it's a steal (and these days you'll probably find it for less, even if you just get it from buying the sequel).

With how good this game is, I would have happily paid $15-$20 for it without question, because Cinderella Phenomenon is (in my opinion) worth it.
I won't ramble on in-depth about the game's plot, because people more articulate than I have laid it all out already. Instead I'll just emphasize how great it is as a story and concept, regardless of it being free or not.
I normally don't like the idea of a "recommended route" because it seemingly takes away the element of 'choice' in a dating sim -- why wouldn't I want to date the boy I think is the cutest first? And yet, with Cinderella Phenomenon, it's so rewarding to do it in their order. Another review said that the game is boring after you finish one route, but I personally disagree. The story unfolds more and more with every romance, clueing you into what the endgame will be, and making the final romance, Waltz's route, all the more enjoyable.
And while the love interests are great, it's refreshing that I found myself loving all of the side characters as well. From King Genaro to Delora to Annice, I adored them all so dearly.
I loved the way the fairytales were utilized, it was fun to wrack my brain trying to remember how a story went in its original tale and how it would manifest in this game. Even when I thought I understood how a curse would work, I found myself pleasantly surprised with the twists!
Honestly, tl;dr if you like visual novels (particularly otomes/games with romance), good character development, and/or fairytales you should give this one a shot. It's free so you have nothing to lose and everything to gain.

For a free game, Cinderella Phenomenon really is good.
There are five playable bachelors, but the last two can only be unlocked once you've finished at least two of the three routes first made available to you.
The developers recommend you play Rod's route first, but that's not really necessary. Rod's route does explain some things, but frankly, he's such a boring and snotty character that it's difficult to get through. Also, he looks about twelve years old, which is so unappealing. Rod fits into the archetypical Serious Otome Boy trope, and it gets real old, real quick.
I liked Rumpel's and Karma's routes (though I do admit I liked Karma's a bit better). They do get repetitive purely because the plot is practically the same, and you have to read the same explanations about the MC's true self and what makes her so special, blah blah blah.
When you finally get to unlock Fritz and Waltz, the game actually becomes interesting.
Fritz's route, for me, was easily the best and most enjoyable. The plot is completely different than the rest of them, so it's actually refreshing, and more things are explained, including certain relationships between characters. Fritz's route makes the entire world and the dynamic between the MC and others more believable. (For example, before Fritz's route I wanted to strangle Delora and could not understand why the MC did not! Fritz's route cleared some things up for me.)
Finally, Waltz's route seems to wrap the entire story of the game up nicely, and his good ending is probably the "ideal" conclusion to the game, if there is one. I did not enjoy it as much as Fritz's, but the story was still better than the first three and Waltz was pretty endearing at times. (Also, adult!Waltz is hot. Good character design, guys.)
To wrap this review up:
Pros
- The game is free, so even if it were crap it'd be worth a shot.
- The writing is above average, especially for an otome game.
- The message of the plot/game is good!
- The MC is not just a pushover, though I did not agree with her reasoning a lot of the time.
- It's a lot of play-time for a free game.
- The art style can be really nice sometimes.
Cons
- The first three routes are really repetitive.
- It seems as if the men fall in love with the MC out of nowhere. Even if you make the wrong choices, the men still fall in love with the MC!
- In the same vein, the bad routes are genuinely just...bad. Not interesting or thrilling or exciting or horrifying. They're repetitive and boring and, frankly, they don't make sense. Seriously, why would these guys fall in love with a girl who keeps doing everything they dislike? (Especially if you're trying to get the bad routes on purpose and just end up insulting the bachelors more often than not...) Only Waltz's bad route was somewhat interesting, and the rest were...blah.
- Most of the time, the art style is just decent (why is every VN anime style anyway?), so if you care about that, it's something to consider.
- Until you play all of the routes, some things are incomprehensible, and the dynamics between the characters change rapidly and seemingly without purpose. This does get better as more things are explained.
- I *hate* how some characters (namely Delora) treat the MC at the beginning of each route. MC was horribly abused by her mother and pretty much everyone is aware of this, but it's almost never mentioned. Seriously, the girl deserves sympathy, not villification.
- No female romance options, no people of color (or, at least, no one who is overtly brown/black). It's 2017, folks. The least you can do is make an inclusive *fantasy* setting. (Karma does dress up like a woman sometimes, so there's that, I guess.)
- Some typos exist, but they're rare and unbothersome for the most part.
In conclusion, I would recommend this game. It's not perfect, but it's good, and Waltz's and Fritz's good routes are worth checking it out.

SIMPLY AMAZING! FANTASTIC QUALITY FOR /FREE/. You go into it not expecting much, like most other sub-par otomes, but the story is so enthralling you never want to stop playing. I highly reccommend playing in the order they suggest (rod, karma, rumpel, fritz, waltz) simply beacuse vaious plot points are slowly given to you and it sucks to have them all spoiled by playing one character over another first. The story is just so deep, there were so many feels, and it's so hard not to fall in love with each and every guy in their path *sob*. Anywho, definitely definitely play.

No joke, this is astonishingly good. Most pleasantly surprising of all is that the story, the characters, and the development of both in all routes are *fantastic.* Let me count the ways:

Everyone (the player character Lucette, the 5 guys, and even the minor/side characters! O.O ) actually feel like real, complete people, with real lives and histories. (Indeed, it's not much of a spoiler to say that the player character is essentially a *villain* at the start, and has to learn how to really live throughout the course of her journey; and all the rest of the characters have great journeys of their own as well.)

The world and magic system are well-developed.

The fairy tales (which are *not* the Disney-fied versions!) and the resulting curses are *very* cleverly implemented, relating to the characters' personalities/issues/etc. in uniquely appropriate ways (and given brilliant twists, to boot).

Every route is completely different in both relationship and plot (and even though there are certain events that are always being planned by the baddies no matter what, they get implemented-- or not-- in quite different ways depending on the circumstances of each route).

The bad ends are downright brutal O_O , and the good ends feel earned and are satisfyingly sweet, yet are often a bit more realistic than fluffy (though the soon-to-be-released fandisc should give us all the fluffy epilogues we could want ;D , and I can't wait for that! <3 ), yet everything that happens in either ending of each route is perfectly logical given each circumstance/choice.

And the way everything builds and unfolds if you go through it in the recommended (really required, IMO) order-- that is, Rod first, then Karma, then Rumpel, then Fritz, and then finishing with Waltz-- is just perfect.

This is *so* good, in fact, that I'd not only willingly have paid full price for it had it not been free, but I actually went and donated to the indie developers because I wanted to thank them and support more of their amazing work.

TL;DR: I cannot recommend this highly enough-- and there's literally nothing to lose, so what are you waiting for? Download it now! :)

I had followed Rakuen’s development for 3 years, ever since composer Laura Shigihara announced she was working on a game of her own, and it definitely didn’t disappoint.
The story is where this game shines. You play as a young boy confined to a hospital. Together with his Mom, he discovers a fantastical storybook world with parallel versions of all his fellow patients and works to learn about their stories. The line between fantasy and reality is hopelessly blurred, but the beautiful thing is it doesn’t really matter – the story’s message is still crystal clear. And the message is truly unique, exploring hope and sorrow in equal measures. There are no miraculous recoveries for these patients – the reward for learning their stories is simply understanding and empathy, both for the patients themselves and for their loved ones.
Another strong point is the music. Shigihara has always been a fantastic composer, and this might be her best work yet. The vocal songs are beautiful, heartwarming, and sorrowful all in one, while the other tracks are a bit bouncier. The story wouldn't have nearly the same emotional impact if it wasn't for the music.
The areas the game suffers most in are all related to its engine, RPG Maker. Though the character artwork is great, the sprites themselves are usually not stellar. Movement is quite sluggish, with no option to speed things up. And the resolution is totally broken, letting you only choose between a super small window and full-screen with the edges cut off. None of thees issues are gamebreaking but they do pull you out of the experience from time to time.
Despite that, I can heartily recommend this game for anyone who likes a slow, emotional story. The To the Moon comparison is apt, as both games scratch the same itch. It mmight not be flashy, but this game is still not to be missed,

Rakuen Review (NO SPOILERS)
When you become really passionate and engrossed in playing several types of video games, you come to a point where you start to experience something called "The Void". The Void is the feeling you get when you experience a game that's SO incredibly good in every single way, that you truly believe that you'll never again play a game as good as the one you've just discovered. The game was so perfect and so magical, that it made a lifelong lasting impression on you that you're never going to forget. It surpasses everything you've seen before it, and you don't think anything you'll see in the future will ever top that. It goes without saying that Rakuen most definitely made me feel The Void.
When Laura Shigihara (also known as Supershigi) first announced Rakuen back in 2014, the trailer alone was enough to tell me that this was going to be an incredibly special game. I've had a lot of times where I buy a game just because of the box art. I just have a feeling that the game will be good, and 9 times out of 10, that method has never disappointed me. It's actually how I discovered my favorite game of all time, NiGHTS: Journey of Dreams. But when seeing Rakuen's trailer, I didn't just think it would be good. I truly believed that it would turn out to be one of my favorite games of all time. And I just HAD to play it.
Fast forward a few years, and Rakuen has finally been shared with the world. Right off the bat, you're able to see that this game is going to be a very emotional experience. But it's actually very surprising in just how many different types of emotions it manages to make you feel. Something that's important to acknowledge is that its not just a compilation of sad stories. They're stories of how to recover from sad events. You'll get attached to these characters and feel heartbroken for the things that they go through, for sure. But you'll also get such wise and powerful advice on how to recover from times like these, if you by any chance can relate to any of these characters. It gives hope in an environment that first appears to be seemingly hopeless. Rakuen will not only make you cry with its sad moments, but feel hopeful and inspired with their conclusions. Not only that, but there's tons of bright and hilarious moments that'll make you laugh out loud, as well as a lot of dark and suspenseful moments that'll truly frighten you. In short, this game has everything.
Now let's move onto the art of this game. I know I'll get a lot of hate for saying this, but I'm usually not that big a fan of pixel graphics. I've just sorta had my fill of them and kinda get underwhelmed, while everyone else around me is going "ERMAHGERD! PIXEL NOSTALGIAAAAA!" But despite this, Rakuen manages to impress me IMMENSELY with its beautiful environments and detailed character sprites. I'd go as far as to call it the most gorgeous pixel art I've ever seen in a game. It also manages to combine pixel areas with backgrounds that look like they were hand-painted, and it all mixes together so well. The game also has these beautiful storybook portraits (drawn by Emmy Toyonaga) that pop up, whenever a character is speaking. This gives the characters so much more personality and brings them to life in a whole new way. Though, there are SOME characters that have SO much personality in both spirit and design, that they don't even need a character portrait to show that. Those who've played the game will know who I'm talking about. ;) From the characters, land, sea and sky, Rakuen's art is truly something to behold.
The hits don't stop there! Not by a long shot! Anyone whose familiar with Laura Shigihara's work knows that she's a phenomenal music composer! You can thank her for the beautiful music in the critically acclaimed "To The Moon". So it goes without saying that Rakuen has the bar set high, for having an awesome soundtrack. And it most definitely does not disappoint. Every scene becomes 10 times more powerful and engaging, with its accompanying track. Music plays such a big role in Rakuen. Not only in bringing more life to every environment and scene, but also in telling its story. I'd go into more detail, but that would just ruin the surprise. Rakuen is very much a game that's best experienced, firsthand.
And that's something I gotta acknowledge. Despite how story driven it is, Rakuen is still first and foremost a game. So how well does it do, in that department? Survey says... just as good as everything else! The main gameplay mechanic comes from exploring all the areas, collecting things that'll unlock new tools that'll unlock achievements or new areas, and solving puzzles. The puzzles are easy enough to not bring your progress to a grinding halt, but are clever enough to make you really stop and think. They're also very clever in the design aspect, as well. Some puzzles are visual based, some are audio based. And sometimes its just as simple as listening to what the people around you say, and not forgetting it. I really like to think that having a story play with your mind counts as a gameplay mechanic, as well. You'll be trying to put all the pieces together, as you gather information on all the big secrets in this game. And if you were to replay this game, you'll end up seeing a lot of subtle hints that you might not have caught, your first time around.
The game also has a lot of side quests, to break up the pace of the main story. The achievements are simple enough to get and fun enough for you to WANT to 100% this game. Besides, if you do the side quests, then that just means that you get to play Rakuen even longer! And that is most certainly a good thing! The game is fairly short, so anything that can keep me in this world for a longer period of time is most welcomed, in my book. I don't know how else I can say it. Rakuen does everything right. Simple as that.
To call this game a labor of love is an understatement. As somebody who was fortunate enough to be one of the beta testers for Rakuen, I was able to see first hand just how much work went into making every detail as perfect as it could possibly be. It's a beautiful piece of art, in both visuals and sound. It's easy and accessible for anyone to get into, regardless of their gaming experience or taste in game genres. And most importantly, its beautiful story and amazing characters are something that'll leave a lifelong impact on you, as well as help you make a difference in your life and in the world around you. From the moment I saw it, I knew I would love Rakuen. And when I finally got to play Rakuen, it met every single expectation I had for it, and so much more. It's something that should be played and experienced by everyone. I hope you all enjoy it as much as I did. Rakuen is and forever will be one of my favorite games of all time.

I got this game for a cent in a Humble Bundle, but it is easily worth full price.
This game is a "bullet hell" style shoot 'em up set in a creative futuristic steampunk timeline where the British Empire have colonized Mars. It's relatively simple, with only three actions (fire, special, and 'vaunt', which defends you from enemy bullets for a temporary period) but provides tons of depth and difficulty. There are five campaigns and a subset of ships for you to choose your own personal play styles with. While five maps may seem very short, the five difficulty modes will keep you coming back for more; the more chaotic the action, the more fun the game really is. Add many secrets and ship types to unlock and you have a decently fleshed out game.
One of the game's strong points is presentation. The pixel art is absolutely gorgeous. We're in an era where every single indie developer can churn out poorly made pixel art in an attempt to be "retro", and it's seem like we've forgotten how good pixel art can be. The only downside is that it make the action seem confusing, with enemy bullets sometimes being indistinguishable from the background. But in addition, you have the soundtrack, which is one of the greatest video game soundtracks I have ever heard for a game of this caliber. It pumps you up for the action and contrasts nicely to the crunchy explosions you'll hear.
The best thing about this game, however, is the local co-op. Supporting up to four players, the game can be played with a mouse, keyboard or controller, and is absolute tons of fun. In co-op play, greater strategy is required through the use of collecting one-ups, but in exchange it allows for greater firepower in the hectic stages. Combine this with a high difficulty and you have some of the most fun you'll ever experience in a shoot em up game, ever. I strongly recommend this for fans of shoot 'em games, especially bullet hell shooters such as
, but everybody needs to give this game a try.

Resident Evil 4 or Biohazard 4 as it's known in Japan is a survival horror game with light action elements. It's a classic, you've heard about this before and for good reason. The plot is rather campy with a lot of B Movie influence, but it really plays off this well with charismatic characters often putting a light hearded spin on dire situations. The gameplay serves to put the player in control, but making it just a bit bulky so you never feel too powerful and really feel the strength of the enemies you're up against. The sound design definitely works in favour of RE4, where guns are loud and pack a real punch, while melee attacks are cruncy and visceral. Everything just works in RE4 and when brought together as a whole, it provides a game with a lot of content (A 16 hour main campaign, 4 hour long extra campaigns and the added Mercenaries mode which can be replayed) and a worthwhile campaign.
All in all, I'd say this game is as close to perfect as you can get. It's a fun game, with a fantastic story and memorable characters. I'd give this a hearty reccomendation and anyone who is even remotely intrigued should give it a go!
EDIT: Do note the extra campaign has FMV cutscene renders from the PS2 game, so they'll be in an extremely low resolution and it doesn't come with English subtitles.

I need to say that I didn't want to make this a thumbs down review. It's really more of an "eh it okay" situation, a 40/100 to be technical. I've compared this game to two others in the series: Medieval II, which came before, and Napoleon, which came after. Both of which I played before getting into Empire.
TLDR: the game is really big and has very few good factions but it is still midly enjoyable and certainly a challenge. Buy Napoleon first, maybe as a bundle like I did.
A common issue people have with Empire is the size. I'm all for ambition and Empire certainly is ambitious, but by no means does that make it good. I can't even begin to play in a scenario surrounded by enemies like France or the Netherlands while at the same time managing the colonies. True, Britain did it well in real life, but I'm not exactly Victorian England's top minister now am I? I doubt anyone playing is. This is where Napoleon learned to keep things central, which makes managing easier and lets me focus on the battles and offense (not worry about defending Louisiana, Paris, and all the shipping lanes in between at the same time) I was still able to succeed in India where competition is sparse and land fertile, but there's no way I'll become a European power any time soon.
I'll another MAJOR issue plainly: They got their history wrong, multiple times in fact. Examples like Mysore, a minor faction in India, being non-playable and feeble despite historically ruling India until 1950 (British puppets but still a powerhouse indeed) are bad enough, but the biggest mistake was in the American Campaign at the start of the Revolution. It begins with the player commanding the American rebels atop Bunker Hill facing off against British Gen. Howe and coming out victorious-- OH but there's one big problem: The Americans didn't win Bunker Hill. The militias ran out of ammo midway through the battle and surrendered. Anyone who so much as glances through an American history book would know that. True, they were martyred by the American rebellion so it was a morale victory, but the battle itself went to Britain. Making such a simple error in their historical content really calls into question everything else the game puts forth. I wouldn't cite this game as a reliable source of information.
The AI to me is a lot more like Medieval II's poor decision-making than Napoleon's AI. In Medieval, you'd get upstart states just randomly jump your regions without any real provocation or reason, and that means you have to throw a lot of money into defense for these AI lapses in judgements, and once you're at war they don't surrender until their last city or obliteration. The same thing happens in Empire. Playing the American campaign I would be on a roll against the Brits until some maurading Spanish or Dutch fleet lands in the New York Harbor and mucks it all up, despite being friends and trade partners. Playing as India I would keep having to fend off futile invasion attempts by Persia, despite the Ottomans sucking up their territory on the opposite side of the country, which should warrant more attention by the AI. When they do finally try diplomacy they ask for a lot for very little. There's no way I was going to give the Mughals their old capital and 3 regions back just to declare a ceasefire, but that's the deal the AI actually sent me. It's very hard to negotiate with the AI because of how high the price of peace is. This just doesn't seem smart to me. I like playing with Napoleon's logical AI and one that is not be a pain-in-my-side without good reason.
A major problem that made me change tactics from other games is that unlike Napoleon you can't liberate regions. I found that trick very helpful, as you can just set up a protectorate, take in protection money, and keep moving your giant army from region to region without stopping, kind of like an early 1800s Blitzkrieg. You don't have to stop and suppress the new region and go years without going on the offensive again, which is what I had often while playing Empire. I made do by splitting up armies and bringing larger invasion forces to compensate, but it is much more expensive and time consuming than Napoleon's Liberation tactics.
For one good thing, Empire has a much more important technology tree than Napoleon. Tech like land rotation and bayonet advancements make the technology tree a lot more useful than Napoleon's, and they have further reaching consequences which is nice too.
DLC for this game varies in quality. The unit ones are actually pretty nice. I like the units that can only be recruited in one region or under set conditions like the Dahomey Amazons and the Swiss Guard. It makes the units and regions feel more unique and important.
Now the Warpath campaign on the other hand is a very different story. It suffers from the same setbacks that Medieval II's Americas expansion and Napoleon's Peninsular War DLC has: gameplay for Total War is not meant for guerilla fighting. Even using the best warriors the Native tribes have to offer they just can't beat Europeans at their own game. Firing lines and close-rank formations are the European style of combat used since the times of Rome and Greece, and work well against other close-rank firing lines. However, that isn't how Guerilla fighting works. You can't make unarmored and out-gunned Native American bowmen stand in a line against Europe's open-fighting musketeers. The Muskets will win everytime even with overwhelming numbers. Total War just can't accomodate Native American style-ambush fighting. The Natives also have a slow and not-very-useful tech tree compared to Europe that doesn't do much to change the outcome of the economy or the battles. Buildings are limited, and getting money is very difficult as a Native Nation. Honestly all you can do is wait for the better-armed, wealthier colonists to march in and wipe you out, which will still take 2-3 turns by the way because the American map is a whole lot of barren land.
All in all, I am able to scratch out some fun playing Empire as centralized factions like Poland and India, but unlike Napoleon or Medieval 2 I just can't imagine playing this for a long time as all the factions.
If there would be more regions, than it would be great. Now it's just very good. Despite of this, I love this historical setting very much.

Pretty usefull peice of hardware. Good for streaming some of the games I like to play, and when you minimize big picture mode, you can just stream your desktop, meaning you can watch netflix/hulu/movies from your pc on your TV with just your Steam Link.

Overall it is a fine addition to my setup, worth considering for yours. My notes that you may find useful:
- Samsung includes a version in their smart TVs now. Pretty sure all criticisms still apply, just one less box and cable. Check your TV first before buying. See the forums.
- Need to have wired Ethernet to the router (or an ethernet powerline adapter network) for BOTH the Steam PC and the Steamlink because over wifi, most games are frustrasting at best, most unplayable. I used a 100Mbps pair for my testing.
- Interface is smooth, setup is a breeze. Device takes over your PC but does not lock you out, so you can always go to your PC and fix anything that doesn't respond (not uncommon on non-controller supported games)
- Uses steam controller just fine, but has no built in bluetooth. Uses Xbox controllers fine if they are wired, or if paired with a bluetooth dongle.
- Basically a set-top box that gives you very fast streaming coupled with shared-screen computing to give you control of your Steam app on any device this is plugged into.
- connection is HDMI out, three USB-A ports. No testing with dual controllers yet but it should handle multiple channels fine; it is supposed to uspport keyboard and mouse.

(Only recently installed through Steam, I have at least a few thousand hours logging in directly through the client and several characters at level cap).
The core game is very good, but the actual experience is plagued with bugs, performance issues and questionable management. Play for free for a while, then decide if you want to commit.
- Gameplay: Positional, third person action RPG based on D&D rules. All the main classes and races are here, and they play as you would expect from the pen and paper (but obviously with different skills and powers due to the different natures of the games). Gameplay is fast, rewards correct positioning and physically dodging attacks and spells is not only viable, but often required. It's more than just amassing big number, even though that's obviously the main goal and the measure of progression.
- Customization: The main strenght of the game. You can mix and match up to three classes on each character, and (almost) each class has 3 skill trees to pick from. No other restricions apply. You can melee with a mage, throw shurikens with a paladin or wield greathammers with a gnome warlock. Tons of loot, (frankly too many) crafting systems and special, named items from various quests. Many cosmetic choices for armor and helmets, not so much for the rest of the equipment.
- Longevity: Over 400 quests (see Business Model below) and a couple dozen raids, which means you can play hundreds of hours to fully explore all content. Quality of course will vary: some revamped classic modules are really good (Haunted Halls of Eveningstar), while many older quests are a bit bland, grey and uninteresting. The main trick however is reincarnation: get to level cap and start again from scratch, with small incremental benefits and the ability to completely reshape the character (including race, class, skills, appearance). The game is based around the concept of performing several reincarnation, growing progressively in power as those boni stacks and you ammass a larger stash of equipment.
- Business model: The premium currency can be earned ingame, so in theory you could experience the entirety of the game for free. That's one of the fairest business models I've encountered, as far as content goes. Turbine, however, is pretty obviously warping a few mechanics around the shop, sadly: a few crafting systems (including some raid rewards) can be bypassed with cash, and the difference is noticeable. I'm ok with convenience and cosmetics (bank space, character slots, cosmetic items, xp boosts), not so much with buying raw power, raw xp and in general progressing without running the content.
- The bad: The game is 10 years old and it shows. It's not graphically impressive, animations are generally bad and you can count polygons on most environments. It's also obviously built on spaghetti code, and every update something completely unrelated breaks and is even fixed way too late, fixed partially or left there. I've experienced crippling lag. I've died for no reason while walking. I've had the game eat my ingredients without rewarding me. I've heard of people losing items while banking them. You need to learn all the quirks of the game and play around them (as in "kill this now or we'll lag out and fail", or "don't use the bank in this area").
My suggestion is to roll a couple of characters, experience the free content as long as one can, buy a couple of adventure packs with the ingame currency earned and by that time you will realize if you want to keep playing. It's a shame a good game is plagued by technical issues and questionable design choices, but what is unacceptable for someone who's been playing for 6 years may be unnoticable to a new player. There is no risk in trying it out.

Well lets get started now. Chasing Dead is a FPS/Sci-Fi Horror game. It's got a unique story.
The story overall was quite cool and it drew me in as I like Zombie games and I'm willing to try a new one out. The alternative universe twist was quite tempting and I couldn't help it, there are a lot of cutscenes to begin with but it's for character development which this game does quite well.
Combat in the game was pretty good, and the weapon selection was quite nice. The boss was quite interesting and fun to play against. There are a few glitches here and there but nothing a patch can't fix. The detection on picking up items was a bit weird, but once again can be easily fixed. The visuals are good looking, and the guns sound good too.
Overall this game is quite fun, and if the developers continue to stick with and support the game, it can be pretty good. I didn't encounter many issues, but thats just me game was fun definitely worth the price.

FPS that has an ambitious story line that I really like but it does come with a few warts.
The zombie angle was the first thing to draw me in as I am a fan of the genre but the idea of an alternate Earth showing up on our doorstep was too good of a story line to resist. The game starts with many cutscenes which develop the story but you soon find your character Jake heading to the alternate earth where he immediately finds action in the form of a zombie infested plane.
The combat was decent although controller support should now be automatic for this type of game and I was shocked to see it missing. Great weapon selection although on the plane there seemed to be a few too many autmatic weapons lying around for a commercial flight. :) The plane boss was unique as it phased in and out almost Predator like which was challenging.
My major beef is that the game is glitchy. I lost count of how many zombies were stuck in seats or in walls and I also found that simple tasks like picking up weapons are hit and miss. Sometimes you have to be pointed in precisely the right direction to grab something which can be frustrating when you have attackers coming at you from 3 different directions.
Graphics are good and sound effects are ok although gunfire sounds a little off to me. The inclusion of hot looking women thoughout the game doesn't hurt this games cause any. :D
Conceptually Chasing Dead is a breath of fresh air but it suffers from some playability issues which can be overcome if the developers continue to stick with and support the game. Clean up the glitches... add controller support and they could have something special here. Keeping my fingers crossed that this happens.

Auch klassische Elemente wie Bosskämpfe oder Gesundheitsbehälter von toten Gegnern, bringen einen schon einmal in schwitzen, selbst auf niedrigem Schwierigkeitsgrad. Es gibt viele Gegnertypen und möglichkeiten diese zu töten. Von Fusstriten, über div. Schusswaffen bis zum Flammenwerfer ist alles dabei.
Wirklich erstaunt, hat mich dass sie echte Schauspieler für Ihre Zwischensequenzen benutzt haben. Das hilft beim erzählen der Geschichte und hilft dem Spiel mehr als nur den Charme, einer Indie Produktion zu geben.
Mir gefällt es und ich mag Indie Produktion, die viel wollen. Man sieht den Aufwand den sie betreiben.

To the point. This is a brutal game. It is unforgiving and the odds are stacked against you. I would say this is less of a "RNG game" than it is a "how you adjust and react to a problematic situations". I say this simply because you will be faced with many rough situations.
It's similar to Valkyria Chronicles with movement and the actions use a action point system in a sense as well. Many who jump into the game never come back because it's tough, it has a steep learning curve but just remember the Warband is what matters.
Do not get attached to characters. They. Will. Die. They will get maimed and nigh useless. You will be forced into making decisions where their is no "good" outcome but "which is less worse".
The warbands, and their are 6, play differently and have a different feel. Weapons balance is wonderful because a daggr can be just as useful, if not more so, than a halbred. A bow better than a handgun, it is up to you to figure out when it is best to use a certain weapon as well as how to build a character around a certain weapon. This game requires you to laugh when things go bad and to learn so you lower the chance of making the same mistake again (because honestly you will make that same mistake again).
The story missions, which each warband has their own, are tough and should be tackled after you spend a decent amount of time learning the basics and gearing your warband out. They aren't amazingly done and honestly, they can be quite frustrating but they do break up the normal gameplay of warband fights and wyrdstone hunting.
The AI is adequate and even though they do one of the largest pet peeves I have with video games (artificial difficulty by giving the AI stat buffs, depending upon the difficulty) it's fun. The AI matches its warband to yours, so if you bring a big guy they do, if you don't they don't. This way you can't rest on your heels with an all decked out warband, the opposing warband will always be a threat.
Ultimately, the game has some flaws but I believe it is a game worth playing for a certain type of gamer. One that tackles a challenge expecting to learn something. Those who go in as an underdog who appreciates when they make a 30% hit 2 times in a row. Those willing to take chances for a big payout, at the cost of possibly suffering complete failure.
As with most games, I recommend getting it on sale.

Almost certainly my favorite game of all-time.  Seven years after BTS was released, I still play it avidly.  Although other games distract me from time-to-time, I always come back to CIV IV:BTS.
By itself, BTS is a fine game, and a decided improvement over vanilla Civ IV.  But the modding community is what keeps the game fresh and interesting.  Fall from Heaven II, Caveman2Cosmos, Planetfall, Realism Invictus, Rise of Mankind (to name just a few) - all are quality mods that change the dynamics of the game significantly to the point that they are almost entirely new 4X games in their own right.  Whenever I get bored with one mod, I'm always able to find another to try out, or an updated version of an old mod that I had previously discarded.
For me, the most fun is exploring the map and the early quest for resources and dominance. After having achieved military, cultural, or economic superiority over the other Civs, however, the endgame often become tedious, and it is rare that I ever actually finish a game.   I don't have any experience with multiplayer, but even as a single player game, I love it.  If I had to erase all games from my Steam account and hard drive save one, CIV-IV BTS likely would be the keeper.

7.5/10
Real review
The premise is interesting, the main character has their own agency and character development, the cast can be charming, and like a fairy tale, the story does dip into being legitimately romantic (at least if you're like me and are a suker for that kind of thing). It's a little short for my tastes, but at least it never felt boring. No scene felt pointless, and every segment felt like it added progression to the plot, which can't be said for some other Visual Novels. I cannot stress enough how refreshing it felt to read through something that didn't feel the need to drag through every stray thought that visited the main character in every conversation. The counterpoint is that some of the elements (especially some of the romance) seems lacking. Not for every route, but it's there for some of them.
Overall, a very solid Visual Novel. As far as it compares to other Otome games, I can't really say. But in the grand scheme of things, you could do a lot worse than this.

Hello, here is my review for Mordheim: city of the damned
Pro:
Nice and rather unique gameplay for a tactical game, you run in 3rd person view around in the levels. That is rather immersive.
Contra:
Difficulty and Balance is all over the place. You can do like 10 games a win and then be slaughtered hard without any possible resistance.
The start is just too hard. Your warband units are just useless, they can't hit♥♥♥♥♥♥ The enemy units have roughly 50% better stats in every category. My henchmen have like 100 hp the enemy henchmen have 150 in a normal mission, not hard or brutal or even deadly. Some faction like the skaven dish out healthy damage like 60 2 times in row, enough to one hit a lvl 0 henchmen or even hero.
Bad Levelscaling:The warband rating raises with every win or levelup of your units. But the combat performance of your men does not rise so fast. So you are outmatched every battle, the sense of progression is just not there. Why even bother with playing the game if you never leave the underdog status. Even the number of enemies is the same as your warband. If you take an impressive with you you will face an enemy impressive. An impressive is a big special unit. The excitement.
Tactics, The only way to win battles is numerical superiority. Building tanks or dodgy characters is just luck. You can win but not consistently, having bad luck just destroys your team. So you try to attack a single foe with all of your men and hope that you can kill them piecemeal before the rest of the enemy warband arrives. So the tactical options are very
narrow in the beginning. Later it could open up, but skills cost a fortune. That leads to the next bad point.
Economy:
You get like 500 gold at the start to equip your warband, but there is not really much to buy in the shops. After each battle you have to treat your fallen wounded warriors or get new men for killed or crippled aka worthless units. That can happen rather quickly. So a small warband that was doing rather fine could be utterly worthless after one battle. I only played like 20 battles until i lost interest. Wound treatment costs like 15 gold per wounded unit. I had many successful missions without any gold income so far. The items found sold for 2 to 5 gold pieces and were really sparse. The wyrdstone collection does not get you much income too. Like 140 for 75 or 380 for 145. But you spent more on warband support und treatment cost then you earn. A really rough start.
Difficulty:
There are not really difficulty options. You can search for easy missions, but that easy missions are not easy at all. The enemy warband is better in every regard then your units. On hard brutal or deadly missions that gets really out of hand. The enemy units have double the hp, can not be hit at all and have double the damage output then your units. And the difficulty rises automatically with time. Yourwand gets slightly better, even non combat stats rise the warband rating, so your units do not get more efficient but the enemy does.
Ranged units are wortless in the beginning. Even when they hit one time a round they do laughable damage. like 15 hp of an enemy unit. In melee they die quickly. Against some warbands that dont use ranged units often you gimp yourself by taking units with you.
There is no saving option for your warband. Hours of progress can be lost in the blink of an eye.
The story campaign missions were too hard, had no chance with a fresh warband in it. You are expected to grind random skirmishes forever to get a maxed out team that is able to do the campaign missions. So there was no story at all for me only random missions.
I played only some matches but this game seems only for expert players or cheaters, the start is so roughly and seems impossible. Hard games like Dark souls are a walk in the park compared to this atrocity. If you like to be hit repeately and punished then this game is perfect for you. If you like random dice rolls that are rigged against you, if you like untouchable enemy units, that you have next to zero hit chance against, if you like AI getting high advantages in every category that is. Everyone else should avoid it like hell. Not fun at all for me.
Thanks for reading have a nice day.

This is, by far, one of the best otome games I have ever played (and I've played a lot!). The store is so interesting with a unique twist on all the cliches of childhood fairytales, fairies, and witches. It's mechanics are easy to use (Ren'Py is wonderful), it's art is pleasing to look at, it's characters are varied (for the most part) in personality and diverse in appearance, the Princess is a dynamic protagnist that genuinely develops as story progresses, the music is not grating, and the dialogue is interesting (a couple parts of the story drag, if you've done multiple routes in a row, but it's in such short amounts that it's barely a bother). Cinderella Phenomenon made a wonderful romance story, and with no fan service, which is something that is REALLY hard to avoid in this genre of games.
By far, my favorite part of this game is that the story is not rinse, wash and repeat with each romance route. Each difference in choice and each romance results in a different ending (whether it's some minor details changing, or the story itself being turned inside out), which BOOSTS replayability. I am STILL playing through a couple of the endings, just because I am so interested in seeing the difference that will occur!
Highly recommend this game! I will remain hopeful for a future installment!

The same mechanics work in your favor as well.
The game is difficult, yes. It's not a game where you can roflstomp the opposition without thought. You have to use strategy and tactics to be successful but there is a huge sense of achievement in victories and even defeats are not the end.
All in all, love the game anf highly recommend it to strategy enthusiasts.

I bought this game because to me, the idea of playing a boy and his mom as main characters is a fresh and unique concept that is rarely explored in a game. So the potential was there; combined with the nice art and really good music, why the thumbs down then?
First of all, the game is not super-bad. I thought long about it but given that we only have the binary choice it tended more to the 'bad' side. The story is very predictable in a bad way. It's just a string of little sub stories to pull your heart strings in the most blatant ways (oh, this poor lonely puppy and her little girl-friend who is poor and has an alcoholic dad, gee, I wonder what will happen???).
The bigger problem is the actual gameplay, though. It's just not engaging in any way. You mostly run around the world and listen to cutesy creatures talking and collect some objects to get to the next plot point. The puzzles are very light and easy, and there aren't that many of them. It's really just running around and talking for the most part. The game is not long, but it still kind of drags on.
I think if you are a parent and you play this with your (really) young kid, than this game is worth playing, maybe. So as a family game, I would recommend it. For everyone else, I would only recommend it if you really enjoy the art and music.

Right from the start, you feel like you are controlling an awesome, destructive power. The energy blasts are wild and the animation conveys a real sense of force. As you unlock power-ups, that destructive power increases dramatically. Once you are fully powered, you will tear through the first portion of the game with little effort. Fortunately, an expansion was released to bring back some challenge and you can start from any level that you've unlocked.
Controls are simple. Aim the curser in the general direction of enemies and fire. The hero is also able to deftly avoid incoming threats by jumping in place, jumping between two platforms, or rolling between the platforms. If an enemy drops a portion of a CD, highlight it and alt fire to rope it in. This is how to unlock power-ups and new music tracks. The power-ups add some more variety to your arsenal and they are straightforward to learn.
The biggest problem with this game is how easy it is once you obtain all of the power-ups. As far as I can tell, there is no way to selectively drop them. The samurai battle requires more rote memorization than strategy. There is, however, an endless mode that gets extremely challenging, although it always requires you to start from the beginning. Another problem is that, on Linux, GOTY mode is unable to load some assets, which causes the game to crash.
I am not a fan of mobile ports. Usually, they feel out of place on PC, but this one was done right. The controls work well, the visuals take advantage of a full sized monitor, and the soundtrack can be enjoyed with high quality speakers rather than headphones. I enjoy this game enough that it is one of very few single player games to which I return after clearing just to kill time. I recommend this game without reservation.

After playing the recently released Sonic Mania, I was in the mood for a bit more 2D Sonic and I had originally missed out on Sonic 4. I do have to say Sonic 4 is both more casual and more frustrating than Sonic Mania at the same time. The levels pose barely any challenge at first and there is even a level (you'll know which) where extra lives are practically thrown at you (about 10-20 at a time). Since one can replay this level as many times as one wants, this essentially means one cannot get a Game Over once one grinds out a few dozen lives.
That doesn't mean the game is easy. While it is casual in its levels, it contains significantly more crushing traps and bottom-less pits than I like in my Sonic games. This isn't helped by the controls being significantly less tight than in the newer Sonic Mania and this is no doubt partially due to the 2.5D plattforming for Sonic not having been perfected yet at the time of Sonic 4 Episode 1's release. The music in the game is also less inspired than usual Sonic Games.
The real bummer about this game isn't any of this, though. The levels are still fun to play casually. The main issue I have with the game are the bosses. There are basically 5 of them. The first 2 are so easy that you likely won't ever get hit by them. Then the third of them is a pattern-recognition and fast reaction based boss that kills you with all of his attacks in one hit by crushing you but each time you die you have to repeat a rather long and annoying bit of the level before facing him again. That third boss is the only way you can ever see a Game Over in this game, since a single mistake (and it's easy to make them with the slightly wonky physics and controls) will result in instant death. A very poorly designed and annoying boss fight. The fourth boss fight is decent in difficulty.
The final boss is usually the most awesome part of Sonic games but in this case, it's a disappointing repetition of all 4 previous bosses (with checkpoints inbetween) followed by a 5th boss which is well designed. But they shouldn't have made you refight the 4 old bosses to get to the 5th boss, it feels like a cheap way to stretch out the game.
Overall, I enjoyed the game. It's rather short but the price is adequate. It has many annoying things about it but if you can get it for a few bucks and you enjoy a very casual, if often frustrating, game then you'll enjoy this despite its many flaws. The second episode is significantly better and owning Episode 1 and 2 gives you a cool new mode in Episode 2 where you can play as Metal Sonic, so if you get Episode 2, get Episode 1 as well.

So, I am not the greatest at writing reviews. So give me a bit of a break.
Mordheim: City of the Damned. A name that would give both a shudder down your spine as well as a sudden urge to play. The lore for Mordheim itself is compact full of dreadfull horrors although with the possibility of great riches.
PROS:
Artwork: Great textures and art that gives the feel of a horrid city filled with death and decay.
Skills and Warbands: You could spend an hour or two just customizing, arming, and leveling your warband. Very complex.
Factions: Each faction plays very differently. Skaven are more speed and rely on dodging in battle. Sisters are more for a defensive and morale attrition with battles. Cultists seem to be more of a high damage with varied specializations. Human Mercenaries are more of a balanced sort of crew, not great at anything but can be good at whatever you want them to be. Do not have DLC factions.
Getting Started: It is actually a very easy game to start and to learn. Not too steep of a learning curve, you can get far with not really understanding the depths of the skills and levels. But getting unlucky at the beginning can be a real turn off if you are just starting.
Simple Gameplay: Things are quite simple but not stupid. You commit actions by using two seperate types of points. Strategic and Offensive points. Most skills with require the use of one or the other.
Cons(Kind of)
RNG: Now I love the RNG, but I hate it with a passion. Everything can be going alright and then you seem to miss every hit and the enemy seems to get criticals. It can be super frustrating but can also feel really good when things go your way or if you just get out of danger.
The Maps and spawnpoints: Most maps are beautifully designed and I enjoy playing them even though there are really not that many. Most maps use the same sort of assets in them and some are just mirror images. But it is not that bad. The bad part is when you either spend all of eternity trying to find the enemy, only to be ambushed into oblivion, or half your band is surrounded and cut into pieces before help arrives.
TL:DR It is a great game that is fun to play in short bursts. If you like heavily RNGed turn based games with a detailed warband leveling systems then this game is for you. But be warned, you will lose warbands. You will die, and you will be very angry. But such is the curse of Mordheim: City of the Damned.

I found it no trouble to replace warriors that died or were too wounded to be useful because of the system that allows you to hire a rotating list of leveled units.
Overall, it's got engaging combat, factions with unique personalities, and gameplay that hooked me. I personally don't think the DLC is worth it, but if you're the type that loves the game so much that you'll start a new warband once maxing your main, then I see the appeal.
