I really want to like this game.
I love the permadeath and character progression. I love the permanent injuries and the brutal fighting.
I played it in early access and I remember thinking the game was cheating me on the To Hit rolls. 90% chance to hit missing 9 times out of ten. What wasn't made clear (and still isn't, unless you're looking for it) is that yes you may pass the To Hit roll 90% of the time, but there's another roll that takes place simultaneously. If you hit, the enemy usually has a chance to dodge or block. If they're really agile they'll dodge maybe half the time. Therfore you feel like you're missing again and again, when actually your sodlier did his part and the enemy jumped out the way.
The combat log tracks all the rolls, which helps ease the feeling of being robbed.
But that isn't my biggest gripe!
In the campaign you're thrown to the wolves immediately, and in a game so heavily reliant on stats and percentages it's just hopelessly unfair unless you're very lucky. It's like the video game version of Monopoly.
Each "day" you pick a mission. They're random in difficulty. The enemies in the mission are random too. On day two I had only 2 choices - a Lethal mission and a Deadly mission. I used the scouting button to find another few missions - both pretty much promised failure.
Thinking this was just the game adding some fluff I headed into the least dangerous one.
I gathered my team and held my ground, hoping to mob the enemy. Except I couldn't because their warband was so much better than mine. My hero would lose over half his health to a single enemy henchman strike (not even critical). My hero and leader had to hit the enemy henchmen around 8 times before they died. Numerically it was impossible, despite surrounding them and trying to pick them off. At a certain point The Numbers dictate the overall outcome.
This is made worse when you realise there are permanent injuries (a good idea in theory) AND time limits for completing shipments which you can only miss 4 of before you fail the game. You HAVE to get into missions, and when those missions are guaranteed to be a disaster I felt like the victim of overly cruel game design. Why not scale the enemy warbands up with you? Why would you ever put the player into a positiion where they are up against brutal, deadly or lethal warbands on day 2?
Some people seem to love this game and relish the difficulty, so I recommend it for people who are drawn to that kind of challenge. But I think most people probably don't want to have to go digging and scraping around the internet for tips and exploits (like, "Don't ever play story missions because they're broken and have infinite waves of enemies" and "avoid missions where there's a chance you could be spread out because it's almost a guranteed fail as the enemy will intercept your guys and pick them off one by one before you can regroup"). If I have to cordon off portions of a game because it's broken or unbalanced then they've done something wrong.

This is a 3D PvP Fighting game. It's not a PvE action RPG. So if anyone complains about, or expects, lots of PvE content then they have unrealistic expectations and are leaving poor reviews. Do you complain that RTS games don't have enough FPS action? Seriously...
I'm a bit biased as I do indeed love this game, having started at launch and not quit (though I only have time for a couple hours a night)
I think if you want a solid indepth review, scroll to find balistafreak's review. He hits all the right points. I'll add some of my 2 cents though on what drew me in:
I've always enjoyed fighting games, but was always more interested in 3D fighting games like Fight Night and UFC. I think this is because I'm not great with reflexes, but I can strategize and develop tactics fairly quickly. So long as the game isn't hyper reliant on 250 ms reflexes, I can compete. Enter Absolver, and while at times it does require reflexes, it more often requires analysis of move characteristics, pattern recognition, pattern training, and some tactical understanding to know how to engage and disengage properly. My old man eyes and brain can work through this better than simply reacting to frames, so that's part of what really got me hooked and made me want to invest my time into this game.
Beyond simply that I am capable of having fun and being good at this game is that the combat system is one of the most unique, fluid, and beautifully made systems I've ever seen. Bar none. Period. The hitboxes still make me giggle like a school girl, especially when two dodging moves flow right past each other, or when a dodging move catches the move its intended to counter and you watch as your opponent's move smoothly misses you and yours cleanly catches them in the ear to send them reeling away. It's glorious.
Another major factor: NO MICROTRANSACTIONS. NO RIDICULOUS GRIND.
Though to be fair, one of the most interesting parts of this game is the fashion, the clothing and gear, which helps you make your fighter look completely unique to you. Loot is found in multiple ways and you really don't have to grind too much to put together a sweet outfit. I almost exclusively  play 1v1 duels and get plenty of gear. You can also get good gear just by going back through the PvE world, perhaps helping a new player or if you just wanted to run through it again. The final boss is an easy win for veterans and she provides good loot options.
But your stats are pretty generic, so don't worry about them. You could level all the way up to 60 and not place a single stat point, remain at base stats, and still do ok in 1v1s if you're a good player and if you have learned enough good moves to make a decent "deck" (personalized combos). And if you don't like how you specced your stats, its darn near free to respec. 3 crystals or whatever. If you do any amount of pvping you'll have crystals and shards coming out of your ears so don't worry, respecs are cheap.
The community here is also solid. Lots of players showing respect and wanting to help you improve. The dedicated players in this game aren't the BM, taunt you all the time people. You may find some players that are kinda rude, but for the most part this community is awesome. As of this writing anyways. If the game population increases significantly I'm sure we'll see more rude people. But generally speaking this game requires a brain, and most BM type people get rekt.
There were and are some problems with the game. At the highest level of skill I believe there's some issues with a few of the moves, so balancing basically. But that's a minor gripe. My major gripe with this game has always been from day 1 connection / netcode. Up until very recently, "inifinite loading screens" and disconnects were fairly common. I'd say on bad days 30 to 40% of the 1v1 matches I attempted to join would just sit on the loading screen forever, or the opponent would just disappear mid fight due to disconnection. This has since been greatly improved with December's update, but there's still an issue with latency. Since 1v1's are a P2P connection, the host has just a ridiculous advantage. Especially at high levels of skill when the players are all very very good, A LOT of the time it comes down to who has host. That's really frustrating. At least with tournaments we can have a 3rd person host the match, so both fighters are mostly equally dealing with latency. I trust they will find ways to improve the host advantage over time, as they have improved the netcode significantly since its release a few months ago.
As I said previously, I encourage you to read balistafreak's review as it contains more technical aspects of the game and is legitimately a great review of Absolver. I do highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fighting games. When you lose a 1v1, and trust me you'll lose hard, ask yourself what happened. Why was I getting hit? Why wasn't I hitting him? And go remedy it in your move list.
Good luck, Prospects.

Okay. I trusted that this would be a really good purchase, and I went ahead and took the risk and I bought it. I don't usually trust games with mixed reviews, and to see
be a victim to that breaks my heart. BUT... having said that I took the risk, I'd like to point out that it was a good risk. I enjoyed what the game has offered so far. Now, all it needs is some love from the players. From the community. Because the number one complaint I read in many reviews that I've read is that the game is pretty much dead, and that is mostly because of the lack of content. Now, while the lack of content may be true, this shouldn't mean the player count should drop. This is such an ambitious game, and I really don't want it to go.
So, the player starts off as a Prospect, and are pitted against the world of Adal, where every Prospect must prove their worth by beating their adversaries to become an Absolver peacekeeper. It's got some RPG-like elements in it, like how you look, and how you'll fight. Since it's mostly an open-world multiplayer game, the story isn't given too much focus.
One way to interact with the world's people, I mean the players, is through the emotes they give you. You can also unlock even more emotes, but yes, it's like sign language. You want to come in peace, bow in respect. You wanna fight, punch the guy. You want him to follow you, fling your hand up. You wanna say hi, wave. And lemme tell you, it works. Players acknowledge this!
I was surprised, because I knew this was going to be a kind of an MMORPG, and the first thing I thought was going to happen to me when I met an online person was "he's going to randomly punch me in the face". But, nope. In fact, some dudes I've met online actually fought with me. WITH me. I mean... not that I need help... I mean, are you kidding? I can play this game by myself, beat everyone by myself. Hah. I just... like helping folks out.
Now, this is where the game takes the cake. It's purely hand-to-hand combat. No guns. No sticks and stones to throw at players. It's raw fist power! Of course, you'll find melee weapons like swords and stuff, but they're not the overpowering kind. The player is also given a massively customizable mechanic called the Combat Deck, in which they can swap their current moves with others so that they can build their own combat deck and put it to good use in the field. So, basically, you make your own moves, and your own play style. There is no "his attack is better than mine". Everyone is given an equal chance. How you play depends purely on how you strategize your moves, and how good you are with the fighting. In other words, with the lack of any better word since I don't use it for games - Skills. Just skills. The skill to strategize. The skill to react in time. The skill to keep everything in control.
There's the thing about control. Everything you do - punch, kick, dodge, parry, etc. - takes away some of your stamina. So, there's some resource management here. You run out of stamina, you're a sitting duck. And if your deck doesn't connect well, you're going to have a hard time fighting against other players. You need to spend some time going through every aspect of your inventory system, to better understand it, so you won't cry about losing later on. Tutorials can't play a more important role in here; you don't go through all of that, you're gonna waste time button-mashing your way through the game, and not take away anything good from it. It won't end well for you.
Of course, there's the level-up system, so that will indeed have a huge impact on how you will perform against other players. But, if you want to level up real good, you gotta get good. You wanna get good, you have to actually put in the effort to getting good.
The weapon system in the game is also balanced. While weapons do extra damage, using it a lot for both offense and defense will result in its wear and tear. Eventually, your weapon will shatter, and you'll be left open by your opponent, and he's going to go to town with you if you are particularly weak in fistfights. And you have three most basic play styles in the game, which I will simply state in basic terms for now - Heal, Evade, and Parry. With Heal, you can take in hits, but if you do the moves related to that style, then you get the bits of health you lost back. With Evade, you can obviously evade the incoming attacks, and with Parry, you can block incoming attacks, and leave the opponent open for hits. You only choose one of the styles.
The combat system in the game is no joke. It's not like
where you keep building up combos and punching your enemy to Valhalla while he just stares helplessly. No. With every hit, you are still leaving yourself open to attacks. If he evades, you're open. If he blocks, you're open. Even if you hit him, you're open! So, the balancing here is done very well. If you rage in the game, it simply means you need to get good. You cannot blame the game for that. (Unless you're lagging. Then, sure, blame your net, or the server you're in)
But, overall, the game does brilliantly with its seamless combat system. But, rest assured, it's HARD to master. Easy to grasp, HARD to get good with. They say it's Dark Souls-like. Well, they're almost accurate with it. Almost. What matters is you have to put effort into it, or you
lose interest quickly. This game is not for scrubs. Best played with a controller, by the way.
The content. There's not much else to do, except explore this big world, fight the CPUs, fight the players, get XP, rack up your level, build your decks, and power up your character. Aaand yeah.
But, hey... here's hoping they'll add more stuff. Like, a singleplayer-only experience. Or arena battles. Or a sort of a battle royale with fists. OR FINISHERS! Can we please have finishers!? It doesn't have to be violent, just a little neck snap, or a hand snap, or some sort of snaps. To show my domination to the enemy. Something like that. Please!
It's so good! It's a vibrant, low-poly-ish environment with a nice colour palette, great particle system, the lighting... not to mention nicely (courtesy of UE4) optimized! Mmm, like, a Bob Ross painting. The music is ambient. The subtle drums when you're fighting. The tense atmosphere it creates. As I look at my opponent's eyes, we circle around each other, waiting for the other to engage, while we switch stances, keeping our guard up... Yeah, no, the combination of the visuals, and the music just makes it all the more immersive. It's a rich experience.

To do that, I urge you to buy this game. It's only been a few months, and people are already complaining that there's lack of content, and that's the sole reason why they're being put off by the game. It's true that the developers are a bit slow with that, but they are releasing updates, and with the latest update giving us private matches, and 3v3, I think it's time we gave the game a chance once again. I have been really hyped about this game for a  long, long time, and I finally get it, and there are some things it gets right, and some things it doesn't. But what game comes perfect?

"Do you recommend this game?"
I see the usual "yes" and "no" options, but unfortunately "absolutely" doesn't cut it.
To set the scene for this game, which I unapologetically call a modern masterpiece-- it was my first Humble Bundle, and enough all on its own to cement HH's legitimacy from a gamer perspective ever since. I remember wondering what it was about, this unknown game with a historical name. And then I installed it.
Hoooly $#%#.
Jamestown harkens back to an era of shmup when the in-game enemies really wanted to murder you in mindless, cold blood. The first two things you'll notice upon opening the application are the beautiful and picturesque, pixelated graphics that range into the higher end of the SNES spectrum, and awesome music that make you feel like you're really in an epic adventure while you're playing the game. You'll soon also notice the plethora of difficulty settings--some of which that have to be unlocked in-game--the potential for four person multiplayer, the 8 total ships with vastly different ammunition capabilities (DLC required for every ship). There is also a shoppe (where you unlock the ships) which contains bonus challenge levels that can be unlocked with money earned by playing through the modes.
The next thing to mention is the very accessible gameplay which is easy to get a feel of, but at higher difficulties is damn difficult to master when the screen is full of bullets, some of which go through the Vaunt shield mechanic at Judgement and above. Couple this with continuously exceptional music, great level design with some quirky enemies and battle mechanics, achievements that are actually noteworthy, and a quirky and interesting story, Jamestown is an easy recommendation.
An easy 10/10.

Rochard is a simple, yet different kind of puzzle platformer. The twist is, that the main character wields a neat gravity gun, which (besides shooting stuff) allows him to control gravity and lift distant objects.
Each room has a small puzzle or challenge, which needs to be solved before advancing. The puzzles are not very difficult, but are never so patronisingly easy that they ruin the game. Additionally, even if the core concept is simple, they manage to keep it interesting by changing the setting, adding different puzzles (a variety of force fields, low gravity, reverse gravity, electric fields, shielded enemies, improving weaponry with new features etc.).
Speaking of enemies, they can be taken out in a variety of ways, such as dropping heavy stuff on them, pushing them into electric surfaces, manipulating giant mining lasers to cut them into pieces, throwing malfunctioning robots at them, or just plain shooting holes in them.
The story is simple, but the nature of the boisterous main character makes it interesting and fun.

Half Minute Hero is an old-school RPG with one twist: you have to win in 30 seconds. You can pay the incredibly frugal Time Goddess to reset the clock, but you can't do it forever. The result is a fast-paced game that cuts out the fluff and has you figuring out how to best spend your last precious seconds. The story is simple and very goofy, but effectively told. The music and graphics are both very good. Controls are bad, though... this game was ported from consoles poorly. You basically need a controller for some modes (not Hero, thankfully).
The game comes with six modes, but Hero 30 is the big draw: the rest pale in comparison. Evil Lord 30 and Princess 30 are fun distractions and don't take long. Knight 30 was okay once I figured it out. Hero 300 is the big climax, and gives you a big payoff for playing the other modes. Hero 3 is infuriating. I didn't try the multiplayer.
Anyone who has enjoyed 8- or 16-bit RPGs needs to pick up this game. Other RPG and puzzle game fans will probably enjoy it as well. It's definitely worth the money.

As a preliminary declaration, I am astonished that an Otome VN with this caliber being a freeware, and it also being the first ever project of Dicesuki development team. I mean, it is surprisingly good for a first trial in the Otome genre, even better compared to products of some veteran developers. Let's take a closer look at the game and discuss its various other qualities aside being free, huh? Because there are many.
Once upon a time, there was a not so sweet little princess named Lucette. Sure she was fair and pretty as most princesses, but she was also cold, rude and mean; taking no interest in any other's feelings or needs whatsoever. She was selfish and cruel also, to a degree that even her own family were wary of her. So... what to do with this little meanie? Why, curse her of course: put a spell on her so everyone would forget that she is royalty, thus living as an ordinary person would teach her some humility, kindness or maybe even compassion in the long run. In her challenge to break her own curse, the princess must accomplish three good deeds. It may sound plain and simple, but not so much for someone who has never committed a single good deed in all her life. For her trial to learn goodness, Lucette choses one of the five fine gentlemen who are also cursed, to serve as a partner and a companion. In trying to help each other breaking their curses, romance arises, but that is not the center of Lucette's story. Things may start simple or even comedic, but given time, Lucette is to find herself in a conspiracy concerning the crown and the fate of the kingdom.
There are five romance paths concerning some really well-written gentlemen here, but I'll get there. In each path, aside the relationship build, you gather different nuances, anecdotes or clues concerning the grand picture. Answers to some questions may lie in different paths, so even though you wouldn’t be interested romantically, I advise playing all paths. When they all are played and their good endings are acquired, the full picture is revealed. Events prior to the story, backgrounds of different romance options, NPCs’ own interrelation and the story consistency itself are gradually revealed and all are imaginative, interesting and attractive. All characters - whether they be main romance options or ordinary NPCs - harbor well thought stories of their own with distinct personalities. I am happy to declare that I didn't encounter any stereotypes in this game. If someone looks like a stereotype, it means that there are things to be revealed about him/her yet. That, I can assure.
What we were saying? Ah, romance options! Sure, this is an Otome in the end, huh? Well, all boys are mostly interesting with well written paths, both their personalities and curses that make their path worthy to play. Rod is our step brother and the current crown prince who lost his voice thanks to the Mermaid's curse. He is stubborn and disinterested mostly, but he has a golden heart. Karma is the pretty, reckless and bohemian creature that no one knows anything about - aside him/her being a master swordsman and a grade A slacker. He bears the Beauty and the Beast curse, and he is one of my favorites in the game. Rumpel was my least favorite, considering his route was mostly slow pacing and his involvement lacks anything related to the main character to begin with. He seems like a womanizer who forgot his own name and throws cheesy compliments around like its wedding confetti, who actually harbors a deep trauma concerning the value of life. Well, then comes Fritz... It's hard to explain about Fritz without giving spoilers but it should be suffice to say that he is our knight, who genuinely likes us and wishes to protect us without any apparent ulterior motive. He is solely a good guy. Huh, who would have thought? Then, my favorite ever - and the last of the routes that should be played: Waltz. He is a street magician by the age of 12 - or is he? Well, telling anything else would spoil the magic. Let’s just say he is older than he looks to be.
The game is made in classical Ren'Py engine. You have 30 or so choices to make in each playthrough to see what happens. Your choices do change the end game, and alter the pace of the main story in some small amount but whatever you do or say, the boy of your choice will love you. Your choices only affect the end game circumstances, which would create either a happy ending or an uncontrollable tragedy. According to the amount of correct choice, you either grab a happy ending by the side of your love, or fail to reach happiness due to a dire mishap. Btw, it might be useful to note that whatever you do, some bloodshed is unavoidable, befitting to any crown conspiracy - especially in a world involving magic.
Art works are not miraculous, but they are beautiful and elegant with an anime style. Background artwork is pretty much run of the mill, but character artworks are especially fetching. I must say that the diversity of expressions used for each character is more than satisfying too. No voice acting present, but CG scenes are plenty and they are plenty pretty. The game soundtrack is more than fitting, and sound effects are well timed with appropriate mood influences. Oh, there are also Steam achievements involved, and all this game has to offer - which is 30 hours or so gameplay - is free.
If you are even remotely interested in the Otome genre or would like to try one without anything to lose, this is one of the better options for you. It doesn't contain any fan service - which is a huge pro for me - and it harbors an elaborate setting that packs a good amount of story. So... go ahead… I bet you'll get a favorite path of your own in no time. As a side note, I would recommend getting the DLC that contains game art to support the developer for a measly 5 dollars. The game itself actually deserves far more, and I hope that it would encourage the developer to bring us other beautiful games like this in the future.

I played RE4 originally back on the GCN. Before Separate Ways, before the PRL 412. I remember having to switch to a second disk when I got to the island. My game ran at 30 fps, and I loved every minute of it.
It was then released on PS2, as a downgrade from the GCN (as in, graphically inferior, no real-time fire effects, simplified enemy AI, etc.). Then it got to Wii, upgraded, and I bought it again (and another copy for a friend). Now, I've got it on steam. 60 fps, bug fixes, updated and more difficult AI, more bonus content. And MODS!?
This is a major improvement.
It's a almost completely linear game, but there's so many styles to play. In practice, I have four playstyles.
I play ultra-conservatively, my first round. I can use anything I want, buy anything I want, to make my job of survival easier. I take my time, explore every nook and cranny, collect every treasure, kill every enemy, and try to survive everything as easily as possibly. This style takes about 10-15 hours to complete, as I go slow and cautious.
Then, I have my "mediumish-hardcore" style. I can only use weapons and items found in the game (meaning Handgun, Shotgun, Broken Butterfly. No rifles. No TMP. For this round, I usually self impose I can upgrade those three weapons only, but no rocket launchers, no tactical vest, and no upgrading my attache case. This playthrough usually takes about 15-20 hours as, smaller attache case means no ammo, means a lot of running around to conserve/pick up.
I've got another "just for fun" style where I use my Infinite Rocket Launcher, Chicago Typewriter, Handcannon, and/or PRL 412 to just mow down enemies like no tomorrow. It's fun, with almost no real chance of failure. Usually, about a 5 hour run, doing just about everything, but taking no time to do it.
Finally, I've got the Speedrun. Where I run past as much as possible, avoid anything extra, accomplish my goals and only my goals as quickly as possible. I've got my time down to just over 2.25 hours.
I've tried to do a knife run, but... I'm just not good enough to pull it off. Look up Kai Wii's knife run on YouTube if you get a chance. That guy's got some real skill!
And that's just the main game! There's about as much playability with the Mercenaries, Assignment Ada, and Separate Ways all thrown in for good measure.
Probably my all time top 5 games.
Cons:
Infrequent audio studders. Sounds like when an old 16bit game would freeze, but only for maybe 0.1 second. Happened maybe 3 or 4 times first 24 hours or so of gameplay. Never happened on either GCN or Wii versions.
Keyboard/Mouse controls are horrendous. Get a controller, or you won't enjoy playing.

In Sum: My all-time favorite PC Game, and probably the best version of Civilization.  5/5.
-----
Ah, Civilization IV:BTS, the game that stole so much of my life.  Civ IV is a classic. After some of the frustrations with Civilization III following the majesty of Civ II, IV felt like a return to form for the series.  It has a lot in common with III, of course, but it made the game feel epic again.  It also resolved some of the awkward controls the series was known for, and added a few intriguing features.  In particular, religion, corporations, and civics (borrowed from Alpha Centauri).
What BTS gets right is amazing. There is a lot of depth to the decisions being made, and it can be a complex game if you want it to be.  The civic system lets you fine tune your own custom government (a theocratic police state with a free market?  Go right ahead!), with the rewards and penalties mixed, like in the classic Civs.  The diplomacy is vital to the game, and the AI's opinions of you actually matter, and can be influenced.
Where it gets it wrong tends to be the tedium and the stacking mechanic.  Civ III and IV suffer from a design oversight that became a mechanic, called 'stacks of doom" in which not only could an army be overpowered by playing upwards of 30-40 units in one tile, but such play became essential to win.  The city attacking and defending mechanics also leave something to be desired, as they are intended for stacks of doom.  The gameplay can be tedious compared to Civ V, many turns can pass without anything happening.
But it's also more satisfying when you get to victory in this game.  And there are more victory options in Civ IV: BTS than any other Civ game, including early game victories such as religious.
This game was so good in its time that even today the Civ fans are divided between Civ IV and V, with many fans preferring this game over the new version.  I do consider it a matter of preference, as I play both.
Last of all, certainly not least, Leonard Nimoy narrates this game in a Leonard Nimoy fashion.  It fits the game perfectly.

Mordheim is a great game well worth its price and your time, although it will not necessarily fit all types of player profiles.
Do not even try if you're the kind of players who build their entire strategy around the idea that percentage equals luck i.e "i missed 5x 80% in a row CHEAT !".
If you do understand, on the other hand that the worst thing you can do in RNG games is to try your luck, and that you should instead build to mitigate bad outcomes, then by all means this game is a delight.
If you just roll the dice you're bound to get lucky or unlucky, but that's the whole point with RNG games, don't try to get lucky.
So you can reroll until everyone crits on the first round, or you can find one of the many strategies at your disposal that will work 95% of the time.
You're going to spend a lot of time before your characters sheets brainstorming builds, synergies and party compositions, if you don't have the patience for it then you will get your booty spanked.
To that effect i highly recommend you get comfortable using this build planner :
considering the game itself doesn't give crucial informations it should have, in my opinion, such as basic important values like how many skill points can a unit have at cap.
The very beginning of the game when all your recruits are fresh is extremely rough since there's no real synergie and you will have to rely on lucky rolls, but that's how it starts and after you begin piling up money and experience everything starts clicking together.
There will be casualties.
There will be mission failures.
But your Warband stands and you can only move forward.
Eventually you will grow more and more comfortable and aside from the occasionnal KO units, failure will become history.
Mordheim does have issues : unintuitive UI, bugs creeping in at the worst time, a general feeling of lacking that last pass of polishing. The tutorials are very helpful but don't really cover every decisive mechanics.
But it's gritty, unforgiving, and deeply satisfying.
I have one real issue with the game overall, the way AI is handled put together with seldom punishing bad rolls successions.
See, the AI doesn't really act like a Warband with a hive mind as yours will since you control everything, they're more like independant suicidal drones going in a bee line for any kill they can grab no matter if they get slaughtered in the process.
This lack of refinement will sometimes lead to the demise of some of your units like a vessel sinking under the weight of countless kamikaze crashing themselves on it, one after another.
While it can lead to some frustrating experiences it's not a real issue as long as you understand that the narrator doesn't ask "Who among us will die today" just to be cute.
All in all a great addition to your library as long as you are a player made of iron, and don't really enjoy make believe sugar coated feel good designs.

I cannot see what is the point of porting the boardgame to video gaming if the developers does not make use of computing to make the final calculation for the player, then for the player to make a risk/reward decision based on the available info given to him.

Unfortunately, I can not recommend this game for three main reasons.
and foremost, as has been touched on by many others, this game employs a Random Number Generator as a core combat mechanic which, in and of itself, would not have been terrible had they not disguised various factors which affect your characters chance to hit. For example, your Hero may well appear to have an 85% chance to hit, but that 85% is not factoring in dodging etc. Whilst 'get good' might well be a valid argument in some cases, it is insanely disheartening to nearly perfectly play a series of moves to corner and outnumber an enemy, only to have them last through 2 rounds of your 4 combatant's attacks, in time for their own team to arrive and seriously hurt your odds of winning.
The
issue flows on from the first, in that the game becomes mind-numbingly repetitive. After around 10 battles, you have seen all there is to see. You do not control your characters in a dynamic sense, only instigating the start of their attack animations whilst moving them around like chess pieces on a board. Once again, this is not an inherently flawed game mechanic, but instead was butchered in implementation. Instead of having suspense, tension and thrills come from, say, an emergent story within the combat wherein your characters evolve through the things they do, the feel of the game is very much, 'move animatronic doll here, whack or miss, rinse, repeat'. This is compounded by the fact that the game very much funnels you into one mind-set; gang up on a single enemy until you kill them, giving you the numbers advantage. Nearly all battles boil down to the same core ideology: gang up on them before they gang up on you. Once more, after a certain amount of battles, you've seen every attack, spell and movement animation your faction offers.
The
issue conveniently flows from the second issue; the atmosphere, whilst very, very immersive, is ruined by the combat mechanics in that the overly-punishing RNG elements detach the player from the game, disallowing immersion as the player is dragged out of the Warhammer universe and into their room, study or basement of choice, becoming a spectator and interloper to the combat as opposed to an active participant. It's hard to feel invested in the characters when you are little more than some omnipresent grand-strategist whose actions have a somewhat open relationship with the gameplay itself. Often I was too focused on not having my squad obliterated to take in the sights of the maps, with their little idiosyncrasies which culminate in what is a rather aesthetically pleasing visual design.
The game is pretty, sporting a rather nice visual design yet shallow game mechanics ruin all immersion and result in slot-machine level frustration. Also, this DLC model is: overpriced, over-reaching and underwhelming.

There are plenty of other Sonic platformers on Steam - Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic CD, Sonic 3 & Knuckles, Sonic Adventure DX, Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic Generations, Sonic 4 Episode II, Sonic Lost World, and Sonic Mania.  All of them are much better than this sad excuse.

I don't recommend supporting Sega. Even buying their good games only supports their current practices but this game isn't one of their good ones.
Sonic 4 Episode 1 is a good example of Sega trying to make a quick buck out of their reputation from their hardware days.
Everything about it has an oddly cheap feel for a game that was marketed as the successor to the classic Sonic trilogy. Perhaps this was a result of its origin as a mobile game. I absolutely don't recommend buying Mania in its current state but there's no denying it's a significantly better game than 4 could ever hope to be.
Dimps can, or at least used to be able to, make a decent Sonic game which plays similarly to his classic games. This is not that game. It's not even as good as their boost-style games. It's Sonic Rush minus the boost and with a few other changes whose end result is probably the blandest game Dimps have ever made.
Not completely awful but certainly not something you'll be in a hurry to play again.
The homing attack is somewhat acceptable as a beginner's crutch but Sega/Dimps seemed determined to make it the big new feature compared to the classic games so it's far more heavily focussed on than Dimps' previous games. This doesn't help make for enjoyable or varied level design.
The game's aesthetics are also pretty terrible. A lot of the assets are technically HD but the art style is awful. It has a kind of pre-rendered look but it’s not remotely as charming as games from the 90s that used that style. The music is worse, arbitrarily adopting limitations the original Sonic already surpassed (such as how short each song is before it loops) without sounding convincingly retro.
It's almost the Mighty Number Nine of Sonic games.
Annoyingly the PC port is locked at a native 720P and merely up or downscales to other resolutions. Considering that my laptop can run the game at full speed at native 480P but not at 720P this is a problem for me.
Sega fixed the resolution option in Episode 2 and Episode Metal which even includes 1 level from each of Episode 1's 4 zones but they didn't bother fixing it in this port. This means my laptop can only run the game using fanmade patches.
To give the game one compliment, I'm one of the few who likes the Special Stage. I like Taito's Cameltry and this is blatantly that but with inferior mechanics. It makes a nice break from the Sonic 2 style half pipe Sega & Dimps are so fond of.

One of the fathers of all modern Army Simulation games. Operation Flashpoint as it was known before.
Where do I begin with this old beast ? It's that kind of game that can entertain you for hours, with its long campaigns (although there are only 2 campaigns here : Cold War Crisis and Resistance. The Russian campaign, Red Hammer, was removed for some reason), its many SP Missions, and the Editor, oh boy, the Editor.
Even if you don't like the campaigns, the Editor will entertain you for days. You can build your own missions, with scripts, even build full campaigns, or just place some soldiers and armored, and start a little battle. It's a lot of fun, and with the possibility to add custom units (well, most of the websites dedicated to that are dead now), you can have a lot of variety !
The father of military sim, and one of the old gems that the gaming industry has made !

For the amount of content that this game has and it being free, there's no reason not to play this game. Pretty much all the routes are good (even the bad routes are well-written and not haphazardly inserted). Only exception is Rumpel's route, but that's only because I found it difficult to relate to him. Only thing I could really critique about this game was the fact that even though the MC was portrayed as a misunderstood villain, the other villains were painted as pure evil. One of the main themes of this game is that no one is completely good nor evil. There's always a balance. And yet, villains like
seemed to be displayed as your typical evil villains. It would have been nice if the game gave the player more insight as to why these characters acted as evil as they did. Even
had reasons for acting evil.

The game could've been great, the different factions are varied enough and theres alot of character progression and customization. But it gets so ruined by horrendous RNG and punishing gamemechanics that only affects you.
Basically it goes like this: You start a mission, deploy your dudes and start exploring. Eventually you run into the enemy warband all bunched up on top of each other more or less. Theyre all in ambush mode, meaning if you get too close they attack. Unless you charge them. But theres pretty much no way of telling how large their ambush range is compared to your charge, you just have to get closer and closer with babysteps trying to get in charge range and pray their ambush range is shorter. More often than not this ends up with you walking into an ambush and getting devastated. If you manage your way around this and end up in a fight thats fair or even in your favor theres no guarantee you will win. Fights boils down to dice throws, and when your dudes and their dudes are equal level you have a pretty good shot at hitting according to the game, 70-80% hit change, which in reality means roughly 1 in 4 because the number shown to you doesnt factor in some of the things that influence combat (such as melee resistance)... The entire game relies on RNG, and the RNGenerator is a joke among jokes, rolling either 1 or 99 half the time. Luckily, the AI is dumb and buggy and can be outmaneuvered alot of the time giving you a pretty good shot at winning most missions anyway.
Long story short, the first issue i have with the game is you get f*cked by RNG alot of the time and your masterfully planned strategy just gets dumpstered by something you have no control over.
The second issue is gamedesign. When you lose a mission (or even win but a guy gets knocked out) you roll for injuries. Alot of the time you get away with nothing big, but occassionally you get hit with a big one, like losing an arm on one of your more important characters. Buying a new one is not really an option as you either get a fresh one with♥♥♥♥♥♥stats that gets massacred by anything and everything or you have to pay a small nations yearly budget to get one with some levels to it, which is generally unaffordable.
And yes, this doesnt affect the computer at all. I've yet to meet an AI warband that has any (visible) injuries at all and you face new, freshly generated warbands each time. This means the AI can play super aggressive (and it will) with no drawbacks. If it loses, nooooo problem! Just generates another fresh warband with no injuries next time!
Basically you play the hardcore difficulty mode while the AI is in sandbox mode, and in the end its all down to RNG anyway.

I am both surprised and not surprised to find this game has mixed reviews. What's more surprising is that a lot of the negative reviews are from people familiar with the tabletop game it was adapted from.
I was a big Mordheim fan in my teenage years despite not having much affection for Games Workshop's more popular products. I loved how it mixed role-playing, which I was a big fan of, and war games. It really felt like a tabletop XCOM.
I hate to say that people nixing this game are playing it wrong, but they are. Your warband is not meant to be eternal. While I think it's a bit of a design hiccup to add a campaign mode, thus the illusion of progression, but the Mordheim I remember isn't about that. It's about seeing how far you can get before you run your warband into the ground. Once you've done that, you're meant to roll up the next warband.
You're not meant to form any kind of bond or attachment to your individual actors. They're tools. In time, they will wear out and break. If you have the gold, you replace them with fresh tools. If you don't, you go out of business. It's that simple.
And while there really isn't a lot of variety to the combat in the early stages of the game...generally it pays to bait the AI into an ambush then gang up on them before help arrives...I don't mind because that's generally how Mordheim always worked. Your individual fighters are so brittle and weak, and risking them can be very costly, combat is all about managing the risk/reward of individual engagements. It's about setting up kill zones to lure enemies into where your best assets are covered by henchmen and efficiently knocking enemies out of the fight.
I only wish maps were either larger or the AI a little less aggressive so that it would be possible to grab more of the wyrdstone and treasure on the map. Unlike the tabletop game, most of your income comes from items collected during the mission rather than rewarded after the fact.
In all, if you enjoy games like XCOM but want something a little more brutal that requires a bit more patience and time to learn, I wholeheartedly recommend Mordheim.

One of the better platformers I've played.  I really enjoy Vagante for good reason, despite being an early access indie game.

The local co-op, or couch co-op as some call it, is tight, works well, and is a blast if you have someone to sit down with you and grab a couple controller.  I've never tried the online multiplayer, but it's there, and I'm sure it only makes the game more fun.
The game has manual melee attack aiming, not unlike Dark Souls III in some senses.  You can jump, attack mid air, or prep an attack mid air, and hit something as you land.  Making it quite interesting to fight certain enemies if you find a way to utilize this.
The enemy and boss designs are all well done and challenge you in different ways, with the end game boss allowing you to cycle through for an NG+ and beyond run.  Where enemies scale and you keep trying to clear the game at harder and harder difficulties.
All in all, I very much enjoyed Vagente, and I highly recommend it for people who enjoy platformers with RPG-mechanics and lots of different playstyles.

To the Moon is one of my favorite games of all time. This game was definitely inspired by it, so picking it up during the latest sale was a no brainer for me. Just finished it today. So here's some thoughts (no spoilers):
- It feels more like a game and less like an experience than TtM. There is much more to collect and do here. Also, it tells quite a few interwoven story arcs, as opposed to TtM's one.
- Therefore this game is much longer. Which is both a good thing and a bad thing. The good: More bang for your buck, and more chances for one of its arcs to emotionally bend you over the proverbial barrel (which, let's be honest, that's what we're all here for, right?). The bad: Some of it's arcs were emotional misses for me, and so felt disappointing.
- The humor isn't always present, but when it is, it is on point, which adds much needed levity. This game gets heavy. To describe it in the words of a great man, "Sad."
- I was quite satisfied by the experience. It never actually got me to cry (TtM got me, twice, by comparison), but I did have my throat catch a couple times, along with some whispered "Oh no"s (let me read that letter next to the marbles, dang it!) and so would very much recommend it.

So I never played any Sonic games as a kid. I started playing all the 2D Sonic games. Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic CD, Sonic 3, and Sonic & Knuckles. I enjoyed all 5 games. The play style was pretty similar so it was easy to go from one to the next. After Sonic & Knuckles I was like okay on to Sonic 4. It immediatey felt so different from its predecessors. It felt like they tried to mix in game mechanics of 3D Sonic games into a 2D Sonic. Your walking speed feels incredibly slow. It takes a while to get up to max running speed. It isn't like old Sonic's where you charge up your spin dash and let it rip and keep going. You constantly need to be holding right. The homing attack kinda oversimplifies a lot of platforming so your basic game strategy is hold right and mash jump.
As far as graphics go it looks like it was a launch game for the Dreamcast. It's still vastly superior to every other 2D Sonic game.
The way momentum works (or rather doesn't work) is so different from all the classic games and also defies logic on a basic fundamental level that it almost completely ruins the game experience.
I got the game in a bundle but it isn't that enjoyable. If you're a fan of the series it might be worth for you just because it's easy and it's still Sonic but at a casual level it's just less enjoyable.

Half Minute Hero is one of those games that once picked up, cannot be put down. With it's whacky sense of humour and retro style this game has it all, packing a plethora of different game modes that can be played in short bursts or happily eat up a few hours of your time. The premise to the games main mode "Hero 30" is different to say the very least. What on the surface appears to be a retro Japanese RPG has actually been condensed into an insane amount of 30 second missions that lampoon traditional RPG tropes. Now this premise may sound completely broken but thanks to a wonderfully helplful deus ex machina known as "The Time Goddess" (who gives our hero some leeway with his thirty second time limit) it totally works.
But that's not all! The game also has a few other modes up it's sleeve to give it a longevity boost that will keep you playing for more than half a minute. Princess 30 is a sidescrolling shooter where you play a kind hearted but borderline psychotic Princess who blasts her enemies with a semi-automatic repeating crossbow whilst being rushed around by a small army of guards. Evil Lord 30 is a real-time strategy game that puts you in the dapper outfit of the fabulous "Beautiful Evil Lord" who has renounced his evil ways so that he can grow flowers and drink tea with his newly beloved. When this peace and tranquility are threatened however the Evil Lord breaks out his summoning skills and unleashes wave after wave of monsters upon the castle's unsuspecting invaders. Knight 30 is an action game where you play as a lone knight protecting a wandering sage from hordes of monsters. The story here plays out a lot like Journey To The West (one of my favourite books of all time) which it clearly takes a great deal of inspiration from. The final two modes are Hero 300 and Hero 3 mode which are expansions upon Hero 30 mode that give you 300 and 3 second time limits respectively.
If like me you are a retro gamer then you will adore Half Minute Hero. It does help if you have a whacky sense of humour, but even if you don't I'm sure you will still be able to appreciate the way the game lampoons those classic video game tropes that we all love and grew up with.

What is "Mile High Horror Shorts"?
It is not, like the title would suggest, some clothes from men in a Mile High club. Rather it is a compilation of ten short stories that are horror themed. They are available only in English, with streaming quality of up to 1090p and only with 5.1 Surround sound. The sound quality is excellent, but as I have only stereo speakers I can't tell if there are any actual surround effects.
Now personally I wouldn't have bought this but a friend wanted me to buy something for him and I told him to get me this in exchange on a 89 Eurocent deal (85 percent off).
The "Devolver Digital Films Horror Screams Bundle" would contain this, the interesting movie The Basement which I have from GOG and yet have to see to the end and The Poisoning, which I don't have.
Since "de gustibus non est disputandum", it is impossible for me to give any objective critic, and I can only give my subjective view. It should be noted that there is a visible production value in almost all segments. Let us get to the single episodes now. These are in the order they appear in the movie, but they are not in any form intertwined - each episode is a short movie of its own. One minus point here is that they can't be watched as separate entries in the Steam library.
1.
(Director: John Gibson)
The entire episode is filmed in black and white. It is about a man named Gillespie who sees himself stalked by a Christian fanatician who seems to know about something bad Gillespie has done. The situation escalates and Gillespie tries to flee, but is enclosed in his home with the stranger...
I liked the story, it was a bit silly, had an interesting but pointless twist, but was okay overall. 6/10
2.
(Director: Brad Stabio)
A hitchhiker finds himself hitching for the first time, entering the car of someone who takes hitchhikers for the first time. But then someone makes noise in the trunk and it turns out the driver actually kidnapped someone...
The story was great, it struck a nerve, but I would rather see it as comedic than horror. Still, exactly my kind of humor. 8/10
3.
(Director: Luke Asa Guidici, based on a short story by Saki)
A new postman takes his job easy until he has a certified letter for a lady. A little girl opens and tells the tragic story of how her uncle died and her aunt does not want to realize that. The aunt insists that the letter is for the uncle and he will be back soon. And sure enough, it seems as if he will be back...
An unnerving story, frightening because it seems as if it could happen to everyone... 9/10
4.
(Director: L. Gustavo Cooper)
A guy finds himself in a zombie apocalypse and his wife is infected...
...and I really did not like the story because there are too many of those zombie apocalypse stories. 3/10
5.
(Director: L. Whyte)
The grisly story of a serial killer in the form of nursery rhymes...
As the episode is told with puppets, it is not really horror. Kudos for the poem, the visuals are nicely done to match, but it is just not really horror. 5/10
6.
(Director: Brandon Laganke)
A boy finds a strange man in a bunny costume on a house entrance...
Silly story, the twist at the end is plain stupid. Thanks for trying, but I can see stuff like this a penny a dozen on Youtube. On the bright side, the visuals are good. 2/10
7.
(Director: Adam O'Brien)
A hair stylist talks with a woman he seems to know for quite a while, but she doesn't seem very talkative...
Fine enough for a Tales from the Crypt premise, but too foreseeable for a stand-alone horror short. 4/10
8.
(Director: Jimmy Weber)
A young man wakes up in a cold bathtub and has a slit on his side. But it seems as if the reason for that was not to steal his kidneys...
This is one that keeps you wondering and then stops just as it is about to get interesting. Bummer! 5/10 for the great suspense.
9.
(Director: Chris Chitaroni)
A young girl complains about monsters in her closet. Her father tells her there are none, but she investigates it herself, just to find herself in a white room without any escape, together with several other people who seemingly all got teleported in from one moment to the other. Is there any way to escape, and is the white room related to the monsters in the closet?
What is there to say? This is brillant, this would in fact make a great Twilight Zone episode if it is a bit more fleshed out. Yes, the premise is known from Cube and Hypercube, but the plot is vastly different. 10/10
10.
(Director: Shane Free)
Two guys fool around with an antique table when one of them gets his head stuck in it. As they test around, the girlfriend translates a book they found in the table that teaches its true purpose... (and no, it was not a table to take a dump in)
What is there to say? Of course, the plot itself is horror by its banality, but everything is so foreseeable. And this is something that just shouldn't be. So again only 3/10 here.
So is the collection worth it? For a small price, as I got it, yes. I wouldn't recommend paying the full six Euro for it, as most short stories are at the niveau you can find on Youtube, and one other is not interesting to me (the zombie apocalypse). The remaining three however are worth paying for.
Recommended: When on a good sale

A decent selection of horror short films for the price. For me, the collection started off strong with Gillespie, Certified, and 46 Miles, which I thoroughly enjoyed. The stories were original, the cinematography was well done, and the acting was fantastic across the board.
Then, it went a little downhill in my opinion. Your tastes may vary...
Either the acting was a little stilted (I realize these are indies and not Oscar material, but when a few of them have stellar acting, the ones that don't stand out like a sore thumb); the story was boring and/or predictable (Bunny Boy, A Little Off the Top); or the buildup ends with a payoff that feels like you've received a surprise package. only to discover the box is empty (Incubator).
I got my copy on sale, but the three I really enjoyed make it worth the full price. If you enjoy indie horror, and are more of an enthusiast than I am, you'll probably really enjoy this collection.

Mile High Horror Shorts is a collection of short horror movies made by various people and won certain awards in festivals. As a long time horror fan and hoping to get into the movie business one day I wanted to get this and check out this package, so here goes. I'll review each short as it's own product and not the entire package in total, so let's start.
The first short is Gillespie. A man is who has sinned is confronted by a door to door bible salesman. The short is advertised as a horror short, but I felt it was more slapstick humor and not much of horror, but overall I still enjoyed it because of the salesman himself. It's not a great start, but overall it's a funny short, which in itself warrants a watch. Gillespie is also available on steam by itself. 5/10
The second short 46 Miles is about two serial killers on the road. It's also not horror and more of a comedy, but it's actually quite funny, but in itself it's one of the weakest shorts in the package. The acting is pretty decent. but I really didn't like the direction of the short, felt sort of all over the place. 4/10
The third short Certified is about a mail man bringing mail to a disturbing family in the middle of nowhere. This short is actually pretty good. The cinematography is pretty decent and the acting is also pretty decent. The pay off is nice and overall it's just good. Definitely worth the watch. 7/10
The fourth short is Velvet Road and I got to say this is probably the best directed short in the entire package. It follows a man on a lonesome road looking for his wife during a zombie apocalypse. It's very well shot and written and the whole style of it is just great. Definitely one of my favorites. 9/10
The fifth short is Nursery Crimes and it's one of two animated shorts and follows on a murderous Bo Peep who kills a lot of nursery rhyme and fairy tale characters. This is one of my least favorite shorts as it's pretty boring to watch, the only saving grace is the narrator who does a fantastic job. 4/10
The sixth short is Bunny Boy and it's the worst out of all of them. It follows on a boy who enters his backyard to find a man in a full bunny suit just sitting there. This short is boring and the pay off is pretty bad as well. There's nothing redeeming about this short and it's just bad in general. 2/10
The seventh short is A little of the top which follows a barber and one his clients, but it takes a turn for the worse for one of them. This is short is also lack luster. The barber himself is decent, but this short really isn't that well made or written for that matter, definitely one of the weaker shorts. 4/10
The eight short is Incubator and follows on a familiar urban legend that a pretty woman takes you to a motel room drugs you and steals your kidney, but this is much much worse. This is probably my favorite short out of the bunch. In the little time it has to set up it drives you to the edge of your seat and the pay off is one of the biggest WTF moments I've seen in a while. Definitely one of the best shorts out of all of them. 9/10
The ninth short is White Room which is the second animated segment which follows on a bunch of strangers in a White Room being killed of one by one. The short is alright, nothing too special. The pay off is nice, but nothing much I can say about this short. It's okay, but nothing great. 6/10
The tenth and final short is called The Table where two friends mess around with an antique table which serves a very dark purpose. This is a very predictable short, but it's really well made and it's a fun watch. 7/10
Overall Mile High Horror Shorts is an alright package there's definitely stuff that's great and could be fledged out into feature films if done right. There is some bad stuff, but overall I enjoyed my time with it and on sale I could suggest to check it out only and only if you like horror otherwise stay away.

Drain's playlist of Resident Evil games:
Originally an exclusive to the Gamecube, Resident Evil 4 has become a classic in horror gaming. While I don't consider this to be the height of glory for the genre, it was definitely when horror started to get really good. Many would say this is the best Resident Evil in the franchise. While I would vote 5 for that; I can't deny that 4 is still good, and it came first, allowing 5 to innovate on many things 4 introduced first. Both of these games also have the best partner systems in gaming, which should have become the standard, but was instead forgotten, even by its own series.
best resident evil game hands down. I haven't played 7 yet so I'm not counting that one.

Mile High Horror Shorts has received some tragically low marks from Steam gamers, but I think for the wrong reasons. As a half-century long lover of horror film, I see absolutely nothing in this collection not worth seeing, and seeing at least a second time (with perhaps a single exception.) This isn’t simply mammary glands and gore, these are stories that (mostly) require active thought. (i.e.- “participation for appreciation”.) Well, more thought that is typical with this genre. Modern horror is often known as a rather “thoughtless” genre, and anyone expecting that here may find themselves badly disappointed. No, these won’t likely show at “Canns”, but the best short works of any form need be lean and hard hitting, and these largely succeed admirably. And at this discount price, ($1.49US!!!!) it should be hard for even a lover of more typical cinema to say “no”.
Gillespie – Also available in another Steam package. Worthwhile story of role reversal…or not. Role something, anyway. Featuring a familiar and talented face.
46 Miles – Wonderful use of humor to turn a much used genre into something for the ages. Very nice acting.
Certified – An old film idea based on an older story idea. Maybe so old it’s new again, and still worthwhile whichever your case may be.
Velvet Road – Instead of humor, social commentary, as with all good zombie stories (especially the first one we oldsters ever saw, and you will know which one that is almost immediately.) Very apt in the age of Trump. (May be the warning we missed…….)
Bunny Boy – You didn’t see that coming. Why didn’t you see that coming? (Oh, right. You’re not American.)
A Little Off the Top – One of my least favorite, but perhaps the story best liked by others. (I do NOT need to know who you are, OK?)
Incubator – Combining two urban legends is NOT synergetic. Well, not this time. But quite well made.
White Room – What can happen when adults play with dolls. “That britch(sic) really DOES have everything!” (Perhaps some issues with sound levels.)
Nursery Crimes – Likely my very favorite. Great stop-motion humor on a subject we all THOUGHT we knew well.
The Table – Based on having seen thousands of films…..end strong, not weak. On second thought, perhaps someone read my first paragraph........
I will watch this well made collection often, and will enjoy some of it more with each watching. Perhaps you should too.
A sincere Thank You to these creators, and to the readers of this review.

I can't really say anything about this game that hasn't been said. All I can say is that this is one of my all-time favorites and I believe it to be one of the greatest action games ever made. The game still holds up amazingly well 12 years after its release, especially with the small texture updates and 60 FPS action. I've seen some people complain about how the game runs on their PC but it runs perfectly fine on mine, and my PC isn't too high end.
If you are one of those people that have somehow managed to never play this game - just keep in mind that the controls might take some getting used to when compared to modern third-person action games. Since this game was a pioneer in the third-person action genre, being one of the first to implement an over-the-shoulder view for aiming,  the controls aren't as easy to get into as they would be if it was made today. While some gamers view the somewhat stiff control as a bad thing, I think it is an essential piece to what makes this game great. It adds an extra element of strategy and tension. Since you can't move while aiming, you need to consider the best way to position yourself and when to fire your weapon. If this game had amazingly fluid control, all of the tension, suspense, and strategy present in the combat would be gone.
Buy this game. It's too good.

I haven't finished this game yet, but oh my dear sweet baby jesus it is sooooo good. There's a lot of content and beautiful art and both heart warming and heart wrenching endings, and I'm honestly in awe that this is a free game. I've paid $20 for games with stories less endearing than these and I've only completed 2 characters (I've gotten both endings for Karma and only the bad end for Rod). This game will make think everything is great and then BAM! turns out you've got the bad ending and your heart is broken
The bad endings hurt so good though, you'll want to experience them, if only to make the good endings better.
My only problem is it can be a little difficult to get the good ending (or at least it was difficult for me) because some of the choices to get the good ending (at least in Karma's case) are opposite of what you might think. I got a bad ending three times in a row before I managed to finally figure it out, but don't let that stop you from playing the game. If you're not super dedicated to playing through the same route multiple times with minor tweaks, there are walkthroughs out there to guide you. Or if you're stubborn and prideful (me), the game does have an amazing fast forward feature to go ahead and get to the choices. The fast forward can be a bit slow or give you an error message if you skip too far ahead (i.e. if the next choice is all the way in the next chapter), but nothing game breaking as far as I've experienced.
The MC actually has a personality aside from the usual ditzy/clueless/airhead/etc. usually found in these types of games, and over the course of the story, you actually get to see that personality change. Some of the love confessions can seem a bit abrupt but they're not nearly as sudden as in other games, and I personally didn't have a problem with them.
Overall, amazing game and definitely worth a look at least. It's free, but worth at least $10, probably more.

Each route is fairly long and distinct from the others, plus the heroine isn't a stereotypical damsel in distress (she's more 'tsundere') - all things which set this above many similar games out there.

What are you waiting for? Try it! It is free, after all.

I wanted to like this game. Honestly I did. I Uninstalled and reinstalled at least 3 times before i left it for good, if that tells you how conflicted i was. I'll throw down some pros and cons then elaborate on specifics.
Pros:
+visually pleasing considering the time
+elaborate and complex combat/level up system
+loot system: special weapons and items can be found at random on quests
+customizable teams: decently customizable. Each individual can have their color and costume changed as well as be given unique items and weapons to improve combat capabilities
+3 playable factions(more with dlc)
+Perma-death and permanent consequences(pro for hardcore game lovers)
Cons:
-Failure Countdown: you are expected to ship a certain number of 'crystals' to your faction leader every few weeks and the number is always ridiculously high at lower levels. you are allowed a few failures on this, but but the game only lasts as long as you can keep sending these 'crystals'.
-No gameplay variance: the only, ONLY way to play this game successfully is with the element of surprise. Stick to shadows and pray to god you aren't spotted first. This style of play can be fun, but it gets old. There needs to be more options than the whole cloak and dagger routine.
-the dlc are in the game already, but you can't use them. They show up when you first select your faction and you think "oh cool, i'm gonna be these undead guys cause that sounds cool" but nope, you gotta buy dlc for that♥♥♥♥♥♥ That's them just flagrantly slapping you in the face with the "you just payed for our game, so we'll try milking you for more money by showing you what you're missing out on by not buying the dlc" card. Real douchey move. Especially for a full priced game.
When all said and done, all of these sins are forgivable. This however, is not. The A.I. is complete BS. They know. They just KNOW. They know where every item on the map is,they know the map layout, they know what to do and exactly when to do it, the only thing they don't know is your position before you are discovered(it's like they're oblivious morons to your whereabouts beforehand), but once you're found, there's no way to escape their pursuit. The most BS thing about their A.I. though, their turn time. Never, not once, did a turn of mine last even remotely close tothe time of one of theirs. Even my longest most thought out turns against their most simplistic, theirs is longer. Too much time is spent watching your troops stand around looking stupid. Seriously, half my time spent in this game was waiting for the bot to finish its turn. And that is an unforgivable, unredeamable flaw. If that were fixed, this would be a highly enjoyable and challenging game. but alas, the developers couldn't figure out how to make their A.I. think its moves a little quicker even though they already know all the details about the map and where they need to go. Good day gentlemen and ladies.

After the first hour you see everything the game has to offer, but it's great fun nevertheless. Kinda like Super Hexagon, very simple gameplay, amazing music, great in short bursts. For the price (especially on sale) it's a bargain.
I liked:
* music
* graphics
I disliked:
* short story mode
Get this if:
* you like shooters and are able to have fun with endless mode
* you like chiptunes (as even if you don't like the gameplay the music is great)
Don't get this if:
* you want to play this for the story

Let me make this very clear right now. This game is not even pay to win. It's pay to play or grind rediculously to play. The free to play in this game is really an unlimited free trial, but that free trial can really let you tell whether or not you want to actually pay for the game. Alternatively you could grind out points you need to buy whatever you want, but this takes a LOT of time and dedication to the game.
But that being said, this game is really good. However, I'm going to start with the cons :
1: This game is old. Very old. It was not released in 2012, it was released in 2006. And you will feel it. The animations can be choppy, things will be buggy and not work quite as well as you'd want it to.
2: Not a huge player base anymore. Most of the playerbase has moved on, But that's not a huge issue.
3: Due to how classes work, this game can be VERY confusing to a new player that's never played a DnD game before, and even worse, if you don't know what you're doing with your class, you have a chance to royally screw it up, making your character worthless. Luckily, there are ways to fix this, but after your first time fixing it per character, it either costs $$$ or you have to get lucky with a drop
Pros:
1: TONS of content, especially for paying players. The amount of quests in this game is quite large, and each quest can be thought of to be similar to a dungeon in other games. Imagine if WoW had 1000 dungeons.
2: Reincarnate system : The endgame for DDO is not very strong, and max level characters, while having things to do, don't have a large amount of repetitious things to do , like raiding for gear or dailies. Instead, what the game has you do is reincarnate your character, which zaps them back down to level 1 and has you relevel it, with a higher xp requirement. In doing so though, you make that character permanently stronger with past life feats. And you can obtain 3 past life feats per class, allowing you to effectively reincarnate your character something like 36(?), each time gaining a little more power than you had. This allows you to experience ALL the content the game has to over multiple times instead of just whats at level cap. You also don't HAVE to do this though, so if releveling the same character (you can change classes and such each time) doesn't sound good to you, you don't HAVE to do it.
3. Classes. If you've ever played a DnD based game, this game is even MORE robust in its available class combinations than most other DnD games, and that's saying something. The only bad thing is that some of the base classes are not well balanced, due to some classes getting reworks while others are still awaiting their reworks.
4. Soloability. Most quests in this game can be soloed, which is why having a small population doesn't mean that much. Each quest scales with the number of people you have, including hirelings, which are AI controlled (kind of) characters you can summon to help you. As thus, if you like to just do things on your own, this game is fantastic for that. Just make sure you plan your character for everything you need in one character. This can be difficult for a newbie that doesn't know the system though.
All and all, this is an extremely fun, but very dated MMO thats great for soloers but also for people who want to things with others when they can. The game doesn't force the social part on you for 90%+ of the quests, but allows you to if you wish. If you do try this game and haven't played a DnD based game (either digital or PnP), definately read up before you make your character though, as you kinda have to plan your character from the beginning, and the premade paths are awful.

Vagante is the perfect mix between a rogue like and an RPG and currently one of my favourite games on steam.
You start each run by choosing one of four classes (Knight, Mage, Thief and the more unconventional"wildling" which involves you hokuto shinken-ing your way through your enemies) and then proceed to venture into a randomly generated cave which will eventually lead to 3 other unique areas, each housing their own stage hazards, secrets, enemies and bosses.
As you progress through each zone you will obtain equipment that carries uniques properties that change the way you can interact with the environment, from double jumping to straight up noclipping for a short time.
Every run involves a sense of adventure, and the different combinations between classes/perks/equipment guarantee that there is always room for experimentation. In a time when rogue-likes of varying quality are crowding the steam store, Vagante manages to shine through as proof that this genre can still be taken further and expanded upon.
Bonus points for having user-friendly and functional online co-op even in Early Access !

Amazing WIP game with great multiplayer!
So, the idea of a rogue-like game with multiplayer greatly intrigued me, and I definitely don't regret buying the game. As with many rogue-like games, the difficulty curve at the beginning can be a bit excruciating. You'll be dying a LOT in the first few levels at the beginning. (And in a rogue-like, a death means game over, go back and start from the beginning). With that said, after playing with friends for a bit under 5 hours, I feel that you really start to get a hang for the game.
At the beginning, the worlds seem endless and mystical, with sooo many items to collect. The basic premise is that levels are grouped in 3 or 4, where those 3 or 4 consecutive levels will be one "area" with a certain theme/enemies, etc. And as you progress you find more areas.
Well, after a decent amount of areas, the whole thing loops again, and you basically replay through every area again, but with much harder enemies the second time around. This is fun and can still provide some challenge, however, once you go through these areas a second time, you just get put into an infinite loop of only staying in one "area" at the end.
At this point, I have played a bit over 10 hours, and I feel that with 2 friends, we can get to the final "area" about half of the time, and once you get there, you just keep looping through the same levels with more and more enemies until it's downright impossible.
There is definitely some balancing that needs to occur, as now that I've played with some friends for a bit over 10 hours, we just continue playing the game until so many enemies start spawning that the server lags and the game becomes quite literally unplayable. However, at the same time, note that we've gotten all of the best gear at this point, and there really isn't much left to do. The only way to beat the levels at that point was basically to use some cheap abilities to just run to the exit unharmed and/or undetected and leave, and repeat. We did this for about 25 levels in the last "area" before we basically quit because the game was so laggy it was unplayable.
With all this said, it is an extremely fun game to learn, and it's still a work in progress so more will be added over time. As of right now, playing with a few friends, I don't know if you'd ever get much more than 30 or 40 hours out of the game at absolute max, but still WELL worth the purchase, and an absolute blast to play with friends.
