This is a hardcore PVP fighting game, not a casual PVE action RPG.
This is a hardcore PVP fighting game, not a casual PVE action RPG.
This is a hardcore PVP fighting game, not a casual PVE action RPG.
Have I made it clear yet? I hope so.
Now, how does this game function as a fighting game? There are two major things that differentiate Absolver from "traditional" 2D fighters, both of which tend to draw the complaints of... to put it politely, plebeians.
Firstly, there are NO confirmed combos. Landing one attack on an opponent gives you frame advantage for your next attack, but never 100% confirms a second attack. The defender ALWAYS has a window of opportunity to respond with one of the following to reverse the flow of battle: an appropriate counterattack, their defensive style, or the basic dodge. The attacker will NEVER feel like he is going through the rote repetition of a combo, and the defender will NEVER feel as though they're a helpless spectator to their demise... well, unless the defender freezes up and loses their ability to interpret the action on the screen, but that's a separate issue.
This lack of clear combos, this complete void of obvious starting and stopping points, means that the MENTAL pace of the fights is LUDICROUSLY fast and the pressure NEVER lets up, despite the relatively slow nature of the individual attacks compared to, say, SF's 3 frame jabs. You're never "waiting around" for the end of a combo or for a reset, like in MvC3... and this means there are no brakes on the train.
This unfortunately means that an unskilled player who has no idea of how to defend themselves can get taken from 100% to dead in one long and uninterrupted chain of attacks. This is why you'll see a TON of negative reviews complaining about "spam". The game is legitimately too intense and information-dense for casual players only a few hours in to hope to compete against longtime veterans. To a newbie, everything looks fast and unreactable and they don't know what's going on and they're blindly mashing buttons but they keep getting interrupted out of their attacks and nothing they're doing is stopping their opponent from continuing to wombo combo them and then they're dead and "wow what a♥♥♥♥♥♥game it's so imbalanced lul".
The second thing that differentiates Absolver is that unlike in other fighting games, where you can simply pick an existing character and put your hope in the developers that whomever you picked isn't meme-tier awful, you have to build your moveset yourself. Competitive wisdom is that a character in a fighting game should "fit your hands" and that you should pick whomever feels best to play for YOU, instead of just looking up some tier list on the Internet. But in Absolver, YOU get to build your own movelist out of a large common pool of attacks available to all players, meaning you get to build, iterate, tweak, and refine your movelist the way YOU want it to feel, flow, and play.
As you might imagine, customized deckbuilding is also a point that absolutely CRUCIFIES new players (and players who refuse to iterate and adapt). The default decks you start with are preeeeeetty garbage compared to the average deck you'll find veterans using. They're the equivalent of going to play rock-paper-scissors with someone playing rock-paper-scissors-lizard-Spock. For those of you not in the know, Spock beats both rock and scissors while only being vulnerable to paper, giving the player with access to Spock a clear-cut, mathematical advantage. This is even before the realization that a well-meaning player can inadvertently hamstring themselves in the process of building their own custom deck. They might say to themselves "well, if Spock is the superior choice in rock-paper-scissors, I'll play nothing but Spock!" Except Spock is beaten 100% of the time by paper, and so they have no hope against an opponent who makes this realization.
Okay, that analogy got pretty butchered. What I'm saying is that movelist customization is an extremely deep part of the game that requires just as much if not arguably more skill than the actual fights themselves. All too many players build a deck they think is cool, get mad when it doesn't perform, and blame the system for being imbalanced or unfair rather than admitting their own ineptitude and lack of insight. Yes, ineptitude and lack of insight can be remedied by research and reflection... but the average gamer these days refuses to do either, it seems.
Now, there DOES exist a sort of soft meta in place as far as move choices and the occasional two-move sequence "motif". HOWEVER, the flexibility of the stancing and sequencing WITHIN a single deck means that almost every player builds their deck differently even when they contain identical moves, and just about every player utilizes a healthy selection of offbeat moves that aren't widely agreed upon to be universally strong, giving their deck its own unique secret sauce. And even if decks were identical, people use the tools given to them in different ways; just look at any other "normal" fighting game with preset characters. Absolver's deck system doesn't feel like a TCG meta with set "netdecks", where you might tweak one or two card choices as "tech"; the majority of most decks out in the wild are more different from each other than they are the same. There are a few basic, easily counterable "scrub strategies" that I see from time to time, generally some kind of "let's put a whole bunch of this one kind of move in my deck while excluding all others", but that's about it. No two opponents whom I've sparred with regularly feel anywhere close to the same.
Finally, I feel I should address the elephant in the room about "content", or lack thereof. Content is a buzzword. Absolver is a game that enables two breathing, thinking human beings to engage in a thrilling battle of wits and reflexes with each other with a hundred different avenues of improvement and study. It will never run out of "content" in the same way that chess, boxing, and chessboxing will perennially remain entertaining pastimes. Maybe you don't enjoy chess, boxing, or chessboxing, but you can't claim that there's "nothing to do" or "that the game needs more work". Humanity's intelligence at large is the game's "content", and Absolver is a damn fine avenue of exploring it. If you think that the game lacks "content"... maybe you don't have very much intelligence. (Yeah, yeah, that came out a bit snarky and fedora-tipping. Something something, obligatory "to be fair, you have to have a very high IQ" copypasta meme.)
I hope this explanation goes a long way towards explaining away a lot of the negative reviews that have been left on this absolute gemstone of a game.

The game mechanic is also very interesting, but the execution is questionable. Being able to build your own combo and style seems fun at first, but it has a very steep learning curve. You'll only understand the value of every single action piece until you have a lot of real fighting experience. The counter intuitive control scheme only makes this problem more severe. What seems a very interesting fighting mechanic quickly descends into mindless button smashing.
This game does a very good job creating an instensive fighting stage. The PvP battles are very engaging and exciting, with the help of those cool kongfu moves, even though most of the time both players are just simply button smashing.
I still would recommend this game hoping that this developer can improve upon the control scheme and the steep learning curve for more casual players to enjoy this beautiful game.

It strikes a really nice balance between puzzles and combat, both which are really well done and quite satisfying. But the best part of Rochard is the amazing physics-based gameplay and how much fun it is to toy with. The game has a quirky sense of humor that really grew on me, and is right at that sweet 8 hour length that isn't too much yet doesn't feel too short. If you like your puzzle platformers with a healthy dose of action, don't skip Rochard.

I was really not prepared for the emotional impact this game was going to have on me. I really wasn't, and towards the end of the game I was genuinely upset, and angry, and thinking on some parts of the game automatically makes tears jump to my eyes. Had I known I wouldve been taken so strongly by the story of the game, I probably would've waited to play it - I'm a bit more sensitive these days due to some rough stuff in my personal life. That said, this is a GREAT game - if it wasn't, I wouldn't be recommending it! It's a beautiful game, with a lot of tie-ins and subtle statements about current events, and even events in the past that still have had lasting effects to this day. It presents them from the eyes of a child, but the discerning eye can catch n pretty quickly with what's happening thanks to all the clever context clues in the scenery and puzzles.
From a gameplay perspective... well, to be honest, there's not much. This is a story driven game, primarily, and the puzzles themselves aren't too difficult. There are a few in-game animations that I think are... weird, such as when using the axe or foraging - the sprites just don't deliver those kinds of actions too well. But they're also the means to an end to deliver you to the story, the true gem of this game. And as I've gone on above - the story will rip you to shreds emotionally if you underestimate how deep it can get.

An amazing first attempt at game making, Laura has put something special in this game, and if you're looking for beautiful pixel art and music, lovable characters, and a true emotional roller coaster, then this game is for you. The fact that this game was able to throw me all around the emotional spectrum, from one extreme to the next, is a true testament to how lovingly this has been crafted and how truly special this is.

I have mixed feelings about when I first got a decent Internet connection, back when I was just a little kid. On the one hand, it made me discover dozens and dozens of free (!) fangames all over the World Wide Web. On the other hand, many of them were, honestly, pretty bad.
What I'm trying to say here is, this feels and plays like a bad
fangame. One of those with very, very low ratings that you downloaded anyway because there was the word "Sonic" in the title.
Supposedly the fourth game in the main 2D series,
doesn't feel at all like the continuation to those games, but rather a terrible rehash of the original. Gone are the different shields introduced in
, gone are the multiple playable characters, gone is even the slightest bit of story or continuity between the various stages. All that's different from the 1991 classic is the presence of the homing attack introduced in
, and the awful controls.
And it's the awful controls one of the biggest flaws that this game has, most notably the complete lack of momentum. As soon as you stop pressing left or right, the titular character immediately stops, even in mid-air, even after being launched by a cannon, leading to unfair losses of rings or, at worst, deaths. Speaking of unfair, the homing attack has also changed for the worse: as soon as Sonic hits an enemy, or even as soon as the forward momentum given by the attack ends, he "cancels out" of his rolling animation, meaning that he's vulnerable to any enemy that may happen to be near him.
The lack of effort put into the controls reflects the low-quality level design. Not only there are merely four Zones that consist of three Acts and a boss battle each (plus a final Zone), but they're all bad clones of pre-existing stages from the first three games in the series, with only a handful of differences here and there. The same applies to the fights against Eggman.
They did try to change things up a bit, but most of the new gimmicks end up being not fun at all: for example, Lost Labyrinth Zone's second Act is almost completely shrouded in darkness (as in, 70% of the screen is nothing but black), and Sonic has to light up torches and blow up dynamites to continue.
What's also not fun at all is the inclusion of a couple of section that were probably meant to be played with motion controls during Lost Labyrinth and Mad Gear. Taking control away from the player doesn't feel good at all, especially when there are almost-invisible spikes you can and will touch.
Also baffling was the decision to make you take on any Act in any order, despite the later Acts and Zones being obviously harder than the first ones. Well, "harder" probably isn't the right word: the entire game is all but a stroll in the park, one that likes to hand you lives as if they were rings, before wanting all of them back during your last encounter with Eggman, which is an exercise in frustration that requires an excessive amount of trial-and-error to finally top.
It took me less than two hours to beat this game -  only seventy-five minutes outside of the final stage - and I highly doubt I'll ever touch it ever again.

On one level, it's an amusing parody of various JRPG tropes. On another, it's a puzzle game that tasks you with solving each scenario, which involves boss fights, side quests, and hidden things to discover, all under the allotted 30 second time limit. Originally released as Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis, this is the game that brought military simulators to a mainstream audience and gave birth to the Arma franchise. You have to be warned that this isn't your typical FPS - it's a military simulator with a steep learning curve.  The combat tries to be as realistic as possible, to the point that it was adapted into VBS1, a training simulator used by NATO.  The gameplay is very unforgiving, but rewards smart, tactical play.
The story is an interesting "Cold War gone Hot" scenario set around a fictional Balkan-flavored island chain and a rogue Soviet general's attempt to destroy the NATO garrison there. It's pretty good overall, though the voice acting is bad and it does strain credibility by just how long the US soldiers have doubts about the enemy their fighting (who are *clearly* Russian.)
The Resistance expansion is a unique campaign where you have to manage a guerilla war against a Soviet occupation of another island in the chain. It has some surprisingly in-depth equipment management, especially for the time, as you have to scavenge gear in order to actually equip your guerilla fighters.
If you're familiar with the original OFP, you might notice that the Red Hammer campaign is not included. This is because it was made by Codemasters and not Bohemia Interactive, and was made after the two had a falling out over the rights of OFP (which led BI to make Arma.) It's possible to mod it back into this game, but honestly, I've played it and it's utterly terrible. Not worth it.

So, the heroine starts out with options of pursuing a crossdresser, a sexpest, or her stepbrother. As I like to call them, the Widow Twankey, Simple Simon, and
. I chose the stepbrother, and it was worth it.
This is a brilliant Otome game, proving once again that psychology beats sex (that's why straight men play Otome games). The heroine is a developed, developing tough-as-nails adorable character with an immediate serious problem; she has lost her place as a princess and no one remembers who she is. Thankfully she has a great chemistry with all five of the chaps who stand ready to assist her. Widow Twankey's hidden depths deserve special mention, but I found each route better than the last; all deeply and excellently characterised, highly tense, but by no means uncompletable. The story is, to be fair, tied to the romantic visual novel route, as it were, compared to even more psycologically innovative stories like Cinders. The writing might also not quite convey so much torrid passion as Amnesia, but what is torrid passion worth without character and originality? And CP has far more of those than Amnesia and many, many other novels.

Positive or Negative? It's a tough call for me. Game play on my Steam Link is hit or miss depending on the demands of the game.

The mystery is that these games are completely playable on my living room TV using my laptop directy - even at high settings. But I can only get about 5-10 minutes of play out of the game when using the Steam Link in the bedroom. Laptop can't seem to handle the mirroring or the transfer and just gives up.
I guess the Steam Link requires the base computer to have more "horse power" than what it typically needs to play the game without the Steam Link involved. Challenging and diverse rogue-like. Think Spelunky, mixed with Risk of Rain, but minus the timed levels. This game rewards thoughtul play rather than rushing through each level, and caters to numerous playstyles with the 3 available classes
. And each class has their own unique skill sets that you level up as you choose, meaning each class can be played a multitude of ways. From a stealthy rogue surgically killing enemies with throwing daggers, to a God-cursed sword wielding Knight cutting swathes through monsters, and the ingenious mage using every spell at your disposal to outmaneuver and obliterate your foes. But not every run turns out with a champion. Spikes, Boulders, Angry Shopkeepers and increasingly fierce monsters will ensure that many adventurers meet their dooms. Although it never felt impossible. Each death felt like it was my own mistake due to lack of skill, and I never felt like there was something unbalanced or unfair.
Vagante features alternate progression routes, a huge variety of item types with randomized stats, procedurally generated levels, multiple classes, and a reasonable learning curve, making it rewarding to progress.
This game is well-worth the price, especially for early access, though at the time of writing this I believe it's very near release state. And as of writing this I haven't even completed everything or played much multiplayer.
TL;DR if you have played platformer and dungeon crawler rogue-like games such as Spelunky, Risk of Rain, or Rogue Legacy you'll feel right at home here. Once you've died a few dozen times of course.

Jamestown is a top down bullet hell shooter, very reminiscent of old school Japanese shoot em’ ups.  It plays great and is a ton of fun, especially with co-op. You control your ship and have two moves, your normal bullets and your special move; you can use each one without limit. They only way to die is if an enemy or an enemy shot, hits the center of the ship, so you can get out of tight spots just protecting your center. You also have a meter that fills up as you kill enemies, which charges a shield to get out of difficult situations as it only lasts for a few seconds. It is easy to get into the game, but hard to master.
It is not that long of a main story, but you can sink many hours just completing the challenges, getting high scores or just playing with friends. Each ship in the game has a different special type of bullet and control very differently, offering great variety and letting the player choose whichever suits their play style best. The DLC adds 4 new ships, which personally I enjoy using more than the default ones. Definitely recommend picking up this game if you like anything mentioned above. It does what it does pretty well!
Original premise, lovely visuals, great soundtrack, tight gameplay, "risk vs. reward" ship choice and level design.  Strongly recommended, and a must-have for all bullet-hell type folks. :-)

The story is completely absurd, and it's sorry it's not sorry, you can purchase an alternate script that's even more childish and might give you a little smirk (Plot included on the Deluxe Pack), it's a pretty wild and crazy story that might intend to make fun of other games stories since in the end people play shoot 'em ups to, well, SHOOT F*ing THINGS UP!
Now this is an area where this game truly shines, I absolutely loved this game's score, kudos to the composer who just nails it in the head with the epic soundtrack, I still hum the final boss' song in my head when I think about this game (mainly because I suffered that freaking boss a loooot of times).

Like so many others, I must say reviews should have an option beyond "Recommend: Yes/No"
As others have pointed out, the game has serious issues.
Flying ships struggle to move around land when they should just fly over it (Unintentionally hilarious when one craft is struggling to move around land and is rammed by another craft causing both to explode) and most/all boats can apparently fly (Not hilarious at all as they bypass the land and fly over your defenses to destroy your home base in large swarms).
The "flying boats" almost feel intentional when I noted the 4th map has a base that is completely surrounded by land. How can a land-only base be threatened by boats? Well, by "flying boats" apparently...
Smoke plumes sprout out of explosions that go off in odd, illogical directions. The drag-and-drop method of upgrading works fine before a fight, but works very much against you during active warfare (your visibility is obscured and sometimes the upgrade doesn't "take").
Hitting ESC is apparently supposed to pause the game but it doesn't (You see Resume/Quit options on-screen, but everything continues on in the background).
Basically, this feels like an unfinished, over priced phone game. Even if everything were working fine, $4 is just too much for something this basic. If the price drops to $2 or less and the programmer addresses the glitches, it would work as an OK little time-waster.
Thumbs up only because the programmer is actually trying to address the issues after taking a beat-down in the reviews...

Pirates Deck has the dubious honor of being one of the few scams that no one bought or even played comfortably sitting at 0 total players until it got into a bundle yesterday: the fact not even the "creator" of this "thing" fired it up once says alot.
This is basically a scam with no redeeming qualities whatsoever sold as a full game to try and get money from careless buyers: onwards to the actual review.
-thankfully no one fell for this scam
-the fact whoever created this was too lazy to even add trading cards means they won't see any money from them
-if you run the executable from the game folder it'll come up as "Spacewar" in your game profile, I don't know if it's bad coding or if it actually contains pirated assets but have contacted Support on the issue
-horrible graphics where jagged edges, washed out colours, ugly textures and a weird blur abound even on Ultra quality: menu graphics are below amateurish
-bad controls, you can't rotate your ship and flying around is awkward not to mention nausea inducing
-dull gameplay, you're supposed to fly around and gather trophies for points until you have enough to interact with an object in the middle of the map and you lose points whenever you die: even if it worked it'd be bad
-only one map and it'd be way too small for MP if people actually played in it
-supports a controller, too bad you can't change direction when you fly, so it's basically useless to try and play with one
-bad weapon design as they all look the same and one even shoots so slowly that, if you fire while moving, you'll zip past your shots (see screenshot) : I can only imagine how horrible it'd be to try and hit a moving target
-technically a mess, it'll often freeze when you try to start a match or refuse to open the options menu when you click on it: I also found no way to make it go fullscreen
The fact the actual game executable shows up as "Pirated_Pirate_MP_Promo" clearly shows this was just something thrown together in a few minutes to try and scam people: a cursory look at reviews and forums also reveals whoever is behind this actually had a completely different game greenlit before putting this mess in the store, clearly showing a willingness to cheat prospective buyers.
You won't be suprised by the negative review, this "thing" is not worth your time or hard disk space and, even for free in the bundle, it's just good for laughing at how bad everything is and at the fact someone thought people would spend money on it. I'm honestly surprised Steam hasn't pulled it.

Of course no game is perfect, but Rakuen comes pretty damn close.
As an avid fan of story-driven games, I absolutely loved Rakuen. The story itself was beautiful, and I quickly became attached to each and every character as the game explores their past and emotions. Though, the soundtrack is definitely one of the best parts of this game.
The only negative thing I could possibly say about this game is a few of the puzzles can seem a bit tedious to complete, however they are very easy and keep you interested as you explore the area surrounding the puzzles. I do recommend keeping a piece of paper and a pencil next to you while playing to write down clues you come across though, which will greatly help you in completing the puzzles. I also read a few negative reviews that said it was difficult to understand what to do next without reading a walkthrough, however for me I was able to complete the entire game without needing one (until I went back to complete the rest of the achievements I had missed). For most of the game you are able to receieve hints in-game whenever you need them, so a walkthrough really is not necessary for this instance.
I also recommend that if you are looking to complete every achievement, you should make sure to interact with and explore everything you possibly can, as there are some achievements that are area or event specific and you cannot get back to them without loading up a save or restarting the game. Other than that, I would recommend an achievement walkthrough if you find that too tedious for your playstyle.
Overall, if you enjoy story-driven games with amazing soundtracks, loveable characters, and an emotional storyline that will have you laughing and crying, I highly recommend giving Rakuen a try. It's well worth the full price, however if you can't pay that much, you can catch it on sale sometimes for about $3 or so!

Mediterranean Chicken and Pasta
Makes: 4 servingsPrep: 5 mins Cook: 15 mins Carb Grams Per Serving: 38
Ingredients
1 6 - ounce jar marinated artichoke hearts
1 tablespoon olive oil
12 ounces skinless, boneless chicken breast, cut into bite-size pieces
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/4 cup chicken broth
1/4 dry white wine
1 teaspoon dried oregano, crushed
1 7 - ounce jar roasted red peppers, drained and cut into strips
1/4 cup pitted kalamata olives
3 cups hot cooked campanelle or penne pasta
1/4 cup crumbled feta cheese (optional)
Directions
Drain artichoke hearts, reserving marinade, and chop them.
In a large skillet, heat oil over medium-high heat; add chicken and garlic. Cook and stir until chicken is brown.
Add the reserved artichoke marinade, broth, wine and dried oregano.
Bring to a boil; reduce heat. Simmer, covered, 10 minutes.
Stir in chopped artichokes, roasted peppers and olives.
To serve, spoon chicken mixture over pasta. If desired, sprinkle with feta cheese.

is, to say the least, a very peculiar experience. While it uses dread and body horror at every turn, the game also features poor characterisation, some painfully cheesy writing and design quirks that break from a lot of what it's trying to imitate: intense, survival horror.
Still, it is interesting to finally play the classic that started it all. Shall we?
You are Leon Kennedy, trusted hair model and ladies' man, and find yourself in the dreary backwoods of Spain on a mission to rescue Ashley Graham; the President’s daughter and a person so incapable of defending herself, it’s a wonder that she’s able to function in everyday life.
Upon “securing the ballistics” however, it’s clear that the Las Plagas parasite and the machinations of the mysterious cult behind it aren’t just going to let the two of you leave. Lock, load and bring plenty of herbs... it’s about to get ugly.
To say that
has had an influential effect on the industry would not only be colossal understatement but also a disservice to all the derivative gameplay mechanics that have appeared in the years since. From
to
, it introduced a standard to action games that revolutionised the industry and genre design.
Though Leon is certainly clunky to control at times, (mouse for laser sight aiming and WASD to orient your position), the stop-and-pop action is surprisingly enjoyable to play. Quite a few people seem to hate it and it’s not hard to understand why, but the gameplay worked quite well, barring the occasional fixed camera issue.
There's an obvious arcade influence, (a nice touch for all the time killers I used to sink money into), and this helps not only the gameplay of
but the campy/pulp tone it has gone for. Make no mistake, the contradictions of action and horror are well and truly on show here.
It’s funny to watch how often Leon will limp around on low health before suddenly kicking a head clean off or gently land from a great height. The shake-off finishers in general deserve a special mention as enemies die with a satisfying splatter, but it does get a little tiresome when you’re prompted for each and every action with a button press.
Speaking of camp however, the writing is markedly less interesting. Capcom always seems to struggle with anything outside of the clichéd and
is no different. While the voice acting does a decent job of selling the material, the cast can ultimately only be as good as what it has to work with.
Conversations with the few NPCs that aren’t totally braindead are hilariously suggestive and Leon’s comments go between stupid observations and smutty wit. The quality of the writing is as trashy and amateur as it gets, but it’s honestly amusing enough that I’m willing to give it a pass.
Despite technical improvements and the impressive visual overhaul that has been rolled into the HD re-release, some noticeable performance issues continue to plague the game. Lip and audio syncing was off significantly during cutscenes, sometimes reaching a few seconds behind the action on screen. Changing the locked framerate setting apparently acts a fix, but I didn’t notice any change between the two.
While the soundtrack does a good job of adding to the gloomy atmosphere, the limited range and repetitive Foley effects really began to grate after a while.
is a challenging game and can be downright brutal at times, so the reliance on gunplay is greatly affected when you’re hearing the exact same effect looped over and over again. QTEs are another unfortunate quirk that takes up a lot of your time, and some of the prompts can be ridiculously quick or just unresponsive, resulting in failure at the worst possible time.
As influential as the material it draws upon,
delivers a solid, action-oriented horror game and a standard for the genre that continues to be replicated to this day. While it is held back by some odd design decisions and the trappings of a fixed camera, this is well worth a look for fans of the series or anyone who wants to just turn their brain off and enjoy some good, ol’ fashioned carnage.

Pros:
Interesting team rpg progression
Strategic gameplay
Different factions offering various playstyles
Lots of replayability
Great visuals
Cons:
Steep learning curve
RNG aspect for calculating hits, dmg, etc, can be frustrating sometimes
Vsing AI can get stale once you start vsing other players
Conclusion
Mordheim: City of the Damned does very well to replicate a tabletop game onto a pc format. The RNG dice rolls for calculations will deter some people, but it's very much like playing cards or gambling. The frustration of fails at 90% chance is superseded by the success of 10% chances. You win some you lose some. The game allows you to strategically play your odds, establishing an interesting core gameplay mechanic.
Trying to level up the henchmen without them dying or getting maimed is challenging and fun. Not a casual game.

I love that the typical submissive or obvious choices are either missing, or they actually aren't received well by the character you're pursuing (I'm annoyed by games where you have to follow the idiot wilting flower choices in order to win the guy). Usually, I prefer a much more involved or active visual novel, like Long Live the Queen where there are many choices and the enedings are diverse and hard to achieve. I'm not usually drawn to those which follow a more traditional otome game format with clear routes and implications about choices, but the writing of this one is so good that I was completely enthralled with almost every route and even replayed some without skipping over everything I've already read like I normally do. I think the choices are also, while clear, still difficult to make and they allowed me to relate to the main character even though I felt very differently than her at the beginning of the game. Happily ever after isn't always perfect and while there will always be an aspect of fantasization to dating simulators like this, I feel it still showed the flaws in all the characters and their imperfect endings while leaving me satisfied with the story I got out of it all. I really enjoyed being in the realm of Angielle for a few days while I completed all the endings and learned all the character's backstories.

I can tell this is going to be a really fun game, but as many people will probably agree that there are a few mechanics that need to be cleaned up, as they actively harm gameplay.
But despite this, I'm already having fun and predict many hours of fun times.
Here's a few examples of some annoying experiences...
Swimming: In order to jump out of a pool of water you must hold up, so if you want to jump out of a pool of water to the left or right, you have to jump out of the water first, then hold left or right. Otherwise you just... float there.
Climbing ledges: If you hold up+left while intending to jump in that direction from a ledge, nothing will happen. You must either hold up OR left. If you want to drop from a ledge, you must hold down. Holding either left or right will not allow you to drop.
Boulders: You cannot grab on to the edge of a boulder. This means that if you push a boulder on top of a row of spikes, dont try to lower yourself down from the boulder onto the spikes. You will die.

Let me start this off by saying I've played this game for far longer than my playtime says. In fact, it was one of the first PC games I ever played, and to this day it's still one of my favorites. The world is interesting, the diversity of spells and abilities you can get is astounding, and it boasts the unique (so far as I know) feature of calculating stats and damage like an actual game of tabletop D&D. You even get a couple Dungeon Masters narrating the things you do, which I always thought was a nice touch. The sixteen-odd classes, with the ability to multiclass up to three times, and various races are each fairly intriguing, though there isn't really much you can do in the way of customization. Still, you can play as a magic robot. That's pretty cool.  The graphics are definitely showing their age, and I've run into my fair share of bugs, but it's never stopped me from having a good time. Still, the game is far from perfect, and there's a few pieces of advice I'd like to give to those interested in picking it up:
1. Get some friends to play with you. This game is fine on its own, but, as with tabletop D&D, a couple friends makes it far better. The playerbase for this game is fairly small, and public groups arent' as common as they once were. If you want to co-op, chances are you'll have to seek outside help.
2. Be prepared to spend money. Not on items, or gear, or things like that, but on adventure packs. This game isn't pay-to-win (how could it be, it's mostly co-op), but you do have to pay for a great deal of content. This can either be in the form of a subscription (I don't know how much that is exactly), or for adventure packs, for which you use TP, the game's freemium currency, to unlock specific quest chains. For some people, that might be an instant turn-off, but if you're like me and have trouble sticking to one game for too long, You'll probably appreciate the ability to pay as you go, rather than keep shelling out money for a game you may not be interested in at the moment. You can, as with most games, go through and unlock all of the areas for free eventually, but not unless you're willing to endure a rather long grind. I'm talking like multiple characters on multiple servers long. If you're not quite sure if you're willing to spend money on a free-to-play game, there's still enough free stuff to get a feel for if you like the game, and you can still have plenty of fun without spending a cent.
Also, not sure if this is on my end or something with the game, but I've found the controls to be a tad slow and unresponsive as of late. Again, not sure if this is the game, or my computer, I've had similar problems in a few other games. To conclude, not a bad game, if you like D&D you'll probably like this. Really I'm just writing this in the hopes of keeping it alive.

I sank a lot more in to this game pre-Steam. DDO remains the best online MMO experience using the D&D 3rd edition ruleset, and is really a great experience, despite the fact that it show it's age. If you prefer soloing or can't find players....a real problem at times....then you need to spend money on henchmen, too; the game is more balanced now than ever for solo play compared to when it started, but forget trying to go it alone without a healer, for example.
DDO is not perfect, and it's aged badly, and I dislike the cash shop's excessive prices (I never bought something if it wasn't on sale as a rule) but it's still an innovative MMORPG and the best such type of game D&D has ever been translated in to.

It's confusing in pretty much every way. I've been playing the game for two hours and I honestly have no idea what I am supposed to do. From what I can gather, it's sort of like Dark Souls in the sense that you wander around, find a boss and kill them. Unfortunatley, the game's actual world is full of awful linear pathways with enemies that will gang up on you when the game is clearly made for 1v1 duels. Every section of the world (and whilst the world is graphically beautiful, but visually failry bland in most respects) looks more or less the same, with a few variations in its theme. There aren't many areas to explore from what I can count with maybe 4 or 5 at the most. AI often seems more of a pain to fight than other players, where as players can actully be good at the game, AI just seems to land blows randomly, even if you are blocking. Other times you are either pushed into a corner by 2 or 3 of them where the camera goes everywhere (this happens on staircases too) and then completely destroyed. Even if you block, your stamina will drain, and then you will be killed. If you try and fight out of it, you will be hit before you can land one of your attacks, simply putting you into a loop.
The only thing I praise about the game besides its graphical quality and art style is the actual fighting mechanics, but be warned, it does take practice. That's a good thing though. What's not good is that most of the player base is no longer around, so you will have to either practice on AI's which I find unnatural to play against, or take your chances with already skilled players in duels.
Lucky I got this on sale. It's not a bad game at its core, but there are too many aspects that let the game down for it to warrant even half its price tag.

Well, maybe, just maybe, someone is interested in reading this. So I want to review not only the positive, but the negative aspects. I do it first for the whole game, then for each story, so it is going to be pretty long.
The game:
+ grafics (i mean if you look at it as a free game. ofc games like Amnesia have asthonishing grafics, but then they are also very pricey)
+ music (i think the music was okay, but got a little bit annoying after a while, when playing different routes with the same bg music...)
+ idea (i think it's not a common idea to use fairy tales as plot for a visual novel. and the idea to reverse them was also really good.)
+ characters (for a free game the characters were unexpectigly deep. they had a personality - it was not like the  focus was on the romance, but also how the characters deal with the feelings, making it more like a story than a otome for me.)
+ plot (it was not really deep (my opinion) but they carried it really well out. the stories were connected and if you played it in the right order, then you also understood the idea at the end)
+ main character (she had a personality, not being a lifeless doll or a total damsel in distress. i liked it)
- main character (she had maybe even too much personality. often i couldn't really emphatize with her. In some routes like Fritz she was overly selfish and like a damsel in distress, but then in the routes of Rumpel or Waltz she was so selfless that I'd call her stupid.)
- characters (somehow, I still think that they had more potential than in the game. e.g. Waltz had really much potential, so that the plot could be much longer)
- plot (well, I'm sorry, but there are some things I don't like about this. The thing with the reversed fairy tales was great. Also the idea about her mother. But then in the plot... I think that the focus lied on the tragic story with the MCs mother, the fairy tale curses making just a shard of the story... I mean, the idea was new, it was great. There could be more done with it e.g. that they lived like in the story: there was peter pan, a child, who couldn't grew up. But he had a lot of friends and the MC became like Wendy for him. But then it was his curse to not leave Neverland and Wendy wanted to leave. So he wanted to stay with her, but he couldn't. MC wants to make a good deed, so she tries to convince him, but then there's captain hook ... and so on )
- choises (God, this really bothered me. I mean REALLY! You just can't get them right. I mean the text on the buttons and the things she said, often don't match. So you need to reload when doing most of the choises at least once every few choises. AND ITS SO FRUSTRATING! Like with Rod, i COULDNT GUESS ALMOST ANY OF THEM RIGHT ON MY FIRST TRY!? And, come on, I'm not so bad at otome games... most of them just didn't make sense for me... like e.g. biting Karmas hand (WHY WOULD U DO THIS?!??!?!?))
Well, I don't want to complain so much, so let's move on to the routes.
Rod:
I think it was the most understandable route of all, although I had a lot of problems with the choises. Rod has the spell of the little mermaid. And it's one of my favorite fairy tales. But well, he is like the mermaid himself. He doesn't want to bother anyone and is pretty shy, so I found him very adorable. There wasn't much of the main story in his route, but well, now we know, why Ophelia married the king (i still think that detail is pretty funny).
Karma:
Well, Karma is Karma. I love guys like him in vn because they are most of the times easy to deal with. Karma wants attention and he wants love. He has the curse... well you will know. But it's my second most beloved fairy tale. And the route itself was a little bit too short for me, but I kind of liked it. But well, the MC wasn't really good in this one I think. If you know, what I mean /coughts bad end /coughts. And that she would learn sword techniques was a little too much for me...
Rumpel:
Ahh, when I started this route, I thought it'd be the funniest one and I was right. This flirty idiot, whom I really wanted to slap a lot of times through the routes... well he had almost the best story (my third favorite). I really enjoyed, how he had grown in the story, realizing that sometimes you need to sacrifice in order to protect. And in this route the main was also really nice. I could almost every time agree with her choises.
Fritz:
Well, this, this is my FAVORITE!!! I ship them. I really do. I think the main and Fritz are meant to be together (and don't you dare to say that Waltz is canon with her DON'T CHA). Fritz has the curse of the tale I think everybody knows. And I think it was the best idea to make it reversed like this in the game. This was the only story, where I really cried. It was killing me, how he was adoring the princess the whole time, willing to do everything just for her to be safe. After ... well when the queen was there and passed away, Fritz always watched her. He wanted her to be happy, to protect her. He wanted to stay with her and he was restless until he found her. Fritz has the saddest curse of all of them I think (besides Rods bad end /coughts), but he still is willing to give up his life for her. He has such strong feelings for her that he could overcome his curse... well... I just loved this story. It's really sad but adorable at the same time.
Waltz:
Last but not least. My favorite character. My favorite fairy tale. And then came the route. It had so much potential, god, but it was too short. I know that it is difficult to write a romantic story, when the hero knows that he loves her and spoils her a lot accordingly. I know that it's not easy to write the conclusion of main story, when you have to mind all the story pieces you had written before. But P L E A S E, don't make a fairy tale curse WITHOUT ALMOST NOTHING BASED ON THE FAIRY TALE (i don't mean the mettaphors e.g. queen = hook). And the MC... I was so devastated at her change. She turned into a person... well she just wanted to sacrifice herself for everyone. And... well I don't like it. The story turned into something like The Maid of Orléans and it displeased me greatly because I'm not fond of people rushing into death. Simply choises like her trying to stab herself, only to save her father... it's just too much drama for me I'm sorry. Nevertheless I loved Waltz personality. So it was nice having at least him around in the route ;)
I completed this pretty quickly, but I like the story and how engaging everything is. Even though I just finished I'll probably continue to play for a long time :)

I was interested in Cinderella Phenomenon because the fairy tale theme intrigued me, had many good recommendations, and happened to be free. This was also my first time playing a visual novel.
The art and the story are so beautiful and I really appreciate the effort that went into making each of the characters unique. Each storyline, while different, also linked in with one another. I highly recommend following the story order recommended by the developers, as more layers were added to the story each time I played it through. I appreciated being able to change the princess' first name and liked doing so for each new character path I took.
The only downside I experienced was that I lack the ability to choose every correct path on my own to get the good endings, which was necessary to unlock the paths of Fritz and Waltz. Thankfully some users have put together extemely helpful walkthough and achievement guides for this game, if you get stuck.

PROS
-FREE TO PLAY! You don’t have to pay a cent for this game!
-Good art. I liked the character design and backgrounds as they were all well done and detailed.
-Compelling characters and character development
-15 plus hours of game play
-Easy to achieve endings. The game has a good ending indicator after every choice and many save states, therefore it is easy to get the good endings.
-Well written and entertaining
-Positive take on cross dressing
-Strong main character (not one of those ninny headed damsels)
CONS and Explanations
-Somewhat similar story lines. Without giving anything away, a lot of the bigger plots are very similar, although the more detailed components are different
-Although the game boasts 60 plus unlockable CGs, I just did not feel like there were enough
-This might be nitpicking, however, I wish there was more after story! I want more love! Each story had a kiss, but sometimes I just need a tiny bit more smut in my life. (Ah to be an old perverted man, but I digress)

An amazing space-age game where you take on the role of a portly miner whose mining operation gets attacked by space bandits. Play around in low gravity, use your  combination weapon—the 'rock blaster' and 'G-lifter'—to solve problems and reach new heights, and collect power-ups to enhance your weapon's capabilities. With incredible gameplay and an enthralling story, it's definitely worth your time to play.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It created little fanfare when it was released, and it hasn't gotten much publicity on Steam since, but it's a solid and entertaining little physics platformer.
It starts off a little slow, with Rochard's abilities being quite limited, and the rock blaster barely able to fire 3 bolts in a row. By the end of the game, though, you will be zipping around in low gravity, blasting turrets in mid-air, while launching sticky bombs at enemies, and throwing their corpses at their friends. In the beginning, it might seem like combat is limited, but sweet merciful crap does it get fun by the end or what.
The music is very well-done, although unfortunately you rarely ever hear it. The song that plays in the casino is amazing, and it made me glad that I bought the soundtrack version. The graphics are also well done, using the Unity engine, although some of the texture work is a little shoddy.
The puzzles are also top-notch. There were only a few that genuinely stumped me for a while, but they all at least require thought and a little bit of planning. Sometimes I evem got the feeling that my solution was not the one the developers intended, and I love when I'm able to do that.
Controls on the 360 gamepad are solid as well, for the most part. There were a few tricky sections where I needed to aim the right analog stick to the right while pressing A and holding down LT, though, which required a little digital (get it? fingers) acrobatics. I didn't have any real issues with it, but I could see it being a problem for some others. I imagine keyboard and mouse controls would work just as well, if not better, but this game seemed to scream "360 CONTOLLER" to me.
The voice acting is really the only sore spot in this game (other than the hilariously flamboyant Skypolice), but as the tone of the game is less-serious, it came across more as funny than anything. Some of the dialog is pretty hilarious as well, but I won't spoil anything.
Overall, I rather enjoyed this game. The gameplay didn't devolve into rote pattern memorization, the combat was very fast-paced and fun, the puzzles were clever, and the sound/music added to the whole experience.
I recommend picking it up. It's a game that almost anyone can enjoy.

I totally love this game ! Sad to see how all the negative reviews have less than 50 hours playtime in this game, not even giving themselves a chance to learn how to play it.
Yes, it is difficult, it is punishing, sometimes even when you did everything right ! Sometimes you will wonder if the gods of RNG hates you and why they would want your elite soldiers to loose their limbs or life. Yes, this is not a game for the soft hearted or for those with anger managment issues, you might just end up breaking your keyboard or computer screen.
But.. once you learn the basics this game is super fun !!
My first warband was a skaven (ratmen) warband, But I had a difficult time managing these squishy creatures, so after some hours I moved on, tried the human mercenaries warband. This went a little bit better, still some deaths and injuries but I got by and kept progressing. After some time I decided to try the skaven again, and this time, after learning the basics, it was a completely different story. Sure there were still have some injuries and deaths, but it went a lot better after learning the basics of the game (and how to avoid doing massive mistakes that ends up killing off your troops for certain)
This is not farmville, it is not CoD, it is not Command and Conquer. This is Mordheim, city of the damned, a stratergy game that punishes bad stratergies and stupid decisions. Only on very rare occations your troops suffer when it was not your own fault. It has a deep learning curve and takes a bit of time to really get into.
Ive played all the warbands to level 10 (max) except sisters of sigmar and cult of the damned. The most enjoyable has been skaven and witch hunters, with the ratmen having a very good all around team and amazing henchmen (warpguard is by far the best henchmen in the game IMO), and the witch hunters having insanely good heroes and leader. In both these warbands you want to go for the optional leader, not the standard one. I dont have a single witch hunter in my witch hunter group, but rather a warrior priest with born leader and a couple of templar knights kicking♥♥♥♥♥ If you are having a hard time with the game try this out, the templars never die, and the warrior priest makes sure to keep them healthy. From my own experience heavy armor and shields with one handed weapons generally works out for the best, accompanied by perks that is useful for people who does many attacks each round, for example "quick insicion".
Anyway, the game.. it has nice maps that always change up, every time you enter a match the map is different created "random", the main story maps are very enjoyable, the skill customizations and how you want to build your group is entirely up to you.
PROS:
Fun and challenging game!
Always a new map. You are in the city of mordheim so the theme of the map is often similar, but in fact the map is always different.
Huge character skill and setup customization.
Active devs ! Every time I was thinking there was some issue with the game it got patched soon after to fix those issues.
CONS:
It is difficult in the start, this is definetly not a game for noobs or impatient people. Your troops will die and you have to decide if you want to ragequit or figure out exactly why they died, because 95% of the times things go bad it is not the RNG fault, it is your own fault because you did something stupid, perhaps got too greedy grabbing that far away wyrdstone away from your group, or you tought your archer was standing in a good spot when soon after realizing he gets trapped on that balcony he was standing on and chopped into bits because you put him in overwatch stance.
I also wish there was more appearance customizations of all the troops. There is usually plenty of colors to choose from, but not a lot of other customization options in terms of how your troops look.
Sometimes the AI go full retard, especially the impressive (huge elite unit), but it has been upgraded/patched and is now a lot better, they rarely do stupid stuff anymore.
The game used to have more cons, like very slow loading times and some annoying bugs, but as far as I can see all those are fixed. Every time I encountered a bug in this game it was just after a new release and it got patched in less than 2 weeks every time.
-----------------------------
This is an amazing game for anyone who wants a challenge and is bored of many of the "fed with teaspoon" games made nowadays that holds your hand trough the entire process. Sometimes you sit there for a match or two, sometimes you sit there all night playing and tinkering with your troops, thinking about how you wish to build them. Tons of replay value and tons of fun once you get into it. A very fine stratergy game indeed !

I really, really wanted to recommend this game, because under it's horrible flaws is hidden the skeleton of something really fun. I even wrote an earlier review to that extent; it didn't post due to an error on Steam. Having played it several days since then, I just can't recommend it now.
There are several minor flaws in things like the UI, AI, weird character animations, et cetera, but most of those are fairly trivial. What it comes down to is that the underlying math is horribly implemented to such an extent that the stats of your warband are essentially a lie. No matter how much you level the stats on your party, your odds of accomplishing any task on the battlefield are no better than random chance. What do I mean by this? I understand that a percentage is a probability. So, if you have say, 70% chance to dodge, it isn't a guarantee; you have 70% chance to dodge, and 30% chance to fail dodging. However,
, statistically, you should dodge roughly 70% of the time.
Instead, a character will get powned again and again in a round, or even an entire combat, with a statistical average of say 0-10%. This results in ridiculous battles where warbands you should slice through like butter due to your superior party members and gear, and your understanding of the game after having played it for dozens of hours, end up handing you your @$$, even if you manage to kill as many of their party as they kill of yours despite the additional obstacle of poor implementation and hence unfairness. This will happen even on normal difficulty combats - the game for some reason has a separate difficulty for combats in addition to the overall difficulty level of the game. This doesn't make the game "hard"... it's not a fair challenge that is simply difficult. Its lack of predictability or reliability makes it aggravating to play. There is no way to improve your skill at psuedo-random number generation. Hard, brutal or deadly combats are impossible. You will also frequently face the somewhat humorous, and much more maddening, circumstance of having your butt kicked by a one-armed and/or one-legged enemy.
I'm a game developer myself. I remember, several years ago, working on a game at a studio that was shut down; and having an argument with a designer about this very issue. Similar to this game, it was a turn-by-turn tactical combat game originally. He wanted me to implement a system that behaves as Mordheim does not. In other words, if you have 70% chance to accomplish something,
, your successes should average out to roughly that percentage. At the time I was resistant, because I hadn't implemented that kind of system before and I knew it would be time-consuming. Unfortunately, we never got to publish that game since, as I mentioned, the studio failed. However, after playing this game, I understand. I mean, I understood the logic of this a while ago, but now I really
.
You will eventually end up in a situtation where you are very far along into the game, and you either have to abandon it because your warband has suffered too many setbacks in the form of defeats and injuries that you cannot recover, or you just become too exhausted to continue playing. I'm at Act II-II and I'm not sure if I'll continue or not.
One last thing I'll say is that it's possible, with all the spells being cast, and gear and what-not, that other parties are simply buffing past all of your stats on-the-fly as it were. That doesn't really improve the diagnosis however, as in that case, the game is simply very unbalanced. Any way you cut it, this game is a tragic failure for the design team. Whether that is inherently due to the design, due to an improper implementation by engineering, or some other factor like poor communication or office politics, which all too sadly sometimes cause these sorts of flaws to appear in games, is pure speculation. Ultimately, for the players - the paying customers - the cause is immaterial. Being a software engineer myself, I doubt there is an easy fix for this problem, since it's a flaw deeply embedded in the entire design from top to bottom - and because, if you did fix it, you would essentially be changing the game fundamentally, which wouldn't be fair to players who had invested so much time into the game before the fix.

Rochard is a physics platformer, and quite a good one at that.  It's definitely not the longest game out there, but the length is quite reasonable for the price.
The game mechanics focus around your G-Lifter, which combines a gravity gun, laser rifle, and grenade launcher into one device as well as gravity manipulation.  You will unlock grenade types as you progress through the game as well as new abilities for the G-Lifter.  The pacing is quite good and new mechanics are introduced at regular intervals.
None of the puzzles are terribly complicated and shouldn't take much thought to complete.  Finding secrets requires a bit more thought and use of advanced game mechanics but are all still pretty easy.  It's definitely not as much of a thinking game as other puzzle platformers like Portal.  That said, it's still quite enjoyable, and I think the game could easily become frustrating if the puzzles were made too difficult.
On the negative side, the voice acting is terrible.  It's not Two Worlds bad, but it's close.  The writing isn't much better, but at least the story is decent.
The DLC is a short series of challenge rooms and much more of a challenge than the puzzles in the main game.  While very short it is quite enjoyable and satisfying to make it through them, especially if you can manage to do it without dying.
If you like puzzle platformers or physics platformers, you should play this game!
A great example how a modern indie puzzle game must be done.

The reason that it’s not stems from a couple of factors, the first one is the rng, on numerous occasions, I found myself missing far more than I should. A great example is during one fight, I failed 4 80% to hit checks in a row, hit once, and missed again. I very frequently got the impression that the number I was being shown for my hit chance was simply wrong. This applies to all elements of the game that are left to chance (and there are many). The next issue is that the enemies you fight will typically be so far out of your league that you won’t be able to win 4 on 1 encounters. I am not exaggerating, when I first started playing, a hero ,a leader,  and 2 of my henchmen lost in a fight with a vampire, they kept failing their fear checks (preventing them from being useful), and kept getting hit. Even in my more recent fights with vampires, I almost lost, I had a vampire lord outnumbered 5 to 1, and it took nearly 3 turns to kill him, he never once failed his all alone checks (I don’t even think he went through any for some reason), and even had enough points to use a skill to lower all of my defensive options for all of my soldiers and do 3 attacks in a row, which he almost never missed. This issue applies to all enemies, not just the vampires, but they were the encounters I remembered the most clearly, and were my kryptonite for some reason. I can’t recommend the game; it’s not that the game is too hard, but that it simply wants to artificially inflate your death count and failures by screwing you. You can start again, hire new soldiers to replace the crippled or dead ones, but it screws you because your new soldiers start out at base level, meaning that their overall combat utility is significantly lower than that of the rest of your squad, and you will suffer for it.
If you still want to play this game, here are some tips; don’t take missions above the hard difficulty setting, try to save up your wyrdstone for a rainy day or required shipment, play the tutorials, always try to move as a massed force or decent sized squads, and focus more on keeping your squad alive than the secondary objectives. Also, be careful about charging, if there are any obstacles in the way your character will simply move forward and do nothing, wasting your offence points. One more thing, if your enemy is moving as a massed force, try to kill them one at a time, as quickly as possible and keep them pinned down or blocked, that or lose, those are your options for fighting massed enemy forces.
Over my time playing, I’ve used ¾ of the original factions, gone through at least 5 maps with each, played 2 story missions, played around 40-50 maps in total (including the tutorials), and at the time of this review, put around 30 hours into this game.
In summary, the game isn’t bad, but it’s not very rewarding because it typically punishes you in ways that seem unfair, be it a single enemy being able to kill most of your party, or the rng screwing you more than you can comprehend.

Initially I wrote a negative review about this game because it spanked me and I ragequit.  I've deleted that review and persisted with the game, read some articles and learned how to play it and I have to say it's a lot of fun.  There's some rich tactical strategy to be had here.
This is a game of positioning and attempting to outmaneuver your enemy.  The combat is quite savage and I think a lot of the negative reviews would go away if the developer simply let the player decide what difficulty level they wished to play at, rather than forcing the player into the way they want the game to be played.
You will get no easy, normal or hard campaign.  Each mission is rated starting at normal, hard, brutal and deadly.  Right from the get go.  The AI stays about the same but the enemies get massive buffs as the difficulty increases.
Of course, you don't have to do these hard missions.  But there are better rewards if you choose to do them.  And it's incredibly satisfying when, either by skill or luck, you win a challenging mission.
There's a lot of customization of your warband and it's a lot of fun naming and making your troops into characters.  Your fighters can be injured and a couple of mine are missing arms and one now has a peg leg.  There are definite consequences in this game and no save scumming.  There's no saving at all, its all autosave and you cannot reload.
I'd say this is an excellent game, but it's also very hard, there's no doubt about it and if you don't like to lose you'll have to get good if you want to survive the deadly streets of Mordheim.

It's good, my favorite of the X-COM-alikes. I played Skaven, Empire, and Undead and progressed until I had a level 10-ish warband in each. A few pros and cons:
Pros:
1. Races feel distinct and none feels too strong or too weak. Weapons and armor feel balanced.
2. The game does a good job in making you use tactics and the environment to win over an enemy that will almost always be stronger than you are. As Empire, I had a clump of ranged that moved around and focused individual stragglers or used chokepoints while my tanks took damage. As Skaven, I was mobile enough to converge first in the missions where you start out in separate packs. As Undead, i'd have zombies distract and occupy enemies while my crypt horror and vampires focused the rest down.
3. RNG is just right for me. Part of tactical games is to have a backup for your tactic; if my 85% chance to hit guy misses...what do I do? I've never had those one in a million streaks some of these other commenters have. One in a thousand? Sure. But not one in a million.
Cons:
1. Campaign missions aren't very good. Endless waves of reinforcements while you try to get that last objective.
2. AI will get stuck on stuff. The large creatures especially will get stuck on stuff. That ends up giving a lot of variance to the difficulty.
3. Many of the skills are almost never worth using.
Overall pretty good and worth buying (maybe on 50% sale, those come around fairly often).

If you're looking to get yourself into these crazy looking shoot 'em ups ("shmups") you've seen out there, like your Touhous, your DoDonPachis, your eXceeds, your Crimzon Clovers and what have you, but still feel too intimidated by being awash in a sea of pretty projectiles decimating your chances of survival, then Jamestown may just be the perfect place for you to get started.
In comparison to all of the other shooters mentioned, Jamestown keeps things relatively simple, not only in its variety of bullet patterns, but the various underlying systems for scoring and survival are fairly easy to understand. With Jamestown you'll naturally learn various techniques that can transfer over to nearly any "bullet hell" kind of game, such as understanding your player character's tiny hitbox (if things hit this, you die!), grazing through tight openings in bullet patterns, and "streaming" various aimed attacks that come at you from one side of the screen to the other, with bullets narrowly missing you.
Key to mastering the game is understanding the "vaunt" system. Vaunting requires only a full vaunt gauge to activate and a single button press. Vaunting affords you some momentary invincibility both upon activation and deactivation, but also serves to double the points you receive from destroying enemies and picking up collectibles as well as doubling the damage you do. It's an ingenius system that can be used for newbies as a way to nullify tricky to dodge patterns and for more advanced players to milk the scoring system for all its worth. In that way, you can almost literally play Jamestown any way you want, be it for survival or gunning for high score challenges.
Though the game is relatively short (five stages total), there's still a really great amount of content to be explored. While playing, you'll unlock four types of ships, challenge maps that will further enhance your understanding of how shmups work, and a whole slew of difficulty modes that are all geared toward creating a smooth level of challenge as you keep moving up and getting better. So, even if the "main game" is a tad on the short side, the game's still feature rich enough to warrant the pricetag.
Jamestown is not only a dandy little shmup itself, but it's also a very comprehensive learning tool that can help new players to the genre come to grips and get over the intimidation factor. The myriad of difficulty selections and stage designs all feel constructed around the idea of getting better as you play. The more you put into Jamestown, the more you'll get out of it. It may be a tad too tame for experienced shmup players, but new players definitely can not go wrong here.

If you thought Civ 5 was disappointing, (as i did), this adds nothing to change your mind.  I was suckered into thinking it was going to be drastically better by the metascores and reviews.  Awful decision.  Still hated it.  It's merely a more complex version of the terd it has always been.

The new mods alone, including space-based and mythological scenarios, are enough to keep a dedicated player occupied for days, and the new civilizations and systems introduce so many new layers to the gameplay that Civilization IV is practically a new game entirely.

In spite of the short time listed here, I actually have played hundreds, if not thousands of hours worth of Civilization IV.  It is, without a doubt, the best 4x game ever made.  That's not to disparage earlier greats in the genre, but Civ IV (particularly the BtS expansion) takes the concept to an extremely high form that would have been unthinkable on any earlier hardware.  The game play is deep, and with dozens of unique leader trait combos, several paths to victory, randomly generated maps, and tons of user mods, infinitely replayable.
The only downsides of this game are its failure to use hexes, failure to have a genuine 3d (as in globe) map, and a particular game mechanic in the combat system that makes crushing the AIs fairly easy when facing even remotely even odds.
There are religious, technological, corporate, political, cultural and military paths to victory.  Each civilization has both a unique unit and unique building, and each leader a unique set of two personality traits that affect gameplay significantly.  The game can be played on small maps, or gigantic.  It can be played in a quick speed - finishing in a couple hours - or in "marathon" speed, a game that can take several days to finish.  There are barbarian hordes that will smash your early civilization, and randomly generated events and quests to vary each game.
It's so infinitely replayable in fact, that I am going to stfu, and go start a new game right now...

"Why does Vagante have an Overwhelmingly Positive score, yet such scathing reviews on the difficulty?"
Well, this is a question I spent my first 15 or so runthroughs with my girlfriend questioning. We went straight into multiplayer, which skips the tutorial aspect of the game... and even with the tutorial, there is a LOT that isn't explained to you when you start out, that you learn through trial... and a lot of error.
This game is hard. If you're looking at this review wondering whether or not you want to buy it, the answer is... do you feel ready to face a Dark Souls level of learning curve? This game isn't forgiving, and very hard to fully comprehend when you start BECAUSE of how much detail the developers put into it. There are strategies, tricks and secret aspects to this game that run so deep that it actually makes getting started quite confusing.
If you want to make this easier, you need to look at the wiki. This isn't all too comprehensive, but try some strategy guides for your class, read up on what your abilities actually do/how to use them... and from there, you can start to make stuff up a little more on your own, but this'll stop you from investing in something that has an application you can't properly utilize.
Is the game itself good? It's rich, deep, and full of promise from some devoted developers who are planning to add more. I would heartily recommend it.
Is it worth $15 in its current state? Yes. 20 hours in and even in co-op we're struggling to beat the last level, and that's on my first class choice- I have three others to test out for entirely different gameplay experiences!
How's the co-op? Thus far, for all the devs warn about it being 'unstable', we've encountered one bug in 20 hours of gameplay and over 50 individual games. The devs know their stuff, and 'unstable' by their standards is far from that of most other indie greenlight stuff.
Is this my kind of game, and will I enjoy the experience? Well, I like to compare it to experiences like FTL over Don't Starve. If you die, you're not going to cry for hours. It's pretty easy to get back to where you are, and much less brutal for ten hours of progress lost or something. For the gameplay itself as opposed to the roguelike side of it, it's very much like the Spelunky era of games, very similar to going caving in Terraria but much more structured and complex.
In its current state, I'd give the game an 8/10. To address the downsides that aren't solely the difficulty curve... It does at this stage lack a little bit of content, the soundtrack leaves something to be desired, and I have no idea how to unlock that %#*$ing chained chest- plus a little more starting character customization would go a longer way. The unlock system is nice as it stands, but I feel like it needs work/more complexity to add a bit more starting flavour than one trait and YOLO it up on the RNG. The new resurrection system (you need a certain amount of health to resurrect your teammates by walking over their graves) is great, though a bit more mechanic specification for co-op would be helpful (took us ages to figure this out.)

I just wanted to say that I am thoroughly enjoying this game. It has a lot of similarities to a lot of other games (the levels remind me a lot of Spelunky, the overall gist of the combat is a bit like Rogue Legacy, the difficulty is a little bit Dark Souls), but it's very much its own thing.
Its world is deadly, but not unfair, and the thematic elements are absolutely lovely! It rewards being meticulous and careful, and also experimenting with your surroundings and the enemies. There is a thoroughly surprising amount of depth packed into the relatively simple tiles. Every mechanic I've encountered so far feels really well thought-out, and they're often quite multidimensional (it took me probably four hours of gameplay to realize I could use the chicken to parachute, a la Ocarina of Time!).
Oh, and the music is fantastic! The small characters and simple graphics may not be for everyone, but the vibe and sense of wonder and discovery about this game are gorgeous.
The last thing I would say about Vagante is that I really love how I can play it for just 10 or 15 minutes at a time. There are progress saves between each level, so it's really easy to play one or two at lunch break, or before heading off to work.
Anyway, enough gushing. I really like this game. If you're looking for something Rogue Legacy ish, but a little slower and more thoughtful, I'd say you can't go wrong with Vagante.

DDO is a mmo co-op dungeon crawler. It uses a hub system with various "dungeons" attached. These usually have a set of objectives that needs to be completed, which is hardly ever "kill 20 monsters". In this way, the game becomes quite different from most other MMO's.
A pro and con, is that the game has almost unlimited character customization possibilities and in my opinion no clear, or dominating, "meta" besides potential flavour of the month. I have never been restricted from joining a group for playing an unorthodox build.
The character customization can make it complex when starting out, but also fun (or self-torturing) as there are many things to try. Generally DDO has a very friendly community. If you are playing a few hours everyday, then doing your time playing/leveling you will certainly meet the same people more than once.
I am in a love/hate relationship with the controls. At times they feel clunky. But depending on class and playstyle you can easily avoid the otherwise standard "Tab-Target stand-still spell-cast-time" combat style of other MMO's. I suggest you don't get too adventurous with your first character, or those controls might give you a "Morrowind-like" combat. DDO is largely numbers-based. (But but! It can be fun to make your own custom character, don't be afraid! ;))
If you want something premade, then I suggest googling "DDO build repository". That post might be gone or old by the time you read this, then you should ask for build advice in the new player section of the forums. As I said, the game has a friendly community. Whatever you do, avoid the pre-set class builds when creating your character. They are old and nobody uses them for good reason.
Two questions I usually see on forums:
- Are people still playing this game? Yes. The player-base on the servers are quite similar, except Wayfinder. Avoid Wayfinder.
- Is the game Pay to Win? Or let me rephrase: Can Free to play get along? Short answer: Yes.
Semi-long: New player builds (see repository) can be made to handle themselves, spend earned in-game currency on adventure packs, and consider spending any minimum amount of real life money on the game to make your account status to premium.
