An oversimplified fighting game, with a short, pointless story. The world is vast and empty with pretty graphics to try and make up for it. Learning new moves is interesting to a point where you get a certain amount of variety and then there's no need for anything else. Everything is a variation of a kick or punch. Every combat style is nearly indistinguishable except for the Drunken style that you cannot start the game with. The concept of building a "combo" in this game is interesting until you play it and find that your combos are just to have access to different single hits as there is no way to chain attacks together against any player that knows how to use their defense ability. The new 3v3 mode emphasizes how underequipped the game is to handlel anything beyond bland two button 1v1 combat. There are no mechanics whatsoever to help a player that is outnumbered overcome their situation. Even For Honor had the revenge system that would allow more skilled players to win while being outnumbered. FOR HONOR. PVP rewards are completely random other than a new currenty you get to unlock little loot boxes or cosmetics. The Student/Mentor system is meaningless with how short the singleplayer content is, and by the fact that why would you be a student of someone to learn their moves when they can just spam the move on you in the open world until you have them all within a few minutes. This game is Dark Souls without the story, and the PvP is somehow even less complex than Dark Souls PvP.
This is not a bad game, it has a good base so far, and I hope to see more of it in the future, because it's so new right now, don't expect too much from the game.

Works great, opens up a new set of game possibilities for couch-gaming.  Bearing in mind, this is using a wired connection.
[SEE EDIT AT BOTTOM: Input Delay Fixed]
The only cons I can think of are the slight increase in input (controller) delay.  It's not a big deal with some games, but others it puts you at a real handicap if you're playing a game online vs other players.
Keeping that in mind, and if you are sticking to local-multiplayer mostly (or single-player), it doesn't really affect gameplay (as I said, it is noticeable but not too terrible; some games it is more prevalent than others).
[EDIT]: I have learned of a way to greatly reduce (almost completely remove) any noticable controller/input delay:  First you change the View Mode on your TV to "Game" or "PC" (if it has it).  Second, in your steamlink before you select which Steam computer to connect to, go to menu/settings and then Streaming, select "Fast" (instead of "Balanced" or "Beautiful") and that should do it.
I did not notice any decrease in resolution by switching to Fast Streaming, only when I changed my TV to Game mode there was a smallish black border as the screen size shrunk down about an inch around the border--which was from changing the setting on my TV, not the Steamlink.  Now, games run as they should and it feels like there is no (or any perceptible) input delay.
If you make these two tweaks I honestly think this is one awesome device.  I'm surprised they don't mention anything about TV tweaks on the main page for this.

Rakuen has the potency of a violinist’s last note. The bow moves, the fingers tighten, and the string sings with a cry of joy,  pain, anguish, or hope.
A spotlight shines down and the musician bows her head in silence, surrounded only by the circle of light and blackness of the stage around her.  The audience, frozen in place from the tenderness of the moment, tries to gather themselves from the emotion of her performance.
Yes, Rakuen is like that.  I never saw it coming.
Here, out of this sweet little game packaged in an RPGmaker wrapper with happy faces and cheerful dialogue, came a tempest of storytelling.  Make your comparisons to other games like To the Moon if you like, but this game can make you pause for a moment, shocked at the very real drama that unfolds within a single scene. One minute I am picking Sila Berries, the next I simply forget to breathe as the tragedy of the story leaves me with that sinking feeling in my gut as if I am falling.  Perhaps it rang too true with me, maybe I’m a softie.  What I can say without a doubt, though, is that Rakuen makes the player actually care about characters like very few games can.
What I’ll begin with is our lead character, Boy, a young child, of perhaps eight years of age.  He is in a hospital, along with many other characters, recovering from an illness.  A doctor informs him of a thief that is stealing items from the hospital, and to the Boy’s surprise, his favorite book, Rakuen, has been stolen as well.  The Boy sets out to find the culprit and retrieve the book, leading to an exploration of the hospital by opening drawers, discovering keys, collectibles, and solving puzzles along the way.  The real meat of the game opens up after speaking with the entire cast of hospital residents and staff. Once the book is retrieved, the Boy’s Mom appears and she stays with him throughout the rest of the story.  She gives him a key to unlock the book’s magical land of Rakuen, which apparently is not just a story, but also a fantasyland juxtaposed to the real world of the hospital.  Strange portal doors begin to be revealed, and the Boy and his Mom travel to Rakuen through these doors.  Once there, they discover the land of Rakuen is in dire straits.  The powerful forest guardian spirit, Morizora, has fallen into a dark sleep due to the negative energy of the Envoy spirits who are changing the forest into a land of doom and desolation.  It’s up to the Boy and his Mom to save the land by helping the inhabitants cope with their problems and collecting parts of a magical song called Mori no Kokoro in order awaken Morizora.  Once awakened, Morizora can grant the Boy a single wish and save the forest.
Right here is where the game takes on some adventure gameplay that feels quite a bit like the Blackwell series of games.  Two characters are being played at the same time, the Boy and his Mom, to uncover clues and find out the tragic story of the other characters with the sole intention of helping those people find peace.  Each time you help someone, you get a piece of the song, Mori no Kokoro.  What you won’t need to worry about, however, is how to combine items.  That part of the game is done automatically once you figure out the puzzles and locate the keys or objects required to progress.  That said, the puzzles are cleverly broken into sections that take some thought to figure out.  There is nothing incredibly hard, yet you may get stuck occasionally due to a single key element that has yet to be uncovered.  Rakuen has the uncanny ability to layer the clues and puzzles in such a way that the answers may be elusive even if the actual solution is right in front of you.  Most of the difficult puzzles are in the first few sections, with the latter half of the game being much easier to get through.
The main part of the gameplay that separates Rakuen from other games is that there are counterparts in the real world of the hospital.  For example, with Winston and Gemma, Gemma is in a coma in the hospital with her husband Winston at her side.  When going to the land of Rakuen, you see the exact same couple with Gemma sick in bed and Winston caring for her.  In order to set these lives straight, you must visit their past, and patch together the story.  The key here is that you interact with their past and show each character how to unburden themselves from the weight of their unhappiness.  Each time a song is sung that becomes a piece of the final Mori no Kokoro song to awaken Morizora.  There is no fighting, no leveling up, or weapons.  Players are only able to help people not fight them.
So, at this point, you may ask, “What’s so special about that?”.  For one, there is the dynamic of a child who is dealing with the arduous task of assisting these people with his mother by his side.  Just like in Blackwell, the secondary character protects the main character, guides them, and helps with useful hints here and there.  It also forms a relationship, one of the key components that made Blackwell successful, when two people are involved with each other you feel that connection between them.  It not only moves the story along, it creates the opportunity for the mother to become a significant part of the plot.
Secondly, and perhaps most importantly, Rakuen creates segmented drama.  There are scenes where you want to continue with the story but have to unlock a series of events that go further than a simple explanation.  A mere storyline is not enough.  There are properly set-up scenes, not unlike a theater play.   Here, Rakuen bravely drops hints of underlying secrets while keeping the big secrets in mystery until the final curtain drops.  You complete one area only to discover another hidden alcove with insight into the backstory of someone, or a tiny snippet of life much like the calm before the storm.  And then, there is the presentation of pacing.  You might be completely unaware of the power of a scene until you get to the center of the story and have your heartstrings pulled when it all finally clicks together.  It takes a lot of care and effort to pull that off correctly, and Rakuen does it in spades.
Ever have someone give you an origami figure that you unfold and discover a hidden story carefully tucked away inside?  That’s Rakuen, a small and compact game which reveals the most endearing game experience I’ve had all year.
Rakuen’s focus is about personal connections.  Each character has lost that connection and it is up to the Boy and his Mom to reassemble those bonds. It’s also about a tragedy, and I’ll warn players that they very well may cry during this game. I certainly did, but I’m prone to that because Rakuen hit a nerve with me.  When I was a little boy my sister had cancer and I remember those hospital rooms full of patients, each with their own personal stories of how they got there.   It’s not easy to manage through that and I’ve never seen it portrayed in a game through a mother and child point of view.  It’s unique and touching, making you feel like you are right there in the hospital with them.
Each scene is carefully constructed, with very close attention to the pacing and timing of select moments. My throat got dry. My eyes welled up. I have to admit, it can be hard to take as the game pulls punch after punch.  Yet, the journey is worth it.  Rakuen aims right at your feelings with no holds barred.  I’ve seldom come across a game that tackles real world tragic events and uses them as core components of a storytelling experience.  The pain you feel is entirely because these things can and do happen.  The fantasy of Rakuen took me to a place I certainly did not expect.  It connected me back to those difficult memories of the hospital that I purposely tried to forget.  I wasn’t sure how I’d feel at the end but I have to say, I am thankful.  My rating is an AutoSave, I encourage anyone who loves storytelling to purchase this game.

Heard this recommended on shmups.system11 as a shmup to not overlook and it was half off on a sale so I took the plunge.
Verdict: Super solid shmup.
While numbers are not everything, I do think they're a big deal in shmups, so here's some quick and dirty stats to entice you, curious buyer:
- There's 6 playable ships, each with two different versions that play almost entirely different (effectively making it 12 ships).
- 5 stages, with completely different alternate versions of stages 2,3, and 4, 2 final bosses, and a true end final boss.
- The game description wasn't lying when it said there's a mix of 40 bosses and mid-bosses. And they're mostly really good.
- Dynamic difficulty system that works surprisingly well.
- Good stage training modes and boss rush modes for practicing.
And it's not just all stats either, it's got the good game design to go along with it:
Some ships function very differently from others and will force you to heavily adapt how you play the game. Bosses are menacing and will not shy away from getting right up in your face, forcing you to leave the comfort zone at the bottom of the screen. Bosses sometimes come in groups and often times have strategic dismemberment.
The dynamic difficulty system affects game speed, enemy attack difficulty, and your own attack power, and will adapt to provide an easier experience if you're struggling, and a tougher experience if you manage to keep up.
The music isn't mind-blowing but it complements the action nicely and some tracks will stick with you.
All in all, pretty great. It's not nearly stellar or stylish enough to threaten Hellsinker's throne, but it's the closest I've seen a shmup get in a long time and you won't want to miss it.

Even if shmups aren't your thing, try this one. It's quite accessible in pretty interesting ways.

I'm always awestruck when the credits roll and there is a single name listed for nearly every position.  I suppose this has happened frequently lately mainly due to the types of games I've been playing.  As you may have already guessed, this is the case with Mecha Ritz: Steel Rondo.  If it weren't for Hanaji Games bringing Yuki Shouhei's (or HEY for short) game to Steam it's likely I never would have played it, which would have been unfortunate as it's one cool shooting game.
Mecha Ritz: Steel Rondo is a Japanese indie shmup that was formed around the goal of creating an STG that could be accessible to players of all levels.  Normally this is achieved by having several difficulty settings, but this game takes quite a different approach.  There is a rank that is adjusted up and down depending on how well you're playing.  I was skeptical at first, but it's handled in an ingenious manner.
One might wager that playing well is defined as avoiding enemy fire, but it's not that simple.  The system takes several variables of play style into account such as using bombs appropriately, avoiding bullets, the speed enemies are killed, and also the distance enemies are killed from.  Rank is adjusted in real time so the challenge will rise and fall depending on your performance.  When starting the game rank is set to zero by default, but it can be increased in order to have a higher difficulty right out of the gate.  The fact that the game is generous with extra lives, shields, and bombs combines well with the ranking system.  I quickly found myself playing aggressively to boost rank as much as I could handle knowing that there were ample resources available.
Playing aggressively will lead to trying to kill bosses as quickly as possible, and killing bosses quickly will lead to different endings.  I've seen three endings and quite a few branching paths for alternate stages.  After playing a small amount of time extra Mecha (ships) will be unlocked.  The Mechas all have a unique primary fire, secondary fire, bombs, and other assorted attributes such as movement speed.  Two Mechas even have an awesome graze mechanic that encourages and rewards riskier play.  Mecha Ritz has a large amount of content, but the game doesn't do the best job at letting you know about it.
There is a text file in the game's directory that should absolutely be read before playing.  I found myself frustrated by the lack of ability to return to the title screen while playing, but it turns out it's possible and explained in the file.  It might have been more logical to simply have a pause menu with a quit option rather than holding three buttons though. There is no notification at all when you unlock a new ship, and I can imagine someone not even knowing that ships beyond the first six exist as they technically don't have icons of their own.  The menu initially felt a little strange to maneuver, but works fine once you get the hang of it.  Other than that, there isn't much else to say that I viewed as potentially negative.
Mecha Ritz: Steel Rondo is a great shooting game that is easily enjoyable by players at any skill level.  Among the things I've already mentioned it also features a decent story, quirky cafe based sense of humor, FM synth soundtrack, and the ability to watch replays of your runs.  It would have been really nice to have Steam achievements and leaderboards, but it doesn't actually detract from the game itself. HEY has truly created an excellent shoot 'em up, and it's probably one of the first games that would come to mind when suggesting a game for someone that wanted an introduction to the genre.  I absolutely recommend Mecha Ritz: Steel Rondo.

This game is truly fantastic. It finds a sweet spot between action and horror and does many things well, though some other things may not please everyone.
Things that tasted real good mmm yeah:
+Some good creepy vibes, especially in the first area and some parts of the latter areas.
+Clunky controls for aiming and maneuvering that really add to the tension of the combat but don't make the game frustrating or un-fun.
+A clever, Tetris-y inventory system that is limited in a way that isn't frustrating or annoying like weight limits.
+Some damn good music that goes a long way in making this game scary.
+Scary and somewhat intelligent enemies (at least compared to zombies).
+Real good level design. Environments are interesting and fun to explore, and for the most part things don't get stale.
+Some clever puzzles.
+Minor bonus content and replayability.
+Boatloads of classic RE cheesiness!
Also, it's just plain fun.
And now, some things I didn't like all that much but ultimately are somewhat minor, nitpicky points that may or may not affect you:
-Some parts of this game are hilariously over-the-top (for example, cultists in a medieval castle equipped with rocket launchers and a gatling gun). This point could actually be a negative or a positive depending on your sense of humor.
-After the halfway point, the game starts to lose focus and becomes less creepy and more silly and stupid. (In terms of gameplay, story, and theme/tone).
-Quicktime events are used too much (especially some during cutscenes that result in instant game-overs).
Overall, this game is great. I certainly enjoyed it, but hardcore, classic-RE horror fans may not as much. Even then, though, it's a definite good time and an example of solid game design.

I've played this MMO for years, before it was even on steam. So really, I do want to recommend it to people. Some people looking at this game have probably felt the sting of Pay to Win games before, and to some extent for new players this can be their initial reaction. Ergo I wish to describe as fully as I can the things that made me a fan of this game, and also concede on points others would have in an argument against it.
Pros:
-This game is 10 years old. That may not seem like a good thing and, it isn't inherently. The way I found this out however, is through the events they recently had for it's anniversary. It celebrated the entire game from it's conception to now, players got to crash an anniversary party, cleave the heads off of some of the more prominent and sometimes frustrating Developers via NPC inserts, in jokes abound from things such as their old web ads and

finding brocolli. (An odd statement to anyone who hasn't played, I'm sure.) My point with this is that it has a
well founded community. A week before this event launched, the Developers had a live stream wherein they went to every server systematically, carpet bombed public areas with loot that you can ONLY be given by devs, and punished greedy players when they stuck around a little
long by spawning dragons, beholders, and giant killer robots in the public areas where they would never have been encountered. The Devs care about the game, and most of the players I've spoken with on my own frequented server are the kind of people you could hang out with without cusswords flung at each other, which is a good thing because...
-This game is highly co-operative. It's possible to solo what easily amounts to 80% of the content, give or take. That doesn't ever mean it's
to run through everything by yourself. Honestly this was the one MMORPG I've tried my hand at where grouping together was genuinely appealing. If I'm playing a Cleric, Wizard, Barbarian, etc. it is, from the perspective of those classes, a very very nice thing to have a Rogue in the party. Every quest is in an instance, and you can either take 6-12 man teams into it depending on the quest/raid. Some of these quests are riddled with traps, hidden doors for extra loot and experience when you crack them open and head through to find some rare enemy that wasn't really on your to-do list. The traps range from easy to walk around, placed in an area you aren't required to go through, to being a repeatedly exploding ball of pure evil that attempts to also paralyze you when you activate it, and again with every blast. Rogues can turn off all of the above traps as you run your way through. That doesn't mean rogue is an easy mode class either, since when it comes to all of the enemies you'll face... playing a Rogue, you would have some of the least HP, and you do greatly increased damage to many enemies when they are ticked off at one of your pals, not looking at you. Grouping together in quests is actually really satisfying, since you can get much more done together than alone.
-EXP availability is high. All of the quests you've done once, you can do again. Furthermore quests give bonus experience for going out of your way to do things like killing a majority, if not just
the enemies in a quest, finding x amount of secret doors, turning off x amount of traps, and even just plain breaking enough things (They had it coming, that table and chair set was ugly and my Barbarian has no care for social standards, earning more XP, Win-Win)
-The sheer amount, and quality of content. Look, I'll be honest here, the level cap is 30. How much content can you possibly cram into thirty levels? Well... a lot, and it isn't poorly made in my opinion either. Since the game started in early beta, when the level cap advancing to TEN was a milestone, the developers have made every quest save for a few, and the stories behind them marvelously. When I hit level 15, one of my very favorite quest/story arcs is "harbinger of madness." Not to spoil too much, but what begins as an investigation into missing persons quickly turns into dealing with
-It stays as true as it can to good old, Pen and Paper D&D. Everything you do in this game is on a dice system. Not one that is ever slow to respond (unless you have a connection lag, which is better than it used to be.) but immediately shows you information like "Okay, I rolled a 20 with my great axe against this beholder. That means I vorpal hit. So, I automatically critically hit the enemy, depending on my weapon's stats and if they are dependant on that roll do a ton more damage, and since I have a great axe, deal triple my normal damage regardless. Hulk smash!" but you don't ever have to wait on that line of thinking, or really pay attention to it in a lot of cases. It will roll for every swing, for granting you every point of damage in real time. Then, remember when I said rogues were great for disabling traps? Well, they have to roll dice the good old fashioned way. They have to roll dice to find it if it hasn't already started being a thorn in your side, and a check to disable device. This is a skill they can train, sometimes so high as to let them guarantee it turns off... sometimes not. When not so, it can hilariously blow up in their face (literally) and no further attempt to turn it off can be made, depending on how poor they rolled.
-It isn't the most impossible thing to obtain paid for content. When you first step into the game, I have no doubt you
be intimidated by the amount of locked races, classes, and quest packs. However, unlike most games with some arbitrary "Trade random player X amount of normal currency for X amount of "paid currency" it isn't the hardest thing to get said paid currency
paying. Every time you run a quest for the first time on a given difficulty, you earn points towards getting a nice chunk of change in the form of Turbine Points. Even more so, the points themselves give you bonuses too. New players might want to get points with "The Coin Lords" for up to 2 extra, FREE backpack slots per character, all while earning progress towards currency to buy that class/race/quest you want, and most of which I've found decently priced... mostly.
I could say so many great things about this game, and while I still recommend it, I can't ignore the negatives.
Cons:
-Plain and simply this is a damn buggy game sometimes. Some bugs are exploitable, some are debilitating, some are a particular place in a particular dungeon which will get you trapped forever, some are ladders which you just can't climb in certain places. The devs are always working on them apparently, and bug reports help, but the flyswatter hardly ever seems to fall on important issues. One of my character's abilities, at the time of writing this review,
It's only supposed to do so in an aoe against the, you know, ENEMIES!
-There are some content pieces which I can't deny, definitely appear to be unreasonably priced. While there are weekly sales which, especially near holidays, cut prices on certain groups of items from the cash shop dramatically... sometimes you can look at two items right next to each other and wonder why the more expensive one is actually more expensive. Like most races costing 995 Turbine points (TP) whereas the most recent costs well over 1,200
-Some of the best quests are paid for. Especially my favorite listed above.
-There is a serious lack of endgame content. The usual system is to, once you reach at least level 20, restart your character at level one, with a choice of any class/race you have, and be stronger every time you restart. However, content at level 20+ seems lacking in scale compared to everything below so... why even push to 30?

If you're willing to be patient and correct your mistakes it will reward you. In my first 50 or so runs I very rarely made it past the Dark Caves, but somewhere along the way I started to get a good feel for the game and now if I don't at least make it to the Catacombs I consider it to be a particularly bad run. Every seemingly impossible challenge becomes trivial as you learn, adapt, and develop strategies that compliment your play style.
Ultimately this is all I'm looking for in a game. Does it reward the time I invest into it or not? And in Vagante's case I would say it most certainly does. If you're looking for a more casual experience I would suggest Rogue Legacy, but if you don't mind putting the work in there's a lot of fun to be had with this game and I look forward to the future development.

Jamestown might be the most refined game I've played in the last decade. A top down bullet hell shooter set in an alternate history timeline (largely mirroring early American history, only this time with aliens), it presents itself with an air of confidence, as if it realizes what a pedigree its of and is determined to make you see so as well.
You can try to break down what makes Jamestown so great into understandable pieces of a larger whole, but it's the combination of them all that pushes it beyond a decent reimagining of classic shmups, into a modern classic. The feel of the ships is relentlessly precise, the action ferocious and incredibly satisfying, and the presentation presenting a remarkably well realized world (despite how little exposition there is).
The more you play Jamestown, the more these elements shine, upping the ante at a breakneck pace, forcing you to improve or perish. However, it does so in a way that allows for a natural increase in skill, letting players ease into the challenge instead of pushing them into it right from the start like the games of the genre are so known for. It also creates a continuous stream of rewards for players that manage to improve past the point of entry, with more elaborate enemy designs, tougher boss fights, and some truly grueling challenge levels. And then you have the coop, the glorious coop, the only flaw of which is that it is sadly local only. Should you get a chance to play with some friends though, it's a fantastic experience that scales perfectly and adds even more replay value as you go through levels that now feel new once again.
At times the action is so intense that it's hard to even keep track of your ship, let alone take in all that Jamestown has to offer, but when you can manage to take a step back it's incredible the level of polish applied to even the smallest areas of the game. I was quite frankly taken aback when I first gave it a try, and this feeling was renewed even up to the very last boss fight, which was as epic and satisfying as I could have hoped for. If you have even the most remote fondness for bullet hell games, Jamestown is about as penultimate an entry point into the genre as you could hope for. Everyone with more than a passing enjoyment of the genre should have played it long ago, but if not, consider this a wake up call that you've been sleeping on something awesome.

To start with, lets establish something: Im a Mordheim nut. Before there was any information about this game really beyond "it sort of exists, a bit..." I pre-ordered it. And i've never stopped regreting the decision.
And it was a mess. The maps were badly designed, the navmeshes were buggy as hell so targeting was a total crapshoot and the stat system was hilariously complex and arcane. But that's early access for you.
Unfortunately, its not much better in full release.
To start with, if you're expecting a faithful recreation of the tabletop game a la Blood Bowl - forget it. This is not that. It sort of limply gestures in Mordheim's direction, but its an affectation at best.
The core of the game revolves around fairly repetitive missions in which your little band of warriors will be scattered around some ruins. These ruins are populated by defined points at which you can climb and descend, knee high walls WILL irrevocably impede your process and no, you cannot climb out of a ground floor window or push open a ruined door.
So far so forgivable.
The issue is that the AI is stupid, but the game is enough of a general crapshoot that it hardly matters. So much is dependent on a random number generator whose margins of favour are so razor thin that the game devolves into a series of coin flips. The only reliably strategy is that if you flip more coins than your enemy, more of them will probably come up heads (no guarentees though!) and you'll win.
And that's about it for depth.
You'll also struggle to get more than a couple of missions into it. Its not brutal in the sense that say, Dark Souls is brutal. Mordheim doesn't teach you lessons, or punish your failure to precisely execute manuevers by setting you back to your previous position and saying "try again, this time don't suck."
No no. It sets you back to your previous position, ties one of your arms behind your back and tells you to try again.
There's no learning curve, really. There's no opportunity to take a mistake learn from it because that mistake will haunt you forever. Every screw up, every misclick, every bad dice roll will be added around your neck like a millstone, and you will never get to remove them. In a purely multiplayer environment this might be a part of the fun. Everyone would acquire these albatrosses and the players with fewer of them would have an edge.
But the AI doesn't suffer these problems.
You will spend your first ten hours of the game being beaten into a bloody smear, winning by hair's bredths and losing by massive margins. When you do lose, and you will, it will set off a landslide of consequences you will never fully recover from.
If I could refund this, I would. If playable demos were still a thing in gaming, this product would never sell another copy.
Its bad. Its not fun. The only reason to peservere with it is spite, but you'll lose more of your life than the sale price is worth. Save yourself the hassle and just play something else.

All in all, the game is fun, with a high replayability. You can quickly get attached to your warband characters and will feel woefully sorry if one of your highlevel soldiers looses an arm or a leg or gets killed on a mission. The six warband all have their distinctive features and play differently enough to use them all. Levelling options give you a great number of choices - better than XCOM2. Character customization is o.k. but  might be improved (more head or at least hat types) and a little less varied than in XCOM2.
The game itself is fair enough, you can choose between "Normal", "Hard", "Brutal" and "Deadly" mission types. So far I have only attempted "Normal" missions, as - depending on your starting position and your opponents - even these may be challenging at times. Story missions so far are o.k. as long as you can avoid mistakes like not keeping your warband together. Beware that the game runs always in "Ironman mode", there is no savescumming and when your characters die or get maimed, they stay dead or crippled. Perhaps the introduction of some exit points on the maps would be a good idea. At the moment you can only "abandon" a mission  at the cost of injuries to all party members or end the mission by failing a party morale check - difficult if you have high leadership stats, as that means you will have to have almost all your high ranking characters out of action before party morale falls below the critical value.
There could be more maps though. However the existing maps are big and as starting positions and weather conditions (day, night, fog) vary it doesn't get too boring. But two or three more maps would be nice.
Hopefully the devs keep adding content to this game. It's much better than "Darkest Dungeon" and almost on par with XCOM2.

I have thought long and hard about buying this game. I am a big fan of the warhammer world and love turn based strategy. However all the negative comments about this game made me doubt.

I am having tremendous fun with my skaven warband, clawing and clubbing my way through bands of enemies. Emptying my warp pistols on them, poisoning them. Ambushing and ganging up on them. In the mean time I have some skaven runners scutteling about, climbing walls, leaping from one terrace to the next collecting weirdstone and other nice loot.
So what about all the negative comments. Well... this is my first warband and in the beginning we did encounter some problems. A warpguard and a hero died but they were easily replaced. One of my star runners lost a leg and I had to fire him. Biggest hit is on my main hero who lost a leg. No sure whetter to retire him or let him limp along.

Is the game difficult? Yes
Does the level of difficulty ruin the game? not for a long shot.

Absolver has not received the best of reviews since its release date. I hope this review can make up the mind of the potential buyer to make him/her realise that this really is a game that they should buy. Seriously, I did not expect to love Absolver as much as I have been. The customisability of your playstyle is insane. It's not just a form of "hardcore batman" that I originally perceived the game to be. There's so much to do when considering which of the moves will chain together, and how you will chain them. Will you have a slower but more damage-intensive moveset or a less-damaging but more pressure-intensive and lightning fast moveset? Or maybe you want the best of both worlds and combine a more mellow but balanced playstyle. Or perhaps you will go for the more confusing, hard-to-read playstyle. This summarises the 4 (archetypal) fighting styles of the game: Kahlt, Windfall, Forsaken, Stagger.
Within just these 4 styles, there is such a broad way to define how you play. Each ability that comes with the fighting styles compliments multiple playstyles, and you're not limited to being a slow fighter if you choose Kahlt, or a faster fighter if you choose Windfall, etc. In fact, on one character alone you can learn all the fighting styles and decide which one you like the best; so you're not stuck with the fighting style you've chosen from the beginning. More than this, one can learn a vast number of moves that fluidly link into one another.
When customising, you have to think hard about which moves you start with, and which moves you end with. You need to give serious thought into how oppressive you want to be. Do you want to be constantly applying pressure to punish the opponent over and over? Or do you want to deal some damage and fall back and allow your stamina to recover? Perhaps you want to be fluid and have a character that can adapt to all kinds of scenarios? There is so much in this game that allows all of this.
Beyond this, there is serious consideration into your stats and your armour. You should consider which kinds of moves you often find most fitting, then adjust your stats accordingly. Absolver have just implemented a system to redistribute attribute points for those who have changed styles over the course of the game. Once you spend enough time deciding, you understand exactly what your character will need. I have only played ~50 hours at the time of this review but I can see as I have not even begun to create my perfect moveset, I have so much room to grow and find out how I play that my stats will be important at a later point. Your armour drastically changes gameplay too. It has a weight that affects damage dealt, but can decrease damage taken. This goes further into playstyles as it allows one to use the lightest armours and be the fastest warriors, or the heaviest ones and be walking tank and so on.
Putting the meat of the dish aside: a great deal of alternative customisability is being added into the game as well, considering the new system to purchase types of end-game armours, emotes and equippable rarities as well. For those concerned with aesthetic, Absolver brings you beauty on a white-gold plate.
The community is fantastic too, often displaying a good amount of decorum online. Of course, you do have the occassional griefer, but even then the toxicity of these players are somewhat dulled because of the lack of in-game speech and text communication - which is something often cited as a flaw, but at least for Absolver, where salt levels can give one high-blood pressure and griefing may be (although isn't) proliferate, the lack of verbal and written communication should rather be seen as a blessing. You also have those kind players who love to help the newer players to defeat bosses, learn new moves and run through the game with. Absolver is in this sense a warm embracing community.
This is to speak in Absolver's favour. Of course, despite its abundance of good, it has its own abundance of flaws.
Absolver is not perfect. Far from in its current state. At least on PC, due to the fact that one can purchase the game on different platforms (Steam and GOG for example), one often finds that they cannot locate the profile of a person they met online and would love to play with again. Absolver does not have an in-game profile system that one can find and connect with other players with. This is something Absolver desperately needs. Imagine finding someone who you love fighting. Once you leave the game, he's gone. It's even worse than this as well. If you die and they do not resurrect you in time, there's a good chance you are spawned into a different lobby, and you cannot join them again. Absolver needs a desperate fix for this.
Online issues are constantly being fixed, but glitches are still commonplace. A common, but humorous, one is if you revive someone and get hit as you are about to lift them. What one often finds is a shadow lying on the floor unable to move and only rotate on the spot with an invisible hitbox. Or one will find a lying body that moves along the ground - while lying down. The only fix to this glitch without logging out is to kill them, which is not a real big problem but better avoided than become Goat Simulator. Lag is still prevalent, with one finding themselves suddenly thrown off ledges, losing progress in the moves they were learning previously.
A common, but often looked over issue is the lack of single-player content. One might be content with a No Man's Sky argument made of "don't go into the game looking for something that was never intended". Of course, Absolver never lied to you, but with a campaign with only 2 measley hours of story, and the actual bulk of the story explained in the Digital Artbook, there is so much rich lore missing that could well have been added. There are stronger versions of the bosses that do provide some vague exposition on the story, but comparing the game to other more mainstream fighting games however, especially the ones within Absolver's specific genre (I'm thinking Batman, Dark Souls, etc.), it's apparent that the game is lacking something. Furthermore, if Absolver could really become competitive, which I believe it can, then a story is somewhat non-essential. But it's not competitive. Because it's a dying game. It's still in its infancy and it's so susceptible to SIDS. There's no interest from the public because they all know just how much it's lacking as a game in itself. Even just a little bit more content would have been more than acceptable. But 8 fairly easy bosses and 1 final boss is just lazy. Without the time spent running around, and just fighting bosses, that's something like half an hour of story for the whole game. And then it's PVP.
The moves you can learn in Absolver, although fantastic, are still somewhat unbalanced. Every top-tier balanced-style and fast-style, even the slower hardhitting style, movesets incorporate at least 3 of the same 5 moves. At higher levels it becomes clear which moves these are. I can't remember the names off the top of my head, but for what it's worth, if Absolver were really balanced, then 5 moves should not really be the crux of the movesets. Every move should be palatable and useful over every other move. Of course, in practice this is extremely hard to do. And most of these moves are in fact easily countered provided you have the know-how.
All that said, I only recently got into fighting games, not Absolver-style ones, proper ones like Tekken, Guilty Gear, Injustice and so on. But Absolver is the game that has captivated my attention. Perhaps it is the fact that it is a little more casual than arcade-style fighting games. Or perhaps it is the customisability of Absolver. Perhaps it's the novelty of it, that it's one-of-a-kind. Perhaps it's the fact that for such a small game, its depth is incredible. Perhaps it's the fact that in this game, I don't learn combos, I learn about myself.

This is a great game in every way except the gameplay itself, which is very boring.
Most of the value in playing Rakuen comes from playing through its story, so I don't want to spoil it here. The story is on the simple side, but it progresses at a quick pace and constantly provides moments of wonder for the player. Parts of it feel very like Alice in Wonderland. It expertly pulls back the curtains little by little and hints at background details effortlessly, making it very rewarding for players who choose to explore the world more. If you're looking for a game with a heartwarming, mature story, a captivating setting, amazing music, and interesting, fleshed-out characters, then this game is one of the best I've ever seen.
There's a big catch, though, and that's the lackluster gameplay. Playing Rakuen consists mostly of three things: walking, talking to people, and collecting objects that serve as "keys" to get to the next area. There are very, VERY few exceptions to this pattern. Basically every puzzle in the game just consist of looking around a room to find the aforementioned "keys", which are usually hidden in drawers or down the sink or something. The story is more than strong enough to carry the game through, but I found myself speeding through the last half of the game because I was so tired of the fetch quests I kept being given. The biggest problem with Rakuen -- and, I think, the only real problem -- is that there just isn't anything to do besides these repetitive puzzles. Even though an enormous amount of time clearly went into building the world, the lack of variety in what the player can actually do makes everything feel a little barren. Part of the wonder in the world of Rakuen is getting to explore more and more, never being sure what you'd find next, but I quickly realized that the only thing I was ever going to find were fetch quests.
Put another way, I think the core gameplay just needs a lot more variation. I would have liked the puzzles to be more interesting and varied, rather than just finding the correct objects in the room. I would have liked some small minigames to play in the Leeble village and throughout the world. I would have liked an incentive to revisit old areas and characters -- it feels like they're just discarded and thrown aside after they're done being useful, a particularly harsh misstep in this narrative. As a quick example, there's a short section in the third chapter of the game where you have to fly over a gap in the attic with an airplane. Why not turn that into a simple minigame where you have to tap a button and angle the plane? It's certainly not a big deal, but it's just one of MANY missed opportunities to make the world of Rakuen feel more surprising and delightful for players.
There are some other minor things, like the text speed is slow, the options select screen is very limited, and the menus could have done with some spit-shine. I realize that most of my complaints are probably due to the choice of RPG Maker as an engine -- but Rakuen is too rich and too good of a world for RPG Maker and they really should have chosen a different engine to begin with.

This is a fantastic shmup experience right here. Wonderful bullet spreads with gameplay that basically changes the better you are. As you do better, the spreads become harder and move faster, enemies power up, and YOU become stronger. It really gives a good sense of synergy for the player and just makes thing flow until you get crushed by a wall of bullets.
Speed, main attack, special attack, and bomb all differ from ship to ship offering unique playtroughs with each one. You're even given options to change certain color aesthetics of the game to you liking with more options unlocking the more you play. The game can also be customized a bit (manipulating the ranking, etc.) before jumping into the action.
The music, sound, and aesthetics of the game offer some kind of retro/cyber punkish kind of feel to it. The tracks in the game are great, sound effects are pleasing and never get old, and the game is colorfull and full of fantastic designs.
This is definitely a title that deserves to be held up above the droves of other shmups that are rushing into the market. Fans of the genre shouldn't think twice about adding this to their library of games. Even at full price this game is less than a premium fast food meal and tastes even better.

Don't let the rough, low-fi graphics fool you. This game has a soul of cast iron. A fast, twitchy shmup in the vein of Cave's best, but with a focus on branching progression (Clear levels fast and efficiently and more routes poen up) and dynamic difficulty. Stay alive and kill quickly and the game gets harder, with bullet patterns becoming more complex and enemies getting new powers. Thankfully, taking hits, using smartbombs or (ithe absolute worst) losing a life will drop things back down to something more manageable.
Even a crusty old coot like me managed to get the most basic ending after a few tries, although I've barely scratched the surface of what the game offers.
A single playthrough of this should clock in at around 25-30 minutes, but if you want to see all 15 stages and unlock every ship? you're going to have to play this A LOT.

It's always nice when you stumble across a game you haven't heard of before and it just blindsides you with its quality.
Mecha Ritz is a bullet hell shmup that packs a downright bold retro aesthetic and a soundtrack that is just gnarly, furthering immersing you in the aesthetic it's trying to pull off (and boy does it pull it off).
You have a great selection of ships with abilities that are fun and more or less equally capable of taking you through the game, a difficulty system that scales itself to how well you're doing, going downright crazy in the harder difficulties,  branching paths leading to multiple endings, great art and enemy designs that are somehow hilarious while still looking badass (There's a boss robot named SOY La-Tay... And a lot of enemies have various coffee themed names that are all pretty clever) and to top it all off, there's a story in between all the bullets that actually doesn't seem too half bad.
A young girl genius named Veloce discovered "Mecha" and has exterminated all of humanity, creating a world of steel machines for her to dominate over. Years pass and one machine, curiously human in its actions, has gained sentience. The collective souls of humanity has somehow converged into the machine, and boy are they ANGRY. You carry out their will and seek to mete out retribution against the tyrannical Volece and give peace to the tortured human souls.
And crazy as it sounds, it ends up being a captivating story. You want to find out what's going on, why things had to be that way, and it just works.
Some other very nice touches were the option to change the enemies bullet and explosion colors. You have to unlock them, but having this option is really appreciated, as if you don't feel the bullets are visible, you can change them to a color that is, and there seems to be enough to satisfy anyone. This to me is a really neat feature as a common complaint in these shmup games is that bullets can be hard to see, so it was smart of them to make it an option to change the colors.
I highly recommend this game and also recommend you pick up the soundtrack. It's amazing and with the bundle provided, it's just a little bit more for a great OST and game that SHMUP fans can enjoy.

I have never played a modern Sonic game, I adored the orginals back in my 16 bit days and played Sonic 2 into dust. I was acutely aware of the issues many people have with the franchise as it has gone on, but I decided to be impartial, particularly as it was on sale for an insanely small ammount during the sale.
All goodwill aside, however, this game has serious problems. The controls are very sticky and the homing addition to gameplay does nothing but make it easier, in earlier Sonic games bouncing from one enemy to another to both protect yourself and also take them out was an act of skill, now its almost a glorified QTE. The pace of the action never quite hits that of the orginals either, you begin to gather the frenetic momentum that Sonic is famous for and it will suddenly drag to a snails pace.
The graphics aren't much cop either, although the zone's look pleasant enough Sonic himself looks utterly awful and his running animations in relation to where he is running from don't seem to make sense at all, if I were to try and define it I'd say to looked cheap.
Finally for a game that also had an amazing score it seems to have been relegated to substandard childrens pop, which although I have no issue with it isn't Mystic Cave's quality music.
All in all I'm a tad disapointed, if not surprised from what I heard of others. If you really want a recommendation I'd say steer well clear and get a copy of Rayman. Its incredibly solid and beautiful and has had great ammounts of attention lavished on it. This however, sadly, has not.

Absolute garbage port of an absolute garbage game. I very stupidly bought it on launch on the PS3 and then picked it up during a sale in a pack with Episode 2 on PC. Where to even begin with this trash?
-Physics are wonky.
-Movement doesn't feel or look natural.
-Building up speed is less organic than it was in any of the Mega Drive games. This makes precision platforming nigh-impossible.
-Graphics are some of the ugliest 2.5D platforming has to offer.
-A series known among its fans for some pretty good or at least catchy music delivers an auditory snoozefest in this game.
-The game calls itself "Sonic 4", but it's too reminiscent of Sonic 1 wth a little bit of 2; there's a throwback to nostalgia and then there is a rip-off.
-This is pre-Generations, so this isn't "Classic Sonic"-- what he is is modern Sonic, with all the annoying Modern Sonic conveniences.
- The port is an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥how. No graphics options beyond resolution, no audio options beyond volume, no way to fix keyboard controls, weird default bindings (D is jump, but it's also "Back", but Space is "accept", which is also jump?!?) and it *requires* you to separately download and install Java for the game to run. You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ me, Sonic Team?
The thing that absolutely breaks the game and makes it a disaster, though, is the horrid level design, accompanied by a completely broken homing attack that doesn't lock on properly and leads to constant deaths in pits or spikes and whatnot.
I usually look for the good things in games and make my recommendations based on whether or not the choice is good for the consumer. I'm way past that point with this game. It's garbage. It's one of the worst things I've put myself through-- twice. There is no price-point, which would make Sonic 4: Episode 1 a justifiable purchase. If given away for free, it would still be too much. It may as well be rebranded as a flash-made "Sanik" game, for it looks and plays like a parody of the real thing and contributes *nothing* to the brand or the series. Literally every other 2D Sonic before it plays better. Go play those. Buy the Mega Drive Collection instead.

Rochard is an overlooked two and a half dimension indie game made by people who apparently really love Valve. The main character has the body of the Heavy, the voice of the Engineer and uses Gordon Freeman's gravity gun to solve cube based physics puzzles.
Well actually he shares the same voice actor as Duke Nukem and it's not exactly Freeman's gravity gun. It's shaped like an old handheld search light and functions as a combination gravity gun, laser rifle, grenade launcher, flashlight, three megapixel camera, calculator, barcode scanner, cheese grater, teeth whitener, guitar tuner, pencil sharpener and it also periodically emits the pleasant aroma of sandalwood.
Armed with only this, and his southern down-home chicken-fried quips about buttscratching, he must travel through space and meet well adjusted characters, a la Cowboy Bebop, to track down a really super serious something or another that his former boss stole because his boss is rich and therefore evil and also because some aliens and ghosts told him to. Okay the writing isn't that sane when you get down to it but when has that mattered?
What is important is the gameplay, and I admit it's quite good. It's all the simple fun you can get from launching heavy steel crates at people or carefully shooting a grenade and watching it bounce it's way to their feet then seeing their body ragdoll through the air. It's very therapeutic. The gleeful murder is broken up by puzzles which COULD be challenging but often isn't once you figure out some of the gamebreaking exploits, such as spamming the gravity gun's recoil over and over to clear gaps and reach high ledges.
The puzzle-exploit scenario reminds me a lot of Trine, specifically playing as the wizard, if the wizard had a gravity gun, laser rifle, grenade launcher, flashlight, blender, blow dryer, paint mixer, food processor, coin sorter, bagel toaster, ceremonial thing-a-ma-jig.
All in all, it's a pretty great game. I thoroughly enjoy it and plan to see this one to the end and if you like sidescrolling platformers with simple but well made puzzles too then I say you should at least give the demo a try cause, after all, it's got balls of steel!

(Note that this game was originally a source mod that was later accepted on greenlight. I played it (or tried, see below) for about a year before it got put on greenlight. Heck, I voted for it on greenlight. So if it shows I've only played for 0.7 hours, that's why. Source mods don't get their hours you've played clocked)
This is an interesting mod. The basic idea is that since they didn't make a Team Fortress game for Half-Life 2 (this mod came out before the Orange Box), the community would make one.
And so they did, and it was pretty faithful. All the classes are exactly as you remember them from Team Fortress Classic (and yes, it was named classic even back when it first came out. It was a mod based on a Quake Mod), with a few additions and changes. The pyro can use his flamethrower to gain lift and jump similar to a soldier, the scout is designed to get the flag and nothing else (which is all he was able to do back in the day), and the spy can now cloak. Yes, I know he can cloak in TF2. He couldn't in TFC, so it's an addition to his skill set. He can also sabotage engi buildings so they turn on their own team before exploding.
This all sounds interesting on paper, so where did it go wrong? Well, first off, there are NO PLAYERS. You can check all of the servers for the game and they have no one playing 96% of the time, fridays usually being the exception. Why are their no players? Because of the community. The players that are there are old players from back in the day who hated TF2 for taking the spotlight away from their beloved TFC. To say that they are toxic about that is to say that the DOTA2 community is civil about mentioning League of Legends. If you come from TF2, or even mention it, they don't want you.
And that is a shame, because there really is a good game here. It's the old TFC with some extra spit and polish, and if people would embrace it, the game would be awesome. However, no players and a toxic group of diehards that refuses to accept that it's precious game has been dead since before the game ever reached greenlight kills any and all enthusiasm one has for this source mod.
Just stick with Team Fortress 2. Valve supports it, there are a lot of players, and fun can easily be had. The exact opposite of Fortress Forever.

Arma: Cold War Assault (Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis) is my most favorite game of all time for a reason.  This is Bohemia Interactive's brilliant 2001 classic that started it all and set the bar for open world military simulators.  No, this game doesn't look that pretty (although i'd argue the visuals were fairly good for their time), yes, it has clunky controls and movement mechanics, but oh man... once you really bite into the game and realize the openworld simulator potential.... holy crap this game still blows my mind 14 years later.  No two playthroughs are ever the same, and in my opinion this one has the most robust and fleshed out single player campaigns out of any of the armas.  It's definitely got a bit of a learning curve if you're not familiar with any of the ARMA games, and it's very difficult and unforgiving (I honestly recommend cadet difficulty if you're playing this for the first time, as this allows you more saves and HUD indicators/map icons that can be confusing for a first timer without).  I'm currently playing through the campaign of this to get me pumped up for ARMA 3, as I plan on getting that soon. God I love this game in all its realistic glory!

It's quite basic, with simple graphics, easy gameplay, and some generic repetitive music (I suggest turning the music off, as it just gets annoying after a while).
All the game comprises of is a woman running away from a lion; she has to jump over an endless stream of cacti; if she touches a cactus plant three times the lion catches her and kills her.
The first time the fleeing woman touches a cactus she loses her shirt, but continues running in her bra.
The second time she hits a cactus she loses her shorts, but continues running in her underwear.
The third time the woman knocks against a cactus the lion catches up with her and kills her (a bloodbath of red pixels ensues).
However, it's hard to finish the game (run 100km) because it's so boring and you have to focus on getting the jumps exactly right for a long time to get the 100km achievement.
Don't play this game when you're tired, because then your concentration will inevitably go awry, and you'll lose the game.
Since Ruthless Safari involves a woman running in her underwear, don't be surprised if the SJW wowsers start complaining about it and try to have it banned.
If there was a statue of this underwear-clad woman in an American city, there would be protests - and it would be torn down by a howling mob, or dismantled by the authorities and snuck away in the middle of the night.
I was tempted to give Ruthless Safari a thumbs up, because it's a cheap game and it doesn't pretend to be anything more than what it is.

It's 1619 and escaping execution by your king you head to The New World, Mars! There you get involved with Captain John Smith, Virginia Dare, Martians and the search for the lost colony of Roanoke.
But this is really a retro style bullet hell shoot'em up. You destroy swarms of alien ships while dancing between the bullets. You can unlock different ships with different types of weapons, Challenge Levels and other game modes. There are five levels to the game, But to unlock the later levels you have to complete the previous ones at higher difficulty settings. You get nine lives for each level, So the game is pretty forgiving in that sense.
On my play through I started at the easiest difficulty setting and had to replay the earlier levels at higher settings. I really didn't mind since it only took me a couple of hours to get to the last level. But the last level took me just as long, If not a little longer, to beat than the rest of the game. I only completed one of the challenge levels and only dabbled a little with gauntlet mode.
I never been big on bullet hell games, but this game is OK. The game looks good and plays good. But there is just too much selecting stuff from menus. It gives the game a disjointed feel rather than a journey. Integrating that stuff into the game would have helped maintain continuity between the levels and taken the player out of the game less often. Basic gameplay is fine.  Though, Maybe I'm just relatively inexperienced in the genre, At times things seemed more like a matter of luck than skill. Having 3 lives and 3 continues (another thing to pull the player out) per level definitely helped me get through the game. This is an Indie game so the music is, as expected, excellent. Not really a big part of the game is the whole colonial Mars story. Which is fine as it's just something to connect the levels and not very interesting otherwise.
In a way this seems more like a taster than a complete game. Aficionados may enjoy it and it is friendly to beginners. But the overall experience could have been better.
Edit - A marginal thumbs up.

I just ♥♥♥ this game. It tries to innovate the (action) RPG genre with a feature that is regularly used in different genres; rewinding time. You control a guy who has to save the world within 30 seconds. Yup, 30 seconds. Let me give you an example; with each level you play you are introduced to a boss. Then you're dropped into the level, populated with towns, caverns, seas, anything really. Please note that the levels are not open, but there are several ways to solve a level. Enemy encounters are random and help you level up, while also earning you money. When the timer is about to hit 00:00 you can pray to a statue in certain towns to rewind time and level up further, finish sidequests and, eventually, kill the boss. You can do this endlessly, but it costs more money every time you do this. So there's a bit of puzzling involved as well.
The graphics are (semi)-retro, and done very well, but the music and sounds are quite basic. One word though: gameplay.
Verdict: a must own !

First of all, buy this and play it already. Don't bother watching it online. It's not as immersive. You have to play it for yourself.
It seems that Freebird Games' Kan Gao has taken Laura Shigihara under his wing. Quite honestly, she has made a masterpiece! I think this game had me in tears on 4, maybe 5, seperate occasions. Both developers are masters at conveying emotion through a game; and to be honest, I think this game may even be better than To the Moon! I'm not going to talk about story, which is the bulk of this game, because you, YES YOU! THE ONE READING THIS! YOU NEED TO PLAY THIS FOR YOURSELF! Seriously it was great. Absolutely nailed it on that story aspect.
Also what I like about Rakuen is that it feels more like a game than To the Moon. Don't get me wrong, I'm not ripping on Kan's masterpiece. I'm just saying that there's a puzzle element to this game that was a lot more present than To the Moon which in turn makes this feel more like a game than an interactive movie.
One other thing that makes this game stand out, was the artstyle. This game is very cute. My mother would occasionally glance at my screen and see some adorable little animations and sprites running around the screen when I played this. Well done there.
I don't have any real gripes about this game but, not going to lie, I needed a guide for a hint at a few certain points. I think one thing that could have made this game better would be a better hint system. Throughout the game you play as a nameless boy and his mother. When you're going through the puzzles, you can turn to mother and ask for a hint. The hints were pretty vague and didn't really help unfortunately. Also perhaps a journal system that keeps track of your quest and puzzle progress would have helped. There were a few quests where you had to find certain items around the map and sometimes I forgot how many of which items I needed to find. I know these are all very minor things but perhaps this could help out in the next game.
Oh and on a side note, it helps to know a little Japanese when you play this game. It is entirely in English but there are some small things around the game that are written in Romaji. Knowing how to read that helps understand the story. It does not at all hinder a player to not know what any of the writings mean, it just reinforces a few story elements if you can understand it.
The music in this game was just great. I knew Laura could sing because of To the Moon, but this is where she step into the spotlight and show us how talented she really is! All of the music was composed and produced by her (with a few guest singers at a few parts). I absolutely loved all of the music in this game!
Unless you don't mind crying in public, I would recommend you play this game by yourself. It is absolutely worth the money and if I could erase my memory and play all 10 hours of this again, I would.

Rakuen is this generation’s Chronicles of Narnia. Except it takes CS Lewis’ concepts and improves them in every way. It’s a game where your verbs are love and hope.
You start as a boy in a hospital, who soon finds a door that sweeps him away into a magical world. In this world of Rakuen — a reflection of our own — the nature and realities of everything around us are made clear in different terms. So you soon find a way to use this spiritual reflective reality to serve and love your hospital mates. This leads to a slow-weaving intersection of each character’s stories.
It resolves in what may be one of the most beautiful and memorable endings in any game I’ve played.
I can’t recommend it enough.

This is the first review I've written in years. It'l be difficult to write, but I feel obligated to. Rakuen doesn't have gameplay that'll blow you away, or visuals that redefine an industry, but you know what it does have? The single most powerful story I've ever experienced. Shigihara tells a story of loss, love, innocense, imagination, wonder, humour, and tearful joy mixed with soul shattering grief. You learn of the patients on your floor of the hostpital. You learn of their struggles, their regrets, and their reasons for having the personalities they do through their alter egos in the world of Rakuen. I won't spoil anything, because this story is something you need to play. But, the ability of this game to get you invested in its world(s) is unmatched by most other titles on this platform, with exceptions like To the Moon. While this game has general value to mean something to everyone, it held a resonance to me that I might hold on to for the rest of my life. I lost my mother to MDS, a bone marrow cancer that disables the immune system, last July before I finished High School. I was overcome with grief naturally, but I began to doubt if I was handling it right. I felt like I wasn't shook enough. I've had these feelings of of doubt and stress for the past year, but after hearing that one of my favorite musicians/ sound desgners made a moving tale about cancer and loss, I immediately picked this title up. I finished it in a day, and I think I cried more after finishing this game than in the past year as a whole. It taught me that I wasn't dealing with loss wrong, because everyone's story with loss is unique. This game gave me peace that no therapist could. Please buy this game. Do not hold back tears. Get invested in the characters and the world of Rakuen, for the payoff is far and beyond worth the sadness this game brings. While you might not experience the same gravity that I did, you will feel. I promise you.
End note: Thank you, Laura Shigihara. You've done something for me that might have changed my life.

Best expansion for the best PC game out there. The base game, Civilization IV, is great. It is a really in depth "civilization simulator." You take control of a civilization starting at the dawn of time all the way to the modern era and beyond. The game is very in depth with all of the options at your disposal for how you manage your government, economy, religion, espionage, foreign policy, and many other factors. You can be Gandhi and set up a fascist theocracy with a socialist economy and nuke everyone on the planet. There is a lot of literature out there about how spectacular this game is so I’ll just stop here.
One of the few flaws is the combat. It is all percentage based, so you can get in some pretty frustrating situations. Maybe you go into a battle where you have and 80+ percent chance of winning, but there is still a chance you can lose. Even at 97+percent I’ve lost some times. This combat system is extremely frustrating when you “get haxed” and lose on battle you should have won. Another issue is that in late game the combat really just becomes “who can have the most units crammed into a tile.” Your (and your opponents’) empire will get so big and have so much production that it becomes quite cumbersome to manage a war with all the military units you’ll have around. Since you can fit literally infinite units in one space, it really becomes a contest of who can get the biggest army and march from city to city. These flaws pale in comparison to how great and addicting this game is, however.
This expansion, beyond the sword, is the best. It adds even more units, buildings, and civilizations to the game. Also, it comes pre-loaded with some of the best mods, including Rhye’s and Fall of Civilization, which takes this game to a whole new level. Over all it’s as close to a 10/10 game I have ever seen. You won’t regret spending the money to buy this, especially when it is on sale.

Man this game is rad.
Mecha Ritz is a shoot em up game with a strong focus on its adaptive rank system which increases and decreases the difficulty depending on your actions in the game. As a result of this system, clearing the game is pretty easy. I'm a mediocre shmup player and was able to clear it on my first attempt with several lives left over. However clearing the game is not really the point. The real meat of this game revolves around the scoring system. The scoring system in the game mostly revolves around trying to push the rank as high as possible as well as speedkilling and point-blanking enemies. It's simple, but due to the games excellent use of the ranking system it always creates an exciting scoring experience for all skill levels. Player's will find themselves at a rank high above where they're comfortable and frantically dodging in order to try and keep it for going down. It's an adrenaline rush that needs to be experienced to be understood.
To top it all off the game has excellent visual presentation, fantastic music, TATE support, and a very customizable practice mode that allows you to switch ship types on the fly. My only real complaint is the lack of leaderboards given the game's focus on scoring. Some achievements would have also been nice but certainly aren't a deal breaker.
Regardless, I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in the genre. There's enough here to engage and challenge both newcomers and veterans to the genre making the game very open to all. If you are unsure, there is also a freeware version available online with less features and no translation but still a similar and exciting experience.

Mecha Ritz is an innovative shmup with a uniquely manic pace thanks to its adaptive difficulty system and creative patterns.
MR's big gimmick is that it adjusts the game's difficulty on the fly, according to players performance's, and awards higher scores to higher difficulty runs. This isn't a new concept, having been done many times before in a variety of ways, but Mecha Ritz executes it with a very special flavor. When you play well, the game's difficulty ramps like an out of control roller coaster, providing instant feedback and a dazzling light show of chaos. "But wait!" you might be shouting while raising your finger inquisitively, "doesn't that mean the game must be really really hard? I don't like the sound of being punished for doing well". Well, actually, the games difficulty drops just as fast and as hard as it rises (once again, going back to the roller coaster analogy). This is both a blessing and a curse, because the game does lack the tension of constantly fighting for your existence that is so vital to the genre, but scoring and seeing how far you can push the chaos takes that drive's place, and allows the game to become even more manic (and at times, completely insane) while feeling rewarding and fair.
Beyond the adaptive difficulty, for me, the game's true strength is more fundamental. Even if the difficulty were set in place, Mecha Ritz is a masterpiece of adrenaline fueled pacing and cleverly designed stages and bosses. Stages are filled with unique setpieces and mini-bosses who rapidly jump in and out of the spotlight like over-excited circus performers relishing their time on stage. Bullet patterns and hazards do a brilliant job of forcing you to keep moving at high speed, as opposed to the slow microscopic dodges in most bullet hell games, and make dodging feel thrilling, free, and fun, without sacrificing any of the engagingly mind-bending chaos of traditional bullet hell shooters.
Mecha Ritz is a game that proves just how vital this oldest and purest of game genres still is, and the unending possibility for creativity that lies within it. With its over the top manic gameplay and quirky audiovisual presentation, Mecha Ritz has easily become one of my top 3 shmups ever made. Highly recommended.
PS: If you're on the fence, try the original freeware version. It lacks much of the polish and content of this version, and annoyingly forces you to unlock any level of difficulty beyond easy, but it's fundamental charm is much the same.

When I saw this game on Steam almost a year ago, it was a pretty big suprise to me. A really cheap game made by the same studio that gave us Owlboy, based on the work of one of my favourite musicans? I just couldn't resist buying it, and man - that was a good purchase.
In Savant - Ascent you play as a powerful Alchemist who is very close to gaining control over a powerful Orb. Suddenly, the Orb violently throws him out of his tower, and takes control over his lab. Of course, our hero is not going to let some shining ball bully him like that, so he crashes back in, ready to fight his way back up. And so begins his Ascent.
Mechanicaly, Savant - Ascent is similiar to One Finger Death punch. You shoot enemies by pressing left mouse button, after gathering enough power can blast them with the right mouse button, and you can jump between two spots to dodge attacks in two different ways - either dash left and right  with A and D, or you can press W to do sick flips from one spot to another. You can also hold S to charge up your power metter, and that's it.
But there's so much more to Savant - Ascent. It's pretty much a bullet hell game where hordes of enemies circle all around you, and you protect yourself by firing
at a very fast rate. While this is realisticaly your only "weapon", this attack sounds, looks, and feels awesome. To make things even better you can listen to Savant's songs like Fat Cat Shuffle or Kali 47. If you're a Savant fan, you will really enjoy this game, and if you're not - you will still listen to some really good music while destroying hundreds of enemies.
Now, the thing with this game is that it's both a great stress reliever, and a pretty difficult game. Gitting gud might take you a while (and the game requires you to survive for a few minutes in endless mode just to unlock the final chapter, which is not easy to do), so you will probably get frustrated quite a lot. At the same time, Ascent is a very fun arcade-style game where you rack up huge combos and watch your score grow bigger and bigger while listening to killer beats.
If you just want to play a videogame that won't bother you with tough moral choices or 80 hours of epic campaign, and instead will let you have good 'ol fun like back at the arcade - Savant Ascent is for you.
In short, a very good title both for fans of Savant, and for people looking for a cheap arcade style game.
