The bullet hell genre has always been dominated by Japanese developers. It is a rare sight to see a bullet hell game from a Western studio, and even rarer to see one that proves to be successful. But Jamestown is one of the few games that fits both of those categories, and by no small margin.
Jamestown tells the story of Riley, a man accused of committing treason against the Great British Empire, and who is consequently sentenced to death. In an effort to escape his penalty, Riley flees to the British colony of Jamestown located on Mars, only to walk right into the middle of an invasion of the said colony by the Spanish Inquisition, aided by the local population of Martian rebel forces. Caught between the choice of meeting certain death at the hands of his pursuers from Earth or throwing himself into the midst of the battle for Jamestown, our hero opts for the latter and charges headlong into the Spanish-Martian ranks.
The story of Jamestown is presented through a series of brief cut-scenes between levels that feature still images accompanied by written explanations of Riley's thoughts on the events taking place. Although each of these is well executed and helps each mission to flow smoothly into the next, it's obvious from the straightforward nature of the events depicted in each scene that the main focal point of the game is the action and not the story.
The gameplay of Jamestown follows the standard formula of any bullet hell game - you shoot the baddies while weaving your way through a hail of enemy fire. As with any shmup, earning points and building up your score plays a crucial role in the game, and is achieved in Jamestown's case by destroying enemies and collecting the score items they leave behind. Aside from your primary, forward-firing attack, you also have a secondary attack your disposal, the nature of which varies greatly depending on the ship; or Conveyance, as they're known in Jamestown; chosen. While some Conveyances utilize secondary attacks that merely provide you with alternative bullet spread patterns, others are designed to be used in conjunction with the machine's respective primary attack. After collecting enough score items, the ability to Vaunt becomes available. Vaunting boosts the player's firepower and renders them invincible for a second or two whilst simultaneously clearing away any bullets in their immediate vicinity, making it particularly useful for escaping situations where you or another player is surrounded by a crowd of enemies with no easy way out. Clearing a level without losing any lives or credits will provide a massive boost to your score, though both are much easier said than done. The end of each level is signalled by the appearance of a boss, who is sometimes aided by a number of regular enemies. The bosses themselves consist of the usual, bog-standard end-of-level baddies found in most games from the genre and range from a giant flying saucer to a multi-eyed blob that dwells within a swamp.
Outside of the main game lies the Challenge mode, which presents a series of short, unrelated stages which see the player placed under strict conditions as they attempt to accomplish specific goals such as collecting a certain number of score items or surviving for a pre-determined amount of time. Playing the main game and clearing challenges earns the player Ducats, which can then be spent at the in-game shop to unlock new challenge levels and Conveyances. When you're not blasting away Martians, the next thing you'll want to be doing is taking a look at the Shoppe for anything that might take your fancy. Tired of that Conveyance you're using right now? Buy a new one! Want to re-experience the story in the form of a self-parody with comical lines and events? Go right ahead.
It's clear that accessibility was a priority during the game's development. Jamestown offers five levels of difficulty across each of its six levels, making the game just as suitable for a newcomer to scrolling shooters as it is for a bullet hell veteran.
With eight flying machines to choose from, there are plenty of choices for players with different playstyles. Those who are familiar with the slow-moving bullet hell player character archetypes should recognise the potential in 'Beam', while players who would prefer to have that extra degree of mobility at the expense of narrowing their bullet spread will find 'Wave' to their liking. Players looking for something new altogether will able to appreciate Conveyances like 'Sword' and 'Ghost' which don't follow of the standard player character conventions common among most bullet hell games.
Up to three other players can join the game on one computer, though you'll need more than just a single mouse and keyboard if you have more than one friend who wants in on the action. Playing Jamestown with others can make things a little easier; especially on higher difficulties when having more players helps keep enemy numbers in check. A pool of lives shared between players replaces the standard lives system during co-op play. An interesting feature unique to Jamestown is the ability for players to revive one another by simply staying alive long enough for a certain length of time after someone goes down. Lives are only deducted from the pool when all players are defeated. This alternate take on the usual opens Jamestown up to those who might not necessarily have had a great deal of experience with manic shooters of any sort. The only major drawback to the co-op experience is the lack of any online support, which is a shame because Jamestown clearly has a great deal of potential as a co-op title.
Jamestown's retro art style works in tandem with the game's premise and its subtle but captivating soundtrack to give it that distinctive arcade feel.  Swarms of flying saucers blanket the play area as a seemingly limitless supply of bullets rain down upon the player. Explosions are big, bright and sound fantastic. Humungous Bosses occupy the entire upper portion of the screen as they frantically unleash wave after wave of projectiles upon the players. Jamestown has everything that one would expect to find in any typical arcade game.
One problem that does present itself is the fact that Jamestown is designed to be played in a 16:9 widescreen format. As such the width of the play area is greater than its height, a trait not shared by many other bullet hell games. The end result is that the player will often end up ducking and dodging through more bullets than they were likely intended to. Unsurprisingly this issue can also lead to scenarios in which a disproportionate number of enemies begin to accumulate on the player's flanks.
Jamestown is an excellent example of a manic shooter from a Western studio. The game is easily accessible for the player yet to become acquainted with the conventions of the genre, yet it still provides an ample degree of challenge for the curtain-fire enthusiast.  All in all Jamestown is a great choice for anyone in search of a bullet hell shooter, regardless of skill level.

Jamestown is a vertically scrolling shoot'em up which supports up to four players locally. The game has four ships each with its own unique attack style. The levels are played asynchronously. In addition to the storyline there are a number of challenge modes which can be completed.
In 1619 Raleigh has escaped execution at the hands of his own king. Desiring to clear his name Raleigh flees the Tower of London and heads to the new world, Mars. Mars is currently being fought over between the English and the Spanish armada. Unfortunately for Raleigh the Martians are loyal to the Spanish and have sided with them. Resting his hopes for clearing his name on solving the mystery of the vanished settlement at Roanoake, Raleigh heads to the Jamestown colony in search of John Smith.
Jamestown is the first alternate history/sci-fi shooter I have ever played and indeed it may be the only one that exists. Storyline is not something I have payed mind to in other shoot'em ups, but it is very present in Jamestown. Before and after every level you get a story update. Happily these can be easily be skipped and even turned off entirely. I don't mind the story, but it's not why I'm playing a shoot'em up.
Jamestown has everything you would expect in a shooter. Destructible enemies to kill, indestructible objects to avoid, bonus items to grab. But the details differentiate it. Before each stage you select a type of ship. At the beginning your options will be limited but as you play the other ships will unlock. You can plays with the Beam, Gunner, Charge or Bomber. Beam and Charge are both listed as standard while Gunner and Bomber are listed as advanced. And I certainly agree with the assessment. The two advanced ships are much more difficult to use effectively.
Each ship has two attack modes. The Beam gives you a wide radius of fire and is the only ship to natively firing range outside of what is directly in front of you. The special weapon here is a high-powered constant beam which fires directly in front of you and rapidly damages opposing ships. The drawback is that your ship moves quite slowly while firing this special attack. The other standard ship is the Charge. The basic weapon is has a smaller firing dispersal and fires fewer bullets than the Beam's basic weapon. The Charge special shot fires a slow moving ball that damages any enemy in its path. It doesn't stop when it contacts an enemy, but rather continues on damaging anything in the path. It slowly charges over time, so that if you wait to use it the ball will be larger and more destructive.
The first advanced ship you will unlock is the Gunner. This ship has a basic weapon very similar to the Charge ship and is unique in that the special weapon is always active. Using the special weapon allows you to change the direction in which the special weapon fires. Thus if you press left while using the special weapon it will fire left. When you let up on the special weapon the direction of fire will lock in place until you use it again. This weapon certainly takes some getting used to, but it is the only weapon that allows you to fire to the left, right or towards the rear of your ship. The Bomber has the weakest basic weapon, a single stream of bullets. But the using the special causes the bullets to explode doing tremendous damage.
When you destroy an enemy, it explodes into a field of golden gears and cogs. Collecting these not only increases your score but also moves increases the Vaunt
meter. Once activated Vaunt has several effects. For a short time it provides a shield around your ship. For a longer but still limited time you will double your score. Collecting gears and cogs during the Vaunt will increase the time your score increases. Vaunt also increases the damage your ships weaponry does to enemy units. The final feature of Vaunt mode is that if you press vaunt again while it is active  you will get a shorter lasting shield, but Vaunt mode immediately ends if you utilize this.
Jamestown ostensibly has five difficulty levels ranging from Normal to Judgement. But make no mistake the first two: Normal and Difficult do not allow you to play the full game. If you play on Normal you can only access the first three levels of the game. You will then be forced to play the earlier levels on a higher difficulty to continue the main story mode. If you should choose to use the Difficult setting you can access the fourth but not the fifth level of the game. This was frustrating to me as a player. I recommend using Legendary (or higher) difficulty from the beginning.
Jamestown offers a number of additional gameplay options beyond the main story mode. There is the Gauntlet mode where you play through all the levels consecutively. You are given three lives per credit and three credits. The credits do not reset during gameplay. Gauntlet is unique in Jamestown in that it is the only mode where your accomplishments in one level have any bearing on the next.
There are also a number of Bonus Levels that can be unlocked. These must be unlocked to access them through a mixture of spending ducats and doing well on the challenges which you already have access to. Most of the conditions for completing the bonus levels are earning certain number of points and activating rings by flying over them, in others you simply have to survive a set amount of time.
Jamestown offers four player simultaneous play. However it is local only. The ships are clearly designed to work well together so that one player can ameliorate the weaknesses of the ship of another, or can activate a vaunt shield to protect a friend. It is unfortunate that online multiplayer was not offered.
Jamestown also offers for additional purchase a DLC pack which has more ships to choose from and bonus levels.
I really like the look of Jamestown which is a throwback to the 16 bit era with pixelization and attractive sprites. The soundtrack is also quite good. Unfortunately, as much as I wanted to like it, Jamestown never captured my interest as much as I was hoping. I think that is largely to do with the fact that the game appears to be primarily designed for multiplayer co-op. If I could play online multiplayer I have a feeling my appreciation for Jamestown would increase tremendously. The other aspect that detracts for me is that each level is its own unique challenge and that your performance in one does not carry over to the next. I tend to most enjoy shoot'em ups where you can continually upgrade your weapons until you can destroy most anything on the screen without trying too hard. And then I can get a bunch of free guys so that by the time the game is challenging enough that I die even with my tremendous fire power and start again with a basic ship I have enough lives that I can brute force my way to the finish. Can't do that in Jamestown. The only way to upgrade your destructive capability is with Vaunt and choosing a more destructive ship, and you can't get any free lives. My guess is that Jamestown is a lot more fun to play multiplayer. But I think it is unlikely that I will ever get a chance to try.

On the surface it seems pretty light hearted with cheerful characters, bright colors and fantastic creatures but it deals with some serious topics. There are some light puzzle solving and fetch questing, giving you more to do than other games of this type like To The Moon. Developed by composer Laura Shigihara of Plants vs Zombies and To The Moon fame, you know the music was going to be awesome. If you can, I'd recommend also picking up the soundtrack.

This is Laura Shigihara's Rakuen, a game crafted with love and passion. You can tell from the heart wrenching story, the colorful and cute artwork, the genuine humor, the multiple levels of personality in every character, and of course, the music that plays an integral role in the game and not just an accessory. You will feel for every character, laugh at their personalities, cry at their struggles, and rejoice in their resolutions through the help of your character. All the while, the game will have developed a love in you for the boy and his mom that you lead through the hospital and the fantasy worlds they discover. Now the game has you right where it wants you... for what happens next. This is a game you don't want to miss, indie at its best.

If you liked To The Moon and/or Undertale, you will love Rakuen. Its well developed and memorable characters will captivate you, its soundtrack and attention to detail will immerse you, its jokes will make you laugh, its harsh realities will make you cry, and its story will enchant you. A must play for anyone who likes an almost entirely story-driven game.

It's all worth it though.

This game is a BLAST. Not everyone's cup of tea, for sure, but it is a quirky, EXTREMELY fast-paced (as the title says) JRPG... thing that definitely brings a smile to my face.
Basically, you have 30 seconds per level to save the world from a terrible spell. A greedy, snarky Time Goddess helps you by rewinding time... that is, IF you pay her good coin to do that!
You run around trying to level up and solve quests within the extremely restrictive time limit.
This game gleefully lampshades every and all JRPG cliches, with its cheerful dialogue and wacky characters.
I especially like the way the game world is visually presented, because you get to choose between two very distinct graphics settings: retro pixelart-ish goodness and stylized cartoonish graphics!
It also has online leaderboards to compete with your friends if that's your thing :)
All in all, this game is cheap, fast-paced and (if you like the whole retro JRPG aesthetics, and I know I do) beautiful.
Definitely recommended!

takes place in the fantasy kingdom of Angielle. The story takes place four years after the Great War between fairies and witches. In this world, witches are generally hated by the populace due to the fact that they are often portrayed as being villainous in fairy tales. You play as Lucette, the crown princess of the kingdom, who is arrogant, cynical, and generally looks down on people. That is until one day she is cursed by a witch. Like others who have been cursed, she suffers a type of "fairy tale curse." Every curse is based on a well-known fairy tale. For Lucette, she suffers from the Cinderella curse. Her previous life of luxury as a member of royalty is gone. She now lives as a poor commoner and everyone, expect magical beings and other cursed individuals, has forgotten who she truly is. Now she must complete at least three good deeds in order to break the curse and return to her former life. Along the way, there is a colorful cast of characters to help her.
This game is a visual novel, a type of game that is entirely story-driven. In total, there are five major routes to choose from in this game, one for each romanceable man, each with his own curse to overcome. Each route has a good or bad ending, depending on the choices the player makes during the game, for a total of ten different endings.
The art in the game is very well done. This goes for all aspects with beautiful and detailed backgrounds and unique character designs. I also thought the music is pretty good, too, and it really helped with the atmosphere of the game.
The main attraction of any visual novel is the story. In this case, I found the game to be quite well-written. It would have been easy just to slap together a cheap romance plot for each guy, but the creators of this game really put in a lot more. To start, the world and lore presented is fairly interesting and as I kept playing I wondered what else I would learn about it. This also goes for the characters. Lucette is not some empty shell visual novel protagonist, but is written as a character  in her own right that fully develops throughout the story. Each of the characters in the game are written well, too, and you learn more about them as the game progresses. With five different routes to choose from, there is plenty of more story to experience on each play-through. You will never find out everything about the story line or the characters through a single route.
Overall, for a free visual novel, this is a fantastic experience. I found this game to have good art and a well written story and characters. I would recommend this to those that like visual novels.

First off, let me start off by saying that I have played many MANY otome games. I started playing otome when I was about 16 (I am 20 now), and I just loved the fact that otome games are like novels/stories where you play the role of the protagonist. This otome, out of the many I have played (many of which I have payed for) is by far one of my favorites along with midnight cinderella (although Midnight Cinderella is mostly P2W). I just cannot wrap my head around how this one is free!? I AM SERIOUS. This otome is truly worth money, and yet here it is for free.. I'm not complaining or anything, I am okay with that since I got to enjoy this, but I wish that the person who created this game would get more for it, since you can truly see all the detail and effort put into every character, story, artwork, and music.
*Beyond this point might be slightly spoilerish as far as the MC goes; no spoilers on  the dateable characters however*
1. I have never been the kind of person to complain about an MC (the heroine) as usually they are written rather blandly so that you can instead project your own personality onto her, but this MC really hit home for me. She is a lot like myself, and it really made me re-evaluate how I see people and the world in general. I am often told that I am cold and should smile more, and I don't allow people into my life nor trust anyone (even family) as I have been shown from a young age that no one can be trusted. Not even family. I won't go into further detail of my past as that is no one's business, but I will say that she (the MC) reminded me so much of myself. I actually cried when I came to that realization, but I was filled with hope seeing as how she was able to change such a demeaner/ way of thinking. I will try to make a conscious effort to do the same as I was very inspired by this story.
2. Each character is so unique and different, all of them warmed my heart. The only route I was not excited about at first was Rumples, I just did not like him to begin with. After finishing his route, I actually liked and respected his character. Surprisingly, there was not a single route that I did not enjoy (which for me is a first... Especially since amnesia and mystic messenger -_-)
3. The artwork is beautiful, and truly amazed me at how many CG's you get for EACH character! Not to mention all of the CG's actually look beautiful, AND IT'S FREE. Truly this game is amazing. I cannot digress how much I have enjoyed this game thus far.
4. The story is so engaging and captivating, and for me very relateable. Maybe not for others (I don't really care), but for me it was. I think that is why this game was quiet dear to me.. I have never related to a main character before, but this one was different. I also enjoy the fact that each route is so unique and different from the other while still maintaining a steady plot. (I love reading, and writing my own stories) and I must say that this one is very well made.
5. The music is beautiful! I will not lie however, when I first heard the intro song, I loved the music until the voice appeared. I scoffed at the voice and thought his voice sounded rather whiney and annoying, but it grew on me. Now, I won't even open the game without letting the intro song play.
10/10 would reccomend. Even if it was not free, this game would most certainly be worth every penny. I hope that more games such as this will be released in the future.
*On a sidenote* The moment I saw Waltz, I knew he would be my favorite character. That still holds true.

When I first heard they were attempting a Sonic 4, I was rather interested. The retro Sonic games are classics, with Sonic 3 & Knuckles in particular being the pinnacle of what a Sonic game can offer. Unfortunately I noticed negative things right from the get go. I've returned to this game many times in the past, removing my nostalgic glasses and trying to find some love for the game, but unfortunately this never amounts to much..
Let's start with the physics. This is by far the worst part of the game. The controls and feel of Sonic resemble older Flash-based fan-made Sonic games from 15 years ago. Sonic is all about movement. This is the most important part to get right. To mess this up, is like crippling Doom guy with ineffectual weapons. It's like nerfing Mario's jump height. Momentum is practically non-existant. The minute you let go, Sonic comes to uncomfortable and unrealistic halt on the spot. This happens when both running and even in mid-air when jumping. To make matters worse, Sonic is unable to pick up proper speed from simply rolling down hills. Instead, aside from the pretty poorly implemented Spin Dash, and homing attack, the only other method of receiving speed is from the overly abundant speed boosters.
This is a critical, fundamental and core problem with the game. In the original games, Sonic had straight forward abilities and behaviours which were the entire basis of the gameplay - you master SONIC. Yet here, Sonic is so crippled, that it becomes more about working with handicapped controls and abilities that are working against you. Sonic has no potential that YOU, the gamer, can bring out or master. Even more out of place, is Sonic's lack of proper acceleration from a stand still. Sonic is an impatient and speed character. In this game, moving from a complete standstill and trying to speed up results in an extremely slow and painful walk. Both this, and the lack of appropriate momentum are easily the worst aspects of the game play. In fact I would actually go so far as to say, that even if we removed the Sonic part of the game, it would still be slow and awkward (most games would make up for this with a run button).
The other issue is that of content. The game has very few levels on offer, all of which are more or less just remakes (visually) of pre-existing levels. This perhaps wouldn't be so bad, except for the fact that the level designs themselves don't necessarily feel too fun. Bosses themselves feel quite heavily scripted, and at times, are often invincible to hits, until they've completed certain animations. One final criticsm is that the music sucks. No really, it does. Eveytime I enter an act 3 boss level, I'm expecting clowns, or Eggman to start juggling. Apparently that particular song is recycled from an old unused classic song, but it's pretty obvious why it was 'unused' in hindsight. Additionally, i'll add that the graphics themselves are rather flat and plastic looking compared with even Episode II.
As a life-long Sonic fan, I don't take any pleasure in giving a negative review. It's not an atrocious game, but rather, an extremely disappointing one. We've all seen what SEGA can achieve at the top of the game and when they're committed to a Sonic game. This is an unfortunate example of a Sonic game, where Sega clearly did not have their heart in it. A great shame.

As someone who's been a Sonic fan my whole life, this is by far one of the worst additions to the Sonic library, and that's not saying much but I'd rather play Sonic 06 any day than to play this boring♥♥♥♥♥game again.
This is pretty much Sonic 1 but if he had a homing attack and "nice" graphics. This adds nothing to Sonic, the levels are boring as ♥♥♥♥ and frustrating as all hell. I can't count how many times I've gotten hit by an enemy that came out of no where off screen and made me lose my chance at the Special Stage.
Don't even get me started on the Special Stages, they're the worst. Think of the Special Stages from Sonic 1 but if you had a time limit and can control the map at will. First of all, you can't proceed through a Special Stage without collecting enough rings in them, this would be fine if it wasn't for the time limit. Some of them start you off with 30 seconds, just because you can collect time bonuses doesn't make the stages anymore bareable. Might as well not even go for the Chaos Emeralds, Super Sonic isn't much different from normal Sonic anyways.

EDIT: I want to reiterate how complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the Special Stages are, I decided to try and get all the Chaos Emeralds in this game I was reminded why these stages were so terrible. The Special Stages literally make you stall for time by making you fall into pits that you have to slowly inch your way out of and the movement in these stages are so wonky that you'll accidentally throw yourself into a ! circle. These stages are by far the worst part of this entire game.
The actual stages are, again, boring as all hell and frustrating. Every stage after Splash Hill Zone revolves around nothing but stupid gimmicks that make the level longer and boring. Casino Street Zone is a huge supporter of this. In Act 2, it revolves around flipping cards and riding on said cards. This level is a great way to gather 1-Ups but that's literally it, the riding sections of this level are boring and make the level longer, again, and the flipping cards sections are frustrating to deal with, considering they flip faster than you can jump on them. In Lost Labyrinth Zone Act 1, the gimmick is literally riding on a rolling ball on a rail for half the level. You have to keep Sonic balanced on this ball or else you'll fall to your death. These sections are, say it with me now, BORING.
Let's talk about Sonic's homing attack in this game real quick because I have lost so many runs to this stupid mechanic. Sonic can homing attack towards anything that has a target over it when he gets close enough. Seems simple right? But a few things can go wrong. The intentional thing that's supposed to happen is that you hit whatever you homing attacked and jump upwards a little bit. However, you might also just hit your target but go straight through, or the more common thing to happen, absolutely nothing happens. You'd launch yourself forward to your target but either get hurt or just... nothing happens. It's a broken mechanic, I'd rather this game not have it at all because the levels are designed for you to use this broken mechanic and it's stupid.
This game has no redeeming factors and nobody should have any reason to come back to this game unless you really want to get all those achievements, which there's an achievement where you have to destroy 1000 enemies. This game is literally stalling itself so that you get more hours into it, it prolongs the game so much and it becomes really annoying.
3 Key Words: Boring, Long, Frustrating.

I played this game at release, quit, played again when they went F2P, quit right before Epic levels were released, and now have started to play again. The game has changed substantially since release, and in its present form is no longer for me. Turbine has made the stats excessively complicated, to the point where the game barely resembles D&D. You thought all you had to worry about was ability points, skills, feats, and equipment. Those, along with buffs, would determine your AC, to-hit and damage, HP, spell DC, etc. Now you need to think about PRR, MRR, % Dodge, Universal Spell Power, Elemental Spell Power, Doublestrike %, whether your bonuses come from enhancement, alchemical, morale, song, profane, psionic, luck, sacred...They have also, on multiple occasions, made build-breaking changes to feats and mechanics in the name of 'balance' in a game where PvP is at best an ancillary feature. The enhancement system has been completely redone at least 3 times, and individual prestige classes continue to be tweaked (or ignored).
The game has been on a freefall slide into a grindfest ever since crafting was introduced. Run raid for mats, run to next raid for loot, run to next raid for more loot, repeat on multiple characters, wait for timers to reset and while you are waiting, grind mats from zones and tokens from epic. This is the essence of DDO today. And what is the reward? Aside from playing through all of the content (much of which is quite good if you take the time to enjoy it), nothing. You can reincarnate your character for a small, stacking bonus and play through all of the content again. But good luck finding groups to run with, as most vets by now are well on their way to completionist status, having reincarnated as every playable class. Not to mention that they are (and this is no exaggeration) months ahead of you on gear. With timers it is temporally impossible for you to craft high level weapons and gear in any reasonable amount of time. You can't even claim that its a social experience. PUGs are virtually non-existent and most people are in guilds only for the buffs.
To be fair, most of the dungeons in this game are very polished, and new content is generally good. Though there is no open, sandbox world, there is a ton of instanced content and occasionally in-game events that the devs put a lot of work into. If you have a group of friends to run with, or can find a good and active guild, this is STILL a great game. Despite what you may hear in-game, you don't NEED crafted gear to complete most of the content in the game, but you can expect challenges along the way. To me that's more fun than mindless destroying content, but most high level players disagree. And who can blame them? They've been playing the same content for
.

The main character is fleeing from the King of England, and is fighting against the Spanish fleet and a bunch of aliens, with steampunk jetpacks things. That’s kind of cool.
Gameplay-wise the most notable thing is that it’s a widescreen, but scrolls vertically. I’m not used to that, as it means a lot of bullets come from the sides, as opposed to games like Touhou and Dodonpachi, but it's nice that the majority of the screen isn't wasted. There’s also a pretty big variety of ships, with very different play styles. But I still stick to the Dodonpachi-style ship, cause that’s what I’m good with.
The pixel art is nice, the music is fitting, and the game difficulty is quite reasonable.

On the one hand this piece of hardware is great. A low cost, low foot print, solution to easily be able to play your PC games from your couch and I totally recommend it. But it also make big shortcomings with the Steam platform painfully obvious, shortcomings that are huge parts of why Steam hasn't really become a viable "replacement" for consoles in the living room yet.
I have had Steam since it's inception and over the years I have built up a library of around 1100 titles.
I have also built up a library of Xbox 360 games during the years and now when I have a family my kids can easily grab one of the games from the shelf and play in one of the many consoles around our house.
But when it comes to Steam, even if I have several gaming worthy PC's and a fleet of Steam links at every TV in the house, my kids are not able to play the games I have bought in a manner even close to the simplicity of the "old ways".
Sure we have Family Sharing, but since it only enables ONE kid to play any of my 1100 games at any given time or NONE of the kids to play if I happen to want to play any of my other 1099 games makes the feature basically useless in a family setting like ours.
That my kids are young also make you perhaps not actually want to create accounts for them so what I would love would be "kids accounts" that are sub accounts of a parents account and controlled by the parent. They have access to the parents games (that the parent have granted access to) and as long as the parent or one of the other kids are not playing a specific game they can play it. This would have allowed the Steam links (because I actually have three) to be used like a true console replacement. With the current system, anything more than one Steam link makes little sense in a house.
I have hoped for Steam to reconsider their highly limiting stance on how Steam could function for families but I'm doubting much will happen. I'm considering buying future titles available on both Steam and GOG on GOG instead so my kids can play my games without affecting my ability to play any of the rest of my games.

As you can see by the many hours I've put into this game, I find it to be the most fun game I've ever played, at least on PC. And I'm a quite a very active player.
As many others beofre me have stated, this game is very punishing and you need to embrace that, or it's not for you. The RNG isn't flawed at all, it's just that because the game can be so punishing, having some bad rolls can make you quite frustrated and think the RNG is broken. That's because most people don't understand statistics. They think two missed 90% rolls is a conspiracy in a gamewhere hundreds of rolls are made per mission. If you have 10 warriors each hitting twice per turn at 90%, there should statistically be two misses. But when it happens, people think RNG is broken.
The game has some DLC but they are not needed to enjoy the game, and the AI will play all DLC races against you even if you did not buy them. There is a lot of grind to be done in this game, adnd I am not even close to be done with all the hours I've put in, but noen of the grind is necessary at all. It's just a nice added incentive to keep going while you develop your warband.
TI haven't even done all the story misisons, but they're pretty fun. Some can be very hard though. For me, multiplayer is where the real fun is. I am an admin of the currently only active MP league, called the Mordheim MP Permaleague. We have a great system for doing fair matches and anyone can join with a new team and play on equal terms against others. What's fun with MP games is that there are tow modes. Exhibition games without permanent effects afterwards, or Contest games with permanent effects. The league I play in do Contest games. So any loot you grab off your opponent you get to keep and they lose it, any injuries you suffer are there to stay, and so on. It's great fun if you can accept that you WILL suffer losses. But league players also get AI games that they can use to recover in when needed.
Unfortunately this game lacks a server based matchmaking system, and that is its biggest flaw.
Pros:
- Best Games Workshop game adaption to date with its awesome fantasy and lore.
- Awesome an helpful community.
- Devs stays in close touch with the players and do balancing changes based on community feedback and they have a great sense of humor and a genuine interest in the game.
- Many different warbands that all have a very unique playstyle and spellcasters (if you own all DLCS, base game has 4 warbands which still is enough for many many hours).
- Very long replayability because there are countless of diffferent viable skill builds to make and toy with for each class and race.
- Lots of skills to choose from, where most of them are quite useful.
- Procedually generated maps and many different deployment types.
- A lot of different runes to discover and enhance your gear with.
- Generally a good economy system where you'll find yourself in short of money for a very long time unless you're quite skilled and know what you're doing.
- The become a "pro" player you will probably need hundreds of hours and understand how to work the RNG in your favor, which is a good thing!
Cons:
- Punishing and unforgiving, can cause serious ragequits.
- Poor AI pathing, especially with Impressives often getting stuck. An issue that's still not been resolved after a year.
- Some very annoying bugs connected to ambushes, stairs and obstacles on the ground, that can cause desyncs in MP games.
- No MP matchmaking system. If you want to play MP you need to find friends, ask in the forums, or join a league.
- Some skills are pretty useless, but they're thankfully not that many and with a lot to choose from it will not impact overall gameplay.
- Devs go very silent between DLCs/patches, and become very active and communicative weeks before such a release. Could be more consistently visible on the forums.
- Lack of customisation options for your warband. There are some, but generally fairly limited. Doesn't bother me much, but for many it does.

8.5/10. This is a very good game. Many people are leaving negative comments that are based entirely on ignorance.
Things you should know before buying; this game:
* has a VERY PRONOUNCED KNOWLEDGE BARRIER. It may take over 20 hours of gameplay to truly understand the game's mechanics. For this reason I would suggest not putting much stock in gameplay reviews from people who have under 20 hours of gameplay time.
- has a similar feel to the original Mordheim board game. It's obviously very different, but it retains its namesake's tactical and challenging appeal.
- is of a similar vein to XCOM. Mordheim does have a lot more punching, and a lot less shooting.
- has a luck component. It is very fair and balanced. The game does not cheat you. Others say that the game actively cheats you; they are both ignorant and incorrect. They do not have a solid understanding of the game mechanics. I have seen statements like the following: "The game said i had a 95% chance to hit, and I missed three times in a row!". This scenario is entirely possible. The % hit chance does not entirely reflect the target's avoidance. Literally every statement that I have seen which disparages the game's luck component originate from stances which are both ignorant and incorrect, and are similar to what I stated above.
- is VERY challenging/unforgiving. Especially if you do not have a very solid grasp of the game mechanics. Almost every turn you take with each of your units has to be well planned and executed. One miss-step could mean a total loss, either of your character or the whole campaign. Also, there is NO saving. Everything is permanent and irreversible.
- does NOT tell you how to play itself, and never explains anything. The tutorial is worthless. You really need to read every aspect of the character sheets to get acquainted with the layout, and then go on the forums and read up on how everything works in-game.
That being said, the game is very fun and rewarding. There is no more problems with loading times. The enemy units do now go after wyrdstone. The AI enemies do play their turns out in real time and may take ~1 minute, so if you are *extremely* impatient, you might want to keep this in mind,
I rated this game an 8.5/10 because, while it is very good, it has a few noticeably detracting flaws:
-Occasionally buggy AI. Perhaps 1 in every 10 games, an AI unit will glitch and stand in a corner. When this happens, the entire balance of the game is destroyed. Even losing 1 unit in a 10 vs. 10 battle is crippling. When this happens, the match's enjoyment is entirely gone. This is the major detractor.
-Often poor AI. The AI are not a match for the player, in terms of skill and tactics. 'Harder' missions are simply ones where the AI units have better gear, more stats, and more abilities than your units. Your tactics might change on harder difficulties, but there is absolutely no scaling in tactical difficulty.
-Antiquated looking graphics. While acceptable, the graphics are sub-par when compared to games of the same generation.
I would only recommend this game if you like a challenging, tactical, and rewarding experience, and you don't mind defeat. Because defeat will happen. Early and often.
If you are a rabid fan of WHFB. and this game's affiliation with WHFB is your primary selling point, then get it. You'll be tickled pink. Just don't try to get too attached to your warband; as I said, they will die =P

First and foremost, I'd like to say I'd give this game a "neutral" review if there was such an option, but since there isn't, I'll opt for a thumbs up, as it has some redeeming qualities (mostly allowing you to play Episode Metal in Episode II).
So, where to begin. Sonic 4 is supposed to be a sequel to the classic Sonic games, and as a huge fan of them (Sonic & Knuckles was pretty much my first console game), I had to get it. And when I saw you could actually play as Metal Sonic in Episode II if you owned both episodes, it was an instant purchase (as a matter of fact, Episode II is, so far, the only game I've ever pre-ordered). However, it seems I'm talking too much about how I got the game, and not about the actual game. Well, plain and simple, this is a subpar Sonic game, especially compared to the older titles (in particular Sonic 3 & Knuckles, which felt huge at the time). It's rather short, with only 4 zones (3 acts + boss fight), and they're all rehashes of zones found in previous Sonic games; the same goes for the bosses. Even the final boss feels uninspired, especially when compared to the final boss in S3&K (yes, I'll talk about that game a lot).
As for the soundtrack, I'd like to say it was good, but I honestly can't remember a single track, whereas there's always a memorable track (if  not the whole soundtrack) in previous Sonic games. It feels kinda generic to me. Another problem with the game is the mechanics. Mostly when it comes to movement: when you start moving Sonic walks slowly before accelerating, and while he's always walked a bit in previous games, the acceleration in this one is slow (not to mention it feels like Sonic's shoes had glue in them, since he kind of sticks to the ground, or even walls); and I guess I should mention the complete lack of momentum, which makes Sonic suddenly stop mid jump if you stop pressing the movement keys.
Even then, despite all its faults, I'd say I had a fun time with this game. I still wouldn't recommend it  on its own; only get it if you're a huge Sonic fan, and want to play Episode Metal as well.

I've been a Sonic fan since 2000 (I'm only 22), but lately the Sonic games haven't been that good. Seeing as how this is an overdue follow up to the classic Sonic the Hedgehog 3, I was eager to try this game. Unfortunately, I did not like it. The level design is rather frustrating and there is no real sense of story. For me, finishing levels was more so based on luck rather than skill. I'm really forgiving when it comes to Sonic games (I actually liked Unleashed), but I just cannot recommend this to anyone.

Sonic 4-I is a game with a long history of memes. See that 9/10 score for Sonic 4-II on Steam? 4-I is a very similar game with many of the same traits, but the memes keep it from ever rising above 6/10. 4-II is ever so slightly better in some small ways, but it's not anywhere near enough for the sharp divide that we routinely see with these two games.
Sonic 4-I has some cool level design, interesting tweaks on bosses (especially in a series that traditionally has poor bosses), and a really great redesign of Sonic 1's Special Stage. There's not much in the way of drawbacks, and the developers even threw in a cool Metal Sonic mode if you own the second game. I have no idea why this game was run into the ground, especially when the largely similar Sonic Advance and Sonic Rush games have a decent reputation. If I could have been there to play this on release date, I probably would have been pretty satisfied with the game.
And let's be real, numbers are questionable. 6s and 7s are supposed to be good games that are worth your time but aren't amazing hidden gems or works of art. That's not what the numbers are ever used for, and anyone who thinks they are is an overly idealistic idiot. 6s and 7s, to the vast majority of human beings, mean worthless trash that isn't even bad enough to laugh at. Oh wait, that's what everyone calls Sonic 4-I. Go ♥♥♥♥ing figure.
If anything, the entire Sonic series has some fundamental game design problems that people cling to out of a sense of nostalgia; the series hit them where it hurts. I can't even say that without being called a hipster or whatever, and there are too many people who think they can say the same about the Mario series (which doesn't have such problems at all).
This game deserves nothing less than a plain old but still shiny blue "Positive" rating.

Sonic the Hedgehog 4 is the canonical sequel to Sonic the Hedgehog 3 & Knuckles that takes place before the Sonic Adventure games. Although canon doesn’t really matter that much in this because it tries to be like the old 2d sonic games where the plot is to just stop Robotnik’s (Eggman’s) plans by beating up a lot.
This game like Sonic Adventure gets too much hate but unlike Adventure, this game doesn’t seem to get much love at all. Yes the game is clearly trying to play off of nostalgia from those who played Sonic in the glorious Genesis era, but that doesn’t make it a bad game. I see people complaining about the controls to this game, but I honestly had no issues during the whole play through.
The game plays similarly but not the same to the old Sonic games with some mechanics such as homing attacks from the 3d games added in. The homing attacks helps the game’s speed which sometimes feels fast but other times feels pretty slow due to level design and Sonic’s starting momentum.
The games graphic’s are honestly not the greatest. The 2.5d graphics and bland colors(at least in this episode, IDK about episode 2) takes away from the nice, colorful Sonic feel. Not only that, but some things such as Sonic himself look fairly ugly.
A few of the bosses are just old ones copied with maybe something added to change it up and a few new ones. I have no real issues with the bosses…except the last one. The final boss has 5 forms with the last one being where the issues come in. This form seems to be designed just to be a pain in the butt and take away lives. After some practice (about an hour for me on the Steam version lol) you can beat him with only slight troubles.
Overall, the game was ok. It did feel pretty empty and uncolorful for a Sonic game but I would still recommend getting it anyway, since it's fun. I mean I bought it twice and played it when my brother had it on the Wii so I think that’s saying something.

Oh god, I hadn't cried in a game since To the moon. You see, I've become interested in this game when I saw so many To the moon references, and they are all accurate. Same (lack of) gameplay, same rich and emotional story. If you really liked To the Moon, playing Rakuen is nothing less than a moral obligation.
You play as "Boy", a hospitalized boy who enters the fantasy world of the book "Rakuen" with his Mom. There's a guardian in the forest who is currently slumbering due to the darkness enveloping the forest. Your mission is to learn a song that will wake the guardian up. To learn this song, you need to help five people.
The fantasy world is (as seen very early in game, so don't worry it isn't a heavy spoiler) connected to the hospital. The patients are characters in the fantasy world and there are some physical mechanics where changing the real world changes the fictional world.
As the game moves forward, you learn about the past of the people being saved and help them to "find closure" (as written in the game synopsis). You actually do that by helping them in the fictional world.
Finally, as in To the Moon, it's interesting to note that you should play this game paying attention to the dialogues and story. There are A LOT of connections between what you are discovering and what a character told you about 2 hours ago. This is specially true for Sue and Yami. I recommend paying close attention to the dialogues between the Boy and these 2 characters.
Now go and build a little world :)
Rakuen is the type of deep, sincerely personal type of narrative we all wish we had in the SNES days. And if you think drama is a drag, don't worry: It's also super fun and charming.
10/10 would cry again

Laura Shigihara is a demon made flesh! A demon that preys upon the feelings of hope, sorrow, longing, loneliness, and oh my god as I write this I realise just how much of an emotional rollercoaster this game was!
Not since To The Moon have I so routinely kept finding dust in my eyes whilst playing a game.
The visuals were very pretty, the characters were relatable. The puzzles had been playtested extensively to smooth off any sharp edges. And the soundtrack? Absolutely central to manipulating my emotions like a harpist on my heart strings.
If you, like me are a very stoic person whose only interaction with your emotions is to wave at them as if from a passing car then this game will be entirely foreign to you. I felt things, even when I desperately tried not to, and I firmly blame Laura!
Buy. This. Game.

Rakuen is an absolutely stunning game with a
storyline about a
boy who sets out to explore a hidden parallel world with his mother, in the quest to have his wish fulfilled. It is therefore more story-based, but does have simpler game-like elements such as exploration, collecting items and solving riddles. Furthermore, the game's creator Laura Shigihara worked on Freebird Games' To The Moon, so it comes as no surprise that Rakuen is heavily inspired by this story-heavy modern classic, and even pays homage through an Easter egg (did you find it?).
As it is a game that inherently stresses the importance of the story rather than the gameplay itself, you will find that much care was put into making the game relatable; as the boy and his mother help people along their way, you uncover some very realistic issues
. I must also applaud the organic mother-son interactions, as well as the use of music and sound to create suspense. They also did a very good job of connecting the two worlds in interesting ways, which made the story a lot more interesting since you must make progress in either world in order to see changes in the other. This constant travel through different portals also nicely symbolizes the dreams and imagination of the little boy.
I do, however, have some criticisms towards this game. One would be that I wish they hadn't been so explicit in giving hints on how to solve some puzzles. Now I'm not talking about the hint function, but rather, when you receive a quest or puzzle you are eager to solve on your own, the NPCs will say something like "Ooooh I would loooove to go to that island, if oooonly I had a boat so I could go there. It would be so great if someone could make me a boat. If only". Now that may perhaps be slightly exaggerated, but my point still stands: the game doesn't always give you chance to solve things on your own, which is quite a shame. The reason I think this is important to mention is that since the game is so story-heavy, I believe it needs to justify itself as an actual game, in order to not come off as just an interactional visual novel.
Now this may just be personal preference, but I find that the frequent use of lyrical songs - although charming when used sparingly, and while it is something that sets it apart from To The Moon - got a bit cheesy. Yes, they were strategically placed throughout the game, but they would still be a bit sudden and made me feel less immersed in the game. That being said, I do think
's song was very suitable and was well integrated into the actual game, rather than just being a random solo in the middle of a conversation.
Overall, it is a lovely game which needs more recognition. It gives you a very fair amount of gameplay (I got about 7 hours and I played it all in one go) and more importantly, it is something I believe is worth experiencing.

Beyond the Sword is the expansion pack that made everything about Civilization IV better, plus is necessary for some of the really good mods outs there such as Fall from Heaven.
So, I am certainly going to recommend it.  It is a strategy game that got a lot right.  The gameplay mechanics encourage expansion, but simultaneously impose reasonable limts.  New technologies can alter the way the game is played, making a very different strategic picture through railroads, airplanes, and democracy.  The religion mechanic adds great flavor and some interesting gameplay.  Diplomacy is easy to understand, but hard to exploit.
There are some flaws.  Get to far behind and you've lost, even if it takes another 100 years for the axe to actually fall.  The end game becomes a bit to grindy with units becoming to common.
Still, the hundreds of hours I've spent playing this game is a testament to both its addictiveness and its quality.

DDO is a pretty decent MMO from a gameplay standpoint. A little dated, and the servers are a bit quiet these days, but... decent.
So why the negative review, you may ask?
The business model is TRULY disgusting. I mean, yes, it's a free-to-play game, you know that they have to keep the lights on somehow. That's fine. But DDO goes way past double-, or even triple-dipping. This is a game that proudly advertises that you can buy healing items direct from their store. This is a game that has a monthly subscription system while still locking classes behind a secondary paywell. This is a game where, if like me, you decide you want to "reincarnate" to use a freshly unlocked class to be able to use skills from that class to any decent proficency (because you're not going to be able to retroactively put points into skills your class couldn't use before, looking at you, Disable Device), you're expected to pay nearly $12 worth of "DDO Points".
And don't get me started on Astral Shards. Yeah, you can add a "funbucks" secondary currency system to the pile of gouging too.
Yes, DDO ticks just about EVERY single box in the pay-to-win checklist. Credit where its due, you can unlock a small number of points by playing the game, and if you pay a subscription you're given a nice bonus of 500 free points per month. This sounds nice in theory, but the payout is not nearly enough.
Let me explain:
Completing quests for the first time (or the first time on one of three difficulties) gives "Favour". Every 100 favour gives you 25 free DDO points, with extra points being given for the first time you reach Favour milestones. So what's the problem?
The problem is the price of the store is inflated to HIGH HELL as a result of this. See, if you reach the game's favour cap (that's 5000 Favour, FYI), you'll have made a tidy 1900 DDO points.
BUT MOST STORE PURCHASES ARE AROUND 1000 POINTS EACH. So if you put in a few hundred hours and complete ALL the quests in the game on the highest difficulty, you'll be able to buy one or two nice little treats. How nice of them.
Oh, but wait! Most of the quests are DLC! So you had better buy a $15 subscription to play them all, because otherwise you're looking at about $6 or more for a few hours of content PER DLC, most of which have virtually no replay value. The Subscriptions don't even unlock all of the classes! If you, say, wanted to play an Artificer, you're out of luck unless you pay 995 TP or farm like hell to complete minigames that clearly weren't designed for solo play but because the game's popularity has waned nobody actually plays. Plus there's two WoW type paid expansions that you have to pay out the nose to get. Credit where its due, even in spite of this, the subscription is actually pretty solid value, and if the game didn't have the amazingly stupid pay-to-win stuff and just sold the subscriptions, I'd be singing its praises.
But they do, and BY GOD does the game try every dirty trick in the book to make you want to spend your DDO points on that sweet, sweet Pay-to-Win. Do you want to revive in the middle of an hour long quest after dying to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t instant kill trap that only Rogues and one paid class can disable, but you're in a room where there's no Rest Shrine because screw you? That'll be 200 DDO points each, thank you! Sure, you can quit a quest, buy expensive drinks at a bar at a respawn spot to get back on your feet and hope like HELL that you make it back to the quest location before the arbitrary timer runs out! Oh, and have a massive XP penalty deducted from the quest reward for not paying us.
What's that? You're a non-magic user who needs to BREATHE to survive an arbitrary three minute swim through an underwater ravine? Well, you're out of luck... but we've got JUST the potions for you! 60 points upfront.
And of course, there's Astral Shards that let you buy exclusive things that are much better than you can with the in-game currency, which you buy with, you guessed it, DDO points.
DDO tries to squeeze money out of its players in a way I've only seen from mobile games. Subscriptions, pay-to-win microtransactions, locking basic content behind paywalls, paid content that is ludicrously overpriced and not covered BY the subscriptions... it has it all.
And the worst part is, there's still a good game in there, begging to be set free, but I just can't overlook how absolutely bonkers the business model is. This game might have Charmed me into giving it a few months of subscription money, but I eventually made my Will save and banished it back to the Nine Hells.
Also the game has inexcusably bad server problems for a game of its age and lag caused by server hang-ups cause all sorts of cheap deaths. Couldn't fit that in somewhere, but worth mentioning.

The basic premise of the game is simple, you have a team of up to 10 characters and you go into a part of the titular city Mordheim to pick up basically money or loot. Rinse and repeat until you level up your characters and equip them enough to try and take on the next mission of the campaign.
You have to really like this sort of gameplay, which is a turn based game from the third perspective with attacks and dodges based on percentages to hit/dodge. It takes a god damn age to set up all your characters in a mission. The first two turns are basically you just moving everybody into a position, if you run ahead with one of your faster characters then be prepared to be caught out of position and take a beating. So you're just inching forwards until you can mob one of the enemies. The game has way too much of that, getting everybody into position, since you're taking control of every single character and moving them as you would a character in a normal third person game, except you're limited by the range you can move. On top of that you have to wait for the enemy to do their turns, which even if you're playing against the AI take way too long. There's no real way to make the AI do their turns instantly.
So you really have to like the gameplay, and since I am a big fan of turn based games this is right up my alley. However even I have a limit, and doing the same set up over and over again in each mission just becomes too annoying. Not to mention that the campaign missions aren't that special either. They at least have unique locations, however the layout of certain maps and where you have to go to complete an objective can be confusing at times. Which really does not bode well when you're against the turn clock, since the enemy keeps getting reinforcments and your guys just get whittled down.
Thankfully since the campaign missions take even longer to complete than a normal mission I did not fail any of the ones I tried. I got very close to that with the last one I completed, which was to kill a sorcerer in a magical library. I was basically down to my last two characters and missing 3 consecutive lethal hits on the sorcerer with a single possible hit remaining, since the next turn the character I had to keep alive would have died for sure due to some ongoing damage. I managed to get that last hit and complete the mission, but just the thought of failing there and then and having to do the whole thing over again totally put me off the game. It really needs some way to cut down on the wasted time spent basically not doing anything. I hope there's a sequel and they manage to fix that part.

There's a lot I like about this game but there's a few infuriating sticking points that made me not enjoy it as much as I should.
Things I liked:
-The harsh difficulty level
-The graphics
-The main skeleton of the game.
-The controls
Things I didn't like (there's a bunch of them but many are small so it looks like they outnumber the good points but that's not really true)
-Even though the Wyrdstone gathering encourages exploring the fact is it's usually too risky to go ham on farming Wyrdstone. The fog of war means you can rarely tell where is safe. The enemy combs the battlefield and once they find you it just descends into a battle. If you try and send out lone guys to find out of the way loot pockets they will most likely get taken out.
-Buildings don't usually make sense. You can't open doors or shoot out of windows. Often you can't jump down or climb up where you want to. You can waste a lot of time messing with scenary with no benefit so it's usually best to not bother.
-Not enough character model options in customisation mode.
-Consumable items mostly suck to the point where I don't usually use them. You can't tell who you're fighting beforehand so taking anti-poison or anti-fear items is a crapshoot as you may not even need them.
-Not being able to get past your own guys in choke points.
-The thing that made me quit in the end was set mission I-III for the human mercenary faction. If you're going to make a game where combat is deadly and consequences of injury are permanent and dire, please please please avoid using a teleportation maze with one-way teleporters. This game is really not suited to missions that require trial and error to find the way around. It's not fun. Not at all. I could have persevered through the rest of the little niggles but this level was too much.

Wow.
First, you should know what you're getting in to. This isn't a typical RPG. It is also free from the RPGMaker stigma of poor quality. If you've played To The Moon and liked it and other story-driven games, then you'll probably like this game. If not, there's not much for you here. There are no combat elements, and only the most basic of puzzles. Most of the game is walking around from location to location, watching cut-scenes and scrolling through dialouge, with a few notable exceptions that I won't get into for spoiler reasons. This is a completely story driven adventure from beginning to end. It's a good thing that Rakuen has compelling characters and great writing, even if pacing feels off at times. Without spoiling things, the sections of the game get shorter and shorter as the game goes on. It'll probably take you about 8 hours to complete, unless you do none of the optional stuff. The game sticks with you long after you finish it, though. You'll probably be humming the songs as well, as the soundtrack is also great. The developer is mainly a composer, so this makes sense.
If you like story driven games and if you want to be sad, then this is the game for you. If you're looking for fun and engaging gameplay and know you don't like this stuff, I'd look somewhere else. If you aren't sure, I'd recommend picking it up. It's an amazing first impression for the genre, and you won't be disappointed.

Having followed the development of this game for nearly 5 years, and also being a huge fan of Laura's work, it is hard to not be biased towards the review of this game. I will, however, be as far from subjective as possible in this review.
The gameplay is obviously the weakest link in the chain. The puzzles make up a big chunk of the gameplay, and can range from somewhat intuitive to a trial-and-error wild goosehunt. The animations are less than stellar, and though some cannot easily look past such aforementioned flaws, the fact that the game was made in RPG maker can allow some slack to be cut.
Character design wise, the game did a great job. The artwork on many of the NPCs felt organic and almost lept out of the screen. The melancholic yet effervescent plot is in also the plus column. Despite the game starting out with the weaker story arcs, it is perhaps the driving force behind players wanting to further progression. I especially loved the indirect storytelling through cartoon reenactments, paralled with real life mementos and areas. The game ends on a truly bittersweet note that is reminscent of To The Moon.
The soundtrack is perhaps the strongest field of this game. Immediately after loading up the menu screen on my first playthrough, an almost magical theme similar to the opening to a great visual novel plays, enchanting me instantaneously. Almost every soundtrack is memorable, and brings life to an otherwise visual-appealing yet generic RPG game. Specifically, soundtracks "Fish Heads" gave an almost PvZ-like vibe, "Morizora's Cave" having chords reminscent of FFVI, and "Welcome to the Forest" giving a vibrant tonality to the main village, just to name a few.

Rakuen is an 8 hour or so rpgmaker style adventure developed by Laura Shigihara, best known for composing for Plants vs Zombies and To The Moon, the latter of which is what this game resembles most. Along the way, you explore dreamscapes and solve various puzzles (nothing too advanced), and if you're so inclined, find collectibles. As expected, the art and music are very well done, way above the standard rpgmaker fare. The writing succeeds at its sentimental melodrama, though some bits felt a bit heavy-handed, and the story is fairly straightforward/conventional fare, don't expect an Undertale surprise or anything. All things considered it was pretty charming.

This is, by far, the best VN I've ever played. Heartwrecking and gentle, it explores such heavy yet familiar to us all topics such as loneliness, abandoment and trust, struggle to be understood and accepted as we are, yet grow and be a better person.
There is really no cons here. The plot is simple, yet holds enough intrigue and depth to keep the reader engaged through all the routes, slowlly unravelling it's little detailes, the futher it goes. It also changes through the routes, so that you never really know what to expect from the next line, that appears on the screen. I also extremely enjoyed the writing itself. There is pretty much no mistakes, it is polished, smooth and pleasant, and you not even notice most of the time, how time flies by over reading.
The Best part for me was the heroine herself. If you, as I am, hate those hollow dummies, that exist only to serv as projections for the reader to emagine the romance Otome provides - well, you will be indeed pleased. Because here princess IS actual main hero, she has clearly defined personality, strengh and weaknesess, history, reasonable reasons for being who and how she is. And not lesser reasons to change, to grow and learn. She is consistent, deep and very real. Here relationships are not the only thing there is to know about her, yet they remain indefinetly important, just as for us our famylies, friends and loved ones.
About the latter... The guys are gorgeous, all of them. Really different from each other, and even though can be define by usual types as the genre intales, they surpass these stereotypes. Just as heroine, they have personality, there own demons (sometimes literally), there own path, which they follow with MC equally, not dragging her behind them as decoration and not dissapearing in her shadow.
And on top of it all, like the cherry on top of a cake, is overall art. Weirdly, my favourite part of it is interface and the chapters pages, along with ends. It is intricate and elegant, perfectly in synch with the rest of the art and the story itself.  The backgrounds are also beautiful, especially the forest, I honestly tried to just hide the interface a few times, simply to enjoy the picture.
Lastly, soundtrack is, as I think must be - is not annoying and not really notecable. As there is no voice acting, the tunes are there enough to not attract to much attention but highlight the story, and it is great. Also never noticed any breakes, music is perfectly looped.
Overall, I think deves should definetely charge for this truly amasing work they've done. Would've paid for the game in a heartbit, and I strongly urge everyone to just try and read it, because that expirience is absolutely worth it.

It's my honest and sincere belief that Civ4, when played with both its official expansions, is the perfect strategy game. I have a lot of trouble getting into most 4X games, even turn-based ones, but what I think makes this game far better, than, say, Galactic Civilizations 2, is that it's complex enough to give rise to various strategies, game styles and outcomes, but you're still presented with enough detail that you can look at your civilization, its cities and its individual units and find out exactly why they're unhappy, or unsuccessful, or unprofitable.
Games like Galactic Civilizations 2 hide the formulas that govern your civilization under the hood, and playing them ends up feeling more like SimCity than Risk or chess: you simply find yourself responding to events as they happen, without a clear understanding of how your actions will affect even your own civilization. Civ4 throws that sort of design out completely--it's detailed, but not ridiculously so (like, say Master of Orion 3, where you feel like you're playing a spreadsheet), and knowing that its design is good, it doesn't feel obligated to hide the details.

When I first saw Vagante, I thought that it would be "just another platformer with RPG/roguelike elements." I am sincerely glad that's not what happened.
Firstly, yes it's a rogue-like. Every floor is randomly generated, every weapon is different from every other weapon either in big or small ways. Even the consumables randomize every character, so the red scroll for your rogue game could be different for the one in your knight game. Some people do
like it when their basic items switch around, but for me it's somewhat refreshing (reminding me of Pixel Dungeon on mobile, actually).
Secondly, it's got progression. You don't have to play the same character every time you play, and I'm not just talking about the classes. Each class has a few different skills that you can level, and they can change the way you play drastically. Can't hit that thing flying above you? Put a couple points in the Sword skill and you'll be able to overhand-chop at it. Really need to boost one of your stats? Sink a point into it and enjoy the strength. And because of these skills, each class can play very differently.
Thirdly,
This game knows how to scratch the looting itch. Every single item you get has different enchantments
that affect the game in different ways. Anywhere from wall-grabbing to stronger arrow shots to even phasing through walls can be on your single piece of armor. There's a variety of different weapons that each have their own kind of "weight" to them, so to say. A sword does not swing like a club does not stab like a dagger does not chop like an axe, if you can process my line of thought. Add in the many kinds of wands and magic spells, and you will not hurt for loot-gathering (that is, until you hit the inventory cap).
This game also has some great music for traversing each area, but I won't go into too much detail on that.
And, as much as I like this game, I have to admit a few faults I've found. The controls are somewhat overcomplicated, but there's a tutorial to get you used to them, and in a few playthroughs you'll learn them pretty well. I've also found that, in each area, there's not the biggest variety of monsters. In the first area, you've got slimes, bats, and goblins. Those are what you're gonna see for the most part, besides the bosses that are placed in each room.
But, all in all this has been one of my favorite games since I grabbed it. I'd definitely recommend this game.

Before there were games like Pathfinder, there was but one big tabletop fantasy game that saw fit to rule them all- Dungeons and Dragons. Anybody who's ever looked at a d20 while cross-eyed has either at least heard of the game, knows someone who plays, or has rolled up a character and found themselves sitting at a table with a two-liter and a bag of cheese doodles. I'm one of the latter ones- I used to have a game night in college- not much any more though. But as far as properties upon Steam, well, there are two of them I pay attention to, and they're both MMO games- and both are free-to-play. Both of them have their ups and downs. In this one, I'm paying attention to the aptly-named Dungeons and Dragons Online.
There are a number of different kinds of MMO out there- there's the kinds that style themselves after WoW, with the open-world, the questing, the grouping up, the tradeskilling... D&DO isn't like that- instead, I liken it to a one-player game of D&D, where the game itself is your own, personal DM to run you through adventures of various length. Adventures are broken up into three lengths- short, medium, or long crawls. Each adventure has specific goals and offers chests full of loot for when you finish them, and the loot tables do not hold back. You won't just find a suit of plate armor, you'll find yourself a suit of plate that has five or six words describing its effectiveness and special abilities, and there are a lot of them out there.
Combat and mechanics are run using either the 3rd or 4th edition of D&D- you'll actually get to see the d20's result on the screen- and yes you can still get nat 20's and absolutely wreck stuff.
There aren't really that many downsides, but they ARE there- for example, if you're limited to solo play, some classes are going to get absolutely wrecked without careful planning and a few barrels of healing potion- most of your casting classes except for healing, for example. I'd recommend a fighter or priest for your first time through, just so you don't get frustrated. Most of your treasure will be sold and converted to healing potions over the course of the game, so don't get too attached to any specific item; you'll be drinking potions like cans of Pepsi.
There is an in-game premium store, but it doesn't take Steam funbucks to buy things- instead, you need to buy something called "Turbine Points" with a credit card or gift card and use those to buy adventure packs and other things. The really crappy thing is that if you don't buy them, you'll end up hitting a level limit, and be unable to progress. They've also hidden a number of options in Character Creation away behind paywalls- races, classes, Epic Destinies (stories tailored around a specific character archetype)- if you want to run something like a half-elf, or a druid, be prepared to fork over. I can understand that yeah, they have to make a profit, but still- really, guys? I'd make an exception if you could buy Turbine Points with Steambucks, but this just kind of irks me.
I think the first level limit is like 20 or 25 but I'm only at level 4 right now, though.
Some adventures are tailored for some classes and playstyles over others. There's an adventure in the second hub of the game that requires you to sneak around to steal a ruby from a bunch of kobolds. You are limited in the number of one type of enemy you can kill, and as it turns out, fighters in plate mail aren't all that good at not making noise, and you'll find yourself swarmed in no time unless you're using the right class.
Of special note is the fact that they managed to get Wil Wheaton to come in and DM an entire adventure pack. I haven't played through it, but to be honest, I kind of want to check it out.
All in all, I have to say that if you're looking for an old-fashioned game of D&D that gives you that feel of being at a table with somebody sitting behind a screen with a stack of adventures, ready to play as much or as little as you want at a time- this is the one you'll want to go for. If you're looking for something more in the vein of World of Warcraft, you'll want to check out my next review.
TL;DR: An MMO that feels like sitting at a tabletop playing your own personal game of D&D. I like that. 7/10.
