Bob made me think I was playing some 3D rendition of Super Meat Boy, which I don't hate.  In fact, I think I was hungry for this type of platforming for a while now.
It's a platformer that sticks to the retro roots, where it's very simple to play, you run, jump, and walljump, and the traps are old-school to the extreme, but Bob is definitely a horse of a different caliber, it's not where you just go from point A to B, it has pretty pronounced difficulty like the aforementioned indie hit.
Throwing this out, you know what I hate about kaizo/impossible grade games?  When you have to do pixel-perfect stunts for long stretches of time, obnoxious traps, and while graphics aren't everything, if your game has no character, no life of its own, don't expect me to care going through it.
Not so much here, this game barely had moments where it was tight as hell to being unfun, like yes it's very hard, I'm not denying that, but there were still some room to maneuver, the difficulty of the normal levels was fairly balanced.  It also helps that the levels are of short length and respawn you quickly after death.  It's weird to explain, but pop in a Kaizo Mario, where things quickly become miserable, and you might understand where I'm going with that analogy.
It even has a system of Normal and Hard levels, the latter being unlocked as you finish Normal levels with the condiment in hand, which often mean risking your neck to get to it.  The Hard levels really are on a whole different level though, it's a much harder rendition of the Normal ones, to the point that they're hardly recognizable.
There were times though where the foreground objects would obstruct my vision from seeing certain traps, especially on Hard, and the camera sometimes doesn't give the whole picture to work with.  Plus, spikes would blend in with the background.
To resume, if Super Meat Boy didn't win you over, you're not going to care about this one, however if you like difficult games that aren't completely baloney, and I know there's this annoying trend of hard platformers for the sake of being hard that are mostly trash, you'll at least spend a good time with Bob here.

A beautiful, unique fighting game that, for all its issues, is definitely worth checking out.
I've always really enjoyed fighting games, even though I've never been that great about them. Absolver is something special. It has a brilliant and unique "combat deck" fighting system, in which you collect new moves by playing against people that use them, and then repurpose them into a custom moveset that you can call your own. You can be mentored by other players and learn completely new fighting styles, or eventually grow your skill until you can start a school of your own. All of these things, plus a really cool setting and fluid, satisfying combat, make this one of my favorite games of the year.
I won't say it's perfect. It launched with some now-probably-notorious serious issues, and it required some serious persistence to really get into at the beginning. But the game itself just felt so darn good to play that I had a hard time putting it down, server issues or no. I also feel like I really wanted to know more about the story and the world: the little taste that they give you is just enough to make you want more.
It's decently content-light, but really fun while it lasts, and is staggeringly unique. It might not be for everyone, but I would definitely recommend it.
My nominee for the "Mom's Spaghetti" award, 2017.

This game is simple but fun and addictive. I found myself playing over and over for hours. Each time I died, I wanted to play again to see if I could get further. The randomly generated levels can get a bit repetitive, but you feel that much more accomplished as you make it deeper into the cave and new content is revealed.
The combat is also simple but fun. I only tried the Knight, but I found it entertaining to time my attacks and kill the little creatures that came after me. The one downfall is that the AI is relatively dumb. You can easily trick the smaller mobs to jump onto a trap, and even the boss/elite mob per level lacks a challange once you learn their several repeatative moves.
Leveling and character building is limited. You have several categories you can invest your points into, but you don't get many skill points to spend, so there's not much room for building your character. Of course-that's likely the point. The further into the Cave you get, the more powerful you'll become. The game simply requires patience to get there.
However, the best part of the game is definitely the randomly generated equipment you find scattered about. You have to identify everything. You can simply equip it right off in hopes you don't receive a cursed item, or find identifying scrolls for a much safer route. The only downfall to equipment (and this isn't important to many, but it is to me) is that your character's look doesn't change when you put on new armor. Again-probably not a big deal to some, but I tend to enjoy games more when my character's look changes like a virtual Barbi/Ken doll :-)
Overall-the game is fun and quite addictive. Keep in mind it's Early Access, so there's still much to come. For now... it's a solid game and well worth the price. I recommend using a controller to play, though.

While the artwork and game setting are very well thought out and portrayed, the longevity of Jamestown is its downfall. There are five campaign levels that must be beaten in Legendary difficulty in order for the player to advance. This difficulty level is appropriate for the first four levels, but on the fifth and final level, this design choice becomes a problem and a hindrance. The last level is so difficult, I consider it to be poorly designed and most importantly, inadequate. It is as if the designers realized they did not have much of a game in their hands, and decided to make the final fifth level nearly unbeatable, in order to excuse the amount of time necessary to complete the campaign. Sure, there are bonus modes/levels to be unlocked, but they are merely side distractions, that do not provide the player with additional entertainment or value. Jamestown is simply too short, in addition to one of its five levels being extremely poor. To add to this insult, the developers have released an expensive DLC for an already overpriced base game, that adds very little. The limited amount of continues is also another bad design choice because of the terrible last level. In the end, the player is left with a clear understanding that the developers resorted to a cheap and unimaginative means of prolonging Jamestown's lifespan by making it artificially and unusually difficult in the last level. Through this, it is very quick to realize that this game does not involve much, and the developers should be ashamed of themselves for charging so much for so little content. There are innumerable amounts of games of this same genre that are incomparably better, and most are more than 20 years older. Jamestown is a prime example of independent developers taking advantage of the scene and overcharging consumers for content that is extremely scarce, poorly implemented, and quite limited. There is very little to do, very little to experience, and very little to enjoy. Jamestown can be beaten in less than one hour, and there are many other games that have a much better value than this. What a waste.

I just started back at Mod 9 Update 29 and played few weeks and got really disapointed. The core mechanics of Dungeon and Dragon are no longer present. There is no longer the rule of 1d20 + attack bonus >= Armor Class. That was a simple rule and easy to understand.
Also now, monsters have ridiculours hp. More than 500 hp for normal mobs is not normal at level 14. For a boss once in a while ok, but really, its gotten out of hand. I prefered before when they had a good AC with a lot less hp.
There is also the guild airship. They can give you buffs, but now there is just too many that you dont care anymore (30+).
Also, even though enhancements (kind of feats) is fun (I used to love it because it adds some customization to the character) it became more powerful than taking a feat. It was really something when you actually take a feat (in most cases you have 7 to choose (for a level 20 char)). You have access to 80 enhancement points and for 1 point, you get 2 AC, etc.
2 AC is what you would get with an epic level feat (21+), not a level 1 character.
The more they update the game, the more they stray from the real dungeon and dragon.
While it still can be a fun game (I did not bother listing the positive and obvious negative such as the outdated graphics), it is shadowed by bad decisions by making it a greedy generic MMO that you would find anywhere.

So many bad reviews are from people who just don't understand how some of the mechanics work.
TL/DR - You'll need to put in 20+ hours to understand all that's happening and really appreciate how much this game has to offer. Go to the forums and ask questions, watch some Let's Play before buying.
Yes, this game is very hard at the start. Hell it doesn't so much have a difficulty curve as a difficulty wall built from the frustration, whining and grief of the people who smash against it.
This game won't hold your hand. It won't tell you everything. It won't show you all the mechanics in action.
It expects you to work some stuff out for yourself. A rarity nowadays in gaming.
BUT
If you persist. Not go rage quitting after a couple of hours, ranting that it's crap & un-fair and the RnG is rubbish, etc you'll find a rewarding unique experience, that I think is the best Games Worshop adaptation doing the rounds.
Yes, there's some DLC, but it's a small developement group that needs to generate funds, not some AAA title house.
You don't need the DLC to enjoy the game anyway, you get 4 warbands with the base game, 2 more through DLC and some DLC hired swords. Wait and pick them up on sale if you enjoy the game.
In summary, it's a game you really need to play for 20+ hours before you start to fully understand what's going on. But it is worth those hours, because 200+ hours into playing and there's still a lot I haven't done. Two of the original campaigns I've not started, two warbands I've not played at all.

It is pretty common to have one or maybe two out-of-action party members per match even when things are going well. And there is always the chance they end up perma-dead or with such a debilitating injury they become next to worthless.
Multiplayer is another matter, there will be players out there that can take your beloved warband to pieces. But you have the option to play in exhibition mode with no permanent repurcussions, but no rewards either. Or just have seperate relatively 'safe' SP and riskier MP warbands.
It's worth knowing that there is a veteran system letting you level up and keep bonuses to running your warband that carries over to the next even if they all end up dead. You even get to choose how you spend your earned bonuses for each warband. I've got 25 hours of fun out of this to date and I've only played with 2 of the warbands on offer so far.
More customisation options would be very welcome, it is hard to make your party members look individual, which is a shame. Another niggle is that the game always suggests a parry stance for my warriors that are better at dodging and vice-versa which gets tiresome after dozens of battles.

Overall still love the game. However, a few issues.
1. Stances. Percent to dodge and block should be automatic. Stance should increase the chance. Do no make my shield useless against an attack if I happen to not be in block stance.
2. Charge VS Ambush. Make the Ambush range reasonable, or the charge range reasonable, or for god's sake put indicators on the ground. I cannot count the number of times I've been approaching an enemy in "Ambush" stance, setting up for a charge, only to get ambushed, when I CAN CLEARLY SEE THEM! On the other hand, I can count the one hundred million times I've been in "Ambush" stance only to be charged by a computer player. Make it fair or f*ck right off.
3. Make the percentage the actual percentage. I wish I knew enough about programming to be able to read whatever code is going on in the background, but I seem to miss a lot more 70%, 80%, or even 95% chance to hit than I should. 7 misses in a f*cking row at 85% to hit isn't fair, and it isn't fun. This doesn't make the game more enjoyable when you do this, it just makes it unplayable.
I've already disbanded several games and deleted the saves because while progressive damage and even losing is fun, it's fun to lose when it's fair. If I go into a "difficult" or "punishing" mission, I expect to lose, or for it to be hard. If I go into an encounter and make multiple mistakes, I expect to lose. If I go into an "Average" mission and miss multiple attacks in the 80% hit chance, only to have the enemy counter, and fail to dodge/parry multiple attacks, and then get my whole warband wiped out because the enemy got 3 criticals and 2 of my guys fail their "all alone" saves, that's not expected, that's not fair, and that's not fun. Why do you guys do this with your games?

Fortress Forever is what I'd describe as "If Team Fortress 2 was good", and "Friendship Ruiner Mk II".
You've got updates that are semi-recent and add things to the game that are something to really experiment with (the latest example being that Pyro now has a jetpack).
The game may not have built-in bot support (which is a shame as I have only one or two friends that are willing to play this) but even 1v1's are intense and serious fun.
Not only that, but it's very well optimised for lower end computers. My friend runs this at around 100+ frames on a♥♥♥♥♥♥laptop with 4gb ram, 2.1ghz processor, 512mb VRAM APU, and an old hard drive that's completely filled with random crap.
On everything max, 1920x1080, 110 FoV, I get an average of 150 frames with a 1060 OC and an i5-6500. It's very well made!
The gameplay is tight and responsive. There have been a couple of times where I've been backstabbed from the front and front-sides with 50 ping, but apart from that, the hitreg and movement is very fluid and is intoxicatingly fun. I've ended up causing more damage in this than I have in Brawl.
This game also pertains moreso towards Team Fortress Classic, and thus does not bode well for heavy TF2 Veterans who are wanting to try something else.
Small changes to classes include:
-Scout is actually terrible (he is equipped with a shotgun that does like 2 damage if people have armour, he himself has little to no armour or health)
-Soldier has been slightly buffed (He now rocks two shotguns, one doing a lot more damage than the other)
-Pyro is almost impossible to stop in a 1v1 situation (He has a molotov, a jetpack, and a rocket launcher. He's a flying monster that thirsts for blood)
-Demoman is more similar to his TFC counterpart (being that the Stickybomb Launcher and Grenade Launcher share the same clip and ammo reserve, and that the DetPack is basically a CS:GO bomb that is plantable anywhere)
-Heavy is an intense counter to any class that is having too much fun (He can push anything away, and is equipped with a armour-shredding minigun, and a slowfield, which slows people down)
-Engineer is a stormtrooper (except he can actually hit his ♥♥♥♥ing shots, and his dispenser is one of the best hidden weapons in the game)
-Medic is a force to be reckoned with (he is only just slower than a scout) and can infect people (meaning they are poisoned for 20 seconds, which leaves them at 1hp)
-Sniper is stupidly powerful (It's the "Classic" from TF2, but it does even more damage and tags people, allowing people to see their health and position at a quick glance around)
-Spy is no longer able to run into danger, instead blessing players who are stealthy (your cloak is asimilar to the Cloak and Dagger [being the more you move, the easier it is to see] and your weapons are not very powerful... apart from the knife)
-The civilian... actually exists. Don't play him though, he's very weak.
TL;DR - Play this game if you're looking for a competitive, yet interestingly fun game to hone your skills at complaining and twitch-shooting. Just don't expect servers from areas that aren't in America. (Oceanic servers don't exist, although I'm not too sure about Europe/Asia servers)
...And don't expect rocket-jumping to come in as handy as TF2 made it. Having 50 armour will make you sustain another rocket jump, although having 50 health and 15 armour is an instant death.
The free Team Fortress Classic!

Ah, Sonic 4. A game loathed by many for its massive differences from the classic games it is trying to mimic. The physics don't work at all like the classic games, resulting in standing on ceilings and losing all of your forward momentum because you thought holding down while hitting a curve would gain you a bunch more speed. The air-dash is present, and for some sections, it is actually NECESSARY to use it, which usually kills off either your momentum, as air-dashing will cancel forward momentum, or you, as you go speeding under it into the abyss below.
The special stages combine the old Sonic 1 special stages with manual controls, and impassable gates that only open when you have enough rings. Combine all this with a background akin to a psychedelic trip, and you've got Sonic 4's special stages.
All the stages in this game are rehashes of old stages from the classics with a fresh new coat of paint. Splash Hill Zone is obviously Green Hill Zone from Sonic 1, Casino Street Zone is Casino Night Zone from Sonic 2, Lost Labyrinth... use your imagination, Mad Gear is Metropolis Zone from Sonic 2, and E.G.G. Station is Death Egg Zone from both games. Of course, these stages have new gimmicks and decorations to make them look nicer, and indeed, they will certainly take your mind off of the inaccuracies for a while. It would have been nice to see some new stages though, for a game titled Sonic 4.
Sonic 4, Episode II is quite a bit better than this one. It has somewhat fixed physics, new levels, and TAILS. Plus, if you have both games, you get to play the Episode Metal, which is a short, story-related episode showing Metal Sonic's return from Stardust Speedway from Sonic CD. This gives you one act from every zone of this game, with the fixed physics of Episode II.
I'm not saying this is a terrible game, but it really isn't worthy of being called "Sonic 4", as it isn't close to the other games at ALL. If you want a true classic experience, you have a couple options. Sega offers emulations of Sonic 1, 2, 3 and Knuckles on Steam, all for cheap prices. You can also buy Sonic CD, which is a much better version of the SegaCD title, or get on your phone/Android emulator and get remakes of Sonic 1/2, all made by the fantastic Christian Whitehead. On the topic of Christian Whitehead, you can also wait for Sonic Mania, which should be coming out in April of 2017.
I received this game as part of a Humble Bundle, so I'm not complaining, as I got many other good games with it (such as Sonic Generations), but if you are going to buy a Sonic game individually, get Episode II. I believe you will have a much better experience with it than this game.

Savant - Ascent is a 2D twin stick shooter developed by small indie dev team D-Pad Studios. The game was made using GameMaker and won the GameMaker GOTY award for 2013, it also won Gullstikka Norwegian GOTY 2014. It’s got much replay value with beating previous high-scores and attempting to be ranked in the leaderboards. It is based on real-life EDM artist Savant (Aleksander Vinter), who also provides the soundtrack straight from some of his albums. Savant - Ascent is available on Steam, Google Play, and the App Store.
Shooting and dodging are the game's main gameplay mechanics. The player shoots a burst of bullets before the shots become rapid-fire, dodging and taking down mobs also builds up energy that make your shots stronger. When enough energy is collected the player can shoot a powerful shot that mostly one-hit-kills enemies.
There is a variety of enemies in the game, ranging from small ones with different amounts of mechanics to big worm-like enemies with destroyable sections. There is also boss battles, which are challenging if the player fails to notice patterns and are careless. The enemies come in hordes, and if they’re not picked off in the order they spawn then you may have some crowd control to deal with, the burst shots help a lot with that. Throughout the whole game there are CD fragments, four of which form one full CD. CDs unlock more songs on the soundtrack and also unlock different abilities and buffs for the player.
There’s Story Mode, Endless Mode, and a Time Attack mode. You unlock latter two modes by beating the Story Mode. In endless you can try and beat your highscore and also rank high on the leaderboards; same with the timed mode, you can try to beat your time and rank high on the leaderboards. Good old arcade-style gameplay model, which give the game a high replay value.
For this game he chose most songs from his dubstep-sounding albums: Alchemist, Cult, ISM, Ninur, Orakel, Vario, and Overkill. Not including the musical scores made specifically for the game.
All in All Savant - Ascent  is a really nice Action Game!

The mother of them all... the orginal, start and birthplace of fantasy games...Dungeons & Dragons. I remember playing this in my uncles basement, rolling die and imagining the beholders and kabolds. Now, I just click click to make a halfling rogue in 2 minutes, then makeing the same character sheet in 30. Times have changed. With free to play abilities D&D is a great game to play. Start from choosing class and race and a rather very in depth face creation hub and your off.  Start with a races human, halfling, elf, dwarf, half -elf, half -orc, warforged with the classes rogue, ranger, artificer, warlock, sorceror, paliden, fighter, barbarian, mage. With a straight foward ''quests lead to a dungeon'' and beat the dungeons with plenty of trainers and merchants around the game. It isn't very difficult to get the hang of. Like its tabletop version, you are pretty much an adventurer off to clear dungeons looking for epic loot. The quests and coupled dungeons do sometimes have a rather good sence of humor to it witch makes for a good read and laugh. The aspect of booby traps and puzzles within the game, in witch you need to use ''example'' my rogues search or disable trap abilities, was rather fun and challanging. The free to play aspect though does get limited as in higher levels you need to unlock along with dungeon/quests of that level. That makes for a lot of stuck between levels grinding for free to play players. Then just getting stuck. Is it a good run until then? YES  but, then the DLC is kinda needed. The graphics are decent with an oldschool feel to it where you can even  change the color of your dice and hubs for custimization. The music is spot on also to what you would expect of the fantasy world and areas. For the nostalgic and those that dont mind throwing some money at to progress.

Discloser: look at my played hours, look at my XCOM1/2, Darkest Dungeon, etc. hours, this is not a rage review. I like difficulty when well designed.
The bad:
. Game has really bad AI. Devs compensate by giving enemy over the top bonuses and say "game is meant to be hard". No, hard games are achieved by good AI not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t bonus/penalties.

You can choose how you level up the skills and abilities of your units but you have to pray to the dice gods to land that sweet 2H sword (which may never happen in extreme situations). No need to explain why this is bad in RNG games, 40 hours of gameplay gone on some bad rolls, or worse due to a bug which this game has quite a few (lost an entire party due to a dmg curse that should last one turn but was bugged so it just kept going until everyone was dead). It is a single player game! I will never understand why would you screw over a player by not letting them enjoy the game their way, when they play it alone and only for themselves! So there are a few things to say about Mordheim. It's a very challenging game for starters. I will say right off the bat to do the tutorials. At least the combat ones. I think I'm decent at X-COM, heard this was similar, and thought those skills would transfer. Hoo was I wrong. If you go in expecting a "Fantasy X-COM" you'll be in for a rude awakening. It's one of the more comparable games out there, but there are still plenty of differences.
The focus is very much on melee in Mordheim. There are ranged units, but pretty much every unit you have will be in melee at some point in their life. The RNG is also much closer to "random". I've had units miss 95% shots/attacks before, but I've seen the AI get just as unlucky. There doesn't seem to be a boost to the rolls for either side from what I can tell. The randomness extends to the injury rolls after combat as well. When a unit is defeated during the mission it isn't instant death luckily. After the mission is over those units roll on the injury table. They can roll a decent variety of injuries, such as missing arms, legs, eye, mental damage, or death. They can also end up fine or with minor injuries, so you aren't guaranteed to have crippled troops, at least not initially.
There is also much less story than I thought there would be. I enjoy the character and warband building/personalization of the game enough to not mind a lack of story. Something to keep in mind if you expect an epic tale, or even a story that further dives into why you're there, how it affects the area or world, etc. The meat of the game is in doing missions to gather resources and level up. Nothing super exciting, but I find the gameplay and warband building enjoyable enough to make up for it.
My favorite aspect of warband building is just how much you can go into it. Each unit has levels, your warband has levels, and you yourself have levels through the veteran system. The veteran system is one of the ways each successive warband you create gets stronger. As you accomplish tasks you'll gain veteran xp. Gain enough and it will increase your veteran rank which gives you a skill point, as well as benefits to buying/selling, and benefits when you create a new warband.
In all I recommend Mordheim to anyone that enjoys tactical games that are truly challenging, as well as anyone that enjoys the Warhammer setting. If you enjoy both, then you should already own this!

I like this game a whole bunch.  Rochard is a 2D physics-based puzzle-solving and combat game.  Nothing it's doing is entirely novel, but gameplay feels good and does a good job of co-opting Half-Life 2's gravity gun while mixing it with variable environmental gravity levels.  The weapons that you eventually acquire are satisfying, but combat is at its best when you use objects and enemies' weapons against them instead of attacking directly.  Likewise, puzzles are fairly straightforward but will sometimes surprise you.  There are a fair few very memorable moments throughout the game.
The whole experience  is imbued with some pretty decent personality and humor; you've seen better characters and more comical narratives, but what's here certainly helps the game to stand out.  It's also filled with beautiful, atmospheric environments and scored with a gorgeous and diverse soundtrack.  Rochard is pretty delightful for its entire 6-odd hours; I definitely recommend it.

This is one of the few games that I loved very hard from drawing phase to art design to sound design, but it ultimately died from a lack of singleplayer content and good, long-living content like proper matchmaking, proper servers, and proper goals [Quests, set arenas, set rulesets] and I can only imagine if this game had a proper story that wasn't 2 hours long, and had far more questings / secrets ala Dark Souls or Borderlands, even Pokemon, it would have had more long term success; but ultimately, it's just another fighting game that failed to grab itself a solid market.
~  GAMEPLAY  ~
Absolver is the weird hybrid of good, 3D fighting games and Catch-Em-All style of games where you have to run around grabbing / learning tons of new stuff.  The fighting itself is somewhat simplistic and ultimately feels very large.  You can make your own deck of moves with all these special things with them: You can also learn enemy moves and then use them to a greater effect or with greater decks.  I did find myself being a tad bit annoyed however with the lack of direction when you build a deck.  I had to try the same idea for a deck 4 - 6 times before I just googled what I would need to do to build a proper deck that actually works and doesn't just look cool, since looking cool decks get you just straight murdered.
And that opens up one of the biggest faults in the gameplay: Decks that are good are often times broken good, with only a few possible combinations of the huge variety of skills being even remotely viable.  And you won't even know what / how to counter certain things simply because the game doesn't give that great of feedback on what you are doing wrong.
Then you have this nice, lush open world filled to the brim with enemies, some ridiculously strong and some pretty easy, ultimately acting as level up punching bags.  But there's a big issue here too: Absolver is absolutely built for single combat primarily, and all of the mobs tend to swarm you at 2 - 4 at a time, even sometimes hitting 6 or 8 enemies if you get unlucky.  Now in other games where you can be easily outnumbered, you could poke / prod an enemy with ranged combat so you get a fair fight, but not here in Absolver!  Your ninja guy refuses to do anything ranged, including picking up a rock, even swearing profanities at the one guy you want to fight is simply impossible.  This problem continues to build up in every area to a huge degree of annoyance.  You ultimately die, not becaues the NPC beat you, but because the NPC's simply had 4 of them with high level moves on one of you, and waiting to fight you is simply too hard.
Then you get into the other bad part which is the somewhat unscripted nature of leveling, deck building, "Questing" and exploration.  It's nice to not have a story in a game for once, but more than a couple of times in my 10 hours of playtime I simply got lost beyond recognition because of the lack of a map.  Then I'd run around the same mob camps only to find the door I needed was in a part of the map I simply overlooked because of how hidden it was.  Well whatever, getting lost got me some XP, so let's level up, and that's where you hit another wall: What the hell does everything I'm leveling up do beyond just the basic flavor text?  The game never quite explains that you can level up indivual styles of moves ontop of your regular stats, for instance, you can increase the strong moves or the quick moves so they work better and go faster, but it didn't occur to me till my 8th hour of play, making it far too late to make a realistic build.  A patch added the ability to reset your skill points, but it still was annoying.  The deck building was covered already, but you have to find several special people who do special stuff, murder them, in order to get to the last boss and murder her.  It's relatively simple, but the game ultimately ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed because once you murdered the 2 bosses [Yes, 2 bosses] and the 4 minibosses they either don't show up or don't give you enough of anything to do anything solo.
The other issues is the fact that this game is P2P, which means that you may sometimes win matches because your opponent can't walk forward, and you may sometimes lose matches because the block you needed doesn't happen for 20 seconds at a time.  A lack of singleplayer content and a multiplayer crowd leaves a lot to be desired.
~  Graphics & Sound  ~
Absolver is painfully pretty and the sound is mediocre, but still good for what it needs to do.  The game looks like any number of somewhat new age low poly games which is a style I dig, and Absolver's use of weird masks and kung fu attire set in super natural, sometimes apocalyptic places makes the game feel even stronger.  Every move looks cool except for the good ones, since they usually don't have time to look cool, and all the gear looks cool with the raw exception of 2 pieces I found in my adventures.
What's nicer is that there are slight varients of all the armor pieces, so if you find one shirt it may be different than another, and another.  It's really cool seeing the same "Core" piece but different colors, wears and tears.  Although, it is never quite clear if the same piece has different stats, but once you find out it does it puts a big damper on your cool dress up minigame.
~ SUMMARY ~
While I loved my time in absolver, I couldn't stand the fact that there wasn't a lot of hand holding, even for the most basic things like a proper HUD or guidance of any kind.  The nail in the coffin is the fact that the game is below 100 players currently and there is practically no reason to try and dive into the singleplayer because it only lasts you 3 hours if you are bad like me.

In terms of actual gameplay, this ranks as my favorite Resident Evil game.
It might take some getting used to, it might feel a bit clunky at first, and it has a certain element that's annoying at times (I'm looking at you, Ashley), but it's so, so worth it. It's one of my favorite games of all time and it's just a blast to play.
Part of the game revolves around escorting a character called Ashley, so if you really hate that type of thing, you should know that right off the bat. It does get annoying at times. However, the game does cut you some slack here and there and it's not so difficult that you'll struggle all the time or anything, but it is worth mentioning for those who absolutely hate babysitting an NPC.
Ultimately, this game was the one that broke the mold and bridged the gap between pure survival horror and more shooty-tooty action horror type stuff - some of the things that illustrate this is the inventory management and the fact that you can't move and shoot at the same time, which adds to the tension and you can't just pick up every single thing you find. Resident Evil 4 (Ultimate HD Edition) is an influental part in the RE franchise with which the series took a step towards action, while skipping the often bothersome and goofy puzzles of the classic episodes. The horror is still present despite changing the fixed camera angle view to over-the-shoulder third-person perspective. By doing so, fighting became more intense and while some people may think otherwise, I believe this shift made the RE series even better.
The main protagonist of Resident Evil 4 is Leon S. Kennedy (the cop from RE 2 - now a special agent) who is searching for Ashley,  the kidnapped daughter of the President of the United States in rural Spain. After finding the girl, Leon discovers a plan of a local cult trying to infiltrate the US government using an ancient parasitic species to manipulate and control people...
Besides appearance, RE 4 is different from the previous episodes in many ways. First of all we control the main character from an over-the-shoulder view, which was revolutionary in 2005, when the game was released. As a matter of fact this was the first game that introduced this perspective, making it popular ever since (think of Dead Space). Its resourcefulness is evident from the start: altough we are still immobile while fighting, we can now freely aim, using the mouse and switch between enemies regardless their distance from us. This allows us to handle multiple enemies at once which we'll need since the game prefers to throw many of them at us at once.
The second thing is the storyline: while not very complex, it's so full of surprises right till the very end there's hardly any dull moment and will definitely keep us on our toes. The characters - for the first time in a RE game - have personalities (altough Leon's behaviour seems inconsistent at times) and we also get to hear deliberately (!) funny dialogues between them (apparently the cultural differences in humor between Japan and Europe/US have been ironed out this time),
Adventure elements are still present, there are puzzles to be solved but not as many and time-consuming as there were before and quest related items won't take up important inventory space anymore. There are plenty of traps instead and quick time events which can even appear during cutscenes (yes, we CAN die during cutscenes).
The typewriters remained (along with the herbs) but we no longer need ink ribbons to save, backtracking is required though to use them again as they are quite scarce.
There's additional content too: we can play through 2 additional side campaigns with Ada from RE 2
and there's a game mode called mercenaries in which we earn points by killing enemies (preferrably in quick succession) within a given time (and stay alive of course). By completing it we can unlock the game's most powerful weapon: the hand cannon.
Thirdly, there are no zombies in RE 4, at least not by conventional means. Mostly we fight humans, but these knife/pitchfork/axe/scythe-wielding villagers and cultist are more frightening and unsettling than the undead from the classic episodes. Fighting the brute(s) from Texas Chainsaw Massacre or the giant lake monster are both memorable moments. And this time, Umbrella is only tangentially involved.
On the fourth place, there's money (peseta accordingly) with which we can buy a variety of weapons and upgrades from shady traders. This feature also makes the optional replays more interesting as we can experiment with various weapons, discovering which suits our style the best. Even the weakest weapons receive an exclusive boost after upgrading them to the max, so it's not always advised to sell our old guns.
We are still unable to buy ammunition though, so saving it and firing considerately is recommended as we can quicky find ourselves standing in front of a boss with no ammo. It's important to mention that whenever we purchase an ammo capacity increasing upgrade, the given gun will be fully reloaded and this can save our lives, so take this into account.
On a side note: weapons can't be reloaded in the inventory screen anymore (which felt like cheating anyway :)).
Grenades are a new addition and are very useful: they are extremely powerful and all 3 of them are effective against different types of enemies. While the flash grenades may seem useless at first, they do come handy against ranged enemies and can also instantly kill those pesky plagas.
Our trusty knife has also been improved, it became quite powerful (as opposed to previous RE episodes) and can even be used against bosses effectively. Its use (especially against downed combatants) is mandatory.
Leon has special moves this time: the roundhouse kick and the suplex can both be performed against disoriented or stunned enemies. The kick is perfect to make some space around us when surrounded by enemies and the suplex is a usually fatal move. While performing these, Leon is invincible, so use them often.
Hitboxes are well placed and headshots aren't always recommended as shooting foes in the knee (thus forcing them to kneel for a suplex) can be more rewarding, not to mention other nasty surprises followed by a wrongfully placed headshot...
The controls as good as they may seem, aren't without major flaws. First of all, Leon is immobile while aiming and releasing the mouse button does not let us move immediately. The second problem is the absence of the autorun function (we do need to run all the time), so that means we'll have to keep a finger constantly on the Shift button (needless to say that it limits our mobility using WASD). While holding Shift we can't use quickturn either: we'll have to let it go for a brief moment (there seems to be a slight delay here too). And thirdly the layout of the quick time event buttons (X and C) cannot be changed.
So it will take plenty of time to practice, but even then, we'll never be able to perform such fluid and quick moves as in Dead Space.
There are bugs in the game, sadly. I noticed that having full health at QTE  events (where we have to tap a button repeatedly) is compulsory, but sometimes the game glitched and I automatically failed regardless (the event never appeared and I was shown the death animation). Only quitting the game and launching it again solved this.
Another QTE glitch is related to boss fights where we can still get hit by an attack depending on where we stand.
Some of these bosses have 'invincible' animations (much like Leon's kick) when they can't be hurt and one must recognize these in order to avoid wasting ammo.
The graphical update is one of the main features of this PC version but I didn't notice that much improvement over the 2005 original. The character models look sharp and some of the environments as well, but there are some outright ugly textures especially towards the end. The rural and castle areas seem nice but apparently the quality from there took a hit. It's hard to understand why they replaced some textures while leaving others on console quality.
The cutscenes however are top quality, but not in Ada's campaigns: for some reason they are extremely compressed and look terrible (even the ones reused from Leon's).
The music is suspenseful and the sound effects are well made. The voice acting is great and the murmurs of the villagers and whispers of the cultist are equally scary.
It's hard not to love Resident Evil 4: despite its numerous faults, the improvements easily outweigh the negatives and the result is a great game recommended to any horror- and action game lover.
PROS
+ action oriented over-the-shoulder view
+ great atmosphere and locations
+ variety of weapons and bosses
+ excellent voice acting
+ additional game modes
CONS
- messed up controls despite the mouse support
- not much change in the graphics
- some bugs
RATING
8.5/10

Jamestown is an extremely solid shmup, with one really fantastic advantage over other shmups.
As a single player game, it doesn't match the classics it takes inspiration from. The bullet patterns and level designs are solid but also a bit bland and lacking in strategic variety. It's good, but not great.
Where it really shines is multiplayer, as unlike the tacked on co op of your average Cave game, Jamestown's mechanics and gameplay were finely balanced around co op from the start. It's probably the best co op shmup ever made, and that's definitely something to brag about.
It also has one of the best and most creative settings and aesthetics for a shmup outside of a Cave game. The theme, music, pixel art, and setting are excellent.
If you don't have anyone to play with (local multiplayer only), than Jamestown is a decent shmup that should probably be somewhere in the middle of your wishlist compared to some of the other excellent PC shmups out there. However, if you have some friends to play with, it's an absolute must buy.

This game is proof that Team Sonic has no idea what they're doing, and likely never did.
The Sonic the Hedgehog franchise is an anomaly of gaming. It has a rabidly devoted fanbase with fanfiction, fan characters, and rule 34 out the wazoo. This makes it all the more baffling that the creators and developers have no idea how to design a good game in the first place.
The levels in STH4E1 play like something created by a computer algorithm. The set pieces are stitched together at complete random with no sense of flow or theme to the levels. One minute you're playing a pinball game, the next you're being crushed by barrels. Some pits kill you instantly, others lead to rewards. Missing some jumps will just cause you to have to take a lower path, others mean certain death, and still others mean having to backtrack and figure out the puzzle yet again. There is no consistency and no way to predict what will happen when you interact with a particular gadget. Bumpers and springs will launch Sonic different heights with no visual indication of what they're capable of. This is a game that not only punishes the player for being not psychic, but also blames the player for their lack of precognitive powers.
Despite how easy it is to die from complete cheapness, the whole game is designed around set pieces that look entertaining, and provide a small burst of enjoyment, but lack any kind of nuance or challenge. Casino Street zone is probably the biggest offender in this regard, doling out extra points, flashy lights, and sparkly bumpers in a pathetic attempt to trick the player into thinking they're playing a good game. This zone contains so many extra lives and free rings, you can practically see the developers going "Love us, please! We'll give you candy!" But they decided to mix a few razor blades in there, because otherwise it would be too easy to enjoy. It's the equivalent of opening your presents on Christmas morning, but your parents decided to randomly put a few boxes filled with millions of spiders under the tree, just so you don't get too cocky and think it's all supposed to be about having fun.
But the real kicker here: This is actually a perfect representation of a Sonic game. Every Sonic the Hedgehog game, with the possible exception of the first two, has been like this. Levels with seemingly random design, enemies that come out of nowhere and punish the player for not being psychic, puzzles that are never explained but nonetheless are required to get through the level. (The Barrel from Sonic 3, anybody?) Intermixed with short bursts of eye candy that's supposed to fool the player into enjoying themselves. It's basically tickle torture.
If you like the previous Sonic games, you'll probably love this, because it's exactly what Sonic is, apparently. It's not good, no. But at least it's accurate.

My favorite MMORPG out of all I've played.
A large portion of this is the extent to which it encourages cooperation with other players. In other MMOs I have played, I've just ended up wandering through the starting area doing quests, never feeling the need to party with other players. In Dungeons & Dragons Online (DDO), if you want to complete the dungeons on the highest difficulty setting, having other players around is a great boon. Traps alone can give many adventurers a lot of trouble, and having(or being) a player that can disable them makes them a valuable member of a party. And, while many experienced players have ways of keeping themselves alive regardless of class, everyone appreciates a good healer.
I also love the high level of customization available in DDO. You have the option to set your own ability scores (STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, and CHA), allocate your own skills (Search and Disable Device are paramount for trappers, while Jump is more generally useful), and choose your own feats, including fighting styles such as Two-Handed, Two Weapon(including "unarmed" combat), Single Weapon, and Shield Mastery. Casters have the option of taking metamagic feats such as Maximize and Empower to increase the destructive(or healing) power of their spells, or Heighten and the various Spell Focuses to make them harder to resist (especially useful for instant kill spells and Crowd Control).
A less desirable feature to many players may be that the game is heavily instanced. There aren't many vast areas to explore; many quest entrances are accessed directly from town, and each party will be in a separate instance of each quest or wilderness zone. While I feel that this was necessary to encourage cooperation to the extent that they have, I can understand players who may think this makes the world feel smaller.
Also, a large portion of the game is behind P2P bars, despite the game itself being Free to Play. You CAN earn Turbine Points in-game and unlock the content of the game without spending a cent, but I have heard that it is better to consider the game a subscription-based game with a limited free trial than a truly free to play game, and I can appreciate that standpoint. If you start playing the game without unlocking any content, you can feel the P2P walls start closing in on you, starting especially around level 6-8 (level cap is 30, so this is higher than it sounds compared to other games).
That said, I feel that the pros outweigh the cons for this game; feel free to jump in for free, and see how well you like it before commiting to paying for anything, and I definitely recommend waiting for sales before purchasing Adventure Packs to make the most out of your Turbine Points.

This is my first visual novel that I've read on Steam at the least and I'm happy to say that this was fantastic. You may find this odd, but this will be coming from a guy (I'm assuming the Visual Novel is targeting girls so I just felt the need to point this out).
Story: I'm a fantasy man. I've read the first two books in A Song of Ice and Fire so far and I'm currently reading The Wheel of Time series. I enjoy a good fantasy story. When I saw that this story was set in a secondary world with a twist on traditional fairy tales, I had to see the novel for myself. I don't know if this helps anyone but if you like the Kingdom Hearts series and how they play Disney Princesses and old fairy tales, and a little bit of romance in genreral, you'd like this.
Characters:
Let's start with the Main Character (I'll be calling her Lucette but the game allows you to name her whatever you want). Some may find her personality in the beginning of the novel annoying or irritating but it serves an obvious purpose since it stems from her past and how she was raised. She is a layered character with flaws and a somewhat dark past. I really enjoyed how the novel developed her. She's rather confident and vocal--a nice change of pace from what I usually recieve which are boring, tasteless, one-dimensional MCs who I honestly do not care for. For once, the MC isn't completely incompetent. I cared for Lucette and wanted to see this character go through this trial that she has to undertake. Also, her character design is absolutely gorgeous, and the novel does well to show her emotions and expressions.
Now, I've only played through Rumpel's route in the story, so I really am in no position to critique the other love interest's personalities, but from what interactions I've seen in my first playthrough, they've peaked my interest enough that I want to play through their route, except for Rod, and not because I don't like him or his character, but I saw the step-brother as something more platonic than romantic (That's just me). As stated previously, I've finished Rumpel's route, both good and bad ending, and I enjoyed it very much. I am curious to see the other gents!
Music -- The soundtrack did well to emphasize a moment in the story whenever it was appropriate. The Main Theme is very enjoyable as well!
Art -- The art style is different from what I'm used to but this wasn't bad in this case. I very much liked the art style, both the design of its characters and the background art too. The only criticism I have is when a character zooms in on the screen, they do look a little blurry and perhaps needs some adjusting. Now this is just me, but I would have liked to have seen some differences or variation in the five main love interests' design. Don't get me wrong, I'm all for pretty boys (I am a seme after all) but having some more 'masculine' or 'macho' looking gentlemen wouldn't have been a bad thing. This is probably my own criticism of Anime-style art and not just this Visual Novel specifically. Other than that, the visuals are beautiful.
Other Criticisms: This might be a major negative for some people, but this Visual Novel does not have voice acting in it. I found it to be no bother personally even though I've grown accustomed to hearing voiced characters. Though I would have liked to seen some voice acting in this, it's still great without it. I don't know any specifics, and I'm assuming, but since this is a free Visual Novel and the developers and creators aren't recieving money from a purchase, I can understand why they'd want to go without voice actors.
This was definitely the most enjoyable Visual Novel I've read in a long time. I hope to read more from these developers and creators!

This game caught my eye a couple of weeks ago, and wanted to give a closer look, despite it being early access and not yet finished. For what it is so far, it's pretty damn good and shows plenty of potential at the stage it's at right now. I've already gotten over 20 hours into it. So I'll go ahead and just list the pros and cons and discuss certain points in further detail...
Pros:
------
+ Concise/Tight controls
+ Streamlined GUI
+ Good Art Design
+ Ambient Music and Good Atmosphere
+ Great variety of Items & Status Effects
+ Difficult and Rewarding Gameplay
+ Great Developer Involvment & Tech Support
Cons
------
- Lots of Multiplayer Bugs
- Level Generation can be Repetitive
- Occasionally frustrating and unfair deaths
- Leveling System is too stringent and one sided
- Lack of Story
=========================================
+ Good Art Design/ Great Atmosphere
One of the biggest reasons why I got this game was the atmosphere and art design. It's very well made and draws you into the game which is accompanied by a great ambient soundtrack. The sound design itself is very tactile and satisfying as well. Feels good everytime you pick up coins, items, and unlock treasure chests which can help keep the player motivated and engrossed.
+ Difficult and Rewarding Gameplay
This game is ridiculously difficult, I've yet to even get to the final area (There's only 4 main areas of the game) let alone complete it. However, it's very rewarding. You have to be very precatious and slow when trecking through the dungeons, learning to manage your resources along the way. For the most part, deaths are pretty fair and can be blamed on just being careless. Even when I get far into the game and end up dying, it's very satisfying just to see what items and weapons I managed to get along the way, and generally doesn't bother me when I have to go all the way back.
+ Great Developer Involvment & Tech Support
What I found the most suprising was how helpful and receptive the developers are for this game, especially it being an early access game where most people tend to just abandon their projects. They seems to really care about their game and are regularly updating and patching the game to make it better. I experienced a graphical error early on in one of the updates. However, they were very quick to respond and fixed the problem the same night. More early access games need this kind of dedication to take off.
- Online Multiplayer
Although I'm sure they're very busy working on making the multiplayer work, it still is a very glaring issue with the game. There are quite a lot of bugs that are very distracting and in some cases make it unplayable. Which is a shame because if it did work properly, this game would be abosuletly amazing to play with a group of friends. At least for the moment, the multiplayer is pretty much unplayable.
- Level Generation can be Repetitive
For a roguelite, the level generation is a bit scarce and repetitive. When you start playing it for a while, and go back to the first area (Trust me... you're going to be there a lot, get comfy) you start to notice the algorythyms of the levels and can generally know what's around the corner without too much trouble. This can make things a little less painless going through the first level, but at the same time can get a little bit boring and predictable.
- Leveling System is too Stringent and One-Sided
Probably one of the most annoying for me personally is the way the leveling system works. Basically you can level up one of two ways. You can either kill the boss thats on every floor in the game which automatically levels you up, or you can get XP by killing a bunch of normal enemies. However, the problem with this is that you can only level up ONCE per floor which is quite frustrating in my opinion and can limit your experimentation with different stats and perks. The stats you can lvl up are either class related, or straight up stats like str, mag, luck, etc. However there isn't much use in lvl'ing up anything besides a couple class related stats. I would personally get rid of lvl'ing up raw stats since you tend to get a lot of gear and weapons that boost your stats anyways.
OVERALL:  8.0/10.0
-----------
All in all, I think it's a pretty fun game that has a lot of potential in the future. The developers regularly work on it and update it. I would definately recommend getting this game. However if you're apprehensive about getting it, nothing wrong with waiting until this goes on sale. So if you like roguelites, or just hard games in general, definately look out for it!

Stage 1 Caves: This is your tutorial of the game, it's mechanics, and with some fairly easy bosses to make you feel good about yourself. If you value your life and valuables I suggest not going into the ruins, you're going to have a bad time.
Stage 2 Forest: Ok, you're doing good you got past the easy part. The forest isn't bad except for the bowman shooting you, the golems with large hp and heavy hits, the birds that throw knifes, and the maneating plants (those f**king maneating plants). The bosses seem overwelming at first but after some deaths you learn their patterns and the best approach assuming you have reasonable equipment.
Stage 3 Catacombs: Awesome you made it to the catcombs, if you thought the caves very claustrophobic then you'll love this place. First off, prepare to die many times. The catcombs are not your friend nor will it ever be. It's not a fun place, if you don't have the right items to make things easier or have the ability to dodge everything and run. Chances are that place will be your catacombs. If you get molested by giant hands don't say we didn't warn you. Now then, the bosses. IF you are not totally insane or you're confident in your skill and equipment you can try the bosses. One of them you can most likely beat. Another will take some time and good dodge skills. The last one you will most likely die, he hits hard and is scary head to toe, not to mention moves fast. But don't bite off more then you can chew because once you reach the catacombs you really get the sense that you'll do anything to survive because you don't want to do everything over again.
Stage 4 The Rift: For completing your periless journey through the catacombs you are rewarded to a beautiful scenery and music. That's pretty much all the reward you'll receive. The enemies are designed to kill you shortly but the biggest obstacle is the fact you're on mini f**king islands that have teleportation doors that need time to charge the first time you use them. But those things are the little concerns you have to deal with. just pray you don't land on an island with the boss. If you are one of those people who needs to fight every boss God Speed you suicidal maniac. 9/10 times you will die in this place, at least you die in the floating sky. But, this is either the hardest stage or the easiest, if you have one item you can complete The Rift will hardly any trouble. But that is up to chance and fate to decide if you obtain it.
End: You reach the end and are rewarded with overhead text that comends your efforts, then you go to new game+ and do it again.
10.1/10 would die countless time to see that ending text again. It's so beautifully written...
Good luck, don't die

Savant - Ascent is a hi-octane, adrenalin-pumping, lightning-fast 2D bullet hell. I'm normally a plodding puzzle game player so this was quite a shock to the system. My poor nerves are still jangling.
You control a masked Guy Fawkes-esque character with a purple cape on a central platform with only two positions, left and right. You dodge and jump from side to side avoiding enemies coming at you from 360 degrees, shooting at them round the clock with unlimited ammo. One certain type of high-hitpoint enemy drops quarter sections of CDs which you collect by flinging your chain-grabber out, and at this point the action is frozen for one second. It doesn't sound like much but it gives you enough of a pause to target the next enemy.
After each 3-life death, of which there are many, the parts you've collected are pieced together and a whole CD awards you a powerup and a new song. You're resurrected at the start of the level you were at with your new abilities allowing you to hopefully progress further than last time. At a certain point you ascend to the next level (of 5) with ever harder, faster, more numerous enemies, culminating in a boss. I'm embarrassed to say I'm still struggling on level 4, it's bonkers! Please don't look at my hrs on record.
After level 3 Time Attack and Endless modes are unlocked for your competitive replay career.
The control settings are a bit flakey in the Linux version. I did manage to get it working with keyboard/mouse at one stage after a lengthy session of plugging/unplugging devices and poking around in the game settings which kept reverting back to what I didn't want, but for the most part it seems to prefer a controller and who am I to argue - I'm happy as long as I can avoid having to boot into that other horrid OS. It works in fullscreen (at full 1920x1200 res) or window but I don't think anyone in their right mind would choose a window for this.
A point to note here is that most Linux-enabled Steam games these days seem to be made with Unity, which simply packages the Windows binary and DLLs with mono to run it all in Linux whereas this game has a proper native Linux binary and music files in open-source OGG format. I for one appreciate the extra effort even if it goes unnoticed 99% of the time.
It's all about the music. Having done a bit of googling I've learned that Savant is a prolific Norwegian electro/dance musician (
); the whole game is based on his music and artwork. 6 striking tracks from various albums are showcased in the game and they are top quality, very catchy. Makes a change from the usual forgettable generic tunes in most games. In some places I noticed the enemies moving to the beat and maybe it would be even more apparent if I was a competent player.
Graphics are easy on the eye but primarily designed for speed and efficiency. There are no overly fancy 3D or artistic elements, just well-designed functional 2D enemies that swarm in packs on a static screen. The result is a highly responsive twitch-reflex environment with zero lag. Any mistakes to be made are down to human error and can't be blamed on the computer, as much as I'd like an excuse for my pathetic scores.
Apart from the slightly flakey Linux control setup it all works smoothly, no glitches, no problems. The menu system is straightforward and includes an integrated achievements list and level selection.
One word...
This is what appeared on my screen every 10 seconds for hours on end (and haunted my dreams) and for quite a while this was followed by "Highscore: 0". I was proud to eventually receive my first points. If there was an achievement for a bazillion deaths I would get it in no time. I daresay if you're a 14 year old with housefly-like reflexes you should fare better than I did.
When using keyboard/mouse, part of the challenge is keeping track of your aiming cursor which can easily become lost in the busy pyrotechnics of gunfire. It has to be placed near the CD part to pick it up. With a controller this doesn't seem to be necessary, you just pull the trigger and the part is retrieved even if you're facing in the opposite direction. The mouse does feel more natural though so it's a tradeoff.
No cards. 14 achievements. I haven't managed to get any yet but hope springs eternal. Apparently some of these achievements tie in with the gameplay, unlocking new abilities. This is an interesting concept I've never come across before. Steam leaderboards are also included but I won't be troubling myself with that.
Everything about this game is tight and compact and the (full) price is no exception. The story mode, at 5 levels, is short but there's a lot of replay in Time Attack and Endless modes. Excellent value.

Colorful, adorable, and heartbreaking. This game will play on your heart strings while telling a beautiful story about the loving bond between mother and child. If you enjoy games with story and good music, I highly recommend giving Rakuen a try.

tl;dr Rakuen and its gorgeous soundtrack is worth every penny at full price and every moment of playthrough. Its emotional storytelling and character-driven narrative will be the something I treasure for the rest of my life, and one that I wholeheartedly recommend to any who enjoy such games and stories.
Rakuen sets its story in a hospital with a young boy as its protagonist, surrounded by various distinct secondary characters whom the boy wants to help. While simple, its execution is anything but average. That so much detail is given to its cast of characters shows how much thought the developer Laura Shigihara has put into them. Even its “tertiary” characters have memorable qualities to them that make the world feel all the more lived-in and relatable.
Its puzzles are as simple but well-executed as its setting and characters. The main bulk of the gameplay, beyond the reading, moving and text reading will be in regards to puzzle solving and fetch quest. If that is a turn off to people, I’d still strongly recommend trying it out and/or attempting to overcome one’s disdain for these gameplay elements. Its puzzles are fairly simple, and even with interesting takes/versions of classics, not nearly as impossible as many a puzzle and rpg games. Its fetch quest also don’t take nearly as long or need as many items, something I greatly appreciate as its story, and not gameplay, were its focus.
The character-driven narrative was what truly kept me invested and interested in playing. With a sprinkling of mystery here and there for good measure. Its coverage of all manner of struggles with characters young and old was very compelling and gripping. I applaud the skill employed in respectfully addressing these issues yet still providing a hopeful and optimistic message for all. There is some ground to say that the message was heavy-handed in some aspects, but I believe it was finely executed and had messages and lessons worth sharing.
Even among all of Rakuen’s notable strengths, special mention has to be given to its soundtrack, a beautiful collection of songs that performs all its functions perfectly. A simple accompaniment to the game as background and theme, a character in its own right and an emotional enhancer when called for, and it is often. Its menu music, titled “The Keepers” in the OST, halted me in my tracks for its duration before starting the game proper. While not the only noteworthy piece, it was certainly my favourite. I feel saying that this quality is expected of a composer is a disservice to her, Laura Shigahara; yes, the creator and composer are one and the same. The choice of pieces and the type of music are incredibly inspired and I look forward to hearing more of her work.
“Unfortunately” I have no deep criticism of Rakuen to balance this review. The following are more minor grievances that bugged me rather than immersion-breaking issues. My understanding however is that most of them are due to limitations of the game engine, in this case RPG maker xp.
•	More resolution options, such as windowed mode (ALT+Enter allows a 640x480 resolution)
•	No steam overlay, which meant no screenshots. I just used printscreen
•	Key rebinding, altering text speed and maybe the font size/type would be nice
•	The direction the character faces bugs out when picking objects up and down, facing left and right instead
As is pretty obvious, these aren’t critical, but it’d be nice to see. And a bit of polish can really make a great game shine even more. As for its graphics, it really does come down to personal taste. RPG maker games have a distinct look and feel to them, and Rakuen is subject to it as well. However, its sprites look anything but unpolished. What’s more, important/significant characters also have unique anime-type portraits given to them that are lovingly designed.
Before my summary, I have to state that I have tried my hardest to avoid a comparison to another character-driven narrative game, specifically To the Moon, which Laura worked on in conjunction with its creator, Kan Gao. I hoped to judge Rakuen on its own merit, rather than in comparison to another, but the similarities/perceived inspirations are hard to ignore. Additionally, the two differ on several key parts; Rakuen is also longer in length, with far more on screen characters and puzzle gameplay. While shorter, To the Moon arguably explores its characters more in-depth and is the first of a series, though with little gameplay. Regardless, having played both I feel confident in saying that those who enjoy one will almost certainly enjoy the other.

As a longtime fan of the original Games Workshop tabletop 'Mordheim' game from roughly a decade ago, it warms the pit of my bitter, cold heart to see such a fantastic digital translation of the game. If anything this version of Mordheim is richer than the original tabletop game, with many more options for customisation of your various warbands, and a bunch of campaign scenarios to battle through as well as random skirmishes.
Great to see the recommended specs aren't that high either which means it'll work on most graphics cards from the last 5 years or so. Workmanlike graphics, but nice models for the warbands, who also reflect the wounds they get along the way - scars, and missing limbs appear on the game models.
People complaining about the 'random number generator' aren't paying attention to the basic mechanics of the game as there's a roll to hit, vs roll to dodge by the target system in play. Means even with an 90% to hit you can still miss if the target has a good dodge ability.
Not a game to be played lightly, as you'll get thrashed unless you apply intelligent use of your warband by flanking and ganging up on your opponents. Never fight 1:1, always gang up on the enemy and Mordheim will reward the unsportsmanlike warband!

The game has serious balance issues. You can be pitted against "hard" and "brutal" difficulty warbands out of the box, making it difficult to progress. There's also something broken with the probabilities in the game. Having an 84% hit chance means you miss repeatedly, dont'cha know. When you beat a mission, you don't get to collect any percentage of the items on the map, you simply get what you got plus a meagre reward. You also don't get back items the enemies stole from your fallen mooks in the event you win by routing the enemy.

If you really like Warhamer / tabletop strategy games, go ahead and get the game. If you don't like endless frustration, avoid it.

A few design decisions broke this game for me.
- Levels are not grid based. This may sound like a weird point to criticize but predictability is very important in these tactical games and this non grid based system makes predictions almost impossible. You don't know what places you or your opponents will be able to reach, often it is unclear where you are in cover and where not.
- Too damn much RNG. Not only when fighting but during pretty much every action. I picked the rat people, supposedly the super agile race, yet I have to constantly roll on these stupid agility tests when scaling walls or jumping down. I saw more rats fall flat on their asses then I ever thought I would. The constant praying to RNG-jesus for such trivial things as movement further makes predictions hard to make.
- Poor tutorialisation. Instead of introducing concepts one at a time in an order that makes sense, it makes you go through a massive tutorial list at the very beginning.
I want to plan ahead and make tactical decisions. I can deal with a fair bit of randomness and realize that a degree of unpredictability is needed to keep things exciting. But the balance of these aspects is very poor, hence the thumbs down.

Steam is full of indie puzzle platformers, and this is one of the best.  The primary gameplay is mixing gravity manipulation with shooting, and it works very well.  The production values on this game are very high.  It's fully voiced, has a polished artistic style, was completely bug free for me and the physics engine worked very smoothly.
However, there are some negatives.  First, the game ends on a cliffhanger.  The developer has talked about a sequel, but none has been announced.  Second, and more imporant, is the fact that the game utilizes some unfortunate stereotypes.  For example, there is a Native American character - he runs a casino and has feathers in his hair.  Also, some of the bad guys have pronounced lisps, like a stereotypical American gay accent.  This really ruined what I thought was an otherwise perfect game.  The developer is Finnish, so they may not have realized the cultural implications, but that's not much of an excuse.

Better than Trine 2, heaps of fun and it got Duke Nukem's Jon St. John lending his voice to the hero. The puzzles are all do-able, nothing too hard, and the characters are all rather charming. I'd call the story a bit shallow, but it's not that bad. Overall, the game is definately worth getting.

The sun shines on the grassy plains. You and your tribe have wandered for many moons. But now the village elders have consulted with the shamans, and have advised you to cease. For you have found the perfect place to call your new home. The grass is green, and ripe for farming. The river sparkles and dances in the golden blaze of the setting sun, waiting to be tamed, to feel the keel of boats along her great girth. And beyond, the distant forested hills call to you. Maybe someday, you and your tribe will dig deep into the womb of the Earth-mother, and harvest the metals that lie within.
You gaze with delight as the procession passes your balcony. The Emperor Jeffersonius himself, in his resplendent robes! His chariot rattles down the cobblestones as the victorious troops of the Ethiopian campaign march trimuphantly behind him, shields and swords gleaming in the summer sunshine. "They have tamed Ethiopia, you know..." you hear your father remark. " We must move to the colonies soon, else there'll be no space left for us!" Your mother laughs gently, and pats you on the head. " We must think of Marcus. His education must take precedence, and you know old Ezrum refuses to travel....." You smile, and throw flowers into the path of those brave legionaires, who fight for the Empire so you may have the best of all  things, here in the capital of the world, Washington.
Your horse gallops wildly through the smoggy streets. Gentlemen of industry, the representatives of the counties, aristocratic ladies, all of them jump and stumble out of the way as you ride past, angrily cursing your receding backside. Along the way, the butt of your rifle thuds against a slow-moving old academic, leaving him senseless upon the cobblestones. You care not, though. You have urgent news for the High Chancellor, and must not be impeded. A rebellion in the Indian colonies! The impertinence astounds you. How dare they, those brown-faced mongrels, rebel against the American Republic? You gallop up the steps of the Palace, and stop to gaze at the Eiffel Tower, under construction on the south banks of the Appatomac River. The fools....the nation that builds such wonders will not fall prey to such nefarious misdeeds! Reflection done, you proceed into the chambers of the High Chancellor to give him the news.
You sigh as you read the fine print of the tender submitted by the cold IronCorp executives. Summary privatization, first right to exploration contracts, government subisidzation of the first twelve months of drilling in the Thames estuary, etecetera, etcetera....your eyes water and you fling the document away, feeling the need for a break. You wipe your glasses and stroll over to the window. You gaze wistfully across the expanse of glass, neon and concrete that obscures your view of the Cristo Redentor, perched high above the city on Zara Yacob Hill. You ponder for a moment....is modernity really worth all this? Did all your ancestors, all the thousands of years of history, all the breakthroughs in science and technology and reason, all the accumulated pride, joy, triumph and defeat of the last four thousand years, lead to this? In the year of our Lord, 1955, you're standing here, in the Pentagon, trying to decide between two equally heartless, vile corporations. Is this what society has become?Ah, well. You wipe your glasses for the last time and shuffle back to your desk, reaching for the legal papers with a weary sigh. You look up at the television to see the newsman babbling about a terrorist attack on the Taj Mahal in Kyoto. Surprise, surprise......
"Oogaboog, wake up!"
"Chief Washington has called a meeting. He want all us warriors to attend. Quickly, get your club."
"....sigh...okay. But remind me to tell you about strange dream I had just now. Big strange."
"Okay, now come , we'll be late!"
You exit, yawning, into the golden rays of the setting sun, hoping that Washington would let you settle here. After all, the shamans did say it was a good place, and you are tired from all the wandering.
