TL;DR : Damn fine game, It's a must buy if you like hardcore platformers.
Vagante is one of those rare gems.  It's the game you've wanted to be playing all of your life.  If you're into tough platformers, this is your dream game.
Vagante plays a bit differently than most platformers.  It rewards meticulous behavior and clear headed judgement calls.  It's not a twitch reaction speed run type game, though your reaction time will be brutally tested.  You will die often, but just as you're about to give up hope (about the 12 hour playtime mark) you'll start to improve.  Spikes will no longer kill you on 90% of your runs.  After the 20 hour playtime mark, the game will just click and Vagante becomes your go to game.
The game is entirely fair.  All the bosses I've seen so far (At this point I've got 48 hrs playtime) have been fair.  They are tough, but they have patterns and weaknesses.  Sometimes they take deaths upon deaths to learn, but the weaknesses are there.
The physics are dead on.  On a platformer the physics make or break a game.  This game has damn good physics.  You'll appreciate them more and more as you put hours into the game.
This leads me to the value of the game.  This game is a steal.  Look at the playtime of most reviewers.  There is a damn lot of bang for your buck.  At 48 hours I feel like I've just scratched the surface.  I think I'm a pretty good player, but I've yet to see the final boss.  The "roguelike" aspects give the game so much replayability as each playthrough feels like a different game.  The random generation algorithm on the levels is great.  Each level feels like it was handcrafted just for you.  The game isn't a traditional roguelike (example: ADOM, Caves of Qud, Brogue), but as I put it, it's as close to a roguelike as you could get and be a real time platformer.
Do yourself a favor and try to not use any guides or wikis.  I feel that part of the fun in Vagante is learning these systems and the surprising ways they interact.  It's pretty fun to share "secrets" and strategies with a similar minded friend or two who don't use guides and wikis.
Character building is a great aspect of the game too.  Leveling up skills lets you guide your character into your playstyle, and lets you try fun new combinations.  Want an archer mage, or a bulwark knight?  Sure, go for it.
Lastly, the graphics are great.  Vagante uses a pixel art style which is extremely well done.  "Low res" pixel art has been played out in the last few years, but this isn't "low res".  This is excellently crafted artwork that's done by a true pixel artist.  This would have felt right at home as a first party Genesis/SNES or later game system.  While it has pixel aesthetic, it's entirely modern and has a great scaling option for all size monitors.  I've played it on everything from a 7" transforming tablet to a 60" plasma television, and you can make it look great on all of these setups with minimal effort.  You just move some zoom sliders and the "pixel perfect scaling" checkbox.
Conclusion: If you like platformers, this is a no brainer.  This will become the bar to which you judge all future platformers.  Don't be scared of it being Early Access.  It's very well optimized, not buggy at all, and has more content than any similarly priced games.  As far as I'm concerned, it's a finished game, just the dev gives us new content every few weeks.  It's like getting free DLC.  The dev is great and really responsive with the community.  I don't know him or anything, but he seems like a stand up guy.  What are you waiting for adventurer?  Your destiny awaits!

One of the best roguelikes you'll play. Really fun, hoping more classes and content keeps being added, but even in its current form its 100% playable and great fun!
This game is like a fighting-oriented spelunky. You progress through 2d levels while looking for items making you stronger. Each level has a boss that you can choose to kill, if you kill the boss you will instantly level up and can assign a skillpoint between levels, else you slowly gain exp by just killing normal mobs.
There is also a shopkeeper you can either rob or buy items from, and many different shrines you need to discover what they do.
The game has a few class-unique skills for each character that you can choose to unlock with skillpoints, it also has general skills for all characters, like strength, vitality, etc.
The game has quite a few different paths you can take your character down and it feels really nice to go from mostly dying on the first 3 levels (one world is 3 levels) to mostly dying on the 2nd world to suddenly almost always make it to the fourth world, every death in this game is caused by you and you yourself, so while you may die a lot when you start out, every death is because of a mistake you made.
If you have any interest in roguelikes at all you HAVE to get this game.

Stunning game! Well made, more save slots than you'll ever need, and the character art and BG art are absolutely beautiful.  The game also had a rich storyline and characters who all felt like people you would want to get to know in real life.
I particularly loved how the MC (Lucette) was a very flawed character. Often, otome games throw you into the action with little knowledge of who the character we are playing is and consequently, the MC tends to feel a little lacklustre sometimes. But this game spends a few chapters building on the characterisation and plot, so you really get to know the MC's personality, relationships, motivations and values before deciding on a route to pursue. I was also genuinely impressed by how the believably the game portrayed the MC and and her love interest help each other become better people.
Although we're only halfway through 2017, this is easily one of the best VNs you'll play this year. There is something for everyone whether you love fairytale tropes, angst, princely characters, action or are just looking for something new to the genre.
Very much recommend it (and in the reccomended play order for maximum plot enjoyment: Rod > Karma > Rumpel > Fritz > Waltz)!

So far after playing the first story, this is a solid Visual Novel story. The story is pretty interesting with fun side characters and music. The curses are actually a lot of fun comedically and for real meaningful moments. I like fairytales in general so having them become curses rather than having someone just plopped into the story is much more intriguing.
I also like the option of having to skip the tutorial and even to each of the prolouge choices that you have to make, if you've already had a run of the game previously. It helps especially when the prolouge is as long as it is which isn't a bad thing because it develops each of the characters' personalities. There's also a nice little tid bit at the end of each completeled Happy Ending which makes you feel acomplished everytime to come to the menu.
I think some of the things that could be improved on the game would be more music scores, fitting slapping/punching sound effects, character involvement and possibly more poses for specific events. There are moments in the game where there are long sincere speeches but instead of the music stopping for dramatic effect rather than having the same song loop for the time you're still reading the speech. There are also times when certain events where a character will hit another character and the game tries to replicate that feeling with the characters moving but it doesn't translate before there's only two hand/body positions. There's a section in one of the charcters does physical violence and the impact sounds like a grasshopper hitting a feather.
There are so many different and interesting characters but since the story might not necessarily need them for a different story, they seem to lackluster when you have such intriguing backstories. It'd be nice to see them involved in a little more epic stuff other than the final battle. I'm not even suggesting the options for your love interest either, I'm talking about the side characters, like the main Witch Delora or the main Fairy Parfait (who's name still makes me hungry.) Both are intriguing characters that I wish would be more involved in your character's development other than as a guide in the beginning.
But overall for a game that's free to play, had so many backers, so much time, effort into the story, writing and programming? I'd give this one a solid 8.5, it still has some wiggle room but I really did enjoy every bit of this game.

Absolver is full of potential.
The core mechanics, AI and level design are competent and thoroughly enjoyable.
The aesthetic suits the tone of the game and is pleasant to look at throughout.
The music never breaches its atmospheric intent and is complimentary to the gameplay.
As many have stated, there have been server issues since launch. However, it is rarely a nuisance and the devs are actively patching the game.
My primary issue with Absolver is the lack of content. From what I've seen, this is the biggest complaint and I can appreciate why. Exploring the entire map and killing all enemies, including bosses will only take a few hours. Basic PVP exists and now there is a deeper reward/ loot system, however it is very rudimentary. The combat system is somewhat imbalanced in PVP as well. However, most people I've played with seem to experiment with their decks, allowing for greater diversity than some people would suggest.
In conclusion, I would recommend Absolver. Whilst it lacks in diverse content, I have enjoyed what is has to offer and will likely sink some more time into it.

This game is what happens if you introduce someone to the original Sonic trilogy for 5 minutes and tell them to make a game. It completely misunderstands what made Sonic's gameplay popular in the first place - momentum based platforming. In general, the physics are very off - you don't gain momentum from rolling down a hill, and one of the staple features of the original games, gaining momentum as you roll, is completely gone. If you aren't holding right, you aren't moving at all. The whole game feels like a cheap cash-in on nostalgia for the first 3 games - several bosses are direct clones of bosses from earlier games, and although there are SOME positive things about this game, those aspects are few and far between. If you want to play a 2D Sonic game, there are many, many better options for you on Steam alone.

That's what SEGA proudly proclaims at the top of this page. And just from looking at screenshots, you would think that this would be the case. It looks like it's a return to form for the Sonic games, even if it's in episodic form (for whatever reason). This is not the case.
Instead of revisiting the fun, fast gameplay of the originals, this game tries to mix things up a bit - and falls into the exact same pitfalls that 3D games in the series have been trapped by for years. The developers sought to add the lock-on jump mechanic that was introduced in the Sonic Adventure series to this game, to no success. It seems like a feature that was added on to help players traverse the levels better - but only because the levels are hard to get through in the first place.
The difficulty in this game isn't the problem - it's the totally incoherent level design. Sonic the Hedgehog was a series known for its lightning-fast gameplay and ability to speed through levels as fast as you can. More recent games, however, focus on putting as many obstacles as possible in your way in order to slow the player down or even make them come to a full stop. One of these such obstacles in this game are vines - no matter how much momentum you have, you have a 50/50 chance of keeping that momentum when you go to make your jump, requiring you to stop what you're doing and build momentum on said vine in order to continue to the next one.
SEGA and Sonic Team have obviously lost their touch when it comes to the Sonic series. The Sonic Rush series on the Nintendo DS did a much better job of carrying on the 2D tradition. Let DIMPS develop all your 2D Sonics, SEGA. You'd do everyone a favor.
Instead of getting this game, maybe fill your 2D Sonic cravings with other games like Freedom Planet or the remastered version of Sonic CD on Steam. Don't buy this retreaded garbage.

Amazing precision platformer! If you enjoy the likes of Super Meat Boy, you will definitely love this game. The controls are spot-on and skill really matters. Speedrunning through a level spiked with hazards truly gives you a sense of accomplishment. The fact that it's 2.5D rather than 2D doesn't really detract from the experience. It's well executed and the camera is mostly well-placed.
The graphics and the odd food theme are perhaps a bit of a weak point, but who really cares when it's this much fun. I found that playing it at a lower resolution than the overly crisp 1080p actually gives it more of a retro feel, making the low-res textures look more flattering, which I kind of like.

I've just played through the Caves (second major area) on normal, and I think this is a really great game. On normal, this game seems more like a Mario game than Super Meat Boy. If they made a sequel, and fleshed it out with powerups and baddies, I would play the crap out of that. If Super Meat Boy is your thing, you'll love the hard mode. Hard mode is definitely a challenge and more indicative of that type of gameplay. It does take a second to respawn from death, so it loses a couple points there. If you're going to die often, it's best to respawn instantly. The camera is also pretty frustrating on hard. Not enough to warrant a pass on the whole game, but the developers have placed a bit too much emphasis on form over function here. Some spikes and traps are hidden from view because the camera is at an angle. Nitpcking aside, probably the best $1.50 I've spent in ages!

Well, it's basically Super Meat Boy with a confusing graphical style (seriously, why have nice 3d enivronments as backdrops when it would make the game a lot easier to utilise them to get past all the tricky platforming, particularly when your main character is an orange ball, the design is all over the place here) and bits wholesale nicked from other games (mine carts any one?).
However, it's responsive, difficult and distracting. As derivative as the core concept is, it holds.

Fantastic game that goes from easy to hard over the course of several worlds. Platforming controls are tight (I'd compare it to Dustforce in this regard), with level designs inspired by Super Meat Boy.

Some of the achievements are almost flat-out impossible (Space Hard mode without deaths?! HAH!), but the sense of achievement from beating a level that has cost you 75 deaths [ I'm looking at you Space-10 凸ಠ益ಠ)凸 ] is absolutely incredible.

Only con are areas where you drop a great distance quickly (mostly a right-to-left scenario), where the camera doesn't pan quick enough. It's not an issue in any hard levels though, just towards the start of the game. Minor annoyance only.

Overall, definitely worth a look if SMB / Dustforce tickled your fancy. In-air controls take a bit of getting used to, but the reward is worth the effort.

Excellent bullet hell shooter. Love the art style and the setting of a 1600s Mars new world. Levels feel somewhat short, and you have to replay them on harder difficulties to progress to the last couple missions (where the 'bullet hell really comes out'), but the difficulty increase makes them still interesting. Awesome music. Highly recommended.

I've played a bunch of bullet hell games (Ikaruga, Radiant Silvergun and Sine Mora to name a few) and while I'm not a real pro, I enjoy and appreciate this genre of games. Jamestown is one of those kinds of games that can get relentlessly difficult, yet give you warm ups to give you the practise needed for the higher difficulties as well as the challenges.
On Normal, the story missions aren't really difficult, but you can only play through the first three missions as each one after the third requires you to beat all unlocked missions on a higher difficulty, and it's through this that you develop the skills needed to complete this game. There are only six missions, but the requirements give each level a fair degree of difficulty to finish the main game.
There are also challenges and a Gauntlet Mode (which sends you through the story mode up to the levels given with the difficult you're on in one straight run. No lives or Credits restored. 2 Continues and 2 lives per continue will be all you get!) which will give you more to do after you finish the game. Not gonna lie, I haven't made much progress with those challenges yet, but completing each one is very rewarding considering how insane some of them are.
The ships themselves differ and cater to various play styles, including the DLC ships. I find myself using the Beam (the default ship) often, but I find the Ghost is a lot of fun, and a neat shout out to Guwange (another bullet hell style game where you control your main character and a spirit, basically how this ship operates).
The music, the style, the gameplay, it's all well done and none of it seems out of place or jarring. The story is a neat throwback to the days of crazy, out there stories, and it's great fun with friends if you can get everything set up to allow them to play, being a local co-op game rather than an online one.
All in all, if you want to pick up a game, blast through some levels and beat scores or take on some harsh challenges, give this game a try!

Length: 10 hours (The other hours were roaming around to create a guide for this game)
Art- Your standard RPGmaker art for human characters and Leebles. However, art for other characters like the Buds and Onions was a lot better. The backgrounds for the fanasty world really stood out to me.
Music and Sound- Beautiful score, songs fit the moment and areas very well. They didn't become annoying at any point. In some parts where there is singing there is voice acting. Keep in mind this is EXTREMELY rare. The voice acting is good, high quality.
Characters- I liked the majority of characters, even one off ones. I wish we could of spent more time with the main characters. You get connected to the characters, but it never feels like the character interacted with you much or connected with you except for Sue and (sort of) Tony. I was always wishing I could do something more for them, even if it was small, because that's kind of what these characters need. I felt helpless watching them, unable to help the way I wanted to. It never got to the point where it was annoying at all, it was more like... just emphasizing with the characters. Of course, that feeling of helplessness is kind of what the game's about. Many of the charcters feel lost and unable to do anything in their situaitions. It's out of their control... Aw man, I thought I was making a negative point but now it's positive! I haven't connected with characters like this in a long while.
Story- Atmosphere is utilized very well. It actually made me anxious at some points, like in the Hospital or during
Character driven.
Gameplay- No combat, that's not an issue for me, but it's important. Consists of puzzles, walking around, talking to characters. Avoid this if you like (or need) your games with combat.

I enjoyed this game a lot! A wide cast  of relatable and enjoyable characters. Puzzles are quite generic most of the time and are a breeze to go through, but when they become a head scratcher it's usually because the puzzle was not explained very well, e.g. the four seasons puzzle it took me quite a lot time to solve it, and I pretty much figured it out after solving the puzzle accidentally.
However I don't believe the joy in playing this game is in the gameplay, much like games of this type such as To The Moon which I'm sure Rakuen will be compared to a lot because of your involvement in it, as these games are all about the journey and the characters which are done extremely well in this game.
Exploring the world is very enjoyable, and it's nice to back track when you gain new abilities and open up new areas. And all the NPCs are fun and quirky and I felt compelled to go around talkig to every single one of them just to be surprised by whatever they say.
And of course, Laura Shigihara's music plays an important part in the emotional delivery, especially the vocal pieces that play during key moments. Just powerful stuff.
Overall, it's a very worthwhile experience and I would recommend this game to any that enjoys a heart felt journey and interacting with a world of interesting characters, definitely take your time with this game to explore as it is very rewarding.
If you liked To The Moon you have to play Rakuen.

What a nice adventure. Like "To the Moon", Rakuen is a more story-driven, rather than gameplay-driven, experience and introduces the player into its universe of stark contrast. A hospital on one side, in which the only joy to be around is brought by the often time rather quirky inhabitants (and yourself). And not-quite Rakuen on the other side: a colorful fantasy world that helps the two main characters - son and mother - not only to explore and resolve the stories of the patients in the "real world", but as well come to terms with the overarching storyline itself.
"Rakuen" is heartfelt. Some parts outright made me sob, while others made me giggle like an idiot. At some moments it feels a bit rushed, only to find back to its strengths a bit later. The songs are nice, but beside one or two exceptions (especially the chorus towards the end got me) unfortunately forgettable. Still, I had a good time with "Rakuen" and will recommend it to anyone who's asking.

I did not have any real expectations for the game, seeing as I paid less than $3. Unfortunately, despite being a decent game, Max is held back by a host of problems that ruined the experience.
The Good: The game has solid platforming, is a decent length for the price, clever puzzles and bright, colourful graphics.
The Bad: Occassional crashing with the Steam overlay enabled, constant hitching when loading a new section, messed up controller configuration (I ended up using mouse and keyboard which works fine).
The game lacks innovation and/or depth [I've had better experiences with platforming games in recent months]. It also uses the Unity engine which  could explain why there are so many problems; every game that uses it seems to be a POS.
Overall, I would not recommend Max: The Curse of Brotherhood, even at a severe discount. A console port with too many unresolved issues.

Dicesuki went above and beyond to deliver an amazing free product! I wish I could recommend it wholeheartedly, but my otherwise enjoyable experience was dampened by some glaring moral qualms (see Weaknesses).
Strengths
+Lucette is a complex protagonist who goes through compelling character growth
+good story-telling that well presents and integrates romances, side character relationships, and overarching plot
+professional quality art and opening, detailed backgrounds
+challenging choices:
+no adult content or tasteless costume designs
Weaknesses
-ethical reservations:
some relationships follow the entertainment industry trend of "crossing a moral line but hey could be worse"
-gameplay:
Good endings allow only 2 wrong choices, and bad endings make sense only with a number of certain wrong choices, not any 3+ out of the 25. The VN's above strengths made this forgivable, but those who care more about gameplay should know that the bad ending is pretty much guaranteed without the right choice indicator.
Suggestions

This game is kind of like Trine: a platformer with a good amount of fighting and some physics puzzles thrown in. Okay, physics is actually a major gameplay element in fights as well as in puzzle-solving: you get to switch between normal and low gravity, and your main weapon is basically the gravity gun from Half-Life.
The visuals and audio aren't as shiny and rich as Trine, instead going (successfully) for a more clean look and feel. Still, the game features Jon St. John (Duke Nukem!) hamming it up as Rochard, and the main theme is done by Poets of the Fall, and everything fits together quite well, with nothing out of place.
The story doesn't take itself too seriously - suffice to say it's your traditional sci-fi action movie stuff.
And there's just something so satisfying in taking out lots of enemies with what's essentially a power tool while hopping all over the place in low gravity.
Great platforming fun!
Good fun right here, a bit on the short side though. Soundtrack was well worth the few extra coins.

This is a brilliantly designed and produced top-down shooter. The retro graphics and soundtrack is charming, the plot melds Victorian-era events with sci-fi and steam punk. The combination makes for a really intriguing mix.
This is a skill-based game and the tight controls and unique ship designs/weapon systems will give you countless hours of enjoyment and frustration. If you die, it's probably your fault. Thankfully, the learning curve is handled well i.e. you can't try more difficult levels until you've managed to beat the previous levels at a certain difficulty.
This is a relatively short game depending on how good you are able to master the ships and become one with the controls. I find myself favoring the game pad though a keyboard + mouse also works well. Multi-player coop is also quite fun.
The charm of this game is that it can also be played in small doses. There was a time that I couldn't beat the final boss. For several nights I try to finish the game to no avail. But after a while, I got the hang of it and managed to kill the boss. This is the point where I realized that all that time, the game was training me to get better and better.

Your soldiers can receive permanent injuries from being knocked out in combat, which comes with visual changes like scars, lost eyes, peg-legs, etc...The style of any given type of weapon is customized to not only the faction, but also the type of unit within the faction (e.g. 'helmet' not only looks different for, say, sisters of sigmar vs mercenaries, but also for hero champions vs henchmen warriors within mercenaries).
There's some recycling of map assets, but there are enough different layouts, orientations, and starting points that you don't really mind, and the story missions add some interesting variety on top of the standard 'route the enemy while collecting wyrdstones'. Also, the reason you can't collect all of the wyrdstones after the battle is that a) you auto collect some and b) lore-wise your soldiers are withdrawing from a dangerous area after some of them were wounded, so they don't have time to scour the whole place (the more are alive after the battle, the more stones you get). Although, I will admit that it is an imperfect solution.
I find that the UI in battle is pretty intuitive, and usable with only a few buttons, but i see that others have criticized it. to each his own i guess.
Some cons:
a little too much waiting for animations and two clicks where one should do. Also, sometimes I wish I could get one unit past another in a doorway, hallway or some other narrow space.
Some of the 'impressive' units are kind of lame. I don't really like the artwork on the ogre, for instance.
I'm not really sure what it is all building towards, and sometimes it seems like the story missions are too few and far between as compared with the normal missions.
face textures can be pretty bad, especially the youngblood mercenary, who has a 'punchable' face
too often i have like a 95% hit chance that misses twice in a row, what is that a 0.25% chance of happening?
theres this animation of throwing both arms back and opening the mouth in a silent scream that happens with almost every action or stance change that feels like a placeholder that should have been replaced
i wish i could move/deploy units from the overhead map mode
hard to tell topographic info from the overhead map
the ai is fairly easy to beat once you figure them out, although i only choose the 'normal' difficulty missions
haven't found much of a good use for the warlock
some tedious, minute upgrading after each battle, and some skills and traits that seem worthless
sometimes RNG is annoying, but that goes with the territory
all of my guys are waiting on me getting enough money for their skill upgrades, which isn't going to happen. I have a dozen guys, each with a few skill points to spend by now, but it costs either 100 or 200 gp to buy each one, and after paying upkeep, medical, recruitment, and equipment costs, i can afford to buy like one skill for one warrior every wrydstone shipment request period (like every 10 game days, during which I'll probably do 5 missions, or like 3 hours of gameplay about)
repetitive loading screen messages
A lot of these cons are the sort of number tweaking or minor adjustment type things that could be done in a single patch (e.g. fix RNG percent chances, drastically lower skills gold costs, speed up or get rid of some animations, write more loading screen quotes, make some better face textures, allow deployment from tactical map, etc...), and I'd like to hope that they will be fixed in an upcoming update, although I have no idea about that.

First off I would like to say that you should ignore all negative reviews by people that played the game for less than 2 hours. They are unlikely to have played the "full game" as there multiple hidden stages and modes, which admittedly can be tricky to unlock. This is because throughout the game you unlock 7 CD's that unlock skills for your character. 4 CD's can be unlocked in the main game and represent your basic abilities. 2 CD's are located in the Endless Mode, unlocked after beating the Story Mode once. Using these 2 CD's it is possible to unlock hidden stages in the Story Mode which (amongst other things) contains the last CD.
The progression of the game is pretty much designed to have you repeat some stages as the order of stages to unlock all CD's is the following: Story Mode (first time), Endless Mode, Story Mode (hidden stages). At the time of writing I have played for 5 hours and have gone through the Story and Endless Mode as well the first hidden stage. I have not even touched the additional free content that was added with the GOTY update and am definitely looking forward to it.
Another concern raised in other reviews is the playability of the game using a controller. I have beaten Story Mode with the controller however in order to unlock the 2 CD's in Endless Mode I had to switch to the keyboard and mouse. However I can't say I was disappointed, as switching to the mouse quadrupled my score. This is simply due to the precision the game requires later on in the harder stages which are incredibly fun to play and represent the main meat of the game. In reality the Story Mode and its 3 levels are essentially a tutorial that explain each of the mechanics in the game and after mastering these one is supposed to play the Endless Mode as well as the Time Attack Mode and the hidden stages in the Story Mode.
TL;DR Overall the game is amazing but fails to tell you that you are supposed to play the Story Mode more after unlocking some new skills in the other game modes. Well worth the price.

Savant - Ascent is a 2D twin stick shooter developed by small indie dev team D-Pad Studios. The game was made using GameMaker and won the GameMaker GOTY award for 2013, it also won Gullstikka Norwegian GOTY 2014. It’s got much replay value with beating previous high-scores and attempting to be ranked in the leaderboards. It is based on real-life EDM artist Savant (Aleksander Vinter), who also provides the soundtrack straight from some of his albums. Savant - Ascent is available on Steam, Google Play, and the App Store.
Savant has been expelled from his tower by an evil Orb, as a result he needs to shoot and dodge his way back up the tower, defeating waves of enemies as he ascends.
Higher up the tower are even more powerful enemies, enemies against which your skill will truly be tested. Are you ready for the challenge that lies beyond the tower?
Shooting and dodging are the game's main gameplay mechanics. The player shoots a burst of bullets before the shots become rapid-fire, dodging and taking down mobs also builds up energy that make your shots stronger. When enough energy is collected the player can shoot a powerful shot that mostly one-hit-kills enemies.
There is a variety of enemies in the game, ranging from small ones with different amounts of mechanics to big worm-like enemies with destroyable sections. There is also boss battles, which are challenging if the player fails to notice patterns and are careless. The enemies come in hordes, and if they’re not picked off in the order they spawn then you may have some crowd control to deal with, the burst shots help a lot with that. Throughout the whole game there are CD fragments, four of which form one full CD. CDs unlock more songs on the soundtrack and also unlock different abilities and buffs for the player.
There’s Story Mode, Endless Mode, and a Time Attack mode. You unlock latter two modes by beating the Story Mode. In endless you can try and beat your highscore and also rank high on the leaderboards; same with the timed mode, you can try to beat your time and rank high on the leaderboards. Good old arcade-style gameplay model, which give the game a high replay value.
Now, the Void Update.
With the Void Update a whole other section was added to the game, and this section is much, much harder. It adds more enemies with different mechanics, and it also adds a new boss, which is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to beat, to say the least.
The graphics are an overload of visual stimulation. The sprites are fairly detailed and animations are fluous. Explosions and shots are brightly coloured and debris and particle effects are eye candy. Amazing art. Just wait until you fight the space-samurai, just wait.
8-bit sound effects and Savant’s music make this game’s audio something unique but at the same time nostalgic. Aleksander Vinter (Savant) has savant syndrome, this makes him able to remember every musical sound he’s ever heard as well as make massive amounts of music in short periods of time. In his lifetime he’s made over 10,000 songs; since adopting the alias “Savant” he has released eleven albums, seven EPs, and twelve singles. He has no definitive genre or sound, and is constantly experimenting with his music.
For this game he chose most songs from his dubstep-sounding albums: Alchemist, Cult, ISM, Ninur, Orakel, Vario, and Overkill. Not including the musical scores made specifically for the game.
Gameplay this simple and this addicting takes ingenuity to develop. D-Pad Studios took a world based on Savant’s music and fleshed it out into a full universe. The Alchemist from the album Alchemist, Vario from the album Vario, and the Samurai from the album Protos.
Personally, I bought this game simply because I’m a huge fan, had ‘Savant’ in its name, and because the trailer was featuring his music. What I was surprised to encounter was a ridiculously fun game with an amazing soundtrack and crazy good visuals. A must have for Savant fans and twin stick shooters alike.

With
the developers from
bring us a new 2d puzzle-platformer, which seems to be an all-around improvement of their previous game named
In this title, we play as Max once again - on a mission to save our annoying little brother Felix, whom we 'accidently' sent away through a portal - to a magical and dangerous place. A place ruled by the fearsome Lord Mustacho; an old, bitter man who wishes to revitalise himself with a young spirit. Armed with a (magical) marker only, the grand adventure to save Felix from Mustacho begins!
Upon arriving the magical lands that we sent our brother to, we receive strange powers for our - at first - seemingly useless marker. Those powers are granted by the wise old lady, who is portrayed as Mustacho's opponent. This new improved marker allows for the creation and destruction of various objects, such as dirt pillars, branches, vines ... which play an essential role in the game's puzzle-platforming sequences. Want to reach the top of a hill? How about you draw a dirt pillar to raise yourself all the way up. How to reach the other side of the tree? Why, just draw yourself a vine and swing across!
stays relatively fresh throughout as new mechanics are regularly introduced and each new chapter grants your marker with new powers, depending on the environment you find yourself in - or so it seemed. It must not have been a coincidence that within the forest, I reveived the power to draw branches and vines, whereas in the wetlands, I was able to create water streams to help me navigate through the levels.
I found the gameplay to be overall fun and exciting. It starts out pretty simple and basic, but in the later chapters you'll have to actively combine certain objects to complete the various puzzles that the game has in store. There are also certain 'escape' scenes to deal with, as in: run away from different threats against time. Most of the puzzles never get really challenging, but that didn't seem to bother me as they were always fun to do and solve. Some of them are quite creative too, which made for an enjoyable experience. Who says games need to be difficult in order to be fun?
The real 'difficulty' comes in another form than puzzle solving, and that is dealing with the somewhat ... clunky controls. More often than not - when I entered a new level -, I could figure out what to do pretty quickly. When I actually wanted to execute my solution, I would regularly fail because of how weird the controls can be from time to time. Jumping/climbing is not always as accurate, and let's not even talk about the amount of times I fell to my death whilst swinging on vines - missing my destination by mere millimeters.
Onto the game's length and replay ability: The game consists of 7 chapters in total and lasts for about 6 to 7 hours, which I found to be just about right. Some additional hours could be acquired by hunting down all of the game's collectibles, which consist of destroying evil eyes and collecting secrets. The great thing is that you don't have to replay the whole game while looking for all achievements, as seperate chapters can easily be accessed in the main menu. Sadly, collecting all eyes & secrets doesn't really hold any significance within the story - it is merely a reason to catch 'em all. However, what good is a platformer without any sort of secrets to track down, right?
If one thing became clear whilst playing
it is how child friendly this game truly is. From the story to the gameplay to the cutscenes, this game strikes me as something that could easily be enjoyed by the whole family. Right from the start - when I loaded up the game for the first time - until the end, I was filled with a somewhat nostalgic feeling, probably because of the charming music, the entertaining cinematics and the loveable cartoony look of the game. In a certain way, it kind of resembles games and cartoons I used to play/watch as a kid. If you're still not convinced, well, the game's antagonist is called Lord Mustacho ... LORD MUSTACHO!
I do recommend this game, but please keep in mind that it is not a perfect game by any means. While the music is very charming and cute, it is rather simplistic and not all that memorable. Secondly, the game's got a sweet look, but don't expect AAA visuals. And lastly (and I mentioned this in the section above), the controls can be a bit odd/stubborn sometimes and can therefore make the game a little bit tedious/irritating at times. In the end, the game feels like an avarage title. Not amazingly good, but not bad either. Just good, but still definitely worth playing in my book.

Just like the music, the level themes and designs are also boring, uninspired, and forgettable. They don't try anything new, and the game suffers for it. I can forgive Splash Hill Zone, every Sonic game starts out with a Green Hill Zone esq level and it's a tradition I like. What I can't forgive is the rehash of Casino Night Zone, (it has its own name but I already forgot it) and the painfully generic levels that come after.
TL;DR this game is a soulless attempt at a cash-grab on older fans' nostalgia. Avoid this, at the very least, don't pay full retail for this monstrosity.

It doesn't live up to the name "Sonic the Hedgehog 4." It's pretty short and takes most of it's inspiration from the original Sonic the Hedgehog but if you ignore the name and just focus on what it is, it's a solid game.
The level design is good, it's a good mix of platforming and puzzles. New gimmicks are introduced every stage, so every level has something new and interesting. The bosses are alright, they move slowly and can sometimes be unpredictable but can all be beaten very quickly if you know what you're doing.
I've heard lots of complaints about Sonic's physics in this game. I can see where they are coming from since they're a lot floatier than the original but it's not like they're bad. Sonic's momentum carries well and is useful for accessing some secret areas. He's also really slow to start running but the addition of Spin Dash and Homing Attack make up for it.
The music is nice. There were only a couple really memorable tracks though. I didn't like that certain elements of the game had no sound effects at all though. It's strange not hearing a thing when Eggman waves agrily at Sonic after being defeated, especially since the game uses their modern designs.
The graphics are a bit bland too. This is especially noticable on the special stages where the background is just a Kaleidoscope.
Overall I liked this game, it has a few weird problems but the gameplay makes up for it. It does not, however, live up to it's name as a sequel to Sonic the Hedgehog 3.

Comparison of this game to To The Moon is inevitable. So I'm going to provide 2 reviews for people who have/haven't played that:
1. If you have
played To The Moon (in which case
) this review is for you:
Ok... So you are contemplating getting this game and you want help on that decision.
It is a linear, simple rpg / puzzle game minus the fights. 10-15 hours max if you take your time reading everything and try to do everything. Much faster if you rush through it.
This game is a project by a professional game musician, so yes the music is strong with this one. But it is at times a bit too eh, you know, kids cartoons style.
Puzles are easy. Actually to make it easier game locks you off a lot of times until you figure something out, so it is hard to miss solutions.
The story is heart-warming. It does have its flaws and at places it feels bits and pieces have been cut off or not fully developed but it is not incoherent at any point. That is important because this game is basically about its story, not gameplay.
Graphics are developed with a heart warming sensation in mind. And it is done properly. The magical world in mind of a child is so beautiful that coming back down to this world felt so cold after finishing the game!
There are a couple of clever things about this game I don't want to spoil. It does have its twists and it does play with your heart but it is not too dramatic.
The phylosophy is quite Japanese. The developer is half Japanese but I did not expect her to see things so Japanese for somebody who lives in US. Some concepts are just very Shinto-like (Final-Fantasy-like if you will).
Overall, it is fun, you get a bit of laugh and tear here and there, and it does leave an impact on you. It provides a perspective without trying to be preaching it. People like developers of this game need our support, not as game developers, but rather as people who live among us. We want more people who think like this among us!
Would I recommend it? If you are not going to expect a gameplay challenge or a long game (and hours of play is the least of my concerns when I rate a game), I very much would recommend it.

2. So, you have played To the Moon and you want to see how this compares. (If you haven't, stop reading right now!) then this is what I'd tell you:
Concept is similar yes, but it is a different game. The answer depends on what you expect. To the Moon nodes to the 80s style rpg genre but does its own thing. This game at times feels quite like a game of that era plus beautiful graphics and sound minus the fights.
To The Moon has a more complex story. Probably this game has more stuff in it, more places to visit, more things to read, etc. (overall I'd say twice as much material) but less twist and turn.
Musically To The Moon is more abstract. It is more of something you'd listen to as an adult. Music of this one at times feels more like going to a theatre with your kid and trying to enjoy what a particular giant media corporation considers good entertainment for children. It may be your thing, it may be not.
Graphics style is a bit more refined. To the Moon is dark and its art style is also dark. This one is the colors of a child's mind.
This game is less emotionally charged. I played To the Moon over a couple of mid-week evenings after work. Sleeping was a bit difficult afterwards with the atmosphere that it created. "For River" was not leaving me alone and still it is one of the most emotionally charged game songs I can think of. I didn't go through anything of that sort here. Don't get me wrong: This is a touching story. And it will have an impact on you after finishing it. But yeah, if you have played To the Moon you know that one is a different beast.
And one last bit, this game starts fairly slow. It grows in pace and material through it. To the Moon was bold throughout. So if you are giving this a try, don't expect things to pick up from get go.
Do I recommend it? If you think this will do to you what To the Moon did to many of us, you may get disappointed. But it is a touching story that you are missing out on if you don't try it.

First lets clear up the "RNG" conspiracy all of the negative reviews are focusing on. When you see 67% for a hit that is what your chance to land a blow is. IF you roll that check and IF you get your 67% your opponent WILL THEN roll their Dodge/Block chance. That is not taken into account into the % to hit chance you see. Settle down and do some research before crying about the difficulty.
With that said this is a great game, it will make you go rage mode but will keep you coming back for more if you truely enjoy tactics games. This game requires that you have overwhelmingly solid tactics making use of choke points etc. You need to keep a pretty deep roster because you will lose guys in a fight. You will need lots of trial and error but that makes a win more rewarding, and unlike some games when your guy gets "knocked out" theres a chance he will make it in the end, albeit with possibly one less arm.
This game has hundreds of hours in it if you want to invest in trying out all of the different factions. I haven't even beat the game yet and have over 80 hours. I recommend this game to anyone who can do the math and do not to those who scream RNG and hit the refund button.

Mordheim is a merger between two of my favorite things, tactical strategy and warhammer fantasy.  Mordheim should be the game that I spend 100+ hours playing, and mucho dinero buying all the DLC. Instead it is infuriating beyond belief.
My complaints first:
Tactical game? -- has no functional top down view, no functional grid, nothing to help chart pathways, lay ambushes, plan charges, nothing. Ambushes often times do not trigger, for reasons unknown to me. Sometimes my warband can charge engaged opponents, sometimes not, seems completely random. I've found my warband stuck in poor situations too often, due to not being able to gauge distances, etc...
Inventory-- is a total joke. Small items do not stack, WTF???? Bob loots 3 coins from a body. Bob gets 5 coins from a chest. Bob has 8 coins, right. No Bob has 3 inventory slots and two of them are occupied by 3 coins and 5 coins. Now Bob previously picked up a total of 27 coins. These 27 coins all fit in one inventory slot, but either Bob is too slow to put all his coins in one slot, or...Same thing with wyrdstones. Small fragments take the same space as clusters, which are 10 x the size? You also can't equip anything you pick up. The helmet you just picked up, which you have a place for, on your head, nope no putting it there, that'll have to wait till after the mission.
Gameplay-- is slow, with unnecessary animations. Opposing warbands are really aggressive, their only tactic is to swarm. Quest goals are sometimes vague and can take forever to figure out, or the quest will just randomly end, regardless of wether you are able to complete the objectives, or not.
And your typical gather wyrdstone quest, goes like this. 3-5 rounds of exploring, looting, gathering. You get noticed by the other warband. They swarm your warband. One leader/hero or another falls. Morale check. Quest over. And this happens over and over again.
RNG-- Game uses rng which can get stuck, causing your warband to suffer, sometimes permanent damage. I just finished a match where the roll was 90 for four consecutive attacks. I lost the objective, due to my hero falling to a zombie with 10 wounds left. Seriously, the zombie has time to destroy my hero, while two other henchmen miss all their attacks. Hero falls, zombie loots the token I took from the other warbands hero, I finally get a shot in on the zombie, morale check and quest over. No objective for you.
My compliments:
Warband develpoment -- Customization on every member of the warband. You can tweak each member of your warband to make them specific, dynami, and unique. There are almost too many customization choices available, which means you can really spend time and geak out.
Landscape-- Mordheim is Warhammer fantasy to a T. It's brutal, trap filled, landscape in ruin. Basically Warhammer fantasy.
Mechanics-- Not fully a plus in my book, but I do like that the warband can do maneuvers and attacks. Different maneuvers use movement points, attacks use offensive points, etc...
I don't know if any of the issues I have with the game will ever be fixed, or if anyone with the ability to mod or fix some of this stuff will. I hope that happens. Like I said, Mordheim should be the game that occupies way too much of my life, except that it isn't.
Turn-based dark souls.

The game has a few good points, but not many.  Expect to spend a lot of time with very few options available as you build your fledgling warband... I'm not sure if it ever opens up, but as far as I got you're stuck with one type of leader, one type of hero and two types of henchmen.  You can fiddle with their equipment a little, but the difference there are relatively minor... leaving you with almost the exact same experience time after time.
Other reviews mentioned how long it takes for the computer to take its turns.  This is true - as is the rather more important matter of a rigged RNG.  My leader had an 82% chance to hit most enemies, but still managed to miss more than half the time.  My opponents, on the other hand, seemed to have little trouble with the most ludicrous of tasks, for instance shooting into a melee.  An opposing archer had a 13% chance to hit with that kind of shot and managed twice in a row.
I don't mind a difficult tactical game.  But losing because you surrounded an opponent who proceeded to outfight all three of your men despite the odds isn't difficult - it's just plain stupid.

Firstly, if you've played the Mordheim tabletop game, THIS IS NOT IT, it merely takes the themes, aesthetics and mindset. As a former Mordheim (coreheim) player, and a fan of this style of dark fantasy, as well as a tactical strategy fan, I'm going to give this game a 9/10 potential with a current score of 7.5/10 because of interface issues and the above complaints.

I love this game.  Feels like a tactical board game brought to life.  It's got a lot of problems:  It's got quite a few bugs, and some clunky UI and controls.  The learning curve is steep and the tutorials suck.  Parts of the core game design look flimsy:  The game is supposed to be unforgiving, and losing a battle means less xp and permanent injuries making your guys less valuable.  But it doesn't stop you from totally avoiding it with an unfortunate exploit.  Just grab a friend to play against, and cut your internet connection during battle and the game rewards you both with a victory.  Makes it kind of trivial to build up a powerful warband.
The objectives are so lame.  I mean, OBJECTIVE, singular.  Always it is to kill the other guys, and collecting loot is sort of a bonus.  It is repetitive, and just assumes that both players will clash somewhere in the middle of the map, or near a big pile of wyrdstone.  Nothing stopping one player from running away forever like a troll, not letting the game end until someone gets bored and forfeits.  IMO the game should also end if all the wyrdstones are collected from the map.  That's like the whole premise of the game anyway.
This is definitely a niche game, for those who love tactical board games and have the patience to figure out the mechanics.  It is a lot of fun if you can look past the bugs, clunky UI and controls, and some poor design decisions.

Fortress Forever (Abbreviated as FF), Also known as TFC: Source (that's what i call it) is a mod from source engine (SDK) 2006 that is inspired (and got most of it's gameplay from) QWTF (QuakeWorld Team Fortress) and TFC (Team Fortress Classic). let's take a look at it's current state and see the pros and cons.
Pros:
-Gameplay keeps itself unique, even though it borrows much from TFC and QWTF.
-Some of the stuff Modders implemented in TFC is now default features in FF (example: two tap grenade binds)
-Free Game.
-The graphics are a huge step up compared with TFC.(even more so with QWTF)
-Suprisingly, Most computers can run this game! (maybe it's because it's very optimized, compared with TF2)
-There's a tutorial to teach you how to do most movements on FF, from conc jumping to trimping.
Cons:
-If you are new to FF, you are going to get destroyed. Same in TFC. but with the limitations imposed by FF and simplifications of some of the stuff from either QWTF and TFC, it's a bit less heavy
-Hardcore TFC/QWTF Fans might not like the slightly simplified content of FF (like auto bunnyjumping for example).
-Since TF2 Released a month after FF, and FF required initially HL2 (Half-Life 2) to play, the mod diden't have much of a chance to get alot of players.
-Has a low ammount of players but this ammount seems to be consistant. for guaranteed decent gameplay, check on weekends (mostly after 12 PM GMT) or at night (from 8 PM GMT) on weekdays.
-FF's Discussion page has some trolls, but it's a bit more controlled.
Overall Score: 7.5/10

1. This game doesn't have any pretense of being too long or involved and really isn't. The hour or so it will take most people to get through the story mode on this is a fun hour w/ really no dull moments. If you are fine w/ that, this game is for you.
2. It sort of feels like an old shareware title from back in the nineties where you got the first episode of the game for free and then had to pay to get the rest. Only in this case you pay up front and there is no more game when you're done.
3. Just kidding, there are actually two extra modes unlocked once you've finished. Not the same as more levels but, hey, it does add some replayability beyond just going for a high score.
4. This game goes out of its way to call attention to its soundtrack but the music is only pretty good.
5. Graphics are also pretty good.
6. Overall presentation strikes me somehow as just feeling very loud, almost feels like the game was designed to stand out in an arcade. I suppose the avalanche of indie titles these days does approximate the din of a packed arcade though so fair enough. I never would have played this were it not for the black metal sounding intro music in the trailer (which sadly devolves into some wubby techno).
7. This controls better w/ mouse and keyboard than with a controller but it controls really well either way. There are definitely frustrating moments in this game but it's because you are a palsied and ill-coordinated nerd and not because you didn't doge in sync w/ your inputs.
8. If you quit before you finish on your first session, you have to start at the beginning again but you maintain all your power ups so it's a bunch easier.
9. There is a weird mechanic in this where you don't get to use any of your powerups until you die. This would make for a great hardcore challenge--to beat the game w/o dying means you don't get to use powerups--but *spoiler* you can't kill the final boss w/o the first power up. I saw an explanation from the devs about this and it still doesn't make any sense.
10. Don't worry. You are almost certainly going to die on your first attempt and many times after that. Nobody who has seen the sun in the past fifteen years has spent enough time playing shmups to crush this thing on the first go.
11. I dig that this is a Game Maker game. I once tried to make a Game Maker game to snowball into the indie game avalanche and only got as far as making a couple sprites flit about randomly while you shot bullets at them that did absolutely nothing.
12. Games don't have to be big and complex to be good. They just have to be good.
13. At the end of the day, my judge of an aracady shmup type game is if when I beat the final boss I give out my secret aracady shmup boss beating victory yell and I did that w/ this game. I call this a win for DPad Studios. I am looking forward to more titles from them.

What a game. What a strange beast of a game. Part twin stick shooter, part platformer, Savant - Ascent is a whirlwind of color, music, and exploding robots. It's also incredibly bizarre as you play a Guy Fawkes lookalike alchemist whose goal is to retrieve an orb that has the essence of a purple Mario clone called "Vario" in it and...yeah. It's a weird game. But it's pretty fun, too, and that's important.
As you play Savant - Ascent, you hop from one of three platforms, dodging enemies and their incoming fire all while firing back at them. That's it. That's the whole game. It's super simple. As you progress through the levels, you can unlock record pieces that, when fully formed, not only grant you new music to listen to, but new upgrades to your own weapon. Very straight forward, but it works well.
Savant is extremely short, however; with determination, you can probably beat it in a sitting, 100%. It's tough for sure, but nothing patience can't fix. If I had a problem with it, it's that when you aim at an enemy, the camera pulls towards them, leaving you blind in the opposite direction. Expect many, MANY, deaths because of that. But still...what to make of the mish mash of steam punk, EDM, and weird Mario insertions?
Fun Fact: I was at work the other day (a supermarket) when I saw a customer walk by with a t shirt with this game art on it. I thought, "Oh, wow, that's cool! I didn't know this game was so popular!" I talk to him about it and learned that Savant is actually an EDM artist. The game, Savant - Ascent, is actually a strange side project featuring his music. IT SUDDENLY ALL MADE SENSE.
I think I got this for a dollar. Buy it. It's worth the one dollar.

I typically avoid writing reviews unless a product gives me a truly good reason to do so. Cinderella Phenomenon has given me plenty to say. In fact, you learn to care about everyone a great deal and the story ensures to bring on the feels. If you are looking for an active game then keep looking as this will not suit your tastes. However, if you are an avid reader and want a good story then I highly suggest picking this up. I do not believe you will be dissapointed.
Note: The creators of this novel suggest going through the paths starting with Rod, then Karma, Rumpel, Fritz and ending with Waltz. There is a very good reason for this suggestion. I do not want to spoil anything but trying it in this order will give you the best experience in my opinion.

The Steam Link is a nice plug-and-play way to get Steam on your TV. One thing I will immediately say before continuing: FOR GABEN'S SAKE, USE THIS WIRED. When hooked up via a wire, the picture quality is excellent and the latency is also excellent on my gigabit network. Wireless, it's jank. That's the one major (and come on, obvious) caveat when using a Steam Link.
Beyond that, it's a neat, inexpensive little device. I got mine for $20, been very happy with it. Setup is a doddle, the UI has plenty of options, etc. The Link essentially uses screen sharing over the network from your PC, so it will support any hardware that is installed on your PC by simply passing the connection through. I use wireless 360 controllers on mine with an adaptor, not a problem. It also has Bluetooth support for keyboards and mice, which is very useful.
I can't speak as to the various apps you can install on it, such as video streaming services, because you, I and your dog can all watch those on basically anything. We don't need yet another streaming video device.
Either way, been loving having mine hooked in next to the Playstation. Pick up a controller, tap a button and I'm in my Steam library.

I don't quite know how to write about this game.
See, here's the thing:  I like shmups, and I like bullet hell shmups.  But I know they're very much an acquired taste, and I also know my own preferences vary wildly from others within this genre.
Anyway, Jamestown feels a bit like "Baby's First Bullet Hell".  It has a pseudo-16 bit art style, but rather than playing like a 16-bit shmup, it plays much more like a modern Bullet Hell (like Touhou or one of the Cave games.)  However, the ship's hit box is fairly large, and the controls are somewhat imprecise.  So, unlike more advanced Bullet Hells, which rely on pinpoint precision, the ability to trace the directions of hundreds of projectiles, and deft maneuvering, Jamestown relys on extremely busy backgrounds (which sometimes make it difficult to separate the projectiles from "noise"), quick reflexes and much larger pattern spreads.
Overall, it does feel like a good shmup for getting your feet wet, and has a bit of variety that I enjoy dipping into on occasion.  If you don't already know what kind of shmups you love, this one might be worth getting a feel for.

This is a Sonic game. The understood story is that Eggman is up to no good again, and it's up to you--Sonic--to save the day.
The game plays mostly like the other original Sonic the Hedgehog games: you jump, roll, attack enemies, collect rings, etc, but now you can use Sonic's more recent homing attack to chain attacks together and jump over wide gaps. If you enjoyed the original's gameplay, you'll like this.
The graphics are strange. At first I was taken back by the strange blend between 2D and 3D visuals, but I soon adjusted. Some areas are very aesthetically pleasing, whereas others fall more on the ugly side. It is more in line with the original's visuals, but carefully avoids straying too far from the modern art style--this might turn off both retro and modern fans.
The music is not bad, but the originals' is better. The sound effects are like the originals', which is fine.
The stages are excellent. Some of the later stages in particular are very creative and are a blast to play. I was pleasantly surprised by how well the stages were designed.
The game is relatively short. I finished all of the stages within 3 hours, which was slightly disappointing. The bosses aren't too varied, but the final boss is incredibly difficult (and a lot of fun). There are plenty of other things to do outside of the main game: time attacks, special stages, collecting achievements, etc. If you're the kind of person who runs through a game's main campaign without doing extras, this game might disappoint you.
I like this game, despite it being short. I plan on going through and collecting all of the emeralds, doing the time attacks, and trying to get all of the achievements. I bet the main game plus the extras will stack up to about 5 hours of gameplay, which is pretty good.

I grew up as a huge fan of the first and second Sonic games on the Genesis.  I finished both, several times.  They have fantastic controls, fluid animation and wonderful music.
Sonic 4 has failed in almost every way the originals succeeded.
The original games had touch-perfect controls.  When you pressed a button, something happened.  This new entry into the series just...ugh.  It has some of the most frustrating controls and camera movements I've ever seen in a platforming game.  For starters, Sonic has incredibly slow acceleration.  For a game character that has always been about speed, it takes a surprisingly long time for Sonic to get moving.  He walks for a few seconds before he starts to really pick up speed.
But even worse, he has no momentum.  What I mean by that is this: he will only move from left to right if you're actively holding the movement buttons (I played using an XBOX controller).  If you let go of the button in mid-air, sonic just stops on a dime right then and there.
Masato Nakamura, who composed the soundtracks for the first two Sonic games, was responsible for some very iconic and memorable tunes from my childhood.  I still catch myself humming them from time to time and they were simply fantastic.
I don't know who composed the music for part 4, but it may as well have been entirely composed by computer.  There is no beauty, no structure, no...good.... in this music.  It is grating, annoying, repetative, flashy, jarring, and just plain horrid.  Absolutely nothing positive about this soundtrack.

It basically amounts to nothing more than moving from point a to point b in such rapid fasion that there is no time to enjoy the journey.  The artwork is somewhat reminiscent of the originals, but lacking all of the depth and charm that they had.  The controls and jerky camera work just compounds the boredom.

This game proved to be far more fun than I originally thought it would be.  I had gotten this as part of the HB Monthly and decided to go ahead and try it out because there was really no point in not doing so.  What I found was a rather impressive take on turn-based strategy that was wholly unexpected.
While the game seems simple at first, the tutorials leave much to be desired and make things a bit more difficult than they have to be as a result.  The tutorials never really tell you how to loot or pick up items, though I was able to figure it out once I completed one of the tutorials.  The learning curve is a bit steep, since this game does things very differently from other strategy games I've played.
What's Different?
First of all, you get to customize a faction all your own.  While you choose the starting race and type of characters you'll play, everything beyond this is pretty much up to how you want to go about things.  You'll start with a small team of 4 characters:  your leader, a hero, and a couple of henchmen, and go out into the ruined city of Mordheim for loot and wyrdstones.  While the customization isn't great, there's enough there that you shouldn't get bored with setting your characters up.
Character movement and actions are handled with a variety of points.  This allows you a bit more freedom with how you can take your turns, but means you have to strategize a bit more.  Henchmen are pretty weak and you don't really want them to rush forward and get slaughtered by a potentially powerful enemy you were unaware of.
Characters can receive lasting/permanent injuries over the course of the game.  Fortunately, this is fairly balanced and doesn't happen too frequently, but when it does, look out.  You may need to retire that character and recruit someone to take their place.  Some injuries are minor and others can be outright crippling, so make sure you pay attention to the details; they are important in this one.
Unlike many strategy games, it isn't necessary to take out all of the enemy to win.  Each mission has a variety of means that you can win, typically, such as routing the enemy, killing a specific character, or acquiring a certain number of resources.  So far, routing the enemy has been how I've completed most missions, as your inventory space is at a premium.
Pros:  Customizable faction, time is a factor on what you do between missions (such as healing and training), lots of variety of weapons and equipment to allow you to further customize your team and how you play the game
Cons:  A steep learning curve, and tutorials that leave much to be desired.
In Conclusion:  A fun game with a lot of nuance, if you like the idea of strategy games where you have to plan a considerable amount more than you may be used to in other games and have a lot of customization options, this is probably the game for you.  If you aren't into learning a new way of playing strategy games and want to stick to the tried and true methods of other games, you may find this one quite frustrating.

Yes the graphics are dated and some of the base D&D mechanics are creaking under the weight of all the add-ons done over the years. Most of the problems with mechanics tend to show up at the upper level ranges (20+)
Many of the recent adjustments to classes has taken some of the difficulty edge off of the lower levels as power creep has reared its head.
-----------
For the absolute best DDO experience:
get 3-4-5 friends that have zero experience playing. Have everyone go through the tutorial (it is solo only).
Set up a schedule of play time and request that no one plays at all outside of the group time, no spoilers!
Dont go read about how best to play the game or the best builds , etc.
The exploration and learning on your own when it is all fresh to the whole crew is priceless.
Some dungeons have you thinking with your fighter ,barbarian or sorcerer you are the baddest MoFo ever.
Next dungeon you are cheering on the rogue who is sneaking around a room full of big, bad Ogres, that would squash him in no time flat if they see him/her, picking up the soul stones(dead PCs) of the entire party to take them back to the shrine to be raised from the dead.
===========================
Lots to do as free to play so no need to pull out the CC right away.
If you follow the above plan for best experience by time you get to where you feel the 'need' to pay, you will gladly be screaming "take my money, now!"
-----------------------
One word of caution about making characters;
Many of the older dungeons have the unfortunate MMO min/maxer design problem.
You will run in to somethings that require X Strength score to open or Y skill points to trick an NPC will seem really high.
The desiginers couldn't make the stat requirements too low where a balanced character could complete with out making things trivial for the min/maxers.
Just keep that in mind when building that maxing or nearly maxing your primary ability scores is suggested and likewise it is better to have a few skills that are maxed rather than a bunch of skills with low investment.

Well, it's been two months since the game was first released, and what do we have so far? To start off with, let's be up-front about it: The game's launch was pretty rough. Servers didn't work half the time, and when they did they were laggy and not exactly conductive to a fun competitive experience. Content was lackluster and the UI seemed like it was put together in a rush. Although I enjoyed it even then, it would've been pretty rough for me to recommend it to anyone who hadn't been as invested through it's development as I had been.
Even today, a lot of those problems still haven't been adressed. We still haven't gotten a major content update. The UI is still pretty rough around the edges. Netcode can still lead to some pretty janky situations in 1v1s, and the team has yet to implement things like 3v3s for PvP. And still, the game's advanced leaps and bounds since it's first itteration in terms of optimization, functionality, balance and quality of life. If nothing else, this helps the game bellow the surface shine even further -- and man, what a game that is.
Quite possibly the most faithful videogame depiction of the feeling and aesthetic of striking-based martial arts, Absolver really does make you feel like you're an up-and-coming fighting legend traveling a vast world, looking for challenges that will net you more experience and sharpen your skills. The way in which this game handles progression -- by having you learn new moves as your opponents use them against you -- is absolutely outstand, and definitely one of the most authentic and genuine looks at the concept I've seen in a videogame.
All around, it's an experience that you cannot find anywhere else, and if that sounds appealing to you then the game is absolutely worth checking out. The dev team behind it is also hard at work on always improving the game's content, so if you like being a part of an active and involved community, this is definitely the place to go.

I was sent a code on Twitch.tv as I showed interest when I first saw the game and was really excited to give this game a try. I am very pleased with my expectations of the game and it's exactly how I thought it would be.
The game is very challenging and addicting, you somewhat become used to seeing the ball get squished and shattered into pieces, but that doesn't leave a sour taste in your mouth in fact it just makes you feel determined to push forward. It feels very rewarding to finally get over a challenging set of obstacles and collect your plater at the end of each level.
One thing I think they should have added is a RGB Color Palette for the Custom Player Color instead of a slider, because at first glance you are not sure what you changing with the fact that the Use Custom Color option is disabled by default. However I do like how the player is situated in the background of the Customize screen and changes color upon selection, it feels really nice. I just think this screen could be more intuitive from the beginning.
The controls feel really nice using a keyboard, some platform style games can give you a feeling that you must plug a controller in as it's so difficult to navigate around, this doesn't. However using a controller did feel a little better, so if you don't have a controller to play with this game, it's still very playable and doesn't leave you frustrated.
The camera tracking is ok, in certain areas it feels like it's too low but nothing that is annoying to the point where it's really spoiling the gameplay.
Graphics are nothing to be amazed about but don't disappoint and are perfect for this style of game, simple yet appropriate.
Game performance is very smooth, very optimized no dips at all, 300fps+ on a MSI R9 280 3GB card. I feel this was a good point to make as you have to be very accurate with your movements sometimes to avoid spikes and close falls.
I have not had a chance to try the COOP out as I don't have any other friends who own it. The game uses its own servers to bypass firewall restrictions which is neat, but it is noted that if their servers go down then you might need to Port Forward.
Overall if you're looking for a challenging and addicting platform game that you can play with up to 8 friends then definitely add this to your shortlist of games to buy.
If I had to rate my experience with the game I'd give it an 8/10.

This game is horribly broken, atleast in my few hours of experience.
I'm not referring to gameplay mechanic or anything like that, that's all well in hand. The thing that kills it for me is the astoundingly horrible AI and crashes/freezing. So I'll go over the good and the bad (Atleast in my opinion).
THE BAD
The AI: It's bad, it's just bad. Keep in mind I've clocked 200+ hours in M2TW and the AI there is bad. The AI immediatly wages war against everything around it, which isn't bad, the problem is everyone is your ally and youre always inclined to help them.  The problem, the ally AI ALWAYS loses, as Britain, both the United Provinces and Portugese were destroyed in a matter of turns when I went to war with them. And keep in mind you remain at war even if you're far away from the enemy faction. Arranging peace I'll get too. But the AI is just outrageously horrible, letting you go nearly anywhere and getting BS forces from nowhere.
Diplomacy: It's worse than M2 standards. Want peace? Too bad, even if theyre down to one province and under siege, they'll want all your colonies. Example; At war with Maratha, offer peace in exchange for some tech and money (No territory owned by me in India keep in mind), what do they do even though it is a useless war? Want Parts of Canada and the Carribean. CANADA AND THE CARRIBEAN, AND THEY'RE BASED IN INDIA!!! Like wtf AI. This makes it impossible tomake peace in these useless wars as you can never bribe them. They either flat out refguse or give you terrible demands, this goes for any other diplomacy.
Freezing/Crashing: Maybe this is just a problem with muy toaster, but every few turns the game will crash or freeze, forcing me to shut down my computer and log back on. Not much else to say.
The Music: Coming from M2TW, I guess I expected grand battle themes, but nope, just some quiet none fun ones.
----------------
THE GOOD
Politics: Love itm, civilian anger to taxes, revolutions, changing governments, it's wonderful as a mechanism to remind you of internal threats. Elections are random, so you may get good, bad, or meh mebers of government, but whatever.
Gameplay Mechanics: Battles are done fairly well and can be engaging in situations such as sieges or big engagements, but small engagements aren't as fun.
Other Bits: The little trinkets of history, economy and other things are also very fun bits to learn about and play around with.
Tech Tree: A bit annoying but great feature to decide what to focus on (Military, farming, philosophy).
----------
Summary: Overall Empire is a meh game for me, the upsides are negated by the problems with it to me, and I find it only enjoyable in small doses. I would recommend it to anyone interested in the time period (18th Century).
I suppose I'll continue playing it irregularly but not as often as I'd like.
(Also you get some stuff for TF2 so there's that).
