Remember back at elementary school when you or some other kid in class used to draw little planes, cars, tanks and people (usually stick-men) on books blank areas? Adding little dots as weapon fire making them fight in an imaginary combat, most of the time resulting in a page full of smudges as explosions happened and stuff were 'destroyed'! Well if you miss that, then Ballpoint Universe: Infinite is right on 'point' to satisfy all the doddle commanders out there!
Ballpoint Universe: Infinite is an arcade shooter with some platforming action and lots of upgrades to choose from! To my big surprise, misled by the 'infinite' of the title, the game has a lovely story that you will uncover step by step as you play. You are a newdrawn doodle exploring an 'almost' 2,5D world (there is the concept of depth and you will notice some models to be closer of further away from the camera in each level), in which you will find doddle npcs to talk to, missions to take, a lot of exploring and some platform jumping. At the beginning you may feel that you have no idea why you do what you do or what is your purpose, these are revealed later on the story. There are tons of collectibles to find called 'golden doddles', some hidden in plain sight, while others through fake walls, also acing a mission will grant you one golden doddle! The main game, the shooter part, happens during the numerous story missions or at the infinite mode. The infinite mode, as the name hints, you play till you die. You gain resources called 'ink' by destroying stuff and you can see all enemies and bosses appearing in this mode. Additionally missions award you ink depending on your performance and for any destroyed enemy, you can always repeat a mission to improve it or to get some ink by the defeated enemies of that mission. With the ink you can upgrade and improve your ship, so you do better at missions or infinite mode thus more ink and more upgrades! Your ship consist of 4 parts, 2 weapons, 1 wing or hull and 1 nose. There are many weapons, from melee blades and shields to shotguns and rockets, each with its very own design, effectiveness and fire mode! The wing affects your hitpoints and may add special abilities, like ink magnet, to your craft. Lastly the nose defines what your special ability will do and how many times you can use it in succession. Each and every part is upgradeable up to level 3, upgrading weapons and noses will increase the overall damage of that part, while wings add durability and special skill effectiveness.

By 'right on point', besides the obvious pun, I want to highlight that everything you will see in this game is drawn by hand in notebooks or blank pages. You 'll be able to see the blue and red lines of a notebook page in many places! The models besides the big variety, feel unique and magnificently well made, even in the tiniest details. From ship parts to bosses, combat backgrounds to the numerous levels you will wonder as part of the story, each feels magnificent and carefully made. Even the level design is superb as many of the golden doodles are surprisingly well hidden!
The game has 3 control options, either keyboard, mouse or controller. Each really easy to grasp and use effectively. Personally I favored the mouse for two reasons, one, I felt it was better during combat, and two, it felt challenging to do the platform jumping with it! However it is advisable to change between them until you find which suits you most. The music, while not something exceptional, feels just enough to highlight each phase of the game, either the platforming or the combat! The only negative for me, is that you can't touch the markings that were created in the back of the page after you finished that well made sketch/doodle! Definitely an unappreciated title as it is a reminder that game development can be an art!

Jamestown seems intent to bring back that closeness that comes with old-school arcade games. Supporting up to 4 player local co-op with any combination of mouse, keyboard, and contollers, Jamestown stands out from the crowd.
On top of the multiplayer focus, Jamestown has a unique setting and great design. The story takes place in an alternate history of the colony of Jamestown on Mars, and that's about all there is to say. The art is great, nothing too special, but the music is fantastic. The epic soundtrack fits the intensity that the game reaches at certain difficulty levels.
The pacing and progression hold Jamestown together nicely. The in game store allows you to buy new difficulty mode and bonus levels that both offer up some intense challenge. The game slowly makes you incrase the difficulty to reach new levels, which pushes you to practice and push yourself. There is also a joke mode that takes the already outlandish story and makes it even sillier.
High scores are the main incentive for replaying. The game offers up a combination of any 4 ships that have their own unique play style, and the combinations  can get pretty insane on-screen. Vaunt mode can be activated after collecting a certain amount of gold and it releases giant shield that can aborsb bullets that will raise your score and save your friends. On top of this, enemies will also offer up bonus points if you hit them at a certain point or time ( I have barely figured out any of these). There are also many difficulty settings that can turn this game into a frantic bullet hell.
This game is highly recommended with some friends. Even though the local co-op only may be a turn off, this will be a great excuse to see some of your friends in person.
***The DLC offers up 3 great new ships and pilots (Guy Fawkes included), and each of them are different and fantastic.

The first Doom and Destiny was an unexpected strike of liquid gold. Despite its generic RPG Maker graphics and sometimes poor translation, it came out swinging as one of the best turn based RPGs since the SNES era. The sequel, however, leaves much to be desired. This review is while the game is still unfinished, but there are some glaring issues not related to bugs, balance, or the unfinished story.
PROS:
- Custom graphics that while cartoony, fit the tone of the game quite well.
- Class system has the potential to be interesting, especially when used to find secrets and navigate terrain.
- Clever introduction to a story: the game functions as a parallel universe to the original story, which has the potential to make a very interesting tale.
CONS:
- The characters fall flat to the original. This is a big problem, as the charm of the dialog was what made the first game so damn good. Toilet humor rules the day in this sequel, and the characters just don't have much in the way of banter, 4th wall breaking, or personality. I played the whole time waiting for Mike to say or do something really zany, but it just never happened.
- The story quickly goes nowhere. Interesting ideas like the frog king trying to marry the characters off to his daughters is quickly brushed aside into a boss battle. Instead this game just seems to have a very generic RPG story with a few eccentric ideas used in the background.
- The class system feels too constrictive. You basically have to dump all your resources to get a decent level for one class per character, leaving the other classes woefully underpowered. This kind of class system would be really good if you could switch between them more liberally and usefully.
- Equipment management is gone. Characters now auto-equip items and there’s no ability to customize your characters in this regard. This is a huge disappointment, as managing equipment is a big part of any RPG, and leaves the full burden of customization to the class system, which is poorly executed.
Overall I’d say this game needs a lot of work to be anywhere near as enjoyable as the first game. As-is, I stopped playing after a dozen or so hours, not because I reached the end of the content available at the time, but simply because I was getting bored. For now, this sequel is simply a disappointment.

Just a bit of a note before you read the whole review: if you use a wifi connection for either your Steam Link or your PC (or even worse, both) DO NOT BUY THIS. Seriously, while wi-fi is an option, you would litterally need a monster internet connection that most people can't afford just for this thing to be playable. HOWEVER, if you are planning to use a wired connection for both your Steam Link and your PC, then read on.
For the people who are going to be using a wired connection, then this thing is really awesome. I use my PC in my room all of the way at the back of my house. It's plugged in directly to an router extender. I put the steam link in my living room, which is at the front of my house and plugged it directly into my router. Once I got the link all set up and updated it worked perfectly fine while streaming at 720p 60fps. There was almost no noticable imput lag with my controller (I didn't test it with keyboard and mouse), however i'm sure if you really care about that kind of thing and try to go for the lowest latency possible, then you probably will notice a difference. I would reccomend it if you are looking to play some more casual games in your living room or if you want to have a split-screen party without having 4 people crowded around your monitor.
(7/10)

I was very sceptical about the steam link having tried similar streaming devices in the past with really poor results. Also, having read a few negative reviews I decided not to buy one. Then it was on sale for £3.99 so I picked one up figuring that even it did not work as expected, I could trade it in for a profit at Cex or Game. Cost of postage was £7.50.
It arrived a week later and was pretty much plug and play out of the box. My rig is connected to my router via ethernet and the steam link is in another room connected via wi-fi (5ghz). Results are great; 1080p, 60fps, little to no input lag. Most controllers are supported, I have used my Xbox One controller and Steam controller.
Very small and slick, great design and has 3 usb ports, hdmi out and ethernet port. Not bad for 4 quid! You are able to stream not only Steam but your desktop too, essentially giving you access to your full PC in another room.

I work at a desk all day so when I come home, I prefer the console style of gaming where I can just sit back on my couch and relax but I also like PC gaming and especially how my PC is stronger than a baseline PS4 I like to take advantage of that. I don't have an HTPC so this was the next best thing.
Is it perfect? No. If you have an HTPC I'd just stick with that but if you're like me and prefer PC gaming but also prefer to game on a couch and don't have an HTPC or the money to build one or a similar living room computer then this is a very good option. It does have some issues, sometimes it gets a little buggy and while it says it is couch based gaming, I reccomend also hooking up a wireless mouse. Some games just need input on a menu and if a game randomly crashes or has issues, that prevents me from having to walk to my PC to solve it. I'd also heavily reccomend using a wired connection unless you have very fast internet.
I bought it on the Black Friday sale. With shipping it came to $13.00 USD. Even at its current price it's more affordable than a HTPC so I'd reccomend it if you don't mind some occassional issues.

I find this item to be very useful for living room parties, and just on the couch gameplay. It is entirely easy to set up, and after a system update works on any controller I connect, with exception of the Nintendo controllers. What's even more on this thing is
- Sweet TV applications you may choose to install on your Steam Link, with up to around a gigabyte of storage for such apps
- Entirely customizable to any kind: Valve is lenient enough to allow the Steam Link for any modifications which are accessible by configuration files on a USB pendrive
Con is that the image quality is lower by the 100Mbit/s NIC limitation of the Steam Link, but you won't notice this if you're far away from the TV or the screen is smaller. Too there is noticable input lag from what I
ranges around 30-70ms, but this is to be expected as this is a stream, not a real-time image from a digital cable, plus your TV model might have input lag on its own.
Summed up short: the Steam Link is a very useful littlle device to forward your gaming experience all the way downstairs on your TV, with additional applications to enhance your experience a little. Not recommended if you're on a busy router switch, or if you're into big accuracy in video games.

Pros:
+Very few latency issues when using ethernet, was able to play a vast majority of my steam library comfrotably on a steam link/steam controller combo
+Doesn't interfere with regular internet usage if you have a decent router
+Great connectivity for its size, most notably a full size HDMI port and 3 full size USB ports with support for hubs
+Defaults to Big Picture mode, but can also be minimized for a stream of your desktop which allows for stuff like playing videos
+Dual monitor setups with varying resolutions seamlessly swap when the cursor moves between them, but not while in game as it locks the mouse automatically
Cons:
-No smart TV, fire stick or chromecast style functionality, this thing literally only exists to stream from a PC
-Wireless connection can be unreliable
-Steam controller onscreen keyboard just doesn't work properly with multiple monitor setups as it will only show on monitor 1
Overall recommended when paired with the steam controller, I wouldn't pay more than $70 for the bundle.

If you think you're the target audience for this game, you probably are.
It's a game with a story to tell, and that's what it does. It's a story about grief and loss and regret and hope and accepting the inevitable. It's about acknowledging the awful unavoidable things that occur in life--disasters, illness, accidents, bad decisions--and how people can decide to handle the awfulness and the importance of understanding.
It's a game split between a hospital filled with patients with long-term illnesses, and a brightly colored fantasy land populated with cute animals that mirror the occupants of the hospital. But the fantasy land isn't really a happy retreat from reality, and it's not a bright paint-job over a horrible truth. The kid-friendly atmosphere isn't trying to hide the brutal reality of what's happening, just to look at it in a different, brighter light.
If a story-driven game with light puzzle elements and an unapologetically bittersweet story sounds good, you'll like the game. If not, you probably won't. To the Moon comparisons make sense, but I do think that Rakuen hits emotional notes that will resonate with a wider audience.
And the game has a dedicated 'talk to Mom' button; more games could use a talk to Mom button.
Absolutely beautiful game, with an amazing soundtrack, great writing and fun puzzles. 10/10 highly recommended

I adore this game. It's a title that appears so simple at first glance, but offers an immense amount of complexity in its narrative, addressing difficult subjects that aren't often found in video game stories. The storytelling is done in subtle ways that truly make you care about the characters and their experiences and emotions. But what truly sets the story apart from other Indie titles like Rakuen is how the creator has imprinted her own Japanese identity into the story and the setting, taking inspiration from many aspects of modern Japanese life that give it almost a shocking sense of realism at times.
Add to that incredibly polished and appealing character and background art and an excellent soundtrack with the high quality you expect from a game music veteran like Laura Shigihara, and you'll find yourself with a game that is truly worth experiencing.
A wonderful and heartwarming game that will make you laugh, cry, and appreciate life. It's a story and puzzle based game that will keep you on your feet with a brilliant soundtrack.

I found this game through Vinny (Vinesauce) and it looked like it was fun.
I have not been disappointed ever since.
As soon as i found out it had coop and my friends were over, we played this together.
We were originally going to play something else as well, but we completely forgot about it.
This game has had me mesmerized from that point.
A lot of the hours spent on this game have been singleplayer however, which is equally as fun (and slightly frustrating)!
This really is a rogue-like game.
One life to get as far as you can.
Did you die? Too bad, try again.
And while this game features many instant kills (watch the spikes and falling heavy objects), it doesn't neccesarily feel cheap.
Maybe the first few times where you discover those insta-kill you, but after a while, you learn how to avoid them.
It helps that the same rules apply to enemies (with the exception of bosses, though they do take damage).
You can knock or lure enemies in traps to kill them without losing anything from it, mostly.
The classes are your typical RPG classes: Warrior, Mage and Rogue (Archer/Assassin blend).
There seems to be more in development, with one other class available right now, but the first 3 are clearly the base classes.
THe game also features a levelling system, you get experience from killed enemies.
After every level, there is a hub area, where you can save for another time, heal up a bit (this is always available, after every level) and you get your level up there.
This will grant you one point which you can spend on either a skill or a stat.
The skills really change the gameplay and while they have a max level, every point spent in them is noticable and changes the way you play a bit.
This way you can specialise, while not limiting yourself.
Aside of that you also have your items to gather (sadly, they are not visible on your character) that range from weapons, armor, spellbooks (spells), potions and more.
While every character has a skill bound to a specific weapon-type, every class can equip everything.
So even the battlemages can work perfectly, they are just not as damaging with melee as a knight would be for example.
There is also a lot of things to discover in every level.
Especially at the start, you will wonder what some things do.
While there is a (mandatory, i think) tutorial at the start of the game, not everything gets explained.
Though some things get hinted at in the tips you see when you have died.
Which will happen a lot.
Trust me.
Tl;Dr:
Fun, entertaining and punishing game.
Fun for up to 4 players in couch co-op (soon to feature online though!) but also fun for solo players.
Certainly recommend it to pretty much everyone.

This game is probably my favourite Choose Your Own Adventure game so far. It's got drama, action, deep and heartfelt relationships, mystery-solving, and lots of intense and even painful moments. You play for the highest stakes, definitely.
Enter you, yet unnamed male protagonist, stumbling back into your old life after surviving a harsh partly robot/mecha war between your Empire and another country. There's plenty of choices to make -- be a faithful soldier, become a traitor rebel, pursue forbidden magics, and pick someone to give your heart to, if you want.
+ The general atmosphere of the novel (Victorian steampunk)
+ Lots of murder mystery solving
+ Great "buddy cop" story with your partner in crime
+ Layered story with political intrigue, including spies and rebels
+ The magic system that's introduced
+ Action! Drama! High stakes!
+ High replay value
+ Save points (!)
- Predictability, even if you're just a bit familiar with the stories this game borrows from (Sherlock Holmes, Jack the Ripper, etc.)
- No skip option for replay purposes
- ???
Sure, I might be biased because I have a weakness for Victorian-style mystery solving and steampunk, but this game really got me invested and involved up to a point where I was genuinely nervous what would happen if I picked a certain choice. The stakes are quite high, and your choices have a huge amount on influence on your relationships with other characters, various story elements, and also on the endings.
10/10 would play again

In this case, due to the length and strong characterization, I would rather stick with my single play through, because I don't want to cheapen that story by going back and seeing how the sausage is made.
In terms of narrative this is, in my experience, the strongest outing yet.

I did not expect this to be the first review I wrote but I'm happy to write it.  As of writing this I have just finished my first playthrough of the game.
The story is enjoyable and well written, the choices non-trivial, there is no "one true path" through this game.  I made some decisions I regret but I loved the bittersweet story those mistakes told.  That is to say, I may have wished I could reload and try again, but I was happy with my regrets.  I am in an odd situation where I want to play again, but I feel like I would lose the story I've already told.
The game centers around you, an ex-soldier doctor with an interesting heritage, working behind the scenes to create a better Mercia.  What exactly that means is up to you.
The mechanics of the game are choice based (as expected) but also stat based.  Your choices change who you are, your skills and outlook, and those stats change what choices you can make (or at least which are viable options).
All in all, great narrative based game, glad that I played it.

It was inevitable, really. I found most twine games on steam to be incredibly pretentious and boring, but reading up on this and tin star, now finding out that they're not twine but rather a different software, I was pleasantly surprised to find that there were damn fine stories being told that had nothing to do with social justice nonsense.

Going into this game, I wasn't sure what to expect: it contained several elements that I had seen attempts at in mobile games and the sort, and those games hadn't overly impressed me. Needless to say, I was apprehensive.
Now imagine an exensive 300+ page novel that is all about you and your adventure. That's what this is. It took 10 hours to finish it for the first time, and every choice I made, every flick of my head or slight wording difference kept me alive and exhilerated to the ending. Even the most trivial of choices contributed to crafting my own personal story; a story that touched, and scared me more than any first person shooter could.
If you like fast-paced novels with biting mysteries and high stake choices, this is a game for you.

Do you remember when Andy lost his dog Whiskey 1998. in "Heart of darkness"? If you do you're probably not a kid any more. The time has come to take on another similar quest. You use magic marker to resolve greatly conceived platform puzzles. Puzzles are just challenging enough for maximum joy without much frustration. As I come from 20 years of console gaming my default setup on Steam is Xbox 360 controller. It held it's own until the last segments of the game when it became impossible to control magic marker with speed and precision needed. Not to worry. When this occurs you grab your mouse for marker control and all is well again.You'll feel omnipotent with controller in one and mouse in another hand :-) Or just play on keyboard and mouse - maybe that is even better, I haven't tried. If you have any interest in this type of games buy this and enjoy. It is just as good as "Limbo" or "Heart of darkness".

♥♥♥♥ing epic, man. The♥♥♥♥♥♥you will pull off in this game is exhilarating. The levels have great verticality, and the vine swinging, oh man that vine swinging. So much of it! And over many vast, vast expanses of open air. Whether it be climbing up the side of towers or plummeting over massive waterfalls,
.
The magic marker mechanic is fun, the highlight being branch+vine creation (and destruction - you can chop off branches/vines from their source to reach higher/lower places). It's the most flexible, figure-it-out-yourself of all the elements you can manipulate, versus the earth pillars, which are fun, but very specific and limited. The player movement controls are precise. You won't find yourself overstepping platforms very often.
The dynamic camera definitely carries some of the epicness of the game, and it's still very effective in letting you see what you need to see. There were two moments when I wish, after zooming out to get a large view of a room, it would zoom in a little sooner so I could control my character with more precision, but it never caused any problems. Overall a great feature.
The tone of the game is silly and childish. The characters are very stock, but that doesn't detract from the experience at all. The voice acting and music are all good, and the art/scenery is nice.
Not sure how long it took me to beat the campaign the first time, but overall it took me 14 hours to complete the story, grab all the collectibles, get all the achievements, and then go back and complete every level without dying (a really fun challenge - you even get little badges to show for it). The puzzles aren't exactly hard, but there were a couple that had me scratching my head for a couple minutes. It's definitely more constant satisfaction than frequent perplexity. You could argue that the game is shallow, in a "little investment of skill or emotion" kind of way, and that would be true for the most part, but there's nothing wrong with that, if you don't mind that kind of thing. It's an Indiana Jones, not a Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥ and that's ok.

This is my first ever review. Mordheim is a brilliant game in every way, or should I say: was. It requires real tactis and battle insight, it gives a very good squad build-up and as such requires long term planning of every single member of the squad. The options you have are endless. The whole system works great and the new races bring even more versatility.
Alas, as of late I can't even get my squad to win missions in such a way that advancement is possible. Planning has no use anymore, it's more about survival in almost every single mission. I know it is meant to be unforgiving and it should, but this is getting out of hand. It's no longer fun if you can't even get a new hero to survive for more than two missions since then the injuries start piling up. I played for (in game) 13 days, a whole cargo assignment cycle and had the feeling my squad didn't advance a bit. Yes the stats did, but no skills, no money, almost no wyrdstone ( at least not enough) so constantly battling for survival in every mission. It feels I'm following the lead instead of leading the dance.
Again, I know it's meant to be tough, and with over 400hrs playtime and many many warbands I think i have no problem with that. But this is getting out of hand. I suppose it's also meant to be fun on the side, and at this point I'm seriously considering quitting all together. The only race I've had successes with ( as of lately) are the vampire counts. The rest are difficulties difficulties and, yes yes, even more difficulties.
Over all, a very great game, I really recommend it, IF some minor changes would be made. Good news is they actually read these things and update regularly. Hence this first and only review ever. I sincerely hope I can enjoy this game again as I used to, till late at night and proud of the (injured) warband I had created, which was able (with injuries) to beat the odds and advance even further and falling "in love" with every squad member, even those with missing eyes and limbs! Fortress Forever is the true successor to Team Fortress Classic. During development, TF2 was changed to an extend that it is a completely different game now. FF compared to TF2 is as follows:
General:
-FF has grenades.
-Classes also have armor.
-Health Pool is different.
-Bhop is possible and is very easy, because it's automatic.
-While in TF2, the best gamemodes are Control Points, King of the Hill and Payload, in FF it is actually Capture the Flag.
Scout:
-In FF, he is used for his speed to cap the flag, rarely fights.
-No double jump. Concussion grenades are used and they are way more powerful.
-No Scattergun, has a weak pellet gun and a Nailgun used against sentries.
Soldier:
-Soldier has normal grenades and nail grenades - which shoot nails in 360 degrees and deal damage.
-Has a weak pellet gun and a more powerful shotgun.
Pyro:
-No airblast.
-Flamethrower deals damage depending on the amount of armor the victim has.
-Has an Incendiary Cannon which acts as a Rocket Launcher, but sets enemies on fire.
-Has normal grenades and Napalm grenades - which set enemies on fire.
Demoman:
-No Stickybomb Launcher, replaced by the Pipebomb Launcher. Pipebombs don't stick to surface.
-The Grenade and Pipebomb Launcher share the same ammo pool.
-Has a pellet gun.
-Has a detpack which has the ability to clear obstacles and open new entrances.
-Has normal grenades and MIRV ones - they split into smaller grenades which explode.
Heavy:
-Alt-Fire enable him to release a shockwave that stops concussion jumping enemies.
-Has a Slowfield grenade which releases a gravity field, slowing enemies.
Engineer:
-Cannot pick-up buildings.
-Has powerful EMP grenades which blow up the enemy's ammo and cause damage.
-His Railgun creates cells used for building. Also used for jumping.
Medic:
-Medic is also used for capping flags because of his speed and concussion jumping ability, but is more powerful than Scout and slower.
-Can infect classes with his medpack.
-No Medigun therefore no Ubercharge.
-His super nailgun is good against sentry guns.
-Drops up to 5 medkits.
Sniper:
-Basically TF2 sniper with the Classic and grenades.
Spy:
-Has a Tranquilizer Gun.
-Has a shotgun.
-Can feign death.
-Has Hallucination Grenades.
Civillian is the last class which is used in special gamemodes.
Teams are pit against each other where Red uses defensive classes to protect their flag from Blue, which use mainly Scouts and Medics to capture it.
It's a game I recommend because it's a lot of fun, despite there being not many servers at a time.

Passing thru the turn-styles for game saves is nice and you never have to go too far or look too hard for them. However, I think this game wouldve worked a little better with a manual save option or an auto-save every time you leave a battle. Its  anice artistic touch but this game already has plenty of wonderful artistic touches. There is such a thing as too much of a good thing.

There are as you may have noticed, several and very differing opinions regarding this game, which gives it a thoroughly "Mixed" (or as I like to call it - "Probably Not Worth My Time") status. But I'd say that the mixed status is very misleading in this regard. The issue here is that old reviews of which some were regarding the servers at release (I'd say it is mostly fixed by now, correct me if I'm wrong), and more recently complaints about price/lacking community. But all things considered, I honestly thing it is still worth it. The combat is intuitive and fast-paced (and more importantly, SMOOTH), and there are so many possibilities. No fighter has the exact same style.
A word of warning though, Absolver is anything but a story- or PvE driven game. It is in it's core a PvP game only. Then of course there are PvE and some, Souls-like and vague story, but what's important to remember is that you don't buy Absolver for doing quests or talking to NPCs, and that is why I think Absolver should be rated higher than 'Mixed' as a LOT of the negative reviews are regarding how little of the forementioned exists. It is very much like judging a fish based only on its ability to climb a tree, and then comparing it to a monkey's results in the same area.
Now there is some truth in it being the of the 'dead' online games-kind, but that can only really be fixed in one way. And that's for more people to start playing it. That's why I think that if you like fighter games (and a real challenge!), you should at least try it out for an hour and a half and make your own desicion wether it's worth the coin or not. Worst case scenario would be that you refund it and then there's no harm done.
Then there's those who are complaining about there being some over-powered style which brings a, and I quote, "Broken pvp system where you can be spamed(sic) to death with no possible way to counter". This is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There are several ways to beat that kind of strategy, and that's the charm of the game, there's always a workaround. That means the skillcap/ceiling is reeeaaally high, and it depends 110% on the player if you are successful or not, as everyone have the same starting point and nothing is pay-to-win. It's all about grinding a little for those sweet moves, then put together a fluid and/or solid deck and lastly to practice. A lot. As with all forms of sparring IRL, or really any skillbased online game.
Lastly it is a blast to figure out, grow with and explore the potential of the combat, all-the-while observing and learning from others, more seasoned or experienced players or maybe a friend.
Do I recomend it?
F**k yes.
Is it for everyone?
No. Definitely not. But that does not make it any less good IMHO, as that's generally the way with everything.
Should you buy it?
Well, yeah, at least try it out for a bit and see if you like it.
PS. Oh, and one more thing. Make sure you play it with a controller. It is specifically designed as controller-played game, and should be treated as such. It even has full support for them (you don't need a third-party program like DS4Windows or similar).

The dark horse of the Total War franchise. The first game released with the warscape engine and the only one with a truly global scope, Empire continued to divide and engage the fanbase for many years after it's initial release.
First, the bad, and the things that caused such a stir back in the day: The A.I. and the bugs. The A.I. has a difficult time handling the scope of the campaign and frequently makes dubius decisions. The only comfort here is that the A.I. is allowed to play badly, without being shoehorned into gamey mechanics designed to obfuscate its incompetence, as happened in some of the later Total War games. The battle A.I. tends to be aggressive, preffering to offer opposition and cause damage rather than implementing advanced and frequently bugged algorithms. Again, this is a mixed blessing compared to some of the later games in the series. Finally, the bugs: Most of them have been patched, but every now and again you will have a botched disembarkment or a failure to intercept enemy armies. On the battle map, river battles remain notoriously unreliable in offering the defender an advantage, and sieges will sometimes drag on for a very long time. Also don't try to board enemy vessel unless you feel really lucky. It is what it is.
On to the positive stuff:
§ The sheer scope and attention to historical detail: The immersion value of this game, especially if you come to the table with an interest in the time period, is almost immesurable. Colonialism, the scientific revolution, the enlightenment, the politics of power, dueling, the age of sail, revolutions, globalised trade, even the manner of speech used by units (in all languages!) contribute to a game experience that feels a bit like visiting a museum but being allowed to play with the exhibits.
§ The research system: Empire total war was the first in the series with this feature, and it is very well thought out. In some of the later games, research feels like a gimmick mechanic tucked on in service to the brand without really representing anything. Here, each technology actually feels like a genuine discovery or invention. Choices matter a lot; upgrade basic units or unlock special units? Increase population growth, town wealth growth, or unlock better mines and logging camps to go for the quick income boost? Play it safe or boost technology rate at the cost of increased spread of revolutionary ideas? All of it feels natural and yet engaging.
§ The armies: Military forces in Empire total war revolve around three basic units: Line infantry and regiments of horse are available from the start, with mobile foot artillery being just a short research away (earlier cannons work the same way except they cant move or hit targets). Using the research system, most upgrades will affect these three unit types and improve their capabilities in one way or another. Line infantry will get improved bayonets, the anti-cavalry square formation, and advanced firing drills. Regiments of horse will get things like diamond formation and improved charge bonuses, and foot artillery will get larger calibers and different ammo types. In addition to this you use research to unlock specialised support units like grenadiers, light infantry, dragoons, howitzers, and late game insanity like the puckle gun or ottoman 60-pounders(!). These units do usually not benefit from the upgrades to basic units, but bring speciallised skills like grenades, skirmishing, fighting dismounted or firing at an angle to the battlefield. The end result of all this is that it is very easy to build a balanced army, but allows a great deal of customization by the player, according to personal taste or strategic decisions. And all of this is achieved without breaking the immersion that you are prioritizing research for your nation and trying to keep abreast of the evolving battlefield tactics of the times.
§ Sail porn: Bit of a personal one here but regardless of how buggy naval battles can be if you try to do something fancy, the ships of this period are absolutely gorgeus. Whenever a naval battle loads up and I see my flagship at the fore of the line, Swedish flags fluttering, boards creaking, crewmen running around on the deck and cannons bristling from each broadside... And then the climax, the moment I face the Danes in battle once again, as it was in ancient times, wooden giants unloading on each other at close range, splinters flying, and then the sudden explosion as a lucky shot hits the powder. Victory. Sinking. Oblivion. Death. Sorry, let's move on.
TL;DR: War, sir, is a terrifying buissness! Empire total war is clunky and sometimes cranky, but it compensates and shines with it's well thought-out game systems and impresses to this day with it's great charm and it's success in immersing the player in the time period.

Now, is this game for you? If you are history buff like me who loves the 18th century and musket warfare, this and Napoleon: Total War are must-buys. The Multiplayer is more active in that game than here and also features better maps, though the campaigns are much more focused.

There's a lot of people super-excited about this game for various reasons, and while I see why, I don't think the game is for everyone.  This game was made to appeal to a specific type of person, and I think enthusiastic hyperbole can backfire when it draws in people other than the intended audience, who are disappointed and end up calling the game bad.  It's not bad, it just fits a relatively small niche.  So I'm going to try to be honest here.
First and foremost, Rakuen is super sugary saccharine sweet.  I'm not saying this as a criticism, I'm saying it because it's a central part of the experience, and the main thing that I think is going to divide opinions on the game.  Imagine the corniest cartoon Christmas special you've seen, then double the dosage of sap, complete with actual musical numbers.  If that sounds amazing to you, go ahead and buy the game.  If it's any kind of a turn-off, you should probably stay away.  If you need more details, well, they're forthcoming.
While the game is sweet, it's also very sad.  The reason the game's world is so sentimental is because the plot is about people who need idealistic stories like that to help them come to terms with the tragedies of reality.  There's a running theme of being distant from loved ones in some way, and seeking any way possible to close the gap.  And, well, heck, the game takes place primarily in a hospital.  What direction do YOU think the story is going to go?
So that covers tone, but is the story GOOD?  Well, I think the game accomplished its intended goals, and that's the only quality I can really measure.  Whether you like it or not really comes down to how you respond to the intensity of the emotions the game is going for.  If you don't embrace it for what it is, you're probably just going to be weirded out or even annoyed by all of it.  But if you're into it, let me tell you, once the game gets going, it does not let up.  Somehow the first time you're left sobbing on the floor isn't enough to prepare you for the two or three times it happens again right after that, even though you will see it coming.  Though to be fair, this doesn't describe the entire game; for the first 2/3rds of the game, you get plenty of breaks to dance around in sunshine and rainbows.  (Seriously, expect to see literal sunshine and rainbows in this game.  How is anyone still this idealistic in TYOL 2017?)
At this point, you may be wondering what the gameplay is like before making a decision on whether the game's right for you.  If so, then you should probably just go ahead and give it a pass.  This is not a gameplay-oriented game.  This is an RPG Maker adventure game without combat, that is to say, gameplay consists of walking around a map and talking to people.  You're given fetchquest-style tasks to fulfill, there's a few light puzzles here and there, there's some items to collect, but really most of that is just to help keep you awake in between the moments that you're talking to people.  If you've played any RPG Maker game like this, you'll know exactly what to expect from this one.  This is a game to play for the story and exploration, not the gameplay.
If you want another specific game to compare it to, I made the connection to To The Moon that a lot of other people seem to have made.  Very similar themes, except Rakuen covers more than just one person's story.
Oh yeah, and it's worth mentioning the music, since it really does stand out.  Music's important to me and I honestly miss the RPG soundtracks from the days of the SNES and the original Playstation, and playing this game absolutely made me feel like I was playing something like Legend of Mana over again.  Arguably you could say that's more of a review of the soundtrack than the game itself, but one of the things I'm specifically nostalgic for is being able to explore a town and talk to all the people in it while listening to memorable music to set the atmosphere, music that was more than just background filler, music with a heart and personality that matched the town I was exploring.  Thanks to Rakuen, I got to do that again.
That's about all I got, hopefully that's enough to make an informed decision.  In summary: Only SUCKAS don't play Rakuen!!!

BTW: If you have the character-stays-in-a-corner-and-won't-movet glitch (that is, sadly, an incredibly common problem all RPGmaker games suffer from), there are a few solutions you can try. Disable your Bluetooth adapters (Control Panel - Device Manager). Do a Google search for Cherry's kbdreset.exe program (resets your keyboard mapping). What worked for me, however, was to shut down the computer, unplug all USB devices (including the mouse and keyboard), turn on the computer and allow it to load completely before plugging in only the keyboard and mouse. (This is a suggestion from Celianna, a well-known RPGmaker pixel artist, that I found online after an hour of searching.) I hope that helps any of you who might experience this issue.

Your enjoyment of the game will be entirely dependent on having a good group to work with. Unless you're able to get into the game with people who are also starting fresh (or willing to make new characters and allow you to play a role you find interesting) you will not enjoy this game at all. There is virtually nothing you can do solo in this game; you NEED to be in a party of several people to accomplish almost anything beyond level 3.
Overall the game feels incredibly slow paced and is clearly outdated. Even setting aside the graphics, there are numerous bugs that feel like they just shouldn't exist in a game that has been around this long. Expect to have to restart the client at least once every couple of hours due to one issue or another. Nothing about this game flows together nicely.
The amount of free content is minimal, at best; you will end up having to grind quests just to continue leveling up, and the interface is littered with frequent reminders of the things you could pay for. Unless you have a VIP subscription ($10/month) you will have only about five quests you can do per level, which will not offer you enough experience to advance, forcing you to redo them for even less XP than you earned the first time. The only workaround is being carried  through the game by someone 2-3 levels above you who can unlock quests on a higher difficulty, but then you'll be doing little more than watching them solo the dungeon. It's not fun, and you'll never catch up to a point where you can actually start having fun with them.

This is actually a hard review to write. I've played DDO regularly for three years, and irregularly before that. The community is great, it has one of the friendliest and most welcoming player bases of any MMO I've joined. The game itself is a steaming mess of bad coding and half-written abandoned systems pasted over old half-written abandoned systems. Content is released with quest-breaking bugs that (more often than not) are not fixed even while it's still the newest release. There appears to be little to no revision control in place, as the few fixes that are implemented are regularly lost in future updates and never replaced.
The lead developer and his assorted team members all routinely admit to being unable to understand systems programmed by previous work teams, as well as not knowing the mechanics and how the game rules work.
That all said, the players are great, and if you ignore anything added after 2013, the content is very fun.

I haven't reviewed many games but looking at some of the recent negative comments I wanted to add my view here.
I strongly recommend this game for anyone who is interested in turn-based squad-level combat games or GW games in general.   There is a lot of strategic depth, many different effective ways to build warbands, and the different factions each have a unique flavor and are fairly well balanced.  While not a direct port of the table top, my impression is the changes make for a better game.
People complaining about the RNG are just complaining because of some bad luck, which does happen.  However, the campaign can be rough at first as there is no ramp-up or difficulty settings and the tutorials don't really prepare you for jumping in.   Opposing warbands always have similar point value to yours with bonuses to hp and damage based on the difficulty of that particular encounter.  Given that a new warband does not have any customization, this means apart from map difficulty your first mission may be your hardest.
Map difficulty does give a challenge later on and advanced players have come up with rule sets to make play more challenging, but it would be nice to have that option coded into the game.  It would also be nice to have a smarter AI ratehr than huge bonuses on the harder misssions.

The first thing you probably notice when first playing the game, is the amount of classes and the different mechanics they revolve around. The classes strike a balance between speed and sheer firepower, with the heavy being the slowest, but most damaging, the scout being the fastest, but having what is basically a BB gun as his primary means of defense. Most classes also have a distinct feature that seperates them; the medic, for instance, has a medkit that heals allies up to full health in one hit, and the pyro can stack afterburn with his three flame weapons, doing up to around 3 damage per second on top of his direct damage.
The second thing you notice is probably the sheer ramp in skill requirements. The biggest problem with getting into this game is the games that are usually populated are filled with people who've played it and/or Team Fortress Classic for years. As new players fill in it will get a little easier to get in games where you won't get destroyed. There is a good tutorial for movement, allowing new players to learn how to reach the high speeds required to play against other players.
The balancing between the classes feels better than TFC, at least to me. The medic isn't quite as able to be as fast as a similarly skilled scout, along with not being able to build jump-pads to allow his team to get to the frontlines faster. Stuff like this helps to keep the classes used more often, instead of being neglected.
The game is real competitive, and not for the faint of heart or anyone prone to keyboard smashing. New players will most likely find it hard to get into, especially without any previous experience with high speed shooters.
7.5/10

At its inception, the main concept behind Sonic the Hedgehog was speed; running quickly across a long, free-flowing area with the occasional obstacle and trick surface to destroy, jump over, activate, or perform a dazzling feat of acrobatics upon before rushing onward. Over time, optional objectives were added to the levels themselves, such as secret treasure troves of rings and portals to bonus levels. But these detours were just that: Optional. Nothing stopped you from just flying across the level in a blur of blue. The physics were smooth, and if you found yourself halted by an obstacle, a couple seconds saw you speeding away once again. At its most tedious and slow, the game saw Sonic jumping nimbly across a series of narrow panels or climbing a treacherous staircase of spikes. Such boxed-in moments were the exception, not the rule. This is where this installation falls short.
There is little-to-no freedom in this game, and the physics engine is sluggish and unforgiving. Sonic scarcely gets to run for more than a second or two before running headfirst into an almost vindictively-placed puzzle or enemy. It's as if he is being punished for moving quickly, which is, as Sega seems to have forgotten here, kind of the core concept of the series. Movement feels stilted and cramped, and more than once I've found myself stuck in a confusing puzzle for a minute or more. This is a large betrayal of what I as a fan expect out of a Sonic game. I don't want tedious corridors and teeming hordes of enemies around every corner, constantly halting my progress. I want to, as the famous lyrics go, "roll around at the speed of sound."
This issue is even present in the bonus levels. While the control system is novel (instead of controlling Sonic in an already-spinning stage, you spin the stage itself and Sonic moves accordingly), the combination of time limit, required ring collection, tricky labrynthian maneuvering, and the occasional EXIT block makes these stages more than unnerving than enjoyable. Compared to the tricky, fast-paced bonus stages of the older games, this can be extremely frustrating and difficult, especially when the Act leading up to said bonus stage is as tedious and stilted as previously described.
Of course, the problem is not the presence of obstacles; it is their frequency. This level of stop-and-go in this game is jarring to the point that, combined with underwhelming graphics and scoring (a notable positive factor in the majority of previous Sonic games), it hardly feels like a true sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles (one of the best platformers of all time, in my opinion). It feels more like an app one might buy off the iTunes store. A pleasant, if not slightly bland, diversion.
If you really feel the need to be a completionist and the game is on sale, go ahead and give it a try. In the end, it's still Sonic. You will do some dashing about, chain homing attacks across groups of enemies, fly through the air, and perform a few tricky maneuvers. The environments are colorful. The array of sound effects is an obvious homage to the old Genesis games, as is the style of the score. With a very positive disposition, you will feel like you're playing a classic Sonic game. But these positives are almost what makes the game so frustrating: It's close, but no cigar. It's quick, but stilted. It's a throwback, but lacks refreshing creativity.
If tedium is a peeve of yours, I would recommend giving this title a pass and moving on to its more successful sequel.

- Graphic is par with PS2 graphic
- Gameplay is fixed at 30 fps. Animations are tied to FPS (common issue with Japanese PC games)
- Very little and vague gameplay tutorial. You are pretty much left to discover everything by yourself
The main point of differentation of WotS series in general is gameplay repetition to unlock everything (swords, endings, etc.) as things, especially storylines, are usually mutually exclusive depending on decision you made. Each gameplay last upto 100 in-game days, but can be cut short for numerous reason (eg. you die).
Overall I still can recommend Way of the Samurai 3 despite its numerous issues. The gameplay and story on itself make the game worth through the troubles

I've been waiting a really long time for Rakuen. I fell in love with Laura Shigihara's music when I first played Plants vs Zombies almost a decade ago and have tried to follow her work ever since. I knew no matter what the outcome of the game she was working on, the music would be phenomenal. That's not to say I didn't expect great things from her across the board, but I definitely came into this thinking primarily of the music.
Of course, the music did not disappoint but I really can't get over how GOOD this game was!!! It's a beautiful game with charming, memorable characters. You can honestly feel how much love went into each and every part of the game from its maps to its sprite designs, to its carefully told story. The world is so colourful and lovely, you can't help but want to explore every nook and cranny. Every NPC has such funny or interesting things to say that you'll find yourself going back through every map over and over just to eke out every bit of dialogue and worldbuilding this game has to offer. The game is pretty short--in an (almost) 100% run, it only took me about 9 hours (be careful--there's some missable collectables that will trip you up in the end if you don't follow a walkthrough), but it's 9 hours well spent. It's just the right length and it manages to get its themes and ideas across perfectly well without dragging it out. (Although I certainly loved the game enough that I was getting melancholic as I reached the end because I knew my time in the game's world was coming to an end!)
And, like I said, the music is wonderful and it matches the game so well. You can really tell how much love went into it and I definitely bought my copy of the soundtrack before I'd even finished the game. :)
tl;dr - This was truly an inspiring game that was worth the wait. I highly recommend it to everyone.

The story is unique in that it wraps complex subjects like Dementia, long term Coma, and illnesses into a whimsical setting experienced through the eyes of a child, and it works.  Like To the Moon, the game focuses heavily in the character development over mechanical gameplay.  The main story is told through experiencing the backstories of several character you meet throughout the game; each with their own arcs complete with high and lowpoints.  The arcs takes you through a main overworld reality and a very stylized "alternate" reality; which, influence eachother at specific points throughout the game requiring the player to switch between them to solve certain puzzles.
Pros:
Neutral:
Cons:
All in all, I enjoyed my time in Rakuen.  Even at full price, it is a game worth picking up.
This game is absolutely incredible, if you're a fan of To The Moon, this game hits very similar emotional notes, but it's a few hours longer, prepare to cry your eyes out.

The good:
I love my Steam Link. I pretty much play PC games exclusively. All the AAA ports from console I have tried work great both with the Steam Controller, and with my wired 360 controller (Many of them are better than playing on PC since they have TV friendly GUI's, and controller friendly controls).  Also I have had great luck playing games that consoles could never dream of. I was even able to get non Steam games to work no problem. To play games that require a keyboard, and mouse you will need a Steam Controller. This is part of the genius of the whole setup. Steam has made it so you can easily program the controls giving them many complex bindings. They also make it so you can select from other users public bindings. Making most games as simple as looking through, and finding a controller config you like then selecting it making any adjustments that you want. I will also say that even though the recomend a wired conection I use mine wirelessly, and besides an ocasional spike in lag don't have the stuttering issues some have experienced. My home network has at times 10+ devices active at once.
The bad:
I won't say that I haven't had any bugs. I will say that with a little effort was able to make it work as intended. Two main issues I have encountered have been: I had an audio issue with my soundcard, and the fact that I had it setup for headphones. This issue seems to have been fixed by Steam, but even before they did I was able to find a work around. The other issue isn't so much a bug, but many PC focused games have UI's that don't scale flawlessly. The Steam Link has a feature that allows you to automatically scale to the TV's ideal resolution. I did have an issue trying to force the resolution on a non Steam game from the early 2000's. It works fine if I just adjust the resolution in the game options. The last issue you will have no matter how you link your PC to your TV in my experience. IMO The Steam Links built in features, and intergration with their own platform seem to offer very good results with minimum setup.
Bottom line:
Don't listen to the haters. The Steam Link is everything it claims to be.

The game is generally fairly enjoyable, if rough around the edges. The move tree builder is pretty interesting, the fact that you can make schools to give other people your move set for them to try/use. But there's a few glaring problems with the moves themselves, learning them is an outright chore. Either you need to get a friend to beat on you a bunch using those moves, or you need to run around for hours to get beat on by enemies where you'll hopefully learn some moves you'll use. Almost 7 hours in and I've only learned 3 moves out of the 70+ and they aren't really moves I even wanted. Meanwhile you have very few moves to start with, trying to PvP causes some serious problems, as most of the other people have been playing longer, so they have much more advanced movesets. So your choices are, hope you have a friend who will help you grind, grind through the PvE and hope you get some moves that you can use, or grind through PvP while at a hefty disadvantage.
There's also the gear problem, gear itself gives armor and weight. Armor reduces damage and weight lowers your mobility, which governs your dash distance, stamina regen, and damage on most attacks. Plenty of armor can be found from exploring, opening chests, and fighting NPCs, who will drop it randomly. You can also get it through PvP, after every PvP level you'll get a special Coin you can use to get a random piece of gear. It should be noted that each coin is at best two PvP wins at worst 5 PvP loses, most matches last anywhere from 3 to 6 minutes. The problem with this is the RNG is pretty heavy, I'm pretty sure I'm just unlucky, but out of the 6 coins I've only gotten gear that you start the game with, and a few duplicates at that.
It's frustrating, the combat is interesting and I really want to enjoy the combo making system, but I literally don't have the moves to do it.
Edit: Geez, I totally forgot about the story, probably because there isn't one. The story can literally be discarded and forgotten, there's almost nothing to it. With a friend's help, I was able to beat the story in around two hours.

I ADORE this game. It's arguably one of my favourite games of all time. Imagine Cities Skylines, but a beautiful, European city/town (based on their real life counterparts) is already completed and it's your job to build a public transport network. It was so ahead of its time, you can track individual cims through their commute and the attention to detail is incredible (every vehicle, animal, building etc. is simulated and can be examined, shows route if possible, background info etc.). You can build from the past (1900s) all the way to present and future times, and the vehicles and city structure reflect this. All the standard modes are here (I have all DLC, so not sure how many are in base game) - buses, trams, metro, ferry, helicopter/blimp, monorail (some maps), trolleycar (some maps).
You are given little missions to do along the way for rewards if you can like some structure, or you can go all out with total freedom and build a network with the widest coverage you can. Unlike Cities Skylines, stops actually show a radius for their coverage zone when building, you need to keep customers happy by running a good service (why don't they care at all in Skylines?), you can easily adjust the type/number of vehicles on a line and you need to take into consideration the pros/cons of each vehicle (fuel consumption, reliability, capacity etc.). It's not ridiculously easy like Skylines and you do need to build good routes (hey, just like real life!).
Get the DLC if you can afford (I'd argue it's necessary), be wary this game is resource intensive and install a few mods (manually, no Steam Workshop here) - must haves are ones that increase vehicle capacity to realistic amounts, or add a first person camera/more camera options to follow your little buses/trains around the city - see the guides for this game and also the Cim Exchange Steam Group. And avoid CiM2! Enjoy :)

There's two ways to look at Cities in Motion.  I could review the game as it was at the time, or the game as it is now.    Now I don't mean patches but rather the landscape as well.
The thing is in neither way can I recommend this game, It's not a "OMG this game is awful" game, but it falls into a common problem of games.  Ultra complex game/systems that don't properly inform the player what they are doing or what is going wrong.   The fact is Cities in Motion might be as complex as a game like Simcity, and that's not a problem.  In fact for a simulation game, you should aim to make this complex as possible.
But there's a problem, where Simcity has a LOT of conversations, complaints and warnings to warn the player when things are going bad, and that's required for this type of complexity.  This game... well there's probably screens that will inform you of these things, but often times when things are going bad... you won't know it until you're in a catastrophe.    Coupled with no autosave, this isn't a good thing.
The bigger problem I have with this game is that it's often VERY stubborn to do anything.  Now this looks like Simcity, but it's not.  You control the public transportation NOT the city itself, you're a transport company.  Interesting Idea, but let's try to do something simple, like make a tram line between A and B?  Unless they are in the same road it's really annoying to draw the line as it feels like if you draw too far the game decides it can't make the line any more.  I'd have loved a way to simple paint on the map, and while it tries to do it, it's frustrating.    Really I want a point A to point B, the game should make it happen to make the gameplay easier for the user.  Since it doesn't all the user gets is a frustration.
Trying to make "Lines" (transportation lines) is a similar problem.  You need to make a complete loop for a transportation line, which means you MUST click on the original location after clicking on all the others.  The downside you also need to watch the direction, the path, and hope the path doesn't do something remarkably dumb.  And that's assuming a full circular path can be made.  if it can't, it silently fails.
But then after you make the path you're good to go?  Well ... sure, but people start getting mad if they are waiting too long at your stops.  Now this could have been solved by something like a "Suggestion box" or a place where you could see simple complaints.  But instead you get a slow ticker that is taking up a small amount of the space.  And even when you see it, the solution is nebulous.  There's a ton of people at this stop on your Line 3.  Great, but what's the solution?  Likely it's more buses, but what if there's two or three lines that stop there, sometimes you add more buses, the problem goes away and then the buses go unused.   Issues like this come up quite often, and I HATE when there's a problem because it stops me from trying to develop a really good transport system.
Actually it does more.  It makes me not want to TRY to develop a transport system.  Screw those people, there's other games I can play.  Games where I can make my own city.   Man I'd love to play a game like that.
And now we come to the true problem with this game.  Well there's a sequel and ... honestly not a fan of either game for the same reasons, BUT there's cities:skylines.  You remember Simcity the online travesty that EA put out?  Remember how everyone just wanted a simple game but EA tried to make it online and now we may never see a Simcity.  Well Cities: skyline is the answer.  It has a few issues (similarly it can be frustrating at times to make those perfect city blocks) but the game is AMAZINGLY fun.  It's what Simcity could have and should have been.    But at the same time, I feel it is a FAR better game than Cities in Motion, if you want a Simcity game.
If you are sitting there saying "But I want to play a transportation company." ok, well honestly why aren't you already playing this game.  If you WANT to play just the transportation company, this is a decent game, but only because that is such a niche that I don't think anyone will compete with this.   If however you want to play a simcity type game, there's a far better one out there, and I highly recommend Cities: Skylines.  But I honestly can't recommend Cities In Motion to anyone who wants anything other than ONLY a transportation game, and even then I don't think it's worth it.
Still the good news is this game lead to Cities:Skyline, same company just an expanded game, and as such I will make the suggestion to go grab that game, instead of this.

My childhood, rests right here. Don't let the title fool you, this is Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis. One of the first milsims of it's time. A decently groundbreaking game back in it's day, with a strong cult following.
It has been renamed as such after the scummy devs from Codemasters fully acquired the rights to the title from Bohemia Interactive, and ruined the franchise to hell and back realising they don't have the "Czech touch" to games like this, spawning awful games such as Dragon Rising and Red River, which weren't QUITE generic cawadooty CQB shooters, but were basically casualised versions of the former games.
Naturally this game got later rebranded after Bohemia released ARMA, the spiritual successor to OpFlashpoint. It lacks one of the expansions, Red Hammer, due to it's partial ownership to Codemasters, but it's easily downloadable and works fine.
My childhood of dicking about in the world editor, spawning in yourself with jets and jeeps to roam the huge islands, and slavic inspired villages, brings a tear to my eye to this day. Naturally this game is even better on LAN or with something like Evolve w/ friends.
Sure, you could buy Arma 3 and tack on hundreds of mods and play in Zeus (which is pretty great by the way), but this is where it all began. Good for a laugh at the primitive graphics or if you want to take a trip down memory lane, and take it for granted.
10/10 buy it now, it's not even that expensive. Buy on sale, or you can buy a certain package with Arma 3 that gives you this game for free. (as a giftable copy, too!)

I have played several of the choose-your-own-adventure stories from the "Choice of Games" series, but this one seems to have touched me the most.  Like with the rest of the games from this series, there lies an complex interplay of character relationships and political factions that provides a wide array of responses and skillsets to help create your persona.  For example, on my first playthrough I played the part of a pacifist medical specialist that chose to partake in the Resistance's efforts to create a more balanced government, but retaining my humanity by saving all my former allies and those that required help.  It felt like all my choices matter, and that there were multiple strengths to build your character across is a plus.  However, it would have been great for an option to choose the gender of your character, as the game automatically assumes that you are playing as a man, which can take people out of the narratice if using a female persona.
Other than that, the story world of this game is great and encompasses many different morally grey areas. A central focus on the game's lore revolves around a group of people known as "the sun-touched", who possess the ability to drain or give life force to other people.  Through this ability, the sun-touched and the vampiric "light-eaters" have created a feudal society at the expense of treating commoners as nothing more than cattle and serfs.  On the other hand, your country Mercia has broken away from such worship and have ushered a technological revolution, with all the pros and cons that they entail, with constant pleas for labor reform and unions.  In fact, the situation can be viewed as so abhorrent that a Resistance has formed to express the discontent of the working class which amounts to a lot of vigilante justice, sabotage, and outright terrorism.  Of course, as the main character, you are one of the sun-touched in hiding, and it is up to you to choose whether or not to develop these latent abilities or master something else entirely.  The friends and lovers that you make, the factions that constantly vie for each other's power and influence, will certainly provide enough intrigue to last a good few hours.
As a result, I would highly recommend this game to people who love a good story due to its longevity and cheap cost.

The game LOOKS fantastic. The basic platforming is adequate. The real attraction of this game is the magic marker, which works SORT OF (very big emphasis on "sort of") like Okami in that it lets you draw things into reality that you can use to overcome obstacles.
The magic marker is an interesting idea that is not very interesting in execution. You can only draw lines when and where the game has predetermined that you are able to draw lines. And you have no control over the kind of thing that you draw, because the game decides that too. It is literally like the game saying, "Now you will draw a vine right here." And you do, because that's all you CAN do. That, in a nutshell, is how the magic marker works. Sometimes there are situations that are somewhat puzzling, but the game always gives away the solution by having the blabbermouth protagonist just flat out tell you how to do it.
The thing that really turned me off on it, though, and decide that I wasn't going to play it anymore, is the way the game spams the abitrary "think fast" type situations. I would have been fine playing it to completion if it were just a sort of platforming adventure with some magic marker puzzles. But as you are making your way through a level, the game likes to suddenly throw a random "think fast" hazard at you, where you have to figure out what you need to do to avoid the hazard in just a few seconds or die and go back to the previous checkpoint. These are made worse by the way the game hijacks and repositions the camera to show you the incoming hazard, so you are also disoriented in addition to needing to think fast. And there is an element of these "think fast" hazards being completely arbitrary, because sometimes the glowing objects you can use via your magic marker don't even APPEAR until the instant the "think fast" hazard appears. This results in most of these moments feeling ill-considered and frustratingly punitive. You know the kind. The trial-and-error, die-repeatedly-until-you-guess-what-the-developer-wants-you-to-right-here type of rigamarole. Apparently most players who picked up this title are cool with it, but it is a HUGE pet peeve of mine. I have very little tolerance for it.
In the end it is a beautiful looking game with adequate platforming, a draw mechanic that is an interesting idea but not very interesting in execution, and (in this player's opinion) a sorry overuse of arbitrary "think fast" moments and chase/forced-momentum sequences.
There is some good to be found here, but it just tends to overuse too many things that are not to my taste and completely turn me off, so I probably will not finish it.
Final verdict:
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is worth full price.
6) A good game that is worth the full price.
5) A pretty good game worth checking out--especially if discounted.
4) A fairly good game, but I'd recommend buying it discounted.
2) Only worth checking out if you are dangerously curious.
1) Avoid at all costs.

I went into this game really expecting to like it. As someone who greatly enjoyed To The Moon, I thought that Rakuen would be perfect for me. However, despite the game's best efforts, it ultimately is crushed under the weight of its own ambition and feels more like a tedious slog than a journey through the highs and lows of the human condition.
It may not be fair to compare Rakuen to To The Moon, but unfortunately the developer opens itself up to criticism when its main selling point is that it is a "To the Moon inspired game." Interstingly enough, the game falls flat on its face whenever it tries to be its own game. To the Moon's gameplay was essentially non-existant, which ended up making it a super tight experience that focused solely on narrative. Rakuen, on the other hand, adds a series of puzzles and quests that feel more tedious than anything else.
These puzzles break up an otherwise excellently written and engaging story that I would love to experience on its own. These gameplay segments are so breathtakingly boring that I ended up stopping halfway threw a chapter because a puzzle demanded that I memorize chess pieces - no really. The game expected me to remember the exact location of chess pieces on a chess board.
Another problem the game suffers from is that it tells its story from two perspectives: one grounded in reality and one grounded in fantasy. The original setting takes place in a hospital, which serves as a perfect backdrop for the very real and serious issues that each character must face. Unfortunately, the drama is severely undercut when Rakuen chooses instead to tell these stories in the fantasy world where people are replaced with humanoid cat creatures and cartoon grizzly bears. I get how the fantasy backdrop is suppose to lessen the severity of the issues but it ends up only softening the emotional gut punch that is the main attraction to these types games.
TL;DR Buy To the Moon instead or play it again if you already have it.

Hello. I'm here to review Absolver.
If you couldn't tell...
Let's get started.
Story first.
Alright, the story isn't great. (Minor spoilers ahead, by the way.) You'll start the game, create your character, go through a cutscene and that's all for a while. Yes, you'll get some dialogue telling you who to kill, some minor hints, and some semi-cryptic stuff. Cut and dy, basically. There's some backstory that you can Google if you want to, but nothing real major. After you kill all the Marked Ones, all the bosses, you'll then get into a tower and climb. Once at the top, you'll meet a pretty scary lady who kills a guy. You fight her and (hopefully) win. Then you're an Absolver with a really heavy cloak that, once I got, I didn't wear. It's not the best story, but it's fairly decent.
Graphics/art style second.
The game looks beautiful. For me, atleast. The different graphics settings don't really make a difference. Anyways, the art style looks amazing and I can't say enough good things about it. It's not realistic or just beautiful by graphic power, but it's great in it's own right. There is a bad thing which really needs to be fixed though. The motion blur. You can't turn it off. I've even tried to go into the game files and turn it off. It's a pretty bad problem, but hopefully the devs will add the option.
Gameplay third.
Imagine this: you rush to the right to avoid a jab to your face, then duck down to dodge a high kick, then you drop down on a knee and punch someone in the stomach. It's amazing and better than the art style. It's smooth and easy to use. At the same time though, it's hard to really be good at it. You may get good, but there will always be someone better. Cheating is a problem though. As with the motion blur, I hope the devs fix it.
Other notes:
Game's sorta short, but it can be played alot.
Matchmaking is kinda bad, but I expect 3v3s to be more balanced.
The community won't attack you often.
The game will expand though, if the recent update notes have anything to say about it.
Deluxe is alright. The art book will be something I'll take advantage of more, as an artist myself.
Well thank you for reading this review, hopefully you'll atleast give it a try and if you don't like it, you can refund it.
