Vagante is an oddly fun and addictive game for how simple it is. It suffers from the usual rogue-like problems where RNG dictates a LOT of the game (gear, map layouts, shrines, etc) but usually you can work with whatever the game gives you anyway.
The Good:
-Diverse Ways to Play. Vagante not only has 4 classes to play, but they can be played in multiple ways. You can play this game for hours and rarely have the same playstyle happen twice in the same sitting.
-Abundance of Danger w/o Being Unfair. This game has spikes and crushing traps that will kill you intantly, not to mention tons of arrow traps and mobs to wittle your health down. However as long as you pay attention and take your time, they are nothing more than keeping you on your toes. Relax too much, and you die.
-Bosses. The bosses are optional big bad guys in each floor. They give you a full level and a key to open a big chest for phat lewts. I have not experienced the new Catacomb bosses yet, since the Catacombs have been owning my butt since they revamped them, but the 7 before the catacombs are very fun and challenging fights. Except the Golem Boss...screw him lol.
-Tight Controls. Much like Spelunky, i never feel like the games' controlling mechanics screwed me over. Every time i died, i knew it was my own fault and not the game.
The Bad:
-Bad or Useless Skills. Some of the skills you can learn when you level up are just total trash. This isnt a huge problem, since its only a glaring issue for a couple of the dozens of builds you can do, but its a problem nontheless.
-RNG for the Wrong Class. Sometimes this happens to me where i'll play a Warrior and get Wand/Book drops left and right. Now, you should have access to everything, but i really wish it would lean more towards gear meant for that class (i.e. swords have a higher drop rate and wands have a lower drop rate as a warrior)
-Useless Gear. Due to the way the Skills work, some gear are useless by default. Things like hammers or maces will literally never be useful to a Warrior, which makes no sense.
-Instant Kill Blade Traps. Catacombs in the old days were more of a placeholder than an actual level. Since theyve been revamped, they are now brutal - and i mainly blame the overabundance of instantdeath traps. Spikes are one thing, but the 10 blade traps one after another while im trying to dodge a jumping Hand is just too much. Really wish they'd be toned down a bit.
-Golem Boss. This is the only boss i have a problem with. He swings VERY rapidly and hits REALLY hard (20-28 per hit) not to mention he chucks boulders that hit just as hard with uncanny accuracy. You'd think something thats suppose to be a living rock wouldnt be so fast or accurate. The crushing thing makes total sense, and that usually never happens unless youre just ballsy stupid anyway. But he can shave your health off REEAAALLLY fast and its hard to land even a single hit without getting whacked at some point.
Overall: 8/10. The game is still early access, but even as it is the game is very fun and addictive. With the exception of the Blade Trap thing i mentioned, all of my quirks can usually be ignored due to the RNG system being in your favor.

Pros:
* Graphics are very good for a platformer, both for character movements and for cutscenes.
* Movements are swift.
* Plot is simple, but ok.
Cons:
* Too simple: just keep moving, everywhere where you need to "draw" something is clearly visible in the game so you need almost no thinking.
* Control: you move with keyboard and, when you get to a place where you have to "draw" something, you have to position your mouse again. Not an issue when you are not in a hurry, but sometimes the baddies are pursuing you. As I said, this game would have made lots more of sense in a touchscreen.
So? If you find it discounted (5€-6€) and you sometimes like simple games to have some relaxing playtime, it may be a good purchase. If not, probably it is not what you are looking for.

Do not let 'free' colour your perceptions of how good a game this can be. While Steam is a sea of shoddy free to play games, this is one of the ones that floats above the rest.
Each character has their own personality, with each route featuring unique scenarios while following key plot points - each of which can and do change depending upon which route you choose. This makes each route interesting in its own right, despite the overarching goal being the same. The game does not shy away from being hard on characters. Background characters have their own stories, and even some 'faceless' characters have reasonable personality and worth here. Not everyone adores the Princess, and it's easy to see why from the start. She has a personality that is deeper than what's on the surface, but is believeably unlikeable for honest and realistic reasons.
Change is not instant. It's gradual and commented upon. She never starts out with the goal of falling in love, rather the emotion develops naturally over the course of the characters' time spent with one another. Two-dimensional it is not, which is quite a lot to say compared to many games that cost money.
The writing is good. Solid, in my opinion and I feel didn't ever feel particularly awkward. The choice of music is excellent and often fit the moods of the scenes. Just as a free game can be good, the choices made from royalty-free music was also very well done.
The game's artwork is beautiful, though some of the CGs suffered from some awkward and sometimes stiff poses. The sprites themselves were top-notch and the colours were all wonderful.
I enjoyed much of the story and many of the routes - both good and bad. I preferred some over others, and even while I admit to not liking one or two of the stories, that isn't to say that they were poorly-done. They simply didn't appeal to me. Overall, however, I really enjoyed every one in some form or other, at least in part.
All in all this is one of the games I shove at people who are looking to try out an otome VN on their own. It's a solid play and very enjoyable.

The Journeyman Project 1 was the very first game I've ever player, so I knew I'll be picking this one up as soon as it gets released. I remember reading about PP way back then (around 1996, methinks), and being incredibly hyped about it - after all it was a remake of the game from my childhood. And then it happened - the game was only released for Macs and PSX (in Japan), so my chances of playing the title I've waited so long for, were pretty much zero. And suddenly in 2014 a PC-compatible Pegasus Prime was released on GOG, and now, in 2017, a Steam port also joined the family. I could finally experience the game I always wanted to play.
Playing Pegasus Prime today is like revisiting your old hometown after several years - things have moved on, some places were built, other demolished, yet everything feels so familiar, welcoming and nostalgic. This is the exact feeling I have while playing PP.
Simply put - it's THE adventure game, now available for our modern machines! The "lost" features of the Japanese PSX version have been restored. It features two difficulty modes, depending on how you want to play. Multiple save slots. The AI commentary, including our beloved Arthur (though you need to find him first!). Updated locations and new puzzles. Cheesy (but in a delightful way) and nostalgic 90's acting. And, of course, the time travel plot and the general world design. It's all here man, it's all here.
Of course it's not perfect, as some people may be irritated by the control scheme, the interface (though there is an overview tutorial, which explains a lot of things), no windowed-mode option, frequent backtracking and unforgiving character deaths (save often!). However, if you played the original, or just want to experience a damn solid late 90's first person perspective adventure game (as well as a damn solid remake), Pegasus Prime is for you.
Now hoping for TJP2 and TJP3 to receive the same Steam treatment!

One of the first games I've ever played, in its definitive form (sure, the original's charm is there, but it's just way too clunky now to play, and this version ties in better with the rest of the series), The Journeyman Project: Pegasus Prime is a very good example of the 90's Myst-like first person adventure games combined with a well written plot and an interesting setting.
Exploration and puzzle solving are its core strengths. While it can be argued that the constant backtracking through multiple time zones to retrieve an item you need in another, or to use a newly acquired item in a previously visited location can get tiresome (since given you're returning to the same exact point in time, all the previous progress through the location is undone), it adds to the setting and idea of jumping back and forth thru time trying to fix everything. Concepts like Gandhi bonuses (whether you deal with the antagonists violently or non-violently) and different puzzle solutions add up to the replay value, which in this particular release is also helped by the various achievements you can get, some of them pretty obscure and/or difficult to unlock.
Working against it are the limited inventory, and the game's decision to automatically discard a "non essential item" that can leave you without an actually important item depending on the specific route you take, wasting time and forcing you to do even more backtracking. Thankfully, due to time travel, any item can be reacquired in the same way you previously did (unless it came from another timezone...), so there's actually no way to get permanently stuck. Another potential flaw are some cheap, Sierra-style deaths that sometimes can make no sense, but since the game allows you to continue immediately from where you were the impact is lessened. Lastly there are some vehicle steering sections that feel forced and unnecesary overall. Puzzles can also get irritating (especially the last one), but the AI companion usually does a good job helping you overcome them, even if she can be a bit annoying from time to time. (There's an easter egg you can find that gives the option to silence her, or more accurately, replace her...)
The acting and overall sound design can be cheesy at times, but considering this is a game from the 90's, that's actually par for the course.
As a final point, while it involves time travel, none of the locations you visit save for a very short one are actual historical locations: they are all in various times during the setting's future (present day being 2318), so that can be a bit disappointing for anyone hoping to travel through the Middle Ages or something. The series takes care of this particular problem in the next two installments.
It's not a flawless game. I wouldn't even go as far as to say it's the best adventure game to come out of the 90's. But it IS an interesting, fun and well thought adventure, and for any sci fi fan, I believe it's a must play.

Pros: Its full of Nostalgic goodness as well as being something new to me (i never owned a mac so i never got to enjoy this remake when it originally came out.) It has Adveneture mode which allows you to experience all the game and walkthru which removes some of the elements to make the experience more casual.
Cons: Compared to what we have today the graphics would be considered horrible (my friends saw me playing and looked at it then began commenting on "how old" it looked. I have also had some weird crashes that just kind of appear out of the blue so save often.
I'm not in this for the Graphics though, I'm here for the story.
A more detailed critique:
I remember the original game tha came on my family's Packard computer back in the late 90's.  It was known as Jounreyman Project Turbo and i played it every chance I got.  I remember looking over every detail trying to find clues and rubbing every item in my inventory over everything always looking for secrets.  This was the game that got me into the "point and click" genre of gaming.
The story is somewhat unique as it similar to Quantum Leap with the "putting right what once went wrong" theme, however you are not lost in time in a broken time travel experiment. Instead you play as a security agent who's purpose is to safe-guard time against anything or anyone who tries to change it.
Now as I mentioned earlier, this is a remake, the major difference between the two besides the original using still images and the remake using something like pre-rendered interactive video. Another difference that it also includes a larger cast (the same cast that appeared in the sequels just not in the original). there are also other subtle differences like adding in and removing of some puzzles as well as greatly expanding the areas you can explore and of course, changing the solutions to some of the puzzles which threw me off when i started playing. This of course made me enjoy the experience more as my memory betrayed me.
Now for the one thing that, while i absolutly loved this character in the sequels, felt bizzarly betrayed by the inclusion of Arthur in the remake.  For those of you who don't know who Arthur is, I'm only going to tell you that you meet him in the sequel "Buried in Time" and he acts as an informative comic relief. While he is an easter egg in the remake and somewhat easy to find, i was kind of hoping that he would have new dialogue and be at least extremly entertaining. Well he wasn't, not that i didnt find myself snickering at his dialogue, its just that i heard it before as it is the same things he says in the sequels all chopped up to make what he says a little more relivant to what you are doing (i will admit that he is less annoying than the AI that noramally assists you in the game).  I will admit there are some moments where he does say something I don't remember him saying in the sequels but i can't help but think now that they could have been things that ended up getting cut out out of the sequels (i find it hard to believe as the creaters left in about 10 minutes of him joking about a hairy rug in "Legacy of Time" that still makes me laugh when i think about it).  I mean I understand his inclusion to help sell the product and maybe give a nod to the fans of the series but it all felt a little "phoned in" by Presto if you get my drift.
In conclusion I feel the game is worth getting, it has good story, the gameplay is a little trial and error, and it's a great game for killing time.

pros: runs stable (most importantly), multiple save files (much needed!), access to hints by selecting the AI chip, 90's cheese soundtrack (remastered) & voice acting (some of the original content with some new), "interface overview" in main menu displays key bindings, lethal & nonlethal options against enemies, upgraded textures compared to the original game
cons: cinematics are stuck at 15fps, random fps drops, unforgiving instant death scenarios (a lot of trial-and-error so prepare for a lot of save-and-load), no windowed full-screen option, RNG color puzzle on mars, hit-or-miss on the final puzzle
Overall, a PC classic for anyone looking to experience some nostalgia. For anyone new to the game - I would encourage looking at the key mapping first, exercise frequent saves on multiple files, & you will need to time travel at different timelines (usually more than once) to acquire items that allow you to progress. I bought & completed this steam release on day one (7-20-2017) to re-experience this game when I was a young kid during the 90's sitting in front of my family's first PC on windows 95. Nostalgia achieved.
Journeyman Project: Pegasus Prime has my recommendation, a PC gaming classic!

Original review:
Ughhhh... you'd think I'd have learned from Way of the Samurai 4 that Acquire and Ghostlight are terrible with PC ports... sadly it seems that much like them, I have much to learn.
Now I loved Way of the Samurai 3 on the 360, it was my overall favorite of the series- 4 had some nice improvements, but as a whole 3 is my favorite, so naturally I was excited when I saw it was seeing a release on Steam... though also reluctant since 4 was pretty glitchy, though after a while they patched it so that it was at least playable (finally adding controller support was nice). So I figured I'd wait a bit until after launch before getting this one, thinking they'd have already patched it... shame about that though.
Enter Way of the Samurai 3, I've managed to play for about 2.5 hours of mostly dicking around getting money and not bothering much with triggering events since I wanted to get a better sword ASAP... it's just a shame that it suddenly crashed when I loaded one of the areas I've been to a dozen times already- ok, no problem, I saved fairly recently... it's just a shame that the game crashes whenever I try to load that save, so I've already lost all my progress. I suppose it's fortunate that I've only put less than 3 hours into it, but add insult to injury it now also crashes whenever I try to start a new game so now I can't do anything besides load up the main menu and think of what could be if I could actually play the damn game.

Steam Link, amazing.
Nvidia Shield, not so much.
Both these products claim to do the same thing, and the Nvidia Shield does do what it says, but all the normal arguments aside here's my biggest gripe with the Nvidia Shield compared to the Steam Link.
Controller deadzones, and input latency.

The Nvidia Shield on the other hand.... not so much. I'm very picky when it comes to these kind of things (IT guy here) and both the input latency, and the deadzones are literally unacceptable on the Shield.
On the Link however, they're awesome. I can finally play my steam library, ANY game, including FPS, and twitch type games (Super Meat Boy, Rogue Legacy, Shovel Knight, etc) with no input lag. Oh yeah, got the link for $5 on BF, jesus this thing is so worth it.
If you do happen to need the best inhome media player, especially now with Google Voice integrated, the Shield is the way to go, it smokes every other streaming device, and I've tested more then a fair handful.

It’s 1619, you’re a guy named Raleigh who’s been busted for your nefarious ways and sentenced to death by the King of England.  You’re not ready to go out like that though; you still have a lot of life in you.  So, you set out for the colonies to make a name for yourself by doing something heroic to put yourself back in the king’s favor.  You set your sights on the lost colony of Roanoke where surely you can become a hero in the war against the Spanish and nab yourself a reprieve on that execution thing.  Except…the colonies, they’re on Mars.  And the Spanish, they fight alongside the Martian Overlords.  And you, you’re going to take them all on with your retro-futuristic wooden sky jet-ski armed with lasers!
I know, it sounds nutty right?  It certainly is.  The story plays directly to fans of science fiction though, especially if you’re a fan of things such as “John Carter of Mars”.   Thankfully, this shoot-em-up packs in plenty of action to spice things up and screens full of bullet hell that will keep you on your toes.  The controls are tight enough to make these moments of on screen chaos manageable.   There are times where Jamestown feels like it might be a bit of an easy mode for the classic shmup fan; Raleigh’s hitbox is very tiny and you’ll find yourself getting away with moves that you know shouldn’t be able to.  The game still manages to be a great time though and the story is so far out there, it feels worth pushing through the levels just to find out where they’re going with Sir Raleigh of Mars.

This is seen in the individual levels, but also in the way Jamestown gates content: you can only play on the easier settings in the early missions - you have to improve in order to unlock the later story missions by beating missions on harder difficulty levels.  Because the gameplay itself is fun, this wasn't a frustration to me, it was a challenge that I was happy to accept.  There are also optional challenges you can complete after the main story content is over, if that's your thing.

Oh, Empire! How I hate loving you. I have ploughed many hours in to this game, and honestly I'm not sure why. Actually I am sure why: long, very long, turn times. Even on decent hardware it takes an age for AI factions to complete their turns, which often kills any enjoyment early in a campaign, and as with most campaigns you will want to play through to the year 1800 for victory, that means 200 long waits. If you're in for the long hall, bring some work with you, or just have a kettle nearby as you'll have plenty of time to get on with other things or make a nice cup of tea while you wait.
That being said, I have enjoyed this game. I love the time period, and it is certainly ambitious as the campaign allows you to battle over multiple continents and grow a truly global empire for your faction. Being British, I also loved the addition of naval combat and the chance to role out First Rate Ships-of-the-Line and wreak merry mayhem across the seas. There is a lot to like about deploying your troops to America and slashing through hordes of Native Indian tribesmen, or establishing a trading post in India and then having to repulse waves of marauding Mughals as you try to set up your tea plantations and secure your trade routes. However, there is also a lot not to like about useless AI that really can't handle large infantry formations, weirdly missing features (such as a family tree, or commanders with personality), uninteresting siege battles, and odd bits that should never have made it passed the Beta testing, like the fact that you can't repair damaged city defenses.
All of these can be fixed with Mods (DarthMod being the go-to), and there is enough here to warrant a recommendation, but it is a close call. The Creative Assembly team dropped many balls with this one, and showed the kind of complacency that reared its ugly head again in Rome II. I do hope they re-visit this time period, and ultimately this game with a Napoleon Total War facelift would be fantastic. If you want to enjoy truly global empire building then dive in, but at a low price as the game is likely to frustrate. However, if you need more polish in the same historical setting, then I recommend heading for the far more reliable Napoleon Total War.

The reason I would not recommend this game is because of the random number generator the game uses for the various tasks your characters perform.  I am not sure if others have had the problems I have, but at least for me, during each and every mission there would be streaks of terrible luck.  There would be six to seven tests in a row where the "80%" or higher chances would fail.  This was not an occasional thing, this was an every mission thing, and almost always took me from having the edge in a mission to either just succeeding or failing miserably.  I played dozens of missions, and these streaks would pop up in every single one.  In addition, though I always equipped my leader with the best parrying weapon and shield combo I could find, I did not make a single parry test the entire time I played, despite there being a "50%" or higher chance to block... and again, I will state that I played dozens of missions, each of which my leader would be hit multiple times while attempting to block.
I do not mind difficult games, I enjoy a challenge, but this did not feel like a challenge.  This was me being (rightfully) punished for tiny mistakes I made, but then being screwed over by the random number generator when I was doing everything right.  I would make tactically sound decisions only to have them blow up in my face- not just occasionally, but EVERY. SINGLE. MISSION. I. PLAYED.  Again, I am not sure if others have this problem as well, but from my experience this game needs either a re-work of their random number generator or a more realistic statement of the odds on a given action.

The soundtrack is wonderful and while it probably won't win any awards, it fits the game perfectly and it was a joy to listen to. I got plenty of genuine laughs from the scenarios that occured in the fantasy world and had plenty of tear jerking moments. The ending hit me so hard I actually couldn't stop crying as the credits were rolling. I think anyone who has dealt with a relative or a close friend who had a long term illness will get more out of the story due to being able to relate to it.
Some of the main problems I have with the game is that it feels at times tonally inconsistent in it's gameplay. You start out doing basic adventure game stuff, i.e finding items, seeing what people want, trying to solve problems, etc. This is how it plays for the first hour or so with no real emotinal punches before  it really gets into the meat of it which is helping and dealing with the problems of the other patients in the hospital. This is where the game gets sad in the story, and inconsistent in how it tells it.
Without spoiling any of the details, the first one you have to go through feels radically different from the others. Going inbetween a completely twisted version of the hospital full of puzzles and enemies, which also gives you details on what has happened in the real world, and with a parallel story taking place in the fantasy world; it works incredibly well in telling an original story. The twisted hospital feels oppressive and creates fear and anxiety with what is happening in the story, through it's gameplay. The main problem is that this is the only part of the game that feels like that.
The second you go through an abandoned house, with no where near the same atmosphere. Still similar puzzles but the oppressive atmosphere is gone. This could be fine if they didn't completely abandon it for the rest of the stories. The 3rd's "puzzles" mostly take place in the fantasy world, completely removed from the character's actual story. This portion while funny and entertaining, it was topped of with what just amounted to cutscenes to tell the story of what happened to the hospital patient. The 4th takes it even further and mostly relegates it to cutscenes with very little gameplay. The shift in storytelling feels bad due to the fact that the first one was more powerful due to how it's told. Being in a hospital is scary. Being sick is scary. Going through that and the catharsis you can get at the end of the first section felt good and you don't really get that in the later ones. It's just cutscenes, and while they are good cutscenes, it makes me upset that the first part was done better.
While this above portion sounds incredibly negative, please don't let that deter you. The game designer in me just got a little upset because it could have been better. This game feels incredibly heartfelt and should 100% be played.
Took me around 5 hours and 30 minutes to beat.

Just finished my first full playthrough.  This is by one of the authors of Choice of Romance (Affairs of the Court), and if you enjoyed that writing style -- intrigue, drama, mysteries, complex plots with great payoffs, and deftly-written characters with a lot of emotional veracity -- this will be exactly the kind of Choice of Game/Hosted Game you're looking for.  In comparison to that earlier work Study in Steampunk is a tad more predictable if you know the basic outlines of the most popular Sherlock Holmes stories, but there are still a lot of other unexpected elements thrown in, and the characters are really fantastic.  For me this is the most important point: I tend to judge CoGs on good characters and good roleplaying choices.  This is a game where just about every time I wanted to say X to a character or respond in Y way to a development, there X and Y were exactly on the menu, which tells me it's been well thought out in a way some games just aren't.  It's also got a pretty good length to it -- some Choice of Games may leave you feeling wanting despite a superficially impressive word count, but this one is truly long and substantial.  This is the most enjoyable CoG I've played in years and I really can't recommend it enough.  The only real flaw in my mind is the lack of ability to play as female, but don't worry, you can still romance men if you want ;)

Disclaimer: If you don't care for the CYOA genre, go ahead and keep walking. I don't waste my time picking on all the pretty tech demos out there; you shouldn't waste your time trying to take some of the most interesting adventure games off Steam just because they're in plain text.
That being said, if you love spies, gamebooks, RPGs, Sherlock Holmes, Victoriana, steampunk, and layers of conspiracy wrapped in morally grey death magic, this is perfect for you. It's also very well-balanced as a CYOA: you don't have to juggle overly complex stats or story, but neither of those things are watered-down until they're pointless or boring, and as far as I can tell, your choices and skills have a very solid influence on the story.

This game is amazing. There are many problems but all in all it's so worth it.
The engine and controls are clunky, the graphics are attrocious (understandably) but it doesn't matter because once you get into it it's so immersive.
So to keep this from dragging on, the gameplay is awesome, it's realistic (as far as a game of this age can go) so one too many shots and you're dead. If you get into an engagment and take hits it's pretty much over, you really need to be the one with the better position or be the one who fires first. This makes tactics extremely important for example positioning yourself, knowing when the move when to stay put, when to fire and when to hold. It could all mean the difference between them getting a few shots off and that'll spell you're end.
And the missions are extremely varied, the story is naf but the missions range from 1-3 men late at night blowing up an entire base (stealth and tactical). Mass infantry+armor operations to attack towns and villages. Helicopter transport/attack etc missions. Tank crew missions (which are awesome fun but take time to get good at) and even more than this. It's seriously awesome.
So i would no doubt recommend this game, it's incredible and I still have fun playing it this long after it was made. The one draw back i should point out is the checkpoint system as you can only save once per mission which means you take 10 minutes longer to do anything which some poeple (including myself) like. However if you dispise this feature and wish to be a little more reckless i will give you this hint/cheat for reading all the way to the end. Go onto the pause menu at any point in a mission and click "shift" and "-" at the same time then type "savegame". You're welcome. :)

Was so hyped, but everything is just locked behind 1v1s. I know this is a pvp game, but it's a one trick pony. The open world aspect was such a nice change, but there's no reward in it.
Also, schools are♥♥♥♥♥♥ I thought the point was to learn the moves of someone else's deck. When I 'unlocked' stagger style, all you unlock s the ability to spin and stuff. There was not enough information in the slightest, so I ranked through the 1v1s and became a disciple of the school. What rewards did I get? Absolutely nothing. The 'rewards' you get along the way, are just school versions of abilities and weapons, which help you rank up in the school faster. They give no benefit.
So, there I was, a disciple of this cool moveset, and yet my character seemingly lost this knowledge of these moves upon going back to my old decks. This meant, once again, standing infront of an NPC and just blocking. Boring, frustrating and cheesy. I thought the point of schools would be to create a nice mechanic of learning these moves and eventually helping new players learn some good moves as they use them, rather than just blocking against a good player with the move (who will kill them). You can block vs NPCs etc, but it is boring and isn't what I signed up for.
Some people will argue that the balancing is incredible, but one of the most common strats is to just use incredibly fast moves. Anyone who doesn't have incredible reaction times will struggle to hit you enough to kill you. Having lost to this in the beta, that was what I tried doing in this game, and indeed it won me so many fights.
I was so disappointed after I beat the story. The main story lasts about 3 - 6 hours depending on your speed and skill. Its not long at all, yet I was still blown away and I really enjoy learning the map and it's secrets. Pity it's all a waste of time as when the story is beaten you just sit there and queue trials (1v1)s. To some, this will be a blast, however, if they wanted to make a game purely about dueling, then don't spend all your time making a 6 hour tutorial and DOUBLE DOWN on the PVP for the fans who want it. Beta told me this was a really neat fighting game with a focus on customisation, but in the end it's just all about the meta and using copypasta movesets (probably mixing them up if you're good at it, but the same moves are used).

This game is incredible, simply put. While it is P2W, there are certainly aspects on in that counter that. The following lists are not complete, I already feel the game calling me back.
Pros:
- customizability coming out of my ears. You can play the same class and race and still end up with totally different character builds from it.
- Leveling system. This is kind of part of the customizability, but on a different aspect. The leveling is much different from normal MMOs, since you get experience from quests and not actually killing monsters. While this makes grinding a bit harder, it also makes leveling more rewarding. There are also two different types of levels, ranks and actual levels. This makes it interesting to rank up due to the different bonuses.
- Addicting. I don't know what it is that draws me to this game, but I just can't stop playing it. It's absolutely amazing and ccompletely fun to play!
Cons:
- P2W aspects. Naturally, there must be money coming to the developers from somewhere since it's F2P. A lot of quests, classes, and races are locked to those who are willing to pay. However, I have learned that simply the experience boost from the monthly VIP is well worth the money.

It is difficult to decide how to rate DDO. On one hand is it' s downsides; including (but not limited to) expencive VIP sub, limited F2P options (starts really limiting you at level 8) and very slow turbine point gain for F2P players, limiting their ability to  purchace adventures. However, for those willing to pay for all the things that would need paying for, it is a jolly old time indeed. It is, by far, the best MMORPG created this side of Ultima online and Wurm. Seriously, the combat is the best I have ever experienced in any MMO ever. The dungeons are instanced: no more fetch 100 slimes or kill 50 goblins! Quests are all interesting and never a bore. Quests could range from having you go through an onslaught of foes to defeat the final boss to having you destroy crates while being unable to kill a certain type of monster. The game follows the lore of DDO very well. There is a HUGE amount of freedom in character creation. However, the business practices of WB and turbine are... questionable. The DLC packs are expencive, and you will find yourself paying for adventures because the subscription is so expencive. Even then, subscribers don't have all the content. You must still pay for stuff. All in all, I recommend this game ONLY IF  YOU ARE WILLING TO PAY SOMETHING. Buying something with real money unlocks character slots and favor growth (which is used to gain rep with factions and get free stuff like races and classes).

In this game, you can kill a man with a green onion.  A chive.  You can pick it straight from the field and beat down the very next person you see.  You cannot eat the onion.
If that doesn't entice you, there's also 100 or so other collectible weapons, each with their own movesets, as well as 22 different endings and the ability to craft your own weapons.
Be aware that the game is not an epic.  It's a short story in a small sandbox, meant to be played several times with different choices along the way.  Your inventory carries over each time you restart, so most of the progression is built around getting all the weapons and developing them, as well as seeing all the endings.  If that sounds awesome to you, then you might love this game as much as I do.  Check out a few videos on Youtube to make sure, since the videos on the store page aren't showing you any real gameplay.
If you try this and like it, check out Way of the Samurai 4 as well.

Full Review here:
Mordheim is one of those games where its a lot less fun in the first 2-3 hours than it will be after, so you have to prepare yourself or just not bother. There are solid tutorials, and a lot of them, but even after those the game still has a steep learning curve in terms of the rules and how things generally work, plus the added complexity/difficulty of navigating the maps with your units the first time around. You will feel lost and frustrated trying to find things, as you will assume an item is on the second floor of a building, only to discover that its actually on the third and there are no stairs up near your unit. Adding to all of this is the game only has one ‘mode’, which is that it saves everything all the time and you can’t reload/undo (think Ironman mode in XCOM).
Now with all of that said, I still think you should press on if you enjoy games like XCOM or other deeper TBS titles. The basics of the game is that you have a warband (squad), and each unit has different classes, stats, abilities, and equipment. You deploy your warband on missions (most somewhat randomly generated, with some unique campaign/story missions), and during a mission they face off against another warband. Currently the game has five different warbands (the 5th, Witchhunters, are DLC), and each plays very differently.
Yeah DLC pricing is annoying but they're a small studio and have to justify cost to keep working on the game. I'd happily pay more to play more as this is a game worth playing.

Well, as a person who has played both the tabletop version (yes, that old, i know..) and this game, i have to bow to the developers for making a computer game worthy of the original. Indeed, the game is unforgiving, even harsh when you are used to other games holding your hand in the beginning, in this game, you lose that hand (but hell, that gives you a bonus to dodge...)
But hanging in and redoing mission after mission with your battered and bloodied team until they finally are unusable (or dead..), then redoing it with a new warband is always fun and never the same.
So is it "too hard"? No, but the tutorials don't even touch the surface of what you must learn to be successful. So you have to learn the hard way. Either you got the patience to do so or you don't. Is ist just "watching guides and yeah...it works" Maybe, but that would take away the fun of finding out.
The developers have made a tough game that gives you the opportunity to earn your medals. The fact that medals don't come easy is common knowledge, so if you give this game a chance, I am sure you will have lots of fun with it. It is beautifully rendered and if you are a fan of the gritty world Games Workshop have created, you will love it for that alone. Performance is fine, my antique gpu  (gtx580) runs it without a hitch @2540x1440 and it hasn't crashed once.

Rakuen is a non-combative adventure RPG that provides a profound emotional experience. With gameplay elements that resemble the older SNES games and a gorgeous soundtrack, be prepared to go on a journey. I found the story in the earlier parts of the game lacking, but it gets progressively better and evolves into a deep and touching narrative.
For a full detailed review please check out:

Rakuen is by far one of THE most beautiful story games I've ever played ^_^ (and yes, I cried my eyes out :)
In the game itself, you play as a Boy living in a hospital, where his Mum reads him his favourite storybook - Rakuen - in which the Boy is told of a place called Morizora's Forest, and the Guardian of the Forest, Morizora. The Boy also learns that Morizora will grant one wish to anyone that can complete his challenges as well :)
After finding out from his Mum that Rakuen is indeed a real place!, secret doors start appearing in the hospital, and the Boy and his Mum travel together to explore this amazing and beautiful world ^_^
Your goal in Rakuen is to help out the residents living with you in the hospital, and consequently, their alter-ego's in Morizora's Forest :D There are a lot of different characters to interact with - some of them include a girl who has lost her best friend and is trying to find her, to a man who has lost his memory.
You play through each of the resident's journeys, quite literally in their own shoes, as you discover how it is they came to be at the hospital, their backstory, and how to help them overcome their own personal challenges :)
I won't spoil anything else, but you do end up learning a lot about the Boy as you complete each of the residents' challenges and progress through the game ^_^
The characters themselves are VERY likeable, and personally, I felt a very strong connection with all of them when I played through Rakuen, which is very rare straight-off :) (Usually it takes me a while to like a video game character until a bit later on in the story, no matter what type of genre of game it is). They also have their own unique personalities and backstories to share, and I loved getting to know each character and sharing in their adventures :D
There is a LOT of music in Rakuen, most of it instrumental, but some of the tracks are also vocal - which are tied with each of the hospital characters you come across :D Laura herself has composed 99% of these tracks, and has done an amazingly magnificent job on them! ^_^ I would DEFINITELY recommend listening to the soundtrack on its own if you get a chance, it's WELL worth a listen! :D
To summarise, if you love story based games with wonderful characters, beautiful music, and a few dungeon-like puzzles, then Rakuen is a game I would highly recommend! Be warned though, the game isn't all cheery and does have some sad parts, so it WILL make you cry on some bits, so I'd have a box of tissues on hand just in case <3
Thanks so much again Laura for making one of THE best and most beautiful story games out there, you are amazing to of come up with something so wonderful! <3

-The caves have instant death-traps but relatively easy enemies.  The spelunking is simple enough to ease you into the game, but watch out, there are some steep falls!
- The forest zone has some pretty tough enemies, some of which will harass you from afar.  There are no real traps here, but some of the platforming can be treacherous.
- The Ruins (or is it Crypt?  I don't visit often...) are definitely a challenge - unforgiving traps and enemies that will mess with your day around every corner.  The platforming here is relatively mundane though, but seriously, watch out for those traps and badguys.
Finding items and equipment is one of those risky things, too, which can ramp up the tension.
Definitely a challenging game but it feels good to play.  The visuals are simply gorgeous as well, it has a really nice artstyle and the music is atmospheric, too (though I personally feel that the boss music needs to be a bit scarier or heavier).

Absolver puts hearts in my eyes. It's like if For Honor were designed competently, if Dark Souls had a high skill ceiling, and if God Hand had online PVP, all in one game.
This is the opposite of a casual experience. It takes hours of learning mechanics, moves, and the style you've forged, before you'll win any games. The community is small, but luckily welcoming and dedicated - it's not hard to find a sparring partner or a mentor after a bit of social exertion.
Seasoned gamers can expect to run through the PVE content in about 6 hours. 8 if you tweak your loadout a lot. It should be treated as an extended tutorial for the competitive 1v1 scene, which has virtually no matchmaker. While ranked games are planned for the future and I look forward to that, I appreciate the absolute chaos of unranked. Being matched vs an absolute monster and getting ♥♥♥♥ing demolished is a great way to expose and learn from your weaknesses,
The dev team is small. Updates aren't much, and they're fairly far apart. But they've proven to me that they listen to their community and are accurate when they evaluate and incorporate balance changes.
Absolver is a very special, unique experience and I can only imagine it improving with age. See you on the path, prospect.

First things first: this game is not a game with both PVP and PVE (at least at the moment). It’s a predominantly PVP game with PVE elements, where both aspects tie in with each other.
Combat is an art in this game, and players need to take note of timing, situation, stance and location to come out on top. This is not an arcade, rounds are not won by memorising combos and button mashing but rather by discerning your opponents’ combat styles and picking the right moves that could allow you to come out on top. Few things are as satisfying as ducking under a jumping kick and catching your foe in the face and sending his disintegrating body flying off over a ledge. To grasp the basics is somewhat easy, but to master it takes practice.
Customisation is well controlled. The first stage is customisation of your combat deck, taking into account starting position, speed, range and power to piece together a combo that fits your style. The next is customising your outfit. The next is customising your character’s equipment. Each article has clean and worn versions with their own protection and weight values and there is a feeling of satisfaction in finding a set that BOTH looks cool and viable.
Artstyle and graphics are beautiful, not much to say there. I do wish there were more areas to explore though, the ruined landscape of Adal leaves plenty of room for imagination.
However, there is still room for improvement. The camera angle when you get cornered is atrocious, having opponents with lousy internet connection makes for matches ridden with rubberbanding, and balance could use some more tweaking. Bugs and the likes still happen sporadically and will still ruin your experience each time it does.
tl;dr: A game that is easy to learn, hard to master, looks aesthetically pleasing, fluid, graceful and yet intense, provides ample opportunities for customisation, yet leaves more to be desired. Thankfully the devs are active on the community chat and will still provide support and updates in time to come. 8.5/10

I've been playing this game since it came out, and still find it interesting at times. It's a shame that it has been superceded by some newer games, so no new content is coming out—if new city DLCs were made, I'd probably still buy them.
Cities in Motion is a public transport planning simulator that lets you build bus, tram/monorail/trolleybus, ferry/waterbus and metro/subway lines. You can control many of the costs involved, and the idea is to make a profit while at the same time making the best public transport system for your city. This is not an official goal by the way—there are (admittedly disappointing) scenarios with clearly set goals, while in sandbox mode you have no specific goal.
The reason I highly recommend this game is that it's surprisingly addictive, and while it cannot serve as an accurate simulator, can give some idea of how public transport planning works; the game calculates the routes taken by all city residents and tourists and calculates if they should or shouldn't use your public transport system. It's extremely fun and rewarding to take a city from 100% car usage to almost everyone using your amazing system!
Unfortunately there are certain major drawbacks. The biggest one by far is technical—the game is not optimized well, and games in large cities with developed transport systems slow down to a crawl even on my top-of-the-line PC. Other than that, there is some imbalance between transport modes, some poorly designed areas in the official maps, almost no ability to customize metro stops (entrances, multiple tiers, etc.), and of course no new content because the game is "outdated".

I was skeptical about this game initially because it was free to play, but the saying "Don't judge a book by it's cover" definitely rings true with this game. I honestly didn't know what to expect at the beginning, but I quickly became enraptured with the storyline, but this was mostly due to the characters in the game. What I'm probably most thrilled with is the main character's development, really well done there. I've partnered with almost all of the characters in the game, and I'm amazed each time at how different the story plays out for each character path. The endings are completely different for each person you choose to be with, and that's what makes each playthrough exciting and leaves me wanting more. Each potential mate has their own unique personalities and has a little bit of something for everyone, depending on your taste. I would suggest playing through each character, as each story reveals more about the lore of the world and the characters in it (Fritz' and Waltz' stories REALLY dig deep, you will not be disappointed).
Overall, this game has replay value for me because I will want to experience the stories again and the characters within them. (Plus there's a handy-dandy fast-forward button to fly through the boring parts if you've already played through the scene once before.)

Having played Way of the Samurai 1, 2, and 4, I can honestly say that this is not only the worst entry in the series, but a terrible port of a bad game on top of it. The control system is near impossible to use competantly, with no viable way to reallocate keys without a third hand, and zero controller support to alleviate the issue. The game itself has issues in it's general design, from a lack of any real tutorial level (which all other entries in the series has had), the worst Time Management system in the franchise, and a difficulty curve that is almost non-existent, regardless of whether you're playing on easy or normal difficulty. The Morality system also has many issues, with harsh penalties for certain actions, but never even telling you what you did to deserve that penalty. This game had a lot of potential to be a good game, had certain changes been made, but overall it's a poor game with an even poor-er porting job. Do yourself a favor and buy 4 instead.

Way of the Samurai 3 is an odd mix of both Open World and Simulator were you can spend your days exploring, fighting or working for one of two factions. The closest comparison I can give to this game has to be the Dead Rising series as both work on a day system where each one leads to unique events as well as both having a bunch of interconnected areas that serve as the world. We play as a nameless and fully customizable character that awakens wounded and battered in the aftermath of a pretty big battle. Right off the bat we are approached by two villagers and are introduced to this games dialogue system where you can either pick from one of three responses or unsheathe your sword  which can lead to either them running in fear or a fight. This title does not hold your hand at all and from the start you can go whatever direction you want and learning as you go.
You can lead a peaceful life and find a partner to settle down with you or you can go up to a faction leader, murder him and get paid for doing nothing but letting your bandit like faction do their thing. Way of the Samurai 3 offers much freedom to the player with noticeable consequences and effects which makes this a highly replayable title. The lack of guidance really harms the experience for the first few hours as you don't know how to fight, you don't know much about what is going on or even what to do. To learn how to fight you must visit the dojo in a location called “Guard Gate”  where you are given basic instructions on how defend yourself. Unfortunately dialogue in this game is a absolute pain since every time you ask a question you are returned to the beginning of the conversation and must make your way back to the questions branch. Kind of a hard thing to describe so I'll use an example. Imagine asking your wife or friend how her day was and she goes on and on with no end in sight. Finally you get to ask a question but if you want to ask another one you will have to listen to how her day was all over again.
All that just to learn how to properly fight and learning about some skills such as jump kicking or throwing weapons at enemies that you will likely not find out about by yourself. The lack of handholding is fine but some form of manual for the basic things such as these would have helped greatly. As for the dialogue there isn't much of it, for better or worse. Outside of the tutorial characters that teach you about the game there is usually only small tidbits text to read so that annoying problem mentioned a while ago becomes rare. This is really not the type of game you get for a compelling story or interesting characters. The story is interesting in that neither of the two factions are benevolent but aside from that nothing of interest is to be found. The few unique characters to be found are bland and unmemorable as well. What makes Way of the Samurai 3 interesting is the effect you can have on the world and characters. Whether they bow down at the mere sight of you, run in fear or plot for your death is solely based on you and your actions.
This however is no GTA game. You are punished for random murder or harming an innocent NPC by losing out on some “Samurai Points” that are given out at the end of a playthrough for all your noble actions. Samurai Points unlock new clothing, fighting styles and other goodies so it is in your best interest to not play like a psycho which is easier said than done. The combination of the awkward combat and the NPCs gathering in a small circle to watch a fight make it very easy for your enemy to dodge a blow causing you to kill or injure an innocent and receive a point penalty. Each area and faction of the game has their own opinions of you so you can terrorize one village and be a hero in the next if you so choose. Those two villages are the only ones in the game, the rest of areas are stuff like guard posts or faction strongholds. It's not a big world by any means and you will have seen every location in no time, especially if you fast travel. What keeps such a small world interesting is all the minor things that can happen the next day that was not there the day before.
Traveling the world is kind of confusing at first as the layout of the lands and where areas lead to feel pretty non-intuitive but with the world being so small you'll know the layout like the back of your hand sooner rather than later. Fast traveling may take up more of the in game's day than simply walking there in real time. The environments hold nothing interesting and with the sever lack of character models you will be seeing the same few people over and over again which doesn't make the prospect of walking to your objective all that attractive. The lack of character modules is one of the major thing that makes this world feel empty especially your first time through when you are wondering which one of these clones are giving out the quests.
Completing quests is the only to gain the respect and the favor of the people your doing them for but none of them are interesting. The first quest you are likely to find and not even realize is the only way to get the villagers to accept you is finding an old ladies underwear. This is not the kind of modern game where items unspeakably glimmer when you approach or you have a waypoint telling you exactly where it is. I'd normally consider that a good thing but finding a pair of randomly generated underwear in a game that is mostly made of different colors of brown is not how I would want to spend my gametime doing. There are much more boring quests to be found such as delivering messages to people seemingly hiding from you and discovering which one of the triplet twins is a thief by waiting for one of them to whistle. Each quest giver has the same two or three quests that they will give out time and time again. It is seemingly designed to give you something to do and a from of making money but get so intolerably boring. One thing that is unnecessary is having to go find a street performer to save and have him talk before letting you save. Minor annoyance that adds humor but an annoyance nonetheless.
Money is used to buy clothing, items and upgrading your weapons. If you have the materials you can even create and name your own weapons as well as choosing one of multiple fighting stances to take when using that sword. Combat is based around stats, hit points and other other RPG aspects so sword play is not all that great as your weapon is either as effective as if it was inflatable toy sword or makes the fight far too easy. It is no doubt a good feeling seeing your weapons becoming more and more effective so be aware the combat is far more RPG centered than action based. You can parry and beat enemies far better equipped than you though the amount of hits they can take make it clear that you are not supposed to beat them. One combat mechanic I found very interesting is the durability meter for weapons. Depending on how much stress a sword is under from too much blocking or hitting it may break leaving you with just the hilt in your hands and your death likely nigh. It keeps you from simply button mashing and makes the fights feel more tactical. This game suffers from a 30fps lock however which really harms the feel of the combat and the overall game unfortunately.
It is a poorly made game with an empty world, uninteresting characters & plot and to top it off that accursed 30 fps lock. Yet it seems to know that it is not all too great and revels in it's weirdness with beat-boxing pedestrians, catgirl companions and old ladies that have the hots for you. Way of the Samurai has a certain uniqueness with it's charming weirdness and all of it's features like being able to attack with the non-lethal blunt end of your sword or just ignore the war entirely and try to get a wife. This is one of those titles that can be is a guilty pleasure which I do want to go and play some more of for some unknown reason.

I'm suprised Max: The Curse of Brotherhood is not widely mentioned, as it is fun little game.
It's supposed to be a sequel to Max and the Magic Marker, which I didn't play. But it is not a big loss. Out of couriosity I checked the other game on YouTube and my conclusion is, that developers where toying with the idea before delivering the real deal which is Curse of Brotherhood. And I'm suprised it didn't get the hype and reach as wide as Ori and the Blind Forest, as both are released by Microsoft studios.
The kid named Max, who got rid of his brother via magic spell that he found on the internet. His brother Felix is captured through portal into another wolrd and Max jumps right after him realizing the consequences of his action. From now on you control Max, who get to use a magic marker. A simple item that let's you solve the puzzles throughout the game mixed with platforming. The marker allows you draw rock pillars, branches, lianes, water geysers at certain spots leaving you to figure out how to do it to proceed further or solve the puzzles. Not all of it will be available from the beginning, but as it is straight-forward side-scroller, there won't be any backtracking.
Now, I need to mention that I play with my X360 controller and I have no idea how the game works with keyboard control. As for the gamepad it felt very smooth, both for controling Max and drawing stuff with the marker. Smooth and nice graphic won't obscure anything and light tutorial won't leave you clueless as to how to interact with objects. You will be able to draw Os from branches, cut them by the base and use it as an object you can climb onto. Some enemies apart from hazzards also serve as a solution to the puzzle. You also have to combine marker's abilities. All of that is explained in the game so you know how, but thankfully doesn't serve as a guide. The difficulty of the puzzles is various however. Normaly you'll be able to go through with very brief moments of reflection. Sometimes you may be stuck for longer, but never long enough to make you frustrated. Colorful and childish theme of the game may suggest it is for younger players and I encourage them to try it.
There are collectibles in the game, but they serve no other purpose, than to chill your eventual OCD. There are evil eyes to collect and these may be placed in the areas that will take you longer to figure acces to. There are also pieces of the amulet of the Old Lady (she's kinda guiding you through the magic land), much harder to get. The main problem with it, is that the camera is very stiff and concetrated on Max. Sometimes you may be able to spot evil eye somewhere on the corner of the screen, but getting some of them requies leap of faith.
The artstyle is simple but gorgeous, there is also superb voice-acting, a bit unexpected from a small game. Normally I play on my PC connected to 32" LED TV so I can enjoy the graphics of such colorful games. However, considering the overall quality of the graphics it shouldn't struggle on older gear, but it does. I own 8GB RAM Laptop with 1GB RAM graphics card and quad core processor and had huge problem with cutscenes. I got the sound without visuals or got it with miserable framerate. No struggles on a PC, though.
As Max: The Curse of Brotherhood is puzzle-platformer, have in mind it will play different than a straight-forward platformer. It is not very demanding game, there's a free demo available on Steam, that I would reccomend to try out first before buying the full game. It was fun for me.

By far the best blending of D&D 3.5 rules with an MMO feel.  While it may take some getting used to, once you grasp the basics, it'll click quite nicely.
This is set in the Eberron world for the most part, not the Forgotten Realms of major fame but don't let that stop you.  The Eberron setting is unique and a lot of fun.
There are several classes available for you to select right from the start, and your four "basic" D&D races, Humans, Dwarves, Elves and Halflings.  And while each race does have a certain feel and flavor about them, as with proper D&D, you are free to combine whatever class you can with whatever race you can.
That said, there are some classes and races that can only be unlocked via Cash Shop.  Or you can get a subscription.  Due note, not all classes are unlocked with a subscription, and they are unlocked only for the subscription.  Best to just buy them outright.
Yes, there's a lot of slow going for this game, you don't just rush to the end.  But when you do get there, you can "reset" your character, causing them to be revived at low level, but with an extra stat points on your build, which lets you make an even more powerful character.
If you're looking for a D&D game that'll get you hip-deep in the mechancis of it, this is the game for you.  If you're looking for something more MMO and modern, look into Neverwinter, which is based on the 4th edition rules.
This is a lot of fun if you have some friends to play it with. There is a lot of room for customization in builds and awesome items.

Ordered it for $5 during Black Friday weekend this year. It just arrived today.
Setup: MOSTLY painless.I plugged it in to the tv in the living room with my keyboard, mouse and gamepad. It ran two updates, and was ready to go. The ONLY snag I hit was that I needed to go up to my bedroom and turn on streaming in my settings panel in Steam. After that, everything just worked.
Pros: Playing from the comfort of your couch in your living room (or wherever)
Streaming works PRETTY well
Easy setup
User-friendly interface
Remote-control of Steam program/library
Compact and light-weight design
Has bonus web apps such as Youtube and a few others. Not really important to me because of my PS4 and smartTV downstairs.
Has 3 USB ports for either co-op or mouse/key/gamepad plug-in
Comes with HDMI, power, AND three wall adapters for different countries
Works with official 360 gamepad (says most gamepads on the box, I'm using wired, don't know if wireless works with it or if only the steamlink controller works wirelessly), so no need to order the steam controller for it
(My personal favorite, and JUST figured it out) The device actually streams your pc, not JUST your Steam library. Just go in to the power setting, and exit Big Picture mode, and voila, you've got access to your desktop. (I used to always drag my tower downstairs when I wanted to play or work from the living room, this is a very nice feature for me)
Cons: Streaming probably isn't strong enough for online multiplayer. (I mostly play single player games anyway though, so it's great for me)
The FPS DOES take a slight hit when streaming. (Should be noted that I'm using wifi for the stream, and not an ethernet cable, so I'm not sure how different it would be hard-wired vs wifi)
All around pretty great device, and at $5 was a DEFINITE steal from the usual $50 price tag. I bought it knowing it wouldn't stream 100% quality, but I'm okay with it. My games actually look pretty good still on the TV downstairs using it. I jumped in to Hitman and State of Decay for a bit and they both ran pretty darn well. The hit in performance was nothing that bothered me enough to not play (but I'm not an elitist when it comes to needing 4K graphics and what-not) If you're the same, and want to be able to just relax on the couch and just enjoy some games without sitting at your computer desk, I'd definitely recommend grabbing this nifty little piece of hardware. I'm happy with it.

It was tough giving this a "not recommended", because I am a big fan of sonic in general, and I do like this game a lot.
But if you are looking for the classic sonic experience, this isn't the game I would recommend.
The game runs completely off nostalgia; the level themes are re-used from other sonic games, and there's not a lot of original things in here.
Worst part is probably the physics engine though, its the engine that was used on the sonic rush games which was designed with a special "boost" button in mind; and that's the thing, there's no boost gameplay from the sonic rush series in this game, and the engine is pretty bad at simulating old classic gameplay.
The level design is fun though, and if you can catch this on a big sale, might be worth checking out. In the end, I recommend Sonic the Hedgehog 2 or 3 or Generations if you want a steam Sonic game.

This game is excellent.
In my opinion, this is the best execution of Roguelike platforming. It's like a marriage between Risk of Rain and Rogue Legacy. The gameplay sort of "slow and tight" like Risk of Rain, but also manages to feel a lot more frantic and fast paced. The different classes have drastically different play styles (in a good way) but there's also the original Diablo principle of 'anyone ~CAN~ learn magic.'
The game's very challenging but also very fair. You'll get punished by visible pannel traps and realize after the fact it was in plain sight, you'll get knocked back into spikes and die and realize it's your fault for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. You'll accidentally summon/anger bosses and learn not to do those things again (or do them again on purpose if that's your thing). For me, it's the perfect level of dificulty to keep me trying and dying and trying and dying.
The 2-4 player co-op in this game is seamless and perfectly done. When a player dies, they can revive as a cannon-fodder skeleton that is essentially useless in combat but can function as a warm body to scout/distract enemies. Dead players are tactically useful, but have no 'actively powerful' impact on the game. It's a clear punishment for dying, but keeps players engaged and useful. If you're lucky, on future floors you may find items that can revive one dead player. If the entire party wipes, of course, it's game over.
I highly recommend this game and really appreciate the developers for creating it.

Back before reviews on Steam was a thing, Ballpoint Universe absolutely absorbed me as few great games are able to do. Growing up with Gradius and a near obsessive love of everything customizable, this game was a shot in the leg of my waning interest in indie titles. A fascinating blend of platforming and sidescroller shooting combined with a stellar hand drawn artstyle really captured what I loved about the booming era of indie, and gave me a lot of hope for the cult classics being made.
2 years later, this game is still gorgeous, still good, and as I just found out, the first game I got all the achievements for (Sorry, Radium). To make up for its fairly short campaign, BU-I offers an infinite shootemup that can go on for however long you survive. Combining previous levels and challenges, it can vary in what exactly is challenging from one moment to the next, but always with fair warning. It gets extremely broken as you go of course, as they stopped worrying about balancing, as I found in the near 100s the screen was practically filling with surrealist inked monstrosities.
The real charm here though is the amount of replayability, even outside of the infinite offered. There are tons of little side missions hidden or otherwise scattered throughout the M.C. Escher landscapes that offer different tiers of reward depending on how well you do. Some unlock new weapons devices to use against the logic horde (your main enemy is a bunch of geometric warriors, against your abstract friends), with all sorts of powers and effects that be further powered through upgrading. No configuration is wrong, either, and while its easy to set yourself into a single set of stuff to upgrade further, variety is often key to get by certain tricky areas and enemies.
I could ramble on, but all this nostalgic speak makes me want to dive back in for a trip through memory lane. If this is a game you're debating whether its worth it or not, make no mistake, this is a genuine gem from a time when Kickstarter was still fresh and exciting. Just do yourself a favor and play it with a gamepad. Platforming with a mouse is the weirdest experience you can imagine.

A cute little action game that feels criminally incomplete. Add more levels, more enemies, more twists on the two-platform system and allow abilities to take effect immediately after you get the CDs for them (the current system is dumb, it forces you to die in order to receive the abilities they grant before actually being able to beat the bosses) and you've got something that could be called an arcade game.
If you're a fan of Savant or electronic music in general, you'll love this game.

When you consider that most commercial music costs
0.99$ for a single song, the same price I paid for this game on sale, it really highlights the great value of Savant - Ascent. The soundtrack alone would be a steal but you get an excellent game too!
The core gameplay of Savant - Ascent is quite simple but don't let that deter you. Its fluid, pulse raising action is a blast to play. The difficulty curve is just right for most of the game but got a bit steep for my liking right near the end. A steady stream of unlocks keeps things fresh throughout the main story and avoids overwhelming you. This isn't a very long game but it includes a few extras like time trial and endless modes that will please you if you like a challenge.
My biggest complaint is that the final boss gets away from the frenetic gameplay and instead becomes an exercise in memorizing a static sequence of attacks. While the fight has an epic air to it, it lost the fun factor for me and became a chore to overcome in order to see the ending. Without spoiling anything, the ending suggests that the developers had more planned but it's unlikely that we'll see an expansion telling the rest. That is disappointing but considering that the story is told solely through short, nonverbal cutscenes, you can't claim that story was ever this game's strength or focus.
If you like electronic music you should enjoy the fantastic soundtrack. All the songs are accessible in .ogg format in the game's main files folder (typically C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\SavantAscent ). It's a testament to their quality that many of the tracks have found their way into my music library.

It was a good game back when I played it on my old account in 2008-2010. A tribute to TFC the game which accompanied my high school years from 1999 to 2002. But now, we are in 2015, and things have changed, moved on.
The rhetorical question I ask is this: was TFC so incredible as to be remade (copy-pasted) entirely, with only a few design and conceptual changes?
The short answer is that it wasn't.
The long answer is that what in my eyes has truly saved tfc back then was the skilled-based movement. The latter being due to a structural bug inherent to the Quake engine and its succesors like Goldsrc and Source, which allowed bunny hopping, surfing, trimping, etc. This almost single-handedly made tfc something more than just a spamfest dominated by Soldiers, Mirv'ing HWGuys and Demomen and the occasional EMP Progineer.
From a game design perspective, FF did succeed in developping and streamlining the player movement, liberating what the Valve devs had tried to restrain in pre-steam tfc, and I felt that explosives had been toned down to be less disruptive in the flow of the game. And I must admit that the amateur team that developped FF really made huge efforts, were open to feedback and fixed A LOT of the bugs that plagued the early versions. And for this I congratulate them for their dedication.
Now to all the vets defending your baby, you can be proud of this great game. But you just have one little problem: outside of the "skill-based movement" niche, there isn't a lot to do, and the game can quickly become stale, very stale (tfc did not have this problem). The action is more sporadic, short. More importantly, explosive spam battles seem to be more an accident than something that was given much thought, whereas they are a central conceptal element in tf2, where spamminess was embraced, with mechanics to make or brake it (such as uber) that were made from the start specifically.
FF is TFC's sequel from the perspective of those who played it and what they turned it into: a fencing-like gameplay with an unassumed and disdained spamminess.
TF2 is TFC as Walker's team initially wanted it to be: a wrestling, tug-of-war-like gameplay which embraces its spamminess and even made it enjoyable.
Do I recommend this game? It's free, so you'd be a fool not to try it :)

40 hours on Steam + at least 3,000 in its own launcher.
The goods:
This game has loads of great aspects to it, ranging from group questing to a 'True Reincarnation' mechanic allowing for endless play.
The party questing allows for some easier playthroughs of the harder quests in the game at low levels and even when you hit the heroic level cap. Each player gets their own loot from chests which can be switched around and given to others via the chest's item drop-down menu allowing for some Bound to Account/Character items to be traded before they're claimed.
The leveling system in this game is real easy to learn but very complex and detailed when you truely understand it allowing for pretty much any combination of classes that don't clash to work. There are thousands of custom player-made builds to try on the forums which give you an edge over a standard build. Being able to combine up to 3 classes will also give you an edge too. Want to play as a caster but still be able to disable traps? No problem! Combine Wizard and Rogue for the easiest of them all.
The True Reincarnation mechanic of this game allows for endless play, as once you hit the heroic level cap of 20 you unlock the ability to remake your character with benefits. You gain +4 points for your build from Adventurer to Hero, +2 from Hero to Legend and it caps at 36. Champion characters will only gain a +2 stat boost going into Hero as they already start at 32 points. Each time you True Reincarnate (TR), you gain extra abilities based on your previous life. For example, if you were a Barbarian in your last life, you gain 10 HP. All passive past life feats stack up to 3 times. Also, you can take an 'Active' past life feat which allows for extra boosts ingame such as Barbarian's 'Berserker's fury' past life feat allowing you to use a Rage like ability in which a Barbarian has as a different class.
Heroic and Epic levels are a fairly new feature of DDO which has only really come around in the past few years and is still massively developing. Now the level cap has been raised to 28 allowing for more Feats and Stats to be gained, giving an even greater advantage over your enemies in quests. With this came a new item system that has 4 different tiers of loot for Heroic and Epic quests. These items are paired with the difficulty they were looted in, giving boosts greater if the difficulty was too.
This is an EXCELLENT F2P game as you NEVER have to buy anything in the game if you decide you don't want to, as you get 'Favor' for completing quests which in turn grants you 'Turbine Points' to spend in the store.
The bads:
DDO has a lot of flaws in its own right, but none more than your average MMORPG. It's always going to have bugs which the community are always trying to stamp out through the use of the public beta test client, Lamannia.
DDO IS a pay2win game. You'll never get to level 28 at the current state of the game unless you get some of the epic-level addon content.
Summary:
Although there may seem more good points than bad, you'll find a lot more yourself from just playing in both aspects. Each person has their own preference of games and whats in them and I love DDO because it's a group-based game. You'll find it much easier to complete quests and objectives if you team up with 5 other people. DDO is an ever-expanding game which is currently on its 25th major update excluding patches for bugs. I could write an essay that makes A Song of Ice and Fire look small and easy to read on whats great and what sucks about the game, but nobody would want to read it. I'd be surprised if people actually read this far into my review. Anyway, going off on a tangent, the game is amazing if you like to team up with friends to go on an epic adventure through the levels, facing different enemies on the way from slimy, annoying ooze monsters that love to break your weapons to Acid-breathing dragons and much more.
I'd give this game a rating of 7.5 out of 10, as it still has a long way to go to be able to catch up with the major MMOs such as Guild Wars 2 and World of Warcraft. On the other hand, it holds its own playstyle I've yet to see in any other MMO of group-based questing from the start.
If you do decide to play the game, Cannith is a great server! Thousands of players always willing to help you, all you need to do is ask. Just remember, asking around for help in the starter area won't get you far, you have to venture out into the world.
Hope to see you in-game soon! ^_^

Awesome game.
See that large number on the time played above? Yeah that has only been since it got on Steam.
