Many of the recent adjustments to classes has taken some of the difficulty edge off of the lower levels as power creep has reared its head.
-----------
For the absolute best DDO experience:
get 3-4-5 friends that have zero experience playing. Have everyone go through the tutorial (it is solo only).
Set up a schedule of play time and request that no one plays at all outside of the group time,  no spoilers!
Dont go read about how best to play the game or the best builds , etc.
The exploration and learning on your own when it is all fresh to the whole crew is priceless.
Some dungeons have you thinking with your fighter ,barbarian or sorcerer you are the baddest MoFo ever.
Next dungeon you are cheering on the rogue who is sneaking around a room full of big, bad Ogres, that would squash him in no time flat if they see him/her, picking up the soul stones(dead PCs) of the entire party to take them back to the shrine to be raised from the dead.
===========================
Lots to do as free to play so no need to pull out the CC right away.
If you follow the above plan for best experience by time you get to where you feel the 'need' to pay, you will gladly be screaming "take my money, now!"
-----------------------
One word of caution about making characters;
Many of the older dungeons have the unfortunate MMO min/maxer design problem.
You will run in to somethings that require X Strength score to open or Y skill points to trick an NPC will seem really high.
The desiginers couldn't make the stat requirements too low where a balanced character could complete with out making things trivial for the min/maxers.
Just keep that in mind when building that maxing or nearly maxing your primary ability scores is suggested and likewise it is better to have a few skills that are maxed rather than a bunch of skills with low investment.
~~~~~~~~

This game has 1 major flaw; it's really gosh darn hard to get into, I really cannot remember how I managed to trawl through the uninteresting mess that are the low levels and starter zone, but I certainly do not regret it; this game is so amazingly unique and I love it <3
Now this game is technically an MMORPG, and MMORPGs have a great level of stigmatism, mostly caused by great numbers of Korean WoW-clone grind fest chatboxes. DDO isn't like that, DDO is focused on the 'game' part; character building (my personal favourite part, just like real DnD) and play-style are very important, so if you want an MMO with unique and interesting gameplay, give DDO a try.
However, this gameplay focus came at a remarkable cost; the social aspect, every quest is an instance, which while making them unique, means you can't just party up with people half-way and make friends easy; you have to make groups beforehand and go into the dungeon together. Of course the Devs don't expect us to do that all by ourselves, so there is a "Grouping" menu, where people can put out server-wide messages to find people to quest with; and it works well enough. But- the DDO community has gained a very... "elitist" edge to it over time, and try as I might, I am not exempt to this rule; many in-game factors make it hard not to become rather "elitist", per se, over time. Many people are interested only in speed running dungeons for optimal xp, and have little-to-no-interest in making friends. This can make things very hard for newer players, who want to take it slow, learn the rather complex mechanics, and make some friends.
All in all, I love DDO and would love to see it thrive, but until the Devs overhaul the starter area, early levels and social aspect, (I say this, I have no idea what they could do to spice them up though :/), I can only really recommed DDO to groups - at least 2 people (max party size is 6) - who are looking for a group based, challenging PvE RPG that rewards effort and planning.

Max.  You little pleasing title you.  Sometimes, during a steam sale, I grab something that looks interesting and just hope it pans out.  This game looked nice. Puzzley platformifisizing and all that.  Figured, why not it's only $3.75.  What a fantastic surprise.
If you are like me and tend to gravitate to action platforming a la Prince of Persia and Tomb Raider as well some some puzzling going on then this very well might fit in your library quite snuggly.
Max's brother is abducted by an evil villain named Mustachio - WARNING:  This title is very anti-mustache and any facial hair aficionados might be offended.  His lil bro is then sucked into a netherworld from which only Max can save him.  I don't know why.  If it was *my* little brother I would be turning his room into a new play room and stealing all his legos.  But I suppose brotherly love must overcome and all that.
Off the bat you'll encounter some tutorials on drawing with your mouse or controller.  Yep, I know it sounds bad, right?  But it's actually pretty easy. I even did it entirely with my controller.  You solve puzzles by drawing vines, branches, water spouts, exploding fire, earth columns, and probably some other stuff I have totally forgotten by now.  These things you draw not only to solve puzzles but also to make up the framework for the platforming.  The puzzles are good, some even causing me to say "what the..".  While being somewhat casual a few  will actually stump you for awhile.  Now, the  platforming is on the medium level until level 6 where is bumps up to a bit-more-than-medium, the majority of the tougher bits towards levels 5 and 6.  And it's done well, usually with a giant monster chasing you.  Very action oriented and guess what?...you have to solve puzzles on the fly while being chased by an evil monster and timing the platforming.  YES.  It's that type of game.
Is it hard?  Before level 5 it is fairly casual gamer friendly.  Level 5 requires more brain activity and Level 6 requires some quick maneuvering.  The final boss is hardish, but once you figure out what to do it's a piece of cake.  Hardness...7/10.  For an extra challenge there are some artifacts and eyeball spy camera plants to uproot.  I got some of those, but frankly my steam library is too damn big to try to 100% a lot of games. Time management yo.
Graphics are sorta kinda Pixar looking. They look great and run well.  I would not say it was stunning, but definitely pretty.  Had zero crashes using a few PC's and ran pretty well overall at 60 FPS with a mediorce system.  Sounds are well done and the menus are easy to navigate.  Save spots are set in good places, and I have to say it was a wonderful produced game all in all.
If you like action puzzle platformers, then give this a go.  Wonderful title and quite enjoyable.

This is a fun little game! You play as Max, who is trying to find his brother, wielding a magic marker with the power to create and manipulate objects in this puzzle-platformer. It's a mix of untimed puzzles, plus ones you have to do (sometimes literally) on the fly. Some of the puzzles require split-second timing where you're being chased, but parts that are super time-sensitive go into a slow-motion for a few seconds to allow you to quickly analyze the situation and act appropriately. They are (usually) very generous with checkpoints, so even if you're not so good at the platforming aspects (like me), you won't have far to go when you have to repeat a level. The magic marker mechanic is really well done, with you being able to adjust the height of pillars for jumping on, create different shapes out of branches for either jumping on or chopping down and using for other purposes, vines for swinging and climbing, water jets where you get to decide their path, and goodness, gracious great balls of fire for blowing up enemies and barriers.
Pros:
+ Good Music
+ Good voice acting (I seriously felt bad for Max when he jumps into lava and screams in genuine agony)
+ Good art (it has characters with a Jimmy Neutron feel but with great backgrounds)
+ Novel mechanic (drawing/manipulating objects)
+ Collectibles for added challenge
+ Puzzles took thought but were not brain-breaking
Neutral:
~ Decent length, though I would have liked more. I got 11 hours out of it, including my bad platforming skills and a lot of redos, and finding all the collectibles. So, not super short, but I would have loved more.
Cons:
- The marker is not always at the ready, making it feel sluggish sometimes as you have to wait for it to appear for use. This doesn't affect the actual game play, since it's created with the sluggishness in mind, but it's a tad annoying at times. Likewise, the effect of your marker (e.g. lifting up a platform) doesn't always keep up with how fast you make it, with a similarly sluggish feel. Not a deal-breaker, since I still played the game to completion, including collectibles, but it was annoying.
- This is not a con for me, but maybe for others: The puzzles aren't maddeningly difficult, as some people may prefer. A lot of the difficulty comes from the split-second timing, but the untimed puzzles take at most a few minutes to puzzle out.
Overall: 9/10. Would replay.

A very pretty game, with a colorful and enticing universe. It's a platformer with a good atmosphere and some imagination. It's rather on the 'casual' side: it's very varied and not too difficult, which will make you feel like you're good at this game.
Graphics: Great. Sometimes you feel like you're into an animation movie.
Physics: Great. All objects behave, move and fall like you'd expect: boulders, vines, branches, roots, water and jets, ...
Game mechanics: Good. You change objects from the scenery with your magical pen to reach your objectives (progress through a level, block enemies, succeed in an impossible jump, ...) You can only do so starting at a few select spots in every level.
Gameplay: Good. It's dynamic, the setting changes often, so you'll have to find new ways to deal with the new challenges, and it's never feels repetitive or boring.
Story/Dialogue/Voice acting: Good (nothing to write home about, but good)
Level design: good to great (some good ideas, lots of imagination in some areas).
Difficulty: never too difficult (At most you'll retry a couple of times before overcoming an obstacle, when you die you lose less than a minute of progression).
Length: Short (about 7 hours to reach the end, a bit more to find all secrets in all levels). The progression is rather fast, so you'd have traveled a long way at the end of the game.
All in all, a good game that kept me wanting for more to the very end.

Nice little platformer which I very much enjoyed.
The game reminded me about the cartoons that I used to watch as a kid, and I was actually quite impressed with how well the developers managed to carry this theme through. The game basicly nailed it, everything from the very basic storyline, the hero and the villain, the dumb evil forces, the big monsters, along with some very convicing voice acting, cartoony graphics, and its very fitting music.
The game itself wasn't super hard, but it wasn't easy either. I am by no means a expert at platformers, and I am sure a lot of people would manage to get through the game with less deaths than I did. The game can be enjoyed by people of all ages, although younger kids might have a hard time at certain points in the game. I personally played the game with a controller, so I can't really speak for how it plays on a keyboard, but I found the controls easy to learn, and even the magic marker was easy getting used to.
+ The magic marker added some very interesting mechanics to the game, that certainly made me think.
+ Good pacing of the game, with new mechanics being introduced through out the entire game.
+ Lots of checkpoints, which is nice for people who are horrible at platformers like me.
+ Achievements, and in-game collectables, which adds some replayability to the game.
+ Most cinematics can be skipped, which is nice for a second playthrough
+ The art style, the music, the cinematics, and the voice acting, all matched each other and was very well carried through. Which made for a very good experience.
- The game has certain parts that require some fast thinking, and change of controls. This means that the game wont be playable for everybody, and that younger kids might not have a fun time. The many checkpoints however helps a great deal with this, so you will rarely have to start all over again, in case you die.

Never before have I played a game that made me so angry and yet made me love it so much. It's a turn-based strategy with RPG elements that will make you want to punch someone out of frustration while at once making you yearn for MORE. If that intrigues you, read on.
Mordheim is a game that I can't play all the time, but when I do, I really and truly immerse myself into it. The basis is that there's a city, Mordheim, that brought the apocalypse on itself, and various powers throughout the world have descended on its ruins like carrion to a corpse. You are leading a warband of such a group, and you're out to achieve your goals by mauling anyone else that comes close to the precious Wyrdstone that everyone wants.
The story itself is a weak point of the game - or, rather, not the point at all. The point of the game is in the strategy, the brutality of gameplay, and in struggling to keep your warband afloat when terrible things can happen at any given moment.
See, this is a turn-based strategy, as I said, and it's got RPG elements in the form of your characters. You end up investing a lot into your characters, and you try to keep them from being knocked out in a fight. If they get knocked out, they may suffer permanent injuries: eye loss, arm loss, leg loss, stupidity from concussions, cracked skulls, psychological disorders... you name it. They can also die from their injuries, though some of these injuries are just as effective as having a dead character sometimes. And the real danger is that since the game has some RNG inherent to its system AND you're always fighting warbands of either equal or greater strength, this can leave you wanting to throw the keyboard across the room and stalk the streets of your neighborhood looking for something to strangle.
Assuming you can control that bloodlust and channel it toward the game itself, though, you'll have a blast.
There's a lot of depth to building your characters, both in equipment and in stats. You learn a lot from your playthroughs, discovering what sort of builds will work for what roles, what sort of builds you wish you hadn't tried, and you'll observe the enemy's warriors and think "Wow, that's a cool ability that I should try." You'll find yourself experimenting a lot (as much as you can afford to, anyway). Finding the faction whose playstyle suits you best is an adventure, too; and sometimes you'll realize that a certain synergy between units - such as the Vampire Counts warband with Poison Globadiers, or a Smuggler to shore up the ranged weakness of the Sisters of Sigmar - just feels right.
One particular talent that you can get I want to make special note of: "The Lad's Got Talent." If you get a Hired Sword minion (read: a mook-level character) with enough character levels (say, 5+), you can potentially get the elite version of The Lad's Got Talent while statting them up. This means they can end up taking a Hero slot and have a LOT of really juicy ability and attribute points to throw around for free. It's one of those nifty things you can discover in the character building process that makes the game that much complex and fun to theorycraft for.
Setting up situations where you can minimize damage to your group can be a challenge, though it's less of a challenge in single player. You'll start your battles off by scouting and figuring out where the enemy is most times, then trying to attack them in such a way that you won't get counterattacked too hard (such as taking out a small group of scouts before gathering your forces for a pitched battle that now favors you). You'll be sending a couple folks around gathering the oh-so-precious Wyrdstone that brings you the money you need to survive Mordheim. I've sacrificed some warriors for the sake of getting enough Wyrdstone to see another day, for sure.
Finally, remember that this is an unforgiving game. You can't get too attached to your characters - one critical hit too many might result in them being in the morgue far sooner than you'd like. Other times you'll have someone become so crippled that having them in your warband actually feels like a detriment, and you decide it's time to put that horse to pasture. Not all injuries are this bad - some people actually LIKE having certain warriors lose an arm, for instance - but it's definitely something you want to avoid.
If you can deal with frustration well, like learning the ins and outs of a complicated system, and enjoy games that are both enraging and engaging, this might be the one for you.
Also, I nominated this game for the made-up category of "I'm Angry and I'm Loving It." It seemed fitting.

A medieval fantasy XCOM on Ironman difficulty, ruthlessly unforgiving, complicated and newbie hostile.
Just like the board game, there is quite a lot to learn in order to play this game effectively. However, success against all  odds feels incredibly satisfying and addictive.
Tactics, objectives, character builds, and random generation (numbers, maps, loot, enemy teams, etc.) reign supreme here.
Before you buy this game, I strongly recommend you watch a bit of gameplay. The battles can feel tedious and repetitive since collecting Wyrdstone is your main source of income. Not to mention how buggy the AI can be sometimes, especially with some large units AKA impressives.
One last thing, multiplayer PVP matches are extremely hard to find. Due to the small growing community and the length of each match, players have resorted to setting up tournaments in the discussions. So if you are looking for a competitive PVP experience you will need dedication.
Overall, if you enjoy very challenging, randomly generated, turn-based strategy with complex unit customization (stat, abilities, appearance), then you will love this game.

While key mapping is quite easy to input, the number of glitches (mouse drift, unrecognized inputs, etc) is enough for me to give up entirely after an hour of technical wrestling.
Hardware is presented neatly and with a number of (some would say needlessly) power adapters, an HDMI, and a CAT5 Ethernet cable. No complaints there. The Link itself is very portable and easy to set up (ignoring software issues for a moment).
In short, Steam's tried to put together a cool streaming feature for multiple rooms, but in practice,  the glitches and instability are far too much to overcome for this to be in any way enjoyable. Unless you have a steam controller or plan to play with a mouse and keyboard (in which case, why bother with a Steam Link at all), avoid this product, save yourself some money, and buy an extra long HDMI cord.

I found this game while looking for something completely different and played it for about an hour and a half before realizing, "Hey, this isn't what I was looking for!" and requesting a refund. Requesting a refund was a mistake and I should have kept this game in my Steam library.
I only played this game for about an hour and a half, so I may not have the best experience of this game, but bear with me.
This game is almost all RNG. Almost. The levels, loot, one time usables like potions and scrolls, and enemies and entities like the shopkeeper and little fae girl are all RNG, and that's really all that matters. Every run is different, and because of that, it is very difficult. You may be running from an enemy down a hallway towards either more enemies, ruthless traps, or a dead end. A scroll that had the "Health Regeneration" effect on a previous run may have the "Remove Curse" effect. A helmet that you find can have any number of enchantments and effects ranging from a larger radius of light, to waterbreathing, to a Curse effect that makes you unable to remove that helmet.
There are Role-Playing Game elements in the pause menu. Equipping armor, weapons, utilities, and spells is the obvious one. At the beginning of each level, you can put one point into any one of your stats, and there are certain perks for every character at each level. Mage, for example, has the perks "Alchemy" "Enchanting" "Spellcasting" and "Wand", each of which effects something different. the first level of "Alchemy" makes it so all potions are identified immediately, which is extremely useful. The first level of "Spellcasting" makes the spells you cast stronger, and the first level of "Wand" increases your effectiveness with wands and staves. I cannot remember what "Enchanting" does, though. It was probably something to do with the various effects that you find on loot. Like I said, I only played this game for about an hour and a half before making a mistake by requesting a refund, so I do not have everything memorized.
The controls are great. Not too floaty like many modern platformers are, and not too static like I find the old Mega Man titles. My favorite feature of the control scheme is the walk button, as your default speed is run/jog. While walking, you can walk off of ledges and grip the edge of them to take a peek below you and decide whether or not you want to jump down or find another way around.
The character types are your typical Knight, Rogue, and Mage. Knight starts with a not-too-good-but-still-effective sword and defensive spells, Mage starts with a crappy staff and offensive/defensive spells that cost zero magic points, and I did not play Rogue, but judging by the character portrait it looks like Rogue would either start with an okay Bow and some Arrows or an okay Dagger of some sort, maybe both.
The color scheme is a little dark, but it fits the setting. There is a radius of light around your character that can be obstructed by obstacles, so while it is possible you can find a mapping scroll which shows you the terrain for that level, enemies and traps are still unknown to you. Not like traditional platformers where everything is all lit up and everything is visible. You should not be able to see what enemies are on a ledge directly above you, and in this game, you can't.
The only problem that I have with this game is an extremely minor one, and likely won't be implimented at all due to the sprite size, but I would like to be able to see the equipment that I put on my character on the in-game sprite.
One of the selling points is the co-op gameplay with friends, but I do not know if it is online co-op or local co-op. The HUD on the menu seems to suggest local only, but I may be wrong. If I am not wrong, then online co-op would be a very nice addition to this game that would make me play it a lot more than I would had I not been dumb and requested a refund.
Overall, I would say that this is a very well put together platformer/rogue-like/dungeon crawler/role playing game. I believe that it is definitely worth the fifteen dollar price tag.

This is one of the best games I've ever played, and it's still in early access. Updates are consistent and there's is absolutely no fear of this title being dropped by the devs.
Vagante is HEAVILY influenced by Spelunky – if you loved Spelunky then not only are you an individual of exceptional taste, then you're in luck. I recently found myself playing Spelunky for the 2 billionth time and secretly wishing that either Derek Yu would come out with a new game, or that Spelunky magically had more content for me to explore. Miraculously, the Spelunky Gods answered my prayer.
Imagine the exceptionally tight handling of Spelunky combined with the RPG elements of, say, Dark Souls, and you've got Vagante. Defeating massive bosses provides you with skill points to level up with at campfires that you find between stages, adding a sort of RPG level progression and skill tree to the already excellent platforming foundation of this game. Dying is permanent, and it's as painful as any hardcore roguelike. That being said, the rewards are equally gripping. Finding a magical lifesteal dagger and a good pair of wall phasing gloves rekindles any sense of lost hope from your last painful, failed mission into the depths of the Vagante ruins. The interactions with enemies is great as well – most enemies don't simply harm you when touched allowing you to learn their tells and evade many of their attacks/spells/arrows.
While it sometimes feels the odds are unfairly stacked against you in Vagante, be sure that the Vagante Gods are watching out for you in their own bizarre way. For the well seasoned platform gamer, Vagante is a diamond in the rough that will require hours of accumulating deaths to finally master; however when that threshold is reached, the perfection of this game is made unmistakably clear. I don't speak hypothetically, I managed to beat this m*&%$#&@#$er (in it's current state).
Well worth the $15, hours and hours and hours of replay value – this will remain at the top of my list of favorite games (indie or not) for many years. Oh, and the multiplayer is pretty fun too :)

At least you tried, Sega… at least you tried…
This game (along with Episode II) are probably the most controversial Sonic games in the whole series.
Before this game came out, the Sonic fanbase had begged Sega for YEARS to make a classic-style 2D Sidescroller Platformer, just like the original Sonic games from the classic Mega Drive days.
Sega heard the cries and they DELIVERED!!! ...but not the way we’d hoped:
I'm not going to grumble about Sonic's design not looking like the original (especially since we got Sonic's classic design in Generations anyway), but the biggest issue with this game I find is I see it as a Modern Sonic Game disguised as an Old-School Sonic Game.
What I mean, is I feel that titling it as ‘Sonic 4’ was a wrong choice.
Because in NO WAY does this game feel like a true sequel to Sonic 3 & Knuckles to me.
Most of the stages (if not all) are just rehashes of Classic Sonic Stages.
No original ideas, no original concepts, just fan-pleasing.
Also, while I don’t seem to mind Sonic’s Homing-Attack ability, I do believe that the rest of the games' physics are poorly constructed when compared to the original Sonic games.
Despite that, I do find this game as a good ‘time-waster’ if I don’t have anything else to play.
Not a bad game, but I wouldn't recommend it to someone that has never played a single Sonic game before in his/her life.

Many years ago in a time called 2001 came a legend called Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis and it gained many rewards along with a expansion pack called Resistance and even got Game Of The Year. But then around a ayear before ArmA: Armed Assault came out Codemasters and Bohemia had some troubles and split and Codemasters took the rights to the name Operation  Flashpoint and got re-released in 2011 under the name ArmA: Cold War Assault.
ArmA: CWA is a military shooter/military simulator that is set during 1985 at the height of the Cold War. Soviet forces invade a bunch of islands and thats where you come in as apart of the U.S. army which is all I know.
The graphics haven't aged well over the years and don't live up to todays standards. Textures being quite blurry and models are low-poly don't look nice but I guess computers weren't power beasts back in 2001 to be able to render some very large maps like Everon, Malden or Nogova which is the largest there.
Sounds aren't to bad, ambient sounds being the best and the weapon sounds are lacking but do deliver a nice feeling of power. There is little ambient combat sounds which makes it hard to detect how far and where the fire is coming from but you do have a direction of where it might be coming from.
You have the basics of shooter elements W,A,S,D move you around the map as a infantrymen. Z prones and Q goes crouch Q stands you up which is odd but you get used to it. Many more controls in-game but I'll explain vehicle controls. The basics when in any ground vehicle Q is slow speed, W is medium speed, E is fast speed, A turns left, D turns right and S goes backwards. Aircraft is a different story which would be best to learn in-game.
There is selection of weapons and vehicles on each side and they have equal power to their opposing side. Sometimes even having a strong point and a weak point like the West side's Jeep is weakly protected but is faster than the more armoured East side's UAZ which is slower but can fit more people. Tanks have equal strength and power like the M60 is equal to the T-72 (unsure about the Resistance T-55.)
Its missions can get buggy and glitchy but thats only the missions.
The multiplayer servers are no longer online but you can download programs to see servers so it isn't fully dead yet.
Overall I think its a decent game worth the money, it may be old but it still lives up as a good game and is GREAT when modded to utter♥♥♥♥♥♥

Having played since launch, I can finally say that I recommend this game. Most server issues and bugs have been fixed, and the team is fairly active at trying to get new content into the game.
If you like fighting games you might get more of a kick out of this than if you don't, and you should get this game primarily for PvP. The PvE, while there, still feels like more of a tutorial to lead you into the PvP once you've mastered most of the moves. Graphically the game looks quite nice, though you'll have to be able to bear the more cartoony stylized style.
The only downside is that the combat can get a bit boring on the long term, so I feel like this game is better in small bursts. While the ability to pick your own moves can be fun, and while it's fun to put together your own fighting style, ultimately fighting itself consists of 2 buttons. Whichever combination of two buttons you press, and which way your character is turned initially, will determine which moves you will do. Now if you care less about execution and more about the way it looks, this is perfect. But if you really like the combo execution in fighting games, then this will turn into a snoozefest in the end I'm afraid. Which doesn't mean the game can't be fun, but I'd take it in small doses in that case.
That said, I would personally value the current game at 20~25 euros. Get it on a 20% or more discount. (Unless you really feel like you love these kinds of games)

The spiritual successor to TFC, Fortress Forever is as skill-based as they come. FF revolves around movement, something TF2 really dissapoints with. Bhopping, conc jumping, and rampsliding are just a handful of the techniques you can use to fly past the enemy team's defenses, swipe the flag out from under some explosives, and get the hell out before they can even react!
One of my favorite Source games to date, Fortress Forever's usage of air control as an actual game mechanic blends graceful midair flights with a fast-paced, explosive FPS experience that feels amazing to play or even watch (check out Voss's scout gameplay). Movement is key when you speed across the map, then hit a ramp and launch into the enemy base.
If you've ever been surfing in any Source game, you'll find yourself speeding along and pulling off amazing stunts very quickly. Even on my first game, I was able to get some great kills and jumps. Those unfamiliar with air control and how it works can play a tutorial that explains how and when to use these techniques, unlike TF2's "USE THE SCROLL WHEEL TO SWITCH WEAPONS OK YOU ARE MASTER AT SOLDIER NOW"
Just don't go in expecting TF2 (aka Valve Team Fortress featuring the names of 9 people we stole).
Its really fun, wish it had an option to play with bots offline, but that's my only complaint.

It's a good game, but honestly I didn't know what I have been doing in this game.

The parts where it's a shooter work okay for the most part. Controls are all with the mouse by default and allows quick movement from one end of the screen to another. As you kill baddies in said shooter you're supposed to collect "ink" to upgrade and buy new items & modifications for your ship. It can be a bit of a challenge of its own to get said ink because they're around enemies & gunfire often and they disappear fairly quickly so you can't necessarily wait for them to come to you all that much. The upgrades and items you buy for the ship with the ink really come in handy though from what I found the guns that spew bullets are extremely weak even when upgraded to the max. To sort of compensate for that you also get a heavy-damage-dealing melee weapon that automatically attacks whatever's in front of the ship so should they come within range. It adds a bit more depth to the gameplay; you can either keep shooting while easily seeing something that can kill you at a safe distance or get close for faster kills while figuring out when to back off when it looks like the ship's in a dangerous spot.
There are a good chunk of shooter levels in this game but unfortunately I found out that I'd have to do a series of very lackluster 2D platforming to even unlock these levels, which is what ruins this game for me.
There's hardly anything to the platforming; jump over here, jump that pit, talk to this person to MAYBE unlock an actual shooter level. By default you use the mouse to run, jump, and interact which feels very awkward to play with. You can set it in the pause menu to move around via the keyboard instead (which works a lot better) however when you're about to get to the shooter levels there's a good chance you'll want to switch back to the mouse controls, at least I did since I got to be more precise with the mouse during those levels.
Navigating and just plain running around through the platforming areas is a tedious task of its own. Anything important you get to do is often a bit of a ways off and the artstyle, though pretty cool, I think makes navigating a lot more confusing, espcially when running to the foreground and background.
It's not something I'd want to finish if it means going through a lot of tedious platforming that hardly rewards much.

I got the Steam Link in a Black Friday Sale for 2 bucks together with the Steam Controller just because it cost almost nothing.
- First of all, the packaging is beautiful. It comes with a fairly long HDMI, Ethernet and power cable/cord, several outlet adapters and a quick set-up guide.
- Setup takes about ten seconds. Plug it in, connect it to your TV and WiFi and your done. I navigated the interface with the Steam Controller which worked perfectly. You have tons of options and preferences to play around with. It also has bluetooth for input or audio devices.
- What does Steam Link do, exactly? It mirrors your pc screen to your TV. With Big Picture Mode or without. It basically saves you the hassle to run an HDMI cable from your pc to your TV.
- Does it anything else than that? Not that I know of.
- Does it work with WiFi? In my case, it didn't. I mean it "works" perfectly fine, but it's unusable for literally anything. It lags even when using the Steam interface. I tried playing a video, nope. I tried playing Superflight as a testrun. Nope. The thing is, everything works perfectly on the PC you are connected with. As in: the video or the game is literally running on that pc. Steam Link doesn't run any programs, it just mirrors your pc screen.
- Does it work with Ethernet cable? Yes it does. No problems here.
So, for the 2 bucks I paid for it, I can't complain. But judging from my experience, it's useless. If you need an ethernet cable, why not use an HDMI cable and just connect your pc with your TV? Same thing. The only advantages Steam Link holds over said HDMI cable would be 1. you can plug in your Controller in the Steam Link 2. you can connect a different pc without unplugging anything. But still need Steam running on that pc, and that pc will be unusable while you're using Steam Link.

Sonic The Heghehog 4 - Episode 1 is a 2D platformer that came out in 2010, later came to Steam in 2012, and is a direct continuation of main trilogy of Sonic games. Sonic 4 project was supposed to have few episode-games, but it only ever reached two. It also should be noted that smartphone versions of this episode have some differences in it, mostly some of gameplay in some levels being different. More carts in mines, I heard.
Though, it doesn't have enough of resolutions. You may want to play in windowed mode so it will not look ugly.
Being episode means that it's not a big game. You got world map where you can select one of the four main zones, each boasting 3 acts, each one using different new gimmick, plus serapate boss act. Plus final level. And plus seven special stages. Actually, if you cound all acts together, it's quite a decent lenght, not much shorter than what Sonic 1 was.
And you know, when the game came out, the critizm was quite extreme. Fans were pushing, kicking and tearing apart Sonic 4 so hard, I actually started to belive that this game is a massive failure. Those videos that showcase inferior physics of main character were quite proving the point. The one where Sonic was standing on the vertical-part of a curve and refused to fall off. They also kept critizing the fact that it had Homing Attack move, the one where you home/zero at the enemy in front of you when you are in air.
And with my very very low negative expectation, I was blown away that this game doesn't suck. It's true that the physics don't work as good as old title, think of Sonic Rush without boost. It doesn't have same rolling physics for sure, so it's more about running and jumping. And yes, the second zone, casino night, with all the pinball bumpers, was showing a weaker side of a game. But as I kept playing, I saw that level design was real nice. It still had few paths you can take. It still wasn't just "run and never jump". It even was introducing new gimmicks each act, like being underwater or getting into cannons that shoot you out, making each act more unique and showing that this game wasn't as lazy job as I was expecting it to be.
And the biggest highlight of it was the second act of Labyrinth zone, which had darkness, Sonic holding light, switches, carts and even usual timed puzzle that platforming genre tend to have. That act is really unique and felt awesome, bringing something fresh to Sonic formula, that even fans themselves beated up badly. Shame that some of Sonic fans didn't play enough of other platformers to be able to figure otu that puzzle and were just complaining about speed and physics, disregarding level design and platforming. The first Sonic wasn't as fast as later ones and that is my favourite.
That, and homing attack is nice there too, with lines of enemies being placed in such way that you can access higher areas if you make use of this mechanics.
But it still quite a weak title, it feels like it didn't want to go too epic, was constraining itself. For example, bosses. They are like the classic Sonic 1 bosses, just eggman taking his time while doing something simple. With a twists. But it still feels on really simple side. At least they were combined in final level for boss rush and then final boss didn't dissapoint. This final boss is going to give you hard time like in all old platformers, killing you until you learn and master all the required tactics and then take him down.
Then again, difficulty is uneven. For most of parts game is easy, with harder parts here and there. And final boss. Though, diffculty does grow slightly as you progress in levels.But my main complaint is lives system. Which is only needed so you wouldn't restart stages from scratch. The thing is, game showers you with lives. You get lives for 100 rings. Then you get life if you finish act with around 100 rings or so, as you will get huge score. And then the second act of second zone throws so many at you at once. Let's say, if in the videogames universe there was market for lives, this game would have make it collapse due to huge inflation.
You also can collect 7 emeralds. They change ending slightly, teasing with what was coming for Episode 2, and they also allows you to transform into Super Sonic. At least, thankfully, transformation is placed on serapate button this time around, so you don't have to worry about accidently transforming into him if you don't like it.
Special Stages are a twist on Sonic 1 formula. You still find Sonic rolling in a maze. But this time around, you control the rotation of maze itself. It was quite hard, but interesting. Much better than Special Stages in Sonic 1 for sure, with additional elements to it too.
Graphics are your usual 2.5D deal. Background are 2D, objects are 3D. They do have simplistic shading that puts many away, but it's fine.
Music, on other hand, is less fine. I can like it for what it is, but if you think of it as trying to emulate music in original Sonic titles, then it comes off as a stereotype, carricature. It's not pretty, abuses same drums and has repetitive tracks. Especially one boss music, which is only few-seconds long or so. I still like them, some even have tense mood that originals tended not to have, but quality is not on the same level.
And that said, physics still do get in the way. Mostly, when you need precise platforming. You have to get used to Sonic stopping suddenly when you release buttons. Being like a tank. On two legs. And jumping one. Yea, Homing Attacks help. And yea, less momentum based, as rolling off the slope still slows you down, like in most modern 2D Sonics. But eh. Still fine platformer.
Though, there is some cheap enemy placement. Like, in darkness level, the first enemy you encounter pops out in front of you, giving a bad impression for whole level, being afraid of other cheap placement. But it's quite rare, actually. That, and rings system of health in Sonic games always made it feel that it's alright to get hit occasionally.
I am not really sure that I can recommend to those who aren't into Sonic. And even then, only those Sonic fans who aren't just there for speed may enjoy this one. It doesn't even feel like proper trilogy continuation, there is no plot or throwback to past events. You just kick Eggman for no reason.
Perhaps I liked it because I had very low expectations. Was expecting a bad game. Horrible one. And I sure can see why people would have made it sound like it, as it was hyped a lot, as continuation to everybody's beloved trilogy.
Think of it as, let's say, Sonic 2D spinoff that would be developed exclusively for smartphone. Yes. Something like that. It's pretty cool this way.

This is another one of those "Steam needs a Mixed option" reviews. Ultimately I am recommending this game because I enjoyed my time with it despite it having a fair number of flaws. I will explain further ahead, I just wanted to get this out of the way first.
is the sequel to the critically acclaimed classic, Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (& Knuckles), a game that, in my opinion, did not require a sequel. Because of how successful Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (& Knuckles) was, it's almost guaranteed that
will be disappointing to any long-term Sonic fan in some way or form, but that isn't to say that the game is a complete disaster, it's actually quite fun if you can overlook some of the bad features it has, which I will cover next.
Right off the bat you will see that this game does not play like any other 2D Sonic game in the past, there is barely any sense of speed and the physics actually feel worse than those in the first and original Sonic the Hedgehog. Spin dashes often slow down your momentum rather than increase your speed and jumping feels very clunky most of the time, this can be especially frustrating on the Casino Street Act 2 stage where you have to use careful platforming to jump across a bridge of moving cards.
Poor physics aside, the levels and stages are fun to play for the most part, but they are sadly just rehashes of previous levels from the older Sonic games, just branded with new names. Splash Hill for example is the same as Green Hill, Casino Street is a mix of Casino Night and Carnival Night, Lost Labyrinth is naturally very similar to Labyrinth from the first game and Mad Gear is Metropolis from Sonic the Hedgehog 2. The boss fights are also rehashes of bosses from the same levels they are almost direct clones of.
as a sequel was essentially expected to have some new levels, unique areas and boss fights, but there are none of the above featured in this game. Everything will feel familiar but different, and unfortunately not in the good way like
was able to accomplish.
What this game (or Episode, as Episode II is supposedly better and I haven't gotten to it yet) lacks is originality, something that all the old games managed to achieve so effortlessly, with all levels and bosses feeling unique despite being so limited at the time, so ultimately as a sequel,
is a disappointment. As a standalone Sonic game however, it can be a fun experience if you take it for just that and not the "successor" to one of the best games ever made, similar to Doom vs Doom 3 as the first example that comes to mind.
Yes, this game has a lot of problems and lacks originality, but I still found it to be fun and I enjoyed my time with it, that is why I'm ultimately going to go for "yes" as opposed to "no". Long-term Sonic fans, take it from another seasoned Sonic the Hedgehog player, you are most likely going to be disappointed, but I wouldn't go so far as to say that you won't enjoy it at all, it takes a little bit of adapting to get used to the the new feeling of movement in this game, but once you get the hang of it, it's a fun to play.
So that's about it, you will either enjoy your time with this or you won't. In the end, my advice is to play it and judge it for yourself.

I don't honestly know whether to recommend this game or not. I have loved the Sonic franchise since I first learnt to actually control anything way back in the Mega Drive era, so the fact the Sonic team decided to continue on from those days was something I had to get in on! But we all know that the Sonic Team of recent years have let us down more times than they've given us anything wonderful. This game somehow lives in between the two.
The visuals, the style, it all harks back to the good old days, and it is wonderfully vibrant. Controlling Sonic though, it's not anywhere near as smooth as it was back then. Sonic feels jerky, and can feel like he has no momentum, though there are times when you manage not to notice this! I think they have hoped this lack of smooth control is made up for by using modern Sonic's new ability to make this sort of homing attack, somewhat negating the need for precise control. This being said, they seem to have enjoyed creating puzzle sections within a couple of the levels, requiring much more control than the game gives.
So much is in this game that should make it great, and nostalgic, and all that. And it sort of achieves this, sometimes. But it doesn't do it well. I want to love it, but the level designs are mostly either lazy or just plain poor. The real work seems to have gone into half cloning a few parts of levels from the 90s to make it familiar, which I find quite absurd considering this is Sonic 4. At no point in Sonic 3 did any of us go "Ah yes, remember this bit from Sonic 1?" It should be a continuation, bringing it into the modern world, but these attempted "homages" only serve to make you notice all the things they've changed about the way the game works, and how you don't like it in this setting.
I'd recommend it I think, because it still has something there, something you can enjoy, but don't expect to get that feeling back, for some reason, although the game is following on from 3, they seem to have targeted it at the kids who would never have touched any form of Sega console and think they have only ever made games for Nintendo.

This game is a lot like the old Goosebumps choose your own ending books where you could have a very long, very short, or moderately long game experience.  Every choice you make determines a lot about your future and opens and closes doors that you won't know exist until you've played the game through multiple times.  Now, there's nothing necessarily wrong with this format, but there should be some sort of warning at the beginning of the game that states that you have to experience each ending to truly appreciate the game because depending on the ending you choose, you could be looking at a 3-hour playthrough with an incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending that would leave you feeling furious and cheated, especially if you payed full price for the game. Now to be fair, I should note before I begin that I've never played any of the other 'Way of the Samurai' games before.  That being said, I found this game to be addictingly fun, and endearingly quirky in a way only obviously Japanese games with questionable translation and terrible voice acting can be.  Once you get the combat system down, normal sword fighting works pretty well, and the push and pull system of blocks is relatively straightforward.  HOWEVER, if you try to use any more sophisticated combat moves such as kicks or throws, you're♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck.
I didn't know that translating the controls of a game from Xbox 360 to PC could be done so horribly.  First off, to even draw your blade, you have to select 'page up' which makes about as much sense as coating your♥♥♥♥♥♥in honey and skull ♥♥♥♥ing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a beehive.  Combat is often thrust upon you quickly, leaving you very little time to react before you're being cut to ribbons.  To remedy this, you could just go around with your sword drawn, but this either scares the locals so much they won't trade with you, or makes just about every dumb ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the area with a weapon attack you, so you can't really do that either.  To kick, you have to hold 'page down' while pressing 'e', which requires that you let go of the mouse and leave yourself open to attack.  All the 'page down' button does is block, which is typically done with 'mouse3', but in order to kick, you have to use 'page down' for some strange reason.
One other gripe I have is that the framerate is locked in at 30 fps, so there will always be a lag, thus blocking three consecutive strikes from even the lowest opponent is damn near impossible.  Once you get to upper level boss battles, if your weapon doesn't have a high defense rating, the boss will execute some ridiculous, ostensibly unblockable combo attack and take out half of your health in one fell swoop.  Now, this is to be expected, and although it's frustrating at times, it happens rarely enough that it doesn't completely destroy the combat experience.
But there is some good news.  The storytelling is fractured and cliché, sure, but thankfully the game relies on storytelling so little that it doesn't really matter.  This game does customization very, VERY well.  You can upgrade swords and spears, or collect parts and create your dream weapon.  Shopkeepers sell different masks and accessories that will offer quite a few cool new looks for your character, and new outfits can be unlocked as you gain samurai points for acting virtuously on every playthrough.  Even though the map is small and you'll probably only get 7 or so hours out of actual storylines, it's still fun for a long time to go around killing other samurai or whomever.
Despite its faults, this game is a lot of fun, but I'd still wait for a sale.  7.5/10.

This game has 1 major flaw; it's really gosh darn hard to get into, I really cannot remember how I managed to trawl through the uninteresting mess that are the low levels and starter zone, but I certainly do not regret it; this game is so amazingly unique and I love it <3
Now this game is technically an MMORPG, and MMORPGs have a great level of stigmatism, mostly caused by great numbers of Korean WoW-clone grind fest chatboxes. DDO isn't like that, DDO is focused on the 'game' part; character building (my personal favourite part, just like real DnD) and play-style are very important, so if you want an MMO with unique and interesting gameplay, give DDO a try.
However, this gameplay focus came at a remarkable cost; the social aspect, every quest is an instance, which while making them unique, means you can't just party up with people half-way and make friends easy; you have to make groups beforehand and go into the dungeon together. Of course the Devs don't expect us to do that all by ourselves, so there is a "Grouping" menu, where people can put out server-wide messages to find people to quest with; and it works well enough. But- the DDO community has gained a very... "elitist" edge to it over time, and try as I might, I am not exempt to this rule; many in-game factors make it hard not to become rather "elitist", per se, over time. Many people are interested only in speed running dungeons for optimal xp, and have little-to-no-interest in making friends. This can make things very hard for newer players, who want to take it slow, learn the rather complex mechanics, and make some friends.
All in all, I love DDO and would love to see it thrive, but until the Devs overhaul the starter area, early levels and social aspect, (I say this, I have no idea what they could do to spice them up though :/), I can only really recommed DDO to groups - at least 2 people (max party size is 6) - who are looking for a group based, challenging PvE RPG that rewards effort and planning.

A great little roguelike! If you like Spelunky, but want a bit more combat like Rogue Legacy, you should definitely check this game out. The initial difficulty is high, but as you begin to figure things out it's very satisfying. And for the most part it feels
, which imo a lot of roguelikes get wrong. When I die I usually feel it's because *I* screwed up - not because the Random Number Generator wasn't in my favor. It's still very difficult, though, and I've come nowhere near beating it.
While the game is a roguelike, with no carry-over between runs, it also has RPG elements. There are three different classes, and you earn points to improve your stats and abilities. You also find a variety of new gear, potions, and scrolls, and can even pray at different shrines for different bonuses. Taken together, all of this helps makes every run feel unique because you never know what you'll find. It also gives both a sense of progression and a sense of investment in every single run.
Visually, I have to say screenshots don't do this game justice. The muted colors really fit the feel, and the reason there is a lot of darkness is because you reveal the map as you explore. You can also only see what's directly in your character's line of sight (like fog of war in strategy games). It's an interesting gameplay mechanic and means you have to be extremely cautious as you proceed. The sound in the game is excellent as well, the music setting a great spooky tone and the sound effects doing their job nicely.
Overall, if you are a fan of roguelikes and 2D platformers this is one for you. It's only in alpha, but it's stable, has plenty of content and features, and is well worth the asking price.

As a huge total war fan, I was very disappointed with E:TW. I couldn't even force myself to put more than a few sessions into the game because of one thing - How awful the battle AI and unit pathing is.
I've put thousands of hours into rome 1 and Shogun 2. Most of them were played on the lowest settings on an old mac before I built my PC, so I'm VERY familiar with the general weirdness of total war AI. Empire takes every weird bug and turns it up to 11. Units won't fire when they're obviously in range. (Yes I know how line of sight works) Movement orders over bridges will often send your units halfway across the map to cross in the shallows. Attack orders can end in a unit casually strolling towards the enemy only to reform at the wrong angle.
Seige battles especially are almost unplayable. Units will not fire off the walls correctly, cannons will not target walls correctly. Good luck trying to order your units through the right holes in the wall, they will just run off to a different side of the fort taking fire.
There's so much potential for an amzing game here but the clunkiness brings it down to the worst Total War game I've ever played. There's no single glaring flaw but the exceptionlly stupid AI makes you micromanage your units constantly. If you don't they will end up taking a route you didn't want them to, getting stuck on terrain or taking casualties you didn't deserve. Nothing is worse than having units get destroyed just because they didn't do what you wanted them to.
I used to think the matchlock units in shogun 2 were bad but now they control buttery smooth compared to Empire. Do yourself a favor and get Napolean (I haven't played but hear it's a lot smoother) or  Fall of the Samurai if you want guns in your total war.

It's one thing to build a city, but another thing entirely to manage it. Games like SimCity are high-level simulations that let you build services like trains and bus stops and then forget about them, trusting their operation to whatever imaginary middle-managers you have. Cities in Motion is the game for them, a simulation entirely concerned with developing and managing transit systems. And while that might not sound like the most thrilling thing in the world, it's presented in such a relaxing, charming way that it's hard not to find joy in.
Each scenario in Cities in Motion sets you in a fully-realized 3D city, where every building and landmark is named and given uses to the populace. You run a startup transportation company, charged with arranging bus lines, tram routes, subway tunnels, and more to achieve goals and turn a profit. The first part is pretty simple and fun, as you get regular missions to connect different parts of the city in various ways. This can be anything from running trains from downtown to the suburbs, to building a bus stop for one very lazy fellow's house.
The second part, turning a profit, is where you might get stuck. There are a LOT of factors to consider when drawing a bus line or even just placing a stop. There are seven classes of people to ferry around, including blue-collar workers, tourists, and retirees. They all live in different parts of the city and have different transit needs, so just running lines from apartments to shopping centers might not cut it if those apartments are where students or CEOs live. There are also a mess of vehicles to outfit your routes with, each with different price tags, speeds, safety ratings, appeals, and fuel consumptions. Add to that your control over wages, ticket prices, and advertising, plus a full economic model for the city that can change the business landscape during recessions and crisises, and you may very well have trouble grasping why you're not making any money.
At least the interface won't be what's standing in your way. Cities in Motion has some very helpful information overlays for the city, as well as useful graphs and charts of your company's performance at all levels. Routes are shown in clear paths overlaid on the city, and floating tabs over your stops display all the key information you need to make informed decisions about your service. The 3D models of everything, from the buildings to the buses to the people, are surprisingly detailed and pleasantly animated. The sound design is exactly what you're expecting as well, with pleasing jingles and chimes over a mostly relaxed soundtrack. You'll find plenty of content to keep you busy as well, with loads of campaigns, scenarios, and sandboxes spread across the many cities of the world. It'll take some effort to break into, but Cities in Motion does everything it can to make the steep learning curve a fun one to climb.

Legionwood 1: Tale of the Two Swords
--Released May 2016: Dark Gaia Studios
Legionwood is a lesser known free-to-play indie game. While the game boasts no impressive programming, having been made entirely on an RPG-making program by its creators, it leaves its own unique mark on the player.
Story
We begin in Legionwood as a young man going to market for vegtables with his younger sister. Somehow, along the way the two are swept into a whirl-wind adventure, one with swords, magic, and monsters. The story develops steadily throughout the entirety of the game, and results in dialog rich and plot heavy gameplay with plenty of action thrown in-between.
Immersion
While Legionwood could be considered open world, it is not free-reign, leaving it lacking on the immersion side of things. However, the compelling story and ease of gameplay will likely have you playing for hours at a time anyway. Just make sure you make it to a save crystal every once in a while!
Game Mechanics
Simply put, the game is simple. Follow the path of quests to get to the other side. There is a set path for your adventure, and deviating from it will lead you to blocked paths and locked doors. So as far as gameplay goes, player actions are quite limited on freedom. Legionwood functions off a similar system to any 16-bit game, and is reminiscent of a classic Final Fantasy in it's handling, right down to the turn-based fighting and party controls.
Controls
While Legionwood requires a very small amount of buttons to play, movement is choppy and uncoordinated when using a keyboard and mouse. For this reason, it is best to take advantage of the full-controller support the game allows.
Graphics & Visual Quality
Again simplicity prevails. In the major portions of the game, mainly during gameplay and traveling the world, Legionwood presents as a classic 16-bit model. However, I will say that design-wise, the game is very well thought-out. There is a great amount of detail work put into every scene and location of Legionwood that helps the game feel rounded and complete. Additionally, the painting style cut-scenes are well done and blend seemlessly into gameplay.
Overall Opinion
The 40 hours I took to lead that young man and his sister through their quest in Legionwood were well-spent. Although it's not a big-ticket game, it constructs a fantastical world and compelling characters. I encourage anyone who's considering Legionwood to download it and give it a whirl.

It's free, I mean it is free!!
Seriously, there a lot of RPGMaker games charging money with lesser content. But this one gives the player 20+ hrs of old-school JRPG style gameplay. I really enjoyed my time with Legionwood 1. The story, while a bit weak in the beginning really got to me after a while. Battle system itself was very nice. However, what I really liked the most was the open class leveling system. Once a character levels up, you will get 10 AP which you can distribute freely on your character, making him/her a mage, fighter, tank etc...and the best is that adding AP to raise stats is not a final commitment. At any given time you can remove spent AP and redistribute it on other stats. This gives room for lots of experimentation.
Now it has to bit admitted that the game is not without it's flaws. One particular annoying fact is the apparently fixed number of steps until the next random encounter happens. This can become a bit of a chore once your party is well levelled and you just want to get to the end of an area. But it's nothing too annoying to keep you from playing.
Overall I recommend this to anybody who likes old-school style (or like me RPGMaker) games. It's free and there is no reason to not give it a shot!!

Lann and Liana are two inseparable siblings like many others. All they wanted was to visit the festival at the city castle, but destiny had other plans. In the world of Legionwood, destiny is more than a word, it's the truth behind many hero's actions.
Created with RPG Maker,
uses all of its abilities, and considering it's a game with over 10 years, it plays really well. The engine gives everything the player needs, to adventure into this impressive world that we have the honour to visit.
Fight with up to 5 characters, find summons to battle at your side, explore a big area with a lot of cities and a handful of interesting side-quests, travel through caves, land, sea, and become the biggest hero Legionwood has ever seen!
is free, and that's a steal! For the content and quality it easily could cost money. We have seen a lot worse for an absurd price. But this is not the case. The design is extremely nice, the areas are well done and you can tell the designers really love what they do, because the attention to details are top of the line.
There are some variations and I never felt I was going to the same area twice (unless backtracking obviously). From forests, to desert, even snowy mountains, the game is well divided and gives you a strong feeling of traveling.
Every city has a very strong personality, and among that the NPC's. Each with a dedicated line, and when events dramatically change, some tend to say new things. I also enjoyed reading the graves, we can expect tips, jokes and some inner developer messages! All that good stuff!
The gameplay is based on the RPG Maker from 2006, therefore some features lack in terms of battles, but everything runs smooth and nice.
The game used to be harder, and the creator level things a bit, with less random encounters and weaker enemies. The game went through some big changes from its first release, and I'm really happy with the final result.
The most surprising factor in terms of gameplay for me was the ability to earn AP for each new level achieved, and can be used on several attributes such as HP, Attack, Defense, etc. The interesting thing is... The player can change them, at any point in the game. Therefore, making a magical user for a battle, and making him a tank holding a strong axe on the next. It's a great idea, and this results extremely well.
The story gave me a few surprises, it's really well directed and interesting, not only that, but gives the player a good idea of the world, and the past history. To understand the future, we must reflect on the past, and so do the heroes, and for a good reason. When games are limited by the engine, it's the story that needs to shine, and it sure does. The game even has  cutscenes with nice hand made drawings that portray the characters.
Overall, I have only good things to say when comes to this game. All the things I dislike are mostly based on the archaic version of RPG Maker, but that's all we had back in 2006.
A game worth being played if you love classic RPG's. A well driven story, a game that respects your time, but also offers a real challenge for those looking to complete 100%.
Has an emotional story that puts the player in front of a terrible enemy, and all cliches aside, I really enjoy it and I recommend it to anyone looking for such a good experience.

Mordheim: City of the Damned has you take control of a warband of eitherReikland Mercenaries, Sisters of Sigmar, Cult of the Possessed, Skaven, Witch Hunters or Undead (the latter two are DLC factions) and fight your way around Mordheim gathering delicious delicious wyrdstone that you collect because whoever you work for wants them for reasons.
Combat is turn based and uses Strategy Points to move, use support abilities, do actions, while spells and fighting use offence points. If you are familiar with the tabletop game, there are no turn phases these actions all happen within a units turn.
The game is perma-ironman so units may (usually will) suffer injuries at points some of which have very real consequences to the characters, such as brain damage that cause stupidity, loss of limbs/eyes, or death. Units also gain stat points that are used to improve their stats (duh) and skill points that are used along with gold to purchase skills. Cultist heroes and impressives can also get a random mutation. This creates warbands that grow uniquely depending on the circumstances of battles.
On higher difficulties a demon (Bloodthirster, Plaguebearer, Daemonette or Pink Horror) or a Chaos Ogre will spawn on maps and depending on how (or if) they enter the fray may help or hinder your efforts. On all difficulties traps are present that may have a positive or negative effect on the units that trigger them.
With the addition of more warbands one of the main downsides, that combat becomes a bit samey because of the limited number of warbands present is somewhat negated. Hopefully more warbands will be released to improve replayability.
A second flaw is that sometimes AI pathfinding gets a bit wonky, espcially with large units trying to get to battle via the shortest route and trying to go through doors that they can't fit through.
Lastly the limited number of maps, while varied, do get repetitive. Different cart deployment locations and wyrdstone/loot points help move things around, but they are the same map.

(Platformer-Puzzle)
We have some basic options:  Vibration (if you're using a controller), Sound Effects, Music, Subtitles (NOT on unless you turn them on), and Use Arrow keys (if you prefer not to use or don't have a controller), and then there are settings for the grapics, low, medium, and high.  There are also six languages to choose from.  The game automatically adjusted for my widescreen, but it can be played Windowed by hitting Alt-Enter, if you wish.
The game begins in a very
-esque way, and it's up to you to save your brother from the trouble you caused for him. ;p  Gameplay starts out as a very basic platformer, but it's not long until you start gaining some powers, and that's where the true charm of the game starts shining through.  The puzzle mechanics are brilliantly realized, ranging anywhere from easy to perplexing, but not to the point of frustration.
I was enjoying the puzzle aspect of the game so much that I was actually a bit disappointed when, in latter levels, we started needing to depend on quick decision-making, and at times, good reflexes!  It wasn't until the final sequence of the game that I remembered -- Oh yeah, this is what platformers used to be all about! (ie. Donkey Kong Country, etc.)  The beauty of these sections is that, while they may be difficult, they are still doable!  It may take a dozen tries, but it CAN be done, AND you don't have to keep starting the level over again to achieve it, as the automatic save-points are well-spaced.
Something I truly love about the game is the graphics.  Sure, they're pretty, but the devs did an amazing job making a side-scrolling platformer *feel* like a 3D game by periodically changing up the perspective.  Beautifully done, devs, I'm very impressed! :D
The music was nicely-chosen, and I enjoyed the voices, as well -- especially some of Max's "YEEES!" moments. lol~
- You can attach vines to a myraid of objects, ranging from branches to boulders and more.
- Items can be cut at the base OR the tip!
- Be creative and don't give up!  The devs give us a lot of freedom with our powers, and sometimes it's going to be trial-and-error figuring things out.
There are a couple of things to be on the lookout for whilst you're running around.  They are beholders (plants with eyeballs at the end of a stalk that allow the user to spy on the world) and pieces of an amulet.  These collectibles are not *needed* to complete the game, but they sure do add an extra bit of fun. XD  You can replay a chapter at any time (even after you've completed the game) from via the menu, and looking at the menu during gameplay will show you how many you have left to find on your current level.  In addition, there are 27 Achievements for you to earn, another plus in my books.
Overall, I found
to be a delightful game, full of beauty, danger, excitement... and tempered with just a splash of good old fashioned platformer-frustration.  I would say that it's OK to play with older kids, but perhaps not little ones.  There's a big scary monster in there (whom I find to be absolutely fabulous!), but it might upset younger children.
Highly recommended!

Doom and Destiny Advanced is a kind of sequel to Doom and Destiny: Spaghetti Fantasy RPG. Never having played the first Doom and Destiny I couldn't tell you what the similarities are. What I can tell you are my first impressions.
You and a group of your friends awaken in a burning castle. As you try to escape you are then teleported back to the real world where you are heading to play Do&De (essentially Dungeons and Dragons).
What this game does well is the humor. From the characters dialogue to the enemies you face there's constantly little things to have a good chuckle. For instance one of the first enemies you face is a giant poop monsters. I mean come on, how stupid is that (It's delightfully stupid that's how much).
The beginning of the game does a good job of taking you through a tutorial without making you feel like that's what it is. Woven into the first parts of the game are npc you can interact with that tell you what different things do. It's an effective way to get you started.
The rpg parts are typical of a top down rpg. You cast spells, level up, heal up and murder ♥♥♥♥♥es. What really sets this game apart is the humor and charm. The story seems deep and enjoyable. Not without it's faults I've seen others report bugs, I personally didn't run into any. It is an early access game so I'm sure there are plenty of bugs. Even their updates point to bug fixes.

is a nice little horror game where you have to survive several nights in the house and complete few puzzles. During most of the gameplay, there is no music which made a bad first impression. However, you do need to listen to sound effects to avoid certain enemies so it makes sense. There are a couple things that could be improved like oversized text boxes but for $1 I can forgive it.
I am having some trouble starting and exiting the game properly. Basically, at the moment I have to start the game from the folder. If I exit it keeps on running. There are several checkpoints but there are no save files so you have to beat the game in one set. The game is about 1-2 hours long so it is not a huge problem. (as far as I can tell there might be 2 endings) You can play with a controller but I don't think you can remap any buttons. The text boxes are a bit of a problem because they hide enemies that you have to jump over.
Movement is a little stiff but I don't mind it because it feels like some of the older games that I like. You will have to do a jump+kick to reach some of the platforms which are tricky.
- I should note that you will probably enjoy the game more if you do not read the rest of the review.
The game has a Night/Day cycle that changes certain things. One of the puzzles, for example, could only be done during the night. Some of the house features change after each day. During the night you can do puzzles but you gonna get chased by all kinds of enemies. Most monsters have a different mechanic, some slow you, some scare you and other just murder the crap out of you. You can speed up the Night cycle by lighting candles so the main goal is usually to survive the night and get next checkpoint. Puzzles were very straight forward so there is not much in terms of thinking or detective work.
House has 3 floors and few locked rooms. Not a lot in terms of exploration but again the game was only $1.
Going back to my earlier point this game does not use a lot of music. I probably could argue that few areas would have benefited from having a theme (even like the first 5 minutes where you just explore the house) Since you do need to listen to sound effects to avoid few enemies I can let it slide. When the game does use music it is enjoyable though. Animations and backgrounds were appealing to me. There are a couple ways to die and I really enjoyed doing so.
I did actually find the game kinda creepy even though I played during the day. It does not create much suspense though. Few areas around the house have unique events that may startle you. Pixel game can only be so scary but in retrospect, I should have played it at night. Like there is this one enemy that always spooks me because it can come out of nowhere with loud sound effect. Jump scares were not always earned but the atmosphere was alright.
Easy 7/10 for me if text size and starting issues are fixed.
I think the concept of solving puzzles while you have to cycle between night/day is kinda neat. They should have capitalized more on the format of the game. If you want a short horror platformer I think it exceeds $1 expectations.

Not the best Sonic outing to date but it was fun.  It tries really hard to relive the Mega Drive/Genesis outings... but it just seems to fall short a bit compared with say Sonic 2, 3 & Sonic & Knuckles.  Let me list some pros and cons:
Pros: Good graphics; saving ability (which is something that Sonic 1 & 2 don't have); controls seem responsive (for the most part); and decent level design (not perfect though); oh and Super Sonic is back (that's if you prefer to play as Super Sonic).
Cons: Way too short.  I feel a bit ripped off in that Sega split Sonic the Hedgehog 4 into two episodes, with only 4 main zones each (well there's the extra episode for Metal Sonic if you buy both Episodes I & II); game physics are not always superb (I kind of got used to it though myself); and probably the thing that bothered me the most about the game is they reused too many of the same boss battles from previous games (with only slight alterations).
Overall I would recommend Episode I (and Episode II for that matter).  However, I will point out that I waited until both episodes were on sale before I bought them.
