Basically this game takes your beloved Sonic 1 and 2 memories and urinates all over them, thanks to the completely absymal player movement. Sonic essentially has no horizontal momentum at all within this game, and is able to immedately stop moving left/rightward as soon as you stop pressing any movement keys. In addition, Sonic has all the initial acceleration of a snail when moving from a complete stop. Those two things together make what should make a simple, fast-moving platforming game annoyingly hard to control, and in sharp contrast to the real Sonic games which have fluid and natural controls, where the character momentum feels right. If it wasn't for the controls, the game would otherwise be decent but completely charmless.
If you want to play a Sonic game that'll satisfy your nostagia but actually has decent controls, just play Sonic Generations instead of this. You'll be better off.

Very good transport manager game. It has a very detailed simulation of passengers, who hop from one means of transportation to another to get to their destination: you can actually see them walk to leave the tram and take the metro, and so on. In that respect I like it better than classics like Transport Tycoon, since that one never bothered to properly model passengers traveling around (OpenTTD attempted it but IMO failed so far).
I can be tough to manage the hordes of angry passengers waiting at your stops, but that problem is handily solved by raising prices for the corresponding transport type really high (thus attracting less users) and using the largest capacity vehicles you can. Don't use too many vehicles on a line or you'll cause traffic jams. Reading community guide on Steam or reading the official Cities in Motion FAQ is recommended if you want to understand the game mechanics in-depth.
I don't find many faults to this game but there are a few:
- Given a crowd of angry passengers at a stop, it's hard to figure out where they want to go. You have to check them one by one. Also some statistics that would be useful are not shown, but you can add a few more by the installation of the Line Statistics Plus mod (see this group for a mod archive:
).

Giving it a finally propper review:
Fortress Forever is inspired from Team Fortress Classic, so many  players can find similarities between those two games and even similarities between this and TF2. Unlike TFC where the maps were plain and dull, Fortress Forever has beautifully designed maps, with cool environments, easter eggs and really really good graphics for a 2007 game, it's one of the best game graphics I ever had the chance to play on in my opinion.
Unlike Team Fortress 2, Fortress Forever is a lot lot more competitive, more serious and fast paced, but players can still have fun. The objectives are pretty simple and basic, but do not get the same feeling from map to map. The community, although relatively small, is quite active and dedicated, this game still kickin' in. There are also unique gamemodes, such as escort mission (ff_hunted) or fun/football (ff_waterpolo and others) that still have the classic fortress feeling, but with a lil' bit of fun added.
Some TF2 and TFC skills can get you well around, but the games simply don't compare to Fortress Forever. FF is nice, unique, fun, polished and has a friendly and dedicated community and best part of all, is really good optimized so you can play regardless if you have a last gen PC or even old crappy computers. I could run this game with absolutely no lag or any problems on my old rig with an AMD Sempron single core 1.5 GHz, 1GB DDR and GeForce 5200 256MB at Medium graphics, so your PC can probably do a lot lot better.
Give it a try, you won't be disappointed. Looking forward to play with you.

Dying is the least of your worries when playing this game, because it's all about the flags and not the frags. Your K/D ratio won't matter a darn while your team loses over and over, and as many victories are forged from the tears of ruthless killing machines. Don't fool yourself into thinking your l33t sniping skills will help you when a Scout is tearing past you at Mach-10 with a flag in hand, at the same time a Spy is driving a knife in your back, because this game's strategy won't allow for that. Only knowledge in maximizing your chosen class' abilities will enable a win, which can transform you into an unstoppable force. Any one player in this game can elevate their team's chances, but a concerted effort from all is truly a sight to behold. Only players with the strongest will need apply, because here is where the short attention-span goes to die.
I thought for sure I'd already posted a review, but for some reason it's not there, and that's too bad because I've loved this game for years. As a fan of TFC before this, I was hoping for a modernized version when Half-Life 2 was released, but the only thing I got from Valve was TF2, which while good, really wasn't the TF I was looking for. What I wanted was the fast paced, super-soldier, flag-capture game that I'd grown to love and respect, and I wasn't the only one.
Enter, Fortress Forever.....an independent MOD crafted to emulate TFC, while also making some major improvements on an already epic formula using HL2's "Source" engine, and marvelously might I add. Ever feel like launching yourself across a map in a deperate attempt to score points by recovering a flag dropped in the middle of a warzone? Maybe you want to be the one defending said flag from an all-out assault? Or maybe you'd just enjoy picking from 9 complexly powerful classes, and playing the equivalent of an online sport, complete with points and objectives that actually mean something? Did I mention it's free? Just download this game, pack a lunch, and strap in for the ride of your life.

The game is really enjoyable if you like face paced old school FPS style gameplay, it's pretty much in the essence of Team Fortress Classic but given a faster pace with some interesting additions.
My only complaint is that engineers sentry is a bit slow... it should be faster to respond to threats.  Other than that, great game.  I'v played this since 2007 and it's evolved quite well.

It only took me 2 minutes in the tutorial map and I was already digging this more than TF2. Fortress Forever is a source port of the original Team Fortress mod for Quake released somewhere in the 90's. You could say it's a rip off, but then again it's made by the same community which probably made your experience joyful in the original game as well. If your d*ck goes hard for two of the following things: TF2 and bunnyhopping, Fortress Forever is a private self-cleaning ejaculation purse for you. There's a fine line between easy and difficult movement. It's relatively easy to bunnyhop, but combining that with rocket jumps and conc-jumps with ramps and slopes makes it a fascinating combination of possible routes and scenarios.
If you're used to modern games, the weapon balance might come as some shock as the weapons in general don't deal as much damage as you'd expect them to. That is because when you're playing as a scout for instance, your objective is emphasized on flag running and swift maneuvers instead of spontaneous fragging sprees on where ever you could reach faster than a Heavyguy could for instance. When you decide to take on a gun fight, it wont be as simple as twitching your mouse over and sometimes hitting a lucky headshot. No, this game grabs you from the nuts and forces you to put some effort to it. Skill and practice is rewarded, unintentional advantages is not.
The bottom line is, none of the oldschool weapon/movement gimmicks or exploits are gone, instead they're cherished and encouraged by the community all the way from the tutorial to those bored f*cks who spend hours teaching new players new tricks and routes. Speaking of tutoring.. There seems to be a variety of flag capture mod types which I'm still quite not used to, there's not really any user friendly implications to what mod you're currently playing, which is my only complaint so far, but that'll pass soon due time I'm pretty sure.. Oh and last time I tried sniper class was broken, or the server had disabled the class. IDK, no implication to that either and I'm not sure whether it's the game's or server admin's fault.
In any case, if you hate hats and how casual TF2 is, then grab a free copy of this and come catch my flag wigging scout butt in game. If there's shortage of players in the area you're playing, join Quakenet #ff.pickup and get involved with the flutter neckbeards.

Jamestown's story is quite unusual. Imagine the 17th century. The colonization of the New World and all that. This English colony is contested by the Spanish. Who are in league with the Martians. Because everything happens on Mars. And you, Sir Walter Raleigh, must stop them. With your spaceship. How crazy is that?
The game itself is of the newly-formed 'bullet hell', a vertically scrolling shoot 'em up genre which emphasises on small Player Character hitboxes and dodging millions of bullets at a time.
You can use any of four ships, associated with four historical characters, each with its secondary fire, and a Vaunt Mode, which can be activated after collecting enough gold from your enemies, and gives you a temporary shield which absorbs all bullets, a double damage boost and a double score boost. The difficulty scales up quickly, and the challenge levels add to it even more. In short, Jamestown is one explosive, manic, and hilarious game. Why not give it a try?

Cinderella Phenomenon was definitely ones of those fairytale game that should not be judge by its cover, I knew dicesuki from previous work but I was rather relutant to play due to the fairytale theme "Cinderella" which didn't interest me as much. After beating the game, I can fully say that I'm glad I didn't brush this game off as another one of cliche meet romantic interest then happily ever after without character depth.
Minor highlights:
-great details to theme (i.e. bad end screen is different each route)
-hidden cameo reference to previous game
-background art is visually stunning
-music and timing for the mood is great
-FOR FREE!
Main highlights:
1) One thing that took me by surprise is the main character is not your typical sweet girl or blank slate, initially not likable at all. she does not go through a sudden change of character easily throughout the story, the change is rather on the perspective, she keeps her character intact. Unlike some other otome games, where there is sudden massive shift in character's personality just because you are on a different route like its a different writter for the script.
2) Not just the main character, but the rest of the cast all have their own flaws and motives which are essentially explored in througout different routes. There isn't a fairytale perfect prince/romantic interest, and the imperfection really builds the character to be more believable. These imperfections are also not cut-paste stereotypes and sometimes diverge from fairytale. Thus, the few seconds of meeting the characters really don't give away how the romance will turn out or how they may react.
3) Each route is interaction and focus theme is different so it never felt like you are redoing the same story. It's more finding more pieces of the puzzle to understand the world, how it works and the characters in the story.
4) Although the endings (good & bad) may not have been unique to many other otome games but it really fitted the world. I do enjoy how there is a short narritive to tie everything together once the game is complete that ties everything, It makes the player feel fulfilled rather than here is an acheivement unlock with say "congratualation"or "thanks for playing" picture exhibited in other games. The extra gesture is nice but I always find this emptiness or the lack of connection or meaning to the actual game.
Minor criticism:
-by utilizing the mouse to interact with the menu screen, load screen was too similiar to the save screeen. So I often save over my saves when I wanted to load previous screen instead. Maybe a different colour background could help seperate the two easier.
-the romance in some routes may not be as furfilling as others due to the pace of events that happens in the game not allow enough time to give more character interaction. Also the emotional impact point may be stolen by other side characters (well developed ones) that the deep romanctic connection at the end lacked impact. This probably would be remedy in the upcoming fandisc.
I enjoyed playing Cinderella Phenomenon more than I thought I would. It definitely has one of the more memoriable main character leads in otome games I've played (on par with "Second Reproduction"'s Christina). Frankly every character in their is quite memorable in itself making the story more enjoyable. Dicesuki is definitely one of the visual novel group that I look forward to seeing more works from.(Although I maybe biased from "Locked Hearts" which I recommend for an enjoyable  short cute otome with teddy bears). Their dedication and attentiveness to the player and the love for their creations really shows!
Please do check the game out =)

This is my first otome game and to be honest I wasn't sure what I was going to expect. After playing mid way in my first round ( I chose Karma's route), I fell in love with the story line and I couldn't stop until I completed all the stories. It's not the typical game I would play but I am so glad I did. And it has a really good plot. I love how it delves into real situations of emotional abuse by someone close, not knowing what to do and learning how to overcome difficulties through opening up to the right people. The heroine, Lucette, is thrown into a life she cannot imagine which is a reverse Cinderella, riches to rags, after being cursed by a witch and has to overcome her situation by trusting people who are luckily kind  to help even though the rest of the town hates her for who she is. The story explains why the heroine is the way she is and why people misunderstood her.  In the end , she breaks her curse and lives happily ever after.
Each story line you choose covers the plot holes and I do recommend playing each character twice to understand the full story.  My favourite routes  would be Karma, Walltz, Rod, Fritz and Rumpel. Though Waltz 's story wins hands down. (lol) Each story is so touching, has adequate humour and enough sadness to make your tears fall like nothing. Every ending is different and I loved the Bad endings as much as the Good endings. The choices you make are limited but they play an important role for what happens next.
Overall, it was an exciting game to play and I'm glad it was Free to play as well. Soundtrack is also amazing. Wished I could download it. You won't regret playing this game :) Looking forward to Dicesuki's next game <3

So I picked up the Steam Link when you could get it for £0.80 in that bundle and since then I have been using it a lot.
I will say before anything else that I use it on a wired connection and live in a really small flat. I don't know how it works over Wi-fi or over long distances.
Pros
+ Works pretty much perfectly out of the box. I didn't run into any trouble getting it linked to my main PC
+ It works with wired 360 controllers.
+ You can automatically wake up your tv by turning on the steam link.(I would guess this might not work with all tv's)
+ Image quality and frame rate seems perfect with most games(more on this in the Cons)
+ Easy to hide away behind the tv.
+ No input lag that I have noticed.
+ You can use it as a slightly round about way to stream video from your PC to your TV.
+ Linking stuff with bluetooth is easy.
Cons
- If you turn it on through your 360 controller it seems to be random if it will actually recognize the inputs. most of the time you have to unplug and plug back in the controller for it to work.
- The built in browser leaves a lot to be desired, at least when you are using a 360 controller it doesn't really want to scroll up and down pages and the lack of being able to install Adblock makes watching streamed content on it a chore.
- Whilst most games I have played on it have worked fine I have noticed that games that put a lot of demand on the your main PC do suffer from frame drops and input lag. It is not massive but it is noticeable.
- Some games that support controllers natively will show up as not and you will have to set up a pointless input map that actually works less well than the games default.
Overall I am pretty happy with it, although if I paid full price I don't know if I would be so forgiving of the janky browser and other quirks.
The other problems I have with it are not really its fault. Games that have third party launchers outside of steam can cause problems and windows pop ups can throw a spanner in the works but those are mostly minor problems. What I would say is launch any games you want to play with it on your main pc first so that you can click through any pop ups with ease instead of having to move from room to room.

Since its free, i will give a quick roundup of things i liked, and things i disliked.
Liked:

you can make all mages if you wish.

Disliked:

- Typos, Grammatical Errors, alot of them.
- Too long and too much rambling conversations to no end.
- Most dungeons were made with a generator tool and are the same.
- Puzzles always end up as pushing buttons and walking to the furthest point
just to open a door that makes you repeat this process till the dungeon runs out of doors.
- Armor/Damagetype system is not explained correctly.
- ALOT of random encounters, you end up being overleveld for the last boss
Making it too easy.

Verdict:
A handful of years back i played alot of RPGMaker games when i lacked the internet, while most not translated in english i sure had fun with those, sadly what they offered lacks in this one, but its free, so i finished it regardless.
Overly if you enjoyed other RPGMaker titles on Steam, you should play this one, it probably had more work in it then others that you pay for.
Bugs and problems you will encounter:
- Dual Wielding does not interact properly with some skills and weapons. Guardman will be casted twice. Ranged, onehanded weapons wont let the 2. weapon attack if its placed in the first slot.
- SP regernation items/tech dont work.
- Monster Ability "Strike All" can stun all your characters and do heavy physical damage, causing instant-wipes.
- Some Bosses dont even attack in any threatening capacity.
- The "Story-Weapon" in late game doesnt actually do enough damage as it was intended to the final boss.
- You can Sequence Break the final fight with Merces by doing high enough damage to prevent his transformation.
And alot more i could mention.
What i suggest is get more patient and proper beta-testers, pay someone if you must, but it feels the problems were never really adressed or ignored.

Vagante is essentially Dark Souls meets Spelunky. Random dungeons layouts, lots of traps, and plenty of character customization options. YOU WILL DIE. This is not an easy game, but it is a fair game. If you take pleasure from getting better at a game, learning from defeat and progressing farther and farther each time, you will love it. Originally the Warhammer Fantasy equivalent of Necromunda, the miniatures game came out in late 1999 if I remember correctly. It is a skirmish game based on gang warfare in the ruins of the doomed city of Mordheim.
All of the basic bands from the core rulebook (Human mercenaries, Skaven, Cult of the Damned and Sisters of Sigmar) are represented in the game, and the rest (Witch Hunters and Undead at this moment, more probably coming in the future) are being released gradually as DLC. The look and feel of the tabletop game are well adapted, without the inconvenience (some may not view it this way) of having to modify the miniatures when some of your warriors inevitably get mutilated or mutated by a wounds/mutation dice roll, or without having to keep an extensive array of scenery in the closet to prevent the games from becoming boring brawls.
Also, the tabletop's ruleset has been well adapted, better than the original IMHO, as it allows for greater granularity and slightly reduces the luck factor from the original (and the power differences a single point in a stat could imply in the tabletop game, but I'm talking from old memories). Graphics are more than good enough for their purpose and don't have huge requirements.
Regarding the gameplay, it fits the grimdark atmosphere of the source material - you hire a bunch of mercenaries to set up your band, and go fight other bands in the ruins of the city for a few fistfuls of wyrdstone, which is fantasy plutonium. Playing the full tutorial is recommended in order to understand all the nuances of the tactical part of the game and the band management part of the game, or you will probably lose hard early on. In line with the grimness (and the darkness) every time a critical strike is landed on someone, or someone is knocked out, a roll is made after the battle and there's a chance that character will end up maimed (this happens to the NPC bands too, and when you encounter them again you will be able to notice the effects of your handiwork on their bodies and minds). Some people get lucky and make a full recovery (or you can get a bunch of one-eyed guys with PTSD or mangled hands - most of the time not all at once). If your guys get knocked out, your enemy can steal their gear, and if you lose a battle you don't even get a booby prize - winner takes all. It's a hard life out there in Mordheim.
If you ever wanted to reenact "Acción Mutante" in a ruined medieval city, play this game. And if you don't get what the hell I'm talking about, go watch "Acción Mutante". You'll enjoy it too.
In short, buy this game. Buy it for your friends, too.

A decent enough casual game where the aim is to fire your balls at the approaching board so that you match three or more of the same colour ball, which causes any now unattached balls to fall off as well. The idea is to clear the board in as few moves as possible, but also against the clock - or rather the board, which moves down steadily (or fast if you haven't made any matches for a few seconds).
It's like one of those other bubble games, but it has something extra. First of all, this has physics. The balls have weight and that means when a group is holding on with just 1 bubble connection, the whole group just swings a bit. The momentum goes away of course, but when it first goes in motion, it can either “catch” the ball you just shot (if you shot it) or it can connect to something else and if the balls are of the same colour, they act as a ball that you shot.
Second neat thing about this game are the upgrades and powerups. You upgrade your launcher to have energy which is gained by bubbles that fall down. Energy you use to activate powerups: launch ball ABOVE the “playground” to selected spot, use a rainbow ball or use a bomb. The powerups themselves are also upgradeable.
There are few flaws though, but they're rather minor. Graphics are a bit bad, too though, but gameplay is what counts. Gameplay first, graphics later.
All in All

Edit: I decided to re-write part of my review, because I think it's a crying shame more people haven't played this.
I've played a lot of arcade shooters, both old ones and ones made within the last year (or five), and I have to say that Jamestown is probably the most aesthetically pleasing shooter I've played in decades, and easily the best western-made shooter by far. The excellent input customization is really crazy compared to other games coming out lately. The game just works right out of the box, period, no matter what input you have or what problems you're used to.
The music is beyond excellent and the graphics are superb, the entire game has a nostalgic quality that comes from successful emulation of older japanese-made arcade shooters from the 80's and 90's. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everyone, you merely need to enjoy old-school shooters to get the full effect of and appreciation for the game itself.  It's quite forgiving at low difficulty, and higher difficulties stay challenging even after a few playthroughs. The highest difficulty levels are pretty rough for me, and I have a penchant for the whole bullet-hell genre. My only 'complaint' is the game is rough on my thumbs!
Dead serious, the game is worth every penny, even if you don't play it long.

Jamestown is a western styled shmup that is a cakewalk for the veterans of the genre but acts as a great game to break in newbies to these style of games. There are various challenge modes to unlock via the token system. The challenges range from flying through checkpoints to staying alive as long as possible and offers quite a variety of things to do if you’re bored trying to hit high scores in the campaign. These tokens are also used to unlock various ships to add spice to your gameplay. Jamestown even includes a local multiplayer mode that allows 4 players through additional controller peripherals. The style is surprisingly unique and creative for a genre that was beaten to death by the Japanese for years. Sadly Jamestown has major flaws that makes it less impressive to the shmup elitists. Jamestown bullet patterns are very predictable and lacks variety. Bosses while visually appealing, don’t really carry the super difficulty expected from bosses in hardcore shmups.

Welcome to FF! As you can see, we have no fancy hotdog hats and Scouts running around playing like a tank instead of grabbing points! Instead we have skill, and bad maps! and Veterans that can kick your♥♥♥♥♥before you can lay one point of damage on him...And rage quitting players...Huh, maybe I overlooked this a bit.
While I haven't been the most "loyal fan" of the TF series I played TF1 then later started playing TF2...Which was a slow god awful cosmetic mess of an online shooter, while addicting at the same time. So I at least have the right to speak my mind about this game both positively and negatively even if I have 10 hours on record.
"So, what is different about FF? Surely it's just a Source port of TFC and nothing more!" Wrong! FF is a nice mix of TFC and TF1=skill based team playing shooter.
The game's classes are a bit more adaptable whereas TF2 had a strict line buried in the sand reguarding what you could and could not do. For example: The medic is only meant to heal in TF2, if he tries anything else other than that you're screwed and that's just how the cookie crumbles. But in FF the medic (while not as fast as the scout) can capture targets/objectives of interest without a sweat if you know how to grenade jump. The medic is also good at defending himself whereas in TF2 the medic is restricted to do one thing: be the heavy's ♥♥♥♥♥.
Which is another class that isn't as screwed up as TF2's version. The heavy is still the lovable tanking one man army, and the TF2 heavy is going through some...Well, terrible unneeded nerfing. TF2's Heavy is worthless without a medic in the area. But in FF the Heavy is perfectly fine on his own, and even better with a medic supplying him with HP.
The Soldier is still your basic hard hitting class and what I like to consider my main class. Yeah yeah I'm a nub for sticking with the starting class. But I would rather play the basics than play around with the Engineer's poorly made building UI. But back to the subject, the Soldier hasn't changed at all other than the fact that he has two shotguns for two different situations. But besides that he's still the same old offensive class.
I don't know if I can mark down all the slight changes within the classes correctly so I'm going to move on to the negatives of this mod.
Starting off with the Workshop...It's a whole lot of empty! I'm not sure if this is the developer's fault or no one with modding talent is interested in modding for FF. But what I do know is, it's an empty feature that no one uses. And in return it brings large disappointment. Meaning no custom maps, no skins, no custom game modes, and no custom classes. I feel that this is potential sitting in front of me rotting away and I can't do anything about it. So it will hurt the game score by a point.
The vet's pretty much serve as a "newbie filter" in other words, new players come in, new players quit because they can't land a hit on these guys. It's not the Vet's fault he/she is good, but it does hurt the community's growth. Even I have this problem fighting vet's since I've played other shooters over the years and those years pay me back by watering my skill down.
I've found a few aimbotters here and there on my team but it's been a fair amount of time since I've seen one so it might not be a problem anymore. But I suggest keeping an eye out just in case.
The final verdict: Fortress Forever deserves a 7/10. It's not the best mod I've seen on Source but I suggest this over TFC and TF2 any day. The current maps could also use work too. I was told that they were returning maps from TFC only because they were popular, but the developers didn't seem to understand that those maps are hard to defend. Having grown up with two younger brothers, I can empathize to Max’s annoyance at his younger brother Felix fiddling with his stuff, making a mess of his room, and seeming to exist only to get on his nerves. I might not have gone so far as to enact an occult rite and banish my brothers to an unknown fantasy world (though I might have wanted to at times), but at least Max realizes the gravity of what he unintentionally did pretty fast and sets off to save his brother from a creepy old man who intends to steal his youth, Gruntilda the Witch style.
A sequel mostly in name and lead character only to Max and the Magic Marker, The Curse of Brotherhood almost entirely ditches the free form drawing that made up the core of its predecessor, opting instead to streamline its mechanics and add a significant amount of cinematic flair, coming together in a far more focused, inspired, and varied experience.
Though it is still referred to as a marker, Max’s tool of choice has been reworked into a powerful instrument with which you can now control various elements in order to help Max traverse through levels. The implementation of this still bares a resemblance to Max’s marker of old, allowing you a small amount of freedom to direct elements into specific shapes and paths, but it’s far more natural and embedded in the experience than before and works well within the constraints of a controllers precision, rarely requiring a great deal of precision and only occasionally imposing any sort of time limit.
The Curse of Brotherhood has rather obviously been designed so as to rarely frustrate the player, or tax them with tricky platforming segments or puzzles, and this simplicity and hand holding is in some ways a bit tedious when the answer is almost always immediately apparent, but overall I actually found the breezy pace rather refreshing. It allowed me to appreciate the gorgeous environments and enjoyably cliched story without many threats or pauses as I got stuck. It provides just enough stimulation to remain engaging, but is accessible enough that it’s a game I could feel confident recommending to a younger player or a parent wanting to play with their child (which is a disappointingly low number of games).
At around 4-5 hours it’s a fairly brisk adventure, but I never felt as if something was cut or missing, nor did any moment feel like needless filler. Every segment is interesting and important to the game, and this consistency and constant variety makes it easy to wind up playing through the entire thing in but a few sittings. That’s not a slight against the game by any means, but a complement to its excellent pacing and inspired level design.
The handful of moments that stand out as poor in my mind are actually those near the end which begin to ask more of the player than before, and the slightly awkward controls have a bit of trouble keeping up. The end boss fight also proved the most disappointing part of the game, with an uninspired encounter that ups the difficulty just enough to be frustrating and would have ended the game on a rather lackluster note had it not been for the charming cutscene immediately following.
It’s probably an understatement to say I was rather taken aback by how much I ended up enjoying The Curse of Brotherhood. Its beautiful scenery pulled me in, and the leisurely platforming and puzzle solving kept me there throughout an experience that continued to surprise me the further I got in. Some may scoff at the low difficulty, but in terms of simple fun and creativity I haven’t played something quite as nice for too long.

Initially, this game was right up my alley.  I am a huge tycoon / sim junkie and I was able to grasp the basics right off the bat.

Optimum lines for doing such tend to be a little too popular and in order to keep up with the demand, you need to add more vehicles.  More vehicles clog up the roadways (which don't seem to thin out no matter how many people you have using the public system in the first place), which deceases your efficiency even more.  In the midst of this entire mess, you have to constantly babysit your wages and ticket prices as the in-game economy fluctuates.  Too high, and your already angry customer base will ignore you completely, leaving you with no income.  Too low, and your lines get flooded, which then turns into a rinse and repeat of the first problem.
I managed to successfully beat the first scenario after a countless number of restarts, and I am still hung up on the second after 22 hours of play.  In the end, you always end up broke and PO'd unless you did things 100% the way the designers intended.  Deviate just a little, and you're toast.
In the end, CiM is just a puzzler pretending to be a sim.  Avoid unless you have the Buddha's patience.

They actually did Sonic some justice in this game. It doesn’t suck like most of the more recent games (looking at you Sonic Boom: Rise of Lyric, Black Knight, and Secret Rings >_>), but it doesn’t copy everything from the past Sonic games. It copies a little, with the side scrolling and level theme borrowing. Then they spiced up his classic look and gave him the homing attack which is the best thing they could have done for the 2D Sonic series. Although the game is great, it does have its flaws. One of these flaws is very tight controls. Sonic games usually do have tighter controls of most games but thats because of the speed aspect. But no. in this game you stop on a DIME. This is super annoying and makes you overshoot or undershoot your position. Also the jumping is hit or miss. You move to the exact location of where you moved and stop. It can be good for tricky platforming but other times you just won’t move. Don’t know if this is a legit problem or if it’s because I’m playing with a keyboard on PC but whatever. The level design is amazing. They are fast paced fun and have enough difficulty to make them challenging. The four main areas are Splash Hill, Casino Night, Labyrinth, and Scrap Brain (not actual names except Splash Hill). The bosses are even better. They put a spin on the classic Sonic bosses that the zones were based off of. The controls are a little weird but again, I’m using a keyboard. The last thing besides the story that I am going to talk about is the music and it is definitely is Sonic quality music. It sets the scene and provides an upbeat fast paced tone that matches the level so well. Some of my favorite tracks are from the new Casino Night Zone and the new Labyrinth Zone. The last thing left is the story. This is literally “Oh no! Eggman stole the animals! Time to go save them and keep Eggman from destroying the world.” A modern touch on a classic formula that is sure to please any Sonic fan. I can't wait to buy the second episode.
Overall I give this game a 7.5/10

I went into this game with few expectations. I was in for a pleasant surprise.
First, I usually cannot stomach otome VNs because the main characters are often too insipid for my taste. It's not about them being damsels in distress. It's that they always seem too eager to please, or they have such shining personalities that every passing pair of pants falls in love with them.
The MC in this game is a delightfully poisonous antidote to that, at least at the start. One great contributing factor is that, unlike most otome VNs, the dialogue here is more... rewarding if the MC stays true to self. She doesn't need to pander, which keeps her behaviour consistent and believable, and the developing lovelines realistic.
It also helps that the plot isn't didactic beyond reason. There's still the standard trope of good vs evil, but it's delivered through storylines that recognise moral greyness to some extent, more so on some routes than others. I can get why some reviewers commented on the skintone/morality thing, but I personally liked those morally grey characters more, heh.
The prose is descriptive without being purple, properly QCed, and the music and art are both lovely. Nice SFX, too.
I'll happily back these guys if they produce another game.

While this is a free visual novel, it is excellent. I would have gladly paid money for it.
Pros:
- The protagonist is quite different from the usual otome main character. She has a strong personality and she's strong-willed. She isn't a one-dimensional, boring character like so many otome VNs have.
- The romantic options (5 men) aren't abusive or problematic. Several otome games feature men who take away the female protagonist's agency or treat her like a child. There are also certain otome games (which I'm not a fan of) that feature men who are r/a/p/e/y as f*ck (yes, Steam censors the word r/a/p/e). All of the men in this game treat the protagonist very well and don't interfere with her agency.
- The game elicited many romantic feelings (butterflies), which is pretty important for me when I play otome games.
- The story is very interesting and well-written.
- Every romance path is VERY different from each other. When you read one character's path, there is no skipping read text when you go to the next character (except for the common route). The paths to the good and bad endings of each character are similar, but the endings themselves are very different
- While the artwork can be slightly awkward a few times, overall, it's quite good. Beautiful illustrations of romantic scenes.
Cons:
- Lack of diversity. Only two of the romance options aren't pale as f*ck, but even then, they're not particularly dark-skinned. Just a shade darker. Everyone else in the ENTIRE game is pale as f*ck. And this time, no one can argue "Well, it's supposed to be Japan" because this story takes place in an entirely fictional world, so there isn't any excuse for lack of people of color.
- No female romance options.
- A couple of typos; no big deal.
- There's an effect that's slightly annoying. The scene shakes around whenever there's a shocking response from someone with exclamation points. It isn't too big a deal, but I thought it was unnecessary.
Overall, this was a great otome VN and I highly recommend it to those who enjoy VNs.

Empire: Total War is a turn-based strategy game that starts in the year 1700. Playable factions are the great powers in Europe, parts of North & South America and Indian subcontinent at the time. The game had a rough start at its release, crashed a lot and wasn't well optimized. Most things have been patched in the meantime though.
Best strategy is to ignore your enemy's army all together and to blitz his regions. His troops will disappear entirely if you have conquered all regions of your enemy's home theatre.
+ The map is quite big
+ a lot of factions to choose from
+ a lot of mods that improve on the base game
+ You can let your people revolt to change your government type. Do it as France to get the cool flag.
+ economy is interesting
+ trading colonial resources is OP
+ research tree
- unit variety is poor. most factions felt the same
- the AI is very bad on the campaign and battlefield map.
- barely any naval invasions
- fort battles are broken
- the Ottoman turn freeze bug and the save corruption bug still aren't fixed.
- still not that well optimized.
- Some factions need more regions. You can finish off some factions like France by conquering their two only regions in their home theatre (here: continent), which is way too easy.
- As soon as one Indian faction unites all of India, prepare to fight a monster. Felt a bit ahistorical.
- Switzerland is not accessable. You can't even march through the country.
- Ottoman turn freeze bug (Ottoman's turn takes a long time: Seize Istanbul and attack all of the little Ottoman armies. But conquering Istanbul helped the most in my experience.
- Save corruption bug (you suddenly can't load your saves anymore): Play one turn to get one autosave. Then, leave the game and go to your save files in C:\Users\yourusername\AppData\Roaming\The Creative Assembly\Empire\save_games
Change the autosave to "Read-only". It didn't happen afterwards for me. Don't forget to still save manually of course.
Replay value: Potentially high (with a lot of factions and many regions)
Rating 8/10
Recommendation: Yes

-----------------NEW REVIEW-------------------- (Current Build)
So now after a lot of time played, and a lot of patience I have finally beaten Vagante almost effortlessly. Regardless, it felt good to finally complete it. I have been trying to play it every once in a while after a new update is released to test the improvements, and I can say these recent improvements have been some of my favorites.
Now however I fear however the game might be too easy. I think it's going to take some time readjusting it and finding the sweet spots. (I managed to find 6 death protection necklaces in one playthrough.)
I do appreciate the developer's watching people's feedback, and working to find that special spot that keeps everyone happy. From the time that I first saw this on indiedb compared to now it's almost a completely different game. (The new hud looks great, and thanks for the new tooltips)
I no longer seem to find random crashes. Attacks are precise, and movement is fluent. I no longer feel like the game is limiting my ability to play. Instead I feel quite the opposite. Vagante is slowly becoming quite the polished game. I think I might have been a bit drastic on my last review, as I didn't give it the level of concentration that I first started the game out with. So for that I'm sorry. The game has indeed improved a lot. (Also please don't confuse me saying the game is being polished just because the difficulty was lowered. I did make it to the very end while everything was overtuned)
Every enemy I fought now had a reasonable weakness or way that it could be killed, and I was able to find that in combat. Loot seemed way more plentiful in single player, and I also think that made a huge difference. (maybe too plentiful or we need a new way to sell gear or do something with it)
Once again though, I think lowering the enemy damage might be a bit too much. (I stormed through the final level like it was nothing, not even fearing enemies, without selecting anything in vitality. (at the end I had 130 hp)) I found the beginning levels to be much more punishing when I was without gear, rather than the other way around.
And finally, now that I've beaten it, I can be less salty about the game's flaws and focus on the things that I like.
The classes feel unique. I'm still not certain if I'm sold on all of the talents yet, but they get the job done. The Wildling is still my favorite class, and I'm glad to see new weapons for it. Getting a 3-4 very fast speed weapon for it made all the difference in my playthrough.
Each enemy has it's own unique way of being dealt with, and I like that. In previous builds, some enemies seemed either impossible to beat, or just way too confusing / full of rng / impossible to kill without losing life / not worth your time. I feel like this has been fixed in the newer builds. Each enemy also has unique ways of dealing with you, which I also like. Some are still a bit unfair, such as the giant rock tree monster being able to 999 you if he lands on you, but I understand the developers want one shot mechanics. I would say a solution to this and the problem I mentioned above would be to make death protection something you can work towards as you play, rather than rng. This would make it so if people spent extra time crafting something, collecting something, giving up something, or a mixture of all of them, then they could craft or receive a death protection item rather than ending up with a lot of them by the end of the game.
I also want to say that there was a point in time where this game's ai wasn't superb, and it made it so enemies felt clunky and out of place, almost just plopped into the game. I no longer feel this way. Enemies seem to have a purpose and seem to thrive in the environments that they are put in. Skeletons still need some work though.
The item list in the game is a decent size, and I'm hoping they continue to add more. I do feel like despite getting a lot of items, I very rarely swapped to new ones though, and this kind of worries me. It made me less inclined to pick up new things. Perhaps increasing the numbers on everything so you have more room to work with numbers in general. Maybe making it so every level adds a bit to the multiplier on new items found, so as you venture deeper, you can expect to find better loot, even if it is just slightly better.
I really enjoy that you can keep playing once you have beaten the game. I love that it's seamless and it just transitions into the next tier of levels, as well as having the increased difficulty. It would be nice to see additional new things on the second playthrough, third playthough, etc.
Another thing I like is that vagante doesn't try to hold the reins too much. You go in, and you view everything in real time. No cutscenes, and quests even happen without the use of interface. I hope they continue to use this, as well as find a way to non intrusively tell a story.
All in all, Vagante has undeniably given me plenty of hours of gameplay. The 15 dollars I have spent I would say is worth it, and if anything I apologize about the last review I gave. It was childish for me to not give you guys the thumbs up at this point. The game is worth the full price, and I look forward to all future updates. I really hope that you guys build a light story around the game, add more quests in the style that you have done, and continue to grow the game out, offering additional levels, new items, new classes, new npcs, and new backgrounds.
As for my wants:
I still want legendary weapons, lol. This also leads to my next want...
I want more / different quests. I know we get the fox quest, and this is a step in the right direction. Seeing more variety will go a long way! Finding precursors for legendaries, or special keys that unlock new areas that you can only find on your second playthrough of the game (after beating it etc) would be wonderful. I want more oh my god moments from the items / quests that I find.
I still think the tarot card reader / fortune teller is a good idea. Being able to find this old hag somewhere randomly in the levels, chance to spawn that gives you a chance to pick a card, with the option of changing your background, even to ones that you can't unlock through normal play.
It would be cool to see the shrines be shrines to gods that you're praying to, and to have them as bosses.
A support class would be very welcome. I would love to see a cleric / bard / shaman.
I still think we should be able to turn while we are attacking.
More npcs would be appreciated, especially ones that effected your gameplay, IE a portal master that maybe asks for something and in return teleports you to a random place, maybe not even on that level. Or maybe make this a bad thing and have it so if you see a portal master, he automatically teleports you somewhere random.
Maybe you find a person / object that if something happens, it curses an item. These types of things would be more than welcome. This would add to diverse gameplay, as well as making sure that no playthrough played the same. Adding enough of these into the game, and keeping their chances of happening low is going to be the key to success there.
More things like the shop keep being angry at you for the rest of the game. We need more decision making in the game, and this is something, that while annoying is exactly what we need. We need more action reaction in the game. "if I pull this lever, level 2 will flood but a new gate will be open"
or "if I scare off this npc I'll see it later on with friends" things of this nature would be very very welcome.

Customization:
This game uses what they term the "AP System" to give you some pretty interesting choices in how to build your characters.  Basically, upon level up a character gains some number of these points, which can then be allocated to things like increasing HP, Defense, Attack, Agility, etc.  In this manner you can customize a character to play exactly how you want them to.  Want a crazy tank?  Put all that character's AP into HP, Defense, Evade, and Threat.  Want an assassin?  Attack, Critical, Evasion, and SP (spell points).  Don't like the way you allocated the points?  Take them back and try again.
All in all it's a very versatile system, and its fun experimenting to see how you can build the characters, even early on in the game at lower levels.
Art Style:
In a phrase: It's nice, well done, and clean.  I haven't gotten to any cutscenes yet, so I can't vouch for those, but the other art is very pretty.  The syle definitely reminds me of Final Fantasy VI, Lufia II, and Chrono Trigger.
Engine:
The engine is ... well, 'meh' about sums up my feelings for it.  First and foremost, I haven't been able to find a way to control the volume, even in the F1 Options menu.  The engine is also a bit "jerky" as it scrolls to follow your party through an area even with the option to reduce stuttering on.
The control customization screen, at least for the keyboard is a bit odd at first glance.  I'm not really sure what half the buttons are for.  Some more descriptive labelling would probably help.
Difficulty:
The game's difficult.  Not like soul-crushingly difficult a-la Dark Souls, but it will still thoroughly beat your a** if you're not prepared.  Save frequently, preferably every time before entering a new area.  Equipment seems to be fairly cheap, at least early on, so upgrade early and upgrade often.
Summary:
To close, Legionwood's pretty fun.  It can be difficult, but it is by no means impossible.  Honestly, the biggest detriment to this game I have found so far is that I can't adjust the stupid volume.

Mordheim, a game I have been playing on and off since early access, is a nice game turn based tactical game - resembling x-com, bloodbowl and other games where you have movement points and fighting points. You will get to know the characters of your warband, develop them and style them. But futher no real stretegic support of your party. You can insert character history and slighty modify their looks. However... the game is also quite merciless. My brave band of imperial mercenaries is led by a one-legged captain, assisted by a one-legged hero; covered by a archer with a permanent open wound; I have to admit. In other games I might have saved my sacred band of brave warriors and my twin-sister smugglers quite often and would have reloaded the missions time and time again to cheat my way out of the leg-losing and thus would have prevented the limitation of the range and actions of my beloved Captain Kenrick and his sidekick the couragrous hero Havok Sparrenschild. I would have re-loaded to avoid the loss of fighting points for my carefully contructed 6th level sharpshooter 'Lars Genade'. But alas. The loss is forever and final.... So much better this paralympic approach to find the green magical shards that are scattered throughout the city.
Ofcourse you have to like the warhammer world to like the game, which is sometime a bit repetitious (but I didn't mind). If you can't stand skaven and ogres... don't buy this game. But if you feel like rampaging with blunderbusses and warhammers through a rotten, deserted, corrupted and decaying city (the artwork is quite nice): it is worth buying. Just be aware that you have to seperately buy the DLC.  That might be the true curse of Sigmar's comet.

Update: I have now spent many, many more hours with the game. My opinion is unchanged. I love strategy games, I love the warhammer universe, and I really want to love Mordheim. I can't though, because the game is clearly bent.
I just went on a 20 win streak against the AI because I forced myself to forgo searching ruins or collecting stones as the primary focus of my excursions and instead focused solely on bottle necking the enemy and mobbing their team one by one as they tried to get into whatever trench I sat and waited for them in. The game is very, very easy when you play like that, because even though at 4 on 1 odds the RNG and designer bias (seriously, +30% wounds just because?) towards the AI is palpable, it's not enough to destroy your fun.
That streak ended the first time I got too comfortable and didn't follow my own advice, open conflict with the AI in this game is laden with blatant weighting to the point it's incredulous. I watched in outright anger as my characters repeatedly missed strikes at 95% success chances, boiling down to an overall real success rate of 37% by the time the game decided to route me. The AI controlled warband on the other hand, only missed 4 times in the entire exchange, 2 of them were on a warrior that their impressive only need to hit once to retire, the third attack landed, not because that's how the dice roll, but because that's how you hide blatant weighting.
I was also hostage to two scenarios where it let the AI's soldier counter attack my engaging character before letting me attack them to begin with. Mordheim is a lot of things, fun is one of them if you're the kind of dullard that is okay with playing every match the same way, over and over. I personally, again, want to love Mordheim, because it has all the hallmarks of a classic small team tactics game. Unfortunately, it also has all the negative attributes of a crapfest thanks to the developers being more concerned with making things hard on you over providing an enjoyable experience.
I cannot give the game a good review even though I'm still playing it and will likely buy the expansion material, because wish I'd never purchased/played it; that is due to the fact that overall it's like dating a pretty girl, that's fun, but has tons of negative baggage and a psychotic streak. You stay because you want the fantasy where everything is right to play out, and it does occasionally, but the reality is that you should leave asap because there is more wrong here than right, and the longer you stay the worse it's going to get for you.
For people who love the Ironman runs in XCOM this game is probably right up your alley. It just isn't something I really got into. Take the review for what it is, my opinion.

Positive reviews for games like this confound me, because I know for a fact that the gaming base by far and large is not made up of masochists, though it is arguably made up of idiots.
Mordheim has a lot in common with xcom, fun is not among those things however. The RNG in the game may in fact even out, as it allegedly does with xcom, but there is no room for tactical mitigation to this abusive mechanism. I actually did grow up playing Rifts, D&D, and Warhammer (as well as the entire White Wolf game world). Bad runs with dice happen, but never at the frequency they do in these games. I spent 3 hours today playing Mordheim on the Xbox One, it was three hours I spend screaming at the TV and scaring my kids because the game put me in such a rage I couldn't even interact with them positively, and not because I'm a sore loser.

If you feel compelled to write a positive review for this because you're just one of those guys that needs to pretend he's part of that 1337 crew, great, good for you, we both know how fake your opinion is. This game sucks, horribly, I would really, really enjoy a true Warhammer game that really brings about the glory, brutality, tactics, and most of all F U N that is associated with the miniatures based table top game.

I was a tremendous fan of the tabletop version way back in the day and when I saw it was being undertaken to make a game version I could barely contain my excitement. One word to new players (even though I'm only a few hours in) getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked in the beginning is part of the process. It's actually more beneficial in the game version than in the tabletop one because your characters actually grow as they recieve desvatating head wounds etc. It doesn't cripple them (usually) but makes them more specialized. Expect a lot of failure before you get the sweet riches of success. So what if a henchman can't use ranged anymore because he's gone insane and wants to tear people apart up close? use him/her/it as a spearhead and keep rolling with the punches. Definite learning curve but once you get sucked in you'll love it. Makes me relive the days that my warband eventually ended up being a group of crippled, maimed, mostly insane zealots that would stop at nothing to destroy the enemy, short of a well-placed warp pistol ball in the chest, and even then, all the sweeter when you plant a good blow and perma-death somebodies favorite character. Haven't gotten far enough to see if they've employed the "peg-leg-peg arm" debuffs yet but we used to go so far as to modify our models to reflect said injuries when playing tabletops was more popular. Well done is well done.

Someone finally nailed tabletop gaming.
If you played Modheim on the tabletop. Or Warhammer FB/40k. Or D&D. Or any other tactical miniature game on the table you recall hours spend crafting the perfect hero, squad, army. You had dream of how it would perform on the table, visions of fantasy glory. But often the game itself would get bogged down in rules and pitched battles would take hours to complete.
The Mordheim successfully captures the enthrawling character/army building process and then pairs it with a very engaging, fluid combat system. You can build, fight, die, and build again several times in one evening. The mechanics are intuitive and easy to grasp but deeply tactical with enough RNG to harken back to those days around the table when a brilliant plan went spectacularly bad or a horrible idea went astonishingly good.
I would love to see more races and more units, though there is a very healthy selection of themes, tactics, and strategies available now. And I would love to see a support tournament and league mode, which would further recreate our collective tabletop experience.
The bottom line is this: late at night, after my family is asleep and my adult responsibilities are done, I can load up this game and push minis across the most beautiful city of the damned ever assembled. No organization, no preplanned event nights, no massive amount of money and time invested in collecting and painting. How perfect is that?

The computer cheats, obviously and often. Rolls are heavily weighted towards the AI, with players missing 80% hit chances 5 times in a row and the AI hitting 60% chances every single time. I particularly hate it when a single hit would finish off a surrounded enemy, but you miss with 4-5 blows because the AI cheats (then it passes its all alone test and proceeds to hammer my sisters).
I have no problem with the permadeath/wounds. I love how every warband tells a story as you play (usually a grim one), but I expect a fighting chance, not this blatant cheating by the AI.
